en: The Imperial Preface:
The Tathāgata’s Treasury of the True Dharma Eye is a separate transmission outside the teachings. It truly contains the principle for penetrating the three barriers.
This is one who speaks the truth, who speaks reality, who does not speak falsely, and who does not speak deceptively. For those with the aspiration for the Way, it is thus:
You must diligently apply yourself to inquiry and investigate with all your might. From the one, you arrive at the three; at every step, there must be a firm grounding.

This is not a matter for superficiality or negligence, nor for self-deception and deceiving others. Since I have deeply realized this matter, I shall not begrudge falling into verbal pitfalls, but shall point it out for you one by one.
Now, when a student first enters the gate of liberation and is newly released from the suffering of karmic bondage, they perceive the mountains, rivers, and the great earth as the ten...
Then the entire void will vanish and perish together. You will no longer be deceived by the ancient "tongue of the iron spike.
Recognizing that this present seven-foot body is nothing more than earth, water, fire, and wind, it naturally becomes thoroughly pure and free from even a single thread of attachment;
this is called the first step in breaking through the kōan. As for "the past and future limits being severed," this occurs after one has broken through the original kōan.
To know that the mountain is the mountain, the river is the river, the great earth is the great earth, the empty space of the ten directions is the empty space of the ten directions,
earth-water-fire-wind are earth-water-fire-wind, even down to ignorance is ignorance, afflictions are afflictions,
and form-sound-odor-taste-touch-dharmas are form-sound-odor-taste-touch-dharmas— all these are one's own fundamental portion. All are...
This is Bodhi. There is not a single thing that is not my body; there is not a single thing that is my own self. Object and wisdom are interfused; form and emptiness are unimpeded.
Having attained great sovereignty, one abides eternally unmoving. This is what is called "passing through the heavy barrier" and what is called "great death and great life.
After passing through the heavy barrier, the home is right within the journey; the journey does not depart from the home.
Abandon it. It is appropriate whether one faces the light or faces the darkness. Stillness is itself illumination; illumination is itself stillness. Practice this and abide in this.

This is its essence and this is its function. This is emptiness and this is existence. This is the ancient and this is the present. Because there is no birth, there is eternal life; because there is no extinction, there is no cessation.
If one practices with such constant alertness, the attachments of ignorance will naturally fall away, and only then can one truly tread [the path].
This is the final barrier. Although it is said that one must pass through three barriers, in reality, there is no passing through them at all.

It is simply that the Tathāgata is thus, and I am also thus. From this point on, one cultivates non-cultivation and realizes non-realization. Wondrous enlightenment is universally luminous, perfectly illuminating the Dharma-realm.
One becomes the infinite, and the infinite becomes one. Within the great, the small appears; within the small, the great appears. One sits upon a mote of dust.
Within the inner turning of the Great Dharma Wheel, he manifests jeweled-king lands upon the tip of a single hair, rescuing and uplifting sentient beings with inexhaustible utility.
Buddha after Buddha, Patriarch after Patriarch, have all appeared in the world for this one great matter of causal conditions. Bodhidharma came from the West;

through successive generations they transmitted and received it. The ancient worthies passed on the lamp within the light of the inexhaustible, within the great perfect mirror—day passes and month follows.

Thus it has continued down to the present day. Although this vast Dharma-gate is entrusted to both the holy and the mundane, and the fragrant ocean of the *Avataṃsaka* is where the subtle and the gross alike find their way home, those who have attained the bone and the marrow are indeed many;
yet how limitless are those who are like hemp or millet! Since the Sage departed, the distance has grown remote and demons and heretics have proliferated.
Failing to comprehend the Buddha’s mind, they recklessly join the seats of the Patriarchs; the Golden Mountain is sealed with mud, and the Sun of Wisdom is obscured by clouds.

Regarding the concealment [of the truth], its errors may also be summarized into three points. The first is as follows: upon merely seeing that the faculties and their objects mutually induce one another, and that the phenomena of the Dharma-realm arise, the mental consciousness flutters about;
realizing that all is nothing but illusion and delusion, one suddenly gives rise to joy and claims this is the "True and Constant.

One then ceases activity and rests, taking emptiness to be emptiness itself, unaware that the ocean of nature is boundless and that the "transformed city" has no fixed abode. If one can truly see into one's nature in this way, [one will not fall into these errors].

At that moment, one is without mind. Since the mind perceives emptiness, it has not yet seen the true nature (*dharmatā*). Consequently, the body is like withered wood and the mind is like extinguished ashes.

When the myriad phenomena arrive before one, even this "emptiness" cannot withstand them. Even if one could achieve standing death or sitting liberation, these would still be but the subtle spirits of karmic consciousness;
how much more so for those who stubbornly cling to the view of annihilation, which will inevitably transform into "mad flowers"—the claim that cause and effect are both empty.

To indulge in such recklessness without returning—could this not be because a single delusion resides in the mind? Amidst the birth and death that occurs as frequently as the sands of the Ganges, how could one fail to create the karma of saṃsāra and sever the root of Bodhi?
Furthermore, those of lesser capacity, upon seeing a state of vivid clarity and spiritual alertness, immediately claim it to be the "Unranked True Person" (wèi zhēnrén).

They say this person enters and exits through the gateway of the face; they point to it when raising an eyebrow or blinking an eye, and identify it when pointing a finger or clenching a fist, treating it as a conscious spirit.
This is their livelihood: they light a solitary lamp beneath the blazing sun; they mistake fish eyes for bright pearls and seek sandalwood in filth and dust;

they swallow iron balls while claiming in their mouths that they are drinking jade nectar. Only when the year ends and their clever devices are stripped away do they realize, as before, that it is still but a vast, groundless void.
Furthermore, those of the lowest sort hang upon the entanglements found within the scriptures, teachings, and recorded sayings. From...
In every direction where they raise their voices, they gather up the spittle and tears of others, giving rise to deranged and chaotic views that obscure their own minds.
They establish illusory forms and sounds as real dharmas, stirring the mental mechanisms toward the realm of True Suchness (*tathatā*).
Within the dharma of non-liberation, they bind themselves; the demonic form is difficult to conceal, as they retreat into the midst of perfect appearances. There is no path of understanding.
Penetrating through, he hides beneath the wisteria vines. Emotions and defilements accumulate and stagnate; the waves of consciousness rush and hasten.

Deceiving himself and deceiving others, betraying his own heart and betraying the Buddha—it is all for the sake of fame and profit, yet he speaks of the "mysterious" and the "original source. It is like a blind donkey leading a blind donkey.
They circumambulate along the grindstone; they realize a delusive dream within a delusive dream. They take a lacquer bucket as an offering of incense.
This is to follow the path of awakening while trampling through the wheel of fire. How could one possibly bring about evil fruits without virtuous causes? Such people are truly numerous;
with the fundamental principle unclarified, they have sunk into the vast eons. I, the Emperor, bear the responsibility of being a parent to the sovereigns of the realm.
I am not one who presides over the hall or wields the whisk. Desiring the peace and security of the people and all things, I follow solely the path of the Duke of Zhou and Confucius;
therefore, since ascending the throne ten years ago, I have not spoken of the Chan school.

Yet, mindful of the sagely life-force of humans and devas—the distinct transmission of the Buddhas and Patriarchs—I have risked letting my eyebrows trail upon the ground to awaken sentient beings, and have preserved the supreme golden elixir to revive the withered and decayed.
How could we allow those demonic influences to blind our true vision and drum the poison of delusion to extinguish the wondrous mind? I truly feel compelled to speak;
I cannot bear not to speak. Recently, during moments of leisure, I have distinguished between the pure and the turbid like the waters of the Zhi and Mien rivers.
Following my inclination, I have examined the records of ancient masters from antiquity and selected those who upheld the ultimate truth and directly pointed to the True Source.
I have also extracted their most profound words and personally edited them. These include the twelve Chan masters:
Sengzhao, Yongjia, Hanshan, Shide, Guishan, Yangshan, Zhaozhou, Yongming, Yunmen, Xuedou, Yuanwu, and Yulin;
as well as the extracanonical works of the Real Man of Ziyang. This is not...
This collection was compiled over the course of several months. As for other works, they have not yet been fully perused, and thus have not yet been excerpted;
this is not to say that there is nothing further worth taking up. Indeed, these several great spiritual friends (mahā-kalyāṇamitra) all thoroughly exhausted the subtle and penetrated the fundamental.
Having thoroughly investigated the ultimate aim and mastered the essential lineage, he deeply accords with the Gate of Non-duality of Vimalakīrti and the principle of the single flavor of Caoxi.
He enables those who have not yet seen to attain the wondrous vision of non-seeing; those who have not yet heard to enter the wondrous hearing of non-hearing;

those who have not yet known to penetrate the correct knowledge of non-knowing; and those who have not yet understood to achieve the great understanding of non-understanding. This is the [path] of humans and devas...

The Eye of the Unsurpassed Vehicle. Regarding the Dharma-gate of the Pure Land: although it appears to have no connection with the Chan School, what hindrance does the practice of *nianfo* (buddha-recitation) pose to the study of Chan?
Indeed, for a practitioner of Chan who has profoundly penetrated the ocean of nature, the pure practices may very well be cultivated concurrently.
Thereby, one rejoices in True Suchness (*tathatā*) and perfectly realizes the wondrous fruit. [From] the Master Yunqi Lianchi... *Fan*... [text fragment].
Regarding the purity of practice, there were those who had once attained realization through contemplation.

Upon examining the work *Yunqi Fahui*, although his discourse did not reach the level of complete penetration found in some other virtuous teachers, it was nonetheless not lacking in right knowledge and right view;

it could certainly not be compared to the writings of those who cling to signs and grasp at existence. I have therefore selected its essential passages and compiled them into a separate volume to be appended here.

Furthermore, by including this single gateway of the Pure Land, it serves as a site for establishing the Bodhi-maṇḍa for those who have not yet attained realization, and as an aid on the path toward the ocean of the fruit of wondrous enlightenment for those who have already attained realization.
Thus, I have composed this general preface to place at the beginning of this work, to be published and shown to those of the present and future, to generously benefit later students.
May they, by following the finger to see the moon, forget the trap upon catching the fish, and shatter the [delusions of] external paths.
Dispelling the obscurity and ignorance that deprives the Hinayana of its narrowness— this is my high hope.

Imperial Preface to the *Imperially Selected Records of Sayings*:

During the reign of Emperor Ming of the Han dynasty, the Buddha-dharma first entered China; it flourished during the Jin and Song periods. Master Huiyuan was among its most eminent and distinguished figures.
This is so. Previously, the core tenets of Nirvāṇa were transmitted; it was through Master Huiyuan that they first became known in this land.

However, when one examines the words of Master Huiyuan recorded in the *Biographies of Eminent Monks of the Lotus Society*, it is clear that Master Huiyuan was certainly not one who thoroughly understood the core tenets of Nirvāṇa;
he merely heard its teachings. Sengzhao was a contemporary of Master Huiyuan. While there was Master Huiyuan in the Jin dynasty, there was also [Sengzhao] in the Qin dynasty.
As for the monk Sengzhao: when it comes to those who advocate for the Pure Land, one looks to Master Huiyuan; when it comes to those who expound the sutras, one looks to Sengzhao.

His followers all regarded him as a follower of the Hīnayāna, claiming he was a man of the era before Bodhidharma, when the principle of the "special transmission outside the teachings" had not yet been heard in China, and thus he could not enter the ranks of the patriarchs.
I have read the *Prajñā-wuzhi* (The Wisdom of Non-Cognition) composed by Dharma Master Sengzhao.
Nirvana is nameless; emptiness and existence do not shift. Regarding the *Xingshan Bibaolu* and other treatises:
were it not for a profound clarity regarding the essential tenets, how could one understand them so clearly? To lecture upon the sutras in this manner is precisely "not relying on words and letters.

How could the wisdom-life of the Buddhas be partitioned by boundaries, or divided by past and present? How, then, could one claim that [the Dharma] did not exist in China prior to the arrival of Bodhidharma?
Since there is no central tenet [to be grasped], I have selected and edited its essential passages, prefaces them, and published them for circulation.
Let scholars not, like those who see wild flowers blooming before their eyes on the single reed across the Yangtze River or the solitary sandal at the edge of Mount Xi, fall into delusion.
Thus they shall know that when Bodhidharma met Emperor Wu of Liang, he came from nowhere; and when he encountered Song Yun, he likewise went nowhere.
Preface to the *Treatise on the Awakening of Faith* (*Zhao Lun*), Selected by Imperial Decree by the Great,
Wise, Perfectly Righteous Holy Monk Master Zhao, on the Full Moon of the Fourth Month in the Year of Gui-chou,
the Eleventh Year of Yongzheng.
Huìdá leads the ignorant. This preface concerns the four treatises—*Zōngběn*, *Bùqiān*, etc.—composed by the Dharma Master Śramaṇa Sēngzhào of Cháng'ān.
It says: "How beautiful is this man! He transcends speech while encompassing silence. When he establishes the fundamental, every sentence deeply penetrates the Buddha-mind;

when he clarifies the derivative, every word fully masters the various teachings. I, Huìdá, am a lowly person who has enjoyed the good fortune of encountering this sublime sound. Whenever I open [these texts]..."

I have sought [the truth] and shall not let it dance out of my hands. I vow that throughout every lifetime, I will exhaust my life in propagating and expounding it. Now, the Way of the Spirits has no fixed form, and the subtle workings of the mind are difficult to depict;

I have merely composed this preface as a temporary寄托 (reliance), requesting that future sages await it. For its profound meaning is largely categorized by the name "Original Non-existence" (benwu). Thus, in establishing the fundamental tenets, I have pointed toward the *dharmatā* (real aspect);
in opening the path of the Dharma of Emptiness, nothing surpasses the relationship between the ultimate and the conventional (*paramārtha-saṃvṛti*). Therefore, I shall explain them in succession.
The Two Truths reveal the gateway of the Buddha’s teaching; as for the cause that is perfectly complete, nothing surpasses Prajñā. As for the ultimate fruit, there is only Nirvāṇa.

Therefore, the derivative is traced back to the fundamental source, clarifying the abode of all the sages. Although the emptiness of intrinsic nature is used to approximate the original ground, it is nevertheless [the means to realize it].

There is no fundamental source that can be named; the discourse on the source transcends words. It is not a realm where the mind operates. Thus, non-transmigration accords with the conventional, yet the conventional is unborn.
Non-reality serves as reality, yet "reality" is merely a verbal designation. If one can revere this single path of the two truths beyond words, [one attains liberation].
Thus, the merit of tranquil illumination is manifest; therefore, while Prajñā is without cognition, the virtue of the Nameless arises, and Nirvāṇa is beyond designation.

I maintain that this teaching is complete and perfect, exhausting the profound ocean of the Buddha’s wisdom. It is vast and boundless, reaching the ultimate limits of the essence and characteristics of all phenomena.
This is the first of the *Honglun* (Great Treatises). Such was the man, Master Sengzhao.

According to the *Chuan deng lu* (Record of the Transmission of the Lamp), while Sengzhao was under sentence of death during the Yao Qin dynasty, he requested a seven-day leave to complete his *Baocang lun* (Treatise on the Precious Treasury).
At the time of his execution, he spoke this verse: "The four elements originally have no master; The five aggregates are fundamentally empty."
"Bringing one's head before the white blade is like cutting the spring breeze. However, this verse was not composed by Sengzhao. Sengzhao was a preeminent disciple of Kumārajīva.

Emperor Yao Xing of the Qin dynasty summoned him to enter the Xiaoyao Garden to assist Kumārajīva in collating and determining the scriptures and treatises, treating him with exceptional honor and respect.
The *Spring and Autumn Annals of the Sixteen Kingdoms*, in the biography of Sengzhao, states that during the Yao Qin...
He passed away in Chang’an in the sixteenth year of Hongshi, which was the tenth year of the Yixi era of the Jin dynasty.

Furthermore, for a person of such dignified character, how could there have been any reason for him to take leave to compose a treatise? Thus, it is indeed true that Dharma Master Zhao entered parinirvāṇa with auspicious signs.
Since the account is as hollow as the "Zi Xu" (The Falsehood), the verse was not composed by the Master; it is merely a corrupted tradition.
Imperial Preface:

When ancients encountered the conditions of time and circumstance, they often spoke of "great awakening beneath a word. Now, as for great awakening beneath a word, awakening does not reside in the words themselves.

To pursue awakening within the words—like Han’s dog chasing after a clod of earth—is to seek it where it cannot be found; such a dream will last until the year of the donkey. This is what is called clinging.
This refers to those who seek the moon by pointing at its reflection. At Huangmei and Caoxi, in the secret chamber during the middle of the night, the robe was transmitted and received;
what single word did he ever speak? Later, when Huangmei escorted Caoxi to the side of Jiuyang Station, the two conversed together.
Caoxi said, "It is only fitting that one should deliver oneself by means of one's own nature. Huangmei replied, "So it is; so it is. Since it is indeed self-nature that delivers itself...
If [the Dharma] has been transmitted, then what was bestowed by Huangmei? And what was received at Caoxi? Nevertheless, this is precisely what was bestowed by Huangmei and received at Caoxi.
Regarding Yongjia’s relation to Caoxi, it can be made even clearer for the world and future generations.
Master Yongjia received his transmission after staying for only one night; thus he was called "The One-Night Awakened One.
Now, observing the words of their questions and answers, Yongjia’s entire approach was one of "rowing against the current," devoid of any intention to "go with the flow.
If this is so, what did Caoxi transmit, and what did Yongjia receive? One must realize that Yongjia precisely obtained the milk of Caoxi from this very point—it cannot be otherwise.

This is a slander. It would be as if there were some actual dharma given to people, and one called it the "milk of the Dharma"—it would be no different from saying that a horse gives birth to a horse or a donkey gives birth to a donkey.

If this were so, demons and heretics would merely produce more demons and heretics; it would be like the long bamboo producing the *qingning* insect, and the *qingning* producing the *cheng* insect—how could such things be called the "life of wisdom"?
The words and phrases of Yongjia are esteemed by those of Western India as the great [teaching] of the Eastern Land.

I have perused this *Cheng lun* (Treatise on the Vehicle). I admire how its cultivation and awakening are both perfected, and how its vehicle and precepts are equally sublime. From the shallow to the profound, the shallow and the profound are of one accord;
it is truly a guiding compass for the followers of our school. Therefore, I have added revisions and edited it for publication to be displayed throughout the monasteries of the ten directions.

On the full moon day of the fourth month in the year of Gui-chou, the eleventh year of the Yongzheng era, the Imperial Selection of the Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Jue of Yongjia, Who Thoroughly Illuminates Sublime Wisdom:

The Master was a native of Yongjia. His surname was Dai. He entered the monastic order in his childhood and extensively investigated the Tripitaka, specializing in the Tiantai school’s *śamatha-vipaśyanā*.
While contemplating the Perfect and Wondrous Dharma-gate, he constantly remained in silent meditative observation throughout the four modes of deportment.

Later, inspired by the Zen Master Lang of Zuoxi, he traveled together with the Zen Master Ce of Dongyang to Caoxi. Upon his initial arrival, shaking his staff and carrying his water jar, he circumambulated the Patriarch three times.
The Patriarch said, "A śramaṇa is one who possesses the three thousand dignified demeanors and eighty thousand subtle practices. Great Virtue..."
“From what direction have you come? You have given rise to great arrogance. The Master said, “The matter of birth and death is great;

impermanence is swift. The Patriarch asked, “How can one realize non-arising? How can one understand that there is no swiftness? [The Master] replied, “Realization itself is non-arising; understanding is fundamentally without swiftness.”

The Patriarch said, “So it is; so it is. At that time, the entire assembly was not without astonishment. The Master then performed his prostrations with full decorum and took his leave shortly thereafter.
The Patriarch said, “Is your departure too soon? The Master replied, “Fundamentally, there is no movement; how could there be ‘soon’? The Patriarch asked, “Who knows there is no movement?
He replied, “It is you, O Benevolent One, who gives rise to discrimination. The Patriarch said, “You have attained the state of non-attainment.”
[The student] asked, "If there is no birth, can there be intention? The Patriarch said, "If there is no intention, who would be able to distinguish?

[The student] said, "Distinguishing is also not intention. The Patriarch sighed and said, "Excellent! Excellent! Stay for one night. At that time, he was called "One-Night Enlightenment" (Yi-xiu-jue).

He returned to reside at Wenjiang, where students gathered like spokes converging on a hub. He was titled the Great Master Zhengjue (True Enlightenment) and authored the *Canyuan zongmen wuxiu yuanman lun* (Treatise on the Perfect and Full Cultivation and Realization of the Chan School).
The essential meaning [of these works] proceeds from the shallow to the profound. Wei Jing, the Prefect of Qingzhou, compiled them into a single volume, entitled the *Yongjia Collection*.
The Emperor composed a preface for over three hundred poems by Hanshan and fifty-odd poems by Shide. They were transcribed by the Tang Governor Lüqiu.
From the Cold Rock [Cave], it has been transmitted throughout the realm of Jambudvīpa.
Those who read it may regard it as vernacular speech, or as verse, or as doctrinal discourse, or as Chan terminology. Like a *maṇi* jewel, its substance is not of a single color;
it is perfectly round in every respect, yet appears according to what each person’s eyes perceive. I, the Emperor, consider it to be neither vernacular nor verse, neither doctrine nor Chan.
This is indeed the direct mind and direct speech of an ancient Buddha. Yongming said: "Cultivate the myriad practices within flowers of the sky;

sit in meditation within a dharma-hall of the moon in water; subdue the armies of Mara within a mirror; and perform great Buddhist services within a dream. Those such as these two Great Beings come close to the ideal:
their right faith is harmonized and straightened, never departing from the causal conditions of their preceptors, and their fullness and radiance extend everywhere.
Pervading the great trichiliocosm, golden phoenixes soar upon branches that never sprout; by the shadowless tree, jade elephants encircle it.
Nature is emptiness yet acts as reality; nature is reality yet acts as emptiness. Falsehood exists while truth is absent; falsehood is absent while truth exists.

Emptiness exists while reality is absent; moment after moment, nothing remains. Reality exists while emptiness is absent; suchness is unmoving. Therefore, with a direct mind and direct speech, it is as follows:

It is thus. When the doubts of the learner are completely purified, they realize True Suchness (*tathatā*) perfectly; they are then able to see existence and non-existence as one body and their nature and conduct as a single thread.
Only then may one read the poems of the two Great Beings (Han Shan and Shide). Otherwise, if one generates interpretations based merely on the literal words, there will be no connection at all.
I have edited and recorded these to bequeath them to future generations. Han Shanzi said: "If there is a Ziqi, he shall discern this."
"Yin. This constitutes the preface.
Written on the first day of the fifth month of the year Gui-chou, the eleventh year of the Yongzheng era, by Imperial Edict.
Indeed, the Buddhas and patriarchs have transmitted the lineage from generation to generation, referred to as "father and son.

Although it is said that they employ worldly names and teachings merely to manifest the true transmission of the transcendental world, through this great death and great life, the life-force of wisdom (*prajñā-jīvita*) is sustained.

When one views that which is composed of hair and skin yet is a harmonious union of the four elements, there is the physical body on one hand and the birthless body on the other; both are equally the ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), fundamentally so.

This is no mere metaphor. Yongming said: "In an instant one leaves the mundane and returns to the True; there is nothing that can match this principle. In a moment one departs from the ordinary and enters the Holy;

it is difficult to repay such grace. Indeed, when one is pulled out of the burning house and ascends Mount Qingliang, or when the clouds of delusion are cleared away and one enters the Ocean of Radiance—looking back upon those times when the head was pierced by spikes and the body was bound like a silkworm in its cocoon—is precisely what [is meant].
It is like a person drinking water: cold or warm, they know it for themselves. How could there be anyone who does not consider the skin, flesh, and marrow from which they originated?
Are these not all fathers and sons? Among them, those who excel in mutual harmony are none other than the lineage of Guishan and Yangshan.

On that day, with a single shout of proclamation, the "cracking" and the "pecking" occurred simultaneously; together they received the true mandate of the Dharma King and jointly manifested the crystal clarity of their realization.
Their golden bodies form a single hall with two lutes: when the *gong* note is struck, the *gong* responds; when the *shang* note is struck, the *shang* responds.
A single casket holds two mirrors: if a Hu arrives, both reflect as Hu; if a Han arrives, both reflect as Han. This unsurpassed, wondrous principle turns the Golden Wheel in unison;
this Dharma-gate of a single generation marks twin Copper Pillars. Indeed, the father and son of Mount Gui and Mount Yang are exactly like Hanshan and Shishi.
I obtained this from my brother. Within the Buddha-dharma, he is like what the world calls a family’s blessing or a rare omen of prosperity.
Therefore, I have compiled these into a single volume to encourage the followers of our school throughout the world and for future generations. This serves as the preface.
Preface Composed by the Emperor on the First Day of the Fifth Month of the Year Gui-chou, the Eleventh Year of Yongzheng:

When Bodhidharma came from the West, he sat facing a wall for nine years without uttering many words or phrases, yet he was able to point directly to the human mind and enable one to see [one's own nature].

He attained Buddhahood by nature and was the first to open the patriarchal style of the land of China. Later generations have chanted, upheld, and transmitted his teachings—his illumination and function, his provisional and ultimate truths.
He beats the drum of lethal poison and brandishes the blade of the Great A sword beyond the reach of words and images, prior even to the emergence of forms and names.
His spiritual capacity is like a flash of lightning or a roll of thunder; his discourse flows like rivers and pours like the ocean. Blue lotus flowers scatter profusely from the root of his tongue.
The Great Lion’s Roar cuts through the ten directions and pierces the auditory faculties of hundreds of thousands of Buddhas. It leaps up to the void beyond the Thirty-three Heavens.
Yet, when one investigates its ultimate destination, it is nothing more than spreading thorns and brambles, with branches growing everywhere;

it is simply the bitterness and sweetness of licorice and yellow-root, which one experiences as sweet or bitter according to one's own mind. Thus, is it not true that benefiting oneself and others does not depend on many words? Zhao.
Chan Master Zhoushen had fully realized the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) and engaged people through the fundamental matter of his own realization.

Like the paulownia tree at Longmen, which stands a hundred feet high yet has no branches, I have examined his words and phrases; they are truly what is called "the skin and flesh having been completely stripped away, leaving only the single reality.
He was indeed one whom Bodhidharma protected and remembered. A single drop of lion’s milk is sufficient to scatter a thousand [other milks].
"A bushel of donkey’s milk. Yet when a Chan Master offers instruction, it is like a bead of five colors.
If one relies on petty knowledge or shallow views to interpret what lies beyond words, one fails the compassion of the ancient Buddhas and the grandmotherly heart that reaches down into the weeds.

Observe how the Master, picking up whatever comes to hand and speaking whatever issues from his mouth, enables all wise ones throughout the ten directions to enter directly into the stage of the Tathāgata at once. It may truly be said:

"Standing like a cliff ten thousand fathoms high; the moon reflected in a thousand rivers. Like Zhaozhou’s way of receiving people, this is truly the direct pointing to the human mind and seeing one's nature to become a Buddha—a teaching of the ancient Buddhas.
Therefore, I have recorded their most essential points here to show future students, so that they may know the model of the True Dharma. Thus it is, thus it is!

During the early Song dynasty, there was the Chan Master Yongming Zhijue of Hangzhou.

Throughout his life, he composed works such as the *Zongjing Lu* (Record of the Mirror of the Source), the *Weixin jue* (Secrets of Mind-Only), the *Xin fu* (Poem on the Mind), and the *Wanshan tonggui ji* (Collection on the Common Return of Myriad Good Deeds). These writings total several million words and are all preserved in the Tripitaka;
some have even been transmitted abroad. As I have perused and recorded them, my feelings of reverence and joy are beyond measure. Truly, they are what is called "clarity surpassing the dawn."
The sun rises high, transcending the Great Clarity; it is like a drum struck with a lion’s string, where all other sounds are silenced.

It is like the manifestation of a *maṇi* jewel, from which five-colored lights radiate. Truly, he is the foremost person after Caoqi, surpassing all the great *kalyāṇamitras* of successive generations.

However, if you have not yet reached the state where bondage and liberation are both empty and where object and wisdom are simultaneously extinguished, you must necessarily rely upon your emotions.

The Chan Master said: "Only by first clarifying the fundamental principle can one advance on the Path; if one pursues only the superficial details, it will truly be an impediment.

Thus, this book should not be read unless one has already attained realization through investigation and awakening; this was the intention of the original Chan Master. Since I have now carved its blocks...
The complete works have been presented to the followers of our school. Furthermore, their most profound words have been selected and appended to this collection.

In that very moment, all is shattered into a hundred fragments, and one encounters the direct, true, and pure essence. This is the practice of the ancient virtuous ones; it is certain.
Regarding "not deceiving one another": the True Person nurtures the "son-jewel" with the divine water of the Flower Pond.

After uniting the three realms within a single body, they are able to employ the cinnabar elixir as speech devoid of conventional meaning. Suddenly turning over and casting it forth, they sweep across the great void;
their entire being is without dependence, and they attain sovereign freedom wherever they go. How magnificent is this immortal, this great man! [End of] chapter.
These words and phrases are a true realization and thorough penetration, a direct pointing to the wondrous perfection.

Among the ancient worthies of the Chan school, such inconceivable self-benefit and benefit for others is truly rare. It is only fitting that figures such as Master Xue Daoguang all took refuge [in this teaching] as disciples.
May this be published for the present and future, so that those who study the Yuan school may know that there exists a True Doctrine.
Those who study the School of the Gate (Zongmen) know that this alone is the one true reality; all else is not the truth. This serves as the preface.

Written on the first day of the seventh month in the year of Gui-chou, the eleventh year of the Yongzheng era, by Imperial Selection for the Greatly Compassionate, Perfectly Penetrating Chan Immortal and True Man of Zi-yang, Zhang Ping-tu.
Postscript to the *Wuzhen pian*:
It is essential to recognize that when a person is born, it is entirely due to deluded emotions that they come to possess a body. Once there is a body, there is suffering.
If one had no body, from where could suffering arise? Now, for those who wish to escape such suffering, nothing is better than embodying the Ultimate Way (*zhìdào*).
To realize the essence of the Supreme Way, there is nothing better than clarifying the fundamental mind. Thus, the mind is the substance of the Way, and the Way is the function of the mind.
If a person can examine the mind and observe its nature, then the perfectly luminous substance will manifest of itself, and the unconditioned function will be spontaneously realized.
Without relying on the exertion of effort, one suddenly transcends to the other shore. This is none other than the mirror of the mind shining brightly and the divine pearl becoming vast and clear.

If one is enlightened, how can one cause all phenomenal marks to be suddenly abandoned, remain unstained by even a speck of dust, attain sovereign mastery over the source of the mind, and be certain of non-arising?
Thus, for those who clarify the mind and realize the Way, the body cannot burden their nature and external objects cannot disturb their truth;
how then could weapons and arms inflict harm, or tigers and rhinoceroses cause injury? How could massive fires or great floods be sufficient [to overwhelm them]?
It serves as a precaution. The human mind is like a bright mirror: it reflects but does not retain; it responds to things according to their conditions, harmonizing rather than initiating.
Thus, it can overcome all things without being harmed. This is what is called the supreme, ultimate, and wondrous Way.
Originally, this Way has no name; the Sage gave it a name by force. Originally, the Way has no words; the Sage spoke of it by force. That being so—
If names and words were silent, the flow of time would have no means to recognize its essence and return to its truth.
Therefore, the sages established teachings and formulated words to manifest the Way. Thus, the Way becomes manifest through words, yet words are forgotten once the Way is realized.
How tragic that this Way is so supremely wondrous and subtle, while the faculties and natures of worldly people are deluded and dull; they cling to the existence of a self-body, and...

People loathe death and delight in life; therefore, it is ultimately difficult for them to achieve awakening. Huang-Lao lamented their greedy attachments and thus employed the arts of cultivating life to accommodate their desires, gradually guiding them.

Since the essentials of cultivating life lie in the Golden Elixir (*jindan*), and the essentials of the Golden Elixir lie in the Divine Water and Flower Pond (*shuishihua chi*), the teachings of the *Daode jing* and *Yinfu jing* were thereby able to flourish widely in the world.
Indeed, people delight in life; yet its words are obscure and its principles profound. Although scholars may recite its texts, none can comprehend their meaning.
Were they not to encounter a supreme person who transmits the oral instructions, even if they were to engage in a hundred kinds of conjecture, [they would remain ignorant].

In the end, none were able to manifest their merit or accomplish the task. Is this not because those who study are as numerous as cow-hair, while those who attain realization are as rare as the horn of a qilin?
In the past, during the year of Jǐyǒu, I met the Master in Chengdu and was taught the methods of the Elixir (dān-fǎ).

That same year, the Master passed away. Since then, I have transmitted these teachings to others three times, yet on each occasion I encountered calamity; in every case, it did not exceed two [years].
Ten days later, he finally recalled his teacher’s admonition: "In the future, if there is someone who unties your halter and removes your shackles, you should bestow [the teachings] upon them;
otherwise, it is not permitted. Thereafter, he wished to be removed from the official registers, yet he was troubled by the fact that this man did not know whether to trust him.

I have thus composed this *Wuzhen pian* (Verses on Awakening to Reality) to record the origins and details of elixirs and medicinal drugs. Once it was completed, seekers flocked to me from all directions.
Observing their diligent intent, my heart could not bear to keep the teachings secret; therefore, I selected those worthy and transmitted them to them.

However, those to whom I transmitted them were none who possessed great power or might, nor those capable of upholding the precarious or rescuing the drowning, but rather those who were resolute, magnanimous, and uniquely discerning, and who were capable and benevolent in clarifying the Way.
The gentleman had previously encountered calamities twice, yet his mind remained unaware [of their cause]. When it reached the third time, he finally reflected upon his past transgressions.

Thus one knows that the method of the Great Elixir (Dadan) is most simple and easy; even a foolish and lowly person may obtain and practice it, thereby immediately transcending to the ground of the sages.
For this reason, the will of Heaven guards it with secrecy, not permitting its light transmission to those who are unworthy. Yet I—[did not...]

I have followed my teacher’s words, yet I have repeatedly disclosed celestial secrets. Because I possess a physical body, I am thus constantly subject to reprimands and calamities; this is Heaven’s profound warning.
Since such divine power is so swift and immediate, how could I not be fearful and self-reproachful? From this day forward, I shall clench my mouth and bind my tongue.
Even if a cauldron of boiling oil were placed before me or a sword were set upon my neck, I would never again dare to speak. This is *Wuzhen* (Awakening to Truth).
Within this treatise, the subtle principles regarding the medicinal substances and the timing of the fire (*huǒhòu*) of the Great Elixir (*dàdān*) are fully and exhaustively detailed.

Those who delight in these matters and possess the innate bone of the immortals will find their wisdom and discernment naturally clarified upon reading it; they can then seek out the text to explain its meaning themselves.
Why should they require my trivial oral instructions? Such [attainment] is a gift from Heaven, not something granted by me at will.

This is a transmission. As for the hymns and praises at the end of the chapters, which discuss the method of realizing one's nature, this is precisely what was referred to above as the path of non-action and wondrous enlightenment (*anabhisaṃskāra-mahābodhi*).
Now, the path of non-action takes the equalization of all things as its core intent; although it reveals profound and essential secrets, it ultimately contains no fault.
Yet, alas, ordinary beings vary in the thickness of their karmic conditions and the sharpness or dullness of their spiritual faculties. Thus, even if they hear a single sound...
Thus, divergent views have come into being. Therefore, the Dharma-treasure expounded by Śākyamuni and Mañjuśrī is nothing other than the One Vehicle;
yet, as practitioners listen and study according to their respective capacities and understandings, the distinctions of the Three Vehicles naturally arise.

Hereafter, if there should be a person of sharp and keen faculties who sees or hears this chapter, they will know that I have attained the wondrousness of the supreme One Vehicle of the Sixth Patriarch of the Dharma.

The essential point is that one may awaken to the myriad dharmas through a single word. If residual habitual tendencies still remain, such that one reverts to views of the Lesser or Middle Vehicles, this is not my fault.

Wuzhen pian Waiji: Verses on the Ground of Being (Xingdi song) I

The Buddha-nature is neither identical nor different; it is like a thousand lamps sharing a single radiance. Whether one increases it, how could it be enhanced? Whether one diminishes it, it remains unharmed.

There is no fault in either accepting or rejecting it; burning it or drowning it does not obstruct it at all. Among the phenomena of seeing, hearing, knowing, and perceiving, there is not a single thing that can be conjectured or measured.
The wondrous body of the Tathāgata pervades as many grains of sand as there are in the Ganges; the myriad phenomena, vast and manifold, are without obstruction.
Only when one realizes this perfect and penetrating true Dharma-eye does one know that the triple world is one’s own home.
If one observes it from three perspectives, its form cannot be seen. Even when called out to it, it responds; do not say this sound is like an echo in a valley.
If there were no valley, what sound would there be?

The four—sound, form, smell, and taste—each contain hearing, seeing, awareness, and cognition. These various sensory objects merely manifest their respective faculties; yet even this single, numinous, and constant entity is not truly existent.
How, then, can these four serve as a basis for reliance?
Without taking a single step, he reached the Western Heaven; sitting upright, the ten directions are present before his eyes. The light behind his crown is still but a phantom;
clouds rising from beneath his feet do not yet make one an immortal.
The six realms of seeking birth are fundamentally unborn; fearing extinction, how could they ever have momentarily ceased? What the eyes see is not as good as what the ears see;
what the mouth speaks cannot compare to what the nose speaks.

There is neither sin nor merit; though one acts all day long, it is as if one has never acted. Though one sits all day long, it is as if one has never sat. Cultivating goodness does not result in the accomplishment of virtue;

committing evil fundamentally entails no transgression. If people of this age have not yet clarified their minds, do not cling to these words and act recklessly; after death, you must face the consequences.
King Yama, one cannot escape the cauldrons and pestles.
The Three Realms are Mind-Only;

All things are myself. When one perceives objects, one perceives the mind;

If one gives rise to conceptual knowledge and understanding, it instead becomes a perverted view. Only when one beholds objects with a mindless heart does one first see the face of Bodhi.

When the perfect penetration sees that true emptiness is neither empty nor non-empty, where would the perfect luminosity not be perfectly penetrating? Within the faculties, objects, mind, and dharmas, there is nothing at all.
Regarding all things: only through wondrous function does one know they are identical to things.

Following along with the myriad phenomena, they manifest freely before one's eyes. Observe their movement and stillness; let them exercise their power. Perfect luminosity and meditative wisdom are ultimately without [duality].

Within the same there is difference, within difference there is sameness. I ask you, puppet: do you know how to dance?
In this verse on the Heart Sūtra, the aggregates, truths, faculties, objects, emptiness, and form—none of these dharmas can be spoken of. Perverted views have been utterly exhausted;
the essence of quiescence is serene and transcendent.
Regarding "The Human and the Self" (also known as "Equalizing Things"):

I am no different from others; it is human minds that differ of their own accord. People have intimates and strangers, but I have neither "this" nor "that. Whether aquatic, terrestrial, or aerial—[all are equal].
Contemplate all as being of one essence; whether noble or base, superior or inferior, head or foot, they are the same as oneself. Since even "I" is not truly "I," how could there ever be a "you"?
When both self and other are absent, all bubbles return to the water.

The true mark is fundamentally beyond words; it has neither low nor high, neither limit nor bound. It is neither form nor emptiness, nor is it a dual nature.

Throughout the dust-motes and lands of the ten directions, it is a single perfect wheel. In right concentration, when has there ever been a distinction between speech and silence? One cannot grasp it, nor can one let it go.
Simply not dwelling the mind upon any marks is the true rule of the Tathāgata. To eliminate deluded thoughts, one sets the real against them;
yet if delusion does not arise, the real also fades away. Only when one knows that both the real and the deluded are non-existent can the true mind be attained without obstruction.
Being unobstructed, one is able to act with sovereign ease; a single awakening instantly dissolves the sins of kalpas beyond reckoning, without the need for further effort.
He has realized Bodhi; from this point on, he will forever leave the ocean of birth and death. My teacher spoke with clarity and eloquence, remaining in the world as a guiding model.

Regarding Precept, Concentration, and Wisdom:
these are the wondrous functions within the Dharma. Although the Buddhas and Patriarchs have spoken of them, those who have not yet attained realization remain attached to them.
I shall now speak of them briefly to assist you in awakening; however, one must transcend both mind and境 (objects).
A single thought unmoving is called *śīla* (precept). The enlightened nature perfectly luminous, with inner and outer clarity, is called *samādhi* (concentration).

Responding to conditions according to circumstances with inexhaustible wondrous function is called *prajñā* (wisdom). These three are mutually dependent for their completion and serve as both essence and function to one another.
When *śīla* is the essence, then *samādhi* and *prajñā* are its functions; when *samādhi* is the essence, then *śīla* and *prajñā* are its functions.
As for the essence of wisdom (prajñā), its functions are precept (śīla) and meditative concentration (samādhi). These three have never been separated from one another for even a moment.
It is just as the sun relies on light to be able to illuminate, and light relies on illumination to be able to manifest clarity; without light, there can be no illumination.

Without illumination, there can be no clarity. To investigate the origins of precept, concentration, and wisdom, they are rooted in the single nature; the radiance of their illumination is rooted in the single sun.
Since even "one" is not truly one, how could there be "three"? When both "one" and "three" are forgotten, all is profoundly still and pure.
Verses on "The Mind Itself is Buddha":
Buddha is the mind; the mind is Buddha. Mind and Buddha have always been but delusive things.

If one knows there is neither Buddha nor mind, Then for the first time one is the Dharmakāya Buddha of True Suchness. The Dharmakāya Buddha has no form; A single sphere of light contains ten thousand things.

The elephant: the body of no-body is the true body; the appearance of no-appearance is the real mark. It is neither form nor emptiness, yet not non-empty; it is neither moving nor still, neither coming nor going.
It is without difference and without sameness, without existence and without non-existence; it is difficult to grasp and difficult to relinquish, difficult to hear and difficult to expect.
Internally and externally it is perfectly penetrating, reaching everywhere through all things. A single Buddha-land exists within a single grain of sand; a single grain of sand...
Encompassing the great trichiliocosm, a single body and mind are identical to ten thousand. To know this, one must realize the dharma of non-mind;
being unstained and unimpeded constitutes pure karma. When the myriad forms of good and evil are not acted upon, one is then the Tathāgata and Kāśyapa.
The Song of Gathering Pearls: The poor man has a pearl within his clothing; it is inherently perfect and bright. Failing to seek it for himself, he instead counts the treasures of others.
Counting another's treasure brings no ultimate benefit; it merely teaches you to exhaust yourself in vain. How much better it would be to recognize your own precious jewel!
Worth hundreds of billions of gold pieces, this precious jewel has the greatest radiance, illuminating the entire trichiliocosm;
from time immemorial, not even a fraction of its light was understood, for it was merely obscured by floating clouds.
Since I have recognized this *maṇi* jewel, who would cherish further these bubble-like bodies and empty flowers? The Buddha’s pearl is identical to my own pearl; my nature thus returns to the Buddha.
The ocean of nature: the pearl is not a pearl, the sea is not a sea. The vast expanse of the mind is level and encompasses the entire dharma-realm;

let the clamor of the dust fill your eyes as you please, yet concentration and wisdom are perfectly luminous and ever-sovereign. It is neither emptiness nor form; internally and externally it is bright and clear without obstruction.
The six supernormal powers and spiritual intelligence are wondrously inexhaustible; benefiting oneself and others—how could there be a limit? To see is to realize; ten thousand things...

When affairs are concluded, one abandons learning and dwells in non-action throughout the entire day. One is as cautious as an infant before birth; in movement and stillness, one follows conditions without fixed necessity.
Do not sever delusion, nor do you cultivate truth; for both the mind of truth and the mind of delusion belong entirely to the realm of dust.

From the beginning, all phenomena are without form (*animitta*); within this formlessness lies the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). This Dharma-body is none other than the Buddha of True Nature, yet it is also not a person.
It is neither a thing; it is vast and fills the space between heaven and earth. It is simply the realm of the rarefied and the silent, the ethereal and the indistinct.
Untainted by defilement, its radiance is self-evident. There is no dharma that does not arise from within the mind; if the mind does not give rise to them, dharmas naturally cease.

Thus one knows that sin and merit are fundamentally formless—there is no form of a Buddha and no dharma to be preached. When a man of integrity possesses such wisdom and insight, his discernment is natural, and his speech emerges [from this realization].
He then let out a lion’s roar, unlike the wild foxes who discourse on arising and ceasing.

This song pointing to the delusions of *dhyāna* and *samādhi* reveals that the nature of the Tathāgata is like water: when its essence is still, wind and waves cease of their own accord; whether rising or dwelling, it remains profoundly serene and ever-pure—not only...
Sitting is precisely what it means [to practice]. When people today sit in stillness seeking realization, they do not say that it entirely depends on seeing one's nature.

If the nature is clear within seeing, then seeing will naturally settle within the nature. Once this settling is achieved, the function of wisdom becomes inexhaustible; this is called the spiritual power of all Buddhas.
I have often sought to investigate its essence and function, yet I see only the empty space of the ten directions. Within this space, there is not a single thing;
nor is there anything subtle, obscure, or elusive. Since the subtle and the elusive cannot be found, to seek them is, on the contrary, to fall into error.
These two characters, "error" and "falling," themselves must not be grasped as a basis for reliance. If the fundamental mind is already like space, how could there be gain or loss, subject or object?
Simply eliminate all phenomena, clearing them away until they are utterly exhausted and without remainder. Suddenly, perfect luminosity will manifest of itself;
you will then be no different from the Buddhas. This physical body is but a shackle for me, so let us simply harmonize with the light and blend with the mundane.
In every movement, remain without intention; what matter is right or wrong, honor or disgrace? This birth-body is merely a temporary lodging; the host of this inn is named Vairocana.
Vairocana neither comes nor goes; thus one knows that birth and extinction leave nothing behind. Someone may ask: "What is Vairocana like? It is simply that having form is not [the truth].
Before one's eyes, leaf by leaf and dust mote by dust mote, these motes and leaves are neither identical nor different.

Furthermore, within each of these motes and leaves, every single one is Śākyamuni and Kāśyapa. If they are different, then all the myriad sounds resound together; if they are the same, then a single wind gathers them all.
If you wish to recognize the *maṇi* jewel, do not say that one must know it only after attaining the Dharma. When there is illness, one employs medicine for its treatment;

once the illness has been cured, what further use is there for the medicine? When the mind is deluded, one must rely on the illumination of the Dharma; when the mind is awakened, the Dharma is no longer required.

It is like a dim mirror that, once polished, naturally has its stains and blemishes eliminated. Since both mind and Dharma are fundamentally illusory, they cause one to depart from and exhaust all phenomenal marks (*lakṣaṇa*).
How is it that one is liberated from all marks? This is called the Unsurpassed Truth of the Tathāgata.

If you wish to adorn the Buddha-lands, practice compassion with equanimity to save those in suffering, and although your original vows for Bodhi are profound, you must by no means grasp at marks. This constitutes the perfection of both merit and wisdom;
such a person shall receive the prediction of enlightenment first. If even a speck of dust of the views of annihilation or permanence stains the mind, one will lack the affinity for the Buddhas.
Turning my thoughts back, I consider how ordinary beings are deluded and attached; they are entirely stained by the habits of emotional craving.

It is simply because their attachment to emotions is so great that they are constantly born from wombs, eggs, transformations, or moisture. Those who study the Way must be taught to be fierce and resolute, with a heart as hard as iron.

Even toward one’s own parents, wife, and children, what difference is there from others? One must constantly maintain a single sphere of light, never allowing the sight of desirable things to provoke thought or deliberation.
All phenomena are simultaneously free from attachment; one speaks of both the deepest hells and the heavenly realms.

Thereafter, my life is in my own hands. Within the void, there is neither sound nor falling. Appearing and disappearing amidst the various Buddha-lands, I never depart from the original seat of Bodhi.
As for the thirty-two transformations of Avalokiteśvara, I shall likewise realize them therein. Manifesting inconceivable emanations, they all emerge from the nature of carefree liberation.
I am a mindless Chan practitioner; I do not discriminate among any matters. In the past, I was a black ox; today, my entire body is white.
Sometimes I sing and laugh to myself, while those beside me say I lack spirit.
Who knows that within this form clothed in coarse hair, I harbor a priceless treasure? Furthermore, if you see me speak of emptiness, it is like swallowing a whole date.
This Dharma can only be known by the Buddha; how could ordinary fools understand its outward manifestations?

Furthermore, there are those superior men who practice meditation, yet they merely learn to wrangle with words and lips, boasting of their quickness in debate while fundamentally failing to recognize the Master.

They all seek only the branches and pluck the leaves, unable to investigate the root. When the root is obtained, the branches and leaves flourish naturally; without the root, the branches and leaves find it difficult to survive.

Thus they flaunt their own grasp of the spiritual pearl, yet the barriers of self and others remain difficult to eliminate; their wondrous awakening to the source of my own nature remains separated by a distance of a thousand miles.

These people are truly pitiable and laughable; in vain they claim to have studied the Way for many years, yet with haughty minds they refuse to seek instruction from others, causing their entire lives to pass in empty old age.
This is due to being dull-witted and deluded, with heavy karma from false views serving as the cause.
If one does not attain awakening in this life, how can one avoid sinking into the depths in future lives?

This verse on "no-mind" is laughable; my own mind is as dull and base as it is. Utterly listless and drifting along, I simply yield to things as they come to rest. I do not know how to practice cultivation.
I have committed no sins; I have never benefited others, nor have I served my own private interests. I do not observe the precepts, nor do I heed taboos and prohibitions.
I know nothing of ritual and music, nor do I practice benevolence and righteousness. Of all that is possible among men, I possess not even one hundredth part. When hunger comes, I eat.
When thirsty, one comes to drink water; when weary, one sleeps; when awake, one walks about. When hot, one wears but a single garment; when cold, one covers oneself with a blanket.
Without thought or deliberation, what cause for sorrow or joy? Without regret or scheming, without mindfulness or intention—such is the nature of all worldly honor and disgrace.
It is merely a lodging house. The birds nesting in the forest trees may serve as a metaphor for it: they come without being invited and depart without being stopped;
they neither avoid nor seek, neither praise nor disparage; they feel no aversion to the ugly and evil, nor do they envy the good and beautiful; they do not hasten toward quiet chambers.

One does not stay far from the bustling marketplace; one does not speak of others' faults, nor boast of one's own rightness; one does not overvalue those who are honored, nor disparage those who are lowly or young;

one treats friends and enemies with equal affection; whether great or small, internal or external, in sorrow or joy, gain or loss, in reverence or contempt, and in danger or ease—the mind perceives no duality.
Serene and uniform, it does not act as the precursor to fortune nor the initiator of calamity. It responds only after being moved and arises only when impelled.

It fears neither the blade of a weapon nor the dread of tigers and rhinoceroses. It adopts whatever name is given according to the object; how could it be constrained by names? The eye does not go toward form.
Sound does not come to the ear. All marks and appearances belong to the realm of delusion and falsehood. The forms and sounds of male and female are entirely devoid of fixed substance.

Since their substance and appearance are without mind, they are neither defiled nor obstructed; they are free and at ease, such that no thing can entangle them. Their wondrous awakening is radiant and perfect.
It reflects and penetrates both inside and out, enveloping the six directions; there is nothing too distant or near. Its radiance is not radiance, like the moon reflected in water.

Since it is difficult to grasp or reject, how can it be compared to anything else? To understand this wondrous function is to transcend all else far beyond. Someone asked: "What is your fundamental principle?"
This is all there is to it. Twelve *Xijiangyue* (West River Moon) Poems,
Part One.
Do not strive further to extinguish deluded thoughts; why must you seek after True Suchness? The Buddha-nature of the original source is cultivated by all equally;
are delusion and awakening restricted to before or after? To awaken is to become a Buddha in an instant; to remain deluded is to circulate through ten thousand kalpas.
If one can, in a single thought-moment, accord with true cultivation, the sins and defilements as numerous as the sands of the Ganges will be utterly extinguished.
These two [aspects] are inherently without arising or ceasing; one merely imposes the distinction between arising and ceasing. Even such things as sin and merit have no root;
how could the wondrous essence ever increase or diminish? I possess a single bright mirror, which has long been shrouded in obscurity. This morning—
Polished and bright, it illuminates heaven and earth; the myriad phenomena are so manifest they cannot be concealed.
The nature of the three selves enters the nature of all Buddhas; the Buddha-nature of all directions is likewise so. Lofty and solitary, its cold reflection shines upon the cold spring. One.
The moon appears universally in a thousand ponds; when small, even a hair’s breadth cannot perceive it; when large, it fills the three thousandfold world-system.
Its high or low position does not depend on the squareness or roundness of one's faith, nor can its length, shortness, depth, or shallowness be described.
The four dharmas are fundamentally non-dharmas; emptiness within emptiness is itself not empty. Stillness and clamor, speech and silence, are by nature the same.
Why labor to speak of dreams within a dream? Where there is function, there is no function within that function; where there is no merit, merit is applied within that merit. It is just like this.
When the fruit ripens, it naturally turns red. Do not ask how it was cultivated or planted;

forget thoughts of the five virtues and evils all at once. Neither prosperity nor decay concerns you; whether in obscurity or clarity, hidden or manifest, let yourself float or sink as you may. Follow along.
Divide the food for hunger and drink for thirst; the spirit is still and profoundly serene, ever in quiescence. It does not hinder sitting, reclining, singing, or chanting.
A pool of autumn water is green and deep; when the wind stirs, do not be startled—just let it be as it is.

Regarding these six pairs reflected in the mirror, there is no need for forced extinction. Bodhi is provisionally established as a mere designation; form and emptiness, light and darkness, are fundamentally equal.
Cease the division between the true and the false into two distinct entities. Upon awakening, it is immediately called the Pure Land; there is no India or Caoxi. Who says...
The Land of Ultimate Bliss lies to the west of heaven; when this is realized, it is Amitābha appearing in the world.

As for the seven types of persons—the self, others, sentient beings, and the life-principle—how could there be any distinction between self and other, or high and low? The Dharmakāya shines universally, transcending all idle chatter. Contemplate this!
In mindfulness, there is no need for seeking; as for what is seen, when was it ever seen? As for what is heard, it is not necessarily heard.
From the beginning, all functions have been mutually unknown; who can obstruct you in birth and death?

Practicing generosity while abiding in the eight stages of meditative concentration yields rewards that do not depart from the realms of devas and humans; it is just like an upward-pointing arrow shot at the floating clouds, which falls only because its momentum is exhausted.
How can this compare to the unconditioned true mark (*dharmatā*), which returns to the source, reverts to simplicity, and restores the state of purity, wherein all objective conditions are forgotten?
When emotions are exhausted, one rests in natural truth; thereby one realizes the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
When the nine fish or the rabbit are returned to one’s hand, one naturally forgets the trap and the snare. It is a raft for crossing the river and a ladder for ascending to heaven. Upon arrival—
All of these must be completely abandoned. Before awakening, one must rely upon verbal expressions; once awakening has occurred, verbal expressions become erroneous.
Although the four propositions belong to the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), even these must still be transcended.

Once the ten [stages] are realized, do not seek quiescent extinction (*śānti*). Follow conditions to guide the masses of deluded beings; only when you sever views of annihilation and permanence and take them up as your own responsibility will you recognize the ultimate destination of the true reality.
Through the five eyes, the three bodies, the four wisdoms, and the cultivation and perfection of the six pāramitās and myriad practices, the radiant light [is perfected].
A single fine maṇi jewel benefits others while simultaneously enabling its own self-preservation.

Eleven: I observe that people nowadays speak of "nature" (xing), boasting only of their quick-wittedness in responding to circumstances; yet when they encounter actual situations, they become even more deluded and confused. Furthermore—
How would this differ from a fool? One must practice what one preaches; only then can it be said that one’s words and deeds are without flaw.
To be able to wield the sword of wisdom to sever the *maṇi* jewel is called the Tathāgata’s Right Wisdom.
The twelvefold desire is to realize the wondrous path of non-arising; one need only perceive the true mind for oneself. The true body is without form and without sound;
the pure *dharmakāya* is simply thus. This path is neither non-existent nor existent; within that which is neither, what is there to seek? [It is beyond] the two extremes.
Discarding both extremes and remaining in the center—seeing through this is called the "superior grade.

In the Imperial Preface to Xuedou, it is recorded that he traveled extensively throughout all quarters, his wit and eloquence being matchless; yet upon suddenly encountering Zhimen, twice the whisk was swept across his mouth.

*Strike!* Suddenly he attained great enlightenment and became a successor of Zhimen. If students can realize this at this point, they should know that the mind does not reside in discursive thought, yet it universally illumines the Dharma-realm;
the mouth need not employ speech, yet it extensively expounds as many teachings as there are sands in the Ganges. As Xuedou said:
"Even if heaven and earth, the great land, the grasses, trees, and forests were all transformed into monks, speaking with one voice in unison—"

Setting aside hundreds of thousands of difficult questions, it does not take the Elder even a single snap of the fingers for him to respond universally to all levels, without any discrepancy between what precedes and what follows.

Nevertheless, within that single snap of the fingers, he spontaneously forms responses according to conditions, just as when the gods of the Thirty-three Heavens eat from a common precious vessel, the color of their rice differs according to their respective merit. Thus, the Sūtra says: "All worthy and holy ones..."
Even with unconditioned dharmas (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*), there are distinctions. This is true even for the mere snap of a finger;
how much more so when there is answering and questioning, words and letters—how could they be treated with such superficiality as to be indistinguishable, without further discernment?

In years past, Xuedou’s eyebrows trailed the ground, leaving behind this tangled vine. Today, Yuanming unties the topknot to retrieve the pearl, adding one more "snake's foot" (a redundant addition). Herein...
This compilation consists entirely of the primary truth (*paramārtha-satya*) and the most supreme vehicle (*yāna*). For those who study it, there is no need to seek elsewhere;

by directly realizing it within themselves, they find that without departing from these very words and phrases, all possess the potential to enter the state of sainthood from the level of ordinary beings.
It is like using fire to melt ice: when the ice dissolves into water, water and ice become of one flavor. Yet, while there is nothing to be attained, fire and water remain distinct paths.
What connection could there possibly be? Nevertheless, the power of fire melts ice; how can its efficacy be denied?
Written as a preface by Imperial Edict on the first day of the seventh month in the eleventh year of the Yongzheng era, the Gui-chou year.
"Calling for Little Yu so frequently—what is the reason? It is because he wishes for the husband to recognize the voice. Chan Master Yuanwu Qin attained sudden enlightenment upon these words.
Are these words frivolous chatter (*ki-oku*)? Or are they Chan talk? At the edge of the "poison-drum," how can one afford to lean an ear toward them?
Yet, if you pause to reflect or deliberate even for a moment upon this frivolous chatter or Chan talk, the sword has already gone far away. Throughout all antiquity...
Pervading the present; pervading above and below; pervading east and west; pervading south and north—all are but atoms of dust. Within each atom, there are established jeweled lands;
within each jeweled land, the Buddha-work is performed. All such Buddha-works fully embody the Tathāgata’s Treasury of the True Dharma Eye and the wondrous mind of Nirvāṇa.
Where could one open one's mouth to speak of it? Where could one lay hands upon it?
To discern it is this very thing; to speak it with the mouth is also this very thing. To apply one's hand to discern it is likewise this very thing.

How could one use "this" to describe "that," or use "this" to select "that"? Should one pause for even a moment to reflect or deliberate, here on this side are earth, water, fire, and wind—the iron mountains loom high;
there on that side are seeing, hearing, knowing, and perceiving—the jade seas lie deep.
How could one let go from a hanging cliff? It is all merely talking in one's sleep with eyes wide open. Thus, an ancient worthy said:

"If you lack even a single dharma, you do not realize the Dharmakāya. If you have even a single dharma in excess, you do not realize the Dharmakāya. If there is even a single dharma, you do not realize the Dharmakāya.
If there is not even a single dharma, you do not realize the Dharmakāya. If you can verify this, then you may speak with your mouth open; you may even take up your hands.
It is also acceptable to select [only those]. However, if you are unable to do so, it would be a great pity to let Master Yuanwu’s lifelong efforts go to waste;
even this single compilation by the "Master of Perfect Illumination" (Yuanying) would then be rendered largely ineffective.
Preface Composed by the Emperor on the Full Moon Day of the Seventh Month in the Year of Gui-chou, the Eleventh Year of Yongzheng:
In ancient times, the Sage Emperor Huang visited Guangchengzi to inquire about the Way; Tang questioned Bian Sui and Wu Guang. These were the sages of antiquity.
Your Majesty, regarding those of lofty character, one must necessarily rely on their cultivation of body and mind as the foundation for governing all affairs.
Even in later generations, when it comes to matters of statecraft and military achievements within the imperial court, such individuals are still difficult to find;
how much more so, then, for matters concerning the nature of the mind? Since time immemorial, the ancient worthies of the Chan school have transmitted the legacy of Vulture Peak.
Among those who possess the lamp of the mind, there are many great men who do not enter the gates of emperors.
Among those who occupy the position of emperor, those who have awakened to the fundamental principle (*zongzhi*) are even fewer.

Occasionally, shallow-minded petty men, floatingly admiring the scriptural teachings (*jiaoxiang*), rashly criticize them by comparing them to heterodox doctrines. Yet, the persons whom they themselves revere and honor often, for the most part, [do not understand this].
This would have been sufficient to win over the world, yet it would only have served to increase suspicion and slander.

Consequently, the glorious deeds of the Yellow Emperor and Tang the Victorious could no longer be witnessed by later generations. When our dynasty first resided in the eastern lands, the customs were pure and ancient;
people were truly loyal and filial, upright in heart and upright in conduct, and were revered through successive generations.
Regarding the Buddha and the devas, there was no distinction made within the Sangha based on rank; they were all revered without exception.
This practice stood in stark contrast to the customs of the Mongols.
During the reign of my Imperial Ancestor, Emperor Shizu (Chang Huangdi), who governed the world, whenever he had leisure from the myriad affairs of state, he [engaged with] Yulinkou and Yang...
The father and son, Seong and Sin, reached the ultimate realization of the study of the nature of mind;
their timely convergence was no different from the encounters between the Yellow Emperor and Cheng Tang. This was not due to our dynasty’s long-standing custom of venerating monks.
I have examined the writings of Yu Linxiu and his son, which expound the wondrous principles of the *zongcheng* (the vehicle of the school). They are truly able to benefit people and save the world:
like the bright sun in the sky, the clouds of delusion are instantly cleared away; like a clear bell ringing through the night, illusory dreams are immediately dispelled.
This will provide inexhaustible benefit for the future "dragons and elephants" (great disciples), and it stands in comparison with the Buddhas and Patriarchs of antiquity without shame. Therefore...

This work was compiled, collated, and published to be transmitted to future generations. It occurred to me that it has been the magnificent tradition of ancient sages for emperors to seek the Way from those of lofty character;
yet, since time immemorial, Confucian scholars have consistently treated the two [Buddhist and Daoist] traditions with narrow-minded discrimination and limitation.
Unable to bear that future generations would remain forever ignorant of this, I have not hesitated to provide a clear analysis of them. Therefore, I write this preface.

The account is as follows. As for the preaching at the West Garden of Wanshan Hall and the various occasions of formal audience and spiritual inquiry, although they are recorded in the *Goryan Sijang Giryol* (Memoranda of Attendant Goryan), these are all matters concerning the Buddha-dharma;
they are not embellished, exaggerated, or erroneous claims. Furthermore, they serve to illuminate the brilliance of the sun and moon of Yulim Hyu, acting as the eyes for humans and devas.

Since there are still sufficient materials to be gathered from the records of the Imperial Household, I have compiled several entries here to respectfully commemorate the gracious treatment bestowed upon me by my imperial ancestor on that day.
Written on the first day of the eighth month of the year Gui-chou, the eleventh year of the Yongzheng era.
From the *Imperial Selection of the Recorded Sayings of the State Preceptor Yulin Xiu, the Great Awakened, Universal Savior, Capable Benevolent One*:
The first day of the intercalary third month in the sixteenth year of the Shunzhi era (Jihai).

At Wanshan Hall, the Master ascended the hall by imperial decree. Upon reaching the front of the seat, he called to the assembly, saying: "Do you understand? If you do understand, this mountain monk has not yet..."
Leaving Jiangnan, he ascended the seat and finished his preaching of the Dharma. "If this were not yet so, look toward the second gate as he unfolds his skillful means.
He then ascended the seat, took up the incense, and said: "This single portion of incense was personally received as a prediction of enlightenment at Vulture Peak.
I burn it in the incense burner to offer my vows."

The Buddha-Mind Deva-son has attained Equal and Perfect Enlightenment. Next, he holds up the incense and says: "This single portion of incense has long been proclaimed throughout the ocean-like assembly of the Flower Treasury.
Burning it within the incense burner, I pray that the Empress Dowager, Mother of Buddhas, may be endowed with a hundred blessings, and that she be protected and assisted."
