A Dharma Talk for Senior Monk Jin of Quanzhan.
The Venerable Jin had served me for ten years without wavering from his level of attainment, yet he would frequently bite through his thumb [in frustration].

At the beginning of the summer retreat, he entered the chamber of Daxiong and heard the phrase, "Where does the one return? He attained immediate and total penetration. He reflected that while self-benefit is easy, benefiting others is difficult;
thus, with a profound and great resolve, he vowed to remain on the stage of a student for the rest of his life. This is what is meant by attaining immeasurable holy bodies, yet still...
"This is not yet the place to moor the boat.
He showed this to the attendant Sengcai.

For those in the family of Chan practitioners, it is difficult to skillfully apply the mind. For those who skillfully apply the mind, it is difficult to attain correct enlightenment. For those who have attained correct enlightenment, [it is difficult to... strike.

One escapes the difficulty of views; one strikes through the difficulty of views. One does not wander into the difficulty of mental proliferation. By reversing these four difficulties into four easinesses, one’s own benefit and the benefit of others will all be fully accomplished.
The ancients said that even after several decades there might still be movement and fluctuation. Some said, "It will take me several decades before I finally achieve a state of being 'one piece.
Setting aside those who have achieved this state for now, as for those who have not yet achieved it: simply take what Caoxi said—"What thing comes thus?"—and examine it at all times.
This will ensure that wherever a patch-robed monk walks, it is like fire melting ice.
A Letter to Master Yue:
Throughout my life, I have possessed no great talents; I am merely one who does not forget even a single word or fragment of a phrase from the past or present.

There is also something for which I take pride in my life: I have not studied the Buddhist teachings or worldly dharmas of other quarters. Alas! How could I not remember the words and phrases of others?
Listen to these words of mine! Entrust this writing to Xingyue, to be shown to those with true understanding throughout a thousand or ten thousand years.
Show it to the attendant Zang in the hall:
do not study the Buddha or the Dharma. Discern the past and clarify the present; you must possess the poisonous eye and the solitary gaze. There is no Buddha.
No patriarch; no person, no self. Let forth a will and spirit that covers heaven and earth:

brushing aside the eastern continent with a horizontal body, stretching out one's legs in the western continent of Aparagoyānī, taking a meal in the southern continent of Jambudvīpa, and voiding urine in the northern continent of Uttarakuru.

Speech and silence transcend ordinary sentiment; movement and stillness are utterly distinct from former habits. Even the heavenly deities have no way to offer flowers; humans and ghosts can only stare.
The Gate of Seizing is Non-existent. If one can truly act in this way—unchanging and unmixed—then to casually raise [the mind] is enough:
even a dull blade can kill, and it can also bring life; it can reflect the liver and gallbladder of others, and it can measure a person’s skill.
Taking up even a single word or half-phrase left behind by the ancient masters of the past seventeen hundred years, whether it be a meeting between adepts or an expression...
"Ke-di-chi. Whether it be solemn and secret, or perilous; whether it be mud filled with thorns, or sand devoid of oil;

whether people regard it as a paradox or as something extraordinary—throughout these thousand paths and myriad divergences, amidst startling forms and strange sounds, if one encounters this blunt blade, one will naturally be like Cook Ding disassembling an ox, or like Yi You circling a tree. How could it be otherwise?
How can those who break through walls, leap over fences, carry wooden boards, or are muddled and fragmented be compared to this? Yet even this is not yet enough.
To realize that even my own monastic instruction in this manner is born of parental affection—failing to notice one's child’s ugliness—is what constitutes a monk of true character and spirit.
As the Patriarch said: "When practice and understanding correspond, one is called a Patriarch. He also said: "Those who understand the Way are many; those who walk the Way are few."

Those who are so [rare] are few. To examine and discern matters in this manner—how could it be a trivial matter? Nowadays, there are those who lack any sense of restraint, yet claim to be descendants of the Buddhas and Patriarchs;

having attained some degree of insight, they fail to cultivate self-reflection entirely. It will be difficult for them to avoid the situation where the power of their karma overcomes the power of the Way.
Furthermore, An hopes that you will penetrate the final phrase; it is a barrier directed upward. Be cautious; exert yourself!
This was shown to Chief Seat Feng.

Regarding Chan Master Chenshi of Changsha: once, because a scholar was reading the *Sūtra of the Names of the Thousand Buddhas*, [Chenshi] asked him: "As for the hundreds of thousands of Buddhas, they..."
Upon seeing his name, [the Master] did not know in which land he resided, nor whether he had returned to transform sentient beings.

Ceng asked, "After Cui Hao inscribed upon the Yellow Crane Tower, has the young scholar ever inscribed there himself? He replied, "I have not. Ceng said, "When you have leisure, you should compose an essay there;
it would be well. Such a response could not be made by anyone who was not possessed of great merit and wisdom.
Exhorting oneself with four vows:
First, to never be separated from one's fundamental practice for even a single act of Buddha-work, down to a single recitation or a single prostration.

Second, to never be separated from one's fundamental practice for even a single person, down to exchanging a single word. Third, to never be separated from one's fundamental practice... [The text continues].

There was no interval. He would read a book or write a character; he vowed never to be separated from his fundamental nature for even a single moment of sitting or standing, or a single word of speech or laughter.
When a guest questioned him—
A guest asked, "How can one study the Way without missing the path? He replied, "Excellent question!

Among those in this world who do not participate in the Chan of the Nirvana Hall, it is difficult indeed for them not to miss the path. Nevertheless, those who transmit the Dharma today fill the world."
I practice universal compassion, making no distinction between the pure and the defiled. I expound the Dharma without restriction, delivering those who harbor doubts and slander.
For those who have already advanced, I take it as my heart’s intent to welcome them extensively; for those who are beginners, I make it my business to ensure they may enter with ease.

As for those whose fame is great but whose substance is decayed, or whose eloquence seems plausible but whose reality is false—can it be said that such people do not exist at all? I dare say they are rare. How could my words alone suffice to judge such individuals?

This is weighty; how could I speak of it deeply with you? The guest pressed his request, saying: "If you do not reject words because of the person who speaks them, I shall venture to speak with you at length.
To study the Way and wish to avoid the lament of 'leaping over the north' and 'flying to the north'—first, one must resolve with perfect sincerity.
If one’s aspirations are small and one’s vision narrow, seeking merely to become a virtuous person of this world, it will suffice simply to read..."

To study the books of the sages and worthies of the mundane world and to practice the deeds of the sages and worthies of the mundane world, or to follow and practice the provisional teaching methods of the Tathāgata to assist one’s cultivation and reflection—these will be beneficial and not harmful.
However, if one desires to ultimately realize the unsurpassed, wondrous Way that transcends the world, one must focus exclusively on birth and death.
Only by focusing exclusively on birth and death can one achieve [liberation]; even with extensive learning and a powerful memory like that of Ānanda, such results cannot be attained otherwise.
One question and ten answers, like Xiangyan; a hundred birds carrying flowers, like Niutou;

a thousand fingers circling the seat, like Jia Shan—even these still required setting aside one’s own views to follow others, let alone those who fall below such levels. To not be occupied with birth and death, one must surely cling to knowledge and views;
yet this Way does not belong to knowledge and views. To not be occupied with birth and death, one must surely strive for functional efficacy; yet this Way does not belong to...

As for spiritual power (*guāngnéng*), one should not pursue it for the sake of birth and death. One must surely aspire to the noble and unrestrained (*háofàng*). This Way does not belong to the noble and unrestrained.

To prioritize intellectual views (*zhìjiàn*) and focus on spiritual power while aspiring to the noble and unrestrained—this leads to being either foolish or mad; one becomes a demon or falls outside the Way.

Such good causes that invite evil fruits mostly arise from those who do not specialize in studying the Way for the sake of transcending birth and death. Is this not a single misstep that leads to eternal straying?

Second, one must apply oneself with diligent and thorough effort. Since you have resolved to study the Way out of concern for birth and death, how can you fail to turn within and reflect upon yourself?
Have you truly possessed the great capacity to attain a thousand awakenings upon hearing a single word? If you have not yet attained this, you must investigate a single phrase of the *huatou*.
If it is not penetrated in one day, continue investigating for one day; if it is not penetrated in one month, continue investigating for one month; if it is not penetrated in one year...
If you do not penetrate it in one year, you must penetrate it in a lifetime; if you do not penetrate it in this life, you must penetrate it in a future life.
Only when there is never any regression or change can it be called "authentic practice.

To fixate upon a single phrase of the *huatou* (critical phrase) is the sharp blade that cuts through the dense forest of intellectual views, the compassionate vessel that crosses the bitter sea of birth and death, and the remedy that neutralizes the various poisons.

It is the sacred medicine that enters the heart; it is the guide for those lost in the perilous straits of ten thousand ages. Without accumulating merit, merit naturally accumulates; without severing evil, evil is naturally severed.
Without observing the precepts, one is naturally disciplined; without practicing meditative concentration, one is naturally settled. Without cultivating wisdom, one is naturally wise;

without reciting the names of the Buddhas, one naturally recites them; without chanting the sutras, one naturally chants them; and without seeking rebirth in superior realms, one naturally attains them.
One will naturally be born in superior realms; without seeking many virtuous friends, one will naturally have many virtuous friends. Originally not seeking praise, one likewise cannot be disparaged.
Thus single-mindedly focused, thus diligent, and thus enduring for a long time—even if enlightenment has not yet been realized, this serves as a model for future learners in the present.
In the future, one will surely attain the heart-essence of the Buddhas and Patriarchs. Should name and form [obstruct you]...
In studying the Way within birth and death, one gives rise to peripheral doubts, seeks outside assistance, develops divergent views, and pursues many external distractions.
One dreads hardship and prefers ease; thus, hundreds of delusions converge. How can the resulting failure be described? Third, one must awaken to the truth with absolute certainty.
Since one is dedicated solely to birth and death, one must investigate with single-minded focus until work is exhausted and effort is spent, so that when the time comes, the principle will manifest.
Manifest! When the life-root is severed, the original face appears. One does not doubt birth and death; one does not doubt past and present.

One does not fall into pits or ditches; one does not forcibly act as a sovereign. One does not recognize the spirit-consciousness; one does not sink into a void. One does not engage in artifice or confusion;
one does not enter the circle of false teachers. One does not violate the discernment of the clear-eyed. If one mistakes fish eyes for pearls, one will sleep through one’s own death.
To accept things with superficiality is taken as having great power; to force matters into place is taken as being free from doubt;

to be coarse and reckless is taken as the "great function" of great capacity; and to be muddled and vague is taken as total liberation without remainder. One fails to advance when one ought to advance at the tip of the staff;

one fails to investigate the words and phrases when one should investigate them; one engages in needless analysis when there is no need for it; and one attempts to suppress what must not be suppressed.

To obliterate [the truth] at the very first step of entering the gate, presenting a jumble of heterodox interpretations—this is precisely what is meant by that which "should cause one to weep and shed tears, and sigh deeply.
Is this not of such a nature? Fourth, the lineage of the teacher must be authentic and correct.

Not only must one avoid following deluded masters who lack a true transmission and fabricate their own doctrines, but even when following an unbroken stream of succession, one must examine the actual conduct and realization of those teachers. One must not...
Carrying a broken length of rope, you mistakenly presume to take charge for yourself. Have you missed the point where the Master acted for your sake?

Have you not failed the Master’s deep thrust from behind the head? Have you not clearly penetrated the fundamental principles of the ancestral school? Have you not, through your biased actions, blinded the eyes of others?
Unless a truly authentic master of the lineage comes to strike out the eye at the crown of your head and seize it from you, [you will never realize it].
If you cast aside the talisman behind the elbow, then even if you possess genuine realization, it may suffice for your own liberation; however, if you employ it for others, calamity will arise.

Should your own vision already be biased and your guidance of others likewise erroneous, while you imagine yourself to be vast and open, you are instead like wood meeting water or space meeting space under the blows of the blind staff and the blind shout.
To falsely grasp the Vajra-precious sword and claim to "sever everything" is not reality.
I know that within the treasury of our King there is no such sword. It is like a blind man leading a crowd of blind men; it is a downward course like rivers flowing into the sea.

Perhaps they have entered a realm of petty and trivial matters, becoming tainted by the flavors of false knowledge and evil interpretations. The poison of error has entered their hearts, just as oil permeates flour.
Furthermore, some do not recognize their error and recklessly claim "self-acceptance" (*ziken*), asserting that they do not rely on others' ultimate realization and thus cannot be turned by them.
Others say, "My view is correct; I simply require its practical application. How can such people be worth mentioning?
Fifth, one must be precise and authentic at the very end. Only the final phrase reaches the secure gate; it is like the mystical tortoise.
To carry the diagram [of the dragon] is, of itself, a sign of one’s own impending ruin. To claim to have attained great capacity and great function without having penetrated the final, solid barrier;
or to claim to possess the fodder of one's own true portion without having penetrated the final, solid barrier—among those who do so, there are few who are not coarse, evil, and mad.
Even if one has attained correct awakening without penetrating this barrier, they may still serve as a guide for a time.

Master: If one lacks authentic awakening and does not recognize this critical juncture, it is rare indeed that they would not confuse the ancient masters' process of inquiry and awakening with their subsequent state of doubt.
To claim that what follows awakening is no different from what preceded it, and to point to awakening itself as delusion, is to slander the former sages and mislead future generations.
All this arises from not knowing the ultimate barrier that transcends [the mundane]. How can one not stand in awe? One’s self-benefit is incomplete and one’s benefit for others is insufficient;

all this arises from not penetrating the ultimate barrier that transcends [the mundane]. How can one not be vigilant and strenuous? Sixth: One must ensure that the Path Truth (mārgasatya) is authentic.
Although one’s initial resolve may be authentic, one’s practice may be authentic, one’s realization may be authentic, and one’s spiritual lineage may be authentic, yet at the very end—
Having attained such thorough penetration and correctness, you must further examine for yourself: Are you of the vessel capable of sudden enlightenment and sudden cultivation?
Are you a true *kalyāṇamitra* of the stage of fruition? Have you integrated [all things] into a single whole as swiftly as Xianglin? Do you avoid the error of wandering astray like Yongquan?
Have the outflows of present karma and consciousness been completely purified? Is there unimpededness in every matter? When practice and understanding correspond, this is called...
The Patriarch said: "Try to examine what the standard of our former masters was. Seventh: One must be sincere and authentic for others. One must not bestow any substantial dharma upon them.
One must not deceive people by claiming to have 'expedient means' that help them enter easily. One must not teach people not to investigate the 'dead phrase.
One must insist that people engage in genuine investigation; one must insist that people attain true awakening; and one must insist that after awakening, they reach full realization."

Regarding the pivotal point for ascending, awakening is definitively defined as the realization of one's nature. One must not recklessly attempt to ensnare people by deceiving them regarding their mistaken perceptions;

that is, falsely claiming they have attained "insight" (*kuan*) when they have merely recognized their own delusions, or claiming they have "entered" (*ju*) the Way when they have simply identified the false as true while their thoughts have not yet ceased.
Such actions are intended only to create a temporary bustle at one’s gate, regardless of the subsequent cycle of errors and deceptions that will spread as these heterodox methods run rampant.

When illness breaks out from this source, it is better to cut off one's lineage than to transmit it in a corrupted manner; only then can one be said to be a person who acts with precision and propriety.

If the first six types [of transmission] lack precision, one errs for oneself; if the final type lacks precision, one leads others astray. Good medicine is bitter to the taste, and loyal words are harsh to the ear.
Out of love for your children, I have entreated you and shown this to you in good faith; do not treat these matters lightly when speaking of them to others.
A monk asked about the karmic occasion: "What is the phrase that 'the casket covers heaven and earth'? The Master patted his belly and said, "I can contain tens of thousands of people like you.
The monk pressed further: "What is the phrase that 'cuts off all streams'? The Master said, "It drives you away until there is nowhere left to go."

[The monk] ran off on foot. [The Master] entered [the hall] and asked: "What is the phrase of 'following the waves and chasing the ripples'? The Master said: "I will allow you to stand here for a moment.
The Master asked a monk: "Xuefeng’s story about the tiger—how do you understand it? The monk extended his five fingers and said: "Teeth and claws."

[The Master] uncovered [the bowl] completely. The Master then struck him and further presented this verse: "Throughout my life I have not left the mountain pass; A single word is transmitted through ancient and modern times.
It is difficult for those with clear eyes to comprehend; You must look further upward."
The Master asked a monk, "Bring forth a single phrase regarding the time before your parents were yet born. The monk replied, "An octagonal millstone rolls through the void.
The Master pointed to an incense box and asked, "What is this? The monk hesitated; the Master struck him immediately. The monk was speechless.
The Master said, "In all sincerity, do not act like a child at play."
He asked the hall attendant, "How many Bodhidharma eyes are there in this rice bucket? The attendant was at a loss for an answer.
He asked the kitchen head, "Do the Buddhas of the three periods of time truly preach the Dharma within the flames? The head was likewise at a loss.
The Master pointed to a monk standing nearby and said, "Only this monk can answer such questions," and then he returned to his quarters.
The head gardener asked, "Has the Master’s illness improved? The Master said, "I have never been ill;
what is there to improve or not? The gardener further said, "I am unable to approach the Master. The Master said, "I am in your garden every day."
Tuigan presented this verse on the World-Honored One holding up a flower: A long sword leaning against the sky, its edge exposed; Who would dare approach it once it is drawn forth?
The decrepit Kāśyapa lightly touched it, And blood splattered from his face in profusion. The Master said:

"You see only the sharpness of the awl's tip, but you do not see the squareness of the chisel's head. [The monk] stepped forward and said: "Yet you have been seen through by the Master. The Master faced the wall.
He said, "Who knows this meaning? It makes me remember Master Pang.
A monk asked, "What is it to have a staff and give a staff? The Master said, "The wind and moon of Chang’an penetrate past and present;
which child would walk by groping along the wall? The monk pressed further, "What is it to take away the staff from one who has no staff?"
[Zhuzhangzi]: “How many people have starved to death at the edge of their own rice baskets?
The Master went to the river to visit his relatives. The elder layman Zhang Jinghan came to visit Shifang Monastery. During their conversation, he asked:
“How can one find the root amidst the toil of worldly life? The Master said: “Layman, from where does this question of yours come? The Layman—

[The monk] remained silent. The Master said: "In the past, although the Great Master Yunqi did not preside over the Chan school, his instructions for people to investigate through *chan* (investigation) were extremely precise and appropriate.
He often highly praised the excellence of people's writings. At the end, he would prompt them, saying:
'You must examine from where this radiance flows forth. To fix your gaze upon this is the shortcut to attaining the source.'"
The layman asked, "How should one apply effort? The Master said, "This cannot be done on behalf of you, layman.

One day, the Master entered the storehouse and, pointing to some steamed buns, asked the storekeeper, "I shall not ask about 'drinking dry the Western River,' but try swallowing these two baskets of buns instead.
The storekeeper replied, "I have swallowed them. The Master said, "Then let the assembly eat them."
"What is this? The monk’s answer did not accord with the Master's intent. The Master provided his own response: "One who rejoices shares the joy.
A monk asked, "Who is it that does not take the myriad dharmas as a companion? The Master said: "The desk and the bench."
Yun Jingbi entered for the third time to practice *samādhi*. The following day, he went to the Abbot’s quarters and said, "I have a certain realization.
The Master asked, "Why does the dog have no Buddha-nature? Yun Jingbi struck the Master’s ribs with his fist and said, "Hitherto I have been stuck at Zhaozhou;
today I have uprooted it here before you, Reverend. The Master then pushed him out. The next day he entered again. The Master said, "It is all..."
"When the great earth bursts into flames, what samādhi must one attain so as not to be burned? Jin replied, "I have come specifically to spend the summer retreat here.
The Master then gave a shout. Bi presented a verse, saying: "Perfect as the full moon, Vast as the great void. Throughout kalpas, it has had no surname."

From the beginning, it has been beyond all climbing or grasping. Sages and ordinary beings emerge from this; the ocean of lands rests within it. From beginning to end, there is no change or variation.
Everywhere, it skillfully accords with conditions. The Master said, "Do you understand that shout just now? Bi then stepped out.
The Master returned from Longyuan and asked the attendants, "In the twelve periods of the day, do you see where thoughts arise?
A student stepped forward and said, "Thoughts are fundamentally unobtainable; what more could one seek as their point of origin?
The Master said, "Just now I saw a block of stone with ninety-nine cracks."
While the Master was conversing with a scholar, he said, "You ought to understand that heaven and earth share the same root and all things are one body.
The scholar replied, "How could it be that I do not understand this? The Master asked, "For what reason, then, do you kill living beings and eat their flesh?"
While performing the ritual for the temple repairs, the Master said, "The Old Śākyamuni turns the Great Dharma Wheel upon the grey tiles.
Who can hear it? The assembly remained silent. The Master said, "Look well! Then the Attendant of the Wall (Bìshìsī) performed a prostration and said:
"Please, Preceptor, provide a turning word in response. The Master said, "Bring forth your question. The monk stepped forward and asked, "What is it like regarding that which has been heard?
The Master said, "It fills the void; the palace is without seams. East, west, south, and north—the lunar disc is crimson."
Returning from the riverbank, the Master asked the assembly, "What kind of person has a realm where not a single inch of earth exists?
A monk stepped forward and said, "This is the house style of the Master. The Master said, "How is it that 'not a single inch of earth' is the house style of this mountain monk?"
The monk was unable to answer. The Master spoke on his behalf, saying: "Changzhou, Huzhou, Hangzhou. The monk asked:
"I do not ask about the great earth, mountains, and rivers; what of the matter upon a single hair-tip?
The Master said: "Swallow seven or eight. The monk pressed further: "I do not understand. The Master said: "Spit out two or three."
A monk asked, "What is the meaning of 'the myriad dharmas returning to the One'? The Master said, "Heaven is round and Earth is square. The monk pressed further, "Where does the One return?
The Master said, "Earth is square and Heaven is round."
A monk asked, "Among the hundreds of thousands of Dharma gates and immeasurable subtle meanings, what is the primary meaning? The Master said, "Horizontal sevens and vertical eights.
The monk asked, "What is one's original face? The Master held up a fan and showed it to him, saying, "Do not call this a fan. The monk prostrated.
[The student] bows. The Master says, "A clever monk.
[The student] asks, "When neither the front nor the back is permissible, what is the place of emergence? The Master says, "Go forward to the Buddha Hall."
Later, when he was about to go to the toilet, he asked a monk, "Speak what was there before your parents were born.
The monk made a gesture with his hands as if embracing the world outside and said, "It has never been hidden throughout the entire realm."
The Master said, "The entire world has never been hidden; why then do you lean toward that side? The monk was speechless.
The Master said, "Why not say, 'I point to the east and draw in the west'?"
A monk came for an audience. The Master said, "I have received you from afar, yet I have nothing to offer as a gift; I shall give you these five meditation halls to swallow in one gulp.
The monk stepped forward and said, "There is not an inch of soil in the great earth; what is there to swallow? The Master said, "How many people speak like this?
Even a broom handle deserves thirty blows."
A monk asked, "When a single speck of dust is penetrated and transcended, the thousand worlds shine with brilliance. Why is it that the Ten Sages and Three Worthies do not understand this principle?
The Master said, "Do not concern yourself with those Ten Sages and Three Worthies. Tell me, how does empty space realize it? The monk stepped forward and said:
[The monk] sought empty space but found it utterly unobtainable. The Master said, "Precisely so. [The monk] further asked, "The Master is a great *kalyāṇamitra* (virtuous friend).

The Master said, "I am specifically waiting for you to examine this. As the monk hesitated, the Master said, "Pass straight through ten thousand layers of barriers; do not linger within the blue heavens."
The Master asked the Hall Attendant of Yuanzhengtang, "When will the incense burner attain Buddhahood? The attendant replied, "It has attained Buddhahood long ago.
The Master said, "Last night it was crushed by empty space; do you know this yet? As the monk hesitated, the Master said, "You deceitful liar!"
The Master returned to Yunfeng’an. A member of the attendants’ office met him on the road. The Master said, “You have arrived late;

I shall take these distant mountains ahead and give them to you as a snack. As the attendant was about to deliberate, the Master struck him across the face with his staff and said, “Add one more portion of *kṣaṇa* (offering money).
The attendant replied, “One must not take another person’s property and treat it as a personal gift. The Master said, “Indeed not.”
Not only can they not digest the monetary offerings, they cannot even digest their morning refreshments.
A verse on an ancient precedent cites Zhaozhou asking Nanquan, "Where do those who know go? Nanquan replied, "To the donor before the mountain."
Jia went out as a water buffalo. Zhou paid his respects and said, "Thank you for your instruction, Master. Quan said, "Last night at the third watch, the moon shone through the window."

The spring colors within the snow are seen upon the tips of the plum branches; the song of the yellow birds is heard, their spirit fresh and new. Their spirit is fresh and new—who knows that the yellow birds laugh so often?
Tell this to those who are elegant and discerning: from this day forth, their eyes shall be as clear as the azure sky, and the fragrance of the blossoms shall be as sweet as last year’s.

Case: Chan Master Guizong Chang was formerly a fellow practitioner of Nanquan. One day, as they were about to part ways, while Nanquan was brewing tea, he asked, "Hitherto, we have discussed and deliberated upon phrases and sayings; both of us already know them.
But if someone were to ask you about the ultimate matter hereafter, what would you say? Guizong replied, "This very patch of ground is excellent for building a hermitage. Nanquan said:
"Setting aside for now the matter of building a hermitage, what is the ultimate point? How is it? Zong struck over the tea kettle and immediately rose.
Quan said, "Brother, you have finished your tea; I, Puyuan, have not yet drunk. Zong said, "For one who speaks such words, even a drop of water would be difficult to digest."

The guest remains a guest from beginning to end; the host remains a host from beginning to end. Each brandishes the skill of its concealed point with a golden hammer—a technique not transmitted from father to son, yet shared by brothers of the same breath.
Mist blends harmoniously upon the jade balustrade; in the depths of the willows hanging over the imperial garden, the birds dwell.
Case: Grand Master Lu Xun said to Nanquan, “Master Zhao is truly extraordinary; he understands that ‘Heaven and earth share the same root with me;
the myriad things are one body with me. Nanquan pointed to a peony flower and said, “Grand Master, when people of this age see this single stalk of flowers, it is like being in a dream.”
A single branch of blossoms brings forth tenfold spring; having thoroughly perceived the source, one holds it in fresh appreciation. How admirable is the Great Officer who lost his nose!
Together we come to laugh and swagger with those of antiquity and today.
Case: A monk asked Master Shushan, "What is the Dharma-body? Shushan said, "A withered stump.
The monk asked, "What is that which is above the Dharma-body? Shushan said, "Not a withered stump."
With one punch, he topples the Yellow Crane Tower; with one kick, he overturns the Parrot Isle. When there is spirit, he adds to that spirit;
where there is no elegance, he is elegant nonetheless.

Case: A monk asked the Patriarch Ciming, "How is it when one seeks stillness amidst the clamor? He replied, "My head rests upon a hemp sack. This was how he caused Wufeng Yang to awaken and enter [the Way].
His sandals were worn through and his feet cracked; he blocked the gateway of the mouth and extended the broad, long tongue. He was like a bell suspended in its frame.
Small and large, slow and fast—strike it and there is a response. The entire body is of metal and stone; three mysteries in a snap of the fingers.
Four views of speech and silence: easy to know, difficult to comprehend; easy to see, difficult to recognize. A lotus boat on Lake Laṅkā; clouds parting to reveal Tuṣita Heaven.
A Poem Presented to Chan Practitioner Luitan, Also Sent to Layman Tiangyi Dingli:
The three peaks rise in formation, piercing the heavens; Though the mountain pass is opened, white clouds remain continuous. A soaring wild goose transmits [this message] to the human world.
Faith. Difficult to rely upon, the stone walls have passed beyond the separate stream;
having entered Qingshan, the style of his reclusive life remains as it was. Before the Hall of Dharma, wild grass grows; do not say that the precincts can remain silent and empty.
Ji: "From of old, few have traveled this path. Shi-tu'an Chongzi:
"Dwelling at Yushan, there are many mountains;
which are more secluded? At Yushan, two bays gather deep azure. Chengjiang: "There is water in the Chengjiang; which is more abundant?"
Sentiments. Before and behind Mount Yu, the waters are level. In those days, my person was as tranquil as water. At night, I followed the bright moon through the deep forest.
I intended to build a "pushing-open-the-curtain" hut on Mount Hua; a small boat, following its whim, could have ventured deep within.

Now you must first decide whether to stay or go for me. Plant many yams on the vacant ground beside the hermitage. Our sentiments of world-forgetfulness are the same, both yours and mine. [The iron sickle for the thatch...]
The pickaxe vibrates with the preceding wind; those who have attained it do not reside within the gate, which is like a marketplace. I still recall the old man from years past who faced the wall.

To a Zen practitioner: when you see the Way, who is there to cultivate it? Forget the mountains and dwell well in the mountains. The snow is deep, the mountain hut is ancient; with a hundred patches upon one body, there is leisure.
Furthermore:
Beneath the layered cliffs, amidst deep and imposing thatched huts, there dwells a recluse who stands in the snow and eats of ice.
Furthermore:
Fine mountains are like paintings; paintings are like mountains. Amidst villages of crimson leaves, one wanders idly with staff and hat. Seeing peach blossoms bloom, a smile arises;
once more, beyond the clouds, I shall seek the thatched gate.
Guarding the stupa while cherishing the past for many years, my physical form is like yellowed leaves. On this day, as I wander about, with whom can I find accord?
Wearing hempen robes and straw sandals, subsisting on breath alone, I call out from before the Elephant Bone Cliff: "Come back!"
I sing of my reflections: at the peak of a thousand peaks, a pointed-roofed hut; Grass mats and a wooden bed, with a single brazier of fire. In thirty years, not a single thing has occurred;
Where among all quarters could one seek out this hidden man?
Quiet Night Thoughts Moonlight on every branch and leaf; Wind, sparse here and dense there. Who walks with me along the flowing stream? Leaning on my staff by the eastern stone bridge.
Inscribed on the Wall.
The stars are high and the moon is bright; rain from the pines fills my robes. Sitting upright on the western ridge, I am so absorbed that I forget to return home.

Spontaneously inscribed: The moon soaks the ten thousand mountains in cold; The wind sounds through the myriad trees with clarity. A single bark from a dog outside the village— Someone is traveling on the road.

A temple with mossy walls in a desolate mountain retreat; a solitary and chilly thatched cottage with no one within. After the rain, I gaze out at the vast expanse; fresh tiger tracks appear in the courtyard mud.
I boil spring water.
How should one extensively cultivate the practice of making offerings? Upon the hundred-boiling clear spring, the Buddha appears; at dawn, vying for beauty, they enter through the gate.
Orioles sing among the ancient trees, their calls like many a *brahma*-sound.
Facing the Mirror (At Huashan Aranya):
Facing the mirror, I am not who I was of old; Touching my heart, my resolve is renewed. How is it that a single branch from a forest Shelters this body of mine through snow and frost?
Winter Days with Regret (Jingshan Luting):
Pine seeds fall upon the empty steps; Starving birds enter the gate. Beneath a thousand-foot precipice, How many plum trees are in bloom?
Gazing toward Mount Taihang, three thousand paths stretch across the vast wilderness; ten thousand people dwell in lofty seclusion. Those stones by the ice from years past await my unreturned body.
Dwelling by boat (three times, then the bamboo grove).

Vast and drifting, cold smoke amidst ancient trees; solitary and suspended, light sails upon snowy waves. It lies right within the ordinary path of travel—far beyond sight, across ten thousand ravines and a thousand crags.
And again:
A single leaf, the waters of a thousand streams; three bowls, the frost of the sixth month. Not rowing my boat when meeting people, I lie high upon my bed facing the slanting sun.

Returning to my thatched cottage in winter, I hide my form while eating cypress seeds; casting my gaze afar, I watch the plum blossoms. Where is the carefree traveler who comes with me to water the ancient fallow fields?
Along the road to Jining, thatched cottages line the stream and trees stand at the eaves; chickens and dogs dwell in harmony in this village by the waters.
The legacy of peaceful governance from the Yu and Xia dynasties endures, as the lands south and north of the river share the same groves and gardens.
Reading the Poetry of Bai Juyi, I Recall Koubing (While Traveling by Boat to Dongchang):
Upon the pond is a small boat; within the boat is an empty folding chair. My heart has long since forgotten the world, yet I am ashamed that I have not yet made the world forget me.
Moored overnight at Jiama Camp, boats on the water are as dense as weaving threads. Human affairs are like the plantain tree; in non-action and desirelessness, who shall wander with me in leisure?
Moderation in food.
Lodging one's form within heaven and earth, eating and drinking merely to sustain the vital breath—such a person dwells in carefree equanimity, clearly realizing this spirit of detachment.

At the southern ravine of Longyuan, sitting by the moon beneath pines of three long and four short spans; upon a stone platform of seven high and eight low elevations. As I sit, the evening sun rests upon the trees; it is time to return.
The moon sets behind the western peak;

my midday nap is like that of a wooden puppet. When the drum ceases, the ropes also come to rest. Whether mountain monks are in motion or stillness, I ask you, all you pillars of dew: what do you say?

Inviting friends into the Way at Jingxi is precisely when the thousand mountains are ablaze with red leaves. Rubbing my hands upon the stone wall, I am moved to compose this verse. Throughout a hundred years, how many flavors can one truly savor from chewing wax?
Let us share the chrysanthemums at the foot of the pine tree, still dripping with dew.

On the walls of the High Ancestor’s sleeping hall, waterfalls hang from the head of the bed; long moss-clad garments grow upon the stupa’s summit. Once settled here, one never enters again; it is only upon reaching this lofty cold that one truly knows.
Addressing the assembly:

Who shares this ten-thousand-li clear sky? The flowers and willows of the third month vie for the traveler's gaze. While the young nobles sleep drunk upon the fragrant grass, how can they compare to those who rinse their mouths with stones and pillow their heads upon flowing streams?
I possess a single leaf of a lotus boat; within it, the sands of the city and the kalpas of mustard seeds are fully contained. Singing aloud, I smash the spittoon;
children emerge and submerge in the vast flood. Dwelling among the mountains.
With not a single concern in my breast, I sit idly all day long. Rising from sleep, I rub my belly; between mountains and waters, I pace with high strides, ascending the peaks to their very summit.
My steps begin from here; though the gentleman’s aspirations are far-reaching, the journey begins from what is near.
I urge the supervisor to establish a retreat and return to the mountain;
within these mountains there is a fine moon, suitable for gazing upon throughout the night. Within these mountains there is a pleasant breeze, where one may lay aside their robes and linger at ease.

The spring murmurs as a thousand peaks fall silent; the pines are still, their single wave cold. Throughout the long day, birds call to one another; in the clear autumn, insects hum of their own accord.
One who understands the melody of the purple mushrooms finds lofty trees upon the tiered ridges. Buried alive beside broken walls, for a thousand ages they look up to the golden lilies.
Ah, the pheasant of Shiliang! Drinking from the snow and feasting on the clouds. At this time, I have composed these lines impromptu:
Over the years, my spirit has gradually returned; in old age, I especially know the leisure of days and months. With full meals and peaceful sleep, there is not a single [care].
The Ritual: Striking the wooden mallet, follow the assembly to view the autumn mountains.
An Inscription on a Rock at Chinqiu Terrace:
The flowing water in the mountains is silent and soundless; a flower blooms upon a withered tree—a spring of its own. Who, arriving here, understands this?
Severed! From the red furnace, a portion of the ten-thousand-year ice is taken.
On the second month of the Gengxu year, inscribed on the wall at Qingshan:
"The countenance is distinct; it is present throughout the entire world. Yet here, in this very place, one receives profound grace. At the third watch under the moon, lingering with hesitation."
Standing here, it is as if I were again attending to his whisk and handkerchief those many years ago.
At the Ching-shan Dust-Waving Terrace (one of the "Ten Poems on Dharma Aid" recorded by my predecessor, bearing this name), I would often sit alone at the foot of the pines;
the rain of flowers did not require planting. I recall in the past, while attending him on a distant peak, though he spoke no word, his voice was like thunder.

Inscribed on the Wall, Gengxu (Three Poems) Originally but a cautious monk seeking self-enlightenment, Content with ample food and peaceful sleep, I have no other ability. To repay my debt of gratitude and honor my ancestors, I emulate the sagely and wise;
In this small room, I burn incense while cherishing the ancients.
A single bowl of frost-flower blossoms, a half-mat of drifting clouds; Without seeking, without joy, and without anger. At the third watch, facing the moon, he sits by the opened door;
How shameful is the one who burns incense and stands in attendance.

Reclining against the green mountains, I dine upon white clouds; the sound of the stream and the songs of birds accompany me through morning and evening. In the empty courtyard, I plant orchids and fragrant herbs in the available spaces;
with my doors sealed and no path for entry, I am beyond both resentment and favor.

Rolling up the curtain, I look out upon the scene; I am struck by its extraordinary beauty. What intention could have placed this entire body within it? Speak these words to my companions dwelling among crags, wood, and stone:
from time to time, cast your gaze wide to recognize the clouds and pines.
Duluo Garden After Rain (Two Poems) A stream surges with silver pheasants and jade dragons;
one can imagine it was here that the name "Frost Flower" was first conceived. Walking to the upper terrace, I forget all need for medicine;
my attendants labor in vain as they urge me to rest again and again.
The Pillow-Stream Stone atop the Pillow-Stream Terrace: those who arrive are taught that it is too late. A flock of egrets flies like snow across a thousand ravines;
a great bell is struck, its sound like thunder across ten thousand mountains.
Patrolling the Quarters at Da-igak (Gui-chu, Before the Lantern Festival):
Flowers fill the cold courtyard, the moon fills the forest; The patrol of the quarters is not yet half-finished, and it is nearly three o'clock. Do not lift the curtain to enter the gate for now;
I cherish the sound of the water flowing before this pavilion.
Presented to Master Hu at the Huan River:

Our bond of true friendship extends from the rivers to the seas; in you, I behold an ancient sage. Your sincere heart is like the moon across a thousand li, and your clear vision is like the bright sun upon a mountain.
Inscribed on a Wall at Chuzhou:
Pale yellow and faint green brush the sparse breeze; Everywhere the willows hang, suiting my indolence. I have found a small boat as large as a melon seed;
A single sail drifts and floats amidst the waters and clouds.
In my fondness for the willows by the guest hall, none equals mine; I stroke them as I pass the years. The guest hall forgets its solitude, for this single tree happens to hang over the eaves.
I open the window.
The sound of the wind and the sound of the rain—every sound enters the ear. The colors of the flowers and the colors of the grasses—every hue is subtle and exquisite.
Regarding your letter, I once again look up to you with deep respect, Minister Tingcheng.
Every place is the layperson’s bodhimanda; every thing is the layperson’s right Dharma-eye; every matter is the layperson’s bodhisattva practice;

every step is the layperson’s nāga-samādhi. Thus, one causes the twelve periods of the day not to be driven by the twelve periods, and turns all objective realms so as not to be turned by them. Such a person is a true seeker of the Way. If there is light in even a single place...
It is not yet transparently liberated. At one time, light is not transparently liberated; this means that one's fundamental portion is not transparently liberated.

One must, at every moment, turn toward the time before one’s parents were born, severing all thought and remaining without dependence. When this is constant and subtle, the time will come for the Way to be perfected.
Only then, with a clear and cool eye, will one realize that everywhere is the site of Bodhi, every object is the Eye of the True Dharma, and every affair is Bodhi.

Every step of the bodhisattva practice is the nāga-samādhi. It causes the twelve periods of the day not to be driven by the twelve periods, and turns all objects of perception so that one is not turned by them.
These words do not deceive people. The light of the Layman’s mind is constantly focused upon the Tianmu Peak;
the wisdom-nature of the Layman is unclouded throughout past and present; and the supreme conduct of the Layman firmly establishes the Dharma banner. With this reply.
[The Master] did not perceive the thread by thread.
He answered the three questions posed by the layman Wang Taiqing:
"It is easy to be a person, but it is difficult to become a true man. I venture to ask about the way of being a man. The Master said: "What you do not desire for yourself..."
"Do not bestow [this] upon others. A question was asked: "What is knowing birth? What is knowing death? The Master said: "Knowing where one comes from is knowing birth;
knowing where one goes to is knowing death. A question was asked: "At the moment of departure, when the mind is not inverted and the consciousness is not distracted, where does one grasp hold?

Only in this way can one fully comprehend birth and transcend death; only then can one exit death and enter birth. What is meant by "comprehending birth and transcending death"?
It is like the great void of space, which existed before heaven and earth were born and will not age after heaven and earth have passed. What is meant by "exiting death and entering birth"?
It is like the great ocean: when the sun shines, its brilliance arises; when the wind comes, the waves stir. Reaching this state, one comes and goes.
He is sovereign. Life and death are not two. Furthermore, there are two ways to maintain mastery at the time of departure.

This constitutes the gathering through "sameness of purpose. Without boarding the vessel of the Tathāgata’s vows, by what means could one be rescued? Generally, in all practice, one must measure oneself and measure the Dharma.

At that time, a woman in the house was in the midst of a difficult labor, and mother and child had not yet been separated. The elder said, "Gautama’s disciple, you are a most holy one;
what dharma do you possess that can alleviate the hardships of childbirth? The Venerable One replied, "I have only recently entered the Path and am not yet aware of this dharma.
I shall wait to ask the World-Honored One and return to inform you. Upon his return, he related the matter in detail to the Buddha. The Buddha told Aṅgulimāla:
"Go quickly and report: 'I have followed the Dharma of the Worthy and Holy Ones; I have never killed a living being.
Aṅgulimāla obeyed the Buddha’s words and went swiftly to inform her. Upon hearing this, his wife gave birth at that very moment. The Master said:

"From antiquity to the present, there have been many who have taken up and discussed this case, yet not a few have misunderstood it. Tonight, Longxi will simply point it out for you: The heavens are vast and blue."
The wilds are vast and boundless; the wind blows through the grass, revealing cattle and sheep. You monks, do you understand? If not, let me say it once more:
The waters overflow and the sky opens over the embankment; flowers fall to fill Long Creek. Wild ducks follow the ebbing tide; as the sun rises, the variegated clouds hang low.
The assembly prostrated themselves; the Master threw down his staff and rose.
Evening *zhan*. The Master said, "The myriad dharmas return to the One. To what place does the One return? Hehe! The student has his own interest;
the Master also has his own interest. With a single sweep of his whisk, he returned to his quarters.
Evening *can*. The Master said: "The phrase obtained before the mountain gate is to be deliberated upon within the meditation hall.
Once you have entered the abbot’s quarters, there is no need to raise it again. Why? Because Tianxi will not let you down."
Evening *can*. The Master said: "The bamboo window opens at night; the moon is bright and the frost is thick. The wild geese enter the clouds; the little mouse scurries through the millstone.
As for you, Great Assembly—walking, standing, sitting, or lying down—tell me, what is this? After a long silence, he laughed loudly and said:
"A bald-headed Turk riding a camel."
An early morning assembly on the Double Ninth Festival. The Master said: "This morning is the ninth day of the ninth month. The monkey climbs the tree and performs somersaults;
turning right, then left; turning left, then right. A master of hand displays his skill among masters of hand. Hehe! Elder Tianxi is truly no good."
Morning Assembly. The Master said: "The flavor of salt in water; the glue and indigo within color. *Du!* I thought the morning star was my own eyes.
With a mouth all over one's body, to whom can one speak? One would drain the entire Milky Way to wash away that iron nail."
Evening *zhan* (informal assembly) in the hall. After the questions and answers were finished, the Master said: "Ajita, why do you smile? A snake pierces through a rat's burrow;
Puhua passes by shaking his bell. Alas! This young fellow’s foot has stepped on a prurient sore. Drawing near the fire, blood stains one's clothes.
Salt and vinegar—old stock. Someone says: 'The old master is kind. If there is tea, please drink it. There is none."
"Tea with boiling water is best. *Cluck.* "Hanxian and Qin Gao rode the red carp; Wang Xizhi wrote characters to exchange for goslings.
After a long while, he said, "Return to the hall."
The morning assembly on the nineteenth day of the sixth month. The Master said: "Red dust rises upon the road; white waves fly across the river. He took up his staff and said:
"Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva arrives! Those with eyes, come forward; those without eyes, step back.

A monk stepped forth, performed a prostration, and as he was about to return to his place, the Master struck him, saying: "It is not so; it must be so. After a long pause, he struck the floor with his staff.
The staff-bearer said: "To prostrate and then return to one's place is truly laughable; thus it is not attained, yet it is attained thus. The maṇḍala points to the ground as a spring;
the great-headed barbarian hammers through the iron mountain. If you understand this, you walk like a dragon and stride like a tiger;
if you are merely muddled, consider how the World-Honored One ascended the seat in silence and Ānanda sent the bhikṣus away. Looking left and right, he said: 'Half...'"
At the Mountain Temple, he went to the Three Tianzhu Shrines and struck them all at once with his staff, dispersing them.
On a snowy night during the evening session, the Master said: "Drink bitter tea and speak plain words; who cares whether it is Buddha-dharma or not?
When Fengyi cuts through the dragon-river silks, the withered willows and plum blossoms are in spring everywhere. Heh! Under the moon, green frost-traces arise."
The Well. Through the lattice window, jade-like flakes fly without a trace; when the wind ceases at the branch tips, they turn to welcome the cold.
Cold people are like birds perching, finding no rest; days grow short and nights long—who perceives this first? A flickering wick, a mournful horn. *Du!
Du!* The Three Barriers of Huanglong; Xiangyan’s Single-Legged Stool.
An early morning assembly on the Winter Solstice. The Master said: "In a cold place, I dreamed of a foolish monk who said:
'Last night at the third watch, during the hour of Zi-Gui, the maples and pines across the valley asked for the pine branches. Where does the snow flying from all sides come from?
The cold plum blossoms lower their heads and smile. He then cried out loudly: 'The Patriarch! The Patriarch! What kind of season is this now?'"

The assembly said, "Let us see. A monk nearby prepared to answer; the Master struck him. Another monk stepped forward and asked, "When one captures a fierce tiger alive and seizes a savage dragon alive, what is it like when such a person arrives?
The Master said, "The laws of the state are like a furnace. [The monk] pressed further: "If one suddenly encounters a golden-scaled fish that has slipped through the net, what then?
The Master said, "Be careful with fire and candles. [The monk] pressed further: "Driving the plowman’s ox, seizing the hungry man’s..."
"Human food—this is not yet the upward-pointing tongs and hammer. What is the upward-pointing tongs and hammer? The Master rebuked him, saying, "Guest from Yangzhou.
The monk hesitated; the Master said, "The assembly, return to the hall."
Evening informal discourse on the anniversary of [the Master’s] passing. The assembly gathered. The Master raised his staff and said, "Is this me? Is this not me? The assembly was at a loss.
The Master cast it down and retired to his quarters.
On the morning of the eighth day of the fourth month, the Master entered the hall for formal discourse and said:
"It has been handed down from antiquity that Śākyamuni Buddha was born today. I do not know whether this is true or not; let me speak of it for you all to examine.

In Xingzi County within Nankang Prefecture, outside Huangmei County, lies Yifeng City—this is the realization of Elder Sen. After a long silence, he asked: "Is the guest master here? The assembly remained silent.
He replied, “I am here. He asked again, “Have the assembly inside and outside recited their morning liturgy? They replied, “We have.
The Master then entered his quarters.
Seeing that many patients were merely pursuing the conditions of suffering, the Master pointed this out, saying: "No! No! No! Illness is the excellent medicine for sentient beings.
When I was still in the secular world, I nearly died of an illness. In the midst of my confusion and distress, I suddenly heard the sound of drums and horns;

only then did I realize that the source of the illness does not come from elsewhere. Thereupon, I resolved to leave the household life, saying: 'The drum and horn clearly pierce the needle of poison. Suddenly—"
Sever the heart of attachment. To die and come back to life—how truly laughable! Even stones and clods of earth are all true companions.
I say to you all: recognize the cause of illness; let us all cast away this dream-body. *Tut! Tut!* If one does not become Vimalakīrti, where shall one seek Mañjuśrī?
A monk asked about the karmic conditions: "What is the mysterious path of the birds? The Master said: "White clouds fly up; red leaves fall. The monk pressed further:
"When a person who masters both civil and martial arts comes, how do you provide for them? The Master said: "I do not permit the drinking of wine or the eating of meat. The monk pressed further.
[The student] asked: "When false teachings are difficult to support, what then? The Master said: "How could such a principle exist? [The student] further asked: "What is the Eye of the True Dharma?
The Master said: "Morning and evening. [The student] further asked: "By what means does one become a person of great capacity? The Master said: "Rice. [The student] further asked:
"What is its great function? The Master said, "Time. The student asked, "How can one act within the realm of different species?

The Master said, "Scales have large and small measures; weights have light and heavy degrees. The student asked, "What is it like when doubt has not yet subsided? The Master said, "When a fish is exhausted, its tail turns red;
when a person is exhausted, their head turns white."
A fellow practitioner asked, "Does the Head Seat truly have seen the Old Man? Is this so? The Master said, "It is. The practitioner asked, "Is there anything extraordinary about it?
The Master said, "Few are those who strike the ice; many are those at Chongfu."
A monk entered the room and requested the Master to resolve his doubts. The Master said, "Master Guiguzi is not at home.
The monk said, "Is there no expedient means? The Master said, "Go back and break tiles yourself by the gate."
A monk asked, "What is the pure Dharma-body? The Master said, "Everyone is working together carrying mud. The monk said, "Why do I not understand?
The Master said, "There is the steward here. The monk asked, "What is the discourse that transcends the Buddhas and patriarchs?"
The Master said, "Practice in accordance with the teaching.
The monk said, "Niu Tou has preached both horizontally and vertically, yet he did not know the pivot. What is this pivot?"
The Master said, "Stop. When the monk hesitated, the Master said, "Go.
A monk asked, "What is the wondrous song that does not touch the tongue? The Master said, "Rarely do we meet one who understands.
The monk asked, "What is the dead snake startled out of the grass? The Master said, "Watch over your life-force. The monk asked, "What is the iron saw dancing? The Master said, "Go."
The Master said, "A dull duck hearing thunder. The monk asked, "What is the 'chanting of the withered bone by one who understands the needle'?
The Master said, "Be careful not to talk in your sleep."
A monk asked, "In the midst of constant clamor and turmoil all day long, what is the Immovable Honored One? The Master said, "When the weather is clear, walk quickly.
As the monk prepared to offer further words, the Master said, "Clapping hands and beating one's breast!"
A monk asked, "When [the wind] comes from the four quarters and eight directions, what then? The Master said, "The stone horse before the gate has its hooves reaching the heavens.
A monk asked, "When the langur monkey hangs by its horns, what then? The Master said, "It makes me laugh."
A monk asked, "All water is of one kind; why is the sea salty and rivers fresh? The Master said, "Do not defile it with excrement and urine.
The monk requested further instruction, saying, "Without using even half an inch of rope, how can one get out of a deep well? The Master said, "Fortunately, you encountered Tianxi.
The monk pressed on, saying, "It seems you have lost a great advantage. The Master said, "Look at your own perversity. The monk said, "I beg the Master for a method."
“Convenient,” the Master said. A monk asked, “What is the mystery within mysteries? The Master said, “The days grow long and the nights grow short.”
A monk asked, "The Buddha-mind is compassionate everywhere; why did the Great Being Avalokiteśvara not go to the kingdom of Goryeo?
The Master said, "Thank you for the steamed buns and noodles."

Returning from a mountain excursion, he asked a monk, "The 'poison-dust drum' kills everyone who hears it; why does the striker not die? The monk offered a response that did not accord with the truth.
The Master then presented this verse: "The leather bag upon the mountain has bought another boat; When will the clear breeze and bright moon ever cease?
If you wish to know the matters of advance and retreat, survival and ruin, Simply ask Zheng Huazhou upon his return."
A monk asked, “In the past, Zhaozhou exposed the old woman of Mount Tai; ultimately, where does he reside? The Master said, “Heavenly Opening River.
The monk pressed further, “I do not know where this falls. The Master said, “To the east of the refectory.
The monk pressed further, “I beg the Master’s compassion to speak directly. The Master said, “Zhaozhou has two eyes; the old woman has one tongue; Mount Wutai.”
[The Master] went up. At Jiu-lu-ling, do not rest.
A monk asked, "What is 'first illumination, then function'? The Master said, "Linji is coming! As the monk hesitated, the Master gave a shout.
The monk asked, "What is 'first function, then illumination'? The Master grabbed him and said, "Speak! Speak! The monk was at a loss. The Master—

He then feigned opening [the door]. The monk asked, "What is 'illumination and function occurring simultaneously'? The Master slapped him and said, "This is not something a donkey can endure. The monk asked, "What is 'illumination and function not occurring simultaneously'?

The Master said, "You ignorant fellow who does not know pain or itch! The monk gave a shout, and the Master said: [Note: This dialogue is from the *Wumen Kuan* (The Gateless Barrier), Case 17. The "Master" is Wumen.]
"Try another shout. The monk shouted again. The Master struck him.
The monk asked, "What is formless nirvana? The Master said, "The five-li pavilion; the ten-li post station.
The monk said, "Why do I not understand? The Master said, "Ahead of the donkey; behind the horse."
A monk asked, "What is Yunmen’s 'looking in the mirror and winking'? The Master extended his hand and said, "There! The monk hesitated;
the Master said, "Finished. The monk asked again; the Master said, "Go!"
A monk asked, "What is it like when [the tiger] comes right at one's face? The Master slapped him immediately as he spoke.
The monk asked, "What is the Buddha-dharma of Mount Daxiong? The Master said, "The white-jawed beast sits in the middle of the road. The monk said, [nothing further].
"Is there also a skillful means? The Master said, "Upādhyāya, do not walk at night.
A monk asked, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West? The Master said, "The people of the South are thin; the people of the North are fat."
A monk asked, "Setting aside for a moment the place where all Buddhas emerge, what is the place where you, Master, establish yourself and sustain your life?
The Master said, "You have leaped well. The monk shouted. The Master said, "Why? As the monk hesitated, the Master struck him and sent him away.
A monk asked, "For what reason do you not light the road lamp? The Master said, "Go ahead and stumble about as you please.
A monk asked, "When one enters the gate and immediately shouts or strikes, what is the meaning? The Master said, "The Patriarch is behind you."
A monk asked, "When one does not admire the thousand sages and does not prize one's own spiritual nature, what then? The Master said, "In that case, you do not even observe the five precepts.
The monk said, "Why did the ancients refuse to dwell here when they reached this point? The Master drew a line. The monk gave a shout.
The Master said, "A fine shout! The monk hesitated; the Master struck him.
A monk asked, "After the golden lock is broken, what then? The Master said, "The crown of the head touches the ground.
Another monk asked, "Piling up cushions and sitting in meditation—what do you seek? The Master covered his nose and said, "Get out!
The monk stood bewildered. The Master said, "Come here. As the monk approached, the Master said, "The Three-Yellow Pill is good."
A monk asked, "How is the ancestral vehicle of the patriarchs to be transmitted? The Master said, "The sun rises in the east; the moon sets in the west.
The monk said, "If that is so, then everyone has their share. The Master said, "Zhang Zhi riding a horse is like riding a boat."
A fellow practitioner asked, "What is the house style of the Head Seat? The Master said, "No fences, no walls.
The practitioner asked, "What if a thief suddenly arrives? The Master said, "It depends on you to search for him."
A monk asked, "Ultimately, what is the Buddha? The Master said, "If it cannot be broken through, burn it.
A monk asked, "What is the mark of the Brahma-voice? The Master said, "The hall steward does not act with finicky precision."
A monk asked, "What is it like when the tips of arrows meet? The Master said, "Stand over there. The monk shouted. The Master smiled.
As the monk hesitated, the Master said, "Truly excellent is the meeting of arrow-tips!"
A monk asked, "How can one turn oneself back into the mountains, rivers, and the great earth? The Master said, "Last night there was fine autumn rain.
The monk asked, "What is your way of benefiting others? The Master said, "Fool! Fool! The monk pressed further, "Without falling [into categories]..."
"How do you express the phrase 'ancient and modern'? The Master said, "Those who hold office for long will surely become wealthy.
He further asked, "Before the Seven Buddhas appeared in the world, where did they practice? The Master said, "Do not employ those who cause suspicion."
A monk entered the room to seek instruction, asking: "The Heart Sutra says, 'Gate gate pāragate pārasaṃgate. What is the meaning of this? The Master said: "Confucius was born in Shandong;

his literary talent is known through all time. When a Great Officer holds sway over the world, even from a humble thatched-roof house, three high ministers may emerge. The monk said: [I do not understand.]
The student did not know where to apply himself. The Master said, "From Wei returning to Lu.
A monk asked, "When one person gives rise to the truth and returns to the source, the empty space of the ten directions all vanishes.
Why then is the mud behind the abbot’s quarters never finished? The Master said, "A ghost eats rancid steamed buns."
A monk asked, “Since you are one who repays kindness, why do you not recognize Mount Jinchē? The Master said, “Watch you circle around me.
The monk gave a shout. The Master said, “When will this ever end? The monk hesitated. The Master said, “Do you still resent me?
He then struck him.
A monk asked, "Do the mountains, rivers, and the great earth have any faults? The Master said, "A toothless man beating a gong.
A monk asked, "What is it like when things suddenly arise and suddenly perish? The Master said, "They are neither ghost-lamps nor fireflies."
A monk asked, "What is the samādhi of Avalokiteśvara? The Master said, "Last night the child cried. The monk asked, "What is the samādhi of Mañjuśrī?
The Master said, "Kicking a brocade ball in broad daylight. The monk asked, "What is the samādhi of Samantabhadra?
The Master said, "Losing the felt bundle in the temple of Lord Bao."
A monk asked, "When both mind and Buddha are forgotten, what then? The Master said, "Who says such a thing? As the monk hesitated, the Master shouted him out.
Another monk asked, "Amidst the vast turmoil of the dust, how does one discern the master? The Master said, "There is too much sand in the rice. The monk said, "Thank you for the instruction, Master.
The Master said, "Do not chew it up in confusion."
A monk asked, "When there is no dreaming and no conceptualization, where is the host? The Master said, "The assembly will laugh at you.
The Master asked a monk, "Where is your native place? The monk replied, "Hepu County. The Master said, "Bring forth the bright pearl and show it to me.
The monk had no reply. The Master said, "I suspect you are a newly ordained monk."
The Master asked the presiding lecturer, "Kongō, stop for a moment. What do you call a sutra? The lecturer hesitated; the Master then smiled.
The lecturer asked, "What is a sutra? The Master called out, "Dharma Master! The lecturer responded, "Yes. The Master said, "A fine presiding lecturer indeed.
The lecturer pointed to his tea cup and asked, "Is there a Zhaozhou here? The Master replied, "It cannot be lifted by a spoon."
The Master asked, "All these complications are like a tile used for knocking on a door. Now that the door has opened, where is the tile?
The monk was at a loss. The Master said, "What a pity—seven bays of the monks' hall!"
A monk asked, "What character is it that does not admit of a single stroke? The Master said, "A large nose and a heart free of poison.
A monk asked, "I do not ask about what was before birth; what is the place where Zhaozhou exposed the old woman?

The Master said, "When one has eaten their fill, they play with their chopsticks. The monk pressed further, "I am not like that. The Master said, "If you want to defecate, go over there. The monk departed.
[The monk] remained silent. The Master said, "Go quickly back to the hall.
A monk asked, "How is it when one has a staff and gives a staff? The Master said, "Clever indeed. The monk said [nothing].
"What is it like to take away a staff from one who has no staff? The Master said, "You foolish fellow.
A monk asked, "When everything before one's eyes has been swept clean, what then? The Master said, "What more would you see in a dream?"
The monk prostrated. The Master asked, "What is your name? The monk replied, "Nanshan. The Master said, "When the clouds rise over Nanshan, why does it rain on Beishan?
The monk was speechless. The Master said, "In spring, there are not three days of clear weather."
A monk asked, "What is it like when one takes a step forward from the top of a hundred-foot pole? The Master said, "The third day of the third month.
The monk said, "I do not know where this falls. The Master said, "Rising from your seat without thanking me for my hospitality. The monk said, "From now on, I have found a place of peace and joy."
The Master said, "In the cemetery of the righteous, traces of tears are many.
The Master asked a monk, "To suppress it and act accordingly—this may be called 'the noble forget much. If you were to attempt to provide an arrangement for that side, what would you do?
The monk had no reply. The Master asked a nearby monk, "If you cannot discern this, it falls to the ground and makes a golden sound. What do you say?"
When a monk was about to prostrate, the Master struck him.
While the Master was traveling to Niushou Mountain, he encountered a practitioner on the road who snapped his fingers once and asked, "What is your fundamental principle?
The Master replied, "A rat eating salt. The practitioner asked, "What is a phrase that conceals its sharp point? The Master replied, "East and West."
[North and South. The student asked, "What is the 'hiding the point' of phenomena? The Master said, "Many drunkards on the opposite bank.

The student asked, "What is the 'hiding the point' of principle? The Master said, "Wild ducks filling the river. The student asked, "What is the 'hiding the point' of both phenomenon and principle together?
The Master said, "A boat in the water; water in the boat. The student asked, "What is the 'neither hiding the point of phenomenon nor principle'?"
Feng. The Master said, "The one above goes up; the one below goes down. The monk then prostrated.
A monk asked, "I do not ask about 'the myriad dharmas returning to the One. But ultimately, where does the One return?
The Master said, "Yesterday the steward came; today the firewood-carrier has gone."
A monk asked, "What is it like when the skull is smashed to pieces? The Master said, "Monks rank by their years of ordination; laypeople rank by their age.
A monk asked, "It is said that making offerings to hundreds of thousands of Buddhas is not as good as making offerings to a single mindless man of the Way.
What fault do the Buddhas have, and what virtue does the mindless man of the Way possess? The Master said, "Beat the drum and turn the prow of the boat."
A monk asked, "The King asks for the *santapa*; what is his intention? The Master said, "Listening to matters without clarity.
The monk said, "The ancients could turn iron into gold; I beg the Master for a direct instruction. The Master said, "Drums from north of the Huai River."

The Master asked a monk who was threshing rice, "Setting aside for a moment the fact that the grain is ripe but you do not attend the field, how is it that the farmer tills the field but does not sow?
The monk had no reply. The Master said, "At Tianhua Temple by Lake Hejia."
A monk asked, "It is not the wind moving; it is not the banner moving. What is it that moves? The Master said, "Zen practitioners have walked right into a lacquer bucket.
The monk asked, "What about you, Master? The Master said, "The Yangxi River is called 'Kindly Old Man' (Ciweng)."
A monk asked, "What is it like when the trees are stripped of their leaves? The Master said, "Excellent! Start from the very beginning.
The monk asked, "And as for 'the golden wind revealing its essence,' how is that? The Master said, "Sing here; weep here. The monk gave a shout. The Master said, "How short is your life!
As the monk hesitated, the Master struck him and sent him away.
A monk asked, "The Ultimate Way is without difficulty; it only dislikes discrimination. Is this so? The Master said, "The double-six has been thrown on the board;
a great cheer! The monk pressed further, "What is the Ultimate Way? The Master said, "Not off by a hair’s breadth. Not off by a hair’s breadth.
The monk said, "Today I have had the fortune to meet the Master. The Master said, "Where did you stay last night, Chan guest?"
A monk asked, “What is the Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū? The Master said, “Beneath the bridge at Gujia.
The monk pressed further, “Why do the Buddha-dharma not manifest before one? The Master said, “The dried tofu at Linping.”
[The Master] entered the room. A monk asked, "What is the direct meaning of Linji? The Master said, "The official is currently beating [me].

The monk pressed further, "If a student does not recognize the fundamental principle, what then? The Master said, "I am the master of Tianxi. The monk pressed further, "How can the eye of the Way be made clear?
The Master said, "A gentleman maintains propriety in his conduct. The monk pressed further, "I beg the Master for a skillful means. The Master said, "You..."
The monk asked, "What? He was at a loss. The Master said, "Come forward. The monk stepped forward. The Master laughed heartily and said:
"The golden wind falls in desolation, washing away the fragrant blossoms; The thousand peaks grow thin until the wild geese begin their flight. A single wave in the South Sea is ever restless;
Do not doubt that half the face of the Western Mountain is not what it seems."
A monk asked, "The swallow is skilled at discoursing on the true mark (*dharmatā*). What is the true mark? The Master said, "Han-lao! Han-lao!
A monk asked, "What is it like when one seizes the moment and goes forth? The Master said, "Mud for making heads."
A monk asked, "What is the mind of the ancient Buddha? The Master said, "Withered branches and crimson trees. The monk asked, "What is the non-transmigration of things?
The Master said, "Leaves floating on the frosty waves."
A monk asked, "When Zen practitioners meet, they merely snap their fingers; how many people can truly know this mind?
What is this mind? The Master said, "Your nose, Reverend, is black."
A monk asked, “What is the Way? The Master said, “Many fine days together. The monk asked, “What is one who is on the Way?
The Master said, “Passing by another household once more.”
A monk asked, "What is Chan? The Master said, "No lamp is lit during the day.
The monk asked, "How was it before Niu-tou saw the Fourth Patriarch? The Master said, "The seventh day of the Qingming festival. The monk asked, "And after he saw him?
The Master said, "The second day of the Gu Yu (Grain Rain) festival."
A monk asked, "Wood above and iron below—what is the meaning? The Master said, "Meeting misfortune, one transforms it into good fortune.
As the monk hesitated, the Master laughed loudly. When the monk asked again, the Master said, "Lately, my practice has been far too leisurely."
The Master asked a monk, “How do you plant a rootless tree? The monk had no reply. The Master said, “I have been quite leisurely on my mountain circuit.
The monk requested further instruction. The Master recounted: Once Xuansha asked Attendant Guang, “Have you finished building the iron boat yet?

Guang had no reply. He requested the Master to provide a substitute answer. The Master said, “Today there is a fine breeze. [Another] asked, “When entering the gate, how do you speak this one phrase? The Master said, “A monkey.”
"Riding on the back of a tortoise. A monk asked, "Since it is already Great Hero Mountain, why do you also say 'Clouds Cover the Hermitage'?
