expounding discourses on dreams, illusions, bubbles, and shadows is like a gourd following its mold. This matter can only be known through personal realization; it is not that one fails to awaken to it oneself.

Within the vast and surging ocean of the Dharma, the supreme and ultimate true mechanism, a gap of even a hair’s breadth creates a separation of ten thousand miles. When a single sound is proclaimed...
It emerges, utterly distinct and clear. As soon as a single character is formed, the great trichiliocosm is revealed. Within genuine gold ore, there can be no trace of copper;
within a great mass of fire, how could a drop of water remain? The stages of the path are laid out clearly, like a series of diagrams;

truth and falsehood, the correct and the deviant, are vividly presented before the mirror. The masses are easily deluded, yet those with clear eyes see no flowers in the sky—just as rain enters [the ocean].

Grass roots have their own hearts; they experience their own bitterness and sweetness. Water returns to its vessel, each manifesting its own square or round shape. Once right contemplation is established, it is difficult to escape the hearing of the divine.
Regarding this matter, I have once applied myself to investigation and deliberation. While in the leisure of the princely residence, I roamed through the City of Transformation.

There, within the midst of non-existence and lack of expedient means, I extended my inquiries with subtle persistence; likewise, in places where thought was utterly extinguished, I humbly conformed to the capacities of those who came to me. How could this be called...?
The journey by ladder and boat has not been without its errors. I have now selected and compiled several volumes to be handed down for future generations;

following the records of the great virtuous teachers (mahā-kalyāṇa-mitra) that were collected therein, these [present works] are also appended for publication. Although I have occasionally discoursed upon the sublime principles in the past, [I have done so only sparingly].

In truth, I have not yet exhaustively perused the various teachings. I have acted according to my own inclinations in unfolding and rolling up [the texts], appearing and disappearing as circumstances dictated;

this was truly due to my own arbitrary fabrications and is not the text of the Dharma-sūtras. Only recently have I begun to uncover the lost writings from within the void and to unseal the accumulated scrolls from amidst the dust.
My desire is to cause the parched and withered thorns to sprout anew and for the decayed, rotten vines to blossom once more with divine flowers. Now, I behold the words of those of former times.
Much of what you have written accords with my own words without prior agreement and harmonizes with them spontaneously without deliberate intent. Such is the nature of the perfect sound;

it cannot help but provoke a laugh. This sufficiently demonstrates that, throughout a thousand years, people from different mouths have spoken with one voice—not because there was any intention to mimic a single word or to engage in plagiarized rhetoric.
Now that I occupy the position of Sovereign Ruler, how could I covet the hollow reputation of a lay practitioner living as a householder?
Having personally visited the site of enlightenment, it is fitting to proclaim the authentic edict of the Great Awakened Dharma King.
It is my desire that people may believe and know that the ancestral seal was transmitted directly with concrete evidence:

that it is primordially complete, that the realm beyond thought and speech is no empty claim, that the principle is manifest—neither existent nor void, neither emerging nor entering—and that this wondrous nature is not distant, nor is clear awakening far away. I, the Emperor...
The reality is fundamentally the perfect penetration of a single nature, yet it is expressed through five kinds of true words. Only this one matter is so;
the other two are not the truth. This is what the ancient worthies have manifested and inherited, and what future generations will silently confirm.

Therefore, I have composed this preface to transmit it, not begrudging the addition of yet another layer of verbal pitfalls. It is not that my own words and phrases can be equated with those of the great virtuous knowers of the past.
This is a record of Shishi (Shi Bi-jian). May those who observe it refrain from deriding it.
Recorded on the eighth day of the fourth month in the Gui-chou year of the eleventh year of the Yongzheng era by the Huoshi Prince Yong and the layman Yuanming.
The Inscription on the Arising of Enlightenment: Buddha after Buddha, Patriarch after Patriarch, have awakened the people; this alone is the one matter, while the other two are not true.
What is this matter? It is the direct pointing to the human mind. What is this mind? It has the illusory and the real; yet the illusory is not illusory, and the real is not real.
Reality is itself illusion; illusion is itself reality. Mind is itself Buddha; Buddha is itself mind. What, then, is called a "sentient being"?

One who clings to the causes of birth and death, turning their back on the Real and uniting with the delusory, thus falling headlong into the cycle of transmigration. If you wish to understand birth and death, do not apply the mind at all.

Do not at all sever delusions; do not at all seek the truth. If all conditions cease, where could there be a cause? To involve oneself even slightly in acceptance and rejection is itself the mind of aversion and attachment.
This very aversion and attachment is the cause of arising and ceasing. This very arising and ceasing is what is called impermanence.
Therefore, through impermanence, true permanence is revealed. What is called "true permanence"? It pervades the entire realm without concealment;

it is manifested in every head and disclosed in every phenomenon. Ten thousand years are but a single thought-moment; things and self are of one suchness. Fundamentally there is no coming or going; how could there be an end or a beginning?

Equally impartial and immovable—this is called True Suchness (*tathatā*). It is the wondrous existence of awakened clarity; it is neither real nor unreal. This wondrous existence of awakened clarity is without deficiency and without excess.
Sages and worthies do not cling to it, while the ignorant and foolish bind themselves to it through false attachment to its false existence, erring further within their errors.
Deluded beings give rise to right and wrong; those who have awakened are free from likes and dislikes. There is no need for deliberation, nor is there any need for conjecture.

The distinction between a Buddha and an ordinary being lies solely in awareness and awakening. Cast away all intellectual understanding, conceptualization, and discursive thought; suddenly, you will achieve resonance, like an echo responding to a sound.
Luminosity and darkness fill the void; there is nowhere it does not penetrate. Perfectly empty yet silently illuminating, it is like the moon encompassing the sky.

Without past or present, without other or self, without duality or unity, its light is profound, clear, and azure. Thus it is, thus it is; such it is, such it is. The Tathāgata, the Tathāgata. Such it is, such it is.
The Patriarch came from the West with a sincere heart to point directly to the human mind. How many scholars have mistakenly identified consciousness and spirit!
All their deductions and explanations are delusory and not true. To chisel stone and polish jade is to labor in vain. There is no need to eliminate delusion; there is no need to seek truth.
Ultimately, how is it? It simply requires the death of the mind. If the one mind dies, then ten thousand minds are all true.
In every dust mote and every world-system, there is direct intimacy. This is called the non-dual, profound, and wondrous Dharma-gate.
The single thread penetrates the gate of non-duality. "My Way is a single thread. This method of one and two is intended solely to still all views.

If views can be stilled, the essence will manifest in its entirety. Abandoning birth and death, abide here in non-discrimination. Without discriminating between right and wrong, hatred and love are but illusions.
Progressing in this manner is called right view. If one proceeds along this path together with others, there is another koan. What follows is a long discourse;
words and speech are cut off. It is neither one nor two. Let this thought remain for ten thousand years.
On the Day of Establishing Spring, the King issued this instruction: "The eighty-four thousand dharmas—some exist, some do not; the twelve gates of emptiness—empty or not empty?
If you can recognize the two pieces of tongue within your mouth, I grant that you possess a single eye.
But if you merely follow that bright red tongue and rely upon those two shining eyes, you will never understand how a snail leaps."
Boarding the boat, I only fear that the toad may not be willing to bark like a dog. The green mountains originally do not grow grass; the clear waters fundamentally do not breed fish.
What need is there to speak of roaming the North Sea in the morning and lodging at Cangwu in the evening? Spring is harmonious and mild; summer is scorching and steaming;
autumn is crisp and refreshing; winter is solemn and freezing. Even if you were to perform a somersault and tumble into the realm of non-being (*asamjñika*), it would still be so.

Even those who conceive of the heavens cannot leap out of this circle. How much better it would be to plunge one's head into the sands of the Ganges, where every atom is as such, every world-system is as such—vast, free, spontaneous, and in accord with the *tathatā* (suchness), even if it means running away from one’s father.
Yet what one actually does is engage in one's own fundamental livelihood. At once, one capsizes the iron boat and sails upon the vast blue sea;

how could this hinder the fact that one’s own kin remain as they were, intimately close? If you still do not understand, I shall provide a further commentary for you. Have you not seen it? In every dust mote and every world-system.
Every land and every atom is I; I am every land and every atom. Who can see every atom and every land? Alas!
The four seasons revolve through the year in turn; try looking: today has begun once again.
To scoop up the ocean of fragrant waters with the palms of one's two hands is the skill of a three-foot-tall child playing with mud balls;
to grasp the trichiliocosm within a single fingertip is the livelihood of a destitute beggar coveting small profits. When traveling companions meet on the road, they pass by shoulder to shoulder.
Zhao Yi said, "How can one person have two heads? Qian Er said, "Suck the Western River dry in a single gulp."
The blind fellow swallows iron caltrops whole; he does not consort with the myriad dharmas. Sun San says: "He still owes the tiger its prey—the great beast has been swallowed.
With staff slung across his shoulder, he strides straight into the thousand peaks. Li Si says: "One must encounter the dead snake and refrain from killing it.
Whether green, yellow, red, white, or black—though these are all colors, one perceives neither sour, bitter, sweet, nor pungent.
Salt. One must taste each flavor individually before it is attained; then one merely performs a somersault within the walls of the Chang’an city.
It cannot be done this way, nor can it be done that way. One must inevitably enter the Han-yuan Hall and perform a full somersault.
Then it can be done this way, and it can be done that way. Therefore, our Great Compassionate Father, the Buddha, said: "I..."
If you press a finger, the Sea-Seal emits light; yet as soon as you stir a thought, worldly afflictions arise first. Tell me, how can this be so?
Today is the eighth day of the twelfth lunar month.
In the three realms there are no dharmas; where can one seek the mind? Since the mind cannot be sought, where shall the dharmas be entrusted?

To pick up the moon at the bottom of the abyss with a staff made of rabbit horns—the essential point remains as it is. To bind the wind at the top of the tree with a rope made of tortoise hair—the manifestation is already complete.
Head and all things, every single object, fill and pervade empty space. Is it the mind? Is it the dharmas? It lies solely in the person’s own recognition. If you say it cannot be depicted...
It is accomplished. It cannot be depicted in painting; it cannot be confined within a cage, nor can it be summoned back when called.
For now, it likely does not even set foot here. (He lets out a shout.)
When you encounter rubble on the road, do not discard it lightly; when you bring it back, it will all be gold.
At this moment, I have bestowed the Jewel-Treasury and the Instructions for the Golden Elixir upon everyone with my two hands. Is there anyone here who knows how to repay this kindness?
Looking left and right, he said: "If you offer even a single interpretation, you will enter hell as swiftly as a shot arrow."
Regardless of whether Zhang San has a beard on his mouth, who cares that Li Si’s body is as black as lacquer? Within the flash of lightning, the mud ox roars;
it moves freely and spontaneously, without any fetters or ties. Watch over the eyebrows as they are arranged upon the eyes;
keep the nostrils intact so you may breathe freely. Setting the eyebrows aside for a moment, tell me: where do the nostrils fall? Drawn eastward, they go to the east.
Dragging it westward, the *Xi Lai* [Patriarch] arrives. The green bamboo—here one stalk, there two; three stalks to the east, four stalks to the west.

The lush yellow flowers—one bloom atop another, two blooms above, three blooms below, four blooms beneath. The pine is straight, the thorn is crooked; not even a fraction of it can be pared away. The crane...
The white crow is black; one cannot apply even a speck of paint to it. For those who have realized it, Mount Sumeru blocks their throats;
for those who have not realized it, the fragrant ocean drowns their blind eyes. Hehe! What possible connection is there?
Wondrous existence within true emptiness; true emptiness within wondrous existence. A single staff is supported by two people. Striking the west, it moves the north.
The fragrant breeze sweeps gently; the seasonal rain falls in mist. *Dong-dong* and *di-di*; *di-di* and *dong-dong*.
When the unperforated flute meets the felt clappers, everyone sings together the "Jade Lotus. As it is said: "To be a monk for even a single day..."
Strike once upon the bell!
Trees are its sinews and stones its bones; water is its blood and mountains its flesh; the sun is its heart and the roads its intestines;
heaven is its hide and earth its skin. Yet there remains the great earth and its sentient beings for whom no place can be arranged—take them up!
Treat it as a parasite in the stomach. Suppose a person comes forward and asks, "Jiyun!
simply wave your hand at him and say, "Scared! Scared! If he says, "Why are you afraid, Great Good Teacher?
just say, "I have never seen such a great monster before. Then laugh heartily.
Sentient beings do not understand this; they are like children flying kites. As the wind carries them away, they let them go; when the wind subsides, they pull them back again.
This constant pulling in and letting go is truly no different from childish play. When will there ever be an end to it?
Therefore, ancient masters would often remark, "Has the red thread beneath your heels been severed yet? These words are profoundly intimate. It is just like a kite.
The thread is severed. Where has the paper swallow fallen? *Chan*.

Seeking a teacher and visiting the Way—how is this different from seeking deer antlers on a donkey’s head? Wandering on pilgrimage to practice *chan*—it is much like seeking pearls from within a tortoise shell.
What is added by seeing with the eyes and hearing with the ears? With the nose straight and the brows arched—what is lacking?
What is it? Those who have realized it take it up at once; those who have not realized it must wait through a thousand births and a hundred kalpas.
But tell me, what is it that they take up? "You are you; I am I. "You are me; I am you.
If you do not understand even this, Yuanming shall provide another annotation: "You are not you; I am not I. You are not me; I am not..."
"It is not you. The King said: "The sea is vast, my fish leap; the sky is clear, my birds fly. My sea allows the fish to leap at will; my sky allows the birds to fly at will.
The sea is vast, so let the fish leap; the sky is clear, so let the birds fly. Of these three lines, there is one line that may be granted [to you].
The Buddhas and Patriarchs are your teachers; examine this closely. If you understand it in a vague or superficial way, you betray the perfect luminosity.
If you attempt to analyze it with conceptual intent, you cannot avoid betraying the former sages. But tell me, how can one truly succeed? [He raises his fist and says:
"A wooden phoenix, donning feathers, dances in the celestial expanse; a stone tiger, carrying a fetus, walks upon the ocean floor."
While appreciating flowers under the moon, he heard the sound of a bell. The King said: "The bell is my own voice, yet I cannot hear it.
The flowers are my own form, yet I cannot see them. The wine is my own flavor, yet I cannot taste it.
The moon is my own body, yet I cannot touch it. He then addressed his attendants, saying: "Today, Yuanying drinks wine and eats meat, yet he discusses [the nature of reality]."
[The Master] spoke of Chan in profound discourse. "Tell me, is there fault or not? The assembly had no reply. The King laughed and said, "Fortunately, it was I who initiated this discussion;
however, you have simply failed to grasp it. *Du!* Was this perhaps talk under the influence of wine? The assembly all laughed heartily. The King said, "It must not be treated so casually.
You should simply focus your minds on recollecting the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha; then naturally, there will be a point of understanding."

Traditionally it has been said: "If one realizes it in the first phrase, one is fit to be a teacher of Buddhas and Patriarchs. If one realizes it in the second phrase, one is fit to be a teacher of devas and humans.
If one realizes it in the third phrase, one cannot even save oneself. Yuanming considers this not to be so.
If one realizes it in the third phrase, one is fit to be a teacher of Buddhas and Patriarchs. If one realizes it in the second phrase, one is fit to be a teacher of devas and humans.
Heaven is the teacher. To attain realization through the first phrase alone is to fail to save oneself.

If you say that perfect luminosity possesses a distinct path for further cultivation—picking up and setting down, overturning and grasping—you still cannot avoid the failure of your eyebrows trailing on the ground once more.
Why is this? Within a single phrase there is a Way that does not exclude the other three; within the three phrases there is no principle that does not include the single phrase. All...
Those who possess the true eye shall discern and grasp this for themselves.
The King said: "The Great Being Hanshan said: 'Anger is the fire within the mind; it can burn down the forest of merit.
If one wishes to practice the Bodhisattva path, one must cultivate patience to protect the true heart. Yuanming says today: 'Affliction is the water within the body; it can delude the *paramārtha*.'"
If one wishes to practice the Bodhisattva path, one must guard the true body by restraining desire. Now, tell me: are these teachings the same or different?
The "four groups and seven elders" of India’s West transmitted a teaching outside the scriptures; this is much like a well-fed man speaking of the pangs of hunger.

The "two or three patriarchs" of our land’s East, with their "one flower and five petals," are all nothing but opening one's eyes to recite dream-poems. If that were so, what would be used to sustain the True Dharma? Wake up!
Ferrying across the multitude of deluded beings, he constantly holds up a single unperforated flute, singing the Song of Great Peace in accordance with conditions.
Utterly pure is this expanse of idle ground; brilliantly manifest is the ancient family style of ten thousand ages, vertically exhausting the three periods of time.
Transversely pervading the ten directions, mountains, waters, clouds, and mists adorn the universe like brocade; the sun, moon, and stars illuminate the cosmos with brilliance.
East, south, west, and north—the eight quarters are clearly arrayed; spring, summer, autumn, and winter—the four seasons are vividly spread.
Spontaneously Avalokiteśvara, Wondrous, Perfect, Pure, and Sublime Sound—proceeding thus, what need is there for further seeking?
A wondrous jewel mirror hangs in the void; there is not a single point of contact. Tell me, how should one practice? After a long silence, he said:
"Even if one were to swallow the Western River in a single gulp, one must still enter directly among the thousand peaks before it is achieved.
Nevertheless, one still lacks the knowledge of how to come thus."
The pure *dharmakāya* is by nature conjoined with emptiness; the hundreds of thousands of millions of *nirmāṇakāyas* are by nature conjoined with existence;

the perfected *saṃbhogakāya* is by nature conjoined with both emptiness and existence. The Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom is both existence and emptiness; the Wisdom of Equality is both emptiness and existence.

The wisdom of wondrous observation knows both emptiness and existence, yet does not perceive them as dual. The wisdom of accomplished action is like a mirror that reflects the three bodies and the three wisdoms;
this is what is meant by the saying: "The Nāga is always in meditative concentration; there is no time when he is not in concentration.

Thus, the three bodies and four wisdoms are fully manifested as a single essence, which is the non-dual Dharma. Since even "one" and "two" cannot be apprehended, how can there be such talk of "three" and "four"?

Furthermore, do you wish to realize how the three bodies and four wisdoms are fully manifested as a single unity? [The Master] snaps his fingers and says: "Above all, do not mistake the nature for a self.
One thought is movement; one thought is stillness. The two aspects of movement and stillness are entirely without fixed definition. One nostril is fragrant; the other..."
The nostrils stink; one cannot grasp them, nor can one let them go. Within this state of unattainability, there is simply attainment. A swift hawk strikes the void and enters the cloud-masses:
wishing to descend, it cannot alight. A mangy dog rolls on the ground and falls into the mud: wishing to rise, it cannot ascend.

Now tell me: is this suffering or joy? Simply wait until the extreme reaches its limit and prosperity arrives; naturally, the myriad yin energies will be stripped away and the single yang will return.
At this point, though the spring may be the same as in years past, you must know that the blossoms opening upon the plum branches are not those of last year.
Just then, a little dog leaps up beside him and cries out, "Gwang! Gwang! Gwang! Gwang! Gwang!"—Perfect!
I spoke inadvertently and was caught by my own words;

I have spoken horizontally across the ten directions and vertically from top to bottom. If you say this is merely following the waves, I have long been concerned about this—it is simply that you yourself have not yet even dreamed of it.
At times it is "Tathāgata" (Thus-Come); at times it is "Come-Thus"; at times it is "Come-Come. There is...
At that time, it is suchness (*tathatā*). If it were not thus, how could it be thus?
If one asks, "What is this 'thus'?"—last night, why did all of you have eighty-four thousand pores, yet one thousand two hundred and fifty were blocked up?
The assembly remained silent. The King said, "This is your own failure; how does it concern Yuanming at all?"

Traditionally it has been said: "The Way is easy to see, but difficult to cultivate; the Way is easy to cultivate, but difficult to maintain; the Way is easy to maintain, but difficult to practice. Yuanming does not agree with this argument.
If one regards the provisional Way as easy to see, then the provisional Way is difficult to cultivate; if the provisional Way is easy to cultivate, [then it is difficult to maintain].

It is difficult to maintain a provisional path; it is easy to maintain a provisional path. It is difficult to travel a provisional path. If one speaks with true words, then traveling the true path is easy;
maintaining the true path is difficult. Maintaining the true path is easy; cultivating the true path is difficult. Cultivating the true path is easy; seeing the true path is difficult.
Once one attains true vision, then cultivation, maintenance, and practice are all easy to accomplish. If one’s point of view is not true, then cultivation and maintenance—

If one does not practice with the single word "difficult," it will absolutely be impossible to achieve success. Therefore it is said: "Investigation must be true investigation; awakening must be real awakening.
Once you have attained the root, what need is there to worry about the branches? Each person should examine their own heart and ask themselves this.
One must not vainly attempt to steam sand in hopes of producing rice; such toil is of no benefit. Unless one reaches the state of great rest, one must not act recklessly.
This is for the sake of rest. Let students exert themselves in this!
At times it is great, at times it is small; at times there is, at times there is not. Being great does not mean it is opened wide; being small does not mean it is squeezed shut.
There being, it is not something separate from non-being; there not being, it is not something separate from being. If one can act in this way—
Only then can one attain suchness. If one can attain suchness, one must not know suchness. If one knows suchness, then one does not attain suchness.
Thus see, thus act, thus cultivate, and thus realize. To those who see alike, act alike, cultivate alike, and realize alike—take heed! Exert yourselves!

It is appropriate for the side of light; it surpasses the radiance of day. It is appropriate for the side of darkness; it is more tranquil than the night. It is appropriate when opening one’s eyes; there is not a single thing that is not my own body.
It is appropriate when closing one’s eyes; there is not a single thing that is my self. To say that originally there are no things is merely excessive verbiage.
To speak of a "unified totality" (yīhéxiàng) is to forcibly assign a name. Who says it extends vertically through the three periods of time and stretches horizontally across all space?
Throughout the ten directions, one merely remains in a state of continuous flow; knowing yet not knowing, subtle and profound; seeing yet not seeing.

Clinging to grass and leaning upon wood, blending with the mundane and harmonizing with the light; when hungry or thirsty, one eats and drinks; when cold or hot, one puts on or takes off clothes; thus going and coming.
The present is the ancient. Listening to Heaven, one is not constrained by Heaven; following destiny, one is not bound by destiny.
Although this is not eternal life, it is nonetheless long-sighted vision. But tell me, what is this long-sighted vision? "A single grain of the Golden Elixir conceals the world;
ten thousand kinds of rare treasures gather on the Mountain of Form. [He lets out a shout. He says: "What connection is there?"
Heaven and hell are precisely this human realm, the Buddha-land. Loyalty and reciprocity, greed and anger, are all the Buddha-mind within the nature of consciousness.
Exert yourself in cultivating wholesome causes to invite auspicious responses; do not sow evil fruits by creating the roots of karma.

Although these are conditioned, illusory fabrications, they are nonetheless firm, formless, and true merit. It is better to follow existence while turning away from existence than to follow emptiness.

To turn one's back on emptiness is to turn away from emptiness and follow existence; thus, one invites evil fruits through good causes. To turn one's back on existence and face emptiness is to invite evil fruits through good causes.

Yet, these are inherently complete within oneself: they are neither facing nor turning away, neither existence nor emptiness, neither having facing or turning away, nor lacking existence or emptiness.
There is no "neither," nor is there "not-neither. There is no "neither-nothingness," nor is there "nothingness-of-nothingness. One who realizes this—
Do not raise [this question] too frequently. Those who have not yet attained understanding should investigate it with care. He drew a single circle (○) and asked, "What are you investigating?
He then drew a circle with a dot inside (⭘) and asked, "What are you investigating? He then drew another symbol (☉) and asked, "What are you investigating?
Finally, he swept everything away and asked, "What are you investigating? "Investigate! Investigate! Investigate!"
To hear sound with the eyes is called true hearing; to perceive form with the ears is called correct observation. This is not a matter of the six sense organs functioning interchangeably;
rather, it is simply the natural law of reality (*dharmatā*). For this reason, the Great Being of Compassion is titled Avalokiteśvara. If it were otherwise, [he would not be so named].
How could one not share the same power of compassion as all Buddhas, and the same yearning of pity for all living beings?

Nevertheless, this is still a gate of transformation for saving sentient beings—a matter of sounds, forms, seeing, and hearing. Suppose there were a man who said, "Set aside this and look toward the path beyond.
Yuanming could only pat him on the back and say, "There is no need to split the discourse into two separate parts."
How many mountain-dwellers remain outside the mountains! How many travelers of rivers and lakes walk upon the surface of the water!
One does not realize that within the imperial court and the cities, every person dwells within the mountains and waters.

Those who do not understand this principle are much like those who speak deceptive words to the common folk; who would not know them to be false speech, unreal speech, superficial speech, and uncertain speech? Why is this so?
"Look at those who dwell on the mountains: who among them does not dwell outside the mountains? Travelers on rivers and lakes:

who among them does not travel upon the surface of the water? People of the court and the cities: who among them does not exist within the mountains and the waters? After a long silence, he laughed loudly and said:
To speak in such a manner may be called truly and certainly deceiving the common folk. Let anyone who finds this unsatisfactory come forward;
let us all together break into a great laugh.
Sentiment creates a barrier to wisdom; the arising of thought clouds the spirit. Right and wrong delude the true nature; like and dislike obstruct the true mind.

When the mind arises, all manner of phenomena arise; when the mind ceases, all manner of phenomena cease. When thoughts of greed, anger, and ignorance arise, if one views the strange as not strange, that strangeness will naturally dissolve.
When the sentiments of precepts, concentration, and wisdom arise, auspicious grass grows before one’s door—better that such "good things" never existed at all. Thus it is said: "Do not see."
The Way: it is through this mind, intellect, and consciousness that one diminishes the wealth of the Dharma and extinguishes merit.

Therefore, the Gate of Chan brings the mind to an end, entering suddenly into the power of non-arising insight. Now tell me: is this power of insight the mind? Is it the intellect? Is it the consciousness?
It is not mind. It is not intellect. It is not consciousness. As for bricks, stones, tiles, and rubble—whether large or small—how can one weigh them by their respective portions?
As for the four directions—east, west, south, and north—whether near or far—how can one measure them in *zhang* and *chi*?
One may only say that the mind is exhausted; one cannot say there is no mind. Therefore it is said: "Do not say that being without mind is [the truth]."
The Way: "To have no mind is already separated by ten thousand layers of mountains. To have a dharma is to have a mind; to have no mind is to have no dharma.
It is not that there is neither dharma nor mind; it is simply that mind and dharma must be one and the same.

A follower standing nearby said, "To make offerings to hundreds of thousands of millions of buddhas is not as good as providing a meal for a single person who has realized the state of no-mind. The King said, "Wait until you yourself have realized no-mind."
I speak to you once more:
My younger brother, Layman Chaoyang, broke through the lacquer bucket in the spring of the Dingyou year.
Because he was able to question that which cannot be known, he humbly requested instruction; I could not refuse him one more time of leaking the truth. Thus, I took up my brush to respond to him.
Yesterday, there was a profound accord regarding the teaching on the correspondence with non-arising and non-extinction.

Now, as for those who have seen that which is non-arising and non-extinguishing, they need not even be discussed. Yet you, my worthy brother, are currently sitting within the armor of non-arising and non-extinguishing.
To sit within the non-arising and non-extinguishing of the physical body is certainly not worth counting; yet now, my worthy brother, you are sitting within the Dharma...
This is that which is neither born nor extinguished within the body. One who can achieve this will find it difficult to encounter another such person even after thirty years.
If one were to turn the Great Dharma Wheel within a single mote of dust or manifest a Jewel-King Land upon the tip of a single hair, one would still not have glimpsed it even in a dream.
Now, regarding the dharma-realm of the physical body, adding a foot to a snake is of no consequence.
Superior: All sentient beings recognize form as themselves; when they happen to be awakened and recognize the original master who is neither born nor extinguished—this is the intermediate level.

All sages and worthies take the great trichiliocosm as themselves; in a single thought of reality, they enter the wondrous, perfect ocean of *bodhi* which is neither born nor extinguished—this is the superior level.
It is just like the longevity or brevity of a person's life, or the shortness [of the lifespan] of things.

Long though they may be, they still belong to the realm of dreams and illusions; how then can they be deemed worthy of esteem? The physical body does not exceed a hundred years, and the world does not exceed a single kalpa.
Therefore, for one who identifies with the physical body, it cannot be called short; for one who identifies with the Dharma-realm, it cannot be called long.
To say that the physical body and the Dharma-realm ultimately come to an end is to imply that there exists elsewhere a place of rest for the self.

To establish the locus of destiny is to split it into two separate fragments. For instance, to claim that the physical body (*rūpakāya*) and the *dharmadhātu* are both inexhaustible treasuries is merely the empty talk of non-Buddhists.
This is because it goes without saying that the physical body—being small and near—is impermanent;

yet even the *dharmadhātu*, being vast and remote, possesses the principle of formation, abiding, destruction, and emptiness. What is realized today is the correspondence with that which is neither born nor extinguished.

This state is still merely a successive unfolding within the sphere of immediate effort. If you take one more step forward, naturally and without depending on even a hair’s breadth of artifice, you will see the three bodies and four wisdoms. Human beings, self, and sentient beings;

the three thousandfold world system and the eighty thousand afflictions—vertically exhausting the three periods of time and horizontally spanning the ten directions—they are neither born nor extinguished, neither extinguished nor born, neither born...

Arising is not the extinction of extinction; arising-extinction is not the extinction of arising; extinction-arising is not the extinction of extinction; arising-arising is not the extinction of extinction.
Even if a Tathāgata were to press down with a single finger and the Sea-Seal (Sāgarāmudrā) were to emit light, one could only say to him:
"This old fellow does not recognize good from evil. Do not say, "This mountain is full of steep precipices"; there is still a highest peak ahead. Traveling together.
"Exert yourself in this! He asked:
"What is the method for crossing the 'heavy barrier'? [The Master replied: "Once the Great Matter is clarified, even if you harbor doubts and seek elsewhere, I fear your footing will not be firm.
Yet many people force themselves to be the master, which leads to error regarding the Ultimate. If you have not yet stepped across the heavy barrier, the greatest thing to avoid is..."
Doubt. To be satisfied with a small attainment and refuse to exert oneself even for a single step of practice; after breaking through the kōan, one must advance by means of doubt;
after passing the heavy barrier, one must enter the reality without doubt. This matter of "ignorance" (avidyā), for instance, originally has no ignorance.
Nor is there an exhaustion of ignorance. Since ignorance is fundamentally non-existent from the start, what need is there to sever it?

If one attempts to still movement with stillness or eliminate delusion with truth—even if one does so for ten thousand kalpas in a single thought-moment—it remains nothing more than the path of the nihilistic outsider. What kind of matter could such a thing possibly accomplish?
The Buddha said: "To mistake the head for its reflection. This is because sentient beings have long been habituated to forgetting their own heads and fixating instead on the reflection.
This is a mistaken and inverted view. Once you have recognized the head, what concern is there for the shadow? Nevertheless, this matter cannot be made one, nor can it be made two.
The shadow is merely a phenomenon occurring at the edge of the radiance of the sun, moon, lamps, or fire; where there is a head, there must necessarily be a shadow.
Where there is a shadow, there must be a head. Sentient beings dwell in the shadow and contemplate the head; the sages dwell in the head and contemplate the shadow.

It cannot be said that one contemplates oneself, nor can it be said that another sees another. Once the four lights—the sun, moon, lamps, and fire—have ceased, how could there be the matter of a head looking at its own reflection?
Since these four lights cannot cease forever, how could the head and its shadow be permanently absent? This is because the habitual tendencies are difficult to exhaust.
It is forgotten. This is why there is the teaching of the seeds of habitual perfuming (*vāsanā-bīja*) accumulated over immeasurable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*).
This single phrase—if misunderstood—has deceived how many people! It is like this: when the sun rises, its shadow follows; when the moon rises, its shadow follows.
Can one then call that shadow the same as the previous one? Originally, it is simply taking birth in its own place.
"Extinction occurs right where it is. As the Sūtra says: "Once gold has been extracted from the ore, it is no longer ore.

When one's efforts are fully integrated, yet one still comes back to identify with reflections or ore, this is not the case; the gold of one's own head does not come to become ore or a reflection. Strive in this!
Question: What is the practice for returning to the source? All sentient beings inherently possess the wisdom, virtue, and marks of the Tathāgata;
however, because of deluded thoughts and attachments, they are unable to realize them. Once the fundamental doubt is shattered, deluded thoughts are eliminated.
Once the heavy barrier is penetrated, attachments are entirely dissolved. Where then is there any wisdom, virtue, or mark that cannot be realized? It is simply this—
For now, do not concern yourself with whether you will return or not, nor with matters of before and after; simply remain still here and wait for it.

Be at ease with whatever you encounter. Though one may speak of the trichiliocosm, viewing it as if it were a mere dwelling, there remains an unavoidable sense of scale—of small and large, near and far. I simply see that every place is fit for sitting.
Whether lying down or rising, what distinction is there between hall, chamber, courtyard, or steps? This is what is called "finding fulfillment in whatever one enters.

One must by no means give rise to the perception of right and wrong, nor the perception of truth and falsehood, nor the perception of rejection and acceptance, nor the perception of departure and abiding.
Such a perception is called Right Awakening (samyak-saṃbodhi). Yet, this is still merely a matter of the shadow of a lamp.
For example, although the substance of a lamp has no function in itself, its function lies in its light; yet that light exists within the substance of the lamp.

"Breaking through the doubt-sensation" (po-can) is like the light near the lamp, while "passing through the heavy barrier" (tòu-chóng-guān) is like the light far from the lamp. If one cannot immediately reach the substance of the lamp, it is because the lamp's light is dim and lacks power.
Therefore, even if one practices for a year or half a year, if one still does not see movement, [it is due to this lack of power].
"Quietude" is still a matter of the heavy gate of practice; it has not yet been thoroughly penetrated.

If you can truly give rise to a single thought of faith and apply effort at that very moment, it will not hinder the re-arising of the state of doubt. As the ancients said: "Merit is never bestowed in vain," and again, "The Buddha-dharma need not fear being ruined.
Even if you were to misapply your mind, it would merely amount to having written several pieces of prose or managed several worldly affairs.
Matters are always clearly recognized. All things are unimpeded: light ultimately can see the essence, and the essence ultimately does not depart from light.
Yet this essence is not within; it truly is within. It is not without; it truly is without.
By no means should you engage in premature calculation; it will only serve as a hindrance to yourself.

Furthermore, do not mistake or misinterpret any particular phrase of the sutra or any specific passage of the text. To become attached to a single state of mind is itself a demonic realm. Nevertheless, that which enters through conditions is not one's own innate treasure.
Even regarding what I, your elder brother, have said above, you should view it merely as a *kōan* (public case); you must not be...
Entangled and bound, one must wait until each [thought] flows forth from within the breast; only then is it the upward path.
Because my worthy brother asked about the "turning back" and how to apply effort—being uncertain as to what comes before and what follows—I have随手 (suíshǒu) [as the occasion arose] written this down.
However, this is merely the principle of immediate practice and the locus where effort is applied. If, furthermore...
To go further would be useless to predict; when the time comes that you have taken this single step, you will naturally experience a joy that will last a lifetime—there is no need for words.
The King said: "The Buddha-dharma saves immeasurable beings; the Buddha-dharma also misleads immeasurable beings. All sentient beings are in a state of burning heat."

Within the icy cold hells, amidst the nine untimely deaths and the eight sufferings, beings undergo a thousand births and a thousand deaths, cycling through the six realms of existence without respite.

This vast and boundless ocean of karma is a pain beyond description. If sons and daughters of noble family can give rise to a single thought of pure faith, awakening a fierce sense of urgency and turning their light back within, they shall immediately ascend to the other shore and transcend the sea of suffering.
This is the immeasurable means by which the Buddha-Dharma delivers sentient beings. Beyond that shore—
Ascending, the myriad karmas melt away like ice; one wanders at ease in the Land of Ultimate Bliss and sports in the Realm of Cool Serenity.

Looking back upon the three realms, they appear like a burning house. It is like a bird wounded by an arrow that soars high and far away, or like a fish escaping through a net that hides deep and flees to distant waters.
Yet, time and again, people mistake the finger for the moon or seek to satisfy their hunger with painted cakes. This is the Buddha.
The Dharma deludes people in immeasurable ways. How could one know that within the cauldrons and burning coals lies the very body of the Dharma King?

The parable of the "transformed city" in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* is most poignant. Among all sufferings, what sentient being does not feel revulsion? Because of revulsion, it is easy to abandon them.
Among all pleasures and benefits, what sentient being does not feel attachment? Because of attachment, they are difficult to relinquish. And so it continues...
Life is inevitably cherished; death is inevitably loathed. Therefore, it is easy to leave death and follow life, but difficult to abandon life and undergo death.
This is why that which is spoken of here is not something generals or ministers can achieve. If one discusses birth within life, generals and ministers can manage it;
if one discusses death within death, generals and ministers can manage it. But as for death within life or life within death, generals and ministers cannot.
"It is possible. Yet one does not see that the Way can be leveled throughout the world, that one may tread upon white blades, but that the Middle Way is impossible to achieve.

Why is it impossible? It is because there is 'ability' that one is unable. At this hundred-foot pole, taking the step of letting go over the precipice requires nothing less than a true man (*mahāsattva*) to accomplish;
it is not for those who seek small gains or who merely draw lines to mark their own boundaries."
This is merely what those of your caliber can conjecture. An ancient said: "Only do not harbor likes or dislikes, and all will be transparently clear.
As soon as there is right and wrong, confusion arises and the mind is lost. He further said: "The mind of acceptance and rejection creates artifice and falsehood.

If you wish to clearly understand this matter, wait until you have cast off your 'sweat-soaked shirt' and severed the life-root; only then will I permit you to realize the eternally abiding true mind."
Do you wish to realize the eternally abiding true mind? When walking by day, you must carry a torch; when sitting at night, do not set up a lamp. Now tell me:
does this save immeasurable people, or does it mislead immeasurable people? (He lets out a shout. He says: "The subsequent text is long; we shall speak of it again tomorrow."
One day, the King said: "This matter exists because it is within, therefore it is not without; it exists because it is without, therefore it is not within;

He did not see this as being like Linji’s saying: "Sometimes one takes away the environment but does not take away the person; sometimes one takes away the person..."
"Seizing the object. At times both person and object are seized; at other times neither person nor object is seized.
