These remarks are like the spring, summer, autumn, and winter of heaven; the east, south, west, and north of earth; and the birth, old age, sickness, and death of humanity; or the sun—[the cycle of phenomena].

These are the directions of the north, south, east, and west; they correspond to the new moon, the first day of the month, the quarter moons, and the full moon. Now tell me: what exists and what does not exist? What is real and what is false?

Fundamentally, existence is manifested through non-existence, and non-existence is manifested through existence. Since both do not exist as such, how can there be existence and non-existence within the four?
When even existence and non-existence cannot be established, from where could truth and falsehood be distinguished? Therefore it is said: "Ignorance is consciousness."
Nature is itself Buddha-nature. The illusory, empty body is itself the Dharma-body.

Since ignorance is itself Buddha-nature and the empty body is itself the Dharma-body, how can Buddha-nature and the Dharma-body be considered noble? How can ignorance and the empty body be considered base?

It is precisely this single distinction between noble and base that gives rise to grasping and rejecting. Once grasping and rejecting arise, then truth and falsehood arise. Once truth and falsehood arise—
Existence and non-existence arise in succession; birth and death follow them. The myriad karmas gather like clouds, all produced from this single consciousness and single awakening.
Therefore, the Buddha said: "If I press my finger, the Sea-Seal emits light; as soon as you stir a thought, the dust of affliction first arises.
This critical juncture is of the utmost importance. If even a single thread is not penetrated, or a single hair is not shed, it is as if—
Pointing at Mount Sumeru as an obstruction—whose fault is this? An ancient said: "When dust and defilements are entirely removed, light finally appears;
when mind and phenomena are both forgotten, the nature is itself the truth. If one wishes to have dust and defilements entirely removed, one must forget both mind and phenomena.
If one wishes to forget both mind and phenomena, one must unify mind and phenomena. As long as there is the perception of "this" and "that," how can one forget them?
The mind. This mind is like a mirror. When the myriad phenomena arrive, they all become dust and grime.

If you cannot merge subject and object, but merely say, "I myself have no mind regarding the myriad things," you have falsely broken the mirror; such words are entirely deceptive, self-deception and self-delusion.
This matter requires one to truly tread upon the ground of non-duality; it is not something that can be understood through intellectual knowledge. Investigate!
The King showed this to a Chan practitioner and said: "Among those who have entered the Way but are unable to break through the heavy barriers, there are three maladies.

First, there is the state of being 'vividly alert,' where there appears to be a great orb of light; whether it is projected or withdrawn, one considers its manipulation to be under one's own control—this is the first.
Second, there is the state of being 'dully vacant,' where there is neither sound nor scent; whether following or seizing, one considers..."

To respond when things come and not retain them once they have passed—this is one. Thirdly, to see red as red and black as black, yet to have something lingering obscurely within the breast as if there were a thing present—this is one. These are all cases where the outflows of consciousness have not been eliminated;
one makes a living within pure appearances and seeks a livelihood within pleasant realms. If you proceed in this manner, even for a thousand or ten thousand kalpas, [you will remain bound].
You are merely a clever being capable of planting the seeds of Buddhahood; when will you ever reach the final goal?

You must leap out of the "transformed city" (the provisional realm) to seek the true state. It should be as if you were still before your great breakthrough—applying even greater diligence than before—and yet you may still fail.
How much less can you afford to be idle and self-satisfied, coveting minor gains and limiting yourself by drawing lines on the ground?
"How could you possibly advance? Wait until your inner and outer are as one, and the present and the past are no longer separated.
When you have taken even a single step from the top of a hundred-foot pole, I shall speak to you again of words that are true and not false."
From the Buddhas above down to the patriarchs below, their myriad explanations have all been for the sake of this very thing. If you can see this, do not concern yourself with it.
If you concern yourself with it, you immediately create a false version of it. If you recognize a false version of it, it is still better than not seeing it at all. Why?
Because deluded thoughts are easy to abandon, but attachments are difficult to dissolve. Those who study later must take heed of this.

To mistake a thief for one's own son, and to consider a small attainment as sufficient—while considering a small attainment as sufficient is a minor matter, once you mistake a thief for your son, it obstructs your journey of ten thousand miles ahead.
Have you not seen the Buddha’s words: "Such a person walks a deviant path; they cannot see the Tathāgata"?
For those who have not yet attained realization, you must leap forward with resolve; do not allow yourself to fall into error.
If an ordinary person wishes to realize this great matter, they can only seek that which is beyond this very thing; once that which is beyond is found, [realization is achieved].
That becomes this; this becomes that. When one reaches this point, one must depart from that.
To depart from that, one must rely upon that. That becomes this; this is that; that is this.
Only when one reaches this point can one deliberate upon true "this. If one sees...
One who has realized this [truth] truly knows that there is neither "this" nor "that. Let it be as it may: "this" is also "that," and "that" is also "this.
Since it is said to be real, and in reality there is neither "this" nor "that," why then do you speak of "that" and "this"?
You simply do not realize that at this moment, "this" and "that" are not the same "this" and "that" as they were before.

If you still do not understand, let me provide a commentary on the final four lines: "In the brief moment it takes for eighty thousand defilements to vanish, the rock contains jade and the earth supports mountains.
The clear breeze and bright moon are unrecognized by anyone; only through direct realization can they be known—they cannot be transmitted. *Chan.*

Investigation must be genuine investigation; awakening must be real awakening. What is meant by "false investigation"? It is seeking to gain the empty reputation of a lay practitioner who has met with an enlightened master.
What is meant by "true investigation"? It is for the sake of resolving the matter of birth and death.

If one truly seeks to resolve birth and death, one must focus the mind on a single point and investigate to the limit. As Zhaozhou said: "If you do not awaken within seven days, I shall take off this old monk’s head."
Go! Yongjia said: "If you deceive sentient beings with false speech, you will yourself incur the punishment of having your tongue pulled out for kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
Observe the earnest and sincere compassion of the former sages; from this, one can personally believe in the truth of this matter. Therefore, Shishuang said:
"Rest! Cease! Let one thought endure for ten thousand years! Be like cold ashes and withered wood! Be like an incense burner in an ancient temple!
Be like a single length of white silk! Be cold and still! If these are but false seekers, upon reaching this point they will claim they have achieved their goal;
they will refuse to press straight ahead. They must examine their own hearts and ask: "Have you truly resolved the matter of life and death? No.

This is to deceive others; it is not to deceive Heaven, but rather to deceive oneself. Not only does one fall into the void of the external paths, but how can one face the karmic retribution for the great sin of deceitful speech?
One who truly seeks the Way through life and death would never, under any circumstances, stop here.
Have you not seen Xuefeng say: "Go on without rest, go on without ceasing; the karmic consciousness drifts on boundlessly, tumbling head over heels..."
They fall headlong; they sit and lie in the clamor of the crossroads; they play among thorns;
they go to the mountains of knives and swords, the cauldrons of boiling water, and the furnaces of glowing coals; they enter the wombs of donkeys and horses.
If you say that these two elders followed a separate path, those who hold such a view truly betray the profound kindness of their predecessors, whose eyebrows trailed upon the ground. Nevertheless...

If one does not reach [the goal], one will never cease or rest; only upon reaching it can one truly cease and rest. If one does not reach [the goal], the karmic consciousness will remain a blur of confusion;

only upon reaching it can one truly enter the state where "one thought-moment is ten thousand years. If one does not reach [the goal], one will remain in the sevenfold perversions and eightfold inversions.
If you cannot truly reach the state of withered wood and cold ashes, you will certainly not be able to truly reach the bustling crossroads.
If you cannot reach the incense burner in an ancient temple, you will certainly not be able to truly reach the single white silk cord.
If you cannot reach the forest of thorns to play therein, you will certainly not be able to truly reach the mountain of knives and the tree of swords.
One may even end up in the womb of a donkey or the belly of a horse; one will certainly be unable to truly reach that state of cold stillness.
Although one has not yet attained liberation from death and rebirth upon reaching this point, one truly sees the path of clearly transcending life and death. This is the statement of Mañjuśrī.
This is the stage when one's power has not yet reached full maturity. Nevertheless, regarding matters of merit and military affairs, Master Xiongquan Xin said:
"Continuity is truly difficult. Do you wish to understand the true face of continuity? It cannot be found by seeking it through hearing or seeing."
Performing good and evil, yet there is no meeting. The profound azure sky, the bright autumn moon shining clear. Throughout the great chiliocosm of dust-motes, the whole body is revealed.
*Tu!* Most strictly avoid hearing with the ears, seeing with the eyes, or understanding with the mind.
Birth and death are but a single matter, like a bubble floating upon the great ocean; fundamentally, they belong to the realm of emptiness and illusion.

Yet sentient beings delusively cling to them as real. This is precisely what my Buddha taught: that all sentient beings have, since beginningless time, continued in the cycle of birth and death because of their obscured ignorance regarding emptiness.
Within this darkness of emptiness, the obscurity coagulates into form. Form mingles with false conceptualization, and these conceptual appearances constitute the body. This...

Because perception is not true, there is cyclic existence. It is like abandoning the clear, vast ocean and instead identifying with the substance of a single floating bubble, calling that the entirety of the tide. As the Sūtra says, all matters are made clear through metaphors.
The Buddha stated that the cause for sentient beings' attachment to existence is like the arising of a floating bubble, which occurs because an object strikes it and the wind stirs it.
When they coalesce, they become floating bubbles; when they disperse, they are but the ocean water. My wondrously luminous enlightened nature is like the ocean water;

the sentient beings of the dust-like lands are like the floating bubbles. There is no day that the ocean water is ever exhausted, and there is no time when the floating bubbles are permanently extinguished.
Although they are born in this very place and extinguished in this very place, even this birth and extinction follows along with the ocean water.
Because it is inexhaustible. Sentient beings take the bubbles for themselves and observe the ocean water; the Tathāgata takes the ocean water for himself and regards the bubbles.

Sentient beings are not apart from the ocean, and the Tathāgata is not apart from the bubbles. One must know that the characteristics of arising and ceasing are identical to the characteristic of eternal abiding.
Therefore, the Buddha said: "This Dharma abides in its own place; the characteristics of the world are eternally abiding."
Furthermore, ignorant sentient beings not only do not know that the ocean is themselves, but they also do not know that their bubble is water.
Those who transfer into a womb or seize another's body are just like abandoning this bubble to take up that bubble.
Those who diligently seek long life are like those who use various skillful means to cherish and protect this bubble.

Those with supernatural powers and transformations are like those who use illusory arts to play with this bubble. Thus it is said: "Even after eighty thousand kalpas have passed, one ultimately falls into emptiness and extinction.
This is something that is both manifest and easy to understand. Good son, a great man should diligently seek this matter.
One must strive to investigate until one realizes that [the mind] is of the same substance as the ocean, and only then can it be called "accomplishing the task.

One cannot sit within a floating bubble and claim that the entire tide has been accomplished. Such people possess only a partial understanding; they are merely slightly superior to the common deluded.
To know that a bubble is water is why one who has not attained "great death" has not yet relinquished this bubble;
to attain "great life" is for the entire body to enter the sea. When it is said that "all worthies and sages have distinctions based on the dharma of non-action," it is like floating bubbles:
they do not exist only in the ocean; rivers, streams, lakes, and seas each have their own bubbles. Yet, the substance of the bubble is water.
The principle of their nature is fundamentally one. The various stages of cultivation and realization by sages and worthies are like rivers, streams, lakes, and oceans;
although they differ in size and depth, they cannot still be called mere floating bubbles. It is the same with Buddhas and sentient beings: their nature is non-dual.
One cannot say that sentient beings possess birth and death, nor can one say that sages and worthies are devoid of birth and death.
If you wish to understand birth and death, you need not seek it apart from birth and death; simply recognize within the floating bubble that the bubble is water.
As the proverb says: "Just go deep into the mountains; why fear there will be no wood to burn? You must by no means consider a small attainment to be sufficient.
Using a mind capable of conceptual inference, one recognizes the principle of the great ocean and then falsely claims to have realized it, ceasing all effort and coming to rest.
Not only does this constitute drawing lines to limit oneself, but it also results in a great deception that leads one to fall into infinite realms of suffering. As the ancients said:

"Those with intellectual understanding are many; those who possess both practice and understanding are not one in ten thousand. The above refers to the wondrous luminosity of the nature-awakening (*prakṛti-bodhi*).
Regarding this teaching, there is furthermore the principle of the luminous and wondrous Original Enlightenment (*ādi-bodhi*), which truly cannot be expressed by words.
If one is a man of iron, upon reaching this point, one will naturally comprehend it; there is no need for Yuanming to laboriously provide further annotations.
At the point where I cast down my brush in shame, thirty years hence there shall naturally be a faceless person who provides verification.
In the monasteries throughout the world, when the masters wield their mallets or raise their fly-whisks, and the Abbot speaks at every turn, saying:
"When letting go, it is thus and thus; when holding fast, it is thus and thus; when picking up, it is thus and thus;
when putting down, it is thus and thus"—this truly makes one burst into great laughter. How can such folly reach this point? Yet they still dare to speak so grandly, claiming this to be "Me."
As a Dharma King, you possess mastery over the Dharma; truly, I do not understand what kind of face or guts these people have.
This matter is fundamentally unshakable—who can let it go or hold it back? It is inherently complete—who can pick it up or put it down?
From the beginning, those who transcend Buddhas and patriarchs, proclaiming the fundamental tenet, sounding like rolling thunder and roaring like a lion, are the great virtuous ones.

There have been those among the learned who have occasionally made such a statement; however, this was merely the compassionate heart of one using yellow leaves to stop a child’s crying, or the talk of a grandfather sending off his grandson.
How could it ever compare to the blind-eyed Chan followers of today, who take this to be the ultimate and final principle?
Even this state of the "transformed city" (the provisional) has not yet been personally witnessed or trodden upon; it still belongs to the category of picking up others' tears.
To treat saliva as a delicacy—this is truly the most pitiable among the pitiable. This is the very root of the consciousness-essence (*vijñāna*) through which one undergoes birth and death.
To hold the heterodox views of annihilationism or eternalism is to mistake a thief for one’s own son; it is not merely to stop at the illusory city on the way.
To be thus self-deluded and ignorant, and thereby to mislead others—how can you bear this in your heart? Do you not fear the Buddha’s words of reproof?
Regarding this precept: when Chan practitioners encounter this teaching on "perfect clarity," they should each reflect upon themselves and interrogate their own minds.
Knowing shame and exerting effort, they should arouse a courageous and resolute spirit, striving to traverse the ultimate barrier and seek that great rest and cessation.

Only by thus continuing the Buddha’s wisdom-life will their renunciation and study not have been in vain; nor will the physical body bestowed by their parents have been wasted. This is what it means to be a "great man"—these three characters.
How much more so when Nanquan has clearly exposed it: "Returning home is entirely the business of the descendants; the patriarch has never gone out from the gate.
However, this single phrase must not be misunderstood. If one were to say that within this skin-bag there is a patriarch, [one would be mistaken].
To hold such a view—that one does not go beyond the gateway of this skin-bag—is no different from sitting in a well and gazing at the sky, or being blindfolded while pulling a millstone.
When it is said that mountains, rivers, grasses, and trees do not go beyond the gateway of mountains, rivers, grasses, and trees;

that dragons, phoenixes, *gūn* and *péng* fish do not go beyond the gateway of dragons, phoenixes, *gūn* and *péng*; and that pavilions, terraces, houses, and buildings do not go beyond the gateway of pavilions, terraces, houses, and buildings...

The patriarchs of the gates of palatial dwellings do not emerge from the gates of birds, beasts, or insects; the patriarchs of the gates of birds, beasts, or insects do not emerge from the gates of empty space;

the patriarchs of the gates of empty space do not emerge from the gates of dust-motes and lands; and the patriarchs of the gates of dust-motes and lands do not emerge from the gates of dust-motes and lands.
If this were so, then both sentient and insentient beings would each have their own ancestors, none of whom would ever leave their respective lineages.
Consequently, this skin-bag [the human body] is but one thing among the myriad phenomena, and it too would naturally possess ancestors who never depart from its own gate.
Investigate thus. Only through such investigation can awakening be attained. Have you not seen Linji say: "There is one person on the road who never leaves home;
there is another person at home who never leaves the road"? Only by understanding these two people will you understand the patriarch who never leaves his door.
But tell me, how do you understand this? To sum it up: returning home, he sits amidst the charcoal.
He asked again, "How does one return? [The Master] replied, "It is simply not returning that constitutes returning. Who can dispute the moonlight and breeze of one's native land?
He gave a shout and said, "A blade or an axe cannot split it open."
The words and phrases of the scriptures are known by all as pointers to the moon and rafts for crossing a river.
Once the Way has been seen, all know that these pointers and rafts must be abandoned; yet who does not realize that these are merely external pointers and rafts? Such is my single insight.
This is a raft marked within one's own body, yet people do not know to abandon it. Why is this? A sutra says:
"To perceive the absence of perception is precisely the untainted true nature. It also says: "At the moment of seeing the seer, that seeing is not [itself] seeing. Therefore, it is said:
When lost, the teacher ferries one across; when awakened, one ferries oneself across. A student must not be careless.
Generally, if one does not apply the utmost effort in learning worldly matters, one cannot achieve mastery.

Once mastery is achieved, one must reach the point where things are grasped spontaneously at the hand, such that there is no concern for the mind and no concern for affairs; only then can it be called refined and pure. Awakening to the transcendental world...
This is the Dharma of the interval. It is not that the ultimate state is without mind; it is simply that one’s awakening has not yet reached full penetration.

Once awakening has reached full penetration, one will necessarily arrive at responding to things according to conditions. When all phenomena are mind and all mind is phenomena, only then is it called the ultimate.

This teaching of perfect luminosity—when observed by those who have not yet attained the eye—is very much like a false discourse on *prajñā*. Who does not know that the ancients said: "Do not say there is no mind"?

This is precisely what is meant by the Way: "The mindless state, conversely, is separated by ten thousand layers of mountains. Allow me to provide a further commentary on this: ordinary people take their illusory minds to create illusory phenomena;
at the ultimate limit, they remain in the stage of the "mindless," which they fail to recognize as delusion and do not bring into the realm of awakening.

Practitioners of the Way dissolve the illusory mind to investigate True Suchness (Tathatā); at the ultimate limit, they reach the stage of the "True Mind," which they recognize as awakening and do not allow to enter into delusion.

This is precisely what is meant by being constantly alert and constantly lucid. This state is that which the Buddha described as abiding thus, maintaining thus, believing and understanding thus, and practicing thus.

Regarding the three seals (trīmudrā) proclaimed by the predecessors, it is often said that when those of superior capacity hear the Way, it is like a seal impressing upon space; when those of middling capacity hear the Way, it is like a seal impressing upon water;

and when those of inferior capacity hear the Way, it is like a seal impressing upon mud. Yuanming considers this to be incorrect. To guide beginners of inferior capacity, it is like a seal impressing upon space;
to guide those of middling capacity who have made progress, it is like a seal impressing upon water; and to guide those returning from the path...
The superior person is like a seal impressing clay. Why is this? If one speaks of the inferior person, they cling to existence and are hindered by words;
for them, how could it be said that they have heard the Way? It is up to those who act with mastery in all directions to examine this.

When a student first hears the Way, it is easy to realize the emptiness of objects, but difficult to realize the emptiness of the mind. Upon reaching ultimate realization, however, it is easy to realize the emptiness of the mind, but difficult to realize the emptiness of objects.

If one realizes the emptiness of objects but not the emptiness of the mind, there will be obstructions everywhere. If one realizes the emptiness of the mind but not the emptiness of objects, one will encounter stagnation at every turn.
One does not see the Way; the mind has passed the imperial examination through emptiness. One should know that outside the mind, what further thing could there be to be emptied?

Outside of things, what further mind could there be to be emptied? Therefore it is said: "I myself have no mind toward the myriad things; how can it hinder the myriad things from constantly surrounding me?
To have even a slight mind of discrimination is not the primary meaning (*paramārtha*). If it were otherwise, it would certainly not be so.
One can guard it;
the wondrously luminous ground of the mind is not difficult to realize. Simply prepare a heart of faith, and it is right before you.
Indeed, the mind of arising and ceasing is the very root of birth and death. All relative conditions—good and evil, right and wrong, self and other, and hatred and love—are but its manifestations.

Acceptance and rejection are both the nature of consciousness characterized by the arising and ceasing of ignorance. Within the wondrously luminous true mind of its original ground, there is truly no such entanglement.
A student of the Way need only recognize their original mind and see through the illusory mind of arising and ceasing;
they will then clearly understand the principle of birth and death. If they can thoroughly master this illusory mind of arising and ceasing, they will transcend the path of birth and death. Observe.
"Breaking through" refers to seeing; "accomplishing" refers to realization. On that path, there is no cultivation or guarding to be practiced.
Unless one has traversed and broken through the successive barriers so that subject and object become one, it cannot be lightly said to be easy.
How does this differ from those who forcibly assume mastery or those of inferior capacity who laugh when they hear the Way? All who enter the Way should reflect deeply upon themselves.
This is one matter. If you attempt to understand it through the extremes of speech or silence, there is no connection at all.
Those who are beginners and wish to clearly realize this matter must, as their primary task, cast aside all clever understanding, verbal expressions, and written characters.
Not a single word can be of any use. As the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra* says: "Rely on the meaning, not on the words. If one can enter directly with such a straightforward mind, [one will succeed].

One must certainly attain clear understanding and take this as the foundation for entering the Way. However, once one has entered, it is not permissible to remain silent and consider that to be the ultimate.
To say, "This single matter does not lie within words and phrases," and then proceed to strive for quiet contemplation of the mind, is what is called "escaping one pit only to fall into another.
Therefore, a sutra says: "Although it is not by means of the path of language, yet one must not be attached [to silence either]."
There is no verbal expression. Why is this? Language is but the name for phenomenal forms (*rūpa-lakṣaṇa*). If one cannot penetrate through its name, how can one penetrate through its essence?

If one is indeed able to penetrate its essence, one will naturally be able to penetrate its name. As long as the dualistic views of speech and silence are not eliminated, they both serve as causes for obstructing the Way.
I have briefly set forth the successive stages and order; those of superior faculties and great capacity will naturally [understand] them.
Understand this: one directly treads upon the Flower Treasury (Avataṃsaka).
When an ordinary person tills the field, they plow and sow from the surface of the earth; when a practitioner tills the field, they plow and sow from beneath the earth.
An ordinary field relies on seasonal rains to nourish the sprouts of grain; the sacred field requires the rain of Dharma to harvest the seeds. Thus, one must attend to the field of the mind.
Examine this carefully. Even if there were those with overweening pride who claimed that they sought the mind but could not find it, what further field would there be for them to plow or sow?
Such people would surely fail to avoid disappointing the Perfectly Bright One.
Those who possess true practice and clear eyes will naturally discern this for themselves.
When a student investigates and realizes the Way, within a mere instant they can clarify the illusory and false causes of birth and death.
They recognize the principle that one is born and dies precisely because one is already free from birth and death. Although this clarity occurs in a single moment, it cannot be limited by time.
If the true mind is not cultivated, there is no cultivation; if the illusory body is not realized, there is no realization. Therefore, it is said: "The Patriarch..."
To externalize the body and yet the body remains. When the Great Master Hanshan speaks of "changing," he means changing its form.

Now, there are two ways of externalizing through change: there is the way of externalizing the body by changing its form from within, and there is the way of externalizing the body by changing its form from without.
If one clings to externalizing from within, it is like being stuck in a shell and deluded by confinement. If one clings to [externalizing] from without...

External shifting is like being demented and running about outside. If one does not understand the two kinds of ways of external shifting, but merely dismisses everything in a vague, general manner and fails to practice the various deeds accordingly, then even if one passes through a thousand lifetimes and a hundred kalpas, it will remain nothing more than empty words.
Though one clearly knows that birth is not truly birth and death is not truly death, why is one still transmigrating under the sway of birth and death?
If you rely solely on your own strength, it will remain insufficient; you will be unable to "step upon solid ground" and fully comprehend the nature of birth and death.
For now, try to contemplate and internalize the principle of the two types of bodies—the internal and external—and how they interchange forms.
If you can grasp this through contemplation, I shall grant that you have understood the unified Way of the Buddhas and Immortals. If you cannot grasp it, you must not proceed.
To cling to a deluded emptiness is to deceive both oneself and others. Even regarding perfect luminosity (*yuanming*), I do not dare to claim it as my own full realization;
rather, what I perceive possesses actual and firm evidence. I merely wish to join with those who see the same truth, pledging together to strive and practice in harmony. Thus it is said.
The fifth day of the tenth month: the anniversary of the Patriarch’s birth. Wáng said: "The Great Being Dànmó was the first patriarch of great kindness to our Zhèndàn.
At the time of his western departure, he compassionately left behind his single sandal. We sentient beings of this eastern land—hundreds, thousands, ten millions, and billions in number—"
Furthermore, the Patriarch’s sandals also transformed into hundreds of thousands of millions of pairs of sandals, which were bestowed upon every person;
they remain before each of you even now. Why, then, do you all disregard this kindness and fail to repay his virtue by casting them aside?
Moreover, the very wall that the Master faced for nine years is likewise present before each of you day after day; why do you not investigate its meaning?
If you do not understand, Yuanming today shall reveal a message to all of you: "Penetrate! See through! Understand! Pass through!
Wang said, "Those who study the Way fail to realize the nature of mind; they do not cling to existence, yet they cling to non-existence.

When they do not cling to these two, they instead engage in conjecture and deliberation within the realm of existence and non-existence. Even when they perceive this illness for themselves, they remain stuck in the 'neither'."

There is neither existence nor non-existence, yet there is attachment to these inversions. For this reason, the ancients earnestly bestowed their instructions, commanding us to distance ourselves from the discourse of the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*).

These four propositions are: existence, non-existence, neither existence nor non-existence, and both existence and non-existence. If one can penetrate through these four propositions, how should one maintain [this realization]?
When encountering any phenomena that exist, I likewise accord with them and allow them to exist. However—
One is not obstructed by this "existence. When encountering all phenomena as non-existent, I also accord with them and treat them as non-existent;

yet this is not the mundane, vacuous negation of non-existence. When encountering all phenomena as both existent and non-existent, I also accord with them and treat them as both existent and non-existent, without engaging in the conceptual proliferation of ordinary minds. When encountering all phenomena as neither existent nor...
"No. I also accord with them by granting that it is neither existent nor non-existent; furthermore, this does not involve mutual contradiction.
This is what Vimalakīrti meant when he said that you would likewise fall into the same error as the six heretical teachers.
If it were not thus, one could not lightly claim to have transcended the four propositions. Take care."
One day, Ou-yun happened to say: "The Buddhas of the ten directions share one single path to the gate of Nirvāṇa.

From of old, when this principle was brought up for discussion, Qianfeng’s staff with its single stroke was considered supreme; yet it cannot be said that he did not err in being too obscure. Today, Yuanming shall once again open another face:
"The years and teeth are similar in form, but the crow and the bird do not share the same heart. Now tell me, is this the same as Qianfeng’s, or is it different?
If you can examine and discern this, I grant that you have found the single path through the gate of Nirvana.

Heaven has no intention to cover, yet it universally shelters; the earth has no intention to support, yet it universally sustains; the three luminaries have no intention to illuminate, yet they universally shine;
the Sage has no intention to act, yet he universally responds. The distinction between the holy and the ordinary is separated by a mere hair’s breadth, existing only in—
It is merely a distinction between having a mind and being without a mind. Thus it is said: "If a person can remain constantly pure and clear, heaven and earth will all return to them.
How much more so for the myriad phenomena of the universe—how could they ever obstruct or hinder me?

Since one has become a human being, why not emulate the heavens and the earth, and follow the Three Luminaries to become a True Person? Would this not be a source of great joy? There was a follower who...
Jin said, "If that is so, then Your Highness is naturally able to transcend the mundane and enter the sacred. The King said, "Bah! What words are these?

He replied, "As for the single character 'sage' (sheng), how could I dare claim it? However, to cultivate without weariness and to instruct others without satiety—this might perhaps be called being such."
A question was asked: "What is the true person of no station? The Master said: "Greed. He added: "This single word has already depicted the playful activities of the true person of no station.
If you do not recognize it, you can only add a superfluous foot to a serpent.
As for what is called the "true person of no station," it is fundamentally not without station; it is merely given the forced name "no station. If one were to say it has a station, then...

This is the state of no-position. To speak of others having no position is itself to have a position. If you wish to recognize the True Person of No-Position, you must understand him from within the realm of positions.
It is like a person who does not abide in the four directions—east, south, west, or north—but stands right here.
If one looks toward this person from the east, one calls him "west"; if one looks toward this person from the west, one calls him "east. The same applies to the south and north.
This is to lose one position and fall into four positions. It is the same for above and below, and so on, even down to every atom and every world-system (*kṣetra*).
Thus, every atom and every world-system is entirely the "True Person with Position. To raise a single word is the True Person with Position;
yet, the hundreds, thousands, ten-thousands, millions, and billions [of words] are the "True Person without Position. From this, one should investigate each instance and expand [the understanding].
How could one be called a "True Person with Rank"? Since he cannot be named a "True Person with Rank," how can he not be the "True Person Without Rank"?
Thus, the name "True Person Without Rank" is established in this way; it is derived from the "True Person with Rank.
Therefore, existence arises because of non-existence, and non-existence arises because of existence. Non-existence is...

This is existence. Existence is itself non-existence. If you seek the "True Man of No-Station" apart from existence and non-existence, even if you were to search until the year of the donkey, you would not dream of finding him. If you still do not understand, investigate!
A monk asked, "How does one protect the true person of no station? The King remained silent for a long while. The monk said, "I earnestly beg for instruction. The King replied:

"To protect the true, simply transform the delusory; as the delusory is transformed, it naturally returns to the true. Through continuous transformation and guidance, when delusion is exhausted, the true is fully realized.
The name 'true' is established because of delusion; once delusion is exhausted, what name can be given to the 'true'? True reality does not establish itself; it is [only known] through this."
[The Master] named it "Protecting the Truth. [The King] asked: "Does Your Highness still expound the teachings, or do you respond to the occasion?
The King said: "First I expound the teachings; afterwards I respond to the occasion. [The Master] said: "A patch-robed monk cannot provide a detailed analysis of this. The King said:

"Does the Great Master understand Avalokiteśvara’s thousand hands and thousand eyes? [The Master] said: "I do not understand. The King said: "If you do not understand, then the eighty-four thousand [pores] of perfect luminosity—"
With his mouth agape, Zhangli could not manage to offer an explanation. The monk bowed in thanks. The King laughed and said, "Why do you not say:
'Today I have finally seen the talkative Prince'?"
A monk asked, "Who is it that does not take the myriad dharmas as his companion? Wang said, "This phrase must be swallowed whole.
The monk said, "I do not understand. Wang said, "Close your eyes and drill yourself into the midst of the sands of the Ganges.

The monk said, "If that is so, then Mazu’s saying, 'Sucking up the waters of the West River in one gulp,' was in error. Wang said, "Those of middle capacity and below certainly cannot [understand this]."
This is because it refers to the supreme.
A monk asked: "It is not mind, not Buddha, and not a thing; what is it ultimately? Wáng said: "It is six."
The monk said, "It goes like this, it goes like that. The King said, "One must still add or subtract a little bit before it becomes perfect.
On the Mid-Autumn Festival, a monk asked, "If the fundamental nature is originally pure, why do mountains, rivers, and the great earth suddenly arise?
The King said, "These twelve characters themselves cannot be dispensed with. The monk asked, "How does one practice? The King said, "When a guest arrives, I..."
He then went out. "How could I fear that we would not be close? The monk asked, "Is there anything further above this? The King said, "Be careful not to celebrate the Mid-Autumn Festival.
The monk clapped his hands. The King said, "I am drunk and wish to sleep; you may go now."
On New Year’s Eve, a monk asked, “What is one’s original face before one’s parents were born? Wang said, “The years slip by;
what leisure is there for idle speculation? The monk said, “I, this humble monk, ask with utmost sincerity and truth. Wang said, “...”
"Next year, on this month, this day, and at this hour, I shall speak it to you. The monk bowed in thanks. The King took his brush, signed with a seal, and said:
"This is established for your records."
At the end of the year, the King arrived at Berlin. He wrote "Spring Blessings" and distributed them to the assembly.
A monk approached and said, "The entire Tripitaka has been given away as alms by Your Majesty. The King took up his brush with his hand and made a dot upon his own forehead. The monk said:
The King asked, "Why do you dot your own forehead? The King said, "I dot it myself so that others shall not dot me.
The monk said, "A master king! Today there are many people and monks here. The King pointed to his forehead and dotted it, saying, "This dot is mine;
it is a person. The monk bowed in embarrassment. The King quickly took an *upānaha* (cloth) to wipe away the ink dot. There was another monk.
Xuchun said, "Gold does not trade with gold. Why did Your Highness wipe the ink from Upa? The King said, "When you visit various quarters, you must never mention this.
One must distinguish black from white. The monk said, "I, a humble patch-robed monk, dare not do so. The King said, "..."
"Washing water is water. An old monk standing nearby said, "Your Majesty’s is truly a divine mechanism (xianji). The King said, "Whether it is a divine mechanism or not has no evidence;
I know full well that you do not understand Buddhist talk. Another monk said, "I beg Your Majesty to speak some Buddhist talk for us to hear.
The King said, "First, write the character for 'longevity' (shòu). The monk said, "What Your Majesty has written is the character for 'blessing' (fú); how can you say [it is longevity]?"
The character for "longevity" (壽). The King said, "Have you not heard it said that among the five blessings of humanity, longevity comes first?

The old monk clapped his hands and laughed, saying, "How interesting! The King said, "An eighty-year-old grandfather chewing on corn stalks. The old monk said, "I, this poor monk, truly do not understand these words.
The King said, "So old and decrepit, when have you ever tasted even a hint of flavor? The assembly laughed, speechless. The King—
He said: "Today, for no reason, I have repeatedly been struck on the forehead.
One day while practicing archery, everyone else drew blanks, yet only I, a skilled archer among the guards, hit the mark with every arrow.

When the rewards and punishments were discussed after the shooting was finished, the King punished me, the skilled archer, and rewarded the others. The man asked: "My arrows all hit the mark; why, on the contrary..."
"Are you to be punished? the King asked. The man replied, "What I was discussing was the middle ground; what you were discussing was the very center. How could I not be punished?
The King said, "If it were discussed in such a manner, it would have been an easy matter. It was originally an easy task; who taught you to make it difficult for yourself?
Everyone laughed heartily, and the King then bestowed a generous reward upon the skilled archer.
One day, the King enjoyed wine while viewing flowers. Returning to his chambers late in the evening, he called for an attendant to bring a lamp.

The attendant held the lamp and entered the room; the King blew it out and said, "Bring a lamp! The attendant relit the lamp and was just arriving when the King blew it out again and said, "Bring a lamp!
The attendant said, "The King is drunk. The King shouted, "Quickly, bring a lamp! The attendant hurried...
He lit the lamp again and entered the room, holding it aloft. The King said, "Look closely under the lamp. [The Master] replied, "It is I who am drunk;
it is you who are drunk.
One day, while fishing, an attendant presented the caught fish to the King. The King asked, "What water did you catch in your net?"
[The Master] did not present them all at once. The King said, "How can a net be used to catch water? The Master said, "Water cannot be caught in a net; how then can fish be caught?

The Master laughed and said, "This very fish is what is caught by the net. The King asked, "What is the net? The Master said: *Note: This dialogue is a classic example from the *Wumenguan* (Gateless Barrier), Case 13, concerning the encounter between Emperor Wu of Liang and National Teacher Huizhong.*
By the side of a pond, the King said, "What a pity! He ordered his attendants to carry the fish away to release them.
One of the attendants asked, "In seeking to realize the Way through Zen meditation, one seeks only the True Self.
What is this True Self? I pray the King will instruct me. The King said, "Water is heavy; mercury is light. The attendant said, "How can water be heavy like mercury?"
Li said, "Your Majesty, if it is as you say, then the entire great ocean is nothing but mercury.
The Emperor said, "In total calculation, naturally there is more water and less mercury. Li said, "Foolish man! Who did not teach you to calculate in total?"
One evening, an attendant requested instruction on the method for realizing the mind and seeing one's nature.
The King said, "If you wish to catch fish and shrimp, you may do so by setting up a lamp within the great ocean. The attendant replied, "How can one set up a lamp in the water?"
The King said, "Since one cannot light a lamp within water, how can the mind be made clear? How can the nature be seen?

The Master said, "If it is thus, does the principle of clarifying the mind and seeing the nature not exist? The King said, "It is not that the principle does not exist; it is simply that there is no such principle.
The Master said, "I am even more confused and do not understand. The King asked, "Candraprabhā (Moonlight)..."
"Not yet. The Master replied, "The moon has not yet risen. The King said, "Wait until the moon rises, and I shall tell you further.
A monk requested instruction and asked, "When one has already trodden through empty space, how should one proceed thereafter? The King said, "Go toward the Great Essence.
The monk said, "Even if there were someone who entered directly into a thousand peaks and ten thousand mountains, would there still be anything left to do?"
[The Master] said, "No. The King said, "A cow passing through a window lattice. The monk asked, "Is this not the place where one establishes one's body and sustains one's life?
The King said, "The body is not the body; life is not life. The monk said, "I, this poor monk, have seen through the King’s wiles."
The King said, "Great Being, how do you address me today? The monk said, "Your Highness, Prince Yongqin.
The King said, "If that is so, I have not yet granted you my full examination."
One day, the King heard the sound of a bell from a watchtower. He asked, "What sound is that? The attendant replied, "It is the sound of a bell.
The King said, "I thought it was the sound of a drum. The attendant laughed and said, "Why do you mistake the sound of a bell for a drum to deceive this humble servant?
The King asked, "Did you see the bell being struck? The attendant replied, "Even though I did not see it, I could hear it was a bell."
[The Master] made a sound. The King shook his hand and said, "It was you who deceived me.
One night, as the King sat, he suddenly heard the wind rise. He called to his attendant; the attendant responded and entered. The King said, "The wind called for you, yet you did not answer."
The King called out, "Come! and the attendant immediately responded. The King asked, "Why is this? The attendant had no reply. The King said, "When the wind calls you, you go at once;
when I call you, you do not come. Why is this? Again, the attendant had no reply. The King said, "The main gate is closed.
The attendant said, "It is not yet. The King said, "Open it! Open it!"
A monk asked, "The boy holds up a mirror; what is the meaning of this? The King said, "The tricks of a small child.
The monk asked, "What is the activity of a great man? The King said, "I am instructing him not to hold it. The monk said, "Your Majesty is truly noble and exalted. The King said, [silently].

"I thought you were a child," the King said. The monk then gave a shout. The King said, "The behavior of a child is fully revealed. The monk said, "By all means, do not suppress the noble to serve the base.
The King said, "The public case is right here before us. The monk said, "In that case, Your Highness has accepted the full responsibility for the matter.
The King said, "I can do nothing but be dragged down by you, Master. The monk said, "It becomes even more unbearable. The King said, "A lacquer bucket! (i.e., a dull-witted person).
This became a laughingstock for practitioners everywhere.
A monk asked, "The great ocean is without waves; why does it surge with wind and billows? Wáng said, "Precisely because it is without mind. The monk said, "..."
"Originally pure by nature, why do you give rise to emotions when encountering conditions? The King said, "It is precisely because there is intention. [The Master] asked, "How do you practice?

The King said, "Where there is intention, there is no mind; where there is no mind, there is intention. [The Master] said, "If that is so, then the blessings and rewards of humans and devas are not lacking;
yet, within the school of the patch-robed monks, you still fall short by one move. The King said, "Try to reveal some news for me. The monk [remained silent].
The monk then gave a shout. The King said, "A fellow with a dragon's head and a snake's tail. The monk asked, "And what about you, Your Majesty?
The King also shouted. The monk shouted again. The King said, "Indeed, you are covered in scales all over. The monk laughed and said, "Withdraw."
While sitting in seclusion, an attendant requested instruction, saying: "The ancient worthies often gave answers consisting of a single word;
what was the underlying meaning? The King said: "Try asking yourselves. [Attendant] asked: "What is the Buddha? The King said: "Heaven. [Attendant] asked: "What is the Dharma? The King said: "Earth.
[Attendant] asked: "What is the Sangha? The King said: "People. [Attendant] asked: "What is... (The King said: "...the same as before."
"It is not the Buddha. The King said, "A thing. [The Master] asked, "What is 'not the mind'? The King said, "The Buddha.
[The Master] asked, "What is 'not a thing'? The King said, "The mind. [The Master] asked, "What is 'the myriad dharmas returning to the One'? The King said, "Open."
Question: What is the meaning of "the one return"? Where does it go? The Master said: "To join. Question: What is the meaning of "the cypress tree in front of the courtyard"?
The Master said: "To enter. Question: What is the intent behind "blowing on the fur"? The Master said: "To follow. Question: [Untranslated] The Master said: [Untranslated]
[Question: What is the meaning of “three pounds of flax”? [Wang] said: *Ci*. [Question: What is one’s original face before birth?
[Wang] said: *Xue*. [Question: What is Zhaozhou’s Barrier? [Wang] said: *Chuan*. [Question: What is the Ruler? [Wang] said: *Ren*. [Question:
What is the Minister? [Wang] said: *Yi*. [Question: What is...? [Wang] said: *...* (The text ends here).
"Ministers serve their sovereign. The King said, "Ritual. [The Master] asked, "What is it for the sovereign to approach the ministers? The King said, "Wisdom.

Jue seems almost to have taken Zhang San for Li Si. This monk was like a Han-lu hound chasing after a clod of earth;

Speaking thus, is there anyone who can examine this? When the wise see it, they call it wisdom; when the benevolent see it, they call it benevolence.
It is not that it is difficult for others to dwell with; rather, for the most part, the distinction between the monastic and the lay must be clear.
One day, during a meal with the monks, the King raised the following case: "In the past, Huanglong Xian and Xia Gongli were discussing the beginning of the Great Treatise on the Awakening of Faith.
They were debating how sentient beings and insentient things share a single essence. At that time, a dog was lying under the incense table. Huanglong took up his ruler and struck the dog;
he then struck the incense table and said: 'The dog has sentience and leaves; the incense table lacks sentience and remains.'"
"How can the sentient and the insentient become one body? Gongli was unable to answer.
Lingyan Yun said, "If you wish to understand how the sentient and the insentient are one body, kill the sentient dog and smash the insentient incense table;
then take them together as a single bundle and cast them into the great ocean. Naturally, they will be free and unencumbered."—Hongjue.
Ming said: "How can one still teach a sentient dog to keep watch? Let the insentient incense table remain for its intended use.
If you wish to realize that the sentient and the insentient are of one essence, simply cut through all that is conceptualized, deliberated, or measured with a single stroke.
Then the ten directions will be vast and empty, and the eternal light will naturally appear before you. What 'sentient being' could there be to call?"
Inanimate objects act as obstacles and conditions for you. From the perspective of Perfect Clarity (*yuanming*), both elders involve themselves in merit-seeking;

One day, while sitting in the company of the monks, the King said: "Mañjuśrī establishes all dharmas from the ground of non-abiding;
Yuanming establishes the ground of non-abiding from all dharmas. I ask you, worthy ones: where do their similarities and differences lie?
Some said, "Clouds when one turns the hand over; rain when one covers the hand. Some said, "Today we gaze up in reverence. Some said, "The Yellow River has nine bends."
Regarding the waters emerging from Mount Kunlun: some say that one must wear precious robes and hang a soiled garment before being worthy of the Prince;
others say that when the Prince ascends the hall, Mañjuśrī dismisses the assembly. The Prince said, "Neither is it so. Mañjuśrī precedes Heaven, yet Heaven does not oppose him;
Yuánmíng follows Heaven, yet he serves according to the timing of Heaven. Now tell me, are Yuánmíng and Mañjuśrī the same? Or are they different?
"Identity and difference. Some say that the Mañjuśrī of the past is the Prince of the present.

Some say that Mañjuśrī’s house is on the road while the Prince’s house is on the road. Some say that if they are identical, they are entirely identical; if they are different, they are entirely different.
Some say that Manjusri does not recognize the Prince, and the Prince does not recognize Manjusri.
Some say it is permissible to call the Prince "Manjusri" and to call Manjusri "the Prince. The King said: "Neither is the realm of perfect luminosity.
Manjusri is perfect luminosity, yet perfect luminosity is not Manjusri."
While sitting in seclusion, the assembly was guarding and attending at his side. One attendant asked, "What is the true self of a servant?
The King pointed to himself and said, "It is I. The attendant replied, "How could a lowly person like me dare to be so? The King said, "This is the truth."
The monk said, "If that is so, what will Your Highness do for me? The King said, "It is you. The monk asked, "How can there be 'master and servant' between you and me?
The King pointed again to another person and said, "It is he. The assembly did not understand. The King said, "In the Buddha-dharma, all things are equal;
there is no distinction between self and other, noble and base, or right and wrong. The monk said, "If that is so, then one would have to call one's descendants by the name of their ancestors."

"Father, is this permissible? The King said, "Excellent is this question! All sentient beings, because they cling to a delusory self, cause both filial piety and compassion to become illusory—illusory filial piety and illusory compassion. Because they cling to a self, there is filial piety and lack of filial piety;
there is compassion and lack of compassion. Because the Bodhisattva is free from the notion of self, he shares in the same power of compassion as all Buddhas."
Below, one shares the same sorrowful longing as all sentient beings; in being filial and respectful toward one’s ancestors, one shares that same sorrowful longing;
in loving one’s descendants, one shares that same compassionate power. Thus, there is only filiality and compassion, and if one seeks unfiliality or lack of compassion, they are utterly unfindable.
This is what is called true filiality. True compassion is this very filiality and compassion; it is the true self. Extending this principle further—
This applies to all things and all principles. The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "Take the bodhicitta as one's home, and take practice in accordance with reality as one's family law.
An ancient master said: "The Buddha-dharma does not destroy worldly appearances. [Otherwise,] one is like a frog at the bottom of a well.
Those foolish people who sit in a well and gaze at the sky slander the Śākya school like the heterodox outsiders such as Yang Zhu and Mo Di, claiming that [the Buddha] has neither father nor ruler.
How is this any different from looking up and spitting at the clouds—only to bring shame upon oneself?

These are all blind arguments by those who have not seen the true countenance [of the Dharma]. You must by no means be deluded by such heterodox teachings. These are the earnest words of our Confucian Sage.
Regarding the dharmas of the mundane world, the Buddha rarely spoke of "fate" (*niyati*) and "humaneness" (*ren*). This was not because he abandoned the supramundane dharma;

rather, it was because he feared that ordinary, ignorant people would become attached to the view of emptiness (*śūnyatā-dṛṣṭi*). When the Buddha explained the supramundane dharma with such urgency, he rarely spoke of "right" and "wrong. This was not because he abandoned the mundane dharma;
rather, it was because he feared that ordinary, ignorant people would become attached to the view of existence (*bhava-dṛṣṭi*). Thus, the teachings of the Śākya are truly existent.

The Sage’s teaching on "cultivating one's own brilliance and transforming the people" and "overcoming the self to return to ritual propriety" truly complements the Buddha’s teachings on precepts, conduct, and merit, as well as the doctrine of causes, conditions, and karmic retribution. These two Sages of the East and West are indeed complementary to one another;
their compassionate grace in transforming beings and delivering the world is truly without difference. This is the subtle essence of the unity of the Sage and the Buddha.
The essential meaning cannot be inferred by the intellectual knowledge of ordinary people, nor can it be demonstrated by speech or pen; it is known only through realization.
That which is difficult to fathom requires each person to exert themselves in investigation. I have indeed attained the principle of the single thread;
this is not a theory established through forced discrimination. You shall certainly not be deceived.

The King said, "Furthermore, you say that the Way has no place of abiding. The Master said, "I, a person of the lowest ignorance, truly have great doubts.
The King said, "Bring your doubts to me. The Master said, "How could I, a lowly person, give my own doubts to Your Majesty? The King said, "..."

A follower asked, "When an ox passes through a window frame, its head, horns, and four hooves all pass through; why is it that its tail cannot pass?
The King asked, "Did you see the ox pass through the window? He replied, "I did not. The King said, "Do not listen to such things for now."
The man was deceived. He said, "How could the patriarchs of the past have spoken deceptively? The King said, "Naturally. How could the patriarchs have spoken deceptively?
[The man] said, "Where is the previous statement of Your Majesty? The King said, "Listen to the truth and do not let yourself be deceived by others.
The man was at a loss. The King laughed and said, "Do not underestimate people. Yuanming is also one who does not speak deceptive words."
A follower asked the Patriarch. Xuan Sha said, "How would you receive someone who is deaf, blind, and mute? If you were to encounter such a person, Prince, what would you do?
The Prince said, "I would receive him with incense. The follower said, "But what if his nostrils were also plugged?"
"What else can be done? the King asked. The attendant replied, "Give him an anesthetic drug to drink.
The Master said, "In that case, he will have no consciousness at all. What then? The King said, "I have already received him for you. The attendant did not understand.
The King said, "It appears that you are even more difficult to receive than this patient."
An attendant asked: "Xiangyan said, 'Mouth holding a tree branch, neither hands nor feet grasping or treading upon it.
