The King said, "As for one with such a bad intention, why would I gather him? Nevertheless, it is only when you descend from the tree that you will find safety."
A monk from Rehe asked, "When a single mote of dust enters into meditative absorption, all motes of dust arise in samādhi. What is the meaning of this?

The Master said, "Our Emperor is on his tour of inspection; those within and without welcome him with joy. The monk asked, "Will he then ascend the precious throne? The Master said, "It is not that he will not ascend it."
[The Master] said, "It is as if we were walking together. [Yunmen] said, "The four seas and five lakes are all within the realm of the King’s transformation.

The King said, "As for the clear breeze and bright moon, the green water and blue mountains—what connection do they have [to this]? [Yunmen] said, "In such a case, one does not speak of difference within sameness;

nor does one speak of sameness within difference. The King said, "If one makes distinctions, it is not permissible. [Yunmen] asked, "How then should one conduct oneself? The King said, "Virtuous One, you speak."
"How far is it from here to the capital? The monk bowed in thanks. The King said, "One must not take the road as one's home.
The monk said, "Furthermore, one's home is never apart from the road. The King said, "I thought you, Venerable One, would understand it in this way."
An attendant asked, "What does the golden fish that has passed through the net eat? The King said, "It eats earth. The attendant said, "I do not understand, Master.

The King said, "If it were escaping from a pit and falling into a ditch, would it not be eating earth? What would it be eating then? Again, [the attendant] asked, "What constitutes the life-force of the golden fish that has passed through the net?
The King said, "Fire is its life-force. The attendant said, "I still do not understand, Master. The King said, "To avoid drowning, one throws oneself into fire."
"Huìhuǒ! Naturally, one takes fire as one's life. The follower remained silent. The King said, "If you understand, why do you remain silent?
If you do not understand, why do you remain silent? He replied, "I still do not understand. The King said, "What fine news! It is a pity that you have merely added 'not understanding' to it."
A monk asked, "What is it that one person cannot enter, no matter how much effort they exert? The King said, "The kite flies up to the heavens.

[The monk] asked, "What is it that one person cannot emerge from, no matter how much effort they exert? The King said, "The fish leap in the deep pool. [The monk] asked, "How far apart are these two people?
The King said, "They are discerned above and below."
A monk asked, "Heaven cannot cover it; earth cannot support it. In the midst of a bustling marketplace as vast as the sands of the Ganges, please, Your Majesty, point out one such person.
The King said, "Why ask about a second moon? The monk asked, "What is the moon? The King said, "When you arrive, do not point it out.
The monk said, "I shall go just like that. The King said, "Guarantee it! Guarantee it!"
An attendant asked, "What is the very essence of the Dharma of the Buddhas and Patriarchs? The King said, "You ask and I answer.
The attendant said, "Your Majesty has not answered. The King said, "I do not answer; you do not ask.
The attendant said, "If that is so, then both asking and not asking, as well as answering and not answering, are all the very essence of the Dharma. The King said, "As for asking and not asking—"
"Whether answering or not answering, both are not the definitive Dharma," [the King] said. The student replied, "I do not understand;

I beg Your Majesty to reveal the definitive Dharma of the Buddhas and Patriarchs. The King laughed and said, "Apart from this, what definitive Dharma of the Buddhas and Patriarchs could I give to you?
The student remained silent. The King said, "The phrase 'pointing directly upward' has already been taken by you; there is nothing more."
It can be so explained.
A monk asked, “When not a single thing is brought forth, what then? The King said, “A greedy official meets with confiscation.
The monk asked, “If all things are complete within oneself, how is that? The King said, “This too is like a beggar obtaining a small profit. The monk asked, “As for these two...”

"On this path, there is neither grasping nor rejecting. How should one practice? The King said, "Remain purely clear. [The Master] asked, "Is this pure clarity the same as being alertly aware, or are they different?
The King said, "There may be times when one is alertly aware yet not purely clear; however, there is no principle by which one could be purely clear and not alertly aware.
[The Master] asked, "Is there still something further beyond this? The King said, "There is. [The Master] said, "I beg the King to point it out to me. The King said:
"When the momentum of a thousand peaks reaches its destination, and the sound of ten thousand streams returns to their source," he said. "At this time and in this place, can a message be conveyed?
Wang said, "Today is the fifteenth; it cannot be spoken of. Wait until the first day of the month, and we shall deliberate together."
A monk asked, "How is it that one person cannot go out from within the gate, while another cannot enter from outside the gate?
The King said, "Why build a wall out of thin air? The monk said, "Yet he is able to come and go with complete freedom. The King said:
"What suffering is there in running out and running in? The monk said, "If that is so, then the imperial wind forms a single expanse;
where can one find boundaries? The King said, "Give me back the tree in the center. The monk said, "From of old, my ancestors have never gone outside the door.
The King laughed and said, "Excellent! Then tear down the wall! The monk made a gesture of clapping his hands. The King said, "This very thing is the wall. The monk gave a shout. The King—
[The Master] said, "The word 'cloud' (yun) is itself the gate. [The Master] said, "I invite Your Majesty to enter and look out.
The King said, "In my royal palace, there are no such slaves as you. The monk remained silent. The King said, "Your skills are exhausted; you have committed no further offense.

[The Master] said, "Having arrived here, what would Your Royal Highness say? The King said, "I shall provide a word for you. Return it to me, my royal palace. The monk bowed his head and said, "Indeed so."
The Prince of Yong, a literary scholar, said: "Fortunately, I am not one who understands the 'inner circle' (the *zhizhen*).
Two monks coming from the south came to pay their respects; as they were just entering the hall, the Prince said, "Virtuous ones, I recognize one of you, but I do not recognize the other.
The two monks replied, "We both see Your Highness for the first time. The Prince said, "Yuanming says..."
[The Master] said, "It is about one's previous life. The monk said, "Does Your Highness perhaps possess the supernormal power of knowing past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-jñāna*)?
The King said, "This is not the perfectly luminous supernormal power of knowing past lives; it is simply that you, Venerable, have not yet understood the talk of before birth.

[The monk] asked, "What is the talk of before birth? The King said, "One is knowing, and one is not knowing. The two monks smiled with joy and prostrated themselves. The King said, "Nor should this be explained as two separate things."
During the tea ceremony, the King said, "One person drinks the tea; the other is drunk by the tea. He then said, "Three before, three after.
The King remarked, "Yet this is not the principle of it."
A monk asked, "If I am 'existence,' what then? The Master said, "One must wait for existence to manifest. The monk asked, "If I am 'emptiness,' what then?"
The King said, “One must wait for the sky to appear. The monk asked, “How shall one settle the entanglements of the past?
The King said, “It is just as if there were an assembly. The monk said, “In the end, this is not the ultimate. The King said, “Use the flameless ice-fire to go forth.

The monk said, “If so, then it is a single snowflake in a great furnace. The King said, “Be careful. The monk performed a full prostration and said, “I offer this body and mind to serve every dust-mote world.”
"How shall I look up to repay the grace of our King? The King said, "One who knows gratitude cannot [be said to] 'attain' it.

The monk wept with emotion and bowed in thanks, saying, "This is yet another layer of grace; how could I not be moved by gratitude? The King laughed and said, "The blind donkey has gone off in that way once again."
A monk from Berlin arrived at the Prefectural Office. During the seating order, the King asked him, "What is the meaning of 'the cypress tree in front of the courtyard'?
The King said, "Tell me, at Berlin Monastery tomorrow they will dismiss the assembly; tomorrow they will serve the midday meal."
A practitioner asked, "The great sun overflows the eyes; ten thousand miles are not hung with a single cloud. What is the meaning of this?
Wang said, "Just go and let others see."

A Confucian scholar asked about the similarities and differences among the Three Teachings. The King said: "If we discuss that which is within the circle [of ultimate reality], the Three Teachings are in truth one and the same Way.
One must not become mired in external signs and forms, nor engage in worldly affairs to give rise to arbitrary distinctions.

Confucianism establishes its teachings through the cultivation of the self, the regulation of the family, the ordering of the state, and the bringing of peace to all under heaven; Daoism establishes its teachings through emptiness and purity. When one investigates the reason why they were shown to people,"

Those who cannot look beyond this very thing, yet whose Buddhist teachings likewise do not abandon this very thing—since they do not abandon it, then speaking from within this very thing, it would be incorrect not to call it a single thread running through all.
If one considers what lies outside of this, the books of Zhou, Confucius, Huang-Lao have never mentioned this; those capable of clarifying it are found only in the Buddhist scriptures.

The inferior person is ignorant and blind; their wisdom is slight and their vision shallow. They claim that since they do not even clearly understand what is within the circle, how could they have the leisure to investigate what is outside it?
Not knowing what is within the circle, they rely on what is outside it to establish themselves.

If one does not understand what is outside the circle, then as for what is within, there is no question of being able to suddenly penetrate through to the ground. Even if one reaches the ultimate limit, it is still...
There is this very circle here. People merely know how to be obstructed and stagnant within birth and death;
they do not know how to exhaustively investigate that which is unborn and undying. This is a great barrier; only by this single path can one penetrate it.

Even when discussing Buddhism from the perspective of the Vinaya, how has it ever not been a single thread with the *zong* (the fundamental principle)? It must be unified and encompassed by the *zong*; otherwise, it is entirely [incomplete].
It belongs to the realm of illusion; the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) is the primary principle. Yet, even "one" is not established—this alone constitutes the intent of the Buddha.

By observing this through that, one clearly understands the definitive doctrine regarding the convergence and divergence of the three teachings. How could Perfect Enlightenment (*Yuanming*) ever willingly endure the slanders of you迂儒 (pedantic Confucians)?
He would never, for all eternity, allow sentient beings to remain submerged in the sea of suffering without being rescued or having their delusions dispelled. Upon hearing this, the scholar...
He was struck with astonishment. He assented and withdrew.
On the eighth day of the fourth month, while sitting beneath the moon, an attendant pointed at the moon and asked, "Why is that other half not visible?
The King said, "It is only natural that it should be so."
A Confucian scholar asked, "What are the six kinds of divine functions? Wang said, "The craftsmen in the cave need only two;
they need not be two.
While taking a leisurely stroll by the stream, a scholar asked, "How can one become as bright and pure as the light of a deep, clear pool? Wang said:
Subtracting a small portion from the present moment.

A monk asked, "Regarding the full illumination of this matter, is there a direct path that points it out immediately? Wáng said, "There is. It does not go beyond the meaning of the Buddha’s scriptures and the patriarchs' intent;
it is simply that people are negligent and do not realize it. Thus, the three piṭakas and twelve divisions of the canon are nothing other than [this].
He expounded that form is emptiness and emptiness is form; this is the separate transmission outside the teachings.
Throughout the generations, the patriarchs have proclaimed nothing other than the single phrase: "Mind is Buddha. You need only understand that form is emptiness and emptiness is form;
form is mind and mind is form; Buddha is mind and mind is Buddha; Buddha is emptiness and emptiness is [Buddha].
This is precisely the Buddha. One who can take these four phrases and synthesize them into a single phrase to take full responsibility for them will have completed their lifelong study of the Way.
A man of the Way asked: "Why did the Bodhisattva Anantagātra not see the crown of the World-Honored One’s head? The King said: "As the text says."
Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva cannot fathom the wisdom of the Tathāgata. [The Master] asked: "Why is it that Mañjuśrī cannot fathom the wisdom of the Tathāgata? The King said:
"It is like the Bodhisattva Anantagātra, who could not see the crown of the World-Honored One’s head. [The Master] asked: "Does the Buddha see the crown of the Bodhisattva Anantagātra’s head?
The King said: "If he sees it, he is not the Buddha; if he does not see it, he is also not the Buddha. [The Master] asked: "Does the Buddha fathom the wisdom of Mañjuśrī?"

"No. The Master said, "If you perceive it as not being the Buddha, then not perceiving it is also not the Buddha. The Way-farer had an awakening. The Master said, "Only when you cast off the cap of the Way will you attain it."
While the attendants were preparing the incense, the King asked, "How can the smoke of this incense be made to have no fragrance? The attendant replied, "I beg Your Majesty to speak for yourself.
The King then covered his nose with his hand.
A monk asked, "What is it like when the lamp of wisdom shines brightly? The King said, "Stretching out one's hand, one cannot see one's own palm.
The monk asked, "What is the meaning of this? The King said, "A torch burning for a li."
When the King arrived at the Baolin Monastery, the assembly came forward to welcome him. Pointing to a dog at the foot of the steps, the King asked the multitude, "One must not call this a 'dog.
Speak a verse! The assembly was speechless. The King said, "It is the permanent resident."
One day, during a tea conversation with the monks under the moonlight, one monk asked, "What is meant by 'when stillness reaches its ultimate limit, light penetrates through'?
The King said, "Look today as you looked yesterday."
A monk asked, "Regarding the teaching that the nature of ignorance is itself the Buddha-nature, how should one understand this principle? Wang said, "There are two ways of explaining this meaning.
Ignorance is likened to waves, and the Buddha-nature is likened to water. One cannot say that the waves are not water, nor can one say that the water is entirely the waves.
Ordinary people perceive the waves and abandon the water; sages perceive the water and discard the waves. Neither of these is True Suchness."
Regarding Buddha-nature, the *Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment* states: "One does not even attempt to extinguish or suppress the various deluded minds. It further states:

"Abiding within the realm of deluded thoughts, one does not apply conscious discernment. The *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* says: "Suchness is immovable. Here, "suchness" is like the waves, and "immovable" is like the water.
For one who has attained thorough realization, the nature of ignorance and consciousness is itself Buddha-nature; for one who has not yet attained such realization—

People, the nature of ignorance and consciousness is not the Buddha-nature. If those who study do not encounter the guidance of an enlightened master, and if they merely recognize the raising of eyebrows, the twinkling of eyes, the shifting of limbs, and the performance of actions—taking this brilliant and numinous awareness to be their own true nature—this is to mistake a thief for one's own son.
Not only does this betray one’s own spirit, but it also slanders the scriptures and misrepresents the Dharma. Students should [be aware of this].

Investigate this thoroughly and exhaustively. Do not allow yourself to fall into error by halting midway based on the provisional teachings of blind-eyed masters of the past and present who have failed to reach the ultimate upward path.
The monk bows his head in prostration and expresses his admiration.
One day, the King said: "Three winters have passed with dripping water and freezing frost; now, fortunately, spring has melted the ice. Everyone, look!
Has a tortoise grown hair in the pond yet?"
An attendant asked, "What is the ghost-king? He replied, "A confused person. The attendant asked, "What is the spirit-king? He replied, "..."
A man of clear understanding asked: "What is the Buddha? The King said: "One who is neither ignorant nor deluded.
He asked: "What is a human being? The King said: "Leave it to you to choose."
A monk asked: "Heaven attains the One and becomes clear; Earth attains the One and becomes tranquil; when a sovereign attains the One, he brings about Great Peace while sitting still.
But as for a patch-robed monk who attains the One—how is it? The King said: "Clear, tranquil, and great peace. The monk bowed in thanks. The King said: "But alas, you are not a patch-robed monk.
The monk asked: "Why am I not one? The King said: "Because you have not yet attained the One. The monk said: "..."
"Who is the patch-robed monk? The King said, "Yuanying is the patch-robed monk. [The Master] said, "If that is so, then Your Majesty has attained one.
The King said, "I, however, am not the patch-robed monk. [The Master] said, "Why do you contradict yourself from beginning to end?
The King struck his knee with his left hand and said, "Patch-robed monk! Then he struck his knee with his right hand and said, "Patch-robed monk!"

A monk asked, "What is the self-nature that is fundamentally neither born nor extinguished? The King said, "Because it constantly undergoes birth and extinction, it is therefore called 'neither born nor extinguished.
[The monk] asked, "What is the fundamental state that is immovable? The King said, "Because it moves at all times, it is therefore called 'immovable.
[The monk] asked, "What is the state that is inherently complete? The King said, "Because not a single thing can be obtained."
[The interlocutor] said, "Therefore, it is said that they are 'complete. How is it that they can give rise to the myriad dharmas?

The King said, "Because not a single dharma can be seen, it is therefore said that they can give rise to the myriad dharmas. [The interlocutor] said, "The King’s words are in great contradiction with the Patriarch’s teaching. The King said:
"If one does not oppose it, one immediately moves toward it. [The monk] asked, "How does one give rise to a mind that dwells nowhere? The King said, "Entering the forest, the grasses move;
entering the water, waves arise. The monk remained silent. The King said, "One must still oppose it before one can attain it."

A monk asked, "What is the 'Ten Wisdoms Identical with Reality'? The Master said, "Fushan’s Nine Baskets, the Eightfold Exposition of Views, the Sevenfold Investigation of Mind, the Six Pāramitās, the Five Positions of Ruler and Minister, the Four Sorts of Discrimination, the Three Essentials of the Mysteries, and the Two Aspects of Guest and Host—these constitute my total answer for you in a single phrase.
The monk said, "Setting aside these complications for a moment, suppose there were someone for whom not even a speck of dust could stand?"
[The Master] said, "How does Your Highness receive it? The King said, "Let those outside the gate listen to the nonsensical talk at their leisure.
[The Master] said, "In every dust mote and every world-system, the whole body is revealed. In whose sphere does this lie? The King said, "Who is there who has no share?

[The Master] said, "If that is so, then Your Highness must grant half the seat to this poor monk before it is possible. The King said, "Does the *Ajari* wish to return to secular life? [The Master] said, "Your Highness..."
He was also not permitted to leave the household life. The King said, "It is a pity that the staff is not in my hand. The monk asked, "Why do you not acknowledge the meaning of my words?
The King said, "From whom would I seek a guarantee? The monk bowed. The King said, "Although it is so, you must know there is more to it. The monk shook out his sleeves and departed.
The King called after him, "Great Virtue, you should remember these words of Yuanming well."
He asked a monk, "If one were to fill empty space with solidity and grasp at solid earth as emptiness, where would one find a place to breathe and stand?
The monk said, "One cannot seek life and find it; one cannot seek death and find it. The Master said, "In that case, have you resolved the matter of birth and death?"
[The Master] asked, "Is it apart from birth and death? [Yunmen] said, "Wait until you have filled the void of space and grasped the emptiness of the earth;
even then, will you still allow me to pass on a message? Wang said, "The message is not non-existent, but first return to me your skill at filling and grasping.

[Yunmen] said, "A non-human being falls prostrate, then rides the ox backward. Wang said, "This too is but a wooden woman and a stone man singing in harmony. [Yunmen] said, "If that is so, then [it is as] Wen..."
[The Master] said, "I have not added a single dot. The King said, "Fortunately, you still have one dot left. [The Master] said, "I am glad it may circulate [widely].
While the King was bathing, as he was drinking tea, he asked his attendant, "The water is within my body;
the water is outside my body. Do you see that my body is water? The attendant said, "How could Your Majesty’s body be called water? The King said, "The human body is originally..."
"This is a composite of the four great elements. Can you believe this? He replied, "I can believe it. The King said, "Come again; consider this carefully.
When fire encounters water, it naturally extinguishes; when earth encounters water, it naturally sinks; when wind encounters water, it naturally floats.
As for the rest that currently exists in union with water—what else could this body be but water? The man said, "Although..."

However, although it was spoken in this way, the principle could not be attained through practice. The King laughed and said, "Since you do not understand the principle, how can I discuss the Way with you?"
The King asked a monk, "Without drawing the bow and without sounding the string, every arrow hits the red heart. Whose skill is this?
The monk said, "To shoot a stone tiger at Lan-tien, one must wait for General Li. The King said, "Do not slander Li Guang."
[The Master] said, "Is it not that great merit lies in non-action, and governance through non-being? Wang said, "Throughout my life, Yuanying has never failed anyone.

[The Master] said, "If that is so, it is like an empty valley responding to an echo. Wang said, "You are a fellow who plunders the void. [The Master] said, "In that case, the great bell is already on its stand.
Wang said, "You are a fellow who merely strikes at the surface. [The Master] said, "How then can one attain it? Wang said, "The chick pecks from within; the mother hen pecks from without."
[The monk] said, "Both are lost at once. Wang said, "Alas, how can it be that a true adept does not 'crack' and 'peck'? The monk said, "Give me back my *huatou* (the critical phrase).

Wang said, "Return it to me! The monk said, "I, this poor monk, am no adept. Wang said, "Then you become more and more like a commoner with every turn. The monk said, "Only when we share it equally with Your Highness shall it be right.
Wang said, "Do as you please; imitate me as you will."
A monk asked, "What is it like when the great ocean has no fish? The King said, "Do you see any sentient beings upon the great earth?
The monk said, "What about when a wealthy man has no grain? The King said, "When you eat rice, do you ever bite into a grain?
The monk said, "How would you explain 'great enlightenment without a path'? The King said, "I knew all along that neither you nor I have yet attained great enlightenment."
[The Master] said, "Prince, how can you judge others by your own standards? The Prince said, "I have been brought low by you, O Ācārya.
[The Master] said, "A heart that does not betray others leaves no trace of shame on the face. The Prince said, "I have often applied myself to this very point.

[The Master] said, "If that is so, then we breathe through the same nostril as the Prince. The Prince pointed to his own nose and said, "Tell me, through which nostril does the Perfectly Bright One [the Buddha-nature] flow?"
[The Master] blocked one nostril. [Wuzhuo] said, "There is no time for explanation. The King said, "If that is so, I do not yet grant you, O Acharya, the right to breathe through even one nostril."
One day there was wind. A monk asked, "Does the sound of the wind come to the ear, or does the ear go out to the wind? The Master said, "A white crane cries in the void; a stone man tilts his ear.
The monk said, "I do not understand, Venerable Sir. The Master said, "There is sound, but no hearing. The monk said, "There is sound, but no hearing."

“What is the meaning of this? The King said, “Because there is a self, there is sound; because there is no self, there is no hearing. [The monk] said, “If that is so, then it is simply the sound itself.
The King said, “That is very much like a clay ox or a wooden horse. [The monk] said, “If that is the case, then it is my own sound.
The King said, “You are a fellow who picks up others’ spittle and saliva! [The monk] said, “I understand! I understand! The King said, “Tell me what you have understood. [The monk] said, “It exists.”
The Way cannot be expressed by the mouth. The Master laughed and said, "I grant you that you have recognized a single star.
A monk asked, "Ānanda said, 'The World-Honored One has opened wide his great compassion and allowed me to enter. I ask: how does one enter?"
The King said, "It is easy for a mustard seed to contain Mount Sumeru; it is difficult for Mount Sumeru to contain a mustard seed.
[The Master] said, "If that is so, then I shall ride off on a blue ox backward. The King said, "Although you know how to go like that, you must also know how to come like that.

[The Master] asked, "How does one come like that? The King said, "A mustard seed contains Mount Sumeru. [The Master] asked, "Does this still require effort and achievement? The King said, "If one relies on effort..."
Xun said, "Both coming and going are illusions. The monk asked, "How should one practice? The King said, "Simply exhaust the present moment, and it will naturally be established.
The monk asked, "Once it is established, what then? The King said, "It is secretly right beside you. The monk bowed in thanks.
The King said, "Be careful not to keep these few phrases within your breast. The monk said, "This poor monk shall not fail you. The King said, "Take care."
A Confucian scholar asked, "Setting aside for a moment the lineage of Caoxi, I request that Your Majesty proclaim the essential tenets of the Five Houses.

The King said, "I, Yuanying, know only the principle of Caoxi; I do not understand the doctrines of the Five Houses. The scholar said, "Are the one principle and the five houses the same or different?
The King said, "When meeting the correct, they are the same; when meeting the deviant, they are different. [The scholar] asked, "What is the principle of the Caoxi lineage?"
"How is it? The King said, "Neither grasping nor abandoning. [The Master] asked, "What is it that you neither grasp nor abandon?

The King said, "I do not grasp at wondrous clarity; I do not abandon clarity-wonder. [The Master] asked, "How do you practice? The King said, "Remain alert. [The Master] asked, "How do you cultivate and realize?
The King said, "Cultivation and realization are not non-existent, yet defilement must not occur. [The Master] asked, "Is there still something further above this?"
[The Master] said: "There is none. The King said: "There is. [The Master] asked: "How does one proceed toward it? The King said: "The Buddha said it cannot be spoken;

how could even a thousand sages proclaim it? [The Master] said: "In that case, it cannot be heard. The King said: "Those who have realized it know it for themselves; it is not something that can be measured."
The officer bowed in thanks.
The King held the fan and asked a monk: "If you say it is an object within the mind, it is missing half; if you say it is the mind within an object, it is missing half;
if you say it is both within and without the mind, it is missing half; if you say it is neither within nor without the mind, it is missing half."
"Half-full. [The Master] said, "Tell me, how can it be made perfectly complete? The monk smiled but did not answer. The King said, "Try asking Yuanming one by one.
[The Master] asked, "Is the object within the mind? The King said, "It is within the mind. [The Master] asked, "Is the mind within the object? The King said, "It is within the object.
[The Master] asked, "Is the object both within and outside the mind? The King said, "It is both within and outside the mind."
[The monk] asked, "Is it not neither within nor without the mind? The King said, "It is neither within nor without the mind. [The monk] said, "If that is so, then all four sides are missing.
The King said, "The perfect realization is already complete; what more could possibly be lacking? The monk sighed in admiration and bowed in gratitude.
The King laughed and said, "You have spoken only half the truth.

Idle words say that throughout the entire realm there is nothing hidden or concealed; not a single thread hangs upon one. Following conditions, one idly drinks and pecks; thus, one is at ease and acts with freedom."
Not knowing the way, the mountains are naturally high and the waters naturally clear. Heaven, earth, things, and the self are all perfectly distinct.
Having momentarily forgotten the path by which I came, I stray instead toward the tracks traveled by others.
Walking at night under the moon, the fish in the pond swallow the bait; the wind comes, and the shadows of the bamboos sweep away the dust. At this moment, self and others are suddenly forgotten;
it is all one seamless flow of original nature.
When the indolent man’s pride awakens and his eyes open, the red sun fills the window as midday approaches. Shake off your lethargy and exert your strength to look:
who could ever oppose the Dharma or worldly laws?

The retribution for good and evil is as difficult to evade as a shadow following a form. Without creating sin or merit, one emerges in equilibrium and enters into equilibrium; this is the true reflection.

however, because they mistakenly identify the conscious spirit—the root of birth and death—as the ultimate principle, they erroneously misrecognize Buddha-nature and slander the precepts and practices. For these reasons, they are termed "externalists" and "demons."

Huangbo said: "People nowadays only desire to know much and understand much, which conversely results in congestion.
They only know how to give their children plenty of butter to eat, yet they have no idea at all whether it will digest or not. All those who practice the Way of the Three Vehicles are like this."
All such cases are termed "undigested food. Thus, one knows that lack of understanding is entirely a poisonous drug, for it is all grasped within the realm of arising and ceasing;
within True Suchness (Tathatā), none of this exists at all. Now, while there are many people who suffer from indigestion, Māgandika and his son were those who had already become satiated with poison.
The Buddha-dharma is non-dual; how can one possibly cling to fixed positions?
Beyond the "Three or Four," there is further the essential principle of the Secret Transmission of Three or Four.

Extensively citing similar sayings from ancient virtuous masters as commentaries, he uses them for cross-examination. He does not establish verbal explanations, but single-handedly upholds the orthodox lineage that points directly upward.
To look up and spit at the clouds is only to soil one's own face. Zhaozhou said: "In this place of mine, I simply use the fundamental..."

To engage people by dividing matters into categories—if one were to teach old monks according to their individual capacities—then the Three Baskets and Twelve Divisions of the Canon would already have sufficed to engage them.

To merely say that there are no signs of right or wrong or discrimination is already not being true to one's own fundamental nature; how much more so to deliberately establish such signs of right and wrong and discrimination?
What the World-Honored One preached for forty-nine years, and what the ancient masters of the seventeen hundred [cases] have said, [is precisely this].

Thus, *gong'an* are entirely composed of language and writing. If you do not recognize this, then even if you imitate every word and phrase exactly as they were written, it will be a demonic teaching;

it will be a slander against the Buddha. Even if you could memorize the Tripitaka and the twelve divisions of the scriptures spoken by the Buddhas and patriarchs, as well as the seventeen hundred *gong'an*, without a single character or phrase being incorrect, this would truly be—

Within the ocean of luminosity, there is much clinging to the dregs of sediment. How much more so once one has fallen into the realm of verbal expression? To fall into verbal expression is to be identical with the characteristics of the teachings (*śāsana-lakṣaṇa*).

Since one is identical with the characteristics of the teachings, then the Three Baskets (*tripiṭaka*) and the Twelve Divisions of Scripture (*dvādaśāṅga-pravacana*) are already present before one. Furthermore, why must one establish the principle of a "separate transmission outside the teachings"?

No matter how they may speak horizontally or vertically, can they ever transcend the Three Baskets and the Twelve Divisions of Scripture? The Sage possesses manifold capacities; this is the Buddha’s [teaching].
The various supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) are not the fundamental basis of the noble path; these powers themselves are not the core tenet of the Buddha’s school.
How could Confucius have ever known the Sanskrit language of the West? Nor could the Tathāgata produce the Tang Chinese language of Zhendan.

Each has its own limits; what connection does this have with the present matter? All the more so regarding the single aspect of written characters—how could the father and son of the Māra-treasury (Mozang) possibly [fathom it] by means of them?
The illiterate mocked Miyun, implying that he was inferior to their own scholarly learning;

they thought that if one were to engage in exegesis or compose literary treatises, there were already scholars available for that, so what use were followers of the Zen school? Whether one is literate or illiterate has no connection whatsoever to this [Dharma].
To be widely versed in the Classics and Histories is like using cut paper flowers to adorn the blossoms on a tree—it is something the eye cannot truly perceive.
The letter "Ding" (丁) is such that when rice is cooked, it does not borrow the water or fire from a neighbor's house.
As for the father and son, Maocang and others, their great root of illness lies precisely in recognizing the letter "Ding" while failing to recognize this very thing.

Now, if a Mongol person comes, one receives them as a Mongol; if a Russian person comes, one receives them as a Russian; if people from Siam, Srīvijaya, Ryūkyū, or Japan come, one receives them accordingly.

We maintain relations with Siam, Sulu, Ryūkyū, and Japan. If we were to wait until they had mastered written characters before establishing these relations, then the Buddha-dharma would be unable to cover heaven and earth.
As for those who harbor demonic and heterodox views, they consider themselves to have every word based on antiquity and every character derived from the sutras;
yet how could they know that the entirety of the Tripitaka and the twelve divisions of scripture—even the thirteen [categories]—[are all contained herein]?

The *Agamas*, the Twenty-one Dynastic Histories, the various masters and schools (*zhuzi baijia*), and all the texts contained within the world’s four treasuries—every single character is threaded together and harmonized until there is not even a hair’s breadth of gap or a seam to be found. Since the coming of the Way and the Buddha, one cannot open one's mouth;
it is precisely that which even a Buddha appearing in the world could not save. For thirty years, Ānanda served as his attendant, yet...
Regarding those who possess much learning and wisdom, the Buddha rebuked them, saying: "Learning wisdom for a thousand days is not as good as learning the Way for a single day.

If you do not learn the Way, even a drop of water will be difficult to digest; how much more so for one like Macang, who uses the heterodox views of external paths to recklessly intrude upon the matters that transcend the Buddhas and Patriarchs?
How could he possibly deserve such a rebuke? He merely deceives those who have eyes but no pupils."
Before those with clear eyes, the demonic form reveals itself. Zhaozhou said, "The teachers of today are like branches growing upon branches;
they are far removed from the sages, with each generation falling behind the last.
As for Nanquan’s usual saying, 'One must walk among the heterodox,' how do you understand it? Nowadays, even children with yellow mouths [at ten years old]..."

On the street, they talk of "ge-teng" (entanglements); they eat their fill and seek only prostrations. Gathering three or five hundred followers, they claim, "I am a good spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*); you are but students.
You should recognize that this is the demonic form of the father and son of the Dharma-treasury (*dharmagañja*).
Zhaozhou had already settled the matter hundreds of years ago; there is no need for it to come before one's eyes to be known. Both awakening and cultivation are approached through this very moment.
Ji’s single blow was intended to point directly to the person; yet Mazu criticized it as "one-stump Chan," a mere trap for evasive dodging.
If one discusses this matter, neither wondrous words nor marvelous phrases are of any use; even a single blow or a shout is but a superfluous expedient.
The ancients used the staff and the shout only when they had no other choice; their original intent was to eradicate emotional views and to point directly to the human mind.

If Mōzang attempts to understand this through emotional views, he commits a most egregious error. Did the ancients not say that a single blow of the staff or a single shout does not function as a mere blow or shout?
How could they have been attached to these one shout or one blow? Mōzang’s intention is merely to reject and dismiss the staff and shout.

"Ha! It is regrettable that he attempts to win a victory by seeking the extraordinary, using the so-called 'one-circle,' 'double-headed,' or 'four-dharma' as the ultimate reality he has falsely established.
He fails to realize that this greatly deviates from the principle of the 'special transmission outside the teachings,' wherein there is no dharma to be transmitted."
Furthermore, in awakening and cultivation, I have never claimed that a single blow of the staff is the ancestor of the thousand Buddhas and ten thousand Buddhas;

yet Mōzang has falsely fabricated the symbol of the "one circle" (○) as the ancestor of the thousand Buddhas and ten thousand Buddhas—is this not merely a case of evading the essential point and falling into a conceptual trap?

To employ the symbol of the "one circle" as a means of *bōdoku* (staff and shout) is still to evade the essential point and fall into a conceptual trap. If one were to take the symbol of the "one circle" as the [ancestor] of the thousand Buddhas...
The progenitor of ten thousand Buddhas is, in truth, nothing but the lair of Māra. National Teacher Zhong showed the ninety-seven [or ninety-one] marks to Tan Yuan;
Tan Yuan showed them to the Venerable Brothers (Miaoxi and Daowu). This was a fabrication by the Māra-store, which they claimed to be the "Unwritten Secret Seal" existing prior to Dīpaṃkara.
On that day when Tan Yuan showed it to Yangshan, Yangshan burned it upon seeing it. Later, Tan Yuan asked him:
Yang bowed. Yang immediately compiled another version and presented it to Yuan; there was no longer any omission.
Furthermore, when Guishan drew a circle (○) with a "one-day" character (日) inside, Yangshan drew a circle on the ground with a "one-day" character inside and then wiped it away with his foot.
Guishan laughed heartily. Mazu’s collection merely marvels at the fact that Yangshan was able to memorize [the teaching] upon seeing it once.
It is marvelous! Yet you do not realize it at the place where Guishan laughed loudly, nor where Yangshan burned the scroll and wiped his feet.
This is what is called "the hound Hanlu chasing a clod of earth.
If you say that the ninety-seven [thousand] marks are extraordinary, I now make eighty-four thousand marks and reduce them to eight thousand three hundred and ninety-seven; they further reduce to—
Seven hundred and ninety-one [marks] return to ninety-five marks; ninety-five return to ninety marks; ninety return to ten marks.
It is just like entering the ocean to count its sands, or playing with a single set of the Flower Treasury World (*Huazang*).
What is so extraordinary about this? As for the Three Mysteries and Three Essentials, since their proclamation by Linji, they have been present throughout past and present.
Among the patriarchs, there were none who did not take up and expound upon these matters, yet none could ever present them with such clarity.

Mazu Zang, however, took Huangbo’s three blows of the staff and used them as a pretext for his own interpretation; he fabricated and rearranged them at will. This was because he fundamentally did not understand the Three Mysteries and the Three Essentials.

Did not Linji say: "In general, when expounding the School of the Patriarchs, every single phrase must embody the Three Mysteries (san-xuan), and within each Mystery there must be the Three Essentials (san-yao).
He first mentions the two terms "expounding" (yanchang) and "singing" (yang), for expounding cannot be without words and phrases.

One must recognize the Mysteries and Essentials within these words and phrases for them to become "living phrases. Thus, the Three Essentials are contained within a single Mystery, and the [Three Mysteries are contained within] the Three Mysteries...

The Nine Essentials must be fully possessed. As for these [diagrams], they are established through the Mysterious (xuán), yet the Essentials penetrate the Mysterious. Without the Nine Essentials, one cannot penetrate the Three Mysteries;
only by attaining the Nine Essentials do the Three Mysteries become complete. Thus, though undivided, they are divided; though divided, they are not divided.
Therefore, the Dharma of the Mysterious and the Essentials encompasses every dharma—just as a single blow of the staff is not merely "one blow."

Regarding the use of shouts (*he*) and blows (*bang*): what is manifest and evident is like the method of the "Fourfold Selection" (*si liao jian*), and also like the four seasons of spring, summer, autumn, and winter.
Although cold and heat shift and change, they do not, in total, transcend this single year; this single year is precisely the staff and the shout.
The Five Ranks (*wu wei*) of Caodong are also like the mutual presence of the five elements (*wuxing*); they do not transcend this single vital energy (*qi*). This...

"Qi" (vital energy) is precisely the "staff and shout. As for Fushan’s Nine Bends, I maintain that within a single phrase one must possess all nine bends, and within those nine bends one must possess fifty-five bundles.

Furthermore, regarding Fengyang’s Ten Wisdoms Identical with Reality, I maintain that within a single phrase one must possess the ten wisdoms identical with reality, and within each instance of being identical with reality one must possess fifty-five realities.
In this way, how does it differ from the essential principle of the profound mystery? If one were to extend this reasoning further, it would be difficult to enumerate all such instances.

In sum, although the ancestral masters of successive generations have assumed various guises to guide sentient beings, they have never departed from the meaning of the World-Honored One’s holding up of the flower or Linji’s staff and shout.
Anything that diverges from this is a demonic teaching. Moreover, these very staff and shouts are capable of embodying all phenomena.
It can dissolve all phenomena. How could this staff and shout have any fixed characteristics? Why would a single staff and shout be used as a single staff and shout?
Mōzang does not recognize this and labels it "one-stump Chan. If one speaks of Chan in this way, even a single stump is already an excessive fabrication.
Mōzang’s intention remains unsatisfied; he does not know how many stumps he must wait for before they will accord with his demonic intent. (3)
"A sudden blow with a staff and three days of deafness"—what further meaning could there be? What connection is there [between these]?
Furthermore, in the preface to the *Record of the Five Schools* (Wǔzōnglù) composed by Mòzàng, a stūpa is used as a metaphor: the nine tiers represent the teachings and meanings of the five periods;
the place where the pinnacle is joined represents Tathāgata Chan; and the thousand-fathom sandalwood pillar that emerges from the void and pierces the pinnacle represents the Chan of the Patriarchs.

He takes the Five-Light Samādhi as the core doctrine of his own school and further boasts that his words are like adding a handful of sand to the pinnacle of a stupa—these are all various demonic teachings.
Indeed, all doctrinal manifestations belong to the category of the "net" (the means); they are like digging the earth to plant melons: once the melons are formed, they are no longer the earth.
Gold is extracted from ore, but can the ore itself be considered gold? Yet he claims that the stages of the teaching have reached their ultimate limit. Such [views] are...

The summit of the karmic bonds is precisely the Tathāgata-dhyāna; it is nothing more than a dream or a delirium. Furthermore, the Great Meaning of the Westward Transmission is the wondrous mind of the Tathāgata’s nirvāṇa.
Although the five houses branched out, they all truly returned to the source. How can one divide Buddhas from patriarchs and further divide them into five houses?
Even the distinction between the Two Vehicles and the Mahāyāna is like that between skin, flesh, bone, and marrow—their respective stages are clearly delineated.

Yet they cannot be separated; how much less so when it comes to the matter of holding directly to the "upward direction"? What connection could there be between the Five Luminaries and the Five Schools?
It is very much like the pedantic Confucians of the Han dynasty who claimed that the twenty-eight chapters of the *Shangshu* corresponded to the twenty-eight generals of the Cloud Terrace.
Such a demonic intent merely seeks to elevate the Five Houses as those who transcend Buddhas and patriarchs, yet it is like gathering grains of sand and placing them upon one’s head. Furthermore—
To surpass the five schools is what the Tathāgata calls the commission of a great falsehood.

Furthermore, Muzhang [Zhao] pointed out that Caoxi’s “originally there was not a single thing” constitutes falling into the externalist path of nihilism; yet even Hongren’s remark at Huangmei, “you have not yet seen your nature,” remains dead within the confines of its phrasing.
Now, if we discuss the phrase “originally there was not a single thing” alone, it certainly seems as though one has attained self-realization.
As for this view, since it is stated below that "how can one remain where dust and grime arise," it may be said that one transcends all merit and achievement and directly reaches the ultimate.
As for the single phrase "Huangmei also had not yet seen his nature," let alone those who die beneath its words; they need not even be discussed.
To say that [the Master] was merely covering people's eyes and ears is also incorrect. How could Huangmei have intended to mislead sentient beings?

As for the response regarding "the rice being white without the need for a sieve," how could Caoxi have been practicing the worldly convention of modesty? Although the distinction between awakening and cultivation may seem somewhat crude, it is nonetheless significant.
Yet Zangren directly denounces [Miyun] as an outsider who has fallen into nihilism; his own vision is thus inadequate.
It is evident that he himself has not yet attained realization, for he perceives the single flavor of conditioned dharmas through distorted knowledge and false views.

Furthermore, Hongren points out that Miyun’s claim that the sentient and insentient are suddenly and brilliantly manifest is merely a matter of domestic triviality, citing Yunmen’s statement: "Directly, the great earth..."
To be free from even a hair’s breadth of fault or affliction is the "turning phrase" (*zhuǎnjù*). Not seeing a single form is the "half-extraction" (*bàntí*).
One must know that there is still a time for the "full extraction" (*quántí*); this serves as the proof.

Little do they realize that the final blow of Mìyún is precisely the full extraction everywhere—the power by which both the sentient and the insentient suddenly manifest in brilliant clarity. Since they have not yet reached the level of Mìyún, [they do not understand].

In his state of realization, he merely cites the sayings of Yunmen to provide a superficial cover, like a fox relying on a city wall or a rat taking refuge in a community altar, causing people not to dare to burn them away.
In the end, the city wall remains simply a city wall and the rat remains simply a rat;
how could they ever be mixed such that the fox and rat become identical to the city wall? Hongren further stated that Master Sanfeng was a teacher of Tiantong. Master...

Regarding its source and lineage: our master was Sanfeng; we are his dharma-milk. One might say that he voluntarily confessed his demonic offenses without being questioned, for did he not realize that, in truth, there is not a single dharma to be attained?
Thus it is called the "source and lineage. Since what has been attained is based on evidence and proof, how could one falsely claim it is merely "dharma-milk"?
When one's practice reaches full penetration and recognizes one's own mind, the way of teacher and disciple merges like a needle and its eye.
They are in perfect accord. Like the simultaneous act of pecking and hatching, this mind-seal of the ancestors has always been nothing more than saying, "You are thus; I am also thus.
Never has there been a single dharma to transmit, for indeed not a single dharma can be obtained.

When there is a single word of transmission and reception, only then is it called the milk of the Dharma. If one harbors the false knowledge and false views of the Mara-heretics and their disciples, [it is not so].
To take secret oral transmissions as "milk" is, in fact, poisonous milk; how can it be called the milk of the Dharma?

I, the Emperor, maintain that Mazu was not entirely without knowledge. It was simply because he left his teacher too early that he fell into afflictions and delusions, becoming arrogant and conceited, seeking only to prevail and wishing to stand alone at the head of the Dharma gate, regardless of the fact that his own footing was not yet secure.

They settle upon the ground, desiring to display a cleverness in their intellectual adornment that surpasses their teachers. They fixate upon such names and characteristics as "the One," "the Ten," "the Four Dharmas," and "the Double-Headed," intending to produce works that transcend their masters.
Every time they establish a false claim, they immediately scour historical records and literature, stitching together the words and phrases of the ancient sages to provide proof for it.
This is exactly as Yongming said: "With a limited mind, one gives rise to partiality."

They perceive by confining themselves to the vastness or narrowness of the great void, and they fix upon the boundaries of the *dharmadhātu*. Consequently, their discriminative emotions do not transcend the realm of manifold sensory dusts.
They stir the mental mechanisms within the sphere of *tathatā*, and they surge with waves of consciousness within the ocean of quiescent extinction.
Keeping their views confined within a narrow tube, they steal light through a crack in the wall; they establish dualistic cognition of subject and object, giving rise to notions of superiority...

The inferior understanding [of these masters] merely matches the literal phrasing while failing to grasp the intended meaning; they dissect the text word by word, establishing separate sects. How could the wings of a gnat ever rival those of the great Peng bird?

How could the glow of a firefly compare to the radiance of the sun? The words and writings of the father and son, Mozhao and Zhiyan, are forever exhausted by the few sentences from the Yongming era that can judge them.
At that time, Mozhao sought favor among the scholar-officials and had them provide protection, causing the monastic community to vie with one another [in their devotion].

Chasing after mere fragments, they have consequently led them to form distinct sects; their followers remain scattered throughout the world to this day, and the decline of the Buddhist schools is largely due to this.
If I do not now suppress and expel them, when will the sorcery of these teachings ever be extinguished?

An edict is hereby issued to destroy all printing blocks for the *Zangnei youcang ren yulu* (Recorded Sayings of the Hidden and Patient within the Canon), as well as the *Wuzong yuan* (Origins of the Five Schools) and the *Wuzong jiu* (Rescue of the Five Schools).

The monastic community is not permitted to privately collect or store [these texts]. Should anyone violate this decree by concealing them, they shall, upon discovery, be judged according to the Vinaya for disrespect.

Furthermore, the *Wujiao jiuyi shu* (A Book of Rescuing the Five Schools) has been individually refuted point-by-point and engraved within the Tripitaka, so that those of future generations possessing correct knowledge and vision may recognize these as demonic heterodoxies and harbor no further doubts. [This concludes the work] of the lineage of Tiantong Miyun Wu. Dharma...
All disciples belonging to the branch [of the lineage] shall be subject to detailed investigation by the Provincial Governors and Commandants of the respective provinces.

All members of this branch shall be completely stripped of their status, and they shall never again be permitted to enter the ancestral temple. Should they be able to study under other masters elsewhere and attain correct insight (*samyag-dṛṣṭi*), such that they may separately inherit another school, only then shall they be permitted to wield the whisk (*vaijayantī*).
On the day this edict arrives, the ancestral temples throughout the realm shall belong to the descendants of Fazang.

Regarding the opening of the hall: the bells and wooden boards must be removed, and no preaching of the Dharma is permitted. The local official shall immediately select a successor from a different branch of the Tiantong lineage to succeed as abbot.
All ancestral temples have been famous monasteries since ancient times; furthermore, the permanent property (changzhu) inherently belongs to the ten directions.

I merely expel those who are outside the Dharma and hostile to it; this has no inherent connection with the permanent monastic establishments (changzhu), nor does it concern the practitioners from the ten directions.
Let local officials not misunderstand my intent. Not a single blade of grass or tree within the monasteries shall be disturbed, and the disciples engaged in study must not be harassed.
Should anyone fail to carry out these instructions properly, they shall be deemed to have disobeyed my decree. As it is said: [followed by the relevant verse].

The disciples under his guidance stubbornly cling to demonic teachings, claiming that their "Dharma-milk" is unerring and that they truly accord with the intent of the separate transmission and have authentically attained the lineage of Linji.
Yet, they refuse to submit with sincere hearts or awaken from their delusion like one waking from a dream or sobering from intoxication.

Let them come to see me so that they may present their views face-to-face; I shall personally weigh their claims against the Buddha-dharma. If they are indeed seen to be superior, [I shall grant them my respect].
Your discourse is particularly profound. I shall immediately withdraw my original decree and reinstate the Sanfeng school.
If you exhaust all your stratagems and remain defiant, refusing to submit while seeking mercy through worldly means, I shall punish you severely according to the laws of the world;

do not leave yourself with cause for regret. From time immemorial, the propagation of heterodox doctrines has easily deluded the human mind; yet, whether within or outside the Buddhist path, [the truth remains clear].
Distinguishing between the heterodox and the orthodox is not difficult; it depends on whether one's practice and teaching are rooted in one’s own inherent nature (*svabhāva*).

That which is rooted in one’s own inherent nature is called "internal" (*neng*). That which is not rooted in one’s own inherent nature, but is practiced and taught through delusion, is called "external" (*wai*).

The Buddhist school often opens the gate of the profound mystery to exclude such [heterodox] views. For example, the Real Man Zi-yang, in his commentary on the *Wu zhen pian*, later separately annotated the *Wai ji* (External Collection), which does not...
A single phrase from the Profound Gate (Xuánmén) unfolds the Chan school from every aspect of its fundamental nature (*xingdì*).
Among the Chan masters of the ancestral lineage, few have been as lucid and unimpeded as this; even those whose works are included within these few chapters are rare to find.
How could one then label such a person "external"? One like a True Man is the internal within the external. As for those like the followers of Mócháng, they are the opposite.
To usurp the Buddha-Dharma and destroy the Buddha-Dharma is to cast what is internal outwards. How could the pure lineage of Caoxi tolerate such a turbid stream?
Moreover, these demonic doctrines and their progeny have fallen into the human world; the junior students receive their inexhaustible lingering poison.
This concerns the very eye of the Dharma and the life-force of wisdom. How could Your Majesty bear not to distinguish between right and wrong? The world...
In future generations, there will surely be those who receive the profound grace of my eyebrows trailing upon the ground.
You must know that this demon must be discerned, for it is a demon within the realm of the Buddha. This anomaly must be sifted out, for it is an anomaly within the midst of the same.
As the transmission says: "Stop heterodox teachings to rectify the human heart. Indeed, the expulsion of the heterodox and the support of the orthodox is what I, the Emperor, intend to do.
This was simply unavoidable. Examining the origins of the names of the Three Teachings, they first appeared during the Jin and Wei dynasties.

Later generations, bound by the hollow prestige of venerating Confucianism, consequently sought to disparage and reject the other two schools. I, however, reflect that Laozi was a contemporary of Confucius;

the intent of his inquiry into the rites and the praise of him as "one who resembles a dragon" are recorded in the historical annals. Thus, he did not belong to a different teaching from that of Confucius.

Furthermore, the Buddha was born in the Western Regions some decades before Confucius. Had Śākyamuni and Confucius been contemporaries, they would surely have exchanged mutual salutations and respect.
For the Five Classics, the Nine Classics, the Three Substances, and the Six Conducts constitute the great outlines and minor regulations for governing the world;
these indeed originated with the Two Emperors and Three Kings and were perfected by our Most Sage [Confucius]. However, it must be...
Only after liberating oneself from all signs can this mind subsequently penetrate the fundamental nature and principles of all things;

this is an absolute certainty. As for later generations comparing the Sun, Moon, and Stars to the Three Teachings—identifying one as the Sun, another as the Moon, and another as the Star—I do not intend to permit such restrictive views. Rather, regarding the Sun...
The moon and the stars share the same source of light; this serves as a metaphor for how the three teachings differ in their applications while remaining identical in essence.
By examining the *Waiji* (External Collection) of the Real Man Ziyang, one can naturally find no cause for doubt regarding the principle that the paths of the immortals and the Buddhas are unified.

Since the Way is thus unified, one can further remain free from doubt concerning the teaching that the three religions may proceed side by side without contradiction. I have therefore appended these remarks here.
This shall cause those throughout the world and future generations who seek the true and ultimate principles of nature to cast aside narrow boundaries and broaden their understanding.
In this, I truly place my high hopes.
It is my view that the Chan school has never been more flourishing than it is today, yet it has also never been more in decline than it is today.
Throughout the provinces, monasteries and temples are spread out like chess pieces, and those who open the hall and wield the whisk are beyond counting; thus, it is indeed most flourishing today.

Nevertheless, among the followers of the school throughout the land, there are few who have truly penetrated the ultimate barrier beyond, and even fewer who can break through their fundamental inquiry (*benkan*).
Those who possess right knowledge and vision are likewise not many; such is the current state of our school’s tradition, which has truly reached its lowest point today.
When Bodhidharma came from the West, he sat facing a wall for nine years before finally transmitting the robe to the Second Patriarch, Huik’e.

Even one who employs the wisdom-power of the Buddhas and patriarchs to guide humans and devas had to wait for the duration of nine years to find but a single successor. Now, throughout the entire land...

Below this [truth], there are ten thousand monasteries and ten thousand monks; ten thousand monks and ten thousand fly-whisks. The Master transmits in blindness, and the Disciple receives in blindness.

Every person proclaims the vehicle of the school, yet each and every one fails to realize their own mind. Does this not cause the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye and the Wondrous Mind of Nirvāṇa to hang by a thread, nearly severed?
Although it cannot necessarily be said that the transmission will always be like that of Bodhidharma to the Second Patriarch, it must nevertheless...

True practice and genuine awakening entail possessing correct knowledge and correct view from within oneself; one must receive these from a person who has attained such correct knowledge and correct view.
How could there be a blind transmission and blind reception that leaves one with no firm foundation?

To claim that this constitutes the revitalization of the Buddha-dharma or the continuation of the Buddha’s wisdom-life—how does this differ from destroying the Buddha and extinguishing the Dharma? At worst, those whose hearts are obsessed with fame and profit commit great falsehoods.
They boast of having realized the Way whenever they move; they shout at Buddhas and revile the Patriarchs; they hold the precepts in no regard and deceive one another;
they hawk fly-whisks and robes like commoners in the marketplace; they treat the life-force of the Buddhas and Patriarchs as mere worldly sentiments.

Though they have stolen the name of being descendants of the Buddhas and Patriarchs, they utterly lack the substance of being teachers and models for devas and humans. Only those such as Fazang and Hongren...
They form alliances with officials and gentlemen, relying on their power and influence as a means to protect the Dharma assembly.
Among these officials and gentlemen, those who delight in assuming the reputation of being "lay practitioners" (upāsaka) accept their superficiality; they mutually extol one another.
Although the World-Honored One, at that time, entrusted the Buddha-Dharma to kings, ministers, and faithful laypeople for its protection, he never commanded them to deviate from the Way.

This is merely following the crowd; how much more so when they do not observe the retreat (jie), do not practice with incense (xiang), and instead devote themselves solely to composing poetry and essays to flatter and please the scholar-officials?

Question regarding the Pure Land:
If the mind of mindfulness of the Buddha is free from distraction and uninterrupted, this is already the perfection of vigor (*vīryapāramitā*). Why, then, is it called "non-retrogression"?
Answer: One might think that it is through diligence (*vīrya*) alone that one is able to avoid falling back; is it not the case that non-diligence itself constitutes non-falling-back?
There are two ways to distinguish this. First, it may indeed be non-falling-back. Why? Although it is commonly said that the essence (*sāra*) is unmixed, [it is so].
Advancing and not retreating. However, these two characters, taken together, encompass the meaning of accomplishment. As the ancients said: "Vigorous effort (vīrya) is the overcoming of indolence.
Since advancing and retreating are opposites, vigorous effort is itself non-retreat. In this context, the emphasis is on how mindfulness of the Buddha universally encompasses all perfections;
the focus is not on the etymological definitions of the two characters "vigorous effort. Furthermore, since it is called "vigorous effort," one is thereby able to be non-retreating. Now...
Those who practice mindfulness of the Buddha never fall back or regress; thus, mindfulness of the Buddha itself constitutes diligence (*vīrya*), and there is no need to seek diligence elsewhere.
As you have asked, it is that one practices mindfulness of the Buddha with diligence; it is not that mindfulness of the Buddha is merely diligence.

why harbor a longing for a land? They argue that an earthworm truly contains mud, yet how could yellow soil ever equal the Golden Realm?
The giant turtle truly bears Mount Tai; how could it possibly grasp the void? This is likely a metaphor for the cinnabar terrace (*dantāi*) and an analogy for the lotus calyx.
The forty channels correspond to the interlacing jeweled nets, and the inner radiance of the single spirit is likened to Amitābha dwelling therein.
Being near the lungs, it approximates the west; connecting to the tongue, it forms a pool. These are merely analogies for the Dharma; they do not describe actual physical realities. Thus:
There are those who claim that the auspiciousness or misfortune of wind and water leads to the rise or decline of one’s descendants;

they take as their model the mutual fusion of the provisional and the real, asserting that the response of the spiritual mechanism is never errant. Yet this still does not clarify the true cause, nor does it exhaustively investigate the Ten Profound Subtleties (*daśa-sūkṣma*).
I further seek your enlightened instruction to overturn these erroneous views.

Answer: "The mind is pure, and the land is pure. These words are indeed true. However, these words carry two meanings. First, from the perspective of principle (*li*), it means that the mind is itself the land;
there is no pure land apart from the pure mind. Second, from the perspective of phenomena (*shi*), it means that the mind is the land;
because the mind is pure, the land is pure. If one adheres to the principle while discarding the phenomena, then what the world calls "tranquility" would be [the land].

O Immortal! Is there no true immortal beyond the state of pure leisure? As for those who, by grasping at the divisions of the body, speak of a "Pure Land"—this is a particularly grave false view, and the retribution for such suffering will be all the more profound.
It is because our Buddha clarified only the single mind, whereas deluded people constantly cling to the four elements.
Therefore, they mistake the network of flesh for the precious net-curtain and point to delusive thoughts as the True Buddha; they take the lungs to belong to the West.
Thus, it is called the Land of Gold; the tongue produces saliva, which is consequently termed the "Flower Pond. The thousandfold paths of base and false doctrines are beyond enumeration.
How could one know that this leather sack is impure and this illusory body is not real? All toil and labor are spent in vain, ending only in decay and ruin.

Yet, in further delusion and ignorance, people secretly align themselves with the doctrine of the purity of mind and the purity of the land—not only do fools and commoners do so, but others follow as well.
They were deluded by it. Even among the scholar-officials, there were those who suffered harm from it; this is truly lamentable.
Question: Some say that the Buddha coerces sentient beings, causing them to abandon their parents and kin, cast off their physical bodies, and leave behind their native homes.
Sent far away to foreign lands, his spirit lingers in obscurity; he enters this dream-like realm where, though he obtains treasures within the dream, every form and color is not real.
Hearing this, one feels profound sorrow—wherein lies any ultimate bliss? Furthermore, it is said that even while alive, existence is but a dream realm.
Since everything is entirely a dream, it is all the more tragic. One might suppose that the Bodhisattva has already awakened, yet he proceeds as if dreaming through the six *pāramitās*.

If it were esoteric, the adornment of the true recompense would become even more ethereal and indistinct. Shall I then return to the Constant Light of Tranquil Radiance? That tranquil radiance is formless;
how vast and boundless, where could one rely upon it? It is better to dwell within the dream of this world, leaving it entirely to the likes of Xianji’s hatred and loathing.
Answer: Within the realm of the void and the floating, that which is dreamlike is not real; within the light of eternal quiescence (*nitya-prabhāsvara*), that which is true is not a dream.
Yet worldly people take dreams for reality and take reality for dreams; such perversion is truly pitiable.

How could they know that bone and flesh are nothing but enemies and grievances, and that the physical form is but a shackle? To attain birth in the Pure Land is to cast off chronic illness and be restored once more.
Having attained a full lifespan, he was released from the prison and returned gloriously to his hometown; to name this state "Ultimate Bliss"—how could it not be so?
As for the practices of a Bodhisattva, although they are said to be like a dream, they are comparable to auspicious visions appearing at night when great joy is about to arrive;
how could they be equated with the loss of dawn due to deep darkness or the portents of evil spirits summoning misfortune? For while a Bodhisattva may be in a dream, [he is] about to...
Awakened! Ordinary beings enter dream upon dream; reaching the Land of Tranquil Light (*sukhāvatī*), however, one awakens from the great slumber with clarity.
Question: Those in the world who seek rebirth are not necessarily those who desire to be reborn immediately, even if they are currently engaged in formal recitation.
At that time, the Buddha appeared before him and led him away toward the west. He declined, saying, "My conditions for conversion are not yet complete, and my marriage arrangements are not finished;
I would be fortunate if I might wait but a moment longer so as not to die. There was another person who differed from the former;

he had diligently cultivated samādhi without ceasing throughout the six periods of the day and night. Fearing that he might later grow weary and lose this opportunity, he then threw himself down to take his own life.

He set fire to himself and burned to death. Since he did not pass away with the composure of one relinquishing his retribution, as if entering meditative absorption, would the Buddha, out of pity for his folly, even be willing to receive him with His own hands?
Answer: When a wise person cultivates the Pure Land, they purify their own minds while alive; when their retribution is exhausted, they simply follow conditions.

To go forth [into the religious life] while unwilling to be born and yet remaining attached to worldly conditions is arrogance. To desire birth so urgently that one destroys one's own body and life is folly.
Such as these, at the light end, will be drawn into the ranks of Māra; at the heavy end, they will sink into the evil realms.
The sunlight shines everywhere, yet it cannot reach the underside of a *pó-é* (a low-hanging fruit). Although the Buddha possesses great compassion, there is nothing he can save.

Question: When kings and ministers attain rebirth [in the Pure Land], they do so without abandoning their state affairs; when lay practitioners (*jūshì*) attain rebirth, they do so without abandoning their household duties.
Now, if a lay practitioner recites the Buddha’s name with single-minded devotion, they may have no other hindrances—just as it is for kings and ministers.
Toiling in the service of the sovereign must not be compared to domestic affairs, which can be shirked.
How could the various masters such as Yang Wuweishang have ever been stigmatized as "widowers in office" (*guanguan*), yet ultimately achieved the welcome of the Buddha?

Is it because military, administrative, and judicial duties do not hinder rebirth in the Pure Land? Or is it because their every thought was never at variance with the true nature of reality (*dharmatā*)?
Answer: For the person who has attained the mind, though there be ten thousand affairs and ten thousand transformations, the administration of the state is not complex.

For those who cling to sensory objects, even a single husband and wife bring about domestic entanglements. This is like a bright mirror reflecting things: it reflects all day long without fatigue; or like an empty valley transmitting sound:
many voices pass through it without exhaustion. In this way, the Great Ruler is no different from the World-Honored One, and the hundred high officials [are no different from the Sangha].

Why would the assembly not gather like the ocean? When there is mutual exhortation and response amidst joy and sorrow, the wondrous Dharma is proclaimed; when there is celebration and reward alongside punishment and awe, true compassion is impartial.
Royal affairs and Buddhist affairs are forged into a single whole—how could it be difficult to be born in the Pure Land?
Question: Those who are deluded today are like people sitting with their backs to a candle; when they turn their heads, there is none who does not see the candle.
If one contemplates the Buddha for even a single thought-moment, one should immediately see the Buddha.

If it must be through the ripening of such contemplation that one sees him, would those who turn their heads to see a candle also necessarily stare fixedly at it for a long time before seeing it? Suppose the Buddha were to employ skillful means (upāya) in this regard...

When one recollects the Buddha, one sees the Buddha in accordance with that recollection; when the mind comes to rest, thoughts are severed, and amidst various distractions, one becomes suddenly oblivious.
Such a person truly recollects the Buddha. How could there be an icchantika among them?
Answer: The sun rises daily in the heavens, yet one wearing a basin on one’s head does not perceive it; a bright mirror is constantly before one’s face, yet the blind have no knowledge of it.
For those who recite the Buddha’s name, every thought-moment is in communion with Amitābha, yet they remain self-obscured and deluded.

How is this any different from these examples? It is simply because the water of the mind is turbid that the moon of the Buddha does not appear; the sentient beings themselves are at fault regarding the Buddha.
What cause for resentment? Moreover, the bright torch is behind one's back; how many people turn their heads to look? Pointing it out is but a futile labor.
To remain stubbornly headstrong and yet blame the Buddha for being difficult to perceive—how truly singular is that!
Question: The *Huangdi Neijing* clarifies the disease of "great delusion," stating that it occurs when there is no apparent cause within the eyes, yet something is suddenly seen.
Now, when a practitioner suddenly sees something within the state of fundamental non-existence, how does this differ from seeing ghosts?

Furthermore, it is said that one receives the guidance [of a Buddha] only at the moment of death; as the saying goes, "When one's time has declined, ghosts play with people. Upon casting off the body...
To follow this [view] is it not a great delusion?
Answer: To suddenly see something without cause—how could it not be false? That what was previously observed now comes to fruition—how could it not be real?
This is indeed the constant principle of cause and effect. A student of pure practice must, during their daily life, investigate the fundamental origins of cause and effect.
One must discern the subtle distinctions between the heterodox and the orthodox. As for what is seen at the moment of death, the difference between Mara and the Buddha will be manifest;

who then could be deluded? For example, if one visualizes a standing Buddha and instead a seated Buddha appears, it is Mara. If the primary retribution and the environmental retribution do not accord with the scriptural texts, it is Mara.
