If one uses the contemplation of emptiness to become obscured by emptiness itself, it is Mara. If it were otherwise, then the pure mind—

It is established that when the pure realm manifests before one, one is welcomed and led to rebirth there. Since this was taught from the golden mouth [of the Buddha], how could it be compared to something occurring without cause or reason?
Question: Some say that the West is a region where heaven collapses and things grow old; that only upon the severance of the dying person's thoughts can they be born there. How is this so?
It is further said: "Where heaven tilts, the earth has a surplus; having this surplus, it can extensively accommodate the multitude who have been reborn there.
It is also said: "Geng and Xin belong to Metal; metal does not change or decay, which demonstrates the meaning of non-retrogression.
Furthermore, it is said: "All things are completed in the west, and all fruits ripen in autumn; the practitioner cultivates causes in the east."
To realize the fruit of enlightenment in the West and secretly aspire for rebirth there is merely a response to the current impulse of sentient beings.

Why not enter the Eastern Repository of Beings instead of entering this land of withering and killing? If one were to point toward the Ultimate Truth (paramārtha-satya), why not directly gather people within the Center?
Is it not simply that you are discussing what is appropriate for a specific moment? As for what is called "the West," it has no fixed location.
Is this a grasping at meaning? Answer:
A single word of the Tathāgata contains many meanings; however, since the heterodox and the orthodox follow divergent paths, it is logically necessary to exercise discernment.

If one says that "thought is severed," then who is it that gives rise to thought? If one says that "the earth contains [all things]," then the capacity of the earth is limited. The nature of gold is immutable. Autumn...

Regarding the title "Director of Accomplishment" (*sicheng*), the two interpretations are close [in validity]. However, when discussed according to reality, it is not entirely so. For while space is inexhaustible, worlds are likewise boundless.
This very land of Sukhāvatī appears as the West when viewed from the East, and as the East when viewed from the West;

the same applies to the two directions of South and North. Because Śākyamuni exhorted [beings] to go there, he spoke of the West; yet when other Buddhas praise rebirth there, they must necessarily designate it [according to their own perspective].

He adheres to the interpretation that the West is the established position, remaining rigid and refusing to reconcile it with other views. Were this not so, why would the Youth have traveled everywhere in his studies, and why would the South be designated as the "Correct Position"?
It was only when the Medicine Master manifested himself that the East was likewise made a Pure Land. It simply comes down to returning the mind to a single point;
once one is single-mindedly focused, success is achieved.
Question: Tuṣita is the palace of Maitreya. In the past, many people frequently made vows to seek rebirth there, and there were established ritual methods for doing so.
Yet, when Dao’ang of the Tang dynasty focused his cultivation exclusively on the Western Pure Land, Tuṣita nevertheless came to welcome him at the time of his death.
If Tuṣita can be attained even without making a vow, it seems that the Western Pure Land might likewise be attained without a vow. Furthermore, some have vowed to take up [the practice of] copper...

If one vows to obtain an iron wheel but instead obtains an iron wheel; or vows to obtain a golden terrace but instead obtains a silver terrace—then it may likewise be uncertain whether one will obtain the pure land of the West instead of the pure land of the East.

Answer: The ten wholesome precepts and meditative concentration are the primary causes for rebirth in the heavens; making vows and dedicating merit are the primary causes for rebirth in the Pure Land.
Thus, while those born in the heavens may sometimes not rely upon such vows, those born in the Pure Land cannot achieve it without them.

This is because although the Pure Land is not devoid of the power of goodness, the vow takes precedence; likewise, while rebirth in the heavens also depends upon aspiration, it is the wholesome roots that serve as the foundation.
The Master of the World. There are those in this world who first cultivate the practices for rebirth in heaven, and later single-mindedly direct their intent toward the Western Land.

Consequently, they manifest at the Jade Capital (Yujing) upon death, yet soon thereafter their traces vanish, only to reappear prominently in the Buddha-land. This is surely the response to focused and dedicated seeking; how could it be achieved through casual cultivation?
It is like when copper and iron do not yet match the standard, while gold and silver remain somewhat distant; such seekers of the highest attain only the mediocre. Nevertheless, in the end...

In the end, it will surely accord with one's wishes. If one’s resolve is set upon the Western Land but one’s merit is not yet complete, one will simply be reborn in the good realms of humans or devas.
If you can apply your mind with single-minded purity and make a firm, sincere vow, then the West is where you shall go; why worry about being born in the East?
Question: In the rites of repentance, one pays homage to all Buddhas throughout the three periods of time; yet, when it comes to the Buddha one contemplates, it is specifically Amitābha alone.
This is surely because the Buddhas of the three periods have no vow regarding the recitation of their names. However, Amitābha also has many names, as fully recorded in the sutras.
Is it permissible to select any one of these names and maintain it? According to the *Smaller Amitābha Sūtra*, [the name] is translated as "Immeasurable" (Amitāyus).
The Buddha of Immeasurable Life possesses immeasurable light; yet, why does the *Amitābha-sūtra* (Contemplation Sūtra) specifically refer to him as "Immeasurable Life"?

Is it that the wisdom by which he is contemplated is itself the light being contemplated? Furthermore, among the Buddhas of the six directions, there is also one named Immeasurable Life in the west—is this perhaps the same Buddha praising himself?
Answer: The names and titles of the Tathāgata are indeed manifold; however, they are intended merely to reach the ears of those sentient beings for whom a particular name is most familiar.

In reality, there is no distinction among them. Only the title of that Amitābha is universally pervasive throughout the ten directions; therefore, it causes all who recite and contemplate his name to attain a single, unified realization.
Furthermore, "Wuliangshou" (Immeasurable Life) is the Chinese translation, while "Amitābha" is the Sanskrit term. Thus, the measure of his lifespan is made manifest.
Equal to empty space, its radiance naturally pervades the universe; its entire substance encompasses all function. It is sufficient simply to call it "Immeasurable Life" (Amitāyus).
As for the Buddhas of the ten directions, when examined, there have been many who shared the same name;

the titles of Śākyamuni Buddha alone are beyond calculation. Why should the Lord of Sukhāvatī be any different? This is not self-praise on the part of the Buddha, nor is there any room for doubt. In the present age...
There are those who cling to Śākyamuni while failing to keep Amida in mind; they consider themselves right, contending with the masses and claiming superiority.
Alas! Śākyamuni has sent you to take Amida as your teacher, yet you do not follow this instruction. It is like a son who defies his father’s command and refuses to attend a wise master;
though he calls out to his father every day, how can he avoid being called unfilial?
Question: The bliss of the Land of Ultimate Bliss arises from consciousness. From the Third Dhyāna upward, one no longer indulges in such pleasure;

yet within the nine grades [of rebirth], one still seeks it. Why is this? If you say that "bliss" refers to the bliss of quiescent extinction (*śānti*), how could it necessarily be called bliss by being naturally free from the manifold sufferings associated with food and clothing? If you say that the Pure Land is "mind-only," then [the mind]...
The essence is eternal bliss. Why, then, is it said that observing the Buddha’s mind consists of great compassion? The answer is:
although the Land of Ultimate Bliss accommodates the ordinary mind, it actually possesses two aspects. First, it is called "Ultimate Bliss" because it is spoken of in contrast to suffering;

as there are no manifold sufferings, it is named Ultimate Bliss. Second, it is called "Ultimate Bliss" when speaking of bliss in accordance with its true nature; as there is neither suffering nor bliss, it is named Ultimate Bliss. This...
How could this true joy be approximated by ordinary consciousness? Furthermore, while the śrāvakas take extinction as their joy, the Great Sage takes compassion as his joy;
thus, is not the mind of great compassion itself the eternal joy? As for worldly people who speak of sorrow with a sense of distress, that is merely superficial.
Question: When one person performs the work of a Buddha, all Buddhas should know it; the Buddhas of the ten directions come to welcome them. Toward whom, then, does this person go?

Since the Buddhas are identical in their essence (*dharmatā*), identical in their traces (*nirmāṇa*), and identical in all their aspects, those who practice mindfulness of the Buddha should be welcomed and guided by all the Buddhas of the ten directions together.
Yet here, only the Three Sages from a single direction go to welcome them. This must be because at the time of their mindfulness...

[The questioner] says: "Your view is biased and shallow. [The Master] replies: "Although the Buddhas are able to know all things universally, they do not confuse their responses to the capacities of beings. Since even a single Buddha diligently applies focused mindfulness, the response and the invocation naturally accord.
For one who cultivates the Pure Land, even if all Buddhas were to manifest simultaneously, there must still be a principal and an attendant. Mī... [text ends]
Only Śākyamuni is manifest, with clouds of transformation-buddhas following him; this is the natural law (*dharmatā*) of cause and effect, not something brought about by partiality or superficiality.

Question: The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states that Śākyamuni also possesses a pure land (*śuddhāvāsakṣetra*). Since our original Teacher spoke these final words of truth during the age of the Dharma’s decay (*paścimakāla*), how could one fail to believe and accept them?
Thus, throughout the six periods of the day and night, one should simply recollect the Buddha Kāśyapa and be born in the country of Duṣprasaha.
Is this not indeed appropriate to the occasion? Śākyamuni extols Amitābha to the utmost; it would be fitting for him to fulfill that wish.
Once you have been born there, what obstacle could there be to my being sent to serve Amitābha?
Answer: Among all Buddhas, who does not possess a pure land? Even Amitābha once had a defiled realm.

This is truly because lands mutually support one another and Buddhas praise one another, much like the worldly practice of exchanging children for mutual instruction, or like grafting branches onto flowers so they may grow. Such subtle functions and hidden skillful means are inconceivable.
How could one know that the realm of difficult-to-conquer evil is not itself a land of purity and peace? Otherwise, how could one discern that Gautama attained the Dharma-less state?
After this [teaching] has been hidden, you should simply follow the present instructions and not seek elsewhere.
Question: It is said that one who has attained great penetration and great awakening may still go on to see Amitābha.

Since such a person has already bypassed all the stages and attained Buddhahood on the spot, seeing the Buddha with the Buddha is like knowing knowledge with knowledge. Is this "one seeing" not redundant?

This is the third [point]. This is the realization. The intention is to provisionally demonstrate a model. Furthermore, although the principle has already transcended all bounds, the body remains that of an ordinary person;
only when one attains wondrous function can one then deliver sentient beings.

Answer: When an ordinary person first attains awakening, their perspective becomes equal to that of a Buddha. Although a Bodhisattva practices reality and possesses boundless capacities, they remain far from Buddhahood;
thus, there is no harm in again relying on the ancient Buddhas to receive new teachings. One should both verify and investigate them—how could they ever be exhausted?
An ancient said that those who leave their teacher too early cannot fully realize its subtlety; how much more so for those who leave the Buddha? If...
To cling to the three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* of refinement belongs to the Hīnayāna of the Tripitaka teachings; yet, like a fledgling flying wildly, one loses much benefit.
Should one not be cautious? Question:
"The pure is the defiled, and the defiled is the pure. Thus, the Western Land and this land do not differ by even a fraction of an inch. Having been born...

This is precisely non-arising. To go is, in truth, not to go. Now, within the span of a single thought-moment of a finger-snap or the bending and extending of an arm—this already defines time—it is as if one has lifted a foot and taken a step. Though this is said to be extremely swift, it still involves two paths.
Answer: When attachments cease and delusions are dissolved, even if the path is obstructed by a thousand mountains, all is integrated and non-dual.

Yet when the emotional barriers and the fetters of consciousness remain, even if one were to transcend them as swiftly as a finger-snap, the separation remains profoundly deep. Nowadays, students seek only for the novelty and cleverness of words and phrases.

They take pleasure in discussing what is defiled as being identical to the pure; they do not realize their heads are submerged in the depths of the Nine Abysses, yet they claim there is no difference between heaven and earth.
Their bodies sink into the midst of stinking latrines, yet they claim there is no distinction between the fragrant and the putrid. Truly, this is to be pitied!
Question: If one were to stop a person on the road and ask them, they would all say that "reciting the Buddha's name" refers to vocal recitation and not mental recitation.
If pressed further, they would say that it is the correspondence between mind and mouth. Now, if mind and mouth correspond, this constitutes sound;

if movement arises because of the mind, this constitutes mindfulness (*smṛti*). How, then, can sound be considered mindfulness? Or, if it is said that all phenomena are but mind alone, what place is there for sound?
[Objection: "Is it not the mind? If so, then the sounding of bells, drums, zithers, and lutes would also be mental volitions (*saṃjñā*). This is quite a muddled argument. [Response:
Although bells and drums possess a grand resonance, they do not sound without being struck. Although zithers and lutes possess exquisite tones, they do not emerge without fingers.
Bells, drums, zithers, and lutes are like the outward extension of lips and tongue; their striking or plucking is like the internal movement of mental volition.
Movement occurs as when one has severed all thought; from where, then, could sound be produced? Therefore, even the incoherent muttering of sleep-talking arises from dreams;

how could the vast resonance of the Buddha’s voice not originate from the source of one's own mind? It is merely that worldly people call upon it by habit, neither with single-minded devotion nor with earnest application.

At first, one relies upon mindfulness. Once the sound is produced, the mind becomes distracted by following that sound; this is called "correspondence," yet in reality, it is not corresponding at all.

As the saying goes: "If the mouth and the mind’s voice correspond sound for sound, and the mind and the Buddha are never parted step for step—practicing mindfulness of the Buddha in this way, one may approach the goal."
Question: When Sudhana visited the Bodhisattva Meghashri, he first came to know the dharma-gate of mindfulness of the Buddha.
Subsequently, after traveling south through a hundred cities and visiting fifty-four teachers, he beheld Amitābha Buddha, whereby his samādhi was perfected.

Later, when Mañjuśrī manifested his body in the Bamboo Grove, he merely instructed people to mindfully recite the name of Amitābha Buddha. Now, by this standard, Sudhana’s rank had already reached the end of the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*).
Why does Mañjuśrī not directly point to Amitābha, but instead cause him to travel through a hundred cities?
For those students who, before even having "sought south," suddenly propose returning west, is this not a premature calculation?
Answer: To begin one’s study by being taught to practice *nienfo* (Buddha-recollection) is to proceed from the source to the flow;

to travel extensively until one beholds Amitābha is to return to the root from the branches. As it is said: "There is nothing that does not flow from this Dharma-realm, and there is nothing that does not return to this Dharma-realm.
Therefore, to inquire southward and return westward—how could this be called returning late? To be reborn and travel everywhere—how can this be called early?
Consider this: when the King of Physicians dispenses medicine, he adapts to the primary and secondary causes as appropriate;
his subtle maneuvers are beyond the comprehension of ordinary minds. Question: "To recite the Buddha's name while encompassing all six sense faculties" is the teaching of Śrī-Ābhāsvara.

Since mindfulness arises from the mind, then for those who make vows, dedicate merit, or perform repentance, every single thought encompasses them. In the world, there is no vow that exists outside of the mind. And...

This is the dedication, prostration, and repentance performed outside of the mind. Now, to single-mindedly recite the Buddha’s name is precisely the bodhicitta (the aspiration for enlightenment) generated by that Buddha;
it is the vow. To focus exclusively upon this Buddha is precisely dedication (*pariṇāmanā*). *Namo* is precisely prostration.

A single thought-moment that eliminates the sins of birth and death is precisely repentance (*pratideśanā*). The rest may be understood by analogy. What is there in the recitation of the Buddha’s name that is not [encompassed]?
"It is sufficient; why cause such confusion that the mind becomes disordered? He replied:

"A single-minded purity constitutes the internal illumination of principle-contemplation (*li-guan*); the diligent exertion of the five limbs is called the external assistance of ritual repentance (*shi-chan*).

While directly contemplating the fundamental mind is indeed the direct and essential path, sentient beings of the Dharma-ending age have meager wisdom and heavy defilements; they must rely upon [external aids]."

The practice of contemplation on principle (*li-guan*) and the ritual repentance of phenomena (*shi-chan*) must attack the internal and external simultaneously; only then may one hope for the stabilization of concentration (*samādhi*) and the perfection of wisdom (*prajñā*), thereby swiftly liberating oneself from birth and death.
Yet nowadays, people maintain only the ritual repentance of phenomena while the contemplation on principle is utterly neglected.

This is especially true when they outwardly display empty formalities while inwardly lacking genuine remorse, causing the hearts of the faithful laity to become distracted and confused, turning their backs on the King of Vows, Samantabhadra, and deviating from the fundamental intent of Maitreya’s Cloud of Compassion.
The Proclamation: Alas! How tragic! This corruption has persisted for a long time.

Question: The *Amitābha Sūtra* states that the mind of contemplating the Buddha is great compassion. If people of the world can release living beings and refrain from killing, showing benevolence toward the people and love toward all creatures, extending this even to the nine classes of sentient beings so that they all attain nirvāṇa, yet do not themselves conceive of "nirvāṇa"—[is this not the contemplation of the Buddha?]
Having transcended conceptualization, he has thus entered into resonance with the mind of Dharmākara. Furthermore, this does not contravene Śākyamuni’s instruction on contemplating the mind.
How can one take the superficial traces of contemplating the body or reciting the name and, conversely, treat the Buddha-mind as a mere auxiliary condition?
Answer: There are two ways of recollecting the Buddha (*buddhānusmṛti*). First is recollecting the Buddha’s mind-nature; second is recollecting the Buddha’s body and name.

Recollecting the mind-nature is to see the True Buddha. This does not preclude beholding the Buddha of radiant marks and signs in the Western Land. Recollecting the body and name is to see the Responsive Buddha (*nirmāṇakāya*).
Yet one can also perceive the Buddha of self-nature and original truth beyond all forms. Thus, both the fundamental and the manifested are realized.
Exposition: Principle and phenomena share a common source; the nature of mind is not merely a secondary condition. How can the physical body and its name be called mere superficial traces?

Today, those who follow the five schools and six volumes of scriptures use "non-action" as a pretext to negate cause and effect, obstructing others from making offerings to images and ridiculing those who recite the Buddha’s name.
An ancient worthy said: "Only when every person is a Danxia can one then split open the Buddha; only when every individual is a Baizhang can one then say 'there is nothing.
If this is not yet the case, you will enter hell as swiftly as a shooting arrow."

Question: Such things as flowers in the sky, a [magical] cloth, or a rabbit [with horns] are what the world calls illusions and falsehoods. All retributions of the environment and its inhabitants (the *āśraya* and *adhiṣṭhāna*) are what the world calls real entities.
If the Buddha says that even these real entities are all illusory and false, then what name should be given to things like flowers in the sky, a cloth, or a rabbit?
Even granting that those real entities are indeed illusory and false, their forms and appearances remain distinct and clear.
As for falsehood, it may suffice to regard it as empty flowers in the sky or a rabbit’s horns; why wait for them to be broken down through analysis before realizing they are illusory and deceptive?
Therefore, that which possesses illusion is like that which possesses illusion; that which possesses delusion is like that which possesses delusion.

Are those who dwell together in the Pure Land illusory and deceptive, or are they like that which is illusory and deceptive? Total delusion is itself reality; total illusion is itself the Middle Way. This is the case even in the defiled land of shared residence.
This is precisely the Land of Common Residence. Is this Land of Common Residence identical to the aforementioned three lands? Answer:

Like flowers in the sky, a cloth, or a rabbit’s horns, these are entirely void and non-existent. Like a flesh-eating hare, a tree-flower, or a phantom, they have from the beginning been illusory and false.

Fundamentally, they do not need to be pushed away to be destroyed; it is simply that one is deluded and does not yet know them as such. Therefore, the actual illusion and that which is like an illusion are no different; reality and falsity—[are likewise non-dual].
How does this differ from the delusory? Dwelling together in the Pure Land, it is both illusion and suchness; it is both the true and the middle.
To speak of it comprehensively, it is both defiled and pure; it is both one and three. Ultimately empty and quiescent, what stages or limits could there be? Nevertheless, although it is thus...

If emotional attachments and biased views have not yet been shattered, and the feelings of longing for the pure and aversion toward the defiled still persist, one must eliminate delusions and realize the true and eternal;

one must abandon this defiled land and seek rebirth in a Pure Land. However, if abandoning the defiled to grasp the pure is merely an activity of birth and death, how could there be such a thing as a Pure Land?
Question: People fear birth and death as a matter of great importance; since impermanence is so swift, they only then develop a fierce desire for liberation, not daring to rest even for a moment.

Yet, upon hearing the principle of suddenly exiting the triple world, the discourse on the shortcut of practice, the texts on eliminating sins through *nien-fo*, and the vow of rebirth with ten recitations, they immediately claim there is a Buddha to rely upon and that their karma is no longer sufficient [to bind them].
Out of fear, they become distracted and ultimately fail to gain efficacy; thus, many fall into the hands of Old Yama. This is because the Lotus School has led them astray.
As for the two gates of the Chan and Pure Land schools, their investigation is extremely difficult, and they do not permit one to see immediate results.
With the two words "birth and death" constantly weighing upon the mind, how could such [distraction] possibly occur?

Answer: Among ordinary people who cultivate the Way, there are those who stop when they hear of difficulty and proceed when they hear of ease; and there are those who exert themselves when they hear of difficulty and become indolent when they hear of ease.
The ancient sages established their teachings each according to what was appropriate for the time. Whether one is able to apply the mind skillfully depends solely upon the individual.
As for the single path of Buddha-remembrance (*nien-fo*), it directly transcends the triple world. Because it is the ultimate expression of Great Compassion, this gateway was opened. If...

Now, negligence leads to ruin; it is sentient beings who delude themselves, not the Buddha who deludes them. "If I desire benevolence (*ren*), then benevolence arrives. Benevolence is right before one's eyes.
"If a madman can maintain mindfulness, he becomes a sage (*sheng*). Sagehood is not remote. Is this, too, making the path easy and thereby leading people astray?
As for the sudden enlightenment through a single word or becoming a Buddha on the spot—this ease of expression in the Chan school is, moreover, [a source of error].
How extraordinary! How could one possibly call this an error?
Question: Fǎnggān was an emanation of Amitābha; Hánshān and Shídé were Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra.
Yet, when Amitābha appeared, he did not lead Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta, but instead traveled accompanied by Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra. This reaches the point of contradiction.

Furthermore, there are many phrases from the Chan school [in this work]. Is it not possible that [the author] considered the practices of mindfulness of the Buddha and visualization of the Buddha to be too restrictive, and thus transformed *Tathāgata-citta* (Buddha-dhyāna) into *Caoxiu chan* (the Patriarchs' Chan)?
Or is it that those who dwell in the Land of Constant Quiescent Light cannot be reached by any means other than this?

Answer: It is true that Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta are called the "two attendants" of the Guide; yet how could Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra ever have been separated from An-yang (Sukhāvatī) for even a moment?
Thus, while Śākyamuni is the transformation lord of the Sahā world, he is always accompanied by Avalokiteśvara. Furthermore, Huangbo was not a patriarch of the Confucian tradition.
The succession of patriarchs has extended and flourished; their harmonious integration and transformative guidance—how could they have fixed limits?

As for the claim that discourse involving the Chan school seems to overturn pure karma, one fails to realize that from every branch of the nine lotus blossoms, the countenance of Kāśyapa unfolds, and with every step upon the railings of the seven treasures, one enters the pavilion of Sudhana.
Upon each of the eight facets of the ūrṇā-kośa, one contemplates the true exposition of the Middle Way.

The six characters of this name reveal, character by character, the esoteric intent of the Western Transmission. Why wait until the Small Vehicle is transformed into the Great, or the particular is changed into the universal, before receiving those of superior faculties and unfolding this profound transformation?
Thus we know that the single path of Buddha-remembrance (*nien-fo*) is the wondrous gate for entering the Principle.
It fully encompasses the five schools and broadly includes all teachings; its subtlety is unfathomable, and its vastness is infinite. For those of dull faculties...
Those with the spiritual faculties who encounter it will swiftly escape the wheel of suffering; those with sharp wisdom who meet it will directly transcend to the other shore.
It appears coarse yet is subtle; it seems easy yet is difficult. May all contemplate this deeply and take care not to treat it with negligence.
Reply to Cao Luchuan (Attached is the original letter).

It has been a long time since I last received your personal instructions; I feel deeply regretful. However, from time to time I have obtained your transcribed teachings, which have guided me in great measure.
My gratitude and thanks! My gratitude and thanks! I look up to you from afar with a profound sense of longing and reliance. Recently, the monk Duanshan Wushang of our district...
I hasten to the foot of the altar; for the sake of seeking the Dharma, I send these words to inquire after your well-being.

I am an untalented and misguided man who has recently guarded the teachings of the East (Confucianism) and from afar revered those of the West (Buddhism). For forty years now, I have been like a woodworm boring into the books of both Confucianism and Buddhism.
I have also received instruction from various masters of attainment and have accumulated some knowledge; I hope that you, O Great One, will correct it.
Good friend, this has been disseminated because Danfan requested it. Now, the Buddha Śākyamuni possesses the teachings of the Three Piṭakas and the Twelve Divisions of Scripture;
these are what are called "casting many nets across the vast ocean" and "the large granaries and small granaries.
One should simply discuss the great so as to encompass the small; how could one possibly advocate for one while abandoning the many? As for me...
Within our school, there are those who advocate the view that the attainment of sainthood over successive kalpas must necessarily be gradual and not sudden.

Now, while the gradual approach is indeed a teaching of the Sage and is by no means incorrect, to reject the sudden approach on account of the gradual is erroneous. The Venerable One [Huiyuan] kept the sudden and perfect teachings hidden within himself.
Furthermore, it is manifest that the Dharma-gate of the Pure Land exists; that all Buddhas possess this is beyond doubt.

Is it not the case that among recent listeners there have been those who, as described in the Lotus Sūtra, upon first hearing the Buddha-dharma, immediately believed and accepted it, contemplating it until they attained realization?
[Yet some] desire to discard the fifteen princes entirely in favor of the single sage Amitābha, [relying solely on the Pure Land...]
To completely discard the Tripiṭaka and the twelve divisions of the scriptures upon encountering a single sūtra is something this unworthy one does not wish to hear.
Although we live in the age of the Dharma’s decline, how could the capacities of these people lack both sharpness and dullness?
It is just as when the World-Honored Śākyamuni spoke thus for Kāśyapa and Kauṇḍinya, yet spoke differently for Sudhana and the Dragon Girl.
Those twenty-five sages each realized their own perfect penetration, as Wen-shu described them.
This is precisely what is meant by "yesterday's certainty is today's uncertainty," and what is meant by saying "I am empty, yet not empty;
I am existent, yet not existent. This is why it is called the "good master of impermanence," lively and vibrant.

It is like pressing a gourd upon water; yet this is not a method of total annihilation. If one were to merely stake oneself to the ground and guard a single cave, how could this benefit those in the realms of humans and devas?

It is my hope that the Venerable One will propagate the Pure Teaching for the great assembly. Encountering those of sharp faculties, you should point them toward the Supreme Vehicle, so that they may achieve perfect, harmonious, and thorough penetration without being obstructed by partiality.
To enable both the great Peng bird and the small sparrow to find their own fulfillment—would this not be the ultimate in beauty and goodness?
Ah! Furthermore, the *Buddhāvatamsaka* is the unsurpassed, perfect teaching of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*), the ultimate expression of the Tathāgata’s nature.
It speaks of that which is neither doctrine nor school, yet is both school and doctrine; it is neither empty nor existent, and is neither defiled nor pure.
Even the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* is but one step inferior to this. As for other vehicles, they seem difficult to compare with it in terms of length or brevity.
To equate this [text] with the *Amitābha Sūtra* (Míto jīng) already seems inappropriate;
therefore, treatises have been composed to elevate it, even placing the Pure Land tradition above the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*. How can one allow the colors of red and purple to be so confused?
To point at each other as being either a deer or a horse—what more can be said? If no one speaks of this, the world and future generations will surely mock us, saying there are no people in Qin.
Furthermore, I pray that the Venerable One will explain the Pure Land for those who are rooted in it.
To preach the *Avataṃsaka* for those whose faculties are suited to the *Avataṃsaka*—do not mock one another, nor do let them become confused.

This is how the Buddha-vehicle is propagated; this is how the five teachings are presented together, so that all three types of faculties are fully encompassed. Alas, why must one seek a sword by marking the spot where it fell from a boat?
It is like shooting at a sparrow while letting a hawk escape. As for the single scripture of the *Avataṃsaka*, it possesses faith, understanding, and practice.
Regarding the realization of the four dharmas: one who skillfully expounds this teaching should not be like Fangshan. His words remain extant today and may be verified.
Now there was Qingliang, whom people called the Avataṃsaka Bodhisattva, yet in reality he did not comprehend the essential meaning of the Avataṃsaka.
He haphazardly split the entire scripture into four parts and assigned them to the four dharmas, thereby [distorting] the wondrous meaning of Vairocana.

I have cast [this matter] among the weeds and brush. I also pray that the Venerable One will distinguish black from white and separate the Jing from the Wei, raising the bright sun over the sky of righteousness.
Alas! Alas! In these times, the eminent figures among both the monastic and lay communities are daily declining.
That which I, the unworthy one, look up to and revere in the Venerable One is like Mount Tai or Mount Song. Therefore, I do not offer praise, but rather counsel; may you know my intent.
This is because there is no self, and I, being without talent, am likewise not a self; therefore, I speak of this repeatedly. I pray that the Venerable One will understand me.

For a long time I have heard that you, Layman, have applied yourself with profound intent to the Avataṃsaka Sūtra, and I have held you in the highest esteem and reverence. Now, having received your letter, its earnestness and directness truly...
To encompass all sentient beings throughout the entirety of the Dharma-realm within the ocean of the nature of the One Vehicle—this is the Great Vow of Samantabhadra.
Although I, your unworthy servant, revere the Pure Land, in truth I revere the Avataṃsaka Sūtra no differently than you, Layman.
For the Avataṃsaka possesses immeasurable gateways; seeking rebirth in the Pure Land is but one gateway among those immeasurable gateways of the Avataṃsaka. Regarding this:
The timing of this opportunity is such that one enters the *Avataṃsaka* through this single gateway; it is not that by citing this one gateway, the *Avataṃsaka* as a whole is discarded.
Furthermore, regarding your letter’s claim that I have composed a treatise because I equated Amitābha with the *Avataṃsaka*, thereby elevating Pure Land above the *Avataṃsaka*:
who is the author of such a treatise? The *Avataṃsaka* is like the heavens.

My son, who has ever placed the feudal lords, kings, great ministers, and hundreds of officials above the Son of Heaven? Yet even those of inferior merit have never been mentioned alongside him in equal rank.
In the *Shuchao*, it is specifically stated that the *Avataṃsaka* represents the ultimate perfection (*pariniṣpanna*), whereas the *Amitābha Sūtra* attains but a small portion of that perfection;
it is a relative and derivative category of the *Avataṃsaka*, not its equal. The ancients have said that the *Avataṃsaka* and—
Other sutras are like the bright sun shining in the sky, eclipsing the brilliance of all other lights; or like Mount Sumeru spanning the sea, surpassing the height of all other peaks.

How could there be anything to rival them? This need not even be discussed. Furthermore, your letter suggests that one should preach the teachings according to the capacities of others—that those who favor the Pure Land should be taught the Pure Land, and those who favor the Avatamsaka should be taught the Avatamsaka. This intention is indeed excellent.
Excellent. However, there are two meanings herein. First, that the myriad capacities are nurtured simultaneously is the work of the Tathāgata appearing in the world;

it is not something an unworthy person like myself can accomplish. Thus, while Caodong was dedicated exclusively to the Chan of direct pointing, does this mean he was不通 (unable to penetrate) other teachings?
While Huiyuan presided over the community at Donglin, did he stop there at merely receiving those of dull faculties? As for Yunmen, Fayan, Caodong, and Guiyang—[the same applies].
Although the Five Houses share a single source, their lineages of transmission differ slightly; that their pedagogical methods vary is but natural, and there is nothing to be wondered at.

How much more so for an unworthy person like myself! If one were to recklessly imitate the ancients—claiming yesterday’s teaching was definitive while today’s is not—and thus act without any formal lineage, creating disorder and inconsistency under the pretext of benefiting others, this would in reality be [nothing but...]

This is misleading. Why? Because I am the Dharma King, possessing sovereign mastery over the Dharma; whereas ordinary people merely style themselves "kings," one must not fail to be cautious regarding this distinction.
Second, when the *Avataṃsaka* is taught, it encompasses the Pure Land; when the Pure Land is taught, it likewise extends to the *Avataṃsaka*.
Therefore, those who teach the *Avataṃsaka* speak of the *Avataṃsaka*, and those who teach the Pure Land speak of the Pure Land—this is indeed so.

These two proceed in parallel without contradicting one another. People today know only that the *Avataṃsaka* is more extensive than the *Sukhāvatīvyūha*, yet they fail to realize that Amitābha is none other than Vairocana.

Furthermore, your letter states that Qingliang failed to grasp the essential meaning of the *Avataṃsaka* and split the entire scripture into four parts to assign them to the four dharmas (*śraddhā*, *adhimukti*, *caryā*, and *sākṣātkriyā*).
Although faith, understanding, practice, and realization indeed permeate the entire scripture, the scripture...
The text, from beginning to end, possesses a natural sequence; it is not that Qingliang arbitrarily imposed divisions upon it.

Its thorough penetration is what is called "perfect interfusion" (yuanrong), and its sequential order is what is called "gradual unfolding" (xingbu). Since it is precisely within this gradual unfolding that perfect interfusion resides, how could the fourfold division be detrimental?
If there were no gradual unfolding, what would perfect interfusion be? If one must eliminate the gradual unfolding, then perfect interfusion [is likewise lost].

If it were fused, it would not be perfectly integrated. Furthermore, from the stages of faith, abiding, practice, and transference, up to the Equal and Wondrous [Buddha-stages], has the Buddha himself torn this complete scripture into fifty-two sections?
Why did he not exhaust the meaning of these fifty-two sections in a single statement, rather than composing such a voluminous text?
Because the cause encompasses the ocean of the fruit, and the fruit reaches back to the source of the cause; cause and fruit have never been separate.
At the same time, it has never been the case that the cause does not arise from its own cause, nor that the fruit does not arise from its own fruit.
Why must you insist on binding eighty fascicles of scripture into a single lump, treating them all as nothing but a solid iron hammer, only then claiming this is "perfect interfusion"?
To insist on a single lump and refuse to allow it to be divided is a dead-end method; it is like nailing down a stake or guarding a den. How can this be right?
In its vitality, Fangshan’s discourse is indeed a magnificent treatise for all eternity.
Yet, every discourse has its own discursive form, and every commentary has its own commentarial form. In comprehensively clarifying the great meaning, Fangshan alone excels;

in fathoming the profound, exploring the subtle, exhausting the minute, and exhausting the mysterious, Fangshan attained the Qingliang [tradition], thereby achieving its first complete perfection. How could this apply to Fangshan alone?
From Dushun down to the successive patriarchs ending with Xianshou, they likewise attained Qingliang and achieved full completion. How much more so for the various patriarchs of the Avatamsaka alone?
As for the Tripitaka, the twelve divisions of the canon, and the commentaries and sub-commentaries of the hundred schools, these too have attained Qingliang and achieved full completion.
Wenzhong’s commentary on the Avatamsaka takes Fāngshān as its primary authority and regards Qingliang as secondary; this is already inappropriate. And...

The layman looked down upon this with disdain. This is something I, an unworthy one, do not understand. Furthermore, Nāgārjuna retrieved the *Avataṃsaka* from the Dragon Palace, yet he vowed to be reborn in Sukhāvatī.
Samantabhadra is the eldest son of the *Avataṃsaka*, yet he too vowed to be reborn in Sukhāvatī.
Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra serve as the two attendants of Vairocana; they are known as the Three Sages of the Avataṃsaka.
Yet, their vows to be reborn in Sukhāvatī are clearly attested in the scriptures, as evident as the sun and stars.

Lay Brother, you intend to proclaim the Avataṃsaka to influence the four quarters, yet you act in contradiction to Mañjuśrī, Samantabhadra, and Nāgārjuna. This is something I, your unworthy servant, cannot understand. How much more so in the case of Fāngshān?

Ten kinds of pure lands are enumerated. Although the Land of Ultimate Bliss (*Sukhāvatī*) is said to be provisional, in the *Avataṃsaka* Sūtra, the provisional and the real are interfused, and phenomena and principle are non-obstructive, such that each phenomenon is non-obstructive with every other.
Thus, even a brothel or a place of slaughter is nothing other than a pure site of practice (*śuddha-maṇḍala*). How much more so, then, is the Land of Ultimate Bliss adorned with the seven treasures?
Even the demoness Pāśupatī and the insatiable woman were all manifestations of ancient Buddhas; how much more so, then, [the beings of] the ten thousand...
Is this Amitābha, whose virtues are fully perfected? You, Layman, sport within the unimpeded gates of the *Avataṃsaka*, yet you obstruct the Pure Land;

this is something I, your unworthy servant, cannot understand. I and you, Layman, are like inseparable friends within the *Vairocanagarbha* world-system, yet you fail to perceive my humble heart. Furthermore, you wish to drag me along with you to the Lotus [Land].
We are brothers of the same flesh from the womb; I hope that you, Layman, will not cast me out. You love me, yet you do not offer praise but rather counsel.
That I now venture to offer this counsel is likewise out of my love for you. With this sick pen, I have briefly set forth the general outline, but it falls far short of fully expressing my intent.
I pray only that you will examine and grant me your understanding.
The Venerable Duanfan of our district has sent a letter of introduction requesting that I write for him, expressing his sincere intentions.
Having received your esteemed letter, I find its instructions thorough and its exhortations earnest; I am deeply grateful, repeatedly thanking you.

Your letter states that while the *Avataṃsaka* possesses immeasurable gates, seeking birth in the Pure Land is but one gate among those immeasurable gates, established according to the capacities of beings at this time. By means of...
To enter the *Avataṃsaka* through this single gate does not mean that by citing one gate the entirety of the *Avataṃsaka* is discarded.
Furthermore, it is a definitive argument to say that the *Avataṃsaka* is the ultimate perfection, such that nothing can surpass it.

However, while the *Avataṃsaka* was spoken by the Dharmakāya Buddha and its wondrous meaning of the One Vehicle is far removed from other sūtras, many people regard it as being on the same level as the sūtras of Śākyamuni.
Therefore, regarding those who have commented upon this sutra: Xian-shou initiated its beginning, while Fang-shan deeply realized its essential meaning.
At Qing-liang, the selection was not yet refined; at Wen-ling, the discourse was not yet detailed.

As for those who composed works titled *Lun-guan* (The Threaded Summary), they were merely concerned with the superficial. Wen-ling states: "Fang-shan represents the primary [teaching], while Qing-liang serves as the auxiliary."
This view is most outstanding; yet the Venerable One considers it inappropriate. It appears he was unaware of Wēnlíng, nor was he aware of Fāngshān.

Various sutras and śāstras of provisional meaning, as well as the independently circulating *Samantabhadra-caryā-praṇidhāna* and treatises such as the *Śraddhotpāda-śāstra*, all proclaim the Pure Land.
How could this be without cause? However, within the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, [it has] never...
This refers to it. It clarifies further the tenth pure land of Fangshan. In the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, the sixteen princes are listed in succession, among whom Amitābha is included;
yet he has never been definitively established as the sole honored one. His praise of the merit of upholding the sutra grants peace and happiness to all;
his actual teaching concerns the causes and conditions of women. In the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi-sūtra*, twenty-five sages testify to their realization of the perfect penetration.
Mañjuśrī makes no distinction of high or low; he merely says that there are many gates of skillful means (*upāya*). He further states that both the direct and the inverse are skillful means.

Yet, by following this with the remark that "the slow and the swift differ in their categories," he shows that even within the absence of such distinctions, there has never been a lack of a specific point toward which one is directed.
Thus, he brings the essential to its ultimate limit in the Universal Gate (*samantamukha*) without self-glorification. Now, as for Avalokiteśvara...
Furthermore, they apply depreciation and denigration, speaking of "impermanence" and "arising and ceasing.

Now, if the World-Honored One had merely taught the Larger and Smaller Amitābha Sūtras, that would have been more than sufficient. Why then was there such a proliferation of the Tripiṭaka and the twelve divisions of the scriptures?
Masters such as Xianshou and Qingliang repeatedly established the five teachings—Small, Initial, Final, Sudden, and Perfect—and all agreed they were appropriate; yet...
The schools that prioritize the Pure Land and the Mind-essence have been utterly swept away by him. Even the words of the Great Mirror (Huineng) have not yet been fully expounded;
let me further cite one or two examples. As Master Zhigong said: "The wise know that the mind is Buddha; the ignorant delight in going to the Western Paradise.
And as Chan Master Qi Ji said: "There is only the direct path of cultivation; it remains, nonetheless, to strike [at the root]."
"Simply recite the name of Amitābha Buddha. It will not do if you merely recite it without attaining realization.
He further said: "All of you come and go day and night along this path; why is it that you pass Amitābha Buddha by right before your faces? He also said:
Should one, following the previous example, abandon their father and flee, wandering aimlessly through foreign lands, bumping into this and that—how bitter it is!
"Amitābha Buddha! These three words may be considered pedantic; yet how could they be without meaning?
There must surely be a path behind those words. As the ancient masters said: "All sentient beings differ in their own delusion and enlightenment. Delusion..."
To perceive [the Buddha] as being outside the mind and to seek the Buddha through practice without awakening to one's own nature is the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna). Furthermore, it is said:
"To realize immediately and directly that this mind is fundamentally the Buddha, such that not a single dharma can be attained—this is the Unsurpassed Way."
This is the Buddha of True Suchness (*tathatā*). A student of the Way need only fear that for even a single thought there is attachment; then one is separated from the Way. Furthermore, it is said:
"There is no dharma before the eyes, yet the intent lies before the eyes. This is not a dharma of the present moment.
If you study from the side of the Buddhas and patriarchs, this person has not yet attained the eye. Why not settle the matter within the midst of birth and death? Where else could it be?
To imitate the Buddhas and the Patriarchs on your behalf regarding birth and death—this is something that a person of wisdom would laugh at you for.

Therefore, those who have attained realization say that the arduous cultivation of practice over kalpas is not as good as attaining the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) in a single thought-moment.

They further say that the non-arising of conditioned origination in a single thought-moment transcends the provisional teachings of the Three Vehicles; how much more so when one does not even distinguish between the Three Vehicles and the One Vehicle? It is essential...
[They] lack the realization of non-self and non-belonging-to-self. Now, regarding those who aspire to be reborn in the Pure Land:

"I" am the subject that is born, and the "Land" is the object wherein one is born. Self and other are distinct; birth and cessation are manifest; and longing for the pure and aversion to the defiled are in full swing. There is much yet to be fully understood.

Looking back at those who have traditionally discussed the Lotus Vehicle (the Pure Land path), they invariably say: "When the lotus flower opens, one sees the Buddha and awakens to the non-arising of dharmas. This implies that one must necessarily wait until [rebirth].
One is born and beholds Amitābha; first through Avalokiteśvara, or Mahāsthāmaprāpta, or perhaps Amitābha himself, who instructs one in non-arising (*anutpāda*).
It is only at this moment that one truly awakens. Is it because those of the highest grade are exceedingly few, while those of the middle and lower grades abound, remaining stagnant for kalpas?
This seems rather circuitous and slow. Moreover, if one wishes to cultivate the Pure Land, one must first practice the sixteen contemplation gates concerning existence, non-existence, and so forth.
I ask you: what are the rules for these objects of contemplation, and how many people are there capable of performing this contemplation?
Those who practice the recitation of the Buddha’s name are as numerous as cow hairs, while those who attain rebirth [in the Pure Land] are as rare as the horn of a unicorn.

Why do you seek the latter in reverse? There are other Buddhas available. When Han-shan exhorted Feng-k’an to go to Mount Wutai to pay homage to Mañjuśrī, saying, "This is not for one of my own kind," it was because he was one who had already attained mastery of the Buddha-way; his words and expressions naturally flowed from such realization.
They are distinct. Furthermore, all paths to Buddhahood take the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā* as their entryway and the *Buddhāvataṃsaka* as their ultimate consummation.
The *Vajracchedikā* states: "In truth, there is not the slightest dharma that can be attained.

Yet, among the two types of ignorance regarding the stage of Buddhahood (*buddhabhūmi*) mentioned in the *Buddhāvataṃsaka*, one is called "subtle ignorance regarding the objects of knowledge" (*sūkṣmajñeyāvaraṇa-moha*), and the other is called "extremely subtle ignorance regarding the objects of knowledge."
To know one's own folly! Thus, when Ānanda himself claimed that he had attained the Dharma-body without passing through the *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*, those who understand still rebuked him.

Therefore, some call it the "sore of the Buddha," while others call it the "demon of the Buddha. When Mañjuśrī momentarily gave rise to the view of Buddhahood, he was nonetheless relegated to the two Iron Ring Mountains.
Alas! Alas! A river of views can sweep away even a fragrant elephant; the Lord of Wisdom does not accept merit.
The mind of the Way has no place of abiding; its traces cannot be sought. Therefore, one does not pass through the provisional vehicles but alone upholds the One Vehicle.
This is precisely what I, the humble servant, have been earnestly devoted to.

Those Buddhas and Patriarchs [taught] for the sake of those inferior sentient beings who cling to a portion of the *ālayavijñāna*, as well as for the disciples of the Small Vehicle, relying solely on a single intent.

As for consciousness, those who reckon that the present aggregates of form, mind, and so forth serve as the basis for defilement and purity, take pity on them when the four great elements have already separated and that solitary spirit has nowhere to return—like a fish out of water, gasping toward its death. Therefore, they cannot help but settle them in a provisional Pure Land;
this is also of the same category as the "transformed city" (nirmita-nagara). It is recorded in tradition: "If one can awaken to the Dharma..."
The Dharma-body and the Dharma-nature land must ultimately return to non-substantiality; this is the true Buddha-land.
Just as in the Flower Adornment Sūtra’s Ocean of Nature, the manifested universal body is like a human body, within which there are eighty-four thousand pores.
In each pore, the Medicine Master of the East and Amitābha of the West each preach the Dharma to deliver sentient beings. If a person were to open these pores and penetrate through them...

The whole body—there has never been a time when it was not so. If one were to cast the entire body into a single pore, it would not only be like turning the bubbles on the ocean upside down, but what could be said of a fly throwing itself against the window paper?

Yesterday, in my humble hand-written note, I stated that it is appropriate to speak of the Pure Land for those who favor the Pure Land, and appropriate to speak of the Avatamsaka for those who favor the Avatamsaka; I considered this to be without contradiction.
The Dharma-gates of all Buddhas are likewise for the sake of the Venerable One’s sincere heart.

Since the Venerable One now wishes to carry me, who am but a lotus-womb, this is what the ancients meant by "if one grasps at things while entering the mired ford," and it is what is called "discarding gold to carry grass.
Furthermore, consulting the words of the ancients: "If you wish to reach the ultimate realization of this matter, you must turn toward the high [peak]."

Standing atop a high mountain peak, yet walking on the bottom of the deepest sea. If one cannot let go of the soft and warm things within the inner chambers, what use would there be [in such practice]?
Furthermore, it is said: "The practice of freedom from anger and resentment as praised in the various sutras—this anger and resentment is not comparable to ordinary worldly sentiments.
As for 'resentment,' it is to resent that all sentient beings possess the wisdom of the Tathāgata."
One possesses the marks of merit yet is unaware of them. As for those who harbor anger, they resent that my deliverance has not yet reached them;
for this reason, one must awaken oneself and awaken others. There is mundane wisdom, supramundane wisdom, and the supreme wisdom that transcends both the mundane and supramundane.
If one employs these to speak with people, they will not encounter resistance or rejection; thus, one may hope to benefit others. Looking back to the three [ancient sages] of old...
When the Sage appears in the world, there is nothing he does that is not for the sake of the One Great Matter. Observe the timing and conditions:
he supplements what is partial, rescues what is decayed, and reveals what is obscure; his essential aim is simply to instruct people regarding the nature of the mind.
Yet today, the pedantic scholars of this world cling stubbornly to traditional commentaries, while the self-indulgent gentlemen drown their wills in empty abstractions.

As for those who hold *mukunoka* beads in their hands while reciting the name of Amitābha, from the great capital to the most remote villages, they dwell in sight of one another and shoulder to shoulder.

That the Venerable One further harmonized with them—was this not what is called "teaching that accords with worldly sentiments," where the waves follow and the wind bends? In this, I, the humble writer, cannot help but feel [a sense of admiration].
I have some doubts. Your letter states that although you revere the Pure Land, you actually hold the *Avataṃsaka* (Huayan) in higher esteem;

it further says that one enters the *Avataṃsaka* through this single gate of the Pure Land. This is as the ancient masters have said: "To propagate the ultimate truth, sentient beings must first be led to believe;

thus, for the sake of the ultimate, one must provisionally employ the expedient. Use the shallow to assist the profound. It also speaks of "employing [the teaching] according to the occasion" (*yòng yù shíshí*). Regarding these points...

Although you speak of the provisional (*upāya*), it does not contradict the ultimate reality within; rather, so long as it enables sentient beings to obtain the various benefits of both the provisional and the ultimate, I, though lacking in talent, truly resonate with this and receive it with reverence.
I am both filled with admiration and comforted. Indeed, among the assembly gathered here, there are those who have traveled from Hangzhou to Suzhou from time to time;
there is none among them who does not take great delight in the Nine Grades [of Rebirth]. When I occasionally converse with them, they show a slight...
When one ventures upon the Supreme Vehicle, people are startled and stare with wide eyes; some even mock it. Is this fault in the disciple or in the teacher?
A great man’s spirit soars to the heavens, yet he regards the salvation of sentient beings as his urgent task. If he were to transcend the world [and remain aloof], how could he fulfill this purpose?
The hall was opened; the seat was spread. Yet, failing to manifest the strategic maneuvers of a great man, he acted only like an old layman or laywoman from the village lanes.

Suddenly, when questioned by a clever person or pressed by one with clear eyes, would he attempt to hide his body within the Big Dipper, or would he hide it within the Iron Ring Mountains? Have you not heard it said: "If it is..."
The great golden-winged garuḍa soars with vigor for hundreds of thousands of yojanas; the divine horse Kanthaka gallops across the four quarters and the eight directions.
Yet neither of them seizes its prey to eat it piecemeal, nor do they bury their bodies wherever they happen to land; rather, they rely upon nothing at all.

The great matters of the Buddha-dharma are not trivial; I pray that the Venerable One will give them renewed consideration. Your letter further states that Amitābha is no different from Vairocana; this is correct.
However, their spheres of transformation and their modes of manifestation each differ. For the teachings of all Buddhas universally take dependent origination as their fundamental principle;
since they fall within the realm of dependent origination, how could there be no distinction between the great and the small? There must certainly be differences in depth and shallowness.
Therefore, if one were to say that the Buddhas are different, then it could not be said that a thousand Buddhas and a single Buddha are different.
If one were to say that the Buddhas are the same, then the two Honored Ones, Samantaprabha and Śākyamuni, would likewise not be distinct from one another.
The ancients held that all dharmas involve a layering of identity and difference; they cannot be entirely identical, nor can they be entirely different. They cannot...
One may take what is entirely identical as entirely different, but one cannot take what is entirely different as entirely identical.

If one is deluded regarding these two gates of identity and difference, then wisdom will not be sovereign. As it is said: "If you intend to seek [the Way] in a place of white snow and reed flowers, would it be appropriate to use Wenzhou orange peel to start a fire?
Shoushan Nian said: "To be a master of the school, one must possess the faculty of discernment."

The Dharma-eye is only then attained. Therefore, since ancient times there have been "picking up the ancients" (niangu) and "verses on the ancients" (sungu), as well as "separate ancients" (biegu) and "constrained ancients" (biegu).
For instance, it is said: "The ultimate Way is not difficult; it only dislikes discrimination. And again: "The ultimate Way is most difficult; it requires discrimination.
Thus, the eighth stage of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: "The realm of true quiescence manifests before one," yet it still says "should respond..."
One gives rise to immeasurable wisdom of differentiation. Furthermore, it is said that one observes and discerns the various dharma-gates;
this is not brought about through deliberate effort. The nature of my own reflective awareness is inherently perfect and luminous, like a great precious mirror.
It distinguishes between Hu and Han without being divided; it appears as blue or yellow without being different, like a wish-fulfilling jewel. If it is thus with all phenomena...
Within the Dharma, one does not give rise to dualistic interpretations. How could a person ever abandon discernment (*viniścaya*) and seek some other "clear and bright" principle?
This very act of discerning or not discerning is precisely what is called the "skillful discriminative wisdom of purity.

Fangshan [Wenxiu] composed the *Treatise* (*lun*), and Qingliang [Xuanzang] wrote the *Commentary* (*shu*); both synthesized the Buddha-vehicle and together elucidated the Perfect Teaching (*yuanzong*). Although this is the *Treatise*...
There is the substance of the treatise (*śāstra*), and there is the substance of the commentary (*vṛtti*). However, one should focus solely on their meaning and not solely on their phrasing;

for while the phrasing may differ, the meaning remains one and the same. If one considers them according to their meaning, the levels of realization (*bhūmi*) appear to be vastly distinct. Thus, when Qingliang expounded upon the various sūtras...
The True Spiritual Friend has provided only a word-by-word gloss and character-by-character explanation of the *Avataṃsaka*.
How could this fail to be of some benefit to Vairocana? Yet, in terms of grasping the collar and pulling the hem [to provide a comprehensive overview], he truly cannot compare to Zao Bo.

If the distinction between Qingliang and Zao Bo is not clarified, the essential purport of the *Vairocanābhisaṃbodhi-sūtra* will ultimately remain obscure—namely, that which is called faith, understanding, practice, and realization.
These four dharmas split the entire sūtra apart like seeds from a melon; this is the most egregious instance, though there are many others besides.

This unworthy one deems such a selection to be unrefined, and it is not for lack of reason. If you should think this is not the case, I beg to further verify it with the Great Being Zao Bo (Nāgabodhi).
I have received your gracious letter, which runs to some two thousand words. Its profound expressions and subtle arguments are vast and layered; I truly admire and look up to them.

Yet, I venture to think that while your affection for me is deep, your words are somewhat excessive. If you truly intend to exalt the Chan school and suppress the Pure Land, there is no need for so many words.
Why not simply say: "The Buddhas of the three periods of time have been swallowed by me in a single gulp"? Once this is said, [the matter is settled].
If not even a single Buddha is established, who else could be Amitābha? Furthermore, why not say: "If a person recognizes the mind, there is not an inch of earth in the great world"?
Since there is not an inch of earth anywhere, where else could there be a Land of Ultimate Bliss?
These two sentences encompass your two thousand words of correspondence without exception. If I were now to provide a response for each and every point, I fear it would lead to a dispute.
[The opponent] disputes [this], but it is not so. Since the Great Way is at stake, one must ultimately not remain silent; I venture to state my views briefly.

Your letter suggests that Qingliang’s selection was not refined. In my humble opinion, I do not know whether Qingliang’s selection of the *Avataṃsaka* was not refined, or whether your selection of Qingliang was not refined.
Furthermore, your letter states that the *neyārtha* (provisional) sūtras merely discuss and describe purity.
I have instead matched it with the "Chapter on Vows and Practices" (*Pranidhāna-paṭala*) and the *Śraddhotpāda-śāstra*.

Setting aside the *Śraddhotpāda* for a moment, as for the "Chapter on Vows and Practices," it subsumes the entirety of the eighty-fascicle sutra within a single chapter. From antiquity to the present, who would dare to claim that this is not of definitive meaning?

The lay practitioner alone esteems the *Avataṃsaka* while disparaging the *Pratideśanā-vidhi* (Vows and Practices). If the *Pratideśanā-vidhi* were of provisional meaning (*neyārtha*), then the *Avataṃsaka* would likewise be of provisional meaning.
Furthermore, in your letter you state that the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* records the rebirth in the Pure Land as the cause and effect for women;
does this not then imply that even the attainment of Buddhahood by the Dragon Girl was merely the cause and effect for a woman? You also claim that Amitābha was one of the sixteen princes.
If that is the case, then Vairocana is merely the thirteenth of the twenty tiers of the Flower Treasury World (*kusumatalagarbha*). Layman, you alone revere Vairocana;

why then do you treat him as equal to Amitābha? Furthermore, in your letter you claim that the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* selects Avalokiteśvara while omitting Śrī-ghana (Potu-shi), and further degrades him to being subject to impermanence and birth-and-death. Yet, [the sūtra] states that Kauṇḍinya awakened to the guest-dust.
The two characters "dust" (chen) may be said to penetrate impermanence and accord with the non-arising and non-ceasing. Why, then, were they not selected for the "Perfect Penetration" (yuantong)?

Truly, one could say that while Guanyin has passed the imperial examination, Shizhi has failed. Have you not heard that the metaphor of the Dragon Gate's "dotting of the forehead" is merely the talk of a rustic from Qi?
Furthermore, in your letter, you mention that Chan Master Qi Ji [took] the ancients' practice of reciting the Buddha’s name...
Each line of the verse is annotated as follows: where it says "only the direct path of practice," the annotation states, "it is simply to strike them according to the old way.
Where it says "just recite the name of Amitābha Buddha," the annotation states, "reciting it will not suffice to save you.

Since the Layman was proficient in the Chan school, how could he not know that this is the Master’s way of directly acting for others to untie their adhesions and remove their bonds? Yet he proceeded to compose [the following]:
"Is it truly the case that one must die beneath the words of the assembly of dharmas? If that were so, as the ancients said:
'To walk upon the crown of Vairocana's head—then not only would Amitābha be of no avail, even Vairocana himself would be of no avail.

Such expressions are found by the hundreds, thousands, tens of millions, and billions in the *yulu* (recorded sayings) and biographies. Even forty years ago, this old man used them for his own pleasure."
His lips were eloquent and his calligraphy was masterful; later, however, he came to feel shame and dared not act as he had before. Even to this day, he remains deeply abashed.

Furthermore, when Qi Ji said to [Shi] Qiu, "Those who seek the West are like sons who abandon their fathers and flee, wandering lost in foreign lands, bumping into things here and there—how bitter it is, Amitābha Buddha!
Qiu replied to him: "Right now, it is rather like a son remembering his mother."
Returning to one's native land—discarding the east to find the west. How joyful is Amitābha Buddha! Now tell me, how far apart is this statement from what Qi Ji has said?

Furthermore, your letter suggests that practicing for many kalpas is not as good as attaining the *anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti* (the patience of the non-arising of phenomena) in a single thought-moment.
Has the Layman already attained the *anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*? If you have, then you should not [speak] of "me."
The mind acts as the producer, and the land acts as the produced. Why is this? The mind itself is the land; who then is the producer? The land itself is the mind; what then is the produced?
One attains rebirth by not perceiving a producer or a produced; therefore, though reborn throughout one's entire life, there has never been a birth.
This is precisely why it is called "true non-birth. It must not be granted that there is birth before it can be so designated.
"Non-arising" (wu-sheng) refers to the emptiness of annihilation; it is not the true meaning of non-arising.
Furthermore, your letter suggests that one must wait for the lotus to bloom to see the Buddha before realizing non-arising, which you deem to be a circuitous and delayed path.

Layman, as one who has mastered the Chan school, surely you know that attaining enlightenment from delusion is like waking from a dream or like a lotus flower blooming. Among those who practice the recitation of the Buddha's name, there are those who realize their nature in this very life.
These flowers may bloom in an instant; there are also those who realize their nature after a long time.

This is because capacities vary between sharp and dull, and effort varies between diligent and lax; thus, the blooming of the flower has its own pace, whether slow or fast. How can one categorically dismiss it as being dilatory?
Furthermore, your letter states that Vairocana and Amitābha are not the same; you liken the Flower Treasury World (*Huāzàng*) to the entire body and the Western Land to a single pore.
To suggest that those born in the Western Land are like grasping the entire body and inserting it into a pore is to invert the relationship between the ocean and its bubbles.
Indeed, the analogy of the large and the small is thus. However, you, Master, are a master of the Huayan school;

why then do you permit only the small to enter the large, yet refuse to allow the large to enter the small? Furthermore, the mutual interpenetration of the large and the small is but one of the Ten Mysterious Gates of the Huayan.
To take the unspeakably unspeakable, infinite worlds of the Flower Treasury World and cause them to enter the Land of Ultimate Bliss—this is precisely such an instance.
Within a single lotus flower, there is not even enough space for one of its petals; how much less would it matter for the entire body to enter a single mustard seed’s worth of space within a petal?
Furthermore, regarding your letter, you state that this mountain monk asks only about the Mahāyāna.
I was struck with awe and stared in amazement. Previously, you spoke of the *Avataṃsaka* to those for whom it was suitable, and of the Pure Land to those for whom it was suitable.
Now, these people of dull faculties are precisely those for whom the Pure Land is appropriate.

Why do you not provide them with medicine suited to their ailments, but instead persist in lecturing them so forcefully? Furthermore, your letter states that since I have left the secular world and opened the hall [to teach], I am not... [end of fragment]
A great man’s strategic maneuvering, yet he adopts the comportment of an old layman or laywoman in the village lanes.
Even if questioned by a clever person or pressed by one with clear eyes, where will he hide? Will he hide within the Big Dipper, or will he hide within the Iron Ring Mountains?
This old man has never dared to assume the name of one who has transcended the world; naturally, he must lack the strategic insight of a great man.

Let us set that aside for now. To disparage those who cultivate the Pure Land as mere "laymen and laywomen" (zhāigōng zhāipó) is, as the ancients said, not to disparage the ignorant husband and wife, but to disparage Mañjuśrī, Samantabhadra, Aśvaghoṣa, and Nāgārjuna. How could it be only Mañjuśrī?

Samantabhadra, Aśvaghoṣa, and Nāgārjuna; as well as our distant ancestors Shandao, Zhiyi, Yongming, Qingliang, Guifeng, Yuanzhao, Zhenxie, Huanglong, Cishou, Zhongfeng, Tianru, and all other bodhisattvas and spiritual friends—do they not all partake of the offerings of the laymen and laywomen?
Liu Yimin, Bai Juyi, Liu Zongyuan, Wen Xiang, and Su Shi.
Yang Wuweï, Chen Yingzhong, and other great gentlemen all practiced as laymen and laywomen who maintained the precepts.

Even if these laymen and laywomen merely recited the Buddha’s name to attain rebirth in the Pure Land, they would immediately reach the stage of non-retrogression; how could they possibly be held in contempt?
Furthermore, those laymen and laywomen who are dull-witted and inferior, yet strictly adhere to formal regulations, are indeed fools.

As for those who are clever and eloquent, who recklessly discourse on Prajñā, and who, having already eaten their fill of meat, come seeking out monks to talk of Chan—[they are even further from the truth].
They are demons. Fools value being fools; I truly examine myself and would rather be an old layman or an old laywoman than an old demon-male or an old demon-female.

As for those so-called clever people and those with clear eyes—when they come to question or press me, those laymen and laywomen need not climb high to the Northern Dipper or seek far away at the Iron Ring Mountains.
I shall simply set up my mat at the throat of the clever man and spread my seat upon the pupils of the clear-eyed one.
Why? It is merely to have him briefly close his mouth in samādhi and turn the light back to reflect within.

Furthermore, while you, Layman, still favor the *Avataṃsaka* and vigorously disparage the Pure Land, I, an old man, practice the Pure Land and most highly praise the *Avataṃsaka*. Layman, in your quietude—

Please consider this for a moment: what exactly is the reason for this being so? Furthermore, regarding your letter’s statement that your exhortation for me to seek rebirth in the Pure Land is like abandoning gold to carry hemp—a perverse act that brings great humiliation—I must say that while this analogy is apt, it is not yet quite precise.
Let me offer a new one: it is like a peasant presenting a visiting card to a wealthy and noble lord.
The gatekeeper invited him into the farmer’s cottage. Those who had heard of this all laughed at him.
The farmer, not knowing how to respond or withdraw, swept the path once more and planned to invite him again. Those who had laughed said, "It was fortunate that your host did not rebuke you just now;
do you wish to be like Feng Fu? The farmer replied, "I have seen among the wealthy families those who possess riches yet lack benevolence, and those who..."

Among those who are wealthy yet inwardly impoverished, there are those who become arrogant before they are truly rich, and those who serve as stewards at the gates of the wealthy while considering themselves to be rich themselves. Moreover, where now are the Jin-gu and Mei-wo mansions?
Yet I, a mere rustic old man, enjoy the happiness of the Great Peace; thus I forgot my own lowliness and did this out of pity for others. Now I realize it was a mistake.
Thereupon, they laughed together and dispersed.
An answer to Master Wu Guan’s letter states:
"I am filled with deep anxiety, constantly fearing that I have not yet attained clear realization of this one great matter. This is the human condition."
What is called "not being a cause for worry" is precisely the primary cause for entering the Way; one simply wishes to single-mindedly investigate the fundamental question.
Furthermore, among the various eminent masters in the *Fushan Records*, all praised the dialogue regarding the black and white stones in the game of Go as a supreme and wondrous discourse.
Although these words have been recited for a thousand ages, the profound depths of Master Yuan do not reside therein. Such [discourses]...
Even people of intelligence today can achieve this. Thus, one need not engage in forced interpretation or seek to reconcile the "nine strands" and so forth;
one simply practices the method of ease and peace taught by Master Yuan. Only when such practice exists will there be such realization.
The ancient masters said: "I only fear that one will not become a Buddha; I do not fear that a Buddha cannot understand human speech. How profound these words are!
May you take heed of them. —In response to Qinglian’s gratitude.

To hold the *huatou* (critical phrase) is the most essential practice for attaining awakening in the Chan school. Those who cultivate the Pure Land should likewise take a single utterance of the Buddha’s name as their *huatou*;
this is a sublime method. However, if the mind is coarse and the breath is restless, one will not yet be in accord with it.
