One must instead remain profound and reflect inwardly until, at the point where strength is exhausted and momentum spent, there is a sudden "crack" of realization that dissolves all barriers.
[The Master] sighed.

He replied, "The inquiry from Jin Guangju concerns the final, critical juncture. [The Master] said, "It is the profoundly deep principle. [He continued,] "It is the resonance with the original ground. [He added,] "It is direct and immediate."

This refers to this very matter. It is urgent, it is profound, it is fundamental, and it is direct—all these are matters of pressing inquiry. Yet it simply requires thinking about what is near at hand.
Apart from this luminous, alert, and penetrating awareness, everything else is lax, shallow, peripheral, and circuitous.

If you can truly perceive through this single thought-moment of nianfo (buddha-recitation), you may be certain that the Great Matter will be brought to completion. Furthermore, one must not [view it] as...

To speak thus and then engage in conceptual deliberation and speculative calculation, or to force an opening through intellectual excavation, is to lose it all the more. Rather, simply investigate with every thought;
through true accumulation and long-term effort, you will realize it spontaneously—this alone constitutes authentic realization.
In response to Zhang Guangjing’s inquiry regarding Yunmen’s words: there is no need to investigate his claim that there is a "separate transmission outside the teachings. Simply look at what he said:
one must take a step back and seek within the very heels of one's own feet to discover what this is. This seeking is not difficult even now.
Once you have established faith in Buddha-recitation, simply look inward at the one who is reciting the Buddha’s name; this is precisely to seek it beneath your own heels.
After doing so for a long time, you will not fail to attain that which was described in the *Zheng'e*: the final stage of exhausting the profound and reaching the subtle.
Answer: For those who have deeply sealed their true faith in the Pure Land and resolved to be reborn there, it does not matter whether they have attained awakening or not.

Even for those who practice the "single transmission" of direct pointing and have not yet awakened—though they may say that their primary task is Chan meditation—it is not an obstacle to making the vow for rebirth in the Pure Land. This is because...
One has not yet attained freedom from future existence, for there remains ultimately a place of birth. This is not a mind of theft, but rather a mind at a crossroads.
Regarding those who have already awakened, an ancient said: "Do you think that with a single awakening you can immediately equal all Buddhas?
Thus, although every atom is the Flower Treasury (*kusumatalagarbha*) and every location is a Lotus Land, the *Bhadracaryā-praṇidhāna* (Chapter on Vows and Practices) [remains essential].

One must certainly be earnestly devoted to the discourse on rebirth in the Land of Peace and Bliss. This is true even for those who have already attained awakening; it can be known to be so for those who have not yet awakened.
When not a single thought arises, this is Chan and not "investigation" (*can*). Only when a thought arises and doubt descends is it called "investigation. As the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says:

Furthermore, using this mind to investigate and examine [the teachings] repeatedly is precisely what is meant by "equivalence. Both during formal recitation (*nian*) and during meditative inquiry (*can*), one remains within the state of having mindfulness;
these are not mutually contradictory.
This is "mind itself is Buddha. If you can truly believe this to its depths and see it through to the bottom, then everything will be resolved once and for all, leaving no further room for doubt.
Only when you are free from stagnation can you proceed spontaneously through time. If this is not the case, you must not yet dismiss the session.

As for great awakening, it may be accompanied by thought, or it may be without thought; this is what is meant by "the inhalation does not dwell within the realms of the aggregates, and the exhalation does not engage with external conditions."
Yongming said: "First, one enters through faith based on understanding derived from hearing; yet he further stated that later, one accords with [reality] through non-thinking.

When one accords with it, the Dharma-body penetrates and emotional consciousness is exhausted. This is both understanding and realization. Is it not fitting, then, for such a person to succeed to the position of the Patriarch?"
If one does not strive for actual practice and realization, but instead uses the samādhi of mere words to display intellectual sharpness and compete for victory or defeat, such speech must not exist.

However, for those who are truly concerned with birth and death but have not yet clarified the ground of the mind, engaging in mutual debate and responding to one another in verse—such speech must not be absent.
Whether one has ascended the mountain three times or nine times, or whether a single phrase remains as vast as a thousand mountains, it matters not if one has not yet awakened.
Even after one has already attained awakening, there remains the final, weighty barrier; the work of inquiry and decisive discernment must not yet be brought to a halt.
—In response to Monk Haiguang.
If you do not exist anywhere at all, who is it that receives the robe? If you pervade all things, in what place does the robe reside?
If you do not exist anywhere at all, then you have been without substance from the beginning; what use would there be for precepts?

If you pervade all things, then you have been without deficiency from the beginning; why seek fulfillment? There is the tree of Bodhi; there is the stand of the bright mirror. From the very beginning...
"There is a thing. These three phrases overturn Caoxi; the final phrase, "originally it does not stir up dust," still falls into his old trap.
Why not say: "Originally there is a thing, which allows it to stir up dust"?
Answer: To Zhou Haimen: "Do no evil;
practice all that is good. At that very moment, the feathers would have covered the ground—what need was there to wait for them to be picked up and blown?
Furthermore, what more need be said of "sameness" or "difference"? Even if they were the same, they would already have become two separate pieces. Master Niaokuo never [intended this].
He neglected the Duke of Bai and showed partiality toward his attendants. Nevertheless, although this was so, he did not misunderstand the profound intent of the former statement;

simply ceasing evil and practicing good will not mislead people. However, if one were to misunderstand the ancient masters’ words regarding "the Tathāgata does not sever inherent evil" or "stolidly not cultivating goodness," the resulting harm would be no small matter.

In response to various questions: the nature of returning to the source is non-dual, yet there are many gates of expedient means. Those who now cling to Chan while slandering the Pure Land have never truly investigated and realized it;
those who cling to the Pure Land while slandering Chan have likewise never truly practiced the Buddha-recitation. If each...
If each of you practices until reaching the ultimate source, you will know that these two paths do not differ by even a hair’s breadth.
To point directly toward the West is not only incorrect for those who have passed beyond this Sahā world-system by ten trillion lands; it is also [inappropriate] to speak...

This very self-nature has already traversed the journey. If one were to speak of the Pure Land in its true reality, not only would the various adornments of jeweled ponds and golden ground be incorrect;
as soon as one clings to "mind-only," it instead becomes defilement. Having departed from these two extremes, what is the Western Pure Land?
In the practice of cultivation, one most fears making discriminations. For those with the resolve to study, there is simply this single right mindfulness ever present within the breast.

It remains so when encountering stillness, and it remains so when encountering clamor. Regardless of the shifting conditions of stillness or noise, this mind of mine shall certainly not be moved or altered.
Only in this way is there no interruption; this is called "skillfulness."
This is indeed the practice of cultivation. Have you not seen the ancients say: "The wise eliminate the mind; the ignorant eliminate objects"?
If you must detest clamor and seek stillness, then you will likely find no time that is still, nor any place that is still.
Now, for one who seeks stillness, nothing compares to the deep mountains. Yet, though the deep mountains are still, the sound of woodcutters' axes is heard across them.
Yun: When the shepherd’s flute resounds in the slanting rays of the setting sun, how can the ears remain still?

Yet, while the axe of the woodcutter and the flute of the shepherd might be warded off so as not to reach our ears, when it comes to the cries of monkeys and the roars of tigers at a clear night, or the chirping of magpies and the cawing of crows during the day—how can one remain still? Nevertheless, as for the cries of monkeys and the roars of tigers, the chirping of magpies...
The cawing of crows may perhaps be driven away so that it does not reach my ears;

yet when a violent wind arises and the myriad apertures roar in fury, or a sudden thunderclap strikes and the thousand mountains tremble—would one who seeks stillness and loathes clamor then seek to block out these sounds or drive them away?
By this reasoning, there is never a time when external conditions are truly quiet.
Indeed, there is absolutely no place that is not still. Students suffer only from a lack of fierce resolve.
If one maintains a fierce resolve, then where could one go that would not be possible?

This shows that, in general, the ancients taught one to draw near to an enlightened teacher and seek out a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*). Yet, such a spiritual friend truly possesses no secret dharma-gate transmitted orally or bestowed through the mind;
rather, simply untying one's adhesions and removing one's bonds on their behalf constitutes the secret. Now, you need only maintain this.

The Name—these eight characters, "Nianfo yixin buluan" (Reciting the Buddha's name with single-mindedness and without distraction), are themselves the secret dharma-gate for untying adhesions and casting off fetters;
they are the grand, open highway for escaping birth and death. Recite them in the morning and evening, while walking and sitting;
let every thought follow the next in uninterrupted succession, and you will spontaneously attain samādhi. Do not seek it elsewhere.

I tell you, Layman Li, there is no need to analyze the two characters "investigate" (can) and "doubt" (yi). Doubt is simply another name for investigation; it essentially conveys the meaning of thorough inquiry and persistent examination.
Simply observe, "Who is it that recites the Buddha's name? and take awakening as your standard. Furthermore, an ancient worthy said: "Observe the phrase."
Do not engage in speculative interpretation or forced analysis; nor should you cast it aside into the armor of non-action.
Simply look in this way—this is the essential instruction.
Tell Da-jun of Wu:

Do not concern yourself with whether there is awakening or not; do not concern yourself with existence or non-existence, internal or external, or that which is in between; do not concern yourself with *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*;
do not concern yourself with whether this dharma-gate is the same as or different from others. Since doubt has not yet arisen, do not concern yourself with who is right and who is wrong.
Whoever merely holds the name, with single-minded focus and undivided attention, practicing it purely and without interruption,
will realize that within the vast and expansive conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*),
awakening, fame, profit, and affection are ultimately empty. Thus, they will penetrate and break through [delusion], and upon the true essence, [realization] is achieved.
To seek birth, old age, sickness, and death and find that they have been fundamentally non-existent is itself the practice. The beginner and the ultimate return to the same source;
the cause encompasses the ocean of fruition. The ultimate and the beginner are not two; the fruition reaches back to the source of the cause. It is simply a matter of clarifying the mind.
There is no separate or distinct dharma. Answer:

Although the moon is bright and pure, its reflection appears different—dim or clear—depending on whether the water is turbid or limpid. The mind is fundamentally luminous and spiritual, yet it reflects good or evil according to circumstances.
Regarding the traces of ascent and descent, how can one claim that because the substance of the moon is inherently devoid of clarity or turbidity, it is therefore better for water to be turbid?

Since the substance of the mind is inherently devoid of good and evil, one might then say that evil deeds do not obstruct it. Yet, if one harbors such a view of emptiness, one immediately contradicts the Perfect Teaching (Yuanzong).
While you may recognize that both good and evil are empty, this is precisely why one should cease evil and practice good. To definitively prohibit evil and practice good is still...
This consciousness-channel is not yet genuine; step by step one walks within existence, yet mouthful after mouthful one speaks of emptiness.
This is the great malady of the "clever people" practicing Chan today.
Answering the Question on Precepts.

To engage in lofty discourse on an age without a Buddha and to point directly to the mind of the person here and now—then not only would the Elder Gautama have no words for the *vinaya*, and Upāli would be ashamed to speak of the *karmavācanā*, but even if one were to bind the five sections of the canon and place them high on a shelf, or strip the three robes and hang them from the tip of a tree, it would not be considered an error.
Were it otherwise, Master Falin would only fear that the forest of Dharma was not dense enough. This is correct.
It is only that one fears not responding when confronted; why should such clamor be wearying? Regarding the two—emptiness and existence:
if one accords with true emptiness, then the myriad dharmas are all complete; what need is there to further practice the *vinaya*? If one falls into a dull emptiness, then all virtues are lost;
does this not surely harm the categories of the precepts? To cling to wild indifference and to slight ritual decorum—their error is great.
When one observes the fundamental substance of the mind-ground as a whole, that substance is but a single thought, inherently perfected from the beginning.

When one minutely analyzes the dharma-gates of the mind-ground, there are ten thousand variations, each belonging to its own category. Therefore, it is said that the thirty minds are all contained within the tip of a single hair.
Furthermore, to assign one or two parts to the characteristics of the precepts (*śīla-lakṣaṇa*) is like growing hair upon the tip of a hair.

For example, although a Heavenly King is titled "Lord of Heaven," he must still be appointed to serve in the six ministries; yet even those six ministries do not encompass everything, so how could he not further open up a hundred offices?
The scripture’s initial designation of "such-and-such a mind" refers precisely to these six ministries. Now, they are further increased.

"Such-and-such a mind. By "such-and-such a mind," I mean the hundred offices [of mental functions]. I have provisionally adopted these terms because their meanings are closely related, so as to allow the rest to be inferred by analogy.
This makes it easy for beginners to understand and simple to practice; for those of wisdom, it requires only the fusion of the spirit and the intuitive realization of the meaning.

He was truly a man of great capacity and vast proportions. Since he was not constrained by whether it was before or after the summer retreat, his spiritual resonance allowed him to manifest both smallness and greatness at will.

As soon as he maintained the precepts, he had already mastered the full extent of the scriptural teachings; while correctly receiving the *vinaya*, he simultaneously awakened to the wondrous essence of the Chan school.
When establishing himself, he gave rise to the myriad phenomena without hindering the six periods of the day; when sweeping away delusions, he eliminated even the finest speck of dust.
How can one maintain even a single thought? Master Huiyuan’s regular prostrations were constant; Master Zhizhe of Yongming never let his personal practice decline.
How could it be that those of inferior capacity treat such matters as trivial? All of us later students, I pray that you each reflect deeply upon this.

This *Brahmajāla Sūtra* takes the mind-ground as its central tenet. There is not a single dharma that does not flow from within the mind-ground, nor is there a single dharma that does not return to the mind-ground.
If the myriad practices of a bodhisattva do not originate from the one mind, they cannot return to the one mind.
This would then not be called the cause of Buddhahood, nor would it be called the fruit of Buddhahood. Now, these flowers emerge from the *citta-bhūmi* (mind-ground) of Vairocana;

they symbolize that the Bodhisattva brings forth immeasurable causal practices from within his own mind. By offering these flowers back to that Buddha, they symbolize that one completes the Buddha who is the fruit of one's own mind by means of the causal practices of one's own mind.
According to the *Avataṃsaka*, the cause encompasses the fruit and the fruit is fully realized within the cause; they are never separate from the cause.
The fruit does not fall because of the cause. When held up, there is not a single thing that cannot be offered to the Buddha; when raised, there is not a single dharma that cannot serve as a cause.
If one insists that the flower must exclusively represent the cause, this is not the meaning of the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao). Why is this?

Sometimes the flower represents the cause and the fruit represents the effect, for it is after the flower opens that the fruit is formed. At other times, the fruit represents the cause and the flower represents the effect, for [the fruit is the seed] planted...

Because the flower arises only after the fruit has ripened, there are times when concentration is the cause and wisdom is the result; because the pure, ultimate light penetrates everywhere, there are times when wisdom is the cause and concentration is the result.
Since delusions are shattered and the mind is at peace, how can one grasp this through a single path or discuss it from a single perspective?
The Tathāgata’s wondrous samādhi is neither moving nor still, yet it is constantly moving and still; it neither emerges nor enters, yet it constantly emerges and enters.
This samādhi is named "Body-Nature Empty Space. Because emptiness corresponds to reality, its body-nature is not empty.

It is like a mountain that does not admit a mountain, or a stone that cannot contain a stone—it would be but a single state of dull stagnation. Since its essence is fundamentally empty space, the Flower-Light manifests freely.
How could it be that once one has entered samādhi, one must simply be reduced to ashes and cease to exist?

In the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* (Complete Enlightenment Sūtra), the Tathāgata enters the Great Radiance Treasury Samādhi and then arises to manifest a pure land, engaging in mutual dialogue with the twelve great bodhisattvas.
What does this mean? Furthermore, there are hundreds of thousands of millions of names for samādhi; it is not merely a single flavor of quiescence. Therefore, [there is...]
As for samādhi, even the followers of the Two Vehicles have not yet heard its name, and Bodhisattvas have not yet understood its meaning.
To cling to stillness and silence is like a lion’s roar and stretch; it all becomes mere clamor. He asked again: "Each of the various samādhis has its own entry and exit.
Why is it that only within this [state] do you speak of entry and exit? He replied: "Entry and exit are not difficult; mastery is what is difficult. Three...

To enter only after withdrawing one’s attention and to emerge only after giving rise to it is not called mastery. Only when one acts with mastery according to the mind is it termed "wondrous concentration.
According to the *Avataṃsaka*, entering and emerging occur simultaneously; the environment and its inhabitants interpenetrate in perfect harmony in an inconceivable manner.
This is merely a minor matter—how could it be considered extraordinary?

In a previous letter to the lay practitioner Liu Luoyang, I specifically urged him to focus on the practice of *nianfo* (mindfulness of the Buddha) to seek rebirth in the Pure Land. Yet this path is most profound and wondrous, and likewise most simple and easy.
Because it is so simple and easy, those of high intelligence and refinement tend to overlook it. Indeed, birth and death do not depart from a single [reality].
Contemplate this: from the mundane to the supramundane, all myriad phenomena do not depart from a single thought-moment. Now, use this very thought-moment to recite the Buddha’s name.
What could be more immediate or authentic than this? If you can penetrate this thought and perceive its point of arising, that is none other than the self-nature Amitābha.

This is precisely the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West. Even if you do not awaken through this very thought, by the power of this mindfulness you shall go to the Land of Ultimate Bliss;
you will thus crosscut the cycle of birth and death horizontally and no longer undergo saṃsāra, for you shall ultimately attain great awakening.
I hope that you, O Elder, will let go of all worldly concerns and maintain constant mindfulness throughout the twelve periods of the day—this is my greatest wish.
It is the seventieth year of Master Fengyun’s life;

how many such centuries can there be? Now, in these final years, it is precisely appropriate to cast off all constraints and see through this world as being like a theatrical performance—what therein is truly real? One need only recite the name of Amitābha Buddha.
Passing the time in this manner, take only the Western World of Ultimate Bliss as your home.
As I now practice mindfulness of the Buddha, I shall be reborn in the West hereafter; what greater fortune could there be? Give rise to great joy and do not produce afflictions.
Should you encounter anything disagreeable, immediately turn your mind toward this single invocation of the Buddha’s name. Uproot the thought with urgency and return to it.
Reflecting back upon this light, one realizes: "I am a person from the world of Amitābha Buddha. Why should I view things with the same common perceptions as worldly people?
Thus, one turns anger into joy and single-mindedly recites the Buddha's name. This is the Dharma-gate of great peace, happiness, and liberation for those of wisdom.
I reply: Your Excellency Yuan, even an infant does not lack the essence of perfect clarity and tranquil illumination; it is simply that they are deluded and thus it does not manifest.
Not only infants, but from childhood through youth, from youth through old age, and from old age until death, there is no one who is not in a state of delusion.

This essence of perfect luminosity and tranquil illumination exists yet does not manifest; it is not non-existent. As for the "water of Caoxi" and the "tea of Zhaozhou," there is no need to force an interpretation based on personal conjecture.
Simply attend to the primary inquiry (*benchan*) in order to seek authentic awakening. What is meant by the primary inquiry?
If you can gain sufficient faith in the practice of Buddha-recitation, then simply inquire: "Who is it that recites the Buddha's name? This is what is called the primary inquiry.
As for Zeng:

when the layman Zhu Xizong dwelt in this world, if he encountered favorable circumstances, his feelings were joyful and at ease; if he encountered adverse circumstances, his feelings were filled with anxiety.
It is perilous. Nevertheless, conformity is not sufficient to be considered fortunate, nor is opposition sufficient to be considered unfortunate.
If one is immersed in what the mind desires, the aspiration for transcendence will not arise. One becomes distressed by failing to achieve one's aims;
only then does one grow weary of the shackles of this world and seek to transcend it. Therefore, when myriad sufferings converge before one, one should simply rely on right wisdom.

Observe: from what does suffering arise? It arises from the body. From what does the body arise? It arises from karma. From what does karma arise? It arises from delusion (*kleśa*). One creates karma because of delusion;
one forms a body because of karma; and one experiences suffering because of the body. If one can only shatter delusion, all things become empty and quiescent.
I venture to ask: what is the method for shattering delusion? It simply requires applying principle to the original *huatou* (critical phrase) of one's inquiry.
Who is it that recites the Buddha’s name? Grasp this doubt and conquer it; all delusions will then be shattered. Reflect upon this without negligence.
In reply to Layman Jiang Guangyou:
Regarding your letter, you ask what retribution awaits Zhu Ziyang for his ultimate slander of the Dharma. I say that each person has their own [karmic destiny].

As for their retribution: those who are virtuous Confucians naturally possess the blessings of humans and devas; however, since they have rejected Buddhism, it is difficult for them to hear the Dharma.
Only when one's own task is accomplished can one then assist others.
The ancients, having attained great and thorough enlightenment and completed their studies, would dwell by watersides and beneath forest trees to nurture the "sacred embryo.
They did not begrudge the growth of mold upon their lips; only when they were finally propelled forth by the dragons and devas did they act as teachers for others.

Therefore, those who leave the seat of the Dharma vow to remain on the stage of learning throughout successive lives to refine themselves. When I left the household life, I faithfully upheld these words, wearing them upon my breast.
Jin. Later, due to illness, he entered the mountains. After a long time, no one was aware of him, and it gradually became a forest monastery.
Even to this day, he does not dare refer to his own dwelling as a "fangzhang" (abbot’s quarters), nor does he dare open his mouth to speak recklessly of the Chan school.

This is because he practices together with the assembly rather than leading them in the Way. Merely being their senior by a single day, he simply encourages and exhorts one another. You virtuous ones, by...
That my friends wait upon me to exhort me toward goodness is a great blessing.

Regarding the twofold benefit of self and others, it has been said of old: "He who is unable to benefit himself yet is able to benefit others first is one whose mind has been awakened as a Bodhisattva. These words are nectar.
If one does not employ it skillfully, it will instead turn into a poisonous drug. Try reflecting upon yourself: Am I a Bodhisattva?

Furthermore, you say that your resolve to attain enlightenment is not yet genuine. Have you not heard of the Tathāgata appearing in the world—one who has personally realized his own perfection and then proceeds to awaken others?
Or, if you claim that one must wait until one’s own perfection before benefiting others, then the work of benefiting others will never be accomplished.
There is no such time. For it is impossible that one who cannot save oneself from illness can save others; such a thing has never occurred.
Therefore, you must give rise to the vast mind of a Bodhisattva and firmly uphold the sincere instructions of the Tathāgata.
Otherwise, you will lead the blind by the hand of the blind; wishing to attach yourself to the rank of a Bodhisattva, you will lose both yourself and others—how can this be called anything else?

The school of doctrinal study (*kyōshū*) ruins the school of the lineage (*shūmon*). It is the school of doctrinal study that ruins it. Someone asked: "Exegesis is for the purpose of clarifying the essence; why do you say it ruins it? I replied:
"The Sūtras, Vinaya, and Śāstras have pathways of meaning; if one does not explain them, they will not be clarified. But the school of the lineage has no pathways of meaning."
To lecture upon it is, on the contrary, to obscure it; one should merely allow others to engage with it so that they may realize it for themselves.
Thus it is said: "Let the blue seas change as they will, I shall never explain it for you. And again: "If I were to break it open and tell it to you, you would later come to curse me.
Nowadays, lecturers have instead turned this into a set formula. That the meaning of the West's coming is not understood is precisely due to this.
Falsely Citing the Circumstances of Ancient Worthies (I):
The Yunqi Monastic Code. Regarding "falsely citing the circumstances of ancient worthies": A monk was expelled from the monastery. Another monk said, "This need not be prohibited."

To prohibit it would sever the conditions for *prajñā*. As for those who slander the *Lotus Sūtra*, once their retribution for hellish offenses is exhausted, they will again plant the conditions for the *Lotus Sūtra* because of that very act of slandering.
How much more so for one who falsely cites it—is this not slander? I said: "Your words are indeed excellent.

However, you know the first part, but not the second. When those who slander the *Lotus Sūtra* emerge from hell and plant roots of goodness, how can they compare [to those who do so through correct means]?"
Those who revere and have faith in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* do not enter hell, for they immediately plant the seeds of virtuous conditions.

Furthermore, to claim that one’s false citations are not slanders while failing to reflect that such ignorant and arbitrary speculations are all termed "slandering the Great Prajñāpāramitā" is a grave error.

Therefore, those who recklessly recount the words of their masters may be rebuked, told: "The former master did not say this; do not slander the former master. This is because they hold their teacher in high esteem; it is not otherwise.
It is slander. To give a mistaken answer to a turning phrase is to fall into the body of a wild fox;
that is an error, not slander. Why then do both become guilty of transgression? The ancients’ single question and single answer both emerged from a state of true realization.
Nowadays, people merely gallop through the samādhi of verbal cleverness; before those with clear eyes, they are like quicksilver entering a red furnace—mere demonic delusions.

This is merely an encounter with a "White Deer" (Bai Ze). If one does not exercise restraint, then with a single punch to the east and a single shout to the west, this person composes a gatha and that person recites a verse;
they become like the wind or madmen, like those playing or mocking, their empty pretenses blazing while their actual practice perishes.
"You consider this to be the restoration of the ancestral school; I consider it the total ruin of the Buddha-dharma.
You recklessly cite the karmic encounters of the ancient worthies.
(2) A monk, displeased, said: "If this is truly so, then is it not impossible even to open one's mouth to offer a single evaluation of the ancient worthies' karmic encounters?"

[The Master] said: "I merely forbade idle picking; I never said that picking was not permitted. When the two monks both rose together to roll up the curtain, the Ancient Sage said, 'One gains, one loses.
You should try to evaluate for me: who is right regarding this gain and loss? The monk remained silent. I said: "An ancient had a saying:
'If one is questioned by a master ten times and fails to answer nine of them, it is not yet a disaster; one only fears a lack of understanding.'"
To engage in idle talk will result in no progress whatsoever; be cautious!

Regarding the Zen school and the Pure Land school, there was once a monk who specialized exclusively in the practice of the Buddha-remembrance (nienfo) method and another monk who prided himself on his Zen realization. The latter said to the former who was reciting the Buddha’s name: "You..."
"Those who practice the recitation of the Buddha's name must wait until they are reborn in the Western Paradise, where they behold Amitābha Buddha, and only then attain awakening.
As for us practitioners of Chan, we attain awakening in this very life. The difference in speed is thus evident. You may cease your recitation and take up Chan; that would be appropriate.

The monk was unable to resolve his doubt and brought the matter to me. I said: "The faculties have their sharpness and dullness; the effort has its diligence and indolence. It all depends on these factors."
Among people, some are naturally faster and others slower; one cannot simply condemn the one while praising the other.

It is like two people setting out for the same place of treasure on the same day—one riding a horse and the other traveling by boat—their arrival times, whether sooner or later, cannot be predetermined.
Thus, the distinction between those who are sharp or dull, diligent or indolent, applies equally to those who practice *chan* meditation and those who recite the Buddha’s name.
This is so. Speaking of slowness: those who practice the recitation of the Buddha's name may have the lotus flower begin to open only after many kalpas;

likewise, there are those who practice Zen meditation who, despite diligent effort over many lifetimes, are unable to see their true nature. Speaking of speed: there are those who practice Zen meditation who attain immediate and complete enlightenment.

Without passing through the *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*, one attains the Dharma-body. Among those who practice Buddha-remembrance (*buddhānusmṛti*), there are also those who achieve thorough penetration in the present life and attain birth in the highest grade at the time of death.

As the ancients said: "It is like a person traveling a long distance; they take reaching the destination as their goal, rather than arbitrarily distinguishing between difficulty and ease along the way."

Regarding dwelling in the mountains, it has been said since antiquity that "dwelling in the marketplace is the lesser hermitage; dwelling in the mountains is the greater. Consequently, there have been those who willingly immerse themselves in the dust and secular world.

However, they do not realize that for one dwelling in the marketplace, blending with the mundane and harmonizing with the light, one finds stillness amidst the clamor—this is the way of the man of the Way, and not otherwise.

This is what is appropriate for those at the beginning of their practice. Some say that Yongjia remarked that if one dwells in the mountains before attaining the Way, one will see only the mountains and inevitably forget the Way;

thus, he did not permit dwelling in the mountains. Each of these views has its own rationale. My praise of mountain dwelling is intended as a warning for those submerged in the dust of worldly affairs.
However, what Yongjia said is itself the correct principle. For those who have left the household life, [the matter is] great...

Since the matter is not yet clear, one must travel thousands of miles to seek teachers and inquire after the Way, drawing near to spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) to attend upon them in the morning and request instruction in the evening.
How could one remain muddled and ignorant, acting like a mountain-dwelling ghost? Therefore, it can be said that traveling abroad comes first and dwelling in the mountains follows;
this does not contradict the words of Yongjia.

It is fitting for those who have become monks to practice filial piety and support their parents; if there are those among the clergy who are unfilial toward their parents, I hold them in deep reproach. Someone may say:

"Since one who has left the household life has already bid farewell to kin and severed attachments, to reproach them would only stir up feelings of affection and love. I reply: How can you speak such words? This is the great filial piety.

The Honored Śākyamuni repaid his parents' kindness over successive kalpas and, by accumulating causes, attained perfect enlightenment. Yet the *Brahmajāla Sūtra* states that although the precepts encompass ten thousand practices, filial piety is their fundamental principle;
and the *Amitābha Sūtra* declares that filially supporting one's parents is the primary cause for pure karma.

In antiquity, there were those who built halls to honor their mothers and those who carried their mothers while begging for food, yet they never allowed such affection to become a burden. How is it, then, that toward one’s own kin...
Having severed his attachments, he nevertheless formed a bond with a patron whose gifts and offerings never ceased; he nurtured his disciples as if they were his own flesh and blood.
Thus, where there was no kinship, there arose kinship; having emerged from one form of attachment, he entered into another. How can such perversity be so extreme?
Moreover, you have already received offerings from the ten directions; having been well-fed and dwelling in peace, you sit by idly watching as your parents suffer from hunger, cold, and desolation.
If you find such conduct acceptable, then do it.

From the *Jingce* (Warning Whip) of the True Friend, Great Master Zhongfeng: "If one who studies Chan must wait to seek out teachers and friends, I fear their practice will come to rest within a single lifetime.
It further says: "Even if it were Bodhidharma or Śākyamuni himself, to attempt to meet them face-to-face would already be falling into a stale convention. This is the very cream of the essence.
These are most excellent words. However, they must not be heard by those of inferior capacity.

If one clings to these words and acts upon them with self-will and self-assertion, no longer recognizing the benefit of seeking friends, they will instead become a poisonous drug. To seek friends is not difficult; it is to find a true friend that is difficult.
Those who pursue one only for food, drink, wealth, and silks are evil friends. True friends are those who exhort one toward what is good and admonish one against what is evil.
He is my true friend. He has opened for me the path of correct practice and shown me the Dharma of the Supreme Vehicle.
He is my lamp, my eye, my guide, and my sovereign physician—a truly virtuous spiritual friend whom I must never be parted from for even a single day.

The masters recorded in the *Chuan Deng Lu* (Transmission of the Lamp) and other such texts—such as those in the successive transmission of the six generations and the branching flames of the five lamps—were all great venerable elders who were among the foremost figures of all time and the world.
As it is said: "Only now do I know that outside of the teachings of the Duke of Zhou and Confucius, there exists another [tradition] of its own."

This is what it means to be a hero. How easy is it to speak of such a thing? Nowadays, some people obtain a mere fragment of knowledge or a slight degree of ease, and immediately consider themselves to have attained great penetration and enlightenment.

Yet, these blind elders further seal them with the "pumpkin seal" (the mark of a blind man). One blind person leading a multitude of blind people not only fails to provide any benefit, but actually causes harm. How deeply lamentable this is!

Yes. Regarding the *Continuation of the Treatise on the Origin of the Teachings* (*Xù Yuánjiào Lùn*), composed by the lay practitioner Shen Shìróng, Court Attendant for the Hanlin Academy at the beginning of the dynasty: its detailed titles and contents are as follows.

The essay "Confucianism and Buddhism" comprehensively enumerates the various worthies of the Tang and Song dynasties, such as Bai Xiangshan, Su Neihan, and even high officials like Prime Minister Pei and Yang Dainian, providing the most precise and thorough analysis of the depth of their Chan studies. It states:
As for figures such as Pei Xiu and Yang Jie, it cannot be said that they lacked realization; however, whether they were able to preserve and maintain [their practice] remains uncertain.
How could there be anyone dwelling in a field of fame and profit, who is not yet a Bodhisattva of the fruition stage, and yet remain free from the subtle outflows of delusion?
Needless to say, those who sport freely within the Dharma-gates need no further discussion; we ourselves are but monastics.
Consider this for a moment in quiet reflection:

those who protect the Dharma know that the external protection of the Buddha-Dharma is entrusted to kings and ministers, yet they do not realize that it is the Sangha who ought to provide that protection.
One cannot but be cautious. There are three ways to protect the Dharma: first, to promote and honor Buddhist monasteries; second, to circulate the Great Teachings;
and third, to encourage and support the monastic community. Why speak of caution? Regarding the protection of monasteries:
since Buddhist monasteries originally belong to temple property, it is only right to reclaim them if they have been seized by the powerful. If one examines historical records and documents, then...

The details are unclear. As time has passed since these matters were first transmitted, the roles of the Zhang and Wang families have been interchanged. Is it appropriate to seize [the property] by force?

To joyfully relinquish one's name for the sake of a "site of auspiciousness" (kṣetra) is commendable; however, to give it away when one lacks the power to defend it is called a "thicket of grievous karma.
If a monk merely exhorts powerful patrons to act as great donors (mahādānapati) for the restoration of an old monastery, yet fails to consider the Buddha...
One must regard all sentient beings as one would Rāhula. When Yang Min established a monastery, its breadth exceeded a thousand *qīng* and its height soared through the nine heavens;

sandalwood formed its groves and pearls and jade served as its ornaments. That which the Buddha pities and loves, yet some do not rejoice in, is such that to have faults without merit is a matter for which one must be most careful—this is the first point.
As for those who protect the Teaching, the works they have composed truly accord with the distant [truth].

The Buddha’s intention was that, having recently grasped the essential meaning of the sutra, one should praise and propagate it. Is it appropriate to offer excessive eulogy based on the superficial talk and biased views of a heterodox outsider?

Furthermore, if Master Sengwei merely solicits prefaces and postscripts from famous officials while failing to consider how this might mislead future students, there will be fault rather than merit; one must be cautious of this. Second, regarding the protection of the Sangha: [text continues].
If a monk is indeed one who has truly investigated and attained genuine realization, possessing great wisdom and insight, it is only natural to honor and pay him respect.
If he is one whose heart and conduct are sincere, and whose integrity is firm and resolute, it is only natural to trust and draw near to him. This is the principle.

But would it be appropriate to honor and trust those who are merely superficial Chan practitioners or base, mediocre folk? If a monk seeks only to curry favor with the noble and powerful, thereby defiling his robes—how could such a person be worthy of respect?
To cover it with cotton, silk, brocade, and embroidery is merely to increase its toxicity; there is harm and no merit.
One must be cautious of this third point. Thus, while the king’s ministers protect the Dharma, the monks destroy it—how tragic!
Verses on Old Cases and Comments on Old Cases (I).
Someone asked: "The ancients all had verses on old cases and comments on old cases; why do you alone have none? He replied: "I dare not."

After the ancients attained great penetration and great enlightenment, the utterance of even half a verse or a single phrase flowed forth naturally from the great treasury of luminosity within their true mind-ground;
it required no deliberation and involved no contrived effort. Can people today do the same?
The venerable masters of the early dynasty spoke of two types of *kōans*: such as "The dog has Buddha-nature" and "The ten thousand dharmas..."
The category of "returning to one" constitutes the first stage. Furthermore, there is the final ultimate point, which is particularly obscure and termed "the single blow behind the head.
It is extremely difficult to penetrate. Previously, regarding the "dog" kōan, I was not yet free from doubt concerning the myriad dharmas; how much more so for this final point?
Therefore, I have not dared to indulge my own arbitrary views by composing a verse commentary.
On the Verses on the Ancients (Sònggǔ) and the Expositions on the Ancients (Niàngǔ) (II):
Someone said, "Are you being modest? Is it that you are able yet show yourself as unable? I replied, "It is not modesty; it is true speech and actual speech.
In the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*, both the teaching (jiào) and the school (zōng) are presented as two-fold paths. While the teaching largely reveals the meaning, the school is largely esoteric."
Therefore, it is further said that there are "words devoid of meaning. Regarding the profound and mysterious aspects of the Teachings (*śāsana*), I am still unable to fully comprehend them;

how much more so, then, regarding the language of the Gate of the Lineage (*zongmen*)? Furthermore, although the dialogues and circumstantial encounters (*jiyuan*) of the Gate of the Lineage are said to be words devoid of meaning, there are some where a small portion of the path of meaning remains such that it can be contemplated, while others are entirely without such a path of meaning.
There are those that are like a solid iron hammer, impossible to drill or pierce; some that are like the vast void, impossible to grasp or fathom;
some that are like iron caltrops, impossible to bite or chew; and some that are like a great mass of fire, impossible to draw near.
It is like the disk of the blazing sun, which cannot be gazed upon directly; it is like arsenic or the feathers of a poisoned bird, which must not touch one’s lips.
How could one dare to offer such reckless judgment? To briefly cite one or two examples from the ancients: when the World-Honored One held up a flower, Kāśyapa broke into a smile.
Have I now been able to intuitively harmonize with the Buddha-mind as Kāśyapa did? When a guest recited the *Vajracchedikā*, the Sixth Patriarch immediately—
At that moment, he attained realization. "Now, am I able to suddenly comprehend the profound sutras like the Sixth Patriarch?
When Linji saw Dayu, he said, 'The Buddha-dharma of Huangbo is not so much. Now, have I truly seen that it is indeed 'not so much'?"
Zhaozhou traveled on pilgrimage even at eighty years of age, saying, "It was only because my mind had not yet become still.
Have I now been able to bring my mind to such stillness? Xiangyan struck a bamboo and it made a sound, whereupon he said, "With one strike, all that I knew was forgotten.
Have I now been able to forget all that I know? Lingyun saw peach blossoms and said, "Even until this very day, I have no further doubts. Have I now...

"Have you already been able to reach the ground of no-doubt with certainty? When Xueyan asked Gao Feng while he was fast asleep—'Who is the master when there are no dreams?'—you were unable to answer. Have I now been able to answer that question?
Furthermore, after three years, you attained great enlightenment at the place where the meditation cushion fell. Have I now attained such great enlightenment? Such were his inquiries.
They are too numerous to mention exhaustively. If there is even one point that remains unclarified, it is uncertain whether the rest are all clear.

This is as when Master Yue of Tuṣita spoke of Zhang Wujin. Not only regarding the ancients, but even concerning the works of people today, I do not dare lightly evaluate their right or wrong or offer arbitrary criticisms. Why is this? Only when one is seated upon the hall can one [truly judge].
They distinguish between the right and wrong of those beneath the hall; furthermore, they have never been registered among the sages and worthies. Alas!
A single erroneous response to a turning phrase leads to rebirth as a wild fox for a hundred kalpas. Laughing at the words of those with clear eyes, one vomits up one's teachings for thirty years.
The overturned tracks are manifest; how can one not be cautious?

Regarding the benefits of renunciation, the ancient masters said: "The most excellent sons find joy in renouncing the world. There is a common worldly saying: "If one son renounces the world, the nine generations of his clan are reborn in heaven.
These statements all praise renunciation, yet they do not explicitly clarify the reasons why renunciation constitutes such a benefit.
How could it be said that there is the benefit of natural clothing and food without plowing or weaving?
How could it be said that there is the benefit of natural peaceful dwelling without purchasing a house or renting a room?

How could it be said that there is [the benefit of] royal ministers protecting the Dharma and faithful donors showing reverence, such that above one is not conscripted by the government and below one is not disturbed by the common people? How could it be said that there is...?
Yet, what benefit is there in this leisure and pleasure? An ancient verse says: "A single grain of rice from a donor is as vast as Mount Sumeru;
if one does not realize the Way, one shall return wearing fur and bearing horns. It further says:
"In the days to come, when Old Man Yama settles your account for the cost of your meals, see what you will have to offer in exchange. Thus, leaving the household life is itself a great affliction.
If even those who are subdued [by such a person] are benefited, how much more so those who are truly helped! What is called the benefit of leaving the household life is this:
by destroying the afflictions (*kleśa*), severing ignorance (*avidyā*), and attaining the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), one emerges from the suffering of birth and death.
This is the most supreme state among gods and humans, and its grace extends to one’s parents and kinsmen. Otherwise, even if one were as wealthy as a thousand granaries or as noble as a master...
What benefit is there in these seven emperors? I am truly filled with great anxiety and fear, and thus I inform my fellow practitioners of this.
The Three Difficulties Regarding the Pure Land.
Someone asked: "The Tathāgata Śākyamuni pressed the earth with his toe and it immediately became a golden world.

Since the Buddha possesses such supernatural powers, why does he not immediately transform this Sahā world—this place filled with mountains of earth and stone and impurities—into the Land of Ultimate Bliss adorned with the seven treasures? Why must he instead cause sentient beings to toil [in saṃsāra]?"
The distance between ten trillion Buddha-lands is vast indeed. Alas! The Buddha cannot save those who lack the necessary conditions;
do you understand this? A pure affinity evokes a pure land. If the minds of sentient beings are not pure, even though a pure land exists, by what means could they be born there?

It is like the case where the practice of the ten wholesome deeds leads to rebirth in heaven, such that even a hell is transformed into a paradise; yet for those sentient beings who commit the ten unwholesome deeds, the Tathāgata... [extends his compassion].
A golden-armed man tried to pull him along, yet he was ultimately unable to cross even its threshold.
For this reason, in an instant, the world of Suvarṇabhāsa was withdrawn by the Buddha’s supernormal power and returned to its former state as the Sahā world. Furthermore, one person asked:

"The sutra states that a single sincere recitation of the name of Amitābha Buddha extinguishes the grave offenses of birth and death accumulated over eighty billion kalpas. What does this statement refer to?"
Is it logic? Alas! The Sūtra says: "A single invocation of 'Namo Buddha' has already established one on the path to Buddhahood. It further says:
"For every single prostration made to the Buddha, from the heels of the feet up to the Diamond Realm, there is the merit of one dust mote equal to the sovereignty of a Cakravartin King.
Now, there is truly no need to debate whether this is a matter of fact or of principle; one must simply apply oneself with utmost sincerity. The only concern is the mind.

If one does not attain [rebirth], do not worry that your transgressions will not be extinguished. When the facts are thus, the principle is likewise; when the principle is thus, the facts are likewise.

Why should there be any cause for doubt? Furthermore, another person asked: "There is someone who, throughout their life, has been diligent in reciting the Buddha's name, yet at the moment of death, they have a single thought of regret and consequently fail to attain rebirth.
Conversely, there is someone who, throughout their life, has accumulated evil, yet at the moment of death, they resolve their mind and recite the Buddha's name."
If the Buddha can thus ensure one's rebirth in the Pure Land, then why would the virtuous suffer loss, while the wicked should instead gain benefit?
Alas! Among ten thousand people, there is but one who, having accumulated evil, maintains right mindfulness at the moment of death.

Were it not for the roots of goodness from past lives, one would be overwhelmed by the agony of death, falling into a state of stupor and confusion; how then could such a person possibly give rise to [right thought]?
Awaken right mindfulness! That a virtuous person should feel regret at the time of death is a case that occurs but once in ten thousand people;
even if it does occur, it must be because they failed to practice the Buddha’s name throughout their entire life. Those who are merely idle are not what is meant by those who are "diligent.
To be "refined" means the mind is free from distraction; to be "diligent" means the mind is without interruption. How, then, could regret arise? This is therefore...
Those who are evil should urgently cultivate self-reflection; do not harbor deluded thoughts that you might have such a stroke of luck at the moment of death.
Those who sincerely seek the Pure Land should simply increase their own diligent efforts; do not worry about falling back or regretting at the time of death.

Regarding the ancient saying that "the world is a dream," it is said that living in the world is like a great dream. A sutra states: "When one returns to observe the world, it is just like the events within a dream.
If one says it is "like" a dream, this is merely a figurative expression used out of necessity; yet, when examined to the ultimate point, it is actually a true dream.
This is not a mere metaphor. Human life proceeds from youth to maturity, from maturity to old age, and from old age to death.
In an instant one enters a womb; in an instant one emerges from a womb; in an instant one enters again and emerges again, in an endless cycle.
Yet in life one knows nothing of the coming, and in death one knows nothing of the going—obscure and dark, through thousands of births and tens of thousands of deaths.
One passes through kalpas without realizing it. In a moment one sinks into the hells; in a moment one becomes a ghost, an animal, a human, or a deva.
Rising and sinking, sinking and rising, in a state of frantic agitation and bewildered haste, one passes through thousands of births and myriad kalpas without realizing it—is this not a true dream?
As an ancient poem says: "In a fleeting spring dream upon the pillow, one travels across all of Jiangnan."
For thousands of miles. Now, being pulled by profit and fame, those who travel back and forth ten thousand li—how could it necessarily be that this is only so upon one's pillow?
Therefore, we know that when Zhuangzi dreamed he was a butterfly, even before he dreamed he was a butterfly, he was already dreaming.

When Confucius dreamed of Duke Zhou, even before he dreamed of Duke Zhou, he was already dreaming. Since the vast kalpas of the past, there has not been a single moment or a single instant [when one is not dreaming].
Yet this does not occur within a dream. Having utterly shattered ignorance, one attains a vast and luminous awakening and says: "In all that is above heaven and below heaven, I alone am honored.
This is what is meant by a person who has awakened from a dream.
Regarding the "turning word" (*ekavāc*), the former masters instructed students, saying: "I shall now say nothing of your meditative concentration, wisdom, supernormal powers, or eloquence;
I require only that you deliver one turning word that is precise and correct. Upon hearing this, the students then studied the turning word day and night.

It is wrong. Since a single turning word is thus noble and thus extraordinary, one knows for certain that it is not something to be conjectured through intellectual consciousness, nor is it something to be appropriated through superficial understanding or conventional knowledge.

It flows forth spontaneously from within true, great, and thorough enlightenment. This is as if, regarding the scriptures and teachings, or regarding the ancestral encounters and dialogues of the ancients—
In the midst of this, those with clever but petty intellects imitate and engage in forced interpretation, seeking distinction through their speech.

While their phrases may indeed be sharp and novel, they are in truth like scratching an itch with a boot on—reaching only the surface. Even if one were to utter as many turning words as there are grains of sand in the Ganges in a single kṣaṇa, what connection would they have with one’s own self?
For now, do not concern yourself with whether these turning words are correct or incorrect; simply cast them aside.
Beyond that which can be said and that which cannot be said, simply hold fast to your original inquiry. Apply your mind with intimacy and secrecy, never abandoning it for a moment.
Once you have attained thorough awakening, how could you worry about having no words? Although I am of dull faculties, I dare not fail to exert myself.
A monk asked an ancient worthy, "What is the original body of Vairocana? He replied, "Give me the whisk."
Shortly thereafter, he said, "Return it to its original place. When the monk repeated his previous question, he replied, "The ancient Buddhas have long since passed away.
He further said, "Listen to a word from one who has not yet attained realization: right now, who is moving their mouth?
Later generations took this to mean that raising a hand, moving a foot, opening the mouth, or making a sound constitutes being a true Buddha. While this is so, it is also truly not so. As it is said:

This is like taking a thief for one's own son. Consequently, [the deluded] take the "cypress tree," the "three catties of hemp," the "green bamboos and yellow flowers," and the "bird carrying a branch or the monkey embracing its young" as being all one and the same.
Is this not a grave error? When Jueyi encountered a question, he would simply raise a single finger;
when Luzu saw a monk, he would turn his body and face the wall. An ancient said, "If I had seen him, I would have snapped off that finger. I, too, [would have done the same].
It is said that he waited for the man to turn his body, then lunged at his chest and kicked him down.
The words of the Chan school cannot be recklessly imitated;
after the great masters attained enlightenment, they spoke horizontally and vertically, speaking directly and speaking inversely, speaking openly and speaking cryptically—each and every word.
These accord with the Buddha’s seal of mind; they are all words of truth and words of reality, not comparable to the parables of Zhuangzi.

Nowadays, those whose minds have not yet attained subtle awakening, yet possess keen natures and sharp eloquence, can merely imitate the questions and answers found within various *yulu* (recorded sayings) upon a cursory glance.
They value nothing more than being unconventional and eccentric, seeking to appear marvelous or startling in order to dazzle the eyes of the vulgar.
It is like midday occurring at the third watch, or the sun rising at midnight; it is like waves surging from a mountain peak or dust arising from the bottom of the sea.
Such various words devoid of meaning are uttered recklessly from the mouth. Those without discernment are unable to examine them, yet they join in praise with one voice.

That person has long been wearing a mask without returning to his true nature, yet they claim he has attained the truth. It even reaches the point where they would say, "Strike him once with a staff and give him to a dog to eat."

"Is there an ancestral teacher within? Call him here and let him wash my feet. In such instances, they likewise show no sense of shame. They often imitate [the ancients] like a person mimicking another's frown. Alas!
To speak recklessly of Prajñāpāramitā is a sin for which there is no pardon. How truly fearsome this is!
In examining the recorded sayings (yulu), one must seek where the ancients applied their minds.
When reading the texts of the ancients' recorded sayings, one must not focus exclusively on a single question and answer, a single "seizing" (nian), or a single verse (song).

The sharpness of his spiritual pivot is steep and keen; in places where his words are exquisite and his expressions marvelous, they refresh my mind and eyes and serve as a resource for my own discourse.
One must thoroughly investigate why he reached this state of great penetration and great awakening. Within it, he himself describes the methods for applying the hand [of practice].
One must apply oneself with diligent effort and practice in accordance with this; this is what is meant by "why not cultivate according to the authentic model?

If one merely plunders and imitates, then even if many years and ages pass, and one becomes eloquent and fluent of tongue, it will still be nothing more than a deceptive facsimile of the ancients—merely flowers made of cut paper or cakes painted on silk. What kind of realization could such things possibly achieve?
When ancient artifacts come into my hands,
people today— regarding even a single ritual vessel, a single jar, a single book, or a single painting whose origins lie in high antiquity and which came from the hands of a master,
things they had long admired and yearned for but could never obtain— will, upon suddenly acquiring them, rejoice with a delight that exceeds their expectations.
He greeted him with joy and comforted him, saying: "This was something mutually cherished by such-and-such a person; now, fortunately, it has come into my hands.
Yet he never considered that since time immemorial, this peerless treasure beyond price would one day fall into my possession.
Moreover, worldly playthings remain outside; though sought, they may not be obtained. But the supreme treasure resides within me—once sought, it is found—and yet he failed to consider this."

"When joy, anger, sorrow, and happiness have not yet been aroused"—this was my initial entry into the Way. I recalled Zisi’s statement that the state where joy, anger, sorrow, and happiness have not yet been aroused is the "Middle" (*zhong*).
I thought this Middle was the self prior to the kalpa of emptiness (*kongjie*). Subsequently, I consulted the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, which says: "Even if one were to extinguish all seeing..."
To hear, perceive, and know, while inwardly maintaining stillness in the profound and secluded, is still but a matter of the shadows of conceptualization regarding mental objects (*dharmas*).

Now, when seeing and hearing have ceased and perception and cognition are cut off—resembling a state where joy, anger, sorrow, and pleasure have not yet been aroused—why is it called "conceptualization of mental objects"?

It is because of the faculty of mind (*manas*) and the mental objects (*dharmas*). When the faculty and the object encounter a favorable condition, joy and pleasure arise; when they encounter an adverse condition, [sorrow and anger arise].

The arousal of anger and sorrow is the faculty of mind (*manas*) discerning the objects of cognition (*dharmāyatana*). When these have not yet arisen, the objects have not yet interfaced with the external, and the faculties have not yet emerged within;
it is tranquil and still. This should be the fundamental substance (*tattva*), which does not know how to move toward conditioned objects.
Now, in relation to a state of stillness, it moves toward the coarse discernment of the objects of cognition; now, it likewise engages in the subtle discernment of the objects of cognition.
These are all matters of reflection; they are not reality. They are called "profound" and "secluded" merely because the profound surpasses the manifest and the secluded surpasses the noisy.
Even before the empty kalpa, one's own true self remains far removed. At this point, you must examine with utmost scrutiny and investigate with precision.
Refine it again and again; exhaust it to its very limit. You must not treat this with superficial haste.

Ji-cen Ji-wu (Quickly Enter, Quickly Realize), known as the Cowherd Layman, was a native of Ancient Hangzhou and a son of the Yu family. He studied under the Elder Wumen and attained enlightenment during the Chunyou era of the Song dynasty.
His words state: "When a person of great intelligence hears of this matter, they immediately attempt to comprehend it through the mind, intellect, and consciousness."

This is why one mistakes a reflection for reality. When the thirtieth day of the twelfth lunar month arrives and the light of your eyes is about to fall, you might say to Old Yan, "Wait until I have clarified my mind and gathered my thoughts; then I will go with you. This is absolutely impossible.
You must investigate urgently and awaken urgently. The words of this "Tending Cattle" [text] are truly urgent. For one who has attained genuine and thorough awakening, during their daily life...
If you can stand firm and secure, steady and composed, without raising a weapon, you will be able to face enemies from all eight directions.
When impermanence arrives, you will remain at ease and self-possessed—neither frantic nor hurried, neither terrified nor confused.
Why then wait to clarify the mind and collect the thoughts, or to struggle with forced endurance? As it is said, "Study urgently and awaken urgently"; we must strive for this with all our might.
There are those who, weary of clamor, seek stillness and practice quietude. They dwell alone in a single room; if there is even the slightest sound of human voice, they consider it an obstacle.

Now, while human voices can be silenced, what is to be done when crows and magpies screech in the courtyard? Crows and magpies can be driven away, but what if tigers and leopards were to roar [in the vicinity]?

As for forests and mountains, what can be done? Even tigers and leopards can be made to be hunted by hunters. But as for the direction of the wind, the flow of water, and the crashing of thunder amidst torrential rain—what can be done about these?
Therefore it is said: "The fool eliminates the external environment but does not eliminate the mind; the wise person eliminates the mind but does not eliminate the environment.
If one wishes to eliminate the environment but the environment ultimately cannot be eliminated, then the Way can never be learned. Or...

It is said: "The World-Honored One did not perceive the sound of five hundred chariots; this was a matter occurring within meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*), beyond the capacity of ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*).
Thus, when Gao Feng was reading his books and did not notice the torrential rain washing away his wheat—at that moment, what meditative state had Feng entered?
To blame him for a lack of firm resolve while resenting the lack of tranquility in his environment is surely erroneous."
Regarding the "Day of Expiation" (*churil*), the ancients considered this day to be one's day of death. It is the conclusion of a year, much like the conclusion of a lifetime.
Thus, Huangbo’s instruction states: "If you have not struck through [the truth] beforehand, when the thirtieth day of the twelfth month arrives, take it for granted that..."
How bustling and noisy! Thus, it is not too early to attend to the affairs of the day of one's passing on the first day of the first month;
it is not too early to attend to the affairs of the day of one's death at the very moment of birth.

How can one endure this slow and gradual drifting, this aimless wandering, until one realizes that youth has become vigor, vigor has become old age, and old age has led to death? Moreover, there are those who do not even reach vigor before they grow old.

Is this not truly a matter of profound lament? Tonight, as the year comes to an end, you ought to feel a sense of urgency and make a vow to yourself, pledging that you will not allow next year to pass by in the same state of procrastination.
Nevertheless, these two characters—*dà* (thoroughly) and *chè* (penetrating)—must not be viewed lightly.
It is not by merely reading through several volumes of sutras and treatises that one attains *chè*; nor is it simply by sitting for a few incense sticks that one achieves it.

If you do not waver when stirred, you will attain thorough penetration (*cheda*). This is not a matter of understanding a few lines of ancient masters' dialogues and *jiyuan* (critical incidents), nor is it a matter of composing a few verses of *songgu* (verses on old cases) or *niangu* (comments on old cases) to attain thorough penetration.

Nor is it a matter of replying with a few words of "verbal samādhi" or slick eloquence to attain thorough penetration. The ancients said that regarding this matter, one must be as clear as when the bottom of a bucket suddenly falls out—refreshing and unobstructed.
It is like waking from a great dream; only when there is not even a hair’s breadth of doubt remaining can one truly proceed. Alas! How could I dare not exert myself?
Reciting the Buddha's name does not obstruct the practice of Zen meditation.
The ancients said that practicing Chan does not hinder the recitation of the Buddha’s name, and the recitation of the Buddha’s name does not hinder the practice of Chan.

Yet, it is also said that one must not allow them to be practiced concurrently. Nevertheless, there were those who combined Chan with the Pure Land school, such as Yuanzhao Ben, Zhenxie Liao, Yongming Shou, Huanglong Xin, and Cishou Shen;
all of these masters were great patriarchs of the Chan school who nonetheless devoted their hearts to the Pure Land.

This does not obstruct one's Zen practice. Therefore, it should be known that although a practitioner of Zen investigates their own fundamental mind in every thought-moment, this does not prevent them from making vows.
One may vow to be reborn in the Land of Ultimate Bliss at the time of death. Why is this so? Although one may attain a state of awakening through Zen practice, [the vow remains necessary].

If one cannot abide in the eternal, quiescent light like the Buddhas, nor attain the state of no further rebirth like an Arhat, then upon the exhaustion of this retribution-body, one will inevitably have a place of birth.
Rather than being born into the human world [again], it is better to draw near to an enlightened teacher now.
How could this possibly compare to the superiority of being born within a lotus flower and drawing near to Amitābha?
Thus, reciting the Buddha’s name not only does not hinder the practice of Zen meditation, it actually benefits it.
That which is obtained by hearing and receiving with the mind is not as extensive as that which is obtained by looking at and reading with the eyes.
That which is obtained by looking at and reading with the eyes is not as extensively vast as that which is obtained by awakening to and clarifying it with the mind.
It is appropriate to take the mind as the sovereign, the eyes as the ministers, and the ears as the assistants and envoys.
To employ the eyes in place of the mind is already base; to employ the ears in place of the eyes is base among the base.
Worldly wisdom should be understood as being twofold: there is worldly wisdom and there is supramundane wisdom. Worldly wisdom is also twofold:

first, those who possess extensive learning, grand rhetoric, specialized skills, and far-reaching strategies, and who surpass others merely by virtue of their great knowledge and many interpretations; second—
This clarifies good and evil and distinguishes the heterodox from the orthodox. To practice what ought to be practiced and to desist from what ought to be desisted is precisely this.

If one attains only the former, it is called "wild wisdom" (*kuaṅ-jì*); such a person shall fall into the three miserable realms. If one attains both the former and the latter, it is called "right wisdom" (*zhèng-jì*);

the retribution for such a person lies among humans and devas. Why is this? One whose virtue surpasses their talent is called a gentleman; one whose talent surpasses their virtue is called... [a petty man].
Such a person is a mere worldly being. World-transcending wisdom (*lokottara-jñāna*) is likewise twofold.
The first consists of those who are well able to discern the Tathāgata’s true Dharma—such as the Four Noble Truths and the Six Perfections—and practice in accordance with them.

The second consists of those who shatter the delusions of ignorance and, with perfect clarity, perceive their own fundamental mind. Merely attaining the former constitutes world-transcending wisdom; it is called...
One enters gradually and simultaneously attains what follows; this is the supreme wisdom of the supramundane, which is called "sudden transcendence.
Why is this so? If one attains the root, there is no need to worry about the branches. Those who attain the branches do not necessarily attain the root.

Nowadays, there are those who, having merely acquired a small portion of worldly knowledge, claim to have achieved great penetration and great enlightenment—how extremely deluded and ignorant they are!

During the daytime, while engaged in affairs, my dispositions were sometimes unsettled and I would fall asleep. Rising at the fourth or fifth watch of the night, right and wrong, what was permissible and what was not, suddenly became perfectly clear to me.
All the errors I had committed during the day appeared therein; only then did I realize that until now, I had been unable to see clearly.
The nature of the mind is such that it is merely its original essence being obscured by agitation and confusion.

An ancient said, "In stillness, one perceives the nature of True Suchness," and another said, "When the water of nature is clear and still, the pearl of the mind appears of itself. How could these not be empty words?
One must not fail to read the Buddhist scriptures.

When I was young, I encountered the refutations of Buddhism by former sages; influenced by these preconceived notions, I viewed them as a "dwarf looking up," remaining entirely unaware of their true nature.

It happened that I requested several volumes of scripture from a sutra shop at a precept platform and began to read them. Only then did I realize with great astonishment: "If one does not read [them], it is like..."
This book—how many have let it pass in vain throughout their entire lives! Yet there are people today who, from youth through middle age to old age and death, never once set eyes upon it;
they may truly be called those who face a mountain of jewels but do not enter it.

Furthermore, there is another class who, though they read it, do no more than pluck its phrases and expressions to serve as conversation pieces or to aid their own literary style, from youth through middle age to old age.
Those who die without thoroughly investigating this principle may be called people who enter a mountain of jewels but do not take any.
Furthermore, there is another class who, though they engage in discussion and lecturing, do no more than explain characters and gloss texts;

they vie for novelty and compete for loftiness, yet from youth through middle age to old age until death, they never truly cultivate or practice. These may be called people who take up the jewels merely to play with them.

They examine it, appreciate it, cherish it, and tuck it away in their sleeves, only to discard it once more. Nevertheless, once it has been imprinted upon the field of consciousness, it will ultimately become the seed of the Way;
therefore, one must not fail to read the Buddhist scriptures.

Regarding the Head Seat Tai, some say that Tai prepared incense and sat in meditation until his passing. Jiupeng did not permit this, because Tai had not yet realized the meaning of Shishuang’s words:
"Go to rest," "Rest," and "Like cold ashes or withered wood. Yet, the Monk Zhiyi was able to go and come. Regarding this—
As for why both [Zhaozhou] did not grasp Shishuang’s meaning and Dongshan also did not approve, what is the reason?

I, the fool, say that if Zhizang had truly attained the state where "the outgoing breath does not involve external conditions and the incoming breath does not dwell within the realms of existence," then he would have been free to go or stay at will;
he should have shared a meal with Dongshan as fools and walked hand-in-hand with him—how could Daoyi have reached such a level? If it were otherwise, he would inevitably fail to avoid [delusion].
This is a fellow who plays with the vital spirit; it is what the ancients called the "livelihood of ghosts and spirits.
Yet Master Tai possessed a truly authentic method of stabilization. It was simply that he became attached to the realm of stillness and failed to understand the phrase for "turning the body.

In this regard, the two were equally afflicted by the same malady. Nevertheless, Zhizai (Paper-Cloth) remained humble and sought clarification from Dongshan, whereas Master Tai departed resolutely for the long journey.
One loses great benefit through self-indulgence; fullness invites loss, while humility brings gain. Those who study Chan should know this.
As for the statement in the *Kongcongzi* that "the spiritual essence of the mind is what is called sagehood," Yang Cihu devoted his lifelong studies to this very principle.
This is taken as the fundamental tenet. As for its relation to "innate knowledge" (liangzhi), how could it not coincide with the Buddha’s teaching of "true knowledge"?
[The opponent] says: "Spirit" (shenjing) is even more superficial than innate knowledge; both are merely ripples upon water. How, then, can they be considered true knowledge?
