Furthermore, if the two characters 'spirit' (shen) and 'energy' (jing) are analyzed separately, each has its own significance; yet when combined to form a compound, they refer to the essence-soul (jingshen), the spirit-consciousness (shenshi), and so forth."
This is what is meant. It refers to the saying of those people of old: "The root of birth and death throughout immeasurable kalpas—fools recognize this as their original person.
This is the habit of the monks.
In the Dharma-ending age, there are monks who practice calligraphy, poetry, and the art of letter-writing. Yet these three are all matters belonging to the scholar-officials;

the scholar-officials abandon them without practicing them and instead practice Chan. Monks, conversely, practice what the scholar-officials have abandoned, while casting aside the great matter of karmic conditions pertaining to their own lot beyond the reach of their concern. How can such perversity be so extreme?
In the encounter dialogues of the ancient masters of the Chan school, their karmic exchanges may sometimes lack meaning or flavor, or they may be startling and suspicious;
they may even seem like insults or jests. Yet all of these arise from genuine inquiry and authentic realization, such that they are as inseparable as water and milk.
The contents of the box and the lid fit together perfectly; not a single word or phrase is applied in vain.

Yet later generations, lacking understanding, merely imitate the frown [of the original], thereby committing no small offense of speech (*vākkarman*). It is like two people from the same town who have been parted for a thousand *li* and suddenly meet;

when they converse with one another using their local dialects, cryptic language, and colloquialisms, those standing by hear them as being devoid of meaning and flavor—strange and suspicious. Thus it is.
Though their insults seemed like jests, in reality, every word and every phrase was a discourse from the depths of their hearts and the essence of their innermost thoughts.
While bystanders certainly did not know what kind of words were being spoken, the two understood each other in silent accord as perfectly as water and milk, or as a box and its lid.
Now it would be better to seal one's mouth and remain speechless; simply exert effort upon the original inquiry. One need only fear not awakening;
one need not fear being unable to speak after awakening, even if one hears slander.
The Sūtra says: "When a person slanders me, at the moment the first syllable is uttered, the subsequent syllables have not yet arisen;

by the time the final syllable is uttered, the initial syllable has already ceased. This is merely the movement of the breath and possesses no reality whatsoever. If one gives rise to anger because of this," [it is a delusion].
In that case, one would have to feel anger at every jay’s caw and every crow’s cry. This argument is indeed most ingenious. Yet some might say:

"If someone were to compose a poem of slander, it would be complete in every character upon a single reading; furthermore, it would endure forever without perishing. What method could possibly destroy it?
But they fail to consider that white is paper and black is ink—what, then, is the slander? Moreover, [the characters] are but one...
Every single character is formed by the combination of radicals and phonetic components from a dictionary.

Thus, having a dictionary placed upon one's desk means that hundreds of thousands, millions, and billions of slanderous texts are present before one at all times. How can one be so deluded? Nevertheless.
This is still a teaching by way of remedial means (*pratipakṣa-dvāra*). If one knows the emptiness of self (*ātma-śūnyatā*), who is there to receive blame?

The Bodhisattva does not currently express surprise that those who create karma are many while those who believe in the Way are few. Since the Bodhisattva has already brought sentient beings across without end, why [should he be concerned]?

Without manifesting as separate bodies, you transform and guide the masses of deluded beings. Furthermore, since the Buddha-Dharma flowed eastward from the Han and Wei dynasties down to the Song and Yuan, spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra) appearing in the world were as numerous as fish scales.
Yet, even during the late Yuan and the early Ming, one or two still appeared; why is it that recently we have heard so little?
If Dizang Bodhisattva vows to deliver all sentient beings, and Avalokiteśvara is said to appear in every land, why is this so?
How could they bear to abandon sentient beings who have not yet been delivered? Could there also be realms where [the Buddha] does not manifest?

After reflecting on this for a long time, I realized that while Bodhisattvas deliver sentient beings according to their vows, they cannot deliver those with whom they lack the necessary karmic affinity.

It is like the moon in the sky: it originally has no intention to cease its reflection in water; yet if the water itself is turbid, the moon will not appear. How much more so now, as we enter the gradual decline of the Final Dharma!

The more profound the defilements of the mind become, the more difficult it is for a Bodhisattva to save sentient beings, even though they constantly do so; yet there will be no ground upon which those beings can receive salvation.
This is like seeking the bright moon while standing before turbid water—how could it ever be attained?

At Caoxi, there was one whose stream of thought was not severed who recited a verse by the Sixth Patriarch: "Huineng has no skill; / The hundred thoughts do not cease. / When encountering objects, mental states arise;
/ How can Bodhi grow? He boasted that he had grasped the essential meaning, and immediately proceeded to let his mind run wild and his body act as it pleased in all matters.
[The Master] was unimpeded. While he sat there, a layman rebuked him, saying: "Great Master, this verse of yours is a medicine for the illness of discursive thought;
it is capable of severing such thoughts. Yet you yourself do not yet have this illness, and you are taking this medicine in vain.

This medicine will instead become an illness itself. "How well said! [The Master replied. "I shall now provide another analogy: Caoxi does not sever the hundred discursive thoughts, just as a clear mirror does not sever reflections."
It is like the myriad forms [contained within] a single image; it is like the unbroken five colors upon a plain silk scroll.
When Caoxi encounters an object, mental states arise, just as a sound arises when a valley is called out to.
When people of today encounter an object, mental states arise, just as smoke arises when dry wood meets fire. Without examining oneself, one merely attaches oneself to...
The former sages said: "Try reflecting on this for a moment in a quiet place.

Regarding the roots, branches, and leaves—the teachings on human karma, the sutras, and the treatises—what they value most often lies in elaborate terminology and complex characteristics that are difficult to remember and uphold."
Regarding those matters where the meaning is profound and the principle obscure, making them difficult to analyze;

and where the phrasing is hidden and the sentences are terse, making them difficult to synthesize—people employ such means to display their eloquence and boastfully flaunt novelty, yet they leave the great matter of cause and condition beneath the feet of the patch-robed monk unheard of.
Furthermore, how could they know that these names, characteristics, principles, and phrases all flow forth from within this very source?
This is to attack the branches and leaves while remaining ignorant of the root and source; it is for this reason that [the Master of] Yongjia sighed so deeply. Thus it is said:
"If you only obtain the root, you need not worry about the branches. I fear only that people of this age lack faith in this and cannot let go.
The various Dharma-gates are like a royal general leading an army into battle; in the clash of combat, victory is achieved by slaying the enemy.
As for this slaying of the enemy, one may use a sword, a spear, a mallet, a halberd, or even arrows and stones—employing whatever is appropriate—but what is valued above all is mastery in their use.
It is merely a single technique. If we take the analogy of a student, then the delusions of ignorance and the obstructions are like those bandits;

the various Dharma gates are like swords, spears, and the like. To shatter and destroy these delusive obstructions is to achieve total victory. Thus, we know that it does not matter what the instruments of killing are;

one simply takes up the task of slaying the bandits. Once the bandits have been slain, the great matter is finished. What are called "instruments of killing" are all merely rafts for crossing a river.
It is not that one neglects the great while being preoccupied with the trivial, claiming that a sword can kill while a spear cannot; how could such a view be reasonable?

Those who practice *chan* (Zen) deride the recitation of the Buddha’s name as being attached to forms (*nimitta*), while those who encourage practice condemn the cultivation of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) as falling into emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
This is just like that. Therefore, a sutra says: "The return to the source has no two paths; the expedient means have many gates. As the former masters said: "It is like..."
When people travel a long distance, they take reaching their destination as the goal; they do not seek to forcibly divide the journey into difficult and easy sections along the way.
Huang鲁直 (Huang Lu-zhi) said: "If one seeks deeply the joy of *dhyāna* and illuminates the root of birth and death, then anxiety, fear, lust, and anger will no longer exist."

"Step firmly upon it; simply wither its root, and the branches and leaves will naturally wither of themselves. This is a definitive argument. However, it does not explicitly state what constitutes the root of birth and death.

Furthermore, regarding the phrase "the essential point of meditative joy (dhyāna-prīti) lies in penetrating through illumination," if one attains meditative joy and considers that sufficient, then remaining inwardly in a secluded stillness is precisely the root of birth and death. One must investigate exhaustively and research with diligent effort to realize this.

When one clearly perceives their own original nature, then birth and death have no place to set foot. When birth and death have no place to set foot, from what source could anxiety, fear, lust, or anger arise?

In the *Ekottarika Āgama*, the Buddha said: "The accomplishment of ethical discipline (*śīla*) is a worldly convention; the accomplishment of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) is also a worldly convention;
the accomplishment of supernormal powers such as flying through the air is also a worldly convention. Only the accomplishment of wisdom (*prajñā*)..."

This constitutes the primary meaning. Thus, one should know that among the three trainings of precepts, concentration, and so forth, as well as the six perfections beginning with giving, wisdom alone is the most weighty and must not be treated lightly; wisdom alone is the foremost and must not be deferred;
wisdom alone penetrates all dharma-gates and is without equal. As the Sūtra says: "Through the precepts, concentration arises; through concentration, wisdom is produced."

This is merely to describe the sequence of its arising; however, one must fundamentally understand what is essential, what comes first, and how to achieve thorough penetration before success can be attained.
Nevertheless, this wisdom is not what is meant by mere cleverness or eloquence. It is like the wisdom of former lives, which should be understood according to the teachings of the Middle Way.

Regarding those who travel on foot and dwell in the mountains, people today see that Xuansha did not cross the ridges and Baofu did not pass through the passes; they simply sat upright and dwelt in peace, their eyes looking down upon the four seas with indifference.
Yet when we look at Xuefeng, who ascended Mount Touzi three times and went up to Dongshan nine times, or Zhaozhou, who traveled even at the age of eighty, [we see a different reality].
To merely wander from south to north and drift aimlessly for a lifetime—both of these approaches are incorrect.

If the mind-ground has not yet been clarified, one ought instead to seek out spiritual teachers (kalyāṇamitra) across thousands of miles. How can you remain idle, guarding your ignorance and sitting empty-handed while harboring self-importance?

Since you have entered the path of life and death to study under a master and inquire after the Way, how can you spend your time merely gazing at mountains and waters, vainly boasting of your travels?
Is it merely this? For a practitioner on pilgrimage, the truth is not so.
When viewing the mountain scenery from nearby, the mountain colors are a profound azure, as green as indigo; when viewing the mountain scenery from afar, they are a dense, lush emerald.
It is like the way indigo is produced from woad: does the color of the mountain truly change? The color of the mountain remains as it was; rather, the power of one's vision has its limits.
As one moves gradually from near to far, blue easily turns into emerald green; as one moves gradually from far to near, [the opposite occurs].
Emerald is easily transformed into green. Thus, it is through the convergence of conditions that it becomes green, and through the convergence of conditions that emerald becomes emerald.
It is not only the emerald that is illusory; green, too, is illusory. Indeed, all phenomena are like this.
The equal value of alertness and stillness, as well as cessation and contemplation, has long been established. Even if a sage were to arise again, he could not alter this.

Yet, some who are slightly lax or overly urgent in their practice between these states say: "The sutras state that wisdom is generated by means of concentration; therefore, cessation is essential. Following this logic, they continue in that manner.
This becomes a habitual practice. Those who cultivate the Way generally emphasize stillness (*śānti*).
Only Yongjia, however, established the teaching of "vividness within stillness" and "stillness within vividness" to clarify their mutual equality.

Yet, his later statement that "vividness is the primary [state] and stillness is the auxiliary" represents a uniquely realized insight that no one has equaled from antiquity until the present. Since then, within the Chan school...
He taught people to examine the critical phrase (kōan) in order to achieve thorough awakening; this was precisely the intent behind Miaoxi’s condemnation of "silent illumination" as deviant Chan.
Therefore, the Buddha is called the Great Awakened One, while sentient beings are called the unawakened. Awakening means being alert and lucid. How subtle is the purport of Yongjia!
For every hundred ordinary people who create karma, there is one or two true practitioners of the Way. For every hundred who practice goodness, there is one or two who turn toward the Way.
For every hundred who turn toward the Way, there is one or two who remain steadfast and enduring. For every hundred who are steadfast and enduring, there is one or two who are even more resolute.
Firmness. After a long time, even after a very long time, there may be only one or two whose bodhicitta has reached the stage of non-retrogression.
Such people as these, called true seekers of the Way at the final stage—how difficult they are to find!
Regarding Tianru’s *Collected Explanations of the Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, some say: "This *Śūraṅgama* by Tianru is not the *Śūraṅgama* of Śākyamuni.
I say that while these words are true, if beginners cling to them, they will consequently seek to completely discard the commentaries of the ancients.

This is incorrect. If one were to completely discard the commentaries and sub-commentaries (*zhùshū*) and retain only the root text (*báiwén*), would it not be the case that this *Śūraṅgama-sūtra* of Śākyamuni would no longer be one's own *Śūraṅgama-sūtra*?
If so, then the scripture itself could be discarded—how much more so its commentaries and sub-commentaries?
Furthermore, if one does not say that one's own *Śūraṅgama-sūtra* pervades all places, then even the songs of woodcutters among the various schools and hundred masters [would not be it].
The recitation of the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* (the "Cows' Song") must not be abandoned; how much less so its commentaries and sub-commentaries!

After his awakening, Master Guishan said: "Now, although the initial mind is attained through conditions, once one has suddenly awakened to the fundamental principle in a single thought-moment, it is even more [so]."

There are those whose habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) from beginningless eons have not yet been suddenly purified; they must be taught to purify and eliminate their manifest karma and flowing consciousness—this is precisely what "cultivation" means.

It does not mean that there is some separate dharma to be taught to them so that they may practice and advance toward it. These words of Master Miu-shan could not have been spoken by anyone who had not thoroughly penetrated the source and bottom of the Dharma.
Now, if one has even a slight awakening, one immediately claims that the task of study and practice for a lifetime is finished.
As for "completion," why is it so?
The cultivation that removes hindrances also has five grades. It is like a single person’s body wrapped in five layers of cloth; the outermost layer...
First, remove the iron armor; next, the leather and fur; next, the cloth robe; next, the gauze shirt; and finally, the fine silk directly against the skin.
Remove them one by one in this order until even the fine silk is gone, and only then is there the bare, naked body itself.
The practitioner removes external coarse obstructions, removing them again and again, until even the most subtle obstructions of fundamental ignorance are completely eliminated.
When all [delusions] have been completely eliminated, this is precisely the fundamentally pure Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).

Once, two monks—one who practiced Chan meditation and one who recited the Buddha’s name—met on a road while debating the nature of Chan and the Buddha. The practitioner of Chan asserted that, fundamentally, there is no Buddha.
"As for 'that which is worth contemplating,' I do not even like to hear the single word 'Buddha. As for 'reciting the Buddha's name,' it means that there is a Buddha in the West named Amitābha;
by recollecting and reciting the Buddha's name, one will certainly see the Buddha. Two monks were arguing incessantly over whether [the Buddha] exists or does not exist.
A young man passing by heard them and said, "What both of you gentlemen are saying is merely the 'Xulu carrying a board' [view]. The two monks rebuked him.

He said, "You are a worldly man; how could you know the Buddha-dharma? The youth replied, "I am indeed a worldly man. Yet, by using the metaphor of a worldly man, one may come to know the Buddha-dharma.
I am a performer from the pear orchard (*li-yuan*). Upon the stage, I sometimes act as a ruler and sometimes as a minister;
I sometimes act as a man and sometimes as a woman; I sometimes act as a good person and sometimes as an evil person—yet I seek only that which is [the truth]."

"Regarding what are called rulers and ministers, men and women, good and evil—those who consider these to exist do so because they are actually non-existent; those who consider them to be non-existent do so because they are actually existent.

Indeed, existence is existence within non-existence, and non-existence is non-existence within existence. Both existence and non-existence are not the truth; I, however, am serene and eternally abiding.
Knowing that I am eternally abiding, why should one struggle for anything? The two monks had no reply.

Regarding Tanzong, before he had left the household life, he once read some sayings from the Chan school and immediately attempted to imitate them with his own intellectual understanding, writing a letter to a presiding abbot that was erratic and incoherent.
The abbot was appalled by it. Several years after Tanzong had become a monk, he met the abbot again at a certain place.
We stayed at a hermitage. During our conversation, I noticed that he was focused exclusively on the Pure Land and did not mention the Zen school.

Startled, he said, "The other day you demonstrated a most transcendent understanding; why is it that today you have turned to something so humble and mundane? I smiled and replied, "There is a proverb:
'A newborn calf does not fear tigers, but one who knows the law fears them. Do you understand this, Master? The Abbot did not answer.

Fame, profit, honor, and substantial gain are what all in the world vie for together. Yet the sages of old said that they cannot be obtained by seeking them, nor can they be avoided by rejecting them.
This single phrase, "they cannot be avoided even by rejecting them," is most profoundly subtle and wondrous. Those who dwell in the world should [reflect upon this].
One may believe deeply and examine it thoroughly, yet it remains unattainable through seeking. If others come to know of it, one cannot avoid it;
who then could know it? If one knows it is unavoidable, why seek it? Furthermore, while seeking it and not yet having found it, one cannot overcome the resulting vexation;
yet once it is found, one cannot overcome the resulting joy. If one knows it is unavoidable, what cause is there for such joy?
Furthermore, one rejoices when one attains [realization] for oneself, yet feels envy when others attain it. If one knows that this [attainment] cannot be avoided, why harbor such envy?

It is hoped that by realizing that all is brought about by one's own past conditions (*pūrvakṛta-karman*) and understanding that the ten thousand kalpas are like empty space, one will become indifferent to success or failure, profit or dullness.
Thus, one should know that these words are profound and subtle.

Supernormal powers (abhijñā) are, roughly speaking, of three kinds: first, those obtained through retribution; second, those obtained through cultivation; and third, those obtained through realization. Regarding those obtained through retribution:

they are brought about by one's own meritorious karma, such as the ability of the various devas to see and hear clearly, as well as the supernormal powers possessed by certain ghosts. Those obtained through cultivation...
The former refers to achieving mastery through study and practice, such as when Devadatta learned supernatural powers from the Venerable Ānanda.

The latter refers to attaining realization by devoting oneself exclusively to the Way without seeking supernatural powers; when the Way is perfected, the powers are naturally possessed, differing only in their speed of attainment.
This is exemplified by the various patriarchs and spiritual friends of antiquity and today. Comparing these two, the attainment of the Way...
One need not worry about lacking supernatural powers (*abhijñā*). Yet, possessing such powers does not necessarily mean one possesses the Way (*mārga*). A former master once said:

"In the marvelous application of supernatural powers, you, O *ācārya*, may be superior; but as for the Buddha-dharma, it must still be left to this old monk. There is a specific meaning behind these words. Let me provide an analogy for you:

Consider the rank, emoluments, official caps and robes, government offices, and ceremonial guards possessed by an official in the world—these are like supernatural powers. Nevertheless, there are three types [of such officials].
That which is obtained as a reward is like a military merit; it exists naturally through hereditary succession.
That which is obtained through cultivation is that which depends on human effort and conditions—precisely what the ancients detested as "not following the Way.

That which is obtained through realization is when the Way is brightened and virtue is established, such that rank follows of its own accord. This is what Confucius meant when he said, "In learning, one's emolument is contained therein. This is it.
Third, their superiority or inferiority can be known.
Among those who were great and noble persons in the world, many have come from the practice of cultivation; yet there are three grades. The first is those who maintain the precepts.

If one cultivates merit while maintaining mindfulness of *prajñā* and right wisdom at all times, then even if one is born in a high position in a future life where the five desires are fully present, the mind will remain constantly within the Way;

this is truly what is meant by being a "shaven-headed monk. Second, if one maintains the precepts and cultivates merit but the mindfulness of *prajñā* becomes somewhat lax, then in a future life one will merely engage in the playful gates of the Dharma (*dharmamukha*). Third, [if one lacks both, one will fall into the realms of suffering].
If one upholds the precepts and cultivates merit, yet remains far removed from mindfulness of *prajñā*, then in a future life they will be deluded by favorable conditions;

turning their back on the good and following evil, there are even those who slander the Buddha, destroy the Dharma, and extinguish the Sangha. When investigating the causal ground of such individuals, they were originally no different from other practitioners of the Way;
yet the disparity between them is so vast. As they pass from one future life to the next, this disparity will only increase further.
"How is it? It makes one's heart tremble with cold!
I recall from long ago, when I was a youth, playing and debating with other youths, saying: 'At the very limits of heaven and earth, one should create...'"
"What is its form? Is it about to become empty? If it is all merely the great void, then where does this emptiness itself abide?
Or is it to become solid like a wall? If it is to become solid, then where does this solidity itself abide? The youths could not respond;
they laughed and desisted, yet for me, a lingering sense of obstruction remained within my breast. This is what is referred to in the *Shanhai jing* as "the east and west facing one another."
It is two hundred million *li* away; from north to south, it spans one hundred and fifty thousand *li*. My knowledge rests upon but one corner, truly like a view through a narrow tube.
Later, upon reading the Buddhist scriptures (*neidian*), I reached the point where it says "empty space is inexhaustible" and "worlds are inexhaustible.
Only then did my mind become vastly expanded. I concluded that none but a Buddha could have articulated this. Alas! This is not something easily spoken of.

"The mind is not within" refers to the investigation of the mind in the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*. To say that the mind is not within points to the true mind (*tathatā-citta*). If one were referring to the deluded mind of conceptualization (*vikalpa*), one could indeed say it is within.
This meaning is subtle and profound; it is not easily explained to those who do not understand it. A worldly text says: "The mind is hidden."
"God. "God" is merely another name for deluded thought (*vikalpa*). What is referred to as the "mind" is simply what we call the physical heart-mass.

When scholars of doctrine hear my words, they shake their heads in disbelief. Now, let me clarify this through actual experience. When a person is fast asleep, if one playfully presses an object against their chest, they will have a nightmare;
or if they accidentally cover their own chest with their hand, they likewise have a nightmare. Furthermore, if one playfully paints on the face of a sleeping person...
There are those who die from nightmares; this is clear evidence of what exists within. The scholar of doctrine says: "If this is so, then the Real and the False become two distinct entities.
I say: You merely know that the Real and the False are non-dual, but you do not know that while the Real and the False are one, they are eternally two.
These two are always one. Have you not observed water and ice? Water and ice are not two; who does not know this?
Yet, once water has become ice, the water flows and moves without a fixed direction, while the ice solidifies and remains in a constant place.

That which is real is without direction, while that which is delusory has a location; it is just like this. Delusion arises from the Real, yet there is no reality outside of delusion—just as ice forms from water.
Outside of ice there is no water; therefore, its substance is always one while its functions are always two. The scholars of doctrine said: "This is merely your own speculative view;

it ultimately contradicts the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*. It may be acceptable if you have a scriptural basis. [The author] replied: "I do have a basis. The basis is found in the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* itself; it is simply that you gentlemen have failed to examine it. The Sūtra says:
'When deluded once, they take this as their mind and are certain to be confused about it being within the physical body. Even though it is within the physical body..."

While being within [the body], it does not hinder its essence from pervading the ten directions; at the very moment it pervades the ten directions, it does not hinder its presence within the current body.
This meaning can only be realized once delusive thoughts are completely shattered. Both you and I still remain within the midst of delusive thoughts;
let us cease this entanglement for now.

The "Poem on the Metaphor of Leaving the Valley" describes a bird as emerging from a deep valley and migrating to a lofty tree; this is a discourse on distinguishing right from wrong and exercising caution in what to adopt and what to reject.
Formerly, when Deshan composed his *Qinglong Chao*, he initially believed that one must undergo cultivation for three great kalpas before attaining Buddhahood. However—
The son of Māra from the south claimed that he had already attained complete enlightenment and said, "I shall go to destroy his lineage to repay the Buddha's kindness.
At that time, a single piece of sincere and good-hearted resolve burned within him, yet he alone did not realize the error of his own vision.
It was only when he received instruction from the old woman and personally visited Longtan that what he had cherished for years...
What was once highly prized, he discarded like withered grass; thus, he was able to ultimately become a great vessel, bringing brilliance to the Dharma of the Final Age.

Had he instead remained stagnant in his preconceived views and been arrogant in his self-regard—like a pauper who treasures a "swallow-stone" (a counterfeit gem) and instead reviles the merchant from whom it was purchased—[he would have failed].
This refers to being envious of one's own treasures. Though one may possess a hundred wives and a thousand dragon pools, what can one do with them?

[The story of] the ball of cake used to deceive the child recalls a time at home: once, when a son asked for noodle soup late in the evening, the market gates had already closed, and the family members were unable to provide it.
He gave him a rice ball, but the child cried and paid no heed. His mother was greatly vexed. I said, "This is a simple matter. I took the rice ball and flattened it;

as soon as it reached the child's hand, he broke into a silent laugh. At that time, people remarked that the child was so easily deceived; from this, one may know that those who today slight the Pure Land while valuing the Chan school are similar to this.
When told that the rice balls were *tangbing* (noodle cakes) from the Pure Land, he cried; yet when the same thing was changed [into a flat cake], he laughed.
To wrap rice in a flat pancake—this is what the Chan school laughs at. How is this any different from the views of a child? Alas!
Those who crave fame know the harm of craving profit, yet they do not realize that the harm of craving fame is even more severe; for this reason, they remain unaware.
The harm of profit is coarse and easy to see; the harm of fame is subtle and difficult to perceive.
Thus, those who possess even a slight degree of self-refinement are able to disregard profit; yet as for fame, even the great sages and those of great wisdom cannot avoid it.

Desiring to establish a reputation, one will deliberately cultivate eccentric conduct; desiring to preserve a reputation, one will craftily devise schemes of concealment. Throughout one's entire life...
One has no leisure to be busily occupied with fame; how then can one find the leisure to cultivate the body and mind?
Long ago, an elderly master remarked, sighing deeply, that there is no one in the world who does not cherish fame. A person in the assembly rose and said, "It is truly as Your Reverence has stated;
you alone are the one who does not cherish fame. The elderly master was delighted and laughed heartily.
One realizes that one has been betrayed by those one knew best. How difficult it is to break through the barrier of fame! It is truly like this.
Observe those in this busy world who have already settled their household affairs; on the final day of the year, they sit at ease and watch the labor of the poor.
To labor for the sake of food and clothing is called "watching the busy. In this world, there are those who have already secured their official titles;
on the day of the great examination, they sit at ease watching the scholars labor busily in their pursuit of advancement—this too is called "watching the busy.

Yet one does not say that there are those in the world whose delusions are shattered and wisdom perfected, who have completed what was to be done, and who sit at ease watching the multitudes of the six realms.
That sentient beings toil incessantly within the cycle of birth and death—is this not what is called "watching the busy"? Alas! The entire world is caught in busyness;
who is there to watch this busyness? An ancient said, "The old monk has his own method of peace and leisure. Is this method of peace and leisure easy to speak of?
Nevertheless, when people of the world watch the busy with a sense of leisure, they harbor a mind of self-congratulation and lack compassion for others.

The mind. When a Bodhisattva perceives the world as being in turmoil, they give rise to a heart of great compassion to universally awaken the deluded masses, hoping that all may together attain liberation.
Thus, these two states of mind are vastly different; this is why there is a distinction between the ordinary and the sagely, and between the small and the great.

Regarding "words devoid of meaning" in the responses of the Gateless Barrier (Wumenguan): what are called words devoid of meaning cannot be reconciled through logic, nor can they be comprehended through discursive thought.
If later generations use their conceptualizing minds to forcefully impose logic upon them, then the more they speak, the further they stray.
Far removed! This is not merely a mistaken explanation; even if one were to explain it perfectly, it would still be nothing more than a parrot mimicking human speech.
Elder Yuanwu said: "If you simply exhaust all conceptual consciousness, intellectual understanding, and every delusive thought, you will naturally comprehend it here.
This is a method already proven by the former masters; it is certainly no empty talk. It is something we, as practitioners, ought to [embrace].
This refers to one who practices with deep faith and vigor.
It is precisely for those who have attained awakening that rebirth in the Pure Land is appropriate.

Someone once asked: "I, so-and-so, have been practicing the Pure Land method. A Zen practitioner said to me, 'Simply awaken to your own Buddha-nature and that is enough; why must you [seek rebirth]? "
To seek another Buddha externally and vow to be reborn there—what is the intent behind this?
I say that while this is indeed the supreme instruction, adhering to it can also lead to error. Please allow me to clarify this through an analogy.

Suppose there were a person whose brilliance and insight equaled that of Yan Hui, yet several hundred or even a thousand *li* away, there was a sage like Confucius who was propagating the Way. Seven...

There are ten sons and three thousand worthies who move about together. You have heard their names; if you were to go and see them, it is not certain that you would not find even greater strengths within yourself.
Yet, relying on your own keen intelligence, you refuse to pay them a visit—is this proper? Nevertheless, you may well attain awakening.
"I do not wish to be reborn there. I venture to say that you, elder brother, have not yet attained awakening. Why? If Heaven were to speak, it would say: "You have merely not yet awakened;
if you awaken, then your birth in the Pure Land shall be such that ten thousand oxen could not pull you back. How profound these words are!
Those who follow teachers and ancient sages have not yet fully realized the fundamental nature of the mind; thus, they travel thousands of miles to seek masters and inquire after the Way.

Once they have found a true teacher, they cast aside their staffs and hang up their alms-bowls. By remaining in close attendance for a long time, they become like Ānanda, who served throughout his entire life.
The Buddha. Subsequently, as for the various worthies of successive generations who studied under masters for long periods, it would not be easy to enumerate them all.
Take, for example, two venerable elders under the old man Ciming: one, Yangqi, assisted him until the end of his life; the other, Qing Su, served him for thirteen years.
Thus, consulting in the morning and being instructed in the evening, their ears were filled and their hearts saturated with the teaching, until they finally attained the Way.
One becomes a great vessel; yet I left the household life late, and my physical strength was frail and weak, such that my vital energy did not assist my resolve.
When my former teacher ordained me, we parted ways immediately as I set out on a pilgrimage beyond the mundane world. At every place I reached, circumstances often obstructed my opportunities.

Or perhaps due to the vicissitudes of illness, I have merely remained stationary; thus it has come to this day that I am white-haired and ignorant, harboring my folly and clinging to my rustic simplicity.

Alas! I could not serve as a messenger boy among the many scholars gathered at the Apricot Terrace or the Si River, but instead must act as a tutor in a village of three households—how deeply lamentable!
Among a thousand monks, there was not a single patch-robed disciple.
Master Jing of Longxing was known by the Great Master Xuefeng, who prophesied of him, saying:

"In the future, when you serve as abbot, among the thousand monks under your seat, there will not be a single patch-robed disciple. Later, Jing accepted the invitation of the Prince of Qian to serve as abbot of Longxing; indeed, it came to pass.
The assembly numbered over a thousand, yet they were all merely disciples who had memorized and recited the Tripitaka, exactly as Jing had predicted.
In the past, when Master Mazu gained so many followers, those who became great vessels reached eighty-eight in number.
Jing left Master Mazu not long ago, yet disciples as rare as these are hardly seen even once among a thousand; how much more so in the present day? People—
If the ten wholesome deeds are absent for even a moment, the celestial realms will decline; if there are no patch-robed monks within the Sangha, the seed of the Buddha will be severed.
Lately, I have not even known what a "patch-robed monk" is. The path of the Dharma stands solitary and alone, like a thread about to snap. How tragic!
On one's birthday, people of the world hold banquets, arrange musical performances, display paintings, and compete in poetic compositions, taking these as their pleasures.
Only Emperor Wen of the Tang did not do so; this may be called transcending ordinary sentiment. Some say that on this day, he did not celebrate.
"If one joyfully recites the sutras, performs repentance rites, and cultivates various meritorious deeds, how would that be? He replied, "Truly excellent.

If one wishes to repay the kindness of one's parents for their toil in giving birth and raising one, and to extinguish the karmic actions performed throughout one’s own life, one should indeed devote oneself to these matters here.
However, this is the secondary; it is not the primary. As the former masters have said: 'Before the parents were yet born, who was it?'"
This is your original face. On this day, is there anyone capable of observing with right mindfulness that face prior to birth, rather than for the sake of pleasure?

If you attain a vast and clear realization herein, then not only will you repay the kindness of the parents of this present body, but the kindness of all relatives throughout countless kalpas will be repaid;
not only will you extinguish the karma of this current life, but [the karma of many lifetimes...]
The karmic obstacles of his past lives were entirely extinguished. Having relinquished the pleasures of the human world, he attained the bliss of Nirvana.
How filial such a person is! How magnificent such a person is!
The doctrine of "closing the gates" while still young has no precedent in antiquity; it arose only in later generations. While it may serve to nourish the Way, it is not the means for creating it.
Furthermore, even those who have already given rise to the great Bodhicitta must still cross oceans and climb mountains, braving the winds and waves.

"Amidst the frost across a hundred prefectures, those who do not accord with even a single word of another will surely pack their bags and don their straw hats to tread upon clouds and waters across a thousand mountains.
For eighty years on pilgrimage, they drive themselves forward in old age; ascending eight times and climbing three times, they never tire of diligent toil.
Who are you that sits idly in a single room? When others come to consult me, do I not seek them out? Formerly, Gao Feng sat...
As for the matter of Zhanggong Cave: there, one builds houses upon the cliffs, suspended in mid-air like birds in their nests. Few people have ever beheld such a place;
it is a state realized only after attaining great enlightenment. If one seeks comfort and security, sealing oneself away for personal ease, this is not it.
This is absolutely impermissible.

As for the matter of monastics keeping servants—where monks possess servants to provide them with service and errands—for one who has left the household life, having disciples to serve them is permissible; why [should this be forbidden]?
He employed his servants [as attendants]. Some say: "The disciples came to seek the Way; they are not people meant for manual labor. Alas!
When the Master visited various states, on one occasion he said, "Ran You is my charioteer," and on another, "Fan Chi is driving.
When Yuanming (Tao Qian) responded to the summons of a friend, one of his students and two sons carried his wicker sedan chair. Later generations depicted and painted these scenes.

They consider this to be a mark of lofty attainment. Yet now, those who have left the household life to become monks treat their disciples with such favoritism as if they were the children of wealthy and noble families, while separately purchasing servants with money to provide cooking, carry firewood, hold umbrellas, and wield staves. Has the corruption of the Final Dharma reached such a state?
Time cannot be spent in vain;
it is the place where worldly people are deeply attached. Without ceasing day or night, they say: "The day is short and suffering is great; the night is long—why not take up a candle and roam?"
To indulge in aesthetic appreciation. "In a hundred years there are thirty-six thousand days; each day one must drain three hundred cups"—this is to indulge in malted liquor.

"The rustic guest finishes his verse by the lamp at midnight"—this is to indulge in poetry and prose. "Throughout the long summer, nothing but a single game of chess can pass the time"—this is to indulge in the game of Go.
They are addicted to gambling and games. There is an ancient, enlightened instruction that says: "As each day passes, one's life span is likewise diminished;

one should exert oneself with diligence, as if putting out a fire on one's own head. Now, while those among the ordained who are addicted to fermented grains and spirits are certainly few, they may still not have avoided these three aforementioned matters.
To let such precious time slip away in vain—how deeply regrettable this is!
"One miss is a hundred misses," as the ancients said: "If one does not practice in this life, one miss is a hundred misses. From one to a hundred—how many misses there are!
It reaches this very point. As the Sūtra says: "It is difficult to leave the evil realms and obtain a human body; it is difficult for a person to be born and encounter the Buddha-dharma."

Nevertheless, to encounter the Dharma-gate of Buddha-remembrance and receive it with faith is even more difficult. As stated in the sutras, an ant has not shed its ant-body since the time of the seven Buddhas;

how can one know on what day it will obtain a human body, on what day it will encounter the Buddha-Dharma, or on what day it will encounter the Dharma-gate of Buddha-remembrance and receive it with faith? It is not merely a hundred missed opportunities—it is indeed a thousand.
Ten thousand errors lead to no end. How tragic!

Regarding the cultivation of merit, there is an ancient verse: "If one cultivates wisdom but does not cultivate merit, the Arhat’s offerings will be meager; if one cultivates merit but does not cultivate wisdom, [one is like] an elephant’s body..."

They hang jeweled necklaces. There are those who focus exclusively on the first two lines [of the verse], busying themselves all day long solely in diligent solicitation for alms, saying, "I am making a Buddha," "I am building a hall," or "I am providing a vegetarian feast for the Sangha. Although these are indeed all gateways to the myriad practices, [they are incomplete].
There are two arguments for this. First, cause and effect must be clearly distinguished. Second, one’s own affairs must be settled first. Someone might say:
"If it were as you say, then Buddhist images would vanish; who would restore them? Stupas and monasteries would crumble;
who would rebuild them? Monks would starve on the roads, unable to find food; who would save them? Person after person...
"Only attend to your own affairs, and the Three Jewels will fall into ruin. He replied, "Not so. My concern is only that the Three Jewels in their essential unity may fall into ruin.

As for the worldly Three Jewels, since the Buddha-dharma entered China, those who have fashioned Buddha images, constructed halls, and provided offerings to the Sangha have done so constantly without ceasing, with such sites appearing everywhere. Why trouble yourself with private worries and excessive anxieties? I—"
I am deeply grieved for those monastics who manage temple affairs; they are ignorant of causes and effects, have no fear of sin or merit, and—
let alone those who embezzle permanent assets or misappropriate offerings from the faithful— even those monastics who merely maintain their assigned duties and are unacquainted with the Vinaya,

thinking only that as long as they do not personally divert funds into their own pockets, they are fine, will then shift resources from the east to the west or substitute item A for item B, or perhaps...
They rush to repay debts or send offerings to lay families, unaware that the money for bricks should be used to buy tiles and the monastic provisions should be used to build halls.

Thus they undergo toil in vain, which instead results in an evil retribution; while heaven has not yet been established, hell is already formed. This is what is meant by "suffering calamity without merit.
Grand Master Zhongfeng instructed the assembly, saying: "Take single-mindedness as the foundation, and the myriad practices will naturally follow."

This follows next: namely, that one’s own primary task must first be accomplished. Once one’s own task is accomplished, when one performs acts of merit, then whatever is done will naturally be appropriate.
How profound these words are! Those who are monks should engrave them upon the very core of their hearts.

The Great Mirror, the Greatly Penetrating Chan Master Dajian Huineng, is what the world calls the Southern School; the Greatly Penetrating Chan Master Daosheng is what the world calls the Northern School.

Yet, although the robe and bowl of Huangmei were not transmitted to Daosheng—who [taught] "constantly wipe away [dust]"—they were instead transmitted solely to Huineng, who [taught] that "originally there is not a single thing."

The Great Mirror of All Things. Why does the *Zongjing Lu* (Record of the Mirror of the Source) say that Dajian [Huineng] possessed only one eye, whereas Datong [Shenxiu] had both eyes perfectly clear?
If this is indeed true, why did he not receive the robe and bowl? Now, Caoqi personally received the lineage from Huangmei;
Huangmei inherited it from Bodhidharma; Bodhidharma inherited it from Kāśyapa; and Kāśyapa inherited it from Śākyamuni. Thus, Yongming transmitted the Way.
Regarding the fact that National Teacher Yao of Tiantai made this statement: why was it so? It was, in fact, a teaching intended to remedy the defects of the times.

An ancient said that since the Jin and Song dynasties, people had vied with one another to exalt meditative contemplation (*dhyāna-vipaśyanā*), no longer understanding the principle of "directly pointing to the human mind to see one's nature and become a Buddha.
Therefore, the First Patriarch came from the West; yet by the time of Yongming, there were again those who— [text continues] —or...

Because awakening once brings immediate understanding, texts such as the *Zongjing* (Mirror of the Source) and the *Wanshan tonggui* (The Ten Thousand Good Deeds Return to One Source) vigorously praise the practice of cultivation.

This suggests that while the Southern School focuses exclusively on sudden awakening, the Northern School maintains both sudden awakening and gradual cultivation, thus possessing both wisdom and practice.
Hence, there is the metaphor of the "single eye" versus the "two eyes. The Elder Wansong alone took up his brush and declared: "This single eye is..."
This is called the single eye of the śramaṇa throughout the entire earth. This is called the eye that grips heaven and earth.

This is called the Vajra-eye at the crown of the head. If those of the new school and those with shallow views cling to what is said in the *Zongjing* (Mirror of the Source) and take it to be substantial dharmas, then Dajian [Huineng] would merely be the truth of emptiness, while Datong [Fayan] would only then be...
"Is it not so that the Middle Way, the Ultimate Truth, is the foremost? Someone asked: 'The transmission of the robe through six generations at Caoxi is something the entire world knows;

yet at that time, why was it that only the Dharma Masters of the two capitals and the Gate Teachers of the two Emperors were seen, while the Northern School was widely renowned throughout the land, and Caoxi was not?
What is the reason for this? I replied: 'Since Caoxi had already received the seal of transmission...'"
Record: He kept his robe and alms bowl secret, acting as a hunter guarding a net, concealing his brilliance and hiding his splendor for eighteen years.

It was only when the Way of Great Penetration flourished that the name of Caoxi became manifest. Upon the dialogue regarding the wind and the banner, his Way was then disseminated for ten thousand generations.
While the Dragon of Caoxi remained hidden in the deep abyss and did not seek self-display, the Dragon of Great Penetration appeared.
Tian did not consider himself full or complete. He said, "He is one who has personally transmitted my teacher’s robe and bowl.
Such is the manner in which spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra) assist one another to achieve success.
A verse in four sections of admonition for practice:

If one performs meritorious deeds but does not recite the Buddha’s name, when the merit is exhausted, one will sink back into the cycle of rebirth. If one recites the Buddha’s name but does not perform meritorious deeds, there will be much bitterness and hardship on the path to enlightenment.

Those without merit do not practice mindfulness of the Buddha; they belong to the multitudes of hell-dwellers, hungry ghosts, and animals. By practicing mindfulness of the Buddha while simultaneously cultivating merit, one shall later realize the state of the Honored One with Two Feet.

It is shown that the various positions [of suffering] arise from the body, and the body arises from karma. By not creating further karma, misfortune is extinguished and merit increases. Thus, practice mindfulness of the Buddha in this Sahā world.
The name "Ultimate Bliss" is established; with single-mindedness and without distraction, one ascends to the highest stage of practice.

As for Xingling, who addressed the assembly of deaf, mute, and deluded monks—his name was Xingling—the good and evil of this world are not worth evaluating, nor are its rights and wrongs, or its merits and defects.
Why must one insist on making distinctions? By not speaking of this, the gate of calamity is closed; by not listening to this, the gate of slander is blocked;

by not doubting this, the gate of faith is perfected. If people can learn from me, ten thousand calamities shall not invade them. Furthermore, if they apply themselves with diligence, [they shall attain liberation].
The Noble Path can be realized.
In seeking the characters for a verse on the Great Text of the Sangha, there is no name outside [of this].
Within the ten thousand phenomena contained in emptiness, emptiness alone is great. Emptiness resides within my own mind, yet it is as minute as a single mustard seed. How vast is the mind!
With whom could there be any correspondence? Because there is no correspondence, there is no exterior.

It is shown that for all things, birth must be followed by death; how can length and brevity be worth discussing? Now that I have attained the marks of a perfect monk, the vows of my entire life are fulfilled.
You should give rise to great joy; by no means harbor grief or distress. Let go of all external conditions and, with single-minded devotion, recite the Buddha’s name.

Focus your thoughts on the Land of Ultimate Bliss, where you shall be born upon a lotus of the highest grade. There, seeing the Buddha, you will awaken to non-arising and return to deliver all beings.
Addressing the Assembly on New Year’s Day:
Today we celebrate the New Year; the seasons have changed once again. But what was it like yesterday? On the twenty-eighth day of the twelfth month.
Lodging at Jizō-in.
In the city of Jining, at the Dizang Monastery, one can still faintly hear the sound of great vows being made. Skillful Chan practitioners return home with empty bowls;
the foolish Daoist sells his robes to buy flour. You who eat the noodles—do not swallow them in haste; take care of the piece of stone within your breast.
A monk who had returned to lay life shaved his head once more and entered Lingyin Monastery;

within a few years, the Buddha hall was overgrown with weeds. In a single instant, the demonic palace was struck with awe and solemnity. This was not a newly established scale, but rather the original face as it has always been.

The mice squeak; the Avataṃsaka is clearly manifest. How extraordinary, Minister Wang! You have been deluded by a beast.
A cat suddenly emerges before the painted hall; at the head of the bed, he preaches the Dharma with no further news.
No further news. The Mahāvaipulya Buddhāvataṃsaka Sūtra, Chapter One: The Sublime Array of World Rulers.
Picking bracken, I sigh;

the Master of Yunqi loves to eat it. The patched-robed disciples gather it together before the mountain. Having returned and finished eating, he sits with his feet washed and speaks earnestly, calling me to discuss the secret of the mind.
What need is there to wait for me to speak this secret of the mind? I have already missed the fine opportunity before the mountain.
The season. Ferns. Ferns. He raises his fist toward you and speaks.
Release the snail;
it will coil itself up, deep and dense. When leaving the gate, it drags water and mud; when closing the door, its traces vanish.
Traces have vanished; I narrowly escaped being refined by the Jade Cauldron and nearly was pierced by the Golden Needle.

Now returning once more to the surging waves, I only pray that I may forever leave behind the entanglements of the net. Do not disdain my slender limbs, nor take offense at the cramped corridors and rooms.
If you know that Perfect Enlightenment serves as the monastery, then what lies before your eyes is none other than the Vajra Cave.
To Layman Shen, who saw Heng fifty years ago:
It is as if one were to paint a form without knowing the face; One seeks to take "non-seeing" as profound cultivation.
A wild fox falsely manifests the golden fur of a lion. I pray you will rely on the Master’s words of truth, Maintaining a sincere heart in every thought.
Unchanging. One day, suddenly awakening to Śūraṅgama Samādhi, when seeing the Seer, it is not "seeing.
I append this verse here to admonish against idle talk and urge you onto the white ox-cart.
A ruler-measure of wood lies across your face; the eye at the crown of your head blazes wide open. True seeing manifests at every moment.
A thousand leagues and ten thousand more—throughout eternal kalpas, how could it ever change? After all, what is this that comes?
A dark-faced barbarian monk sits by the wall; seeing thus, not a single thing exists.
The great sound is a rare silence, like the profound stillness of an empty valley. A single call echoes throughout the ten directions; the thunder is silent.
A single roll of the drum shakes and awakens a hundred li. As for the spring birds crying by day and the autumn insects chirping by night, they merely multiply their sounds.
It is merely a small sound. Therefore, the World-Honored One remained silent for a long while, yet the heterodox practitioner claimed that his clouds of delusion had been dispelled.

Having already selected and carved the recorded sayings (*yulu*) of Chan masters such as Sengzhao and others, during my leisure moments in the long summer, I desired to peruse in their entirety the exhortations and clarifications of the ancient worthies of successive dynasties, recording those whose teachings were most sincere and authentic for the sake of others. There was no time to spare. Among my ministers and officials, there were none with the visual acuity of Zen monks capable of discerning the difference between the waters of the Zhi and the Mien rivers.
Finding no such person, there was no one who could be appointed to divide the labor of translation and present the works for my imperial perusal.

Having no other recourse, I have therefore selected certain passages from the two books: *The Treasury of the True Dharma Eye* compiled by Miaoxi and *The Record of Pointing at the Moon* carved by Huanji.

Thus, these *gong'an* were presented for the instruction of future students. Indeed, the two works—the *Zhengfayan zang* (The Treasury of the True Dharma Eye) and the *Zhiyuelu* (Record of Pointing at the Moon)—have circulated throughout the land for several hundred years.
From the forty-seven patriarchs of India to the twenty-three [patriarchs] of China, there is not a single word from the Buddhas and ancestral masters that lacks profound meaning.

To this day, throughout the entire realm of Jambudvīpa, from desolate mountains and ancient monasteries to vast hermitages for Chan practice, where staffs and meditation cushions stand and sons of the Śākya lineage dwell, all have been able to unroll and behold [this teaching], and to hear its proclamation. The merit of Miaoxi’s illusory sojourn is indeed indelible;
yet, it is a pity that none have yet attained the eye that penetrates the barrier, which is why he has now taken up and expounded upon it.
Having already lost the advantage for oneself, one is like snow amidst flour or ink within soot; how could one possibly distinguish them with accuracy?
To cast away gold to take up rubble, or to prize a fish-eye gem while discarding a *maṇi* jewel—such errors are certainly unavoidable.

Therefore, beyond the *Zhengfayan zang* (Treasury of the Eye of the True Dharma) and the *Zhiyuelu* (Record of Pointing at the Moon), there still remains the Essential Pivot of the True Body and the Miraculous Mirror of Genuine Radiance, which shall now be opened.
As for the *Shizhigui* (Pointing Out the Goal) and the *Biyi Moshai* (Benefiting the Final Age), as they have not yet passed before My eyes, there is nothing that can be done.
Within these two works, however, you may confidently choose one or the other without omitting anything; those with clear vision will naturally be able to discern and select between them.

The sayings and phrases collected within this volume are not like those selected by Miaoxi or Huanji, who merely prized the novelty of their phrasing and the agility of their *jīfēng* (critical pivot).
They did not consider whether these words had any connection to the fundamental ground of the mind; they focused exclusively on pointing toward the "upward" direction.
While these were indeed highly esteemed by people of the time and widely circulated among the common folk, they were truly not [the ultimate teaching].

The First Patriarch, Great Master Bodhidharma, received the Dharma from Venerable Prajñātāra and propagated its transformation in his own country. At that time, there were two masters; one was named...
The first was Buddhadasa; the second was named Buddhasanta. Buddhadasa encountered the Venerable Prajñātāra, whereupon he abandoned the Hinayana and turned toward the Mahayana.
Together with his master, he transformed beings, and they were known at that time as the "Two Gates of Ambrosia. Furthermore, Buddhasanta divided his followers into six schools:
first, the School of Characteristics (*Lakṣaṇavāda*); second, the School of Non-characteristics (*Alakṣaṇavāda*); third, the School of Samādhi and Wisdom (*Samādhiprajñā*).

The first was the School of the True Principle; the second, the School of the Non-Being; the third, the School of the Emptiness of All Dharmas; the fourth, the School of Preceptual Practice; the fifth, the School of Non-Attainment; and the sixth, the School of Quiescence.

Each clung to their own understanding and separately expanded their sources of conversion. The Patriarch sighed deeply and said, "If even one of those teachers has already fallen into the tracks of an ox, how much more so for these who have fragmented [the truth] into six schools?
If I do not eliminate this, they will remain forever entangled in false views. Having spoken, he subtly manifested his supernatural powers and arrived at—
In the school of the Sarvāstivādins (the School of Characteristics), it was asked: "What is called the 'true mark' (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) of all dharmas?
A venerable elder named Sarvaloka among that assembly replied: "Among all marks, not mutually [confusing] the various marks—this is called the true mark. The Patriarch said:
"Regarding all characteristics, if they do not mutually correspond, and if one were to call them 'true reality' (bhūtalakṣaṇa), how could they be fixed? He replied:
'Among all characteristics, there is truly no fixedness. If characteristics were fixed, how could they be called true? The Patriarch said: 'All characteristics are not fixed.'"

"This is precisely what is called the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). You are currently not fixed; how then can you attain it? He replied, "My statement that I am 'not fixed' does not refer to various marks;
rather, it is precisely to speak of various marks, and its meaning is likewise so. The Patriarch said, "Your statement that you are 'not fixed' shall itself become the true mark."

"Because it is fixed and not fixed, it is not the true mark (dharmatā). He replied, "Since what is fixed is not fixed, it is not the true mark; because one knows that 'I' does not exist, it is neither fixed nor changing.
The Patriarch said, "If you are now unchanging, how can you be called the true mark? That which has already changed and passed away is no longer present."
The meaning is likewise. He said, "The unchanging must exist; because it both exists and does not exist, the changing is the true mark (*dharmatā*), which thereby establishes its meaning.
The Patriarch said, "If the true mark is unchanging, then that which changes is not the true mark. Within the realm of existence and non-existence, how can it be called the true mark?"

Sāvala, knowing in his heart that the Holy Master possessed profound and hidden understanding, pointed with his finger at empty space and said, "This is a conditioned phenomenon of the world, yet it can also be made empty.
Can my body become like this? The Patriarch replied, "If you understand the true mark (*dharmatā*), you will see that which is not a mark.
If you realize that which is not a mark, its form is likewise so. You must not lose yourself within form."

"The substance of form is not obstructed by existence within the signless; if one can understand it thus, this is called the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). When the assembly heard this, their minds became clear and bright; they paid homage with reverence and accepted it with faith.

The Patriarch suddenly vanished from sight and went to the school of the Signless (*animitta-vāda*), where he asked: "You speak of the signless; how do you realize it? Among the assembly there was one named Pratītya who replied: The substance of form is not obstructed by existence within the signless; if one can understand it thus, this is called the true mark. When the assembly heard this, their minds became clear and bright; they paid homage with reverence and accepted it with faith.

The Patriarch suddenly vanished from sight and went to the school of the Signless, where he asked: "You speak of the signless; how do you realize it? Among the assembly there was one named Pratītya who replied:
He said, "I clarify formlessness because the mind does not manifest. The Patriarch said, "If your mind does not manifest, what is it that you clarify?
He replied, "I clarify formlessness; the mind neither grasps nor rejects. At the very time of clarification, there is also no one who clarifies.

The Patriarch said, "If the mind neither grasps nor rejects existence or non-existence, and there is furthermore no one who clarifies, then all clarifications are absent. He replied, "One enters the Buddha’s three..."

[The Master] said, "If even samādhi cannot be attained, how much less can one know the signless (animitta)? The Patriarch said, "Since you do not know the sign, who speaks of existence or non-existence?
If there is nothing to be attained, what is it that you call samādhi? He replied, "I speak of non-realization; realization is that wherein there is nothing to be realized.
Because it is not [ordinary] samādhi, I call it samādhi. The Patriarch said, "That which is not samādhi—how could it be given a name? You..."
"Since you have not realized it, what is there to realize that was not already realized? Upon hearing the Patriarch’s analysis, Boluoti immediately awakened to his original mind.
He prostrated in gratitude to the Patriarch and repented for his past errors. The Patriarch prophesied: "You shall attain the fruit;

you will realize it before long. There is a demon in this land whom you must subdue. Having spoken, he suddenly vanished. Boluoti then went to the abode of Dinghui Zong and asked: "What do you study?"
"Are concentration and wisdom one or two? A man named Bharanda among the assembly replied, "This concentration and wisdom of mine are neither one nor two.
The Patriarch said, "If they are neither one nor two, why are they called concentration and wisdom? He replied, "In concentration, it is not concentration."
"Abiding in wisdom is not wisdom. One is not one; two is also not two. The Patriarch said: "When it is one, it is not one; when it is two, it is not two.
Since it is neither fixed wisdom nor insight, by what means can it be defined as wisdom or insight? He replied: "Neither one nor two—this is what fixed wisdom and insight are able to know."
"It is the same for non-concentration and non-wisdom. The Patriarch said, "Because wisdom is not concentration, how then can one know it?
It is neither one nor two; what is concentration and what is wisdom? Upon hearing this, Vairocana’s doubts were completely dispelled.

He then went to the abode of the fourth master, Śīlabhadra, and asked, "What is called 'precept' (śīla)? What is called 'practice' (caryā)? In relation to these precepts and practices, are they one or are they two?"
Among that assembly, there was a worthy man who replied: "One and two, two and one—these are all produced from them; by relying on the teachings, one remains untainted.

This is called the practice of precepts. The Patriarch said: "Your statement that one 'relies on the teachings' implies there is still defilement. Both 'one' and 'two' are thus violated. How can you say you rely on the teachings?
These two are contradictory and do not reach the true practice. When what is internal and external is not clear, how can it be called precepts? He [the worthy man]...
The monk said, "I have 'inner' and 'outer,' yet he has already understood this to its conclusion. Having attained thorough penetration, this is itself the practice of precepts.

If one speaks of contrariety, then both 'is' and 'is not' are present; when speech reaches purity, it is both the precepts and the practice. The Patriarch said, "If both 'is' and 'is not' are present, how can you speak of purity?
Since thorough penetration has been attained, why discuss inner and outer? Upon hearing this, the worthy man immediately felt ashamed and submitted. This concludes the passage.
Regarding the school of Non-attainment (*wude*), a questioner asked: "You speak of non-attainment; how can there be attainment through non-attainment?

Since there is nothing attained, there is likewise no 'attainment-of-attainment'. Among that assembly was one named Baojing, who replied: "I speak of non-attainment, yet it is not the case that there is no attainment-of-non-attainment.

I shall explain the attainment-of-attainment: non-attainment is itself attainment. The Patriarch said: "If attainment is already non-attainment, then attainment is also non-attainment. You have already spoken of attainment..."
"Attainment. "What is attained by attainment? He replied, "Seeing attainment is non-attainment; non-attainment is attainment. If one sees non-attainment, it is called 'attaining attainment.
The Patriarch said, "Since attainment is non-attainment, attaining attainment is non-attainment. Since there is nothing to be attained, how can there be 'attaining attainment'?
Upon hearing this, Baojing was suddenly freed from the net of doubt. He went to Jijing’s dwelling and asked, "What is meant by 'quiescence'?"
"Within this Dharma, what is stillness and what is tranquility? A venerable one among the assembly replied, "That this mind does not move is called tranquility;
that it is unstained by phenomena is called stillness. The Patriarch said, "If the original mind were not already tranquil, it would require the cultivation of tranquility.
Since it is tranquil from the very beginning, what need is there for tranquility? The other asked, "All phenomena are originally empty; they are empty because of emptiness."
"Because it is empty within that emptiness, it is called 'quiescence'. The Patriarch said, "Emptiness is already empty; all dharmas are likewise so.
Quiescent and signless—what is there to be quiescent, what is there to be still? Upon hearing the Master’s instruction, Venerable Śānta attained sudden and complete enlightenment.

Thereupon, the six assemblies all vowed to take refuge in him. His transformation spread throughout Southern India, and his fame resounded across the Five Indias. For sixty years, he delivered immeasurable beings.

The assembly [listened]. Master [Hui]nian reflected that, according to the Buddha’s prophecy regarding the Eastern Land of Zhendan (China), during the final five hundred years, the lamp of Prajñā-wisdom would spread its light there.
He therefore entrusted his disciple Prajñāmitra to remain in India to transmit the Dharma, while he himself traveled to Zhendan. Thus...

He took leave of his ancestral stupa and bid farewell to his fellow students. Setting sail across the vast ocean, he reached the South Sea; this was the seventh year of the Putong era of the Liang dynasty, the year of Gengzi.
Xiao Ang, the Regional Inspector of Guangzhou, prepared formal ceremonies to welcome and provide for him, and submitted a memorial to Emperor Wu.

The Emperor dispatched an envoy bearing an imperial edict to invite him. In the tenth month, he arrived in Jinling. The Emperor asked him, "Since I ascended the throne, I have constructed monasteries and transcribed scriptures."

The Emperor said, "The number of monks you have ordained is beyond reckoning. What merit does this constitute? The Patriarch said, "There is no merit at all. The Emperor asked, "Why is there no merit?
The Patriarch said, "These are merely the minor fruits of the realms of humans and devas; they are causes subject to outflows (*āsrava*).

Like a shadow following a form, though they exist, they are not real. The Emperor asked, "What, then, is true merit? The Patriarch said, "Pure wisdom is wondrously perfect; its essence is itself empty."
Ji said, "Such merits as these are not sought through worldly means. The Emperor asked again, "What is the primary meaning of the Noble Truths?
The Patriarch replied, "Vast emptiness; there is no sage. The Emperor asked, "Who is it that faces me? The Patriarch replied, "I do not know. The Emperor did not attain awakening.
The Patriarch crossed north of the Yangtze River and took up residence at Shaolin Temple on Mount Song. He sat facing a wall, remaining silent all day long.
A monk named Shen Guang came to attend upon the Patriarch; however, as the Patriarch constantly sat upright facing the wall, no instructions were heard.
The Master stood in the snow until it reached his knees and severed his own arm to seek the Dharma. The Patriarch then changed his name to Huik’e. He asked: "The dharmas of all Buddhas..."
Huineng asked, "May I hear about this seal? The Patriarch said, "The Dharma-seal of all Buddhas is not obtained from another person.

Huineng said, "My mind is not yet at peace; I beg the Master to bring it to rest for me. The Patriarch said, "Bring forth your mind, and I will bring it to rest for you. After a long while, Huineng said, "I have searched for my mind, but it is utterly unobtainable.
The Patriarch said, "I have finished bringing your mind to rest for you. Nine years later, wishing to return to India, he looked back.
Huike then addressed him, saying: "In the past, the Tathāgata entrusted the Eye of the True Dharma to Mahākāśyapa. This great being passed it down through successive transmission until it reached me.
I now entrust it to you; you must protect and uphold it. I also grant you this cassock as a token of the Dharma.
Internally, I transmit the Seal of the Dharma to accord with and realize the mind; externally, I bestow the cassock to establish the fundamental tenet. Up to this point...

Two hundred years after my parinirvāṇa, the transmission of the robe will cease, while the Dharma will pervade the entire realm of saṃsāra. Those who clarify the Way will be many, but those who practice the Way will be few;
those who expound the principle will be many, but those who penetrate the principle will be few. There will be more than ten million who secretly correspond with and secretly realize [the truth].

You should propagate it and never underestimate those who have not yet awakened; in a single thought-moment, if they turn their faculties, they will be identical to the original attainment. Listen to my verse: "I am originally..."
He came to this land to transmit the Dharma and save those lost in delusion. One flower opens into five petals; the fruiting occurs naturally.
Once, a lay practitioner over forty years of age—whose name and lineage were not disclosed—came to pay his respects to the Second Patriarch, Master Huike, and asked the Patriarch:
The disciple said, "My body is afflicted by a wind ailment; I beg the Master to repent for my transgressions. The Patriarch said, "Bring forth your transgressions, and I shall repent for you.

The disciple remained silent for a long while and said, "I have searched for my transgressions, but they are utterly unfindable. The Patriarch said, "I have finished repenting for your transgressions. You should now abide in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha.
The disciple said, "Now that I see the Master, I already know what the Sangha is. But I do not yet understand what is meant by 'Buddha' and 'Dharma'. The Patriarch said:
"This mind is the Buddha; this mind is the Dharma. The Dharma and the Buddha are non-dual; so too is the Sangha Jewel.
The scholar said, "Today I have finally realized that the nature of sin is neither within, nor without, nor in between. It is just as this mind is: the Buddha-Dharma is non-dual.
The Patriarch held him in high esteem and immediately shaved his head, saying, "He is my treasure. He should be named Sengcan."
The Patriarch then entrusted him with the robe and the Dharma, saying in verse: "Originally, there was ground due to conditions; From the ground, flowers grew from seeds.
Originally, there were no seeds; Thus, flowers have never been born."

To the Layman: You dwell in seclusion within the forests and fields, eating from the trees and drinking from the mountain streams. At the beginning of the Tianbao era of the Northern Qi dynasty, hearing that your Master’s transformation of beings was flourishing, you sent him this letter:
"Shadows arise from forms; echoes follow sounds. To toy with shadows is to weary the form, yet one does not realize that the form is the root of the shadow.
To raise a sound is to produce an echo, yet one does not know that the sound is the source of the echo. To eliminate afflictions and seek Nirvana is like... [the analogy follows].
To seek a shadow by departing from form is like seeking the fruit of Buddhahood apart from sentient beings; it is analogous to seeking an echo while remaining silent.

Thus we know that delusion and awakening share a single path, and folly and wisdom are not distinct. Where there is no name, one creates a name; yet because one relies upon names, right and wrong arise.
To take what is irrational as rational, and because of that rationalization, disputes arise. Illusions are not real; who is right and who is wrong?
They are empty fabrications without substance; what is void and what exists? One should know that there is nothing gained in gain and nothing lost in loss.
