[The Master] said, “Power. He asked, “What is the meaning of coming from the West? The Master said, “Ask the pillar. [The student] said, “I do not understand. The Master said, “...”.
"I certainly would not," Daian replied.
Dongshan asked, "To say 'it exists' or 'it does not exist' are both slanders. Please, Master, eliminate them for me. The Master said, "There is not even a single thing. What is there to eliminate?
The Master then asked, "Close off your throat, lips, and mouth, and bring forth your words. Daian said, "I have none such."
The Master said, "If it is so, you have entered the gate.
Dowu asked, "What is the great meaning of the Buddha-dharma? The Master said, "One cannot but know it.
Dowu asked, "Is there any further turning beyond this? The Master said, "The vast sky does not obstruct the flying white clouds."
Question: "What is Chan? The Master said: "An ordinary brick. Question: "What is the Way? The Master said: "A piece of wood.
Because the Master was reading the *Zhao Lun* (Treatise by Sengzhao), he reached the passage: "Only the Sage can take the myriad things as himself. He then struck the table and said:
"The Sage has no self, yet there is nothing that is not his own self. The Dharma-body has no form; who would speak of self and other? It is the numinous round mirror."

Illuminating that which lies between them, the myriad phenomena manifest spontaneously within the profound mystery of their essence. Since object and wisdom are not two, who can speak of coming and going?

How sublime are these words! Thereupon, I closed the volume and fell asleep without realizing it. In a dream, I traveled with the Sixth Patriarch, riding upon a single tortoise as we swam within a deep pool.
Upon waking, I reflected: "The numinous tortoise is wisdom; the deep pool is the ocean of nature. I—"
Riding upon the same numinous wisdom as the Patriarch, he roamed the ocean of nature. He then composed the *Cantong qi* (The Mysterious Coincidence). Entering the hall, he said:
"My Dharma-gate is that transmitted by the Buddhas of the past. It does not concern itself with meditative concentration or diligent effort, but only with attaining the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
'Mind is Buddha'—mind, Buddha, and sentient beings; awakening, enlightenment, and afflictions—though their names differ, their substance is one. You all..."

You should know that the substance of one's own mind is free from annihilationism and eternalism; its nature is neither defiled nor pure. It is profoundly still and perfect, equal for both ordinary beings and sages.
Its applications are limitless and it transcends mind, intellect, and consciousness. The three realms and six paths are merely manifestations of one's own mind;
like the moon in water or an image in a mirror, how could they have arising or ceasing? If you can understand this, there will be nothing that is not fully prepared within you.
Chan Master Niaoke Daolin had an attendant named Huìtōng.
One day, wishing to take his leave, the Master asked him, "Where are you going now? He replied, "Huìtōng has left the household life for the sake of the Dharma.
Since the Master does not deign to grant me compassionate instruction, I am now going to various quarters to study the Buddha-dharma. The Master said:
[Daowu] said, "If this is the Buddha-dharma, we have a little of it here as well. [Daowu] asked, "What is the Master's Buddha-dharma?
The Master picked up some cloth-pelts from his robe and blew on them. Daotong thereupon attained realization of the profound principle.
Emperor Suzong asked National Teacher Huizhong of Nanyang, "What is the Tamer of the Ten Bodies? The Master rose and said, "Do you understand? The Emperor replied, "I do not understand.
The Master said, "Hand the pure pitcher to me, old monk. The Emperor asked again, "What is the Samādhi of Non-contention? The Master— [remained silent].
The Master said, "Donor, you are walking upon the crown of Vairocana’s head. The Emperor asked, "What is the meaning of this? The Master replied, "Do not mistake it for your own pure Dharma-body."
When Emperor Suzong arrived, the Master pointed to a stone lion and said, "Your Majesty, this stone lion is most extraordinary.
Please provide a turning phrase for it. The Emperor said, "I am unable to provide a turning phrase; I ask you, Master, to provide one. The Master said, "This mountain monk commits a transgression.
Later, Tanyuan asked, "Does the Emperor understand? The Master said, "Setting aside whether the Emperor understands for a moment, how do you understand it?"
The Master asked Attendant Zilin, "What is the meaning of 'Buddha'? He replied, "The meaning of awakening. The Master said, "Has the Buddha ever been deluded?
He replied, "Never. The Master said, "If so, what use is awakening?"

[He] was serving as an attendant while [Master Linji] was commenting on the *Suyāma-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*. The Master said, "In general, when annotating a sutra, one must first comprehend the Buddha’s meaning before it can be done.

[The attendant] replied, "If one does not comprehend the Buddha’s intent, how can one possibly explain the commentary? The Master ordered his attendant to fill a bowl with water and place seven grains of rice inside it.

A single chopstick was placed across the face of a bowl. [The monk] asked, "What is the meaning of this? Fung was speechless. The Master said, "I myself do not yet understand the old monk's intention;
how much less could I understand the Buddha’s intention?"
The Master asked a Zen seeker, "From which direction have you come? The seeker replied, "I have come from the South.
The Master said, "How do the masters of the South instruct people? He replied, "The masters of that region directly point out to students that 'this very mind is Buddha.
Buddha has the meaning of awakening. You now fully possess the nature of seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing. This nature is well able to raise an eyebrow and blink an eye."

The functioning of coming and going pervades the entire body: when the head is touched, the head knows; when the feet are touched, the feet know. Therefore, it is called "Perfectly All-Knowing" (Samyak-saṃbuddha).
Apart from this, there is no other Buddha. This body indeed undergoes birth and death, but the nature of the mind has never been subject to birth or death since beginningless time.
As for the birth and death of the body, it is like a dragon shedding its bones, a snake sloughing off its skin, or a person leaving an old dwelling.
"The very body is impermanent, yet its nature is eternal; such is the general teaching of the South.
The Master said, "If that were so, there would be no distinction between this and the non-Buddhist Śreṇika.

If seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing were the Buddha-nature, then Vimalakīrti should not have said, 'The Dharma is apart from seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing. If one practices seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing, this is..."

"Then seeing, hearing, perceiving, and knowing are not the seeking of the Dharma. The monk asked again, "The *Lotus Sūtra* is of definitive meaning; it 'opens up the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. How is this so?
The Master said, "The sūtra says it 'opens up the Buddha’s knowledge and vision,' yet it does not even mention bodhisattvas or those of the two vehicles.
How could the deluded and inverted perceptions of sentient beings be the same as the Buddha’s knowledge and vision? The monk asked again, "Which one is the Buddha?"
[The monk asked about] "mind. The Master said, "Walls, fences, tiles, and pebbles are it. The monk said, "This greatly contradicts the sutras.

The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states that because it is apart from walls and insentient things, it is called 'Buddha-nature. Now you say these are the Buddha-mind. I do not know whether mind and nature are distinct or not.
The Master said, "In delusion they are distinct; in awakening they are not distinct. [The monk] said, "The sutra says that Buddha-nature is..."
[Question: "The nature is constant, while the mind is impermanent. Why do you now say they are not distinct? The Master said: "You rely only on the words and do not rely on the meaning.
For example, in a cold month, water freezes into ice; when it becomes warm, the ice melts back into water. When sentient beings are deluded, their nature binds itself to form the mind;
when sentient beings awaken, the mind releases itself to become the nature. If you cling to the notion that insentient things lack Buddha-nature," [you have not understood.]

[The Master said: "In that case, the Sūtra should not have stated that 'the three realms are mind-only. This is clearly your own contradiction of the Sūtra; I do not contradict it. [The student] asked:
"If insentient things possess Buddha-nature, do they also understand how to preach the Dharma? The Master said: "They preach it incessantly and without interruption.
[The student] said: "Why is it that I do not hear them? The Master said: "It is you yourself who do not hear. [The student] asked: "Who is it that does hear?"

[The monk] said, "I have heard [it]. The Master said, "The various sages have attained hearing. [The monk] said, "Then sentient beings must have no share in it? The Master said, "I speak for the sake of sentient beings;

I do not speak for the sake of the various sages. [The monk] said, "I am deaf and blind; I do not hear the insentient preaching the Dharma. You, Master, ought to hear it. The Master said, "I, too, do not hear it.
[The monk] said, "If you, Master, do not hear it, how can you know that the insentient are able to preach the Dharma? The Master... [remained silent].
[The Master] said: "I am fortunate not to have heard it. Had I heard it, I would have been equal to the various sages. You, however, did not hear me preach the Dharma. [The monk] asked:

"Master, you speak only of insentient things having Buddha-nature. As for sentient beings, what of them? The Master said: "If even insentient things are thus, how much more so sentient beings? [The monk] asked:
"If that is so, then the spiritual friends of the South say that seeing, hearing, perceiving, and knowing are themselves the Buddha."

[The interlocutor] said: "In terms of their fundamental nature (*dhātu*), they should not be judged as being the same as non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*). The Master said: "I do not say that they lack Buddha-nature.

Do non-Buddhists not also possess Buddha-nature? It is simply because their views are mistaken; within a single dharma, they give rise to two views, and for that reason, it is said they are 'not' [Buddhists]. [The interlocutor] asked: "Why?"
“The Buddha’s body is without obstruction. Now, to fashion a Buddha-body out of conditioned things that are obstructive—is this not contrary to the Sage’s intent?
The Master said, “The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* states: ‘One cannot speak of the unconditioned apart from the conditioned. Do you believe that form is emptiness?
He replied, “This is the Buddha’s sincere word; how could I dare not believe it? The Master said, “Since form is emptiness, how can...”
[The student] said, "There are obstructions. The Master said, "The Buddha-nature is of one kind; is it not so? The student said, "It is not of one kind. The Master asked, "Why?

The student said, "In some cases it is entirely without arising or ceasing; in others it is half-arising and half-ceasing, or half-non-arising and half-non-ceasing. The Master asked, "Who provides this interpretation?
The Master said, "In my tradition here, the Buddha-nature is entirely without arising or ceasing. In your region to the south, the Buddha-nature is half-arising and half-ceasing."

"Extinction. Half is neither arising nor extinguishing. The student asked, "How are these distinguished? The Master said, "In this state, body and mind are as one, with nothing remaining outside the body;
therefore, it is entirely without arising or extinguishing. You of the South hold that the physical body is impermanent while the spiritual nature is permanent;
therefore, for you, half arises and half extinguishes, while half neither arises nor extinguishes. The student asked, "Master, how could your physical form possibly be the same as the Dharma-body?"

[The monk asked: "Is it neither arising nor ceasing? The Master said: "How have you fallen into the way of heterodoxy? [The monk] said: "When did this student fall into the way of heterodoxy? The Master said:
"Have you not read the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, which says that 'to see forms or seek sounds is to walk the way of heterodoxy'?
Is what you have seen not exactly like that? [The monk] said: "But you, Master, also say that 'this very mind is Buddha,' and the teachers of the South say the same. Why [is there a contradiction]?"
There are similarities and differences. A teacher should not consider themselves right and others wrong. The Master said: "Sometimes names differ while the substance is the same;

sometimes the name is the same while the substance differs. It is because of this that confusion arises. For instance, *bodhi*, *nirvāṇa*, *tathatā*, and *buddha-nature*—these have different names but the same substance.

The true mind and the deluded mind, or Buddha-wisdom and worldly wisdom—these have the same name but different substances. It is because those in the South mistakenly took the deluded mind [to be the true mind]..."
To claim that this is the true mind is to mistake a thief for one's own son. To possess worldly knowledge and call it the Buddha-mind is like confusing fish eyes with bright pearls;
they must not be treated as the same, for the matter requires careful discernment.
The monk Lingjue of Changzhou asked, “I have set my mind on leaving the household life, originally intending to seek Buddhahood. I do not know how one should apply the mind to achieve this.
The Master said, “If you can employ a mind that is no-mind, you will immediately attain Buddhahood. He asked, “If there is a mind that can be employed, who is it that attains Buddhahood?
The Master said, “No-mind itself attains Buddhahood; even the attainment of Buddhahood is no-mind. He asked, “If no-mind is precisely Buddhahood...”
"Has the Master already attained Buddhahood now? The Master said, "Mind itself is already non-existent; who says one attains Buddhahood?
If there were a Buddha to be attained, there would still be mind. Where there is mind, there is outflow (āsrava); how could one find that which is mindless?

[The student] asked, "Since there is no Buddha to be attained, does the Master still employ the function of a Buddha? The Master said, "Mind itself is already non-existent; from where could its function arise? [The student] asked, "..."
[The student] said, "I am utterly bewildered and have nothing at all. Am I not falling into the view of nihilism? The Master said, "Originally there is no view; who says it is 'cut off'?

[The student] said, "If originally there is no view, am I not falling into emptiness? The Master said, "There is no emptiness into which one can fall. [The student] said, "Is there anything that can be fallen into?
The Master said, "Since emptiness itself is non-existent, from where could a fall arise? [The student] said, "If I encounter tigers or wolves in the mountains, how should I apply my mind?"
The Master said: "To see as if not seeing; to come as if not coming—such a one is without mind, and even ferocious beasts cannot harm them.
[The student] asked: "That which is tranquil and without affairs, solitary and detached, and without mind—what is it called? The Master said: "It is called the Vajra Mahāsattva."
[The student] asked: "What is the physical form of the Vajra Mahāsattva? The Master said: "Fundamentally, it has no form or segment. [The student] asked:
"Since it has no form or segment, what thing do you call the Vajra Mahāsattva? The Master said: "I call it the Vajra Mahāsattva who is without form or segment. [The student] asked: "..."

"What are the meritorious virtues of the Vajramahāsattva? The Master said: "If for a single thought-moment one attains resonance with the Vajra, one can extinguish the heavy sins of birth and death accumulated over as many kalpas as there are grains of sand in the Ganges. One shall behold as many Buddhas as there are grains of sand in the Ganges.

The meritorious virtues of this Vajramahāsattva are immeasurable; they cannot be described by speech nor recounted by the mind. No one is able to destroy them. There is no further need [for elaboration]."
Question: You travel at will, solitary and free from fear, always protected by sages and saints as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.

Wherever you are, you are constantly revered by devas, nāgas, and the eight classes of beings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, and as many benevolent deities come to guard you so that you are forever without hindrance. Where, then, could you not roam with ease?
A monk asked: "An ancient worthy said, 'The verdant green bamboos are all the Dharmakāya; the lush yellow flowers are none other than Prajñā.
Some people do not allow this, calling it heterodox teaching, while others believe it, calling it inconceivable. I do not know how to deal with this. The Master said:
"This is the realm of Samantabhadra and Mañjuśrī; it is not something that ordinary beings can believe or accept. All [the monks] were silent.
This accords with the intent of the definitive Mahāyāna sūtras. Thus, the Avataṃsaka Sūtra says: "The Buddha-body fills the Dharma-realm;
it manifests universally before all sentient beings. Responding to conditions and meeting with those who seek it, there is nowhere it does not reach, yet it always remains upon this seat of Bodhi.
Since green bamboo does not exist outside the Dharma-realm, is it not indeed the Dharmakāya? Furthermore, the Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra says: "Form..."
"Because it is boundless, Prajñā is also boundless. Since yellow flowers do not transcend form (*rūpa*), are they not Prajñā?
These profound and far-reaching words are difficult for those who do not understand to grasp. Thereupon, the Chan guest paid his respects and departed."
A monk asked, "How can one attain Buddhahood? The Master said, "Cast off both Buddha and sentient beings at once; liberation occurs right where you are.
The monk asked, "How does one achieve resonance with this? The Master said, "When neither good nor evil is contemplated, the Buddha-nature reveals itself spontaneously."
[The student] asked: "How does one realize the Dharmakāya? The Master said: "Transcend the realm of Vairocana. [The student] asked: "How does one attain the pure Dharmakāya?
The Master said: "Do not seek it from the Buddha. [The student] asked: "Which one is the Buddha? The Master said:

"The very mind is the Buddha. [The student] asked: "Does the mind have afflictions? The Master said: "The nature of afflictions is inherently detached. [The student] asked: "Is this not severing [afflictions]?"
"Yes. The Master said, "One who cuts off afflictions is called a follower of the Two Vehicles. That afflictions do not arise is called Great Nirvana.

[The student] asked, "As for sitting in meditation and observing stillness, what is this? The Master said, "It is neither defiled nor pure; why would you need to give rise to a mind to observe the mark of purity?
[The student] asked, "Does the Chan Master see the empty space of the ten directions as the Dharma-body? The Master said, "This is grasping with a conceptualizing mind."
This is a perverted view. [The questioner] asked: "If 'this very mind is Buddha,' should one still practice the myriad deeds? The Master said:
"Even the various sages all possess the two kinds of adornment; how could one possibly deny cause and effect?"
As the Master was about to enter nirvana, he took his leave of Emperor Daizong. The Emperor said, "After the Master’s passing, by what means shall your disciples commemorate you?
The Master replied, "Inform the donor that they should construct a seamless stupa. The Emperor said, "I request the Master to provide me with a model for the stupa."

The Master remained silent for a long time and then asked, "Do you understand? The Emperor said, "I do not understand. The Master said, "After this poor monk has passed away, my disciple Yingzhen will know this matter.

I beg Your Majesty to issue an edict to question him. Later, an edict was issued to question Yingzhen regarding the previous words. After a long silence, Yingzhen asked, "Does Your Majesty understand?
The Emperor said, "I do not understand. Yingzhen recited a verse: "To the south of Xiang, to the north of Tan, In between there is a yellow..."
Gold fills the entire country. Under the shadowless tree, they board the same boat; atop the lapis lazuli palace, there is no one to recognize them.
Chan Master Danyuan Yingzhen was asked by Magu:
"Is the Twelve-Faced Avalokiteśvara not a sage? The Master said, "Yes. Magu then gave the Master a blow.
"Snap! The Master said, "I suspect you have not yet reached this state.

When the Monk Guifeng Zongmi was questioned by the Minister Shan Nan Wen Zao: "Does a person who has realized the principle and stilled delusion no longer form karmic bonds? For the duration of a single lifetime..."
"After one's life has ended, upon what does the spiritual nature rely? The Master said: "All sentient beings are without exception endowed with the awakened nature (*buddhadhātu*).

Its luminous clarity and empty stillness—how is it different from that of a Buddha? It is only because, since beginningless kalpas, they have never attained realization, and thus falsely cling to the body as the mark of self (*ātman-lakṣaṇa*).

Consequently, they give rise to emotions such as attachment and aversion; following these emotions they create karma, and following their karma they receive retribution: birth, old age, sickness, [and death]."
One dies and wanders through saṃsāra for long kalpas; yet the enlightened nature within the body has never been born or died.
It is like being driven to labor in a dream, while the body remains fundamentally at ease; or like water turning to ice, while its moist nature does not change.

If one can awaken to this nature, it is the Dharmakāya, which is fundamentally unborn—how could there be any dependence? It is spiritually lucid and unclouded, clearly and eternally aware, without anything [to grasp].

From the beginning, there has never been anything that comes, nor is there anywhere to which it goes. Yet, through many lifetimes, false attachments have been formed until they become one's very nature;
thus, joy, anger, sorrow, and pleasure flow on in subtle currents. Although the True Principle may be suddenly realized, these emotional habits are difficult to eliminate abruptly.

One must constantly maintain awareness, diminishing them again and again, just as when the wind suddenly ceases and the waves gradually subside. How could the practice of a single lifetime be equal to that of others?

The power and function of the Buddha can only take emptiness and stillness as its own essence; do not identify with the physical body. Take spiritual awareness as your own mind; do not identify with deluded thoughts.
If deluded thoughts arise, do not follow them at all. Then, at the moment of death, karma will naturally be unable to bind you.
Even if you pass through the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), your destination will be free and unimpeded; whether in the heavens or among humans, you may take rebirth wherever you wish.

If the thoughts of attachment and aversion have already dissolved, one will no longer receive a body subject to分段 (fen-duan) birth and death; one can naturally transform the short into the long and the coarse into the sublime.
Zongmi has an eight-line verse that elucidates this meaning, which I shall recite for you in the presence of the Minister of State.
The verse says: To perform actions that accord with what is meaningful is a mind of clarity; to perform actions that accord with what is meaningless is a deluded mind.
A deluded mind follows emotional impulses, and at the moment of death, one is dragged away by karma. A clear mind does not follow emotions; at the moment of death, it is able to transform karma.

If, within the flow of emotion, you feel the urge to act but perceive through reason that it is improper, you must stop immediately. If, within the flow of emotion, you have no desire to act but perceive through reason [that it is necessary], [you should proceed].
This is appropriate; one must act immediately based solely on the principle of right and wrong, rather than out of feelings of attachment or aversion.
Thus, at the moment of death, karma will not bind one, and one will attain mastery over one’s destiny, whether in the heavens or among humans. Generally speaking, this is so.
However, during the morning and evening, one's actions are led astray by the dust of the emotions (*kleśa*). Thus, at the moment of death, one is led away by karma and undergoes rebirth.

If one's actions and conduct are based on awakened wisdom rather than the dust of the emotions, then at the moment of death, one undergoes rebirth through the sovereignty of the self (*ātman*) and not by means of karma.
You should know that this is how to verify whether one possesses sovereignty over rebirth at the time of death.
"Freedom? It simply depends on whether you examine your ordinary mind as it engages with sensory objects to see if it is free or not.
An old master of no name said:
"The Patriarch sat facing the wall for nine years in search of one who could understand him. If you understand it in this way, you will deserve a blow from an iron staff."

The Master is here. When the Patriarch sat facing the wall for nine years, how could he not have felt shame? If you understand it in this way, you will still need to buy straw sandals and travel on foot for another thirty years.
One day, Mazu asked Chan Master Baizhang Huaihai, "Where have you come from? The Master said, "From behind the mountains. Mazu said, "Did you encounter anyone there?
He said, "I did not encounter anyone. Mazu said, "Why did you not encounter anyone? He said, "If I had encountered anyone, I would have raised [the matter]."
[The monk] acted as if he were the Master. The Patriarch said, "From where have you obtained this news? He replied, "It is my fault.
The Patriarch said, "Rather, it is my own fault."
The Master said to the assembly, "There is one person who has long gone without eating rice yet does not say he is hungry; there is another person who eats all day long yet does not say he is full.
One day, while the Master was walking with Mazu, they saw a flock of wild ducks fly past. Mazu asked, "What is that?"
The Master said, "Wild ducks. The Patriarch asked, "Where have they gone? The Master replied, "They flew past. The Patriarch then seized the Master by the nose and twisted it;
the Master cried out in pain. The Patriarch said, "And you say they flew past? At these words, the Master attained realization.
The Master instructed the monk, "Go to Zhangjing’s place. When you see him ascend the hall to preach the Dharma, you should immediately spread out your sitting mat, prostrate, and then stand up;
take one of his shoes, brush away the dust on it with your sleeve, and turn it upside down to cover [the shoe] with its sole.
The monk went to Zhangjing and followed the Master's instructions exactly. Zhangjing said, "I, this old monk, am at fault."
A monk asked, "I come to you, Master, bearing my uncut jade; I pray that you will examine it for me. The Master said, "Last night, a tiger on South Mountain bit a large beast.
The monk said, "That is no error in the true teaching. Why do you not bestow a skillful means? The Master said, "You are a fellow who covers his ears while stealing a bell."
[The monk] said, "If I had not met the discernment of Minister Zhong, I would have been no different from firewood in a rustic shed. The Master struck him. The monk cried out, "Heaven! Heaven!
The Master said, "To have such a garrulous mouth! The monk said, "Rarely does one meet a true connoisseur," and shook out his sleeves and departed.
The Master said, "Today Baizhang has lost half the battle."
While Chan Master Nanquan Puyuan was playing with the moon, a monk asked, "When will I become like this? The Master said, "In my youth, twenty years ago, I also came along in this very way.
The monk asked, "How about now? The Master then returned to his quarters.
The Master asked Huangbo, "Regarding the study of the equality of concentration and wisdom to clearly see the Buddha-nature—what is the principle of this?
Huangbo said, "In the twelve periods of the day, do not rely on or depend upon a single thing. The Master said, "Is this your own realization, Elder? Huangbo said, "I dare not say so."
The Master said, "Let us set aside the matter of the money for rice and water for now; who will repay the cost of the straw sandals?
The Master, along with Lu Zu, Gui Zong, and Shan Shan—four of them in total—departed from Mazu’s place and each planned to establish a hermitage.
As they were parting ways along the road, the Master planted his staff in the ground and said, "Even if you can speak, you are obstructed by this; if you cannot speak..."
[The Master] was also obstructed by this very thing. Zong pulled his staff and struck the Master once, saying, "It is also just this.
What does Old Wang say about being obstructed or not? Lu said, "This single phrase alone has spread throughout the world."
Grand Master Lu asked the Master about the Dharma Master Zhaor. "He is truly extraordinary," he said. "He explains that 'Heaven and earth share the same root as I;

the myriad things and I are one body. The Master pointed to the peony flowers in front of the courtyard and said, "Grand Master, when people of this age see this single stalk of flowers, it is like being in a dream. Lu was unable to fathom this.
A monk asked, "When the Master returns to his chamber, what will you use as a guiding pointer? The Master said, "Last night at the third watch, I lost the ox;
when I rose at dawn, I had lost the fire."
The Master addressed the assembly, saying: "To call it 'suchness' (tathatā) is already to have altered it. Now, monks must walk among the heterodox. Guizong said:
"Though one performs the deeds of an animal, one does not receive the retribution of an animal. The Master said:
"Alas, Old Man Meng has gone off in that way again!"
The Master asked a monk, "There was a fine wind last night. The monk said, "There was a fine wind last night. The Master said, "It blew down a pine tree in front of the gate.
The monk said, "It blew down a pine tree in front of the gate. Next, he asked another monk, "There was a fine wind last night. The monk said, "What kind of wind was it?
The Master said, "It blew down a pine tree in front of the gate. The monk said, "What [kind of tree]?"
"Mosong. The Master said, "One gains, one loses.
The Master said, "The Buddhas of the three periods do not know it exists; the wildcat and the white ox, however, do know it exists.
Daopei Zhi said, "If the Buddhas of the three periods do not know it exists, then how could the wildcat and the white ox have ever dreamed of it? It is evident."
One must know that only those who have realized the ultimate and possess the fundamental ground can attain this.
The Master asked the *karmadāna*: "What are you doing today during the communal labor? He replied, "We are hauling the millstone.
The Master said, "You may haul the millstone as you wish, but you must not move the central pivot of the millstone. That monk was speechless.
While the Master was in the abbot’s quarters warming himself by the fire with Shanshan, the Master said, “Without pointing east or west, speak directly of the matter of your own fundamental division.
Shanshan inserted his fire tongs and stood with hands clasped. The Master said, “Even so, you are still one thread behind Old Wang.”
A monk asked National Teacher Haiqing (Haichang) of Qian’an, “What is the original body of Vairocana? The Master said, “Bring me the pure water pitcher.
When the monk brought the pitcher, the Master said, “Put it back in its original place. The monk returned it to its place and came back to question him again.
The Master said: "The ancient Buddhas have long since passed away.
Zen Master Guizong Zhichang once traveled with Nanquan; later, one day as they were parting, while Nanquan was boiling tea, he asked:
"I have been discussing these phrases with my senior brother for some time now; we both already understand them.
Hereafter, if someone asks about the ultimate matter, what will you say? The Master said, "This patch of ground is excellent for pitching a hermitage.
Nanquan said, "Setting aside the hermitage for a moment, what is the ultimate matter? The Master then overturned the tea kettle and immediately rose. Nanquan said, "Master..."
The elder brother had finished drinking tea, while Puyan had not yet drunk any. The Master said, "To speak such words as these makes it difficult even for a drop of water to be digested.
This was Chan Master Baoji of Youzhou.
Ascending the hall, [the Master] said: "Now, the moon of the mind hangs solitary, its light swallowing the myriad phenomena. The light does not illuminate objects, nor do objects exist.
When both light and objects have vanished, what is this thing?"
Ascending the hall, he said: "Virtuous Chan practitioners, you may study the Way within this school. It is like the earth supporting a mountain, unaware of the mountain’s towering loftiness;
or like a stone containing jade, unaware of the jade’s flawlessness. If one can act in such a manner, this is called 'leaving home. Thus the Guide said:"
Phenomena are fundamentally non-obstructive; the three periods of time are likewise so. Even for one who is unconditioned and inactive, it remains as difficult as a golden chain.
Therefore, the spiritual source shines alone; the Way is absolute and birthless. Great wisdom is not "bright," and true emptiness leaves no trace.
True Suchness, ordinary beings, and sages are all but dream-like words. Buddhas and *nirvāṇa* are both merely figurative designations. Zen practitioners, you must simply look within yourselves.
There is no one to replace me. Entering the hall:
In the Three Realms there is no dharma; where can one seek the mind? The four great elements are fundamentally empty; upon what does the Buddha rely to dwell?
The celestial sphere is unmoving; it is silent and wordless. Face-to-face presentation—there is nothing more. Be careful.
Cen Master Huizang of Shigong asked Xitang, "Do you understand how to seize empty space? Xitang said, "I can seize it. The Master said, "How do you seize it?
Xitang reached out his hand and grasped at the empty space. The Master said, "You do not understand how to seize it. Xitang then asked in return:
“Brother, how do you catch it? The Master grabbed Xitang by the nostrils and pulled. Xitang made a cry of pain and said, “You are pulling at a person’s nostrils far too hard;
I feel as though they are about to come right off! The Master said, “You must catch empty space in this very way before you will succeed.”

When Chan Master Dayi of Gehu was summoned to the Linqide Hall by Emperor Xianzong of the Tang dynasty to debate the principles of the Dharma, a Dharma Master asked: "The desire realm has no dhyāna; dhyāna resides in the form realm.
Upon what basis does one establish dhyāna in this world? The Master said: "Dharma Master, you only know that there is no dhyāna in the desire realm; you do not..."

[The Master] knew that the realm of dhyāna is free from desire. He asked, "What is dhyāna? The Master pointed at the empty space with his hand. The Dharma Master was speechless. The Emperor said, "The Dharma Master has lectured on infinite sutras and śāstras, yet he cannot even manage this single point. The Master then asked the eminent virtuous ones, "In walking, standing, sitting, and reclining, what ultimately constitutes the Way? One replied, "That which knows is the Way. The Master [continued]: The Master asked, "If you know it, why do you not know yourself? The one who had replied was speechless. The Master said, "I have already told you that the Way is not something to be sought externally; it is simply your own original mind. You seek it outside yourselves and thus fail to recognize it.

He then asked the assembly, "If you do not see it within yourselves, where else would you go to find it? If you do not see it within yourselves, how can you claim to understand the Way? The assembly remained silent. The Master said, "To understand the Way is to understand the self. To understand the self is to forget the self. When the self is forgotten, there is nothing to attain. When there is nothing to attain, the body and mind are both cast off. When body and mind are both cast off, delusions vanish and the traces of enlightenment disappear. This is called 'the great liberation. It is like the great earth: when rain falls upon it, it does not choose between high and low ground, but moistens everything equally. The Way is likewise: it does not choose between noble and base, but illuminates all things equally. Therefore, the sages of old said: 'The Way is vast and boundless; it is not something that can be grasped by the mind or intellect. He then recited a verse: "The Way is originally not difficult; Simply do not create complications. When the mind is pure and still, The Buddha-nature is revealed. He further said, "If you wish to enter the Way, you must first abandon all conceptualizations. Do not grasp at forms, do not dwell on names, and do not cling to anything. Just maintain this state of non-attachment, and you will naturally accord with the Way. The assembly was greatly enlightened. The Emperor was deeply moved and paid homage to the Master. He then invited the Master to reside at the Great Ci'en Monastery. The Master accepted the invitation and lived there for many years, teaching and transforming disciples. His reputation spread throughout the land, and he was revered by both the clergy and the laity. At the age of seventy-eight, he passed away peacefully. The Emperor mourned him deeply and bestowed upon him the posthumous title "Great Master of Universal Wisdom" (Guanghui Dashi). His remains were enshrined at the monastery, where they remain to this day. His legacy continues to inspire practitioners across generations.
[The Master] said: "It cannot be known by means of wisdom (*jñāna*), nor can it be cognized by means of consciousness (*vijñāna*). How, then, can one know that which knows? A student replied:

"It is that which is without conceptual discrimination (*avikalpa*. The Master said: "You are well able to discern the characteristics of all phenomena (*dharma-lakṣaṇa*), yet you do not waver from the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*)."
"How can there be non-discrimination? [A monk] replied, "There is a counterpart; the four dhyānas and eight samādhis are it.

The Master said, "The Buddha-body is unconditioned and does not fall within the realm of numerical categories. How could it reside within the four dhyānas and eight samādhis? The assembly remained speechless.
Chan Master Zizai of Funiu at Ique ascended the hall and said:
“‘This very mind is Buddha’ is the phrase of seeking medicine when one is not ill. ‘Neither mind nor Buddha’ is the phrase of counteracting the disease with medicine.
A monk asked, “What is the phrase of liberation? The Master said, “Under the foot of Mount Funiu, past and present.”
*Chuan*:
Zen Master Weikuan of Xingshan was asked by a monk, "Does a dog have Buddha-nature? The Master said, "It has. The monk asked, "Does the Master have it as well? The Master said:
“I have none. [The monk] asked, “All sentient beings possess Buddha-nature. Why do you alone, Preceptor, lack it? The Master said, “I am not among all sentient beings.
[The monk] asked, “If you are not a sentient being, are you perhaps a Buddha? The Master said, “I am not a Buddha. [The monk] asked, “Then what are you?”
"What, ultimately, is this thing? The Master said, "It is not even a thing. [The monk] asked, "Can it be seen or can it be conceived?

The Master said, "It is beyond the reach of thought and cannot be grasped through deliberation; therefore, it is called 'inconceivable' (acintya). [The monk] asked, "Where does the Way reside? The Master said:
"It is right here before you. The student said, "Why do I not see it? The Master said, "Because you have the notion of 'self,' you do not see it. The student asked, "..."
"If there is 'I' because of 'me,' then one does not see. Does the Preceptor still see? The Master said, "If there is you and there is me, we simply do not see each other.
[The monk] asked, "If there is neither 'I' nor 'you,' do you still see? The Master said, "If there is neither you nor me, who is it that seeks to see?"
Chan Master Yangqi Zhenshu addressed the assembly, saying:
"The myriad spirits share a single source; this is provisionally named 'Buddha. Though the physical body is exhausted and form dissolves, it does not perish;

though the metal flows and the ingot disperses, it remains ever-present. When the ocean of nature is windless, the golden waves surge spontaneously; when the spiritual mind is free of signs, the ten thousand phenomena are in harmony."

Illumination! Those who realize this principle do not speak, yet they traverse as many worlds as grains of sand; they do not act, yet their merit increasingly benefits the profound transformation of beings.
How can one turn one's back on awakening and instead conform to worldly toil, falsely imprisoning oneself within the aggregates and realms?

Chan Master Shanjue of Hualin in Tanzhou was in the habit of carrying his staff at night as he walked among the forested foothills. Every seven paces, he would shake his staff once and recite the name of Avalokiteśvara once.
Jia Shan asked him, "I have heard from afar that you, Master, chant the name of Avalokiteśvara; is this true? The Master replied, "Yes. Jia Shan said, "Then ride upon it!"
“How is it when the head appears? The Master said, “If it appears, you may ride it; if it does not appear, what is there to ride? Shan had no reply. A monk came for an audience;
as he was just unfolding his sitting cloth, the Master said, “Slowly, slowly. The monk asked, “What do you see, Master? The Master said, “It is a pity.”
"Granted," he said. [The monk] struck and broke the bell tower; from this, the monk attained awakening.
When the Inspector Pei Xiu visited him, he asked, "Do you have any attendants? The Master replied, "There are one or two."
"However, you must not see the guest. Pei asked, "Where is he? The Master then called out, "Dàkōng! Xiǎokōng!
At that moment, two tigers emerged from behind the hut. Seeing them, Pei was struck with terror. The Master said to the tigers, "There is a guest; depart for now."
The two tigers roared and departed. Pei asked, "What practice did you master, Master, to have elicited such a response?
The Master remained silent for a long while and then said, "Do you understand? He replied, "I do not. The Master said, "This mountain monk constantly recites the name of Avalokiteśvara."
The lay practitioner Pang Yun of Xiangzhou went to Mount Yao.
The Master of the Mountain ordered ten Zen guests to escort him to the gate. Upon reaching the entrance, the layman pointed to the snow in the air and said:
"Fine snow! Each flake falls nowhere else. A Zen guest named Quan said, "Where does it fall? The Master then gave him a slap. Quan said, "You should not be so hasty.
The Master said, "If you call yourself a 'Zen guest' like that, the Old Man Yama will not let you go.
Quan asked, "What about you, Layman? The Master slapped him again and said, "Seeing with eyes as if blind; speaking with a mouth—"
It is said to be like a mute. The verse says:
"The mind is as it is, and the objects are likewise; they are neither real nor unreal, neither existent nor non-existent.

They are not sages or worthies, but ordinary people who have understood the matter. It is easy, indeed, very easy. Within these very five aggregates there is true wisdom, throughout the ten directions."
The world is one in the Single Vehicle; how could there be two in the signless Dharmakāya? If one abandons afflictions to enter Bodhi, one would not know where else the Buddha-ground exists.
Chan Master Yaoshan Weiyan went to pay his respects to Mazu.
Upon hearing Mazu’s words, he attained realization and immediately prostrated. Mazu asked, “What principle have you seen that you prostrate?
The Master replied, “When I was with Shitou, it was like a mosquito on an iron ox. Mazu said:
"Since you have been thus, protect and maintain yourself well.
He served [his master] for three years. One day, the Patriarch asked, "Son, what is your current realization? The Master said, "My skin and flesh have fallen away completely;
there remains only the one true reality. The Patriarch said, "What you have attained may truly be called being in accord with the essence of the mind."
"It shall spread through the four limbs. Since this is so, take three strips of rattan and bind them around your belly, then go to dwell in the mountains wherever you find one.
The Master said, "Who am I that I would dare say I will dwell in the mountains? The Patriarch said, "It is not so.

There has never been constant movement without stillness, nor has there ever been constant stillness without movement. To seek benefit where there is no benefit, and to act where there is nothing to do—"
"You ought to act as a vessel for others; do not remain here for long. The Master then took his leave of the Patriarch and returned to Shitou.
One day, while sitting on a rock, Shitou asked, "What are you doing here? The Master replied, "I am doing nothing at all.
Shitou said, "If that is so, then you are just sitting idly. The Master said, "If it were idle sitting, then I would be doing something. Shitou said, "..."
"You say it is 'not doing. Not doing what? He replied, "Even the thousand sages do not recognize it. The Master praised him with a verse:
"From the beginning we have lived together, yet you do not know its name; Spontaneously following along, you simply walk on. Since antiquity, even the most eminent sages have failed to recognize it;
How could ordinary people in their haste possibly understand it?"
Shitou gave a "hanging word," saying: "Words and activities have no connection [to the truth]. The Master said: "Neither words nor activities have any connection [to the truth] either.
Shitou said: "In my place, not even a needle can pierce through. The Master said: "In my place, it is like planting flowers upon a stone. Shitou approved of this.
During a sitting session, Daowu and Yunyan were standing in attendance. The Master pointed to two trees on the mountain, one withered and one flourishing, and asked Daowu, "Which is it?
The withered one, or the flourishing one? Daowu said, "The flourishing one. The Master said, "Truly, in every place there is radiant brilliance. He then asked Yunyan, "Which is it?

The withered one, or the flourishing one? Yunyan said, "The withered one. The Master [said], "Truly, in every place there is radiant brilliance. (Note: The Master’s concluding remark is understood to apply equally to both responses.)
The Master said, "Clearly, let everything everywhere be released into a state of withered stillness. Gao the Śrāmaṇera suddenly arrived, and the Master asked, "What is the withered?
What is the flourishing? Gao replied, "As for the withered, it withers of its own accord; as for the flourishing, it flourishes of its own accord.
The Master looked toward Daowu and Yunyan and said, "Not so! Not so!"
A monk asked, "In the level fields and shallow grass, the deer and roe form a herd. How does one shoot for the lord among the deer?
The Master said, "Watch the arrow! The monk threw himself down and fell. The Master said, "Attendant, drag this dead man out! The monk then ran away. The Master said, [and the monk did not return].
"What limit is there for this fellow who plays with lumps of mud?
While he was reading a scripture, a monk asked, "Master, you usually do not allow others to read scriptures; why then do you read them yourself?"
The Master said, "I only intend to cover my eyes. The student asked, "If I were to study under you, Master, would I be able to achieve the same?
The Master said, "If you look, even an ox hide must be pierced."
While the Master was seated, a monk asked, "What are you pondering so intently? The Master said, "I am pondering that which cannot be pondered.
The monk asked, "How can one ponder that which cannot be pondered? The Master said, "It is not pondering."
Li Ao, the Prefectural Governor of Langzhou, asked the Master, "What is your surname? The Master replied, "It is precisely now.
Li did not understand this and instead questioned the head of the monastery, "A moment ago I asked the Master his surname, and he said, 'It is precisely now. I do not know what his surname is.
The Head said, "In that case, his surname must be Han. Upon hearing this, the Master remarked, "How can you be so incapable of distinguishing between good and evil?"
If one were to face him during the summer, he would be of the "Hot" surname. Li Chuxiang, having long admired the Master’s profound transformation, invited him repeatedly but was refused each time.
He then went in person to visit the Master. The Master held up a scroll and paid him no heed. The attendant said, "The Governor is here.

Li, being of a narrow and impatient disposition, remarked, "Seeing the person is not as good as hearing of his reputation," and brushed his sleeves, departing at once. The Master said, "How could the Governor have acted thus?"
"Cherishing the ear and despising the eye," Li Hui bowed in thanks. The Master asked, "What is the Way? The Master pointed up and down and said, "Do you understand?
He replied, "I do not understand. The Master said, "Clouds in the blue sky; water in the pitcher. Li joyfully prostrated himself.
He spoke in verse: "Refined, my body has taken on the form of a crane; Beneath a thousand pine trees lie two caskets of scripture.
I have come to ask about the Way, with no other words— Clouds in the blue sky, water in the pitcher. Li asked again: "What are precept, concentration, and wisdom?"
The Master said, "In this humble monk’s place, there are no such worldly furnishings. Li did not fathom the profound intent.
The Master said, "If you, Prefectural Governor, wish to take responsibility for this matter, you must stand atop the highest mountain peak and walk upon the deepest ocean floor.
If you cannot let go of the things of the inner chambers, that constitutes a leakage."
Chan Master Kuang of Changzhi in Tanzhou was a disciple of Caoxi.
Having returned from paying homage at the Patriarch’s stupa, he went to visit Shitou. Shitou asked, "Where have you come from? He replied, "From Lingnan."
Nanquan said, "At the head of Dayu Ridge, there is a single set of meritorious works. Is it finished yet? The Master said, "It has been finished for a long time;
it only lacks the application of the eye. Nanquan said, "Do you not want the eye applied? The Master said, "Please do so.
Nanquan then lowered one foot. The Master prostrated himself. Nanquan said, "What principle have you seen that you prostrate yourself? The Master said, "According to..."
What I have seen is like a single speck of snow upon a red-hot furnace.
Chan Master Daowu of Tianwang went to visit Mazu.
Mazu said: "Recognize that your own mind is fundamentally Buddha; it does not belong to gradual stages, nor does it depend on external aids."
He practiced until his essence was naturally *tathatā* (suchness), and all virtues were perfected. Under these words, the Master attained great enlightenment.

The Patriarch instructed him, saying, "If you take up the position of abbot, do not leave your former location. Having received this command, the Master returned to Jingmen. Not far from the city walls, he constructed a thatched hut.
When the regional inspector came to visit, the Master did not offer him special courtesy. The inspector became enraged, seized the Master, and threw him into the river. Upon reaching...

Upon his return, he saw that fire had broken out throughout the entire yamen, and he heard from the air the sound of the Heavenly King’s wrathful reproach. He immediately repented with sorrow and prostrated himself;

the smoke and flames were instantly extinguished, and everything was restored exactly as it was before. He then went in person to the riverbank to welcome the Master, only to find the Master standing in the water.
His robes did not become wet at all. [The Master] grew even more self-respectful and, to the west of the prefectural seat, built T’ien-wang Temple to provide for his teacher.
Long-t’an Hsin asked, “How is the matter handed down from the ancestors? The Master said, “It is not that you cannot understand it;
it is that you have not yet realized where you came from. Long-t’an said, “How many people possess such an eye? The Master said, “In shallow grass, reeds grow easily.”
The Master often said, "How happy! How happy! Yet when his time of death arrived, he cried out, "Alas! Alas! and further said, "King Yama has come to take me away.
The head monk asked, "When you were thrown into the water by the military commissioner, your countenance remained unmoved.
Why now do you act in such a manner? The Master raised his pillow and said, "Tell me, was it as it was then?"
At this, the abbot was speechless. One day,
after returning from the communal labor of clearing fields, Zen Master Huangbo Xiyun asked Baizhang, "Master Yun, clearing these fields is no easy task."
The Master said, "I shall join the assembly in their labors. The Abbot said, "This will trouble your practice. The Master said, "How would I dare decline such toil? The Abbot said, [silently].
"How much field have you cultivated? The Master struck the ground three times with his mattock. Zhaozhou then shouted. The Master covered his ears and departed.
One day, he took up his bowl and sat upon Nanquan’s seat. When Nanquan entered the hall and saw him, he asked, "Venerable sir, for how many years have you been practicing the Way?
The Master replied, "Before King Bhīṣmagarjitasvararāja. Nanquan said, "You are still but the descendants of Old Master Wang; get down from there!"
The Master then passed over the second seat and sat down. Nanquan retired from the conversation.
One day Nanquan said, "I have a 'Song of Herding an Ox'; I ask you, Elder, to provide a response. The Master replied, "I already have my own teacher.
When the Master took his leave of Nanquan, Nanquan saw him off at the gate; picking up the Master’s straw hat, he said, "Elder, your physical stature is immeasurable."
"Large! Your straw hat is too small for you. The Master said, "Even so, the great trichiliocosm is entirely contained within it.
Jianquan asked, "What about Wuzhuo? The Master donned his hat and departed.
One day, Prime Minister Pei placed a statue of the Buddha before the Master and knelt, saying, "I beg the Master to bestow a name upon it.
The Master called out, "Pei Xiu! The official responded, "Yes. The Master said, "I have finished bestowing the name upon you. The official bowed in prostration.
One day, the Master clenched his fist and said, "All the old monks of the world are gathered right here.

If I let slip even a single thread of a path, you may run wild in every direction; but if I do not let it pass, it will not take more than this one clench. A monk asked, "What is it like when you let slip a single thread?
The Master said, "Running wild in every direction. The monk asked, "And what about when you do not let it pass and it does not take more than this one clench?"
"What? The Master replied, "Universal.
He then said to Pei Gongmei: "The Buddhas and all sentient beings are nothing but this one mind; there is no other dharma apart from it."
This mind, from time immemorial, has never been born and has never ceased;
it is neither blue nor yellow, formless and signless, belonging to neither existence nor non-existence, reckoned as neither new nor old, neither long nor short, neither large nor small.
This one mind alone is the Buddha. Between the Buddha and sentient beings, there is no further distinction. If one contemplates the Buddha as pure, luminous, and liberated...
The mark of liberation: to perceive sentient beings as having the marks of defilement, obscurity, and birth-and-death.
One who forms such a view will, even after passing through kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, never attain Bodhi, because they are attached to marks. Only this one mind exists;
not even so much as a speck of dust of a separate dharma can be found. This very mind is Buddha. Now, practitioners of the Way who do not awaken to the essence of this mind, instead—
To give rise to thoughts within the mind, to seek the Buddha outwardly, and to practice while clinging to signs—all these are evil dharmas;

they are not the path to Bodhi. "Vimalakīrti" means "Pure Name. "Pure" refers to nature (*dhātu*); "Name" refers to characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*). Since nature and characteristics are not different, he is called Vimalakīrti.
That which is manifested by the great Bodhisattvas exists within every person; it is not separate from the one mind. To awaken to this is—
It is so. Now, practitioners of the Way do not awaken within their own minds, but instead cling to external appearances and grasp at objects outside the mind;

all such actions turn their backs on the Way. As for the sands of the Ganges, the Buddha said they are sand. When the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Śakra, Brahmā, and the various devas walk upon them, the sand does not rejoice;
when cattle, sheep, insects, and ants tread upon them, the sand does not feel anger. Precious...
Whether it be the fragrance of jewels or the stench of excrement and urine, the sand remains neither greedy nor loathsome. This mind is the mind that is no-mind; it is free from all marks.
There is no further distinction between sentient beings and Buddhas. To simply be able to be without mind is itself the ultimate realization.
If a student of the Way does not directly become mindless, they will never achieve the Way even after practicing through many kalpas. [Created] by Daoxuan.

Committing evil or performing good are both attachments to signs (*nimitta*). To commit evil while attached to signs is to undergo the cycle of rebirth in vain; to perform good while attached to signs is to undergo toil and hardship in vain.
Neither is as good as immediately recognizing the fundamental Dharma for oneself upon hearing these words.

This Dharma is the mind; there is no dharma outside the mind. This mind is the Dharma; there is no mind outside the Dharma. The mind itself is mindless, yet there is also no one who is "mindless. Take this up...
The mind is no-mind; yet the mind becomes existent. It is merely a matter of silent resonance, transcending all thought and deliberation.
Therefore it is said: "The path of language is cut off; the sphere of mental activity is extinguished. This mind is the Buddha of primordial purity; everyone possesses it.

From the wriggling insects to the sentient beings that harbor life, they are of one essence with the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, no different at all. Deeply awaken to this through personal realization; right here and now is it. It is perfect and complete.
It is complete; nothing more is lacking.
The Master said: "If you wish to know the essential secret, simply do not place a single thing upon the mind.

It is said that the Buddha’s true Dharma-body is like empty space. This is a metaphor for the fact that the Dharma-body is precisely empty space, and empty space is precisely the Dharma-body. Ordinary people..."
This means that the Dharma-body pervades all places of space, and space contains the Dharma-body.
One does not realize that the Dharma-body is itself space, nor that space is itself the Dharma-body. If one definitively asserts that space exists, then space is not the Dharma-body;
if one definitively asserts that the Dharma-body exists, then the Dharma-body is not space. However, do not interpret it as being space; space is [the Dharma-body].

Regarding the *dharmakāya*: do not form a conceptual understanding of it as a "body. The *dharmakāya* is itself empty space (*ākāśa*). There is no distinct characteristic between empty space and the *dharmakāya*.

There is no distinct characteristic between the Buddha and sentient beings. There is no distinct characteristic between birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) and nirvāṇa. There is no distinct characteristic between afflictions (*kleśa*) and awakening (*bodhi*).
To be free from all characteristics is itself the Buddha. Ordinary people grasp at objects; practitioners of the Way grasp at the mind. Mind and objects...
The simultaneous forgetting of both is the true Dharma. Forgetting the objective realm is relatively easy; forgetting the mind is extremely difficult.

People do not dare to forget the mind, fearing they will fall into emptiness where there is no place to grasp. They do not realize that emptiness is fundamentally without emptiness, being nothing other than the single True Dharma-realm.
Now, for one who studies the Way: if at all times the mind harbors the view of permanence, this is the eternalist heresy;
if one contemplates all phenomena as empty and forms a view of emptiness, this is the nihilist heresy. Therefore, the three realms are but mind, and the myriad dharmas are but consciousness.
If one speaks only of the derivative and not the fundamental, speaking only of awakening and not of delusion, [one remains within these extremes].

He does not speak of essence; he speaks only of function. There is, in total, no place for you to engage in discourse. All dharmas are fundamentally non-existent, yet now they are not non-existent either.
Conditioned arising is non-existent; the cessation of conditions is not non-existent. They were fundamentally non-existent because the fundamental itself is not fundamental.
The mind is not mind, for the mind is non-mind. Characteristics are not characteristics, for characteristics are non-characteristics. Thus it is said:
"Without dharmas and without the fundamental mind, one first understands the mind and mental phenomena. Dharmas are themselves non-dharmas; non-dharmas are themselves dharmas.
Without dharma and without non-dharma, this is precisely the mind and mental phenomena. Since this is so, one knows that the nature of all dharmas is inherently thus. This is...

Do not worry about it or overthink it. If one says that the preceding thought is ordinary and the succeeding thought is holy—like the turning of a hand over—it represents the ultimate of the teachings of the Three Vehicles.

According to our Zen school, however, the preceding thought is not ordinary, nor is the succeeding thought holy; the preceding thought is not the Buddha, nor is the succeeding thought a sentient being. Therefore:
All forms are the Buddha’s form; all sounds are the Buddha’s sound. To apply this to a single principle, it is so for all principles.
To see one thing is to see all things; to see one mind is to see all minds; to see one path is to see all paths.
There is nowhere that is not the Path. To see a single speck of dust is to see the mountains, rivers, and great earth of the worlds of the ten directions.
It is so for all things. To see a single drop of water is to see all the waters of the nature of the worlds in the ten directions.
Furthermore, to see all phenomena is to see the universal mind. All phenomena are fundamentally empty, yet the mind is not non-existent. That which is not non-existent is wondrous existence.
Existence is also non-existence; non-existence is itself existence. This is the wondrous existence of true emptiness.
Since this is so, the worlds of the ten directions do not transcend my single mind, and all lands of even the finest dust do not transcend my single thought.
If this is the case, what can be said of "internal" and "external"? It is like the nature of honey being sweet: all honey is thus. Thus does the world arise.
The world—including the six realms and four modes of birth, the mountains, rivers, and the great earth, whether possessing nature or lacking it—is fundamentally of one single substance.

To say they are "the same" means that names and appearances are empty; existence is empty, and non-existence is empty. Throughout worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, there is fundamentally but this one emptiness.
Therefore, when Master Bodhidharma came from the Western Heaven to this land, having passed through countless countries, he...
Having found a single Great Master, he secretly transmitted the Mind-Seal (citta-mudrā) to seal your original mind.

Using the mind to seal the Dharma, and using the Dharma to seal the mind—since the mind is thus, the Dharma is also thus. Identical to the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi), equal to the nature of phenomena (dharmatā).

Within the emptiness of the nature of phenomena, who is the person receiving the prediction (vyākaraṇa)? Who is the person becoming a Buddha? Who is the person attaining the Dharma? He clearly [said] toward...
"You say that Bodhi cannot be attained by means of the body, because the body is without marks; it cannot be attained by means of the mind, because the mind is without marks;
nor can it be attained by means of nature, because nature is precisely the original source-nature, the true and heavenly Buddha."
One cannot attain Buddhahood by means of a Buddha; one cannot attain the signless by means of the signless; one cannot attain emptiness by means of emptiness;
one cannot attain the Path by means of the Path. Originally there is nothing to be attained; even non-attainment cannot be attained.
Therefore it is said: there is not a single dharma that can be attained. It is only to cause you to realize your own original mind. At the moment of realization, there is no mark of realization;
even the marks of neither realizing nor not realizing cannot be found. Regarding such a dharma, those who attain it simply attain it.
Those who attain it do not consciously perceive it as attainment; those who do not attain it likewise do not consciously perceive it as non-attainment. Such is this dharma. From...
Since the time [the Buddha] ascended to heaven, how many people have been able to know this? That is why it is said: "How many people in the world have forgotten themselves? The Master said:

"Ordinary people are mostly hindered by objects in their minds and hindered by affairs in their principles. They constantly wish to flee from objects in order to settle the mind, and to screen out affairs in order to preserve the principle.
Yet they do not realize that it is actually their own minds that hinder objects and their principles that hinder affairs. One must simply cause the mind to be empty so that objects..."
It is empty by its own nature. One should simply allow the principle to be tranquil so that phenomena are naturally tranquil; do not apply the mind perversely.

Ordinary people for the most part are unwilling to let the mind be empty, fearing they will fall into nihilism, yet they do not realize that their own minds are fundamentally empty. The foolish eliminate phenomena but do not eliminate the mind;
the wise eliminate the mind but do not eliminate phenomena.

Addressing the assembly: Since the Tathāgata entrusted the Dharma to Kāśyapa, mind has been sealed with mind; mind and mind have not differed. If the seal is applied to emptiness, the seal does not produce a pattern.
If the seal is applied to phenomena, the seal does not produce a dharma. Therefore, it is by means of mind sealing mind.
Mind and mind are not different. That which can seal and that which is sealed are both difficult to bring into accord; therefore, those who attain it are few.
Yet, mind is itself no-mind, and attainment is itself no-attainment.
One day he said: "A student of Prajñā does not perceive that there is a single dharma to be attained. They sever their intent toward the Three Vehicles, for there is only the one true reality.
It cannot be called 'attained through realization. To claim, 'I can realize' or 'I can attain,' is the mark of those with overweening pride (*adhimāna*).
Those who rose and left the assembly at the Lotus Sūtra were all of this sort. Therefore, the Buddha said: 'In truth, I have no [realization] regarding Bodhi...'"

What is attained is merely a matter of silent resonance. When an ordinary person is about to die, they should simply contemplate that the five aggregates are all empty, the four elements are without self, and the true mind is not permanent—neither going nor coming. At the time of birth, the nature does not come; at the time of death, the nature does not go.
It is profoundly still and perfectly quiescent, where mind and object are one as such. If one can thus directly and suddenly realize this, one will not be [bound by it].
Though bound by the three periods of time, one is indeed a person who has transcended the world. One must not harbor even a fraction of intentional striving.
If auspicious signs appear—such as the Buddhas coming to welcome you or various manifestations appearing before you—one should have no mind to follow them.
If inauspicious signs appear in various ways, one should likewise have no mind of fear. Simply forget the mind and become identical with the Dharma-realm; thus one attains [liberation].
"Self-mastery. This is precisely the essential point.
The Master said, "In this Chan school of mine, which has been transmitted from antiquity, we have never taught people to seek knowledge or seek understanding."

To speak merely of "studying the Way" is already a term used for the purpose of guiding others. Yet, the Way cannot be studied; if one harbors an attachment to intellectual understanding, one instead becomes deluded regarding the Way.
The Way has no fixed location and is named the Mahayana mind. This mind does not exist within, without, or in between.
In reality, it has no location or direction. First, one must not form conceptual understandings of it. When emotional measurements are exhausted, the mind has no location or direction.
This Way is celestial and natural; fundamentally, it has no name.

A monk asked, "Delusion can obstruct one's own mind; I wonder, by what means may delusion now be dispelled? The Master said, "To give rise to delusion and then seek to dispel it also constitutes delusion.

Delusion originally has no root; it exists only because of conceptual discrimination. You need only exhaust all emotional attachments regarding both the ordinary and the sagely, and delusion will naturally vanish.
You must not harbor even the slightest trace of reliance or attachment. The monk said, "Since there is no longer any reliance or attachment, then—"
"How is it transmitted? The Master said, "It is transmitted mind-to-mind. [The questioner] asked, "If it is transmitted as mind, why do you say that mind also does not exist?
The Master said, "Not grasping a single dharma is called 'transmitting the mind. If one realizes this mind, it is precisely no-mind and no-dharma."

[The student] said: "If there is neither mind nor dharma, how can it be called 'transmission'? The Master said: "When you heard that the mind was transmitted, did you think there was something to be obtained?
Therefore, the Patriarch said: 'When one recognizes the nature of mind, it may be called inconceivable;
when it is clearly understood, nothing is obtained; when it is obtained, one does not speak of knowing. If I were to try to make you understand this matter, how could you possibly endure it?"
Question: "The Master is currently preaching the Dharma. How can you say that there is neither Sangha nor Dharma? The Master said:
"If you perceive that there is a Dharma to be preached, you are seeking me through sound and voice. If you perceive a self, that is a locus. There is neither Dharma nor non-Dharma;
Dharma is itself the mind. Therefore, the Patriarch said: 'When this mind-Dharma is transmitted, what dharma is there to be transmitted?'"

The Dharma has never existed; there is no dharma and no fundamental mind. Only when one first understands that every moment of mind and its phenomena are truly such that not a single dharma can be apprehended is this called "sitting at the site of enlightenment" (*bodhimaṇḍa*).
As for the "site of enlightenment," it is simply the non-arising of various views and the realization that all dharmas are fundamentally empty; this is called the "empty *tathāgatagarbha*.
Originally there was not a single thing; where could there be any dust? If one attains the meaning within this, what need is there for anything else? One wanders freely and at ease.
Treatise. Question:

"If the sage’s lack of mind is itself Buddhahood, then when an ordinary person lacks mind, does he not sink into empty stillness? The Master said: "In the Dharma, there are no ordinary persons or sages, nor is there any sinking into stillness.
The Dharma is fundamentally non-existent; do not form the view of 'non-existence. The Dharma is fundamentally non-non-existent; do not [form the view of existence]."
To create views of existence or non-existence is entirely a product of emotional perception; it is like an illusory cataract. Thus it is said:
"Seeing and hearing are like illusory cataracts; cognition and awareness are but sentient beings. Within the school of the Patriarchs, one speaks only of ceasing mental activity and forgetting views.
Therefore, when mental activity is forgotten, the Buddha-way flourishes; when there is discrimination, the demonic armies blaze.
Question: Since the fundamental nature is already Buddha, how can there still be the various different forms and appearances of the four modes of birth and the six realms? The Master said:

"The essence of all Buddhas is perfect and complete, with nothing further to increase or decrease. Flowing into the six realms, it is perfect everywhere. Amidst the myriad species, every single one is Buddha.
It is like a ball of quicksilver that, when scattered in various places, remains perfectly round in every single grain."
There is no distinction of time; it is simply one single mass. This one is all, and all is this one. These various forms and appearances are like houses:

leaving the house of an ass, one enters the house of a human; leaving the human body, one reaches the body of a deva, and so on, up to the houses of śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and buddhas—all these are places where you take up and discard.
It is for this reason that they appear distinct, yet their fundamental nature remains the same.
How could there be any difference?
Chan Master Changqing Da'an of Xuefeng once entered the mountains and found a piece of wood; its shape resembled a snake. He inscribed upon its back: "The Original..."
It is naturally so; it requires no carving or polishing. Entrusting this to the Master, the Master said: "A mountain dweller of true character leaves behind no traces of axe or hatchet.
— Master Qingtian.
While the Master was brewing tea with the Senior Monk Tiao, the Master struck the rope-bench three times. Tiao also struck it three times.
The Master said, "When this old monk strikes, there is a skillful means; when you, Senior Monk, strike, what principle is there? Tiao replied, "It is I who strike."
"There is a skillful means. The Master struck [the table]. "What was that? The teacher held up a tea bowl.
Tao said, "The eye of a good spiritual friend must indeed be like this. After the tea was finished, Tao asked again, "Master, what was the meaning of holding up the bowl just now?
The teacher said, "It cannot be anything other than this."
Chan Master Huánzhōng of Mount Dàcí in Hángzhōu:
Chan Master Huánzhōng of Mount Dàcí in Hángzhōu was a native of the Lú clan from Púsān.

Having studied under Bǎizhàng and received the mind-seal, he took his leave and went to Chánglè Temple on Mount Nányuè, where he thatched a hut upon the mountain peak. One day, Nánquán arrived and asked, "What is..."
"Who is the master of this hut? The Master said, "Heaven! Heaven! Nanquan said, "Setting aside 'Heaven' for a moment, who is the master of this hut?
The Master said, "If you understand, then understand; do not be so talkative. Nanquan shook out his sleeves and departed.
The monk took his leave. The Master asked, "Where are you going? He replied, "To Jiangxi. The Master said, "I have a certain matter that troubles me;
can you take it with you? He asked, "What matter do you have, Reverend? The Master said, "Can you take this old monk along?
He replied, "Even those who are superior to the Reverend could not take him along either. The Master then desisted. Later, the monk related this incident to Dongshan.
Dongshan said, "How can you, Reverend, speak in such a manner? The monk asked, "How about you, Master? Dongshan said, "Attained.
Dongshan then asked the monk, "What other words or phrases did Daci have? The monk replied, "At times he addressed the assembly, saying:"
"To speak ten feet is not as good as practicing one foot; to speak one foot is not as good as practicing one inch.
Dongshan said, "I do not speak in that way. [The monk] asked, "How then, Master? Dongshan said, "Speak that which cannot be practiced;
practice that which cannot be spoken."
A monk asked Chan Master Shishuang Xingkong, “What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West? The Master said, “Suppose there were a person in a thousand-foot well;
if you could get this person out without using even a foot of rope, then I would answer you regarding the meaning of his coming from the West. The monk said, “Recently, Chang [of Hunan]...”
When the Master [Nanquan] appeared in the world, he spoke of this and that for the sake of others. The Master called out, "Novice!
Drag this corpse out! This novice was Yangshan. Later, Yangshan asked Danyuan, "How can one get the person out of the well?
Danyuan said, "Tsk! You fool! Who is in the well? Yangshan then asked Guishan. Guishan called out, "Huiji! Yangshan responded, "Yes?"
Yangshan said, "He has emerged. After Yangshan took up residence [at Mount Yang], he would often cite these former words to the assembly, saying, "I received my name at Danyuan's place;
I received my ground at Guishan's place."
Chan Master Jingcen Zhaoxian of Changsha ascended the hall and said:
"If I were to exclusively exalt the teachings and the tradition, the grass before the Dharma Hall would surely grow a fathom deep.
Having no other choice, I shall speak to you all: the entire world of the ten directions is the eye of the śramaṇa; the entire world of the ten directions..."
The realms constitute the entire body of the śramaṇa. The worlds of the ten directions are one's own radiance;
the worlds of the ten directions are entirely contained within one's own radiance. Throughout the worlds of the ten directions, there is not a single person who is not oneself.
I have always told you all: the Buddhas of the three periods of time and the sentient beings of the dharma-realm are the light of Mahāprajñā.
Before the light has been emitted, where do you all turn for full understanding? Before the light has been emitted, there is not even a trace of Buddha or sentient beings;
from where could mountains, rivers, and lands have come? At that time, a monk asked, "What is the eye of a śramaṇa?
