Although the Master had traveled extensively through various monastic communities, he had merely followed the crowd and had not sought out any instruction or inquiry.

A monk asked Zen Master Fayan, "How can one suddenly bring all conditions to rest throughout the twelve periods of the day? Fayan said, "Is emptiness a condition for you? Is form a condition for you?"
"Is it that which serves as a condition? [The master asked. "If you say emptiness serves as the condition, then emptiness fundamentally has no conditions.

If you say form serves as the condition, then form and mind are not two. In your daily life, what thing actually serves as a condition for you? When the teacher heard this, he was struck with awe and marveled at him.
Furthermore, another person asked: "What is one drop of water from the Cao source? Fayan said: "This is one drop of water from the Cao source. Thereupon—
The Master attained great enlightenment beneath the seat; all the doubts and stagnations of his life were dissolved like melting ice.
Moved to tears that soaked his robes, Fayan said, "You shall greatly propagate my school. Go now; do not let yourself be hindered."
Master Ming of Xingjiao asked: "Kāśyapa held Śākyamuni’s robe—sixteen feet in length—at Mount Kukkuṭapāda, awaiting Maitreya’s descent.
When he shall don that sixteen-foot robe upon his thousand-foot body, it will fit perfectly according to measure."
"If Śākyamuni’s body is sixteen feet tall and Maitreya’s body is one thousand chi tall, is it that his body understands shortness, or is it that his robe understands length?
The Master said, "You understand this, after all. He then vigorously shook out his sleeves and went out.
The Master said, "Little fellow, had I answered you as 'not so,' there would have been cause and effect. If you are not [as you claim], I shall see to it."
On the seventh day after Ming’s arrival, he spat up blood. Master Fuguang urged him, saying, “Go quickly to repent.
Ming went to the master’s quarters and wept bitterly, saying, “I pray that the Master will have compassion and grant me permission to repent.

The Master said, “It is like a person who falls to the ground and rises by means of the ground; I have never taught you how to rise from a fall. Ming spoke again, “If you grant me permission to repent, I shall—”
He served the Master for the rest of his life. The Master spoke these words for him: "The Way of Buddha after Buddha is equal, yet it appears as high and low;
Śākyamuni and Maitreya are like a seal impressing clay."
A monk asked, "I have heard it said of old: 'If a person sees Prajñā, they are bound by Prajñā;
if a person does not see Prajñā, they are also bound by Prajñā. Since they see Prajñā, why are they instead bound by it?
The Master said, "Tell me, what do you see when you speak of seeing Prajñā? The monk said, "Since one does not see Prajñā, why is one also bound? The Master said, "You..."
Where does the Way not see *prajñā*? It is said: "If one sees *prajñā*, it is not called *prajñā*;
if one does not see *prajñā*, it is likewise not called *prajñā*. Furthermore, how can one speak of seeing or not seeing? Therefore, the ancients said:
If one dharma is lacking, the Dharmakāya is not realized; if one dharma is superfluous, the Dharmakāya is not realized.
If there is even one dharma, the Dharmakāya is not realized; if there is not even one dharma, the Dharmakāya is not realized. This is the true essence of Prajñā.
Addressing the assembly: The True Teaching is non-dual; the myriad virtues are beyond words. At this very moment of clarity, it is like a king’s precious sword.
Therefore, the Tathāgata attains equal and perfect enlightenment in all places; he attains equal and perfect enlightenment even upon mountains of knives and trees of swords.
One attains equal and perfect enlightenment within the cauldrons and burning coals; one attains equal and perfect enlightenment beneath the staff;

one attains equal and perfect enlightenment beneath the shout. Therefore, whether in motion or stillness, departing or arriving, arising or ceasing, there has never been the slightest mark of difference, nor the slightest mark of distinction;
there is not even a hair’s breadth or a thread’s width of anything further to be done.
The mind-consciousness understands through seeing and hearing. Why is this? It is because the path of right and wrong is utterly severed; it is the wondrous nature and celestial faculty.
Thus it is said: "When you are born, I am also born; when you kill, I also kill. Birth and killing are the mechanism of the Wheel-Turning King, racing back and forth like flashing lightning.

Ascending the hall, he said: "The Buddha-dharma is already perfected; all things are fully complete. Have you not heard it said: 'Perfectly identical to the great void, lacking nothing and having no excess'?
If this is so, then who is deficient and who is redundant? Who is right and who is wrong? Who is one who understands and who is one who does not understand?
Therefore it is said: 'Going eastward is also the Venerable One; going westward is also the Venerable One. South..."
Going west is also the Elder; going north is also the Elder. For what reason do they instead become east, west, south, and north?
If you can understand this, the paths of seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing will naturally be cut off, and all dharmas will manifest before you. Why is this so?
Because the Dharmakāya is formless, yet forms appear before every eye; Prajñā is without cognition, yet it reflects in response to conditions—all at once.
"Understand this thoroughly, all you elders. How should one who has left the household life act?
This is the principle inherent within; it is not something extraordinary. To recognize the mind and reach the source is why one is called a śramaṇa.
If you recognize the mind, it is luminously clear, truly without the slightest obstruction. Elders, you have stood for a long time; take care."
Ascending the hall, [the Master said]: "The skillful means of the ancient sages are as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. The Patriarch said: 'It is not the wind or the banner that moves;
it is the mind of the wise man that moves. This is the Dharma-gate of the unsurpassed Mind-Seal. We are disciples under the Patriarch’s lineage; how should we understand the Patriarch’s intent?
Do not say that the wind and banner do not move while your own mind moves falsely. Do not say that you do not stir the wind."
Regarding the "banners": this refers generally to both the wind and the banners. Do not merely ask, "What is it that moves when the wind and banners move?

Some say that one clarifies the mind by means of objects, yet need not recognize the objects themselves. Others say that form is itself emptiness. Still others say that it is neither the wind nor the banners that move;

rather, one must have a wondrous realization. If one understands and interprets it in such ways, how does it relate to the intent of the Patriarch? Since such interpretations are not permitted, [what then is the truth?]
All you elders should know this for yourselves: if one attains thorough awakening here, what dharma-gate would not be clarified?
One will simultaneously and completely penetrate the skillful means of hundreds of thousands of Buddhas; what further doubt could there be? Thus the ancients said:
"One thing understood, a thousand things are clear; one thing deluded, ten thousand things are confused."

Ascending the hall, [the Master said]: "A hair swallows the vast ocean, yet the nature of the ocean remains unimpaired. A tiny speck is cast upon a sharp blade, yet the keenness of the blade remains unmoved.

Whether one sees or does not see, whether one realizes or does not realize—it is known only by me. Thereupon, he spoke this verse: "Having momentarily descended from the high peak, it has already been proclaimed:
Prajñā is perfectly pervasive throughout the ten directions. The vast expanse of humans and devas is without distinction; The Dharma-realm extends vertically and horizontally everywhere."

"Manifested in the dwelling. Take care. He ascended the hall and said: "The ancients said: 'What is Chan? The three realms are vast and continuous. What is the Way? The ten directions are expansive and boundless.
Why do they say 'the three realms are vast and continuous'? Where is the principle of the 'ten directions being expansive and boundless'? He paused, seeking [a response].

Do you understand? The eyes are blocked; the ears are blocked; the tongue, body, and mind are blocked. There is no place for vacancy, and there is no place for movement. How do you, Venerable One, understand this?
It cannot be grasped horizontally; it cannot be grasped vertically; it cannot be extended; it cannot be seized.
There is no place for the application of the mind, nor is there any place for contrivance. If you can understand in this way, only then will you understand the Dharma.
The gate is cut off from discrimination; all speech is cut off from leakage. Once there was a monk who asked, "What is speech that is cut off from leakage?
I said to him, "The mouth is like the nostrils—how excellent! If you, Elder, understand it in this way, naturally there will be no passing through.

[The Master] ascends the hall. A monk asks, "One who wishes to enter the ocean of non-action must first board the boat of prajñā. What is the boat of prajñā?

Question: An ancient worthy said, "To ascend to heaven one does not rely on a ladder; throughout the earth there is no path to walk.

What is "to ascend to heaven without relying on a ladder"? The Master said: "Not leaving behind even a single thread or hair's breadth of ground. [The questioner] asked: "What is 'throughout the earth there is no path to walk'? The Master said:

"What did I just tell you? He replied: "The hundreds of thousands of gates of samādhi, the hundreds of thousands of gates of supernatural powers, and the hundreds of thousands of gates of wondrous function—all do not transcend the ocean of prajñā.
Why is this? Because all dharmas are established upon the foundation of non-abiding. Therefore it is said:
birth and extinction, coming and going, the heterodox and the orthodox, movement and stillness—these thousand transformations and myriad changes are [all within it]."
The great samādhi gates of all Buddhas do not surpass this. All you venerable elders, investigate this thoroughly!

Soil. Question: "A student has come here; we request the Master to preach the Dharma. The Master said: "Birds chirp in the forest; fish swim beneath the water. Ascending the hall:
On the summit of Mount Sumeru, the golden bell is not struck; within the Bimbā Rock, no one gathers. This mountain monk rides backward upon the Buddha Hall;
all you people wear straw sandals on your heads. In the morning you roam Mount Tandi; by evening you arrive at Mount Luofu. [Holds up] the staff.
[The Master] took up a needle case himself.
He ascended the hall and said, "Though patch-robed monks may speak horizontally or vertically, they do not yet know the eye upon the crown of the head.

At that time, a monk asked, "What is the eye upon the crown of the head? The Master said, "The robe is worn through and the bare bones are exposed; the roof is broken and one sleeps gazing at the stars."
Ascending the hall, when the assembly had gathered and settled, he said: "If you say 'Not well? upon entering, it can exhaust ten thousand taels of gold.
If you say 'Take care' upon leaving, it can likewise exhaust the offerings of the four worlds. If you treat this as a matter of Buddhist doctrine..."
"A single drop of water is difficult to dissolve. If you deliberate upon this as if it were a matter of no concern, you are like someone with grit in their eye.
But how is it, then? After a long silence, he said: "Do you understand? Take care."
Ascending the hall, [the Master] said: "To be a true patriarch, one must drive the plowman’s ox and seize the hungry man’s food;
when encountering the base, one makes it noble, and when encountering the noble, one makes it base. Driving the plowman’s ox ensures his crops flourish;
seizing the hungry man’s food ensures he is forever freed from hunger and thirst. Encountering the base and making it noble means turning soil into gold; encountering the noble and making it base..."
I transform gold into earth. This old monk neither drives the plowman’s ox nor takes the hungry man’s food.
Why is this? What use have I for the plowman’s ox? What food have I to eat?
I do not grasp earth and turn it into gold, nor do I transform gold into earth. Why? Because gold is gold, and earth is earth. It is jade.
This is jade; that is stone. This is the monastic community; that is the laity. The heavens and earth of past and present. The sun and moon of past and present.
The mountains and rivers of past and present. The human relations of past and present. Although it is thus, once the Great San Pass is broken through, how many will encounter Bodhidharma while lost?

Ascending the hall, [the Master said]: "A wild goose flies across the vast sky; its shadow sinks into the cold water. The goose has no intention of leaving a trace, and the water has no mind to retain the shadow.
If you can be thus, only then will you understand how to walk among those of different species. There is no need to lengthen the ducks or shorten the cranes, nor to level mountains or fill valleys.
When let go, there are a hundred uglinesses and a thousand clumsinesses; when gathered in, there is a clutching and a grasping. To employ it..."
"I dare to compete with the Eight Great Dragon Kings in wealth. "Not needed; it is not worth even half a cent. [Case closed. Ascending the hall, he said:
"The skull is constantly interacting with the world; the nostrils touch upon the family style.

When the banana tree hears thunder, it blooms; the sunflower turns toward the sun. You people of virtue, when the banana tree hears thunder and blooms, does it have ears? When the sunflower turns toward the sun..."
It turns. Is there still an eye? If you can understand this, the Western Heaven is this very land. If you cannot understand it, seven times nine is sixty-three. Pack it up!

Ascending the hall, he said: "The spiritual source is devoid of traces, yet the physical body manifests everywhere. The Dharma is free from the extremes of annihilation and permanence; existence and non-existence cannot be pointed out. Therefore it is said:
'In every speck of dust one does not see the Buddha; in every world-system one does not hear the sutras.

If you wish to understand the direct transmission received at Vulture Peak, look at the sun by day and the stars by night. After a long silence, he said: "If you go to other places, do not speak of this mistakenly. Study!"
Ascending the hall, [the Master said]: "The realms of infinite lands are not separated from one another by so much as a hair’s tip.
Tell me, what Dharma does the Tathāgata of the Immovable World, Wondrous Joy, preach? The ten ages of past and present do not depart from the present moment.
As for the very first assembly of the Buddha King of Awesome Sound—how many people did he deliver? If you are a master who penetrates all quarters, try to explain."
"Look at the Way. After a long silence, he said: "Difficult is the journey! Difficult is the journey! Look for yourself at the summit of the ten-thousand-fathom peak.
Ascending the hall, a monk asked: "Heaven cannot cover him; earth cannot support him. Pray tell, who is this person? The Master said:
He dug into the ground and buried [the object] deeply. He asked, "Will this person still receive an arrangement? The Master said, "Add more mud upon the earth.
The Master asked a monk: "A handless man can throw a punch; a tongueless man understands speech.
Suddenly, the handless man strikes the tongueless man. What does the tongueless man say?"
Two Verses on the Emptiness of Form: Form is empty; emptiness is form; form is empty; emptiness is form. The pass at Tongguan is blocked, and the road is impassable.
When the kalpa-fire blazes forth and even the finest hairs are consumed, the green mountains remain as they were amidst the white clouds. East, west, south, north—ten thousand eight thousand li.

Chan Master Yuquan Chenghao was nicknamed "Hao the Cloth Pants" by the monastic community. One day, for the sake of Zhang Wujin, he cited the verse of Master Fu Dashi:
"Holding a hoe in empty hands, Walking while riding a water buffalo. A person passes over the bridge; The bridge flows, but the water does not. Furthermore...
The case is cited. Dongshan’s verse says: “On the summit of Mount Wutai, clouds steam rice; before the steps of the Buddha Hall, it is a dog-urine sky.

A monk asked Chan Master Yongming Yanshou, "What is the wondrous principle of Yongming? The Master said, "Add more incense. The monk said, "Thank you for your instruction, Master."
The Master said, "For now, rejoice that there is no connection. The monk bowed. The Master said, "Listen to this verse:
'If you wish to know the purport of Yongming, there is a lake before the gate. When the sun shines, radiance arises; when the wind comes, waves stir.'"
Question: "What is the Great Perfect Mirror? The Master said: "A broken sand pot. Two monks came to attend upon him.
He then asked the head monk, "Have you ever been here before? He replied, "I have been here. He then asked the second senior monk, "Have you been here before?
He replied, "I have not been here. The Master said, "One has gained; one has lost. After a short while, an attendant monk asked:
"Regarding those two monks who just arrived, I do not know which one gained and which one lost. The Master asked, "Did you ever recognize these two monks?
He replied, "I have never recognized them. The Master said, "There is no different soil within the same pit."
The method of pointing [to the truth] takes the words of the Buddhas and Patriarchs as its standard. It is said: When Kāśyapa first heard the verse—"All phenomena arise from conditions;
all phenomena cease through conditions. My teacher, the Great Śramaṇa, has often spoken thus"—this was the very marrow and bone of the Buddhas and Patriarchs.
Nāgārjuna said: "There is no thing that arises from conditions; there is no thing that ceases through conditions. Arising is merely..."

Regarding dependent origination: when conditions cease, it is simply the cessation of those conditions. Thus one knows that when form arises, it is merely the arising of emptiness; when form ceases, it is merely the cessation of emptiness.
For example, the nature of wind is fundamentally non-moving; it moves only because of dependent origination. If the nature of wind were inherently moving, [it would never cease].
How, then, could there ever be a time of stillness? If there were wind within a sealed room, why would the wind not move?
If there is no wind, it arises as soon as it encounters conditions. It is not only wind that is thus; all phenomena (*dharma*) are likewise so.
Vimalakīrti said to Mañjuśrī: "He comes with the mark of not coming; he sees with the mark of not seeing. Mañjuśrī then replied: "It is so, Layman. If...
Having come, it does not come again; having gone, it does not go again. Why is this so? That which comes has no place from which it comes;
that which goes has no place to which it goes. What can be seen cannot be seen again. This is the principle of dependent origination as non-arising.

The intent of the teachings and the intent of the patriarchs share the same expedient means; ultimately, there is no separate principle. If he understands it clearly, then this too will be manifest.

One will also constantly see the Bhikṣu Meghaśrī, never for a single moment being parted from him. Do you still believe this?
Three Verses by Master Shuilu Benxian:
It is not the wind or the banner that moves; it is the benevolent mind that moves. This has been transmitted from antiquity down to the present day.
If those who wander as water and clouds wish to understand this hereafter, the Patriarch was truly a connoisseur of the Way. Furthermore, he said: "If you see form and [immediately]..."

Ascending the hall, [the Master] said: "The Avataṃsaka Sūtra proclaims that the Buddha-body fills the Dharma-realm. Is this truly so?

Now, if the Buddha-body already fills the Dharma-realm, then in the realms of Bodhisattvas, Pratyekabuddhas, Śrāvakas, humans, devas, asuras, hungry ghosts, hell-beings, and animals, there would be no place for them to stand.
To argue in such a manner is utterly preposterous. He searched for [a way to resolve this].

I have always taught that all phenomena which arise are but manifestations of the mind. Now tell me: are the six objects currently confronting your six sense faculties the same as you, or are they separate?
If they are the same, why do they not become a single mass? If they are separate, how can it be said that there is only this one mind?
You must apply yourself with great vigor; the Buddha-dharma is no trivial matter.
Ascending the hall, [the Master] said: "In the teachings of Tiantai, the three gates of Mañjuśrī, Avalokiteśvara, and Samantabhadra are explained.
The gate of Mañjuśrī is all forms; the gate of Avalokiteśvara is all sounds; the gate of Samantabhadra is to arrive without moving a step.
My teaching, however, holds that the gate of Mañjuśrī is not all forms; the gate of Avalokiteśvara is not all sounds; the gate of Samantabhadra..."
"Gatekeeper! What is this? Do not speak as if you have left behind the teachings of Tiantai.
There is nothing to it; withdraw for now. Ascending the hall, he said: "All of you, when you sleep soundly at night, you are unaware of anything.
Since you are unaware of anything, let me ask you: at that time, does your original nature exist, or does it not exist? If you say it exists..."

To be unaware of anything at all is no different from death. If one says that the Way has no original nature, yet when suddenly awakening from sleep, one’s awareness is as it was before—do you understand?
To be unaware of anything at all is no different from death; when suddenly awakening from sleep, one’s awareness is as it was before. At such times as these, what is this?
If you do not understand, each of you must investigate it for yourselves. There is nothing else to it; do not be idle.

Lilxingjiao Hongshou Chan Master was once working together with National Teacher Huizhong when he heard a piece of firewood fall and attained realization. He composed a verse, saying: "The falling was not caused by anything else."

After he had finished his discourse, the Minister Wang Sui came to visit the Master one day. The Master sat naturally, wrapped in a coarse woolen robe and basking in the sun.

The Minister bowed down; the Master pushed aside his rush-mat seat and sat on the bare ground with him. They conversed with laughter all day long before the Minister departed. A disciple remonstrated with the Master, saying:
"This entire assembly looks up to him; how can you fail to show him due respect? Later, when the King came again, the Master went forward to meet him.
The King said, "Why do you not appear as you did on the previous day? The Master replied, "I would have been able to do so, Minister, but what of the administrative official's anger?
The King held him in even higher esteem.
Master Yunju Daoji said to his disciples:
"Dharma Master Bodhidharma stated that among the scriptures of this land, only the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* can serve as a seal for the mind.
As I read this sūtra, there is a verse which says: 'All dharmas have no essence; it is taught that they are nothing but mind. If one does not perceive one's own mind...'"
Yet, discrimination still arises. This may be called the Great Compassionate Father’s discourse on reality as it truly is;
we ourselves simply fail to receive it, carrying our ingratitude back like the sands of the Ganges. Someone asked: "In that case, does one sever discrimination upon seeing one's own mind?
The Master said: "It is not so. It is like training a horse: when the horse sees its own reflection, it is not startled. Why?"
For this reason—because one knows for oneself that the shadow arises from one's own body—I know by this that one must not cease discernment, yet must also relinquish the characteristics of the mind.
Observe now before you as it truly is; not even a hair’s breadth is to be seen. The Patriarch said:
If one perceives the present, one should likewise perceive the past and the future; if one does not perceive the past and the future, one should likewise not perceive the present.
These words are clear and distinct, yet people remain deluded and confused.

When a monk was standing in attendance upon Zen Master Huanglong Huinan, the Master gazed at him for a long time and then asked, "I shall tell you of all the hundreds of thousands of samādhis and immeasurable wondrous gates as a single phrase;
will you believe it? The monk replied, "If these are the Honored One’s sincere words, how could I dare not believe them? The Master—

Pointing to his left, the Master said, "Come over this way. As the monk was about to move toward it, the Master rebuked him, saying, "Chasing after sounds and pursuing forms—when will you ever reach the end?
Get out! Another monk, understanding this, immediately stepped forward. The Master repeated his previous words and questioned him.
The monk replied, "How would I dare not believe? The Master again pointed to his left, saying, "Come over this way. The monk stood firm and did not go.
The Master rebuked him again, saying, "You have come to attend upon me, yet you do not listen to my words. Get out!
Later, when the old man Shun was in his twilight years, he had this to reveal: "Fundamentally, there is nothing to do; why seek anything from me?

Upon hearing this, the Master said to his attendant, "The old man is in his dotage. How can he take that which has business and make it non-business, or take that which is non-business and make it [so]?"
There was an occasion when he spoke of purifying the Buddha-land and bringing sentient beings to maturity.
In his quarters, the Master would regularly ask the assembly: "Every person has their place of birth; where is the Venerable One’s place of birth?"
While they were in the midst of a vigorous exchange of questions and answers, he reached out his hand and said, "How is my hand like the Buddha’s hand?
He then asked about what the masters from all quarters had attained through their studies, and again lowered his foot and said, "How is my foot like a donkey’s foot?

For over thirty years he presented these three questions, and no student was able to penetrate their essential meaning. The monastic communities throughout the land came to refer to them as the "Three Barriers."

as for the great earth, mountains, rivers, light, darkness, form, and space—all these phenomena manifest before you. How can you explain the principle of 'abandoning' them? At this point—

The Chan Master Yuanzhao, whose dharma name was Huelin Zongben, was visited by Uichon, the State Preceptor of Goryeo, who had been dispatched to the imperial court as a prince on a mission from his kingdom.

Having heard of the Master’s reputation, Uichon requested an audience in the manner of a disciple and inquired about what he had attained. When [Uichon] cited the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* in response, the Master said: "The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* is the three bodies..."
"Does the Buddha speak as the Reward Body (Sambhogakāya), the Transformation Body (Nirmāṇakāya), or the Dharma Body (Dharmakāya)? The student said, "He speaks as the Dharma Body.

The Master asked, "The Dharma Body pervades all lands throughout the sands of the Ganges. Where, then, were the members of the audience standing or sitting at that time? The student was bewildered and had no reply.
Chan Master Huanglong Zuixin Huītáng Bǎojiào was conversing with Xià Yìgōnglì.

When they reached the section in Sengzhào’s *Treatise on Awakening* concerning "uniting all things within oneself" and "sentient and insentient beings sharing a single substance," there happened to be a dog lying beneath the incense table. The Master struck the dog with his ruler and struck it again.
Xiangzhuo said, "The dog has sentience and thus departs; the incense table lacks sentience and remains stationary.
How can sentience and insentience become one body? Gongli was unable to respond. The Master said, "As soon as one engages in discursive thought, it becomes a superfluous dharma.
When have you ever realized that the myriad things are oneself?"
Ascending the hall, [the Master said]: "If one clarifies only the self but does not awaken to what is before one's eyes, this person has eyes but no feet.
If one awakens to what is before one's eyes but does not clarify the self, this person has feet but no eyes.

According to these two types of people, throughout the twelve periods of the day, there is always something harbored within their chests. Since that thing is in the chest, the state of unease is constantly present before their eyes."
Since it is already present before you, every touch and movement becomes an obstruction. How can one attain stability? Did not the Patriarch say:
"To grasp it is to lose the measure; one will inevitably enter a deviant path. To let go naturally, its essence has neither going nor staying"?
In his room, the Master constantly raised his fist and asked the monks, "To call this a 'fist' is to encounter it;
not to call it a 'fist' is to turn one's back on it. What would you call it?"

He addressed the assembly, saying: "Where there is obstruction, it is not the wall; where there is penetration, there is no empty space. If you can understand it thus, mind and form are fundamentally the same.
This whisk is form; which one is mind? A person of keen intelligence, upon hearing this mentioned, sees the horns through the wall and immediately knows it is an ox.
If you hesitate or engage in deliberation, white clouds will stretch for thousands and tens of thousands of miles."
On the day Master Zhenjing Yun’an Baofeng opened the hall for formal discourse, he said:
"Cease your questioning for a moment. You know only to ask about the Buddha and the Dharma, yet you do not realize the source from which the Buddha-Dharma comes.
Tell me, from where does it come? He extended one leg and said: "In the past, Huanglong personally performed this."
An edict! None of the Buddhas of the ten directions dare to disobey it; none of the successive patriarchs or all the holy sages dare to transgress it.
All the immeasurable Dharma gates and all the wondrous meanings—the tongues of the old monks throughout the world have been sealed with a single seal from beginning to end.
None dared to differ. Since there was no difference, let us set it aside for now. Where is the seal? Do you see it? If you see it, you are neither monk nor layman;
without bias and without faction, I shall entrust it to each of you individually. If you do not see it, I shall take it back myself. Having finished collecting [the items], he gave a shout and said:
"The army follows the seal; the general pursues the talisman. The Buddha’s hand, the donkey’s feet, and the circumstances of birth—Old Man [Huangbo]."
"A good pain for thirty blows. Is there anyone in this assembly here who does not feel a sense of dissatisfaction?
If there is, it is truly extraordinary. If there is none, then the new Elder has been deceiving you all.
Chan Master Baoyun Shouduan addressed the assembly:
"If you can truly achieve a moment of breaking into a sweat, then upon a single blade of grass, the jade palaces and crystal halls will immediately manifest.
If you have not yet truly achieved a moment of breaking into a sweat, then even if there were jade palaces and crystal halls, they would instead become obstacles."
"A single stalk of grass covers it all. Now tell me, how can one get out of this sweat? After a long silence, he said:
"I have always had a pair of hands for the destitute; I have never easily performed the Three-Platform Dance."
Master Baoning Yong addressed the assembly, saying:
"That which belonged to the ancients is used by people of today; that which belongs to people of today was practiced by the ancients. Between ancient and modern, there is no front or back."
How many people have known this from ancient times to the present? Ye-wo-yi! Nineteen and twenty-nine—when they meet, they do not reach out their hands. It is also said:
A seedless spiritual sprout is planted in the midst of fire; iron flowers bloom upon the treetops. Suddenly, a round fruit is formed;
it is pointed out to people of the age as something found through diligent practice.
In the meditation hall, Zen Master Huanglong Siji Wuxin asked a monk:
"On the night of the last day of the month, when the sky is shrouded in darkness, suppose one were to apply five colors within that gloom.
If a hundred, or even ten thousand people, were to look at those colors in the night, would any of them be able to distinguish blue, yellow, red, or white? The monk remained silent.
The Master spoke on their behalf, saying: "Every single one is blind. He addressed the assembly, saying:
"Outside the mind there is no dharma, yet dharmas can be clarified. Outside dharmas there is no mind, yet the mind can be penetrated.
When it can be penetrated and can be clarified, mind and dharma constitute the complete school. When the school is complete, every dharma is the school; when the mind is complete, the mind..."
The mind is no-mind. Since the mind is already no-mind, one proceeds directly to its source. Having attained the source, one manifests a great body that fills the void of space;
one manifests a small body in which not even a speck of dust can stand. How is it that not even a speck of dust can stand?
After a long silence, he said: "A single drop of ink forms two dragons."
Chan Master Qingyuan Weixin ascended the hall.
The Master said: "Thirty years ago, before I had studied Chan, when I saw mountains, they were mountains; when I saw water, it was water.
Later, however, after I personally encountered a teacher and attained an entry point, when I saw mountains, they were not mountains; when I saw..."
Water is not water. Now one has attained a place of rest; as before, seeing mountains, they are simply mountains; seeing water, it is simply water.
Great assembly, are these three kinds of insight the same or different? Is there anyone who can distinguish between them?
"I grant you permission to see the old monk in person.
When the three Buddhas were conversing with Chan Master Wuzu Fayuan atop a pavilion at night, they returned to find that the lamp had already been extinguished. In the darkness, the Master said:
"Each of you must provide a turning word. Fojian said, "A colorful phoenix dances in the crimson sky.
Foyan said, "An iron snake lies across the ancient road. Foguo said, "Look beneath your feet. The Master said, "It is Kechin who will extinguish my school."
Addressing the assembly, [the Master] raised the following case: When Deshan answered a monk, "In my school there are no words or phrases," Xuefeng heard this and attained realization.
Later, Xuefeng said, "At that time, I went empty-handed and returned empty-handed. Regarding this causal occasion, the Master said:
"Today Baiyun will explain it for those who have not yet penetrated it. It is like a person coming from Dongjing; if you ask him where he has come from, he instead..."
He came from Suzhou. I asked him how matters were in Suzhou, and he said, "Everything is just as usual.
Even so, he could not deceive Baiyun. Why? It was simply because their dialects differed. But in the end, what is it?
The water chestnuts of Suzhou; the lotus roots of Shaobu.
The Master ascends the hall and says: "Regarding the matter of human life and destiny, first of all one must have the ○. If you wish to achieve this ○, you must first guard against the ○.
If you are a true ○ person, you will [attain] the ○○."

He addressed the assembly, saying: "I have come to this land from the outset to transmit the Dharma and save deluded beings. One flower opens and five petals emerge; the fruition is naturally accomplished.
Master Bodhidharma came with his feet and spoke with his mouth; yet the descendants of later generations have mostly fallen into calculating deliberation.
Do you wish to understand the place where the flowers bloom and the fruit ripens? Pear trees in Zhengzhou, jujubes in Qingzhou—among all things, nothing surpasses these."
This was an auspicious occasion.
When Guo Gongfu first arrived at Wuzu’s monastery, he requested that the Master ascend the seat. Gongfu stepped forward, offered incense, and said:
"This single portion of incense, burned within the brazier, is offered to my Dharma-brother, the Zen Master of the Hall. I humbly pray that you, from this vast and expansive seat..."
[The Master] opened wide his face and manifested the form of his former teacher for the others to sketch.
Why was this so? "We met long ago by the cliffs of Baiyun; the matters of those days are not the same as today. The night is still and the water cold, yet the fish do not bite;
a single incense burner drifts away from White Lotus Peak. The Patriarch then said: *Namo satvata paraya*.
"Thus, thus. How many times have I gazed upon the white clouds above the stream? The yellow plum blossoms open amidst the snow.
"Not thus, not thus. The tender willows hang down golden threads; one must simply wait for the opportune moment. Have you not seen how Layman Pang asked Great Master Ma:
"Who is it that does not take the myriad dharmas as a companion? The Master replied: "Wait until you..."
"I tell you all: swallow the waters of the West River in a single gulp.
Ten-thousand-fathom deep pools are exhausted to their very bottom; the footbridge is not Zhaozhou’s bridge. How can bright moon and clear wind compare [to this]?"

In the meditation hall, Chan Master Letan Jingxiang asked a monk, “When Bodhidharma returned to the West, he carried a single sandal in his hand. Why did he not take both sandals with him at that time?
The monk replied, “This land also required a trace of his presence. The Master said, “One foot remains in the Western Heaven; one...”
"One foot is in the Eastern Land; what cause for this is there? The monk was speechless. [The Master] asked the monk:
"There is but one firm and dense body, which manifests within all atoms. What is this body that manifests within the atoms?"

The monk pointed to the incense burner and said, "This is the incense burner. The Master said, "It brings all the Buddhas of the three periods of time down with you, causing them to fall into hell alive.
The monk was at a loss for words. The Master then struck him.
When Chan Master Cishi Rui arrived at Touzi, Guangjian asked, "Where is your native place? The Master replied, "Dongyue in the Two Zhe regions.
Guangjian asked, "What is it like in Dongyue? The Master said, "Mount Qinwang is high; Lake Jianhu is vast. Guangjian said, "Mount Qinwang..."
"Are you the same as yourself or different from yourself? The Master said, "In India it is called *brahman*, in this land of Tang it is called 'Dharma'.
Jian said, "This is still just the formal exchange used in monasteries. Ultimately, are they the same or different? The Master gave a shout; Jian struck him.
The Master said, "A great kindness is difficult to repay," and then he prostrated himself.
The lay practitioner and Minister Zhang Shangying once said:

"What the Buddhas of the past have taught—that within the tip of a single hair one manifests jeweled royal lands, and while seated within a mote of dust one turns the Great Dharma Wheel—is the ultimate truth.
At the assembly of the Lotus Sūtra, the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna was present within his jeweled stupa."
He shared half his seat with Śākyamuni Buddha; past and present Buddhas sat together in one place. Such a thing truly occurred;
it was not merely a symbolic representation of the Dharma.
When Chan Master Huìqín Fójian of Tàipíng and Chan Master Wénshū Xīndào first traveled to study under various masters, they arrived at Tàipíng.

There, they heard the Master’s night discourse on Zhaozhou’s “Cypress Tree” koan, specifically the passage where Jué Tiězu said, “The former master did not say such words; do not slander the former master. Because of this...
Great doubt arose. After a long period of intense mental exertion, one night he suddenly attained clarity. He immediately hurried to the master’s quarters, intending to recount his realization.
When the Master saw him approaching, he closed the door. Daowu said, "Master, do not deceive me. The Master said, "The ten directions have no walls;
why do you not come inside? Daowu punched through the paper of the window. The Master immediately opened the door, grabbed him, and said, "Speak! Speak!"
Daowu cupped his teacher’s head with both hands, made a sound with his mouth as if sipping, and departed. He then presented this verse: “Zhaozhou has a story about the cypress tree;
Zen students have passed it down throughout the world. Most merely pluck leaves and seek branches, Unable to understand it directly at its source.
Jue says there were no such words; This is truly like reviling someone face-to-face with foul language. Zen practitioners—
"If one possesses the all-pervading eye, one should skillfully distinguish the true from the false within this. The Master deeply approved of this.
Chan Master Foyan Qingyuan of Longmen addressed the assembly:
"A thousand explanations and ten thousand expositions are not equal to a single face-to-face encounter. Even if nothing were said, it would still be perfectly clear. King [Wang]...
The parable of the son and the precious sword; the parable of the blind men feeling the elephant; the matter of beckoning across the river in Zen study;
the matter of meeting at the Wangzhou Pavilion; and the matters of remote, uninhabited places and deep mountain cliffs—these are all seen face-to-face;
they do not reside in words.
Ascending the hall, he said: "Great assembly! Suppose someone calls out, 'Venerable One! and the Venerable One responds.
Even if he were not to respond, he must still internally acknowledge it. Nowadays, students simply say that the one who responds is right, and the one who acknowledges it is right."
If you understand it in this way, you are a son of hell. Let that be for now; tell me, who is it right before you calling your name?
Is there someone calling you, or is there no one calling you? Can you yet reach a definitive judgment?
If it is someone calling you, then when mountain spirits and ghosts call you, or when celestial demons and heterodox teachers call you, what will you do?
Clarification: If it is said that no one is calling you, and yet you are neither deaf nor foolish, how could there be no one calling?
This is the matter of the headway of birth and death throughout the twelve hours of the day. Can all of you understand this? When someone calls, confusion arises;
when no one calls, one is entangled in fetters. If you can act accordingly, birth and death are severed—ten thousand ounces of gold would never be exchanged for it.
Descend from your seat.
The Master then spoke three verses on pointing out the Way. The first says: *Following the Stream* The numinous traces of a thousand sages lie at the tips of the hundred grasses.
Standing forth and letting go is called "following the stream. Let it be that for ten thousand ages no one recognizes it; It brings to laughter the water-buffalo of Mount Mui.
The second is called "Meeting the Tracks": "The moon in the water is the moon at the edge of the sky; north, south, east, and west, there is no difference between them.
When the blacksmith of Silla strikes the iron and sparks fly, burning one's fingertip is what is called 'meeting the tracks. The third is called "Singing in Unison":
"Severing all diversities at the head of the ancient path, he unmoors the boat that ferries people from the empty shore. Clearly and brightly, a single phrase encompasses the multitude of phenomena."
How can one seek the soundless through skillful chanting?
Chan Master Jingyin Jicheng,
together with Chan Master Tongyuan Wuzhuo, Fazhen, Cishou, and ten great Dharma masters— along with a thousand monks of both Chan and Exegesis— attended the banquet hosted by the Grand Marshal.
At the private residence of Lord Chen Gongliangbi, Emperor Huizong went there in person to observe the ceremony.

There was a man skilled in the Avataṃsaka Sūtra, a "tiger among scholars" of the Xianshou school, who addressed the assembly, saying: "The Buddha established his teachings, ranging from the Small Vehicle up to the Perfect and Sudden."
Having swept away both emptiness and existence, one alone realizes the true and eternal; only then, adorned with the myriad virtues, is one truly called a Buddha.
I have often heard it said that a single shout of the Chan school can transform the ordinary into the holy, which seems to contradict various sutras and treatises.
Now, if this single shout can enter the five teachings of our school, it is a correct teaching; if it cannot so enter, it is a false teaching. [End of] Various [Texts].
Chan Shi addressed the Master. The Master said, "What the Dharma Master has asked is not sufficient for the response of the three great Chan masters.
The junior Elder of Jingyin may be able to free the Dharma Master from his delusions. The Master summoned Shan; Shan responded with an assent.

The Master said, "That which the Dharma Master calls the teachings of the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) is the meaning of existence. That which is the Initial Teaching of the Great Vehicle (Mahāyāna) is the meaning of emptiness."

The Mahayana Final Teaching (Zhongjiao) refers to the meaning of neither being existent nor being empty. The Mahayana Sudden Teaching (Dunjiao) refers to the meaning of being both existent and empty simultaneously.
The One Vehicle Perfect Teaching (Yanjiao) refers to the meaning of being existent without being existent, and being empty without being empty.

"My single shout," [the Master] said, "is not only able to penetrate the five teachings; it can even penetrate the arts and crafts, as well as all the various schools of thought and the hundred masters.
The Master let out a thunderous shout and asked Shan, "Did you hear that? Shan replied, "I heard it.
The Master said, "Since you heard it, this one shout is 'existence' (yu); it can penetrate the Hinayana teaching. A short while later, he asked Shan again, "Did you hear that?"
[The student] said, "I did not hear it. The Master said, "Since you did not hear it just now, my single shout was 'non-existent.

This can lead one into the Initial Teaching (Shijiao). Then he looked at Shan and said: 'When I first gave a shout, you said it was existent. Now that the sound has long since faded away, you say it is non-existent.

To say it is non-existent implies that it was originally real and existent; to say it is existent implies that it is now actually non-existent. Being neither existent nor non-existent can lead one into the Final Teaching.'"

Teaching: When I let out a single shout, there is "existence" that is not existence; it exists because of non-existence. When there is no single shout, there is "non-existence" that is not non-existence;
it is non-existent because of existence. Being both existent and non-existent, one can enter the Sudden Teaching.

You must know that this single shout of mine does not function as a mere shout; existence and non-existence do not reach it, and both emotional understanding and intellectual interpretation are forgotten. When the Way is present, even the finest...
When dust does not arise and the Way is non-existent, it pervades the void horizontally. This single shout enters hundreds of thousands of myriads of kotis of shouts;
hundreds of thousands of myriads of kotis of shouts enter this single shout. Therefore, one can enter the Perfect Teaching. Shan then rose and bowed twice. The Master spoke again, saying:
"It is not only this single shout that is thus; even down to a single word, a single silence, a single movement, and a single—"

Quiescence. From antiquity to the present, throughout the empty space of the ten directions, amidst the myriad phenomena of the universe, the beings of the six realms and four modes of birth, the Buddhas of the three periods of time, and all sages and worthies—the eighty-four thousand dharma-gates, the hundreds of thousands of samādhis, and the immeasurable subtle meanings that accord with principle and respond to capacity—these are of one substance with heaven, earth, and the myriad things;
this is called the *dharmakāya*. The three realms are but mind; the myriad dharmas...
Consciousness-only: throughout the four seasons and eight nodes, yin and yang are of one accord; this is called the Dharma-nature. Therefore, the Avataṃsaka Sūtra says:
"The Dharma-nature pervades all places; whether with form or without form, in a single sound or a single color, it is entirely present within a single mote of dust."
It encompasses four meanings: phenomena and principle are boundless; they are all-pervasive without exception; they interpenetrate without being confused; they blend together yet are not one.

All of these are fully present within this single shout. This is still merely the establishment of the gateways of transformation and instruction—a provisional means according to capacity—termed a "small resting place.
It has not yet reached the Precious Abode. Little do they realize that beneath our ancestral masters, mind was transmitted through mind. Through...
The Dharma-seal is a teaching that does not rely on words and letters; it is the realization of one's nature to become a Buddha.

There exists a supreme path that has not been transmitted by a thousand sages. Zhishan asked again, "What is this supreme path? The Master said, "For now, you should understand it from the perspective below.
Zhishan asked, "What is the Precious Place? The Master said, "It is not within your realm. Zhishan said, "I hope the Chan Master will show me compassion."
"Alas! The Master said, "Even if the vast ocean were to change, I would never speak for you. He then left with his mouth firmly sealed.
The Emperor was greatly pleased, and all who heard of it did not fail to express their admiration and respect.
Chan Master Guoqing Miaoyin ascended the hall and said:
"Why is it that those who can speak from their full mouths do not know 'having' (the truth)? And why is it that those who know 'having' fully cannot speak?
Tell me, where does the crux lie? If you know this place, I grant you the power of simultaneous illumination and function."

At the same time, both light and darkness are clearly perceived. Should this not yet be the case—whether you can speak it or cannot, whether you know it exists or do not know it exists—the stone tiger of the Southern Mountain knows how to let out a lion’s roar.
One day, Chan Master Anmin of Huazang Minyin said to Yuanwu, "Master, please refrain from citing stories; let me speak of them. Yuanwu consented.
The Master said, "Is it not the case that when you habitually brandish the mallet or raise the whisk, you are acting in accordance with what the sutras say: 'All worlds and all things that exist...'"
“Phenomena are all the wondrously luminous true mind of bodhi. Yuanwu laughed and said, “So you have been making your living right here all along!
The Master further said, “When you let out a shout or strike the meditation seat, is that not ‘returning the hearing to hear one’s own nature,’ whereby that nature accomplishes the unsurpassed Way?
Yuanwu replied, “Have you not seen it stated in the sutras: ‘The wondrous nature is perfectly luminous, transcending all names’?”
Xiang was suddenly enlightened upon hearing these words. When Yuanwu left Sichuan and resided at Jia Shan, the Master (Xiang) ceased his lectures to serve as an attendant during his travels.

One night, while Yuanwu was addressing the assembly, he cited the kōan concerning the ancient sail that had not yet been hoisted. The Master heard it but did not grasp its meaning, so he sought a definitive resolution. Yuanwu said, "Ask me.
The Master repeated the previous story, and Yuanwu replied, "The cypress tree in the courtyard. At that moment, the Master attained thorough penetration.
Ming said to Yuanwu, "The ancients said that it is like a single drop cast into a vast ravine; yet they failed to realize that the great ocean can be cast into a single drop.
Yuanwu laughed and said, "What can be done about this fellow? Shortly thereafter, he ordered Ming to share his seat.
A monk asked Chan Master Daomeng Fatai:

"Principle conforms to phenomena, encompassing all existence as a single expanse of void and stillness; phenomena follow along with principle, equalizing all differences as they return to the ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).
What is the dharma-realm of principle? The Master said: "Mountains, rivers, and the great earth. [The monk] said: "As it is..."
"What is the Dharma-realm of phenomena? The Master said, "The myriad phenomena in their dense array. He asked, "What is the Dharma-realm of the non-obstruction between principle and phenomena?

The Master said, "East, west, south, and north. He asked, "What is the Dharma-realm of the non-obstruction between phenomena and phenomena? The Master said, "Above, below, and the four intermediate directions."

One day, while Zen Master Shanwu of the Upper Hermitage at Yunju was staying there, a monk had his foot bitten by a snake. Foyan asked him, "Since you are from Longmen, why have you been bitten by a snake?
The Master immediately replied, "Indeed, he has manifested the marks of a great man. Foyan held him in even greater esteem. Later, this was transmitted.
These words reached Zhaojue. Yuanwu said, "Is there such a monk at Longmen? The Dharma lineage of Dongshan has not yet become desolate.
This refers to Chan Master Baiyang Fashun.

The Master relied upon Fuyan. Hearing a general discourse that cited the *Mind-King Inscription* by Dashi Pudu, he said: "The flavor of salt in water, the glue and blue pigment within color—these are certainly present, yet their forms are not seen. Upon these words, he attained realization. Later, while contemplating the rapid turning of the *Precious Treasury*, he suddenly clarified the Great Dharma. He hurried to the Master’s chamber, prostrated, and presented this verse: "A summit rises distinct from the peaks; A stream flows apart from the rivers. The moon does not enter the mirror; The mirror does not go out to meet the moon. The myriad phenomena are all thus; The true mind is naturally so. The Master said, "In the past, you were a man of the Way; today, you are a man of the Way. He then gave him the name Changqing Huileng. Subsequently, he went to Mount Donglin to visit Xuefeng. Xuefeng asked, "Where have you come from? He replied, "From Changqing. Xuefeng said, "What is the teaching of Changqing like? He replied, "It is like a great dragon soaring through the void. Xuefeng said, "Is there anyone who can soar with it? He replied, "There is no one who can soar with it. Xuefeng said, "If so, why did you not soar with it? He replied, "I was afraid it would be misunderstood. Xuefeng said, "How could it be misunderstood? It is like a great pearl rolling on the ground. He then composed a verse: "The dragon soars through the void; The pearl rolls on the ground. The myriad phenomena are all thus; The true mind is naturally so. Xuefeng said, "This is the teaching of Changqing. He then bowed and withdrew. Afterward, he visited Deshan. Deshan asked, "Where have you come from? He replied, "From Donglin. Deshan said, "What is the teaching of Donglin like? He replied, "Like a great pearl rolling on the ground. Deshan said, "Is there anyone who can roll along with it? He replied, "There is no one who can roll along with it. Deshan said, "If so, why did you not roll along with it? He replied, "I was afraid it would be misunderstood. Deshan said, "How could it be misunderstood? It is like a great dragon soaring through the void. He then composed a verse: "The pearl rolls on the ground; The dragon soars through the void. The myriad phenomena are all thus; The true mind is naturally so. Deshan said, "This is the teaching of Donglin. He then bowed and withdrew. Subsequently, he visited Yunmen. Yunmen asked, "Where have you come from? He replied, "From Deshan. Yunmen said, "What is the teaching of Deshan like? He replied, "Like a great dragon soaring through the void. Yunmen said, "Is there anyone who can soar with it? He replied, "There is no one who can soar with it. Yunmen said, "If so, why did you not soar with it? He replied, "I was afraid it would be misunderstood. Yunmen said, "How could it be misunderstood? It is like a great pearl rolling on the ground. He then composed a verse: "The dragon soars through the void; The pearl rolls on the ground. The myriad phenomena are all thus; The true mind is naturally so. Yunmen said, "This is the teaching of Deshan. He then bowed and withdrew. Afterward, he visited Yangshan. Yangshan asked, "Where have you come from? He replied, "From Yunmen. Yangshan said, "What is the teaching of Yunmen like? He replied, "Like a great pearl rolling on the ground. Yangshan said, "Is there anyone who can roll along with it? He replied, "There is no one who can roll along with it. Yangshan said, "If so, why did you not roll along with it? He replied, "I was afraid it would be misunderstood. Yangshan said, "How could it be misunderstood? It is like a great dragon soaring through the void. He then composed a verse: "The pearl rolls on the ground; The dragon soars through the void. The myriad phenomena are all thus; The true mind is naturally so. Yangshan said, "This is the teaching of Yunmen. He then bowed and withdrew. Finally, he visited Linji. Linji asked, "Where have you come from? He replied, "From Yangshan. Linji said, "What is the teaching of Yangshan like? He replied, "Like a great dragon soaring through the void. Linji said, "Is there anyone who can soar with it? He replied, "There is no one who can soar with it. Linji said, "If so, why did you not soar with it? He replied, "I was afraid it would be misunderstood. Linji said, "How could it be misunderstood? It is like a great pearl rolling on the ground. He then composed a verse: "The dragon soars through the void; The pearl rolls on the ground. The myriad phenomena are all thus; The true mind is naturally so. Linji said, "This is the teaching of Yangshan. He then bowed and withdrew. He then returned to his own mountain. One day, while sitting in meditation, he suddenly heard the sound of a stone striking bamboo and attained great enlightenment. He then composed a verse: "Top of the head, a distinct peak; At the bottom of the feet, a clear stream. The moon does not enter the mirror; The mirror does not go out to meet the moon. The wondrous nature and the spiritual palace—why need they undergo refinement? The mind is a mind of non-action; the face is the mother-born face.
Though the kalpa-stone may be moved, herein there is no change. Non-action is fundamentally non-action; why need one read written words?
Eliminate the root of self and person; merge in secret with the meaning herein. All manner of laboring the sinews and bones is not as good as sleeping soundly beneath the forest trees.
Raising one’s head, one sees the sun is high; eating a meal, one proceeds from the very beginning. To employ effort upon effort is but a revolving muddle.
If you grasp it, you will not obtain it; by not grasping it, you naturally penetrate it. I have a single word: cut off deliberation and forget all conditions.

It cannot be obtained through clever speech; it is transmitted only through the mind. Furthermore, there is another phrase: nothing surpasses direct bestowal. It is as fine as a hair-tip, yet vast beyond any spatial location.

Originally perfected by nature, there is no need for the toil of weaving. Worldly affairs are wearying; they are not as good as the mountain peaks. Green pines obscure the sun; azure streams flow on forever.
Mountain clouds serve as curtains; the night moon acts as a hook. Lying beneath the wisteria vines, with a block of stone for a pillow.
I do not attend court for the Son of Heaven; how could I envy kings or lords? Having no anxieties regarding life or death, what more need I worry about? The moon in the water casts no shadow;

I am always simply at peace. All phenomena are thus; they are fundamentally unborn from the beginning. Sitting upright and free from affairs, when spring comes, the grass turns green of its own accord.
The Great Master Fashun composed a verse on the Dharma-body as follows: In Jia Prefecture, the ox eats the grain; In Yi Prefecture, the horse’s belly swells.
Seeking a physician throughout the world, One applies moxibustion to the left shoulder of a pig.
A great virtuous one asked Zen Master Nanyue Huairang:
"When a mirror casts an image, once the image has been formed, I do not know where the light has gone. The Master said:
"When you were a young boy, Great Virtue, where was your appearance? [The monk] said: "But once the image has been formed, why [is it that way]?"
"Does it not reflect? The Master said, "Although it does not reflect, one cannot deceive it by even a single point.
When Mazu Daishi was propagating the teaching in Jiangxi, the Master asked the assembly, "Is Daoyi preaching the Dharma for the community?
The assembly replied, "He has already preached the Dharma for the community. The Master said, "Yet no one at all has brought back any news of it. The assembly was speechless.
He sent a monk away, instructing him, saying: "When he ascends the hall, simply ask him, 'What is it? and memorize the words he utters.

The monk went and followed the master's instructions exactly. Upon his return, he said to the master, "Master Ma said, 'Since the time of confusion, for thirty years I have never lacked salt and sauce. The master approved of this.

Cen Master Xingxiu of Qingyuan was staying in seclusion when Xiqian went to pay his respects. The Master asked, "From where have you come? Xiqian said, "From Caoxi. The Master asked, "What have you brought back?
He replied, "Even before arriving at Caoxi, I did not lose it. The Master said, "If that is so, why did you go to Caoxi?"
Xuefeng asked, "What does Caoxi do? Baizhang said, "If you had not reached Caoxi, how would you know that [the mind] is not lost?
Xuefeng further asked, "Does the Great Master of Caoxi recognize you, Reverend? The Master said, "Do you recognize me now? Xuefeng said, "Even if I recognized him, how could I truly recognize him?"
The Master said, "Though there may be many horns, one qilin is sufficient. Xian asked again, "Since you left Caoxi, Master, when did you arrive here?
The Master said, "I know, however, at what time you left Caoxi. Xian said, "I, Xian, did not come from Caoxi.
The Master said, "I also know where you have gone. Xian said, "Fortunately, Master, you are a great man."

"Do not act rashly. On another day, the Master again asked Xian, "Where have you come from? He replied, "From Caoxi. The Master then raised his whisk and said, "Is there such a thing as this at Caoxi?
He replied, "Not only at Caoxi; even in the Western Heavens it does not exist.
The Master said, "Have you perhaps been to the Western Heavens? He replied, "If I had been there, then it would exist. The Master said, "That is not yet it. Speak further."

The monk said, "The Master must also speak for half of it; do not rely entirely on this student. The Master said, "I do not refuse to speak to you, but I fear that in the future there will be no one to take it up."
A monk asked Master Mazu Daoyi, "Why does the Master say 'this very mind is Buddha'? The Master said, "To stop the crying of small children. The monk asked, "When the crying has stopped, what then?
The Master said, "Neither mind nor Buddha. The monk asked, "If someone comes who is neither of these two types of people, how will you point it out for them?"
[The Master] showed [him something]. The Master said, "I told him, 'It is not an object. [The monk] asked, "What if someone who has realized it were to come?
The Master said, "Just let him realize the Great Way."
One night, while Xitang, Baizhang, and Nanquan were attending him as they gazed at the moon, the Master asked, "At this very moment, how is it?

Xitang said, "It is precisely the right time for making offerings. Baizhang said, "It is precisely the right time for practicing cultivation. Nanquan brushed his sleeves and walked away. The Master said, "..."
The Sutras have entered the Canon; Chan has returned to the sea. Only Puyan alone transcends the mundane world.
During a monk’s formal visit, the Master drew a perfect circle and said, "Strike if he enters; strike if he does not enter. As soon as the monk stepped inside—
The Master struck him. The monk said, "Master, you should not strike me. The Master leaned on his staff and desisted.
A monk asked, "How can one attain accord with the Way? The Master said, "I have long been out of accord with speaking of it."
A junior disciple named Danyuan returned from his pilgrimage and drew a circle before his master. He then prostrated himself upon it and stood up.
The master said, "Do you not wish to become a Buddha? The disciple replied, "I do not know how to press on my eyes. The master said, "I am not as good as you.
The junior disciple remained silent.
Deng Yinfeng took his leave of his teacher. The teacher asked, "Where are you going? He replied, "To Shitou. The teacher said, "The path at Shitou is slippery.
He replied, "Carrying my staff and wood with me, I shall perform my art wherever the stage appears," and he departed.

As soon as he arrived at Shitou, he circumambulated the meditation seat once, shook his mendicant’s staff once, and asked, "What is the fundamental principle? Shitou said, "Heaven! Heaven! Yinfeng was speechless.
He returned and reported this to the Master. The Master said, "Go back and ask him again; when he gives an answer, you should simply let out two sighs.
Feng went again and asked as before. Shitou then let out two sighs. Feng remained speechless once more. He returned and reported this to the Master.
The Master said, "I told you that the path of Shitou is slippery."
A monk drew four lines before the Master; the top line was long and the three bottom lines were short. He said, "One must not say that one line is long and three lines are short.
Apart from these four words, I ask the Master to answer. The Master then drew a single line on the ground and said, "One must not speak of long or short. My answer to you is complete."
The Master asked a monk, "Where have you come from? He replied, "From Hunan. The Master said, "Is the water in Dong Lake full yet? He replied, "Yes."
"Not yet," the Master said. "The rainwater has not yet filled it after all this time.
Zen Master Shitou Xiqian’s disciple Wendu asked, "Who has attained the essential meaning of Caoxi? The Master replied, "Those who understand the Dharma attain it. Wendu asked, "How so?"
"Can you return, Master? The Master said, "I cannot. "Why cannot you? "I do not understand the Buddha-dharma," he replied.

When Chan Master Faring of Mount Niutou was nineteen years old, his mastery of the classics and histories was thorough. He subsequently studied the extensive *Prajñāpāramitā* sūtras and attained a profound understanding of ultimate emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
One day, he sighed and said: "Confucian studies and worldly scriptures are not the ultimate Dharma; the true contemplation of *prajñā* is the vessel for transcending the world. Thereupon, he...

He lived in seclusion at Mount Mao and shaved his head under a master. Later, he entered a stone chamber on the northern cliff of Youqi Temple on Mount Niutou, where there was the marvel of hundreds of birds bringing him flowers.
The Fourth Patriarch, observing the atmosphere from afar, knew there was an extraordinary person on that mountain;

he went in person to seek him out and asked the temple monks, "Is there any practitioner of the Way here? They replied, "Which one among those who have left the household life is not [a practitioner]?"
"This is a man of the Way. The Patriarch asked, "Which one is the man of the Way? The monk had no reply.
Another monk said, "About ten *li* from here in the mountains there is one named Lanrong; he does not rise when seeing people, nor does he join his palms. Could he be the man of the Way?
The Patriarch then entered the mountains and saw the Master sitting upright and composed, with no concern for anything around him. The Patriarch asked, "Are you here?"
"What are you doing? the Master asked. The Teacher replied, "Contemplating the mind. The Patriarch asked, "Who is it that contemplates? What is this mind? The Teacher had no reply.
He immediately rose, prostrated himself, and asked, "Virtuous One, where do you dwell in seclusion? The Patriarch said, "I have no fixed abode;
I go either east or west. The Master asked, "Do you know Chan Master Daoxin? The Patriarch asked, "Why do you ask about him? The Master said:
Having long admired his virtue, I hope to pay my respects once more. The Patriarch said, "I am that very Dharma Master Daoxin.
The Master asked, "For what reason have you deigned to come here? The Patriarch replied, "I have come specifically to visit you. Is there perhaps another place for us to rest?
The Master pointed toward the rear and said, "There is a separate small hermitage. He then led the Patriarch to the site of the hut; as they circled it, they saw only tigers and wolves.
The Patriarch then raised both hands in a gesture of threat. The Master said, "There is still this one remaining. The Patriarch asked, "What is this?
The Master was speechless. After a short while, the Patriarch then inscribed the character for "Buddha" upon the stone where the Master sat in formal meditation.
The Master looked at him and was struck with awe. Nanyue said, "There is still this one remaining.
Prince Boling asked, "When one is precisely applying the mind, how can there be peace and ease? The Master said, "When one is precisely applying the mind, it is precisely the non-application of mind.
To speak circuitously of names and forms is wearying; to speak directly of the absence of such things is free from heaviness. When there is no mind, it is precisely so."
"Exactly as used; when used constantly, there is nothing 'exactly. Now I speak of the state of no-mind; it is not different from that which has mind. A questioner asked:
"The Wise One cites wondrous words, yet they should accord with the nature of the mind. If the words differ from the path of the mind, then when joined, they will be a myriad times more discordant.

The Master said: "Wondrous words are spoken as skillful means to break through the illnesses of sentient beings; they do not concern the discourse on the original nature. They emerge once again from emptiness and transform back into it."

It is created. Taking non-thought as the true constant, one shall ultimately sever the path of the mind. When detached from thought, the nature is unmoving; arising and ceasing are free from contradiction or error.
As the echo in a valley possesses sound, the reflection in a mirror can look back.

A monk asked Zen Master Tianzhu Chonghui, "Before Bodhidharma came to this land, was there still the Buddha-dharma? The Master said, "Setting aside for a moment the time before he came, what is the matter right now?
The monk said, "I do not understand. I beg the Master for instruction. The Master said, "Ten thousand ages..."

"Vast emptiness. One morning, wind and moon. The monk remained silent. The Master asked again, "Do you understand, Ācārya? He replied, "I do not understand. The Master said, "What is it on your own account?
What does it have to do with whether Bodhidharma came or did not come? His coming here was much like a fortune-teller;
seeing that you did not understand, he broke open the lines of the divination for you. As soon as there is good or bad fortune produced..."
"It all lies within your own sphere; look for it all yourself. A monk asked, "What is one who understands divination?
The Master said, "The moment you step out the door, you have already missed it."
When Mazu sent a messenger with a letter to Chan Master Daoqin of Jingshan, the letter contained a circle. Upon opening the seal,
the Master placed a dot within the circle and returned it sealed.

The Master replied, "Your Excellency, the Prefect, is in even greater danger. Bai said, "I, your disciple, hold a position that commands the rivers and mountains; what danger could there be? The Master [continued]: The Master said, "The perilousness of my abode lies merely in the falling leaves and drifting snow. Your peril, however, lies in the fact that you are a high official who must constantly attend to the affairs of state, never finding a moment of rest. You are like a bird perched upon a tree branch, fearing the wind at every moment. This is far more dangerous than my life hanging by a single thread. Bai was deeply moved and attained realization.
