Baizhang said, "Fuel and fire intersect; the nature of consciousness does not rest. Is this not perilous? He asked again, "What is the great meaning of the Buddha-dharma?
The Master said, "Commit no evil; practice all that is good. Baizhang said, "Even a three-year-old child understands how to say that.
The Master said, "Though a three-year-old child can say it, an eighty-year-old man cannot act upon it. Baizhang bowed.
Having paid his respects, he withdrew.
Chan Master Daoshu of Shouzhou received the Dharma from Xiu of the Northern School. He selected Mount Sanfeng in Shouzhou, where he constructed a thatched hut to dwell. There was always a wild...

The man’s appearance was simple and unadorned, yet his speech was strange and eccentric. At times he would suddenly transform himself into the forms of Buddhas, bodhisattvas, arhats, or celestial immortals;
sometimes he emitted divine light, and at other times he produced miraculous sounds. When the master’s disciples witnessed these things, none could fathom them.
After ten years had passed in this manner, he suddenly vanished without a trace or shadow. The master addressed the assembly, saying: "A rustic man has displayed many colors."

Their arts may dazzle and delude people, yet it requires only that this old monk neither see nor hear them; thus their arts will eventually come to an end, while my state of not seeing and not hearing is inexhaustible.
The Master Puzhao Duoheshang of Mount Song did not have his name or lineage recorded.
His words and deeds were unfathomable. He lived in seclusion on Mount Song, where there was a shrine in a mountain valley that was considered highly efficacious.
Within its hall stood only a single hearth, yet offerings from far and near never ceased; many living creatures were slaughtered for sacrifice. One day, the Master...
He led the temple monks into the shrine and struck the hearth three times with his staff, saying, "Ho!
This hearth is merely composed of clay and tiles. From where does the 'saint' come? From where does the 'spirit' arise? Yet you slaughter living beings in such a manner!

He struck it another three times, and the hearth immediately collapsed and fell apart. After a short while, a man appeared wearing a green robe and a tall cap; he prostrated himself before the Master. The Master said:

"What kind of person are you? He replied, "I am originally the hearth god of this temple. Having long endured the retribution of my karma, today I have been fortunate enough to hear the Master preach the Dharma of non-arising.
I have attained liberation from this place and shall be reborn among the devas; I have come specifically to express my gratitude. The Master said, "This is your own inherent nature;
it was not something I spoke of by force. The spirit bowed again and vanished. A short while later, an attendant monk asked, "We [monks]..."
“I have served the Master for a long time, yet I have not received any instruction. What essential principle did the stove god obtain that he was able to be reborn in heaven?
The Master said, “I simply told him that it is composed of clay and tiles; there is no other principle to impart to him.
The attendant monk remained silent. The Master asked, “Do you understand? The monk said, “I do not understand. The Master said, “Why do you not [realize] the nature that is inherently present?”
[The assembly] gathered, and the attendant monks prostrated. The Master said, "Broken! Broken! Fallen! Fallen!
Chan Master Yuangui of Songyue had received the Dharma from National Teacher Huizhao. He lived in seclusion at Pangwu on the mountain. One day, a divine being led a retinue [to his dwelling].
He went to visit the Master. Upon seeing his appearance, which was extraordinary and magnificent beyond the ordinary, the Master asked, "Welcome, O benevolent one!

For what purpose have you come? The other replied, "Do you perhaps recognize me, Master? The Master said, "I regard Buddhas and sentient beings as equal; I view them all with a single eye. How could I make such distinctions?
The other said, "I am the deity of this mountain. I can bring life and death upon people. How is it that you, Master, have attained [this state]?"
"Behold me! The Master said, "I am fundamentally unborn; how can you cause me to die? I regard my body as equal to space, and I regard myself as equal to you.
Can you destroy space and yourself? If you could indeed destroy space and yourself, then I would be neither born nor extinguished.
Since you cannot even do this, how could you possibly bring about my birth or death? Shen bowed his head in reverence.
The leader said, "I am also wise and upright compared to other spirits; how could I have known that you, Master, possess such vast wisdom and eloquence?
I pray that you will bestow upon me the true precepts, so that I may cross over this world. The Master said, "Since you have requested the precepts, you are already possessed of them."
"Why is this? Outside of precepts there are no precepts; what, then, would 'precepts' be? The deity said, "This is the principle. I have heard it only in a state of profound obscurity.
I merely seek a teacher to instruct my person as a gate-disciple. The master immediately prepared a seat, held up the incense burner, and straightened the desk.
The Master said, "I shall confer upon you the five precepts. If you can uphold them, you should say 'I can'; if you cannot, you should say 'No'.
He replied, "I respectfully accept your instruction. The Master asked, "Can you refrain from sexual misconduct? He replied, "I am married. The Master said, "That is not what I mean."
The Master said, "This means you have no desire for gain. The man replied, "I can. The Master asked, "Can you refrain from stealing?
The man replied, "What lack do I have that I would need to steal? The Master said, "I do not mean this. I mean that you reward the licentious while bringing calamity upon the virtuous.
The man replied, "I can. The Master asked, "Can you refrain from killing? The man replied, "I truly hold the authority over life and death; how could I say I do not kill? The Master...
[The Master] said, "I do not mean this. I mean that there is confusion, error, doubt, and entanglement. [The student] said, "I can [avoid these]. The Master said, "Can you avoid being insincere?
[The student] said, "I am upright; how could I be insincere? The Master said, "I do not mean this. I mean that your actions before and after do not accord with the Will of Heaven.
[The student] said, "I can. The Master said, "Are you not ruined by alcohol? [The student] said, "I can. The Master said, "As for the above,"
This is the Buddha’s precept. Furthermore, it is said: "To uphold with a mind yet remain free from the attachment of a mind;

to act for the sake of others with a mind yet remain free from the thought of a self-body. One who can do so was not born as a vital essence before heaven and earth, nor does one die as an aged being after heaven and earth.
Throughout the day one undergoes transformations yet is not moved; throughout one's entire life one remains in silent stillness yet does not rest."

Believing this, then although one marries, it is not [the act of] taking a wife; although one faces [others], it is not [the act of] seeking them out; although one holds office, it is not [the exercise of] power; although one acts, it is not [acting on] purpose;
although one is intoxicated, it is not [a state of] delusion. If one can be without mind regarding the myriad things, then though one is caught in desires, it does not constitute lust;

though fortune favors the licentious and calamity strikes the good, it does not constitute theft; though there is excess, error, suspicion, and confusion, it does not constitute killing; though preceding and succeeding events violate the Way of Heaven—
To be deluded, dazed, and inverted is not to be intoxicated; this is what is called being "without mind. Without mind, there is no precept.
Without precepts, there is no mind, no Buddha, no sentient beings, no you, and no self. What, then, would constitute a precept? The Spirit said:
“My supernatural powers are second only to those of the Buddha. The Master said, “Regarding your ten points on supernatural powers, five are abilities and five are incapacities.
For the Buddha, however, of his ten points, seven are abilities and three are incapacities. Shen bowed deeply, withdrew from his seat, and knelt to ask, “May I hear these explained? The Master said:
"Can you cause the Supreme Deity to turn back? Can you make the Seven Luminaries travel westward while the Eastern Heaven moves east?

He replied, "I cannot. The Master said, "Can you seize the Earth Deity? Can you melt the Five Sacred Peaks and congeal the Four Seas? He replied, "I cannot. The Master said, "These are called the five impossibilities.
The Buddha can empty all phenomena and perfect the wisdom of all dharmas, yet he cannot immediately extinguish fixed karma. The Buddha...
One may know the nature of all beings and exhaustively understand the events of billions of kalpas, yet one cannot transform and guide those who lack the karmic affinity.
A Buddha can deliver immeasurable sentient beings, yet cannot exhaust the realm of sentient beings. These are the three things that cannot be done. Even fixed karma is not eternal;

even the absence of affinity is but for a single lifetime. The realm of sentient beings is fundamentally without increase or decrease; throughout all time, there is not a single person who can [exhaust it].
"It is the master who presides over the Dharma; where there is Dharma but no master, this is called 'no Dharma. Where there is no Dharma and no master, this is called 'no-mind.
As I understand it, even the Buddha possesses no supernatural powers (*abhijñā*); he is simply able to penetrate all dharmas through no-mind.

The deity said, "I am truly shallow and ignorant, having not yet heard the meaning of emptiness (*śūnyatā*). I shall faithfully practice the precepts you have bestowed upon me. Now I wish to repay [your kindness]."

"Cizhi, imitate what I am capable of. The Master said, "I contemplate the body as being without substance; I contemplate all phenomena as impermanent. Being but a clod of earth, what further desire could I have?

The spirit said, "The Master must surely command me to perform a worldly task to display my minor divine powers, so that these five types of people—those who have already resolved [to attain enlightenment], those who have first resolved, those who have not yet resolved, those who lack faith, and those who will certainly gain faith—may behold me."

The Spirit said, “I know there are Buddhas, there are spirits, there is capability, and there is incapability; there is that which is spontaneous and that which is not spontaneous. The Master said, “Non-action is it. Non-action is it.
The Spirit said, “Even the Buddha employs spirits to protect the Dharma. Would you, Master, dare to fall into rebellion against the Buddha?
I pray that you will deign to instruct me as you please. The Master, having no choice, spoke: “The barrier of Dongyan Temple is vast and wild.”
"However, there are no trees here; they exist only on the northern peak, yet its slope does not form a natural screen.

Can you move the trees from the north to the eastern ridge? The deity replied, "I have received your command. However, there will surely be great commotion during the night. I pray that you, Master, do not be alarmed. He then prostrated himself and departed.
The Master saw him off at the gate and watched until he was out of sight; he beheld his retinue winding along in a manner like that of a sovereign.
That evening, indeed, there was a violent wind and a roar of thunder, and the buildings shook and swayed. The Master said, "The words of the spirit have been verified; you may all be free from fear.
At dawn the next day, when it had cleared and become sunny, the pines and cypresses of the northern cliff had all been moved to the eastern ridge, standing in dense, orderly rows.
The Master said to his disciples, "Do not let outsiders know of this; people will regard me as a sorcerer. He added, "I originally resided on the eastern ridge of the temple."
"Extinction! You must place my remains there. Having said this, he was like one casting off a sloughed skin.
A monk asked Master Jùngjí of Mount Song:
"What is the person who practices goodness? The Master said: "Shouldering the cangue and wearing the shackles. [The monk] asked: "What is the person who acts..."

The practitioner of evil conduct said, "I practice meditation and enter samādhi. The Master said, "You are of shallow capacity; I ask that you request the Master to provide direct instruction. The Master said:
“You ask me about evil; evil does not arise from good. You ask me about good; good does not arise from evil. After the monk had been silent for a long time, the Master said, “Do you understand?
The monk said, “I do not understand. The Master said, “The evil person has no thought of good; the good person has no mind of evil. Therefore it is said:
‘Good and evil are like floating clouds; both have no place of arising or ceasing. At these words, the monk attained great enlightenment. Later, he broke the hearth.
Duo Wenju said, "This son has realized that all dharmas are unborn.

When the National Teacher Huizhong of Nanyang and the Tripitaka Master Mahākarṇa from India arrived at the capital, the latter claimed to have attained the supernormal power of knowing others' minds. The Emperor ordered the National Teacher to test the Tripitaka Master.
As soon as he saw the Master, he prostrated himself and stood to the right. The Master asked, "Have you attained the supernormal power of knowing the minds of others?
He replied, "I dare not say so. The Master said, "Tell me, where am I now? He said, "The Master is the teacher of the entire nation;
how could you have gone to West Shu to watch the boat races? After a long silence, the Master asked again, "Tell me, where am I now?"
"Right now, where am I? Zang said, "The Master is the teacher of the entire nation. How can you be here on Tianjin Bridge watching monkeys perform?
After a long silence, the Master asked again, "Tell me, where am I right now? Zang was unable to fathom it.
The Master rebuked him, saying, "You wild fox spirit! Where is your 'penetration of others' minds'? Zang had no reply.
"Yes. One day, he called to his attendant. The attendant responded. He called him thus three times, and the attendant responded three times. The Master said, "I thought it was I who had failed you;
it turns out it was you who have failed me."
Nanquan arrived for an audience. The Master asked, "Where have you come from? He replied, "From Jiangxi. The Master said, "Have you brought the portrait of Master Mazu with you?
He replied, "This very one is it. The Master said, "What about the one behind it? Nanquan then remained silent.
Danxia came to visit while the Master was asleep. He asked the attendant Danyuan, "Is the National Teacher here?

The attendant said, "He is indeed here, but he simply does not see guests. Danxia said, "That is far too deep and remote. The attendant said, "Do not say so; even with the Buddha-eye, one cannot see him.
Danxia said, "A dragon begets a dragon; a phoenix begets a phoenix. Then the Master woke from his sleep.

The attendant reported this to the Master. The Master struck him twenty blows and drove him out. When Danxia heard of it, he said, "He is truly not mistaken in being called the National Teacher of Nanyang.
The Master asked the Imperial Official Zilin, "Where have you come from? He replied, "From south of the city. The Master said, "What is the grass like south of the city?"
[The Master] said, "What color is it? [The boy] replied, "It is yellow. The Master then asked the boy, "What color is the grass south of the city wall? [The boy] replied, "It is yellow."
The Master said: "Even this very boy may be granted purple robes before the imperial curtain and discuss the profound mysteries in the presence of the Emperor.
Regarding Chan Master Dengyuan Yingzhen of Mount Dengyuan in Jizhou: when he was serving as an attendant to the National Teacher, one day the National Teacher was...
In the Dharma Hall, as the Master entered, the National Teacher lowered one foot. Upon seeing this, the Master departed. After a long while, he returned.
The National Teacher asked, "What was your intention just now? The Master said, "To whom could it have been explained?
The National Teacher said, "I am asking you. The Master said, "Where would you see me? The Master then asked, "If someone should come after a hundred years..."
A question was asked regarding the matter of the ultimate limit. The National Teacher said, "Fortunately, you are already here; why must you seek a talisman for protecting the body?"

On the anniversary of the National Teacher’s death, a vegetarian feast was prepared. A monk asked, “Will the National Teacher come? The Master said, “I do not yet possess the power of knowing others’ minds.
The monk asked, “Then why is this feast being prepared? The Master said, “I do not sever conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).”
One day, Emperor Taizong of the Song dynasty visited Xiangguo Temple and asked a monk who was reading a sutra, "What sutra is this? The monk replied, "The Benevolent Kings Sutra. The Emperor said:

[The Emperor] said, "Since this is the scripture of the Sovereign, why is it in your hands? [The monk] was speechless. [The Emperor] took the opportunity to open the treasure pagoda and asked a monk, "Who are you?
The monk replied, "I am the master of the pagoda. [The Emperor] said, "This is my pagoda; why do you act as its master? [The monk] was speechless.

When the monk was attending court, Zongzao asked him, "Where have you come from? He replied, "From the Woyun Hermitage on Mount Lu. [Zongzao] said, "I have heard that deep within Woyun [there is a place of] profound stillness."

[The Emperor] did not look up at him. "For what reason have you come here? [The monk] had no reply. After the monk entered for an audience, he addressed the Emperor, saying, "Does Your Majesty remember?

[The Emperor] said, "Where did we last meet? [The monk] said, "Since our parting at Vulture Peak, it has been until this very day. [The Emperor] said, "What proof do you have? [The monk] had no reply.

A fire broke out at a temple in the capital, and the Tripitaka scriptures were destroyed. The monk requested that they be granted anew by imperial decree. He was summoned and questioned regarding the past.
[Meng] Teng was not burned. Why, then, is he burned now? [The monk] was speechless. Zong once dreamed that a divine being informed him, saying, "I request Your Majesty to give rise to the bodhicitta.
Consequently, during the early court audience, he questioned those at the palace gates: "How does one give rise to the bodhicitta? [They] were speechless.

The Master Yushan of Chaling had never traveled on pilgrimage. Once, when a transformation-monk arrived from Mount Lu, they discussed matters concerning the Gate of the Patriarchs (Zongmen). [Yushan] was instructed to contemplate the question:
"When one is atop a hundred-foot pole, how does one advance further? Fodeng replied, "Agh! This lasted for three years. One day, [he suddenly attained realization].
While riding a donkey across a bridge, he stepped upon a plank and fell; suddenly, he attained great enlightenment. He then composed a verse:
"I possess a divine pearl, Long confined by the dust of worldly toil. Today, the dust is cleared and its light shines forth, Illuminating the myriad peaks of mountains and rivers.
Because of this, he no longer traveled to seek teachers elsewhere.
The Master Louzi was a man of unknown origins; his name and lineage were likewise unknown.

One day, while wandering through the streets and markets, he happened to be adjusting his socks and sash beneath a wine tavern when he heard a song being sung by someone on the floor above: "Since you have no heart, I..."
He then desisted. Suddenly, he attained great enlightenment and was consequently named Lousi (The Tower Master).
A lay practitioner once asked Chan Master Yungting of Fuzhou:
"Dongshan said, 'There is one thing that reaches up to heaven and down to earth. I do not know what this is."
"What kind of thing is this? The Master said, "Carrying an iron yoke; eating iron blows. [The monk] said, "Heaven and earth grow dark; mountains and rivers flee.
The Master said, "One more ghost is added before the Hall of King Yama; he shall lie for a thousand years beneath Mount Beimang. [The monk] said, "How joyful! How joyful! The Master said:
This is also like a wild fox swallowing a mouse.
An unnamed old master spent an entire summer without speaking a word to the monks. A monk sighed and said, "I have merely passed this summer in vain."
Xia said, "I do not dare hope for the Master to preach the Buddha-dharma; it would suffice for me to hear even the two characters 'right cause' (zhengyin).

Upon hearing this, the Elder said, "Disciple, do not speak so hastily. As for the right cause, there is not even a single character. Having finished speaking, he clicked his teeth and said: *Recorded by Xia.*

"What you have just said was groundless; it was not right to speak in such a manner. An old master living in a neighboring wall heard this and remarked, "What a fine pot of soup that has been ruined by a single mouse dropping!"
An unnamed old woman and her daughter supported a mountain hermit for twenty years, constantly sending a young girl of eighteen to serve him with meals.
One day, she ordered the girl to hold the master firmly and asked, "At this very moment, what is it? The master replied, "A withered tree."
Leaning against a cold rock, he had no warmth for three winters. When the woman reported this to the old woman (the abbess), she said, "For twenty years I have supported nothing but a common man.
She then sent him away and burned down his hut.
There was a monk who went to visit Mihu. On the road, he encountered an old woman living in a hermitage.
The monk asked, "Do you have any kinsmen? She replied, "I do. The monk asked, "Where are they? She said, "The mountains, rivers, and great earth;
whether grass or trees—all are my kinsmen. The monk said, "Are you not coming here as a nun? She replied, "What do you see in me? The monk said, "A laywoman."
The woman said, "You cannot be a monk. The monk said, "Old woman, do not confuse and muddle the Buddha-dharma.
The woman said, "I am not confusing the Buddha-dharma. The monk said, "If you act as you do, is that not confusing the Buddha-dharma?
The woman said, "You are a man and I am a woman; how could we ever have confused one another?"
Chan Master Faha Li of Chuzhou:
Because Emperor Huizong had converted his monastery into a Shenxiao Palace, the Master ascended the seat and addressed the assembly, saying:

"It is precisely because you have not yet attained thorough penetration that you speak of right and wrong; it is because you lack true realization that you distinguish 'this' from 'that. Even my own body..."
Furthermore, since they do not exist, what is there to say about that which lies outside the body? Viewed through the correct eye, it is but a source of laughter.
Now, as the Sage Ruler has issued his decree to convert monasteries into temples of Shenxiao, adding a crown to the Buddha’s head—considering it, what could be wrong with this?
Today, this mountain monk cannot help but slung his staff across his shoulder and hang his alms-bowl bag high, heading toward the seamless stupa.
Establishing one’s dwelling and securing one’s livelihood, beneath this rootless tree, one whistles at the moon and chants to the wind.
Let the cloud-riding immortals come as they please to recite incantations, write talismans, and perform rites by clapping their teeth.

In years to come, when you have attained the Way and ascended on white clouds, you will be able to repay the unrepayable debt of gratitude and assist in the transformation of non-action. I only fear it may not be jade; yet if it is jade, how truly marvelous! Nevertheless...
"Even so, tell me: how would you express the monk’s turning-about? Do you understand? Having said this, he cast down his whisk and immediately passed away.
The Prefect submitted a memorial, and by imperial decree, the name of the temple was again changed to "True Body."

Formerly, when the Duke Wenzhong of Ouyang was serving as an official in Luoyang, he once went on a journey to Mount Song. Leaving his attendants behind, he proceeded at his own will until he reached a mountain temple.
Upon entering, he found the courtyard filled with tall bamboos; the frost was clear and birds were singing, the scenery vivid and bright. There, Wenzhong rested.
At the palace steps, there was an elderly monk nearby reading a sutra with complete composure. When Wen Zhong spoke to him, he did not look back or respond much.
Wen Zhong found this strange and asked, "Has the practitioner lived on this mountain for long? He replied, "For a very long time. Wen Zhong asked again, "Which sutra are you reciting? He replied:

Regarding the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, Wenzhong asked: "Among the eminent monks of antiquity, when facing the threshold of life and death, they all for the most part cast off their bodies with talk and laughter.

What path led them to this? He replied: "It was simply the power of meditative concentration and wisdom (*samādhi* and *prajñā*. Wenzhong asked again: "Why is it that nowadays such instances are silent and non-existent?"
"Why is this? the old monk asked with a smile. "The ancients," he said, "were in meditative concentration and wisdom at every moment; how could they have been disturbed at the time of death?

The people of today are in a state of distraction at every moment; how could they attain stability at the time of death? Wen Zhong was so greatly delighted that he did not even realize his knees had bent.
An anonymous monk who was serving as an administrative official (*karmadāna*) under the assembly at Yanguan Temple suddenly saw a ghost messenger come to pursue him.

The monk said, "I am an administrative official and have not yet had the leisure to practice. I beg you to grant me seven days; would that be possible? The messenger replied, "Wait, I shall go and inform [the authorities]."
"O King, if you grant permission, I shall come after seven days; otherwise, I will arrive in an instant. Having spoken, he vanished.
When the seven days had passed, the king searched for the monk but could not find him at all. Later, someone questioned another monk:
"If you were to be caught, how would you evade them?"
Furthermore, there was an anonymous monk who stayed within the sutra hall and did not read the scriptures, but sat in meditation every day. The Librarian asked, "Why do you not read the scriptures?
The monk replied, "I am illiterate. The Librarian said, "Why do you not ask others? The monk stepped forward, joined his palms, and bowed respectfully.
[The Master] asked, "What character is this? The Abbot of the Repository had no reply.
A monk entered the underworld and saw Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva. Kṣitigarbha asked, "What practice have you cultivated throughout your life?
The monk replied, "I recite the Lotus Sūtra. [Kṣitigarbha said], "'Cease, cease! Do not speak; my Dharma is subtle and inconceivable. Is this speaking, or is it not speaking?"
The monk remained silent.
One day, when a nameless ancient master did not attend the hall, his attendant requested that he go to the hall. The master said, "Today I am eating at the manor."
"Oil-cakes have satisfied me. The attendant said, "The Master has not been out. Deyi said, "Go ask the village headman.
Just as the attendant was about to leave the gate, he suddenly saw the village headman coming to thank the Master for visiting his village.

The Dharma Master Zhengwu of India was a disciple of the Dharma Master Bai-lu Xian. He once lamented that students were confined by names and forms, even to the point of regarding the Tiantai school as merely a study of words and letters, while the Southern School looked down upon it.
Thereupon, he went to visit the Chan Master Ciyuan Yuan of Huguo. During their conversation one night:
The Master cited the verse by Dongpo on staying at Donglin and said, "It is not easy to reach such a state.
Yuan said, "I have not yet even seen the path; how can you say I have 'reached' it? The Master said, "As for what he said: 'The sound of the brook is itself the broad and long tongue.'"
"Are these mountain colors not the pure body? If one does not reach this state, how could there be such news?
Yuan said, "That is merely a man from outside the gate. The Master said, "Venerable One, do not be stingy; you may explain it for me.
Yuan said, "Instead, right here, exert your utmost energy and look closely to catch him. If you can catch him and see through him, then you will know the source."
He instructed Yuan Chenluo on the place where he should reside. The Master did not sleep for the entire night. At dawn, as the bell tolled, he removed his secret concealment and spoke another verse:
"The Layman Dongpo is far too talkative; In the gateway of sound and form, he wishes to pass through.
If the stream is sound and the mountain is form, Without mountain and without water, one is a person of sorrow. He specifically told this to Yuan. Yuan said, "To you..."
Dao was a man from outside the gate. The Master bowed in thanks. Not long after, there was one who had repaired the roof tiles of Mazu’s hall and requested words to promote [the teaching].
The Master wrote: "Send word to the old adept of Jiangxi: Let him be scorched by the sun and blown by the wind as he pleases.

It is not that his descendants lack the means to manage it; He simply wishes to see the moment when it melts like ice and crumbles like a wall. When Ciana saw this, he laughed and said, "One must indeed..."
Only this master could achieve such a feat.

The nun Jingju (Pure Abode) constantly practiced meditative concentration within a stone grotto on Mount Dayi (Great Sun). One day, she suddenly thought to herself: "The nature of phenomena is profoundly still."
Fundamentally, there is neither going nor staying. To loathe clamor and hasten toward stillness—how could this be considered realization?
Thereupon, he went to visit Xuefeng. Xuefeng asked, "Where have you come from? The Master said, "From Mount Daji. Xuefeng said, "Has the sun risen yet?
The Master said, "If it had risen, it would have melted away Xuefeng. Xuefeng asked, "What is your name? The Master said, "Xuánjī (Mysterious Pivot). Xuefeng said, "It weaves by day."

"How much? The Master replied, "Not a single thread hangs. He then bowed and withdrew. As he had walked only three or five paces, Xuefeng called out, "The corner of your cassock is trailing on the ground!
The Master turned his head; Xuefeng said, "Truly excellent—'not a single thread hangs.'"
A salt-seller encountered a monk who was heading toward Fushan. The monk asked, "Which way does the road to Fushan go?
The salt-seller remained silent for a long while. The monk asked again, to which the salt-seller replied, "Are you deaf? The monk said, "Tell me."
"What is it? the old man asked. The monk said, "I tell you, it is the path of the overturned boat. The old man said, "Do you not understand Zen? The monk said, "Do not say that I understand Zen;
I have exhausted all the Buddha-dharma as well. The old man said, "Then try to explain it to me. The old man lifted up his salt basket. The monk said, "Difficult.
The old man said, "What do you call this? The monk said, "Salt. The old man said, "What connection is there [between that and the Buddha-dharma]?"
Shè asked, "What do you call this? The monk replied, "I cannot say to you again that it is salt.
This monk was Wéntōnghuì of Báiyún Monastery in Kāifēng, Hénán. His master ordered him to attend to the washing basin; by chance, there was fresh produce from the market.
While he was washing his feet in a basin, Wen became angry and struck him; the monk suddenly fell. He then fled secretly to Zongchi Monastery in Huazhou.
After a long time, he became the abbot (changlao), a position he held for more than twenty years. One day, he suddenly said to his disciples, "The case from twenty years ago must be settled today.
When the assembly asked for the reason, he replied, "At noon you shall know it yourselves," whereupon he sat in meditation (dieduo).
He sat there waiting. At that time, Zhang Jun was leading his troops to Guanzhong. A soldier carrying a bow and arrows arrived at the Dharma Hall;
he stared intently at Wen and was about to shoot him. Wen laughed and said, "I have been waiting for you, old monk, for a long time.
The soldier said, "We have never met before. Now that I see you, my anger cannot be restrained; I wish to kill you immediately. Why is that? Wen told him of their past connection.
Suddenly, he spoke a verse, saying: "Enmity begets enmity; when will it end? Kalpa after kalpa, we entangle one another—is this by mere chance?

It would be better to resolve this together with my teacher; Right now, standing here, I depart for the Western Heaven. Upon looking at him, he was already standing in the state of transformation (parinirvāṇa).
Wen then sought out a brush and wrote a verse: "For thirty-three years I have wandered, Assuming various forms along the way. Who would have known..."
Meeting today, it was actually an obstacle that had appeared before me. Having finished writing, he passed away peacefully.

When National Teacher Baizhang Huaihai went to see Mazu Daoyi, as soon as the assembly had gathered, the Master stepped forward and rolled up the seat. Mazu immediately descended from the seat, and the Master followed him to the hall.
The Master said, "I have not yet spoken a word; why did you immediately roll up your mat?
The teacher replied, "Yesterday, I was pinched by the Master until my nose ached. The Master said, "Where did you direct your attention yesterday?
The teacher replied, "Today, my nose does not ache anymore. The Master said, "You have deeply understood what happened yesterday. The teacher then paid his respects.

He withdrew. The Master went for a second audience. While standing in attendance, the Patriarch looked at the whisk in the corner of his corded seat. The Master said, "Is it used right here? Or is it apart from this?
The Patriarch replied, "When you open your two flaps of skin [your mouth] in the future, with what will you save people? The Master took the whisk and held it upright.
[The Master] rose. The Patriarch said, "Is it by using this? Or is it apart from using this? The Master hung his whisk back in its original place.
The Patriarch let out a thunderous shout, which left the Master deaf for three days straight. Not long after, he resided at Mount Daxiong;

because the cliffs and peaks there were so steep and lofty, it was named Baizhang. Scholars from all directions flocked to him like deer. One day, he said to the assembly, "The Buddha-dharma is not..."
"It was a minor matter. In the past, when I was struck by Mazu Daoshi’s single shout, my ears were deaf for three days.
When Huangbo heard this being mentioned, he involuntarily stuck out his tongue. The Master said, "Will you not, in the future, become a successor to Mazu? Huangbo replied, "Not so.
Today, because of the Venerable Master’s mention of it, I have been able to see the great functioning of Mazu’s dynamic power; yet, I still do not know Mazu himself."
The Patriarch said, "If you succeed Mazu, you will cause me to lose my descendants. The Master replied, "So it is, so it is.

When one's insight is equal to the teacher's, they have halved the teacher's virtue; only when one's insight surpasses the teacher's is one fit to receive the transmission. You possess an insight that greatly transcends your teacher's."
Huangbo then prostrated.
After he took up residence there, Master Ma sent three jars of sauce as a gift. The Master assembled the community and ascended the hall;

having opened the letter, he took up his staff, pointed at the jars, and said, "If you can speak, I will not break them; if you cannot speak, I shall break them. The assembly was speechless. The Master struck them.
He broke off and returned to the abbot’s quarters.
While Guishan, Wufeng, and Yunyan were standing in attendance, the Master asked Guishan, “Set aside your throat, lips, and mouth;
how would you speak? Guishan said, “I beg the Master to speak for me. The Master said, “I am not unwilling to speak to you, but I fear that in the future...”
"You have lost your children and grandchildren. He then asked Wufeng. Wufeng said, "The Master must also shut it all up together.

The Master said, "In a place where there is no one, I will clench my fists and gaze at you. He then asked Yunyan. Yunyan said, "Does the Master have it yet? The Master said, "I have lost my children and grandchildren."
Whenever the Master ascended the hall, an old man would follow the assembly to listen to the Dharma. One day, when the assembly had withdrawn, only the old man remained.
The Master asked, "Who are you? The old man replied, "I am not a human being. During the time of the past Kāśyapa Buddha, I once dwelt on this mountain.
At that time, because a student asked me, 'Does a great practitioner of the Way still fall within the realm of cause and effect? I..."
He replied, "It does not fall within cause and effect. Consequently, he fell into the body of a wild fox for five hundred lifetimes.

Now he requests the Master to provide a turning word on his behalf, so that he may be liberated from this wild fox body. The Master said, "Ask me. The old man asked, "Does a great practitioner of the Way still fall within cause and effect?
The Master said, "One does not obscure cause and effect. At these words, the old man attained great enlightenment. He prostrated himself and said:
"I have already cast off my wild fox body and now reside behind the mountain. I venture to request that you provide me with the funeral rites accorded to a deceased monk.
After the meal, the Master led the assembly to a cliff behind the mountain, where he used his staff to pull out a dead wild fox and performed its cremation according to the Dharma.
When the Master arrived for the evening lecture hall, he recounted the preceding karmic incident.

Huangbo then asked, "The ancients fell into the body of a wild fox for five hundred lifetimes because they gave one erroneous response to a single phrase. Had they not erred at every turn, what would they have become? The Master said, "Come closer, and I will tell you.
Huangbo stepped forward and struck the Master with his palm. The Master laughed and said, "I thought the beard was red, but it turns out it is the chin that is red."
Furthermore, there was a red-bearded barbarian. At that time, Guishan was serving as the kitchen steward (*diànzuò*) in the assembly.
When the Head Dharma Master Sīmā raised the story of the wild fox and asked the steward, "How would you handle this? the steward shook the door panels three times. Sīmā said, "That is too crude."
Zuo said, "The Buddha-dharma is not a matter of this kind.
While they were all being pressed into labor (pǔqǐng) to dig with pickaxes, a monk suddenly heard the drum signal, raised his pickaxe, laughed loudly, and went back.

The Master said, "How brilliant! This is the gate through which Avalokiteśvara enters the principle. When the Master returned to the monastery, he called that monk and asked him about what had just occurred.
"What principle have you seen that leads you to act in this way? The monk replied, "Just now I was hungry; hearing the sound of the drum, I went back to eat.
The Master then smiled.
A monk asked Xitang, "Setting aside the case of having a question and receiving an answer, what is it like when there is neither question nor answer? Xitang said:
"I am afraid it will rot away. When the Master heard this being cited, he said, "From the beginning, I have suspected this old brother.
[The monk] said, "Please, Master, speak. The Master said, "A unified totality (ekapiṇḍa-lakṣaṇa) cannot be apprehended."
Yunyan asked, "For whom do you labor so diligently every day? The Master said, "There is one person who needs it.
Yunyan asked, "Why do you not let him do it himself? The Master said, "He has no means of livelihood."
Zhaozhou went for an interview. The Master asked, "Where have you recently come from? He replied, "From Nanquan. The Master said, "What words or phrases did Nanquan speak recently?

He replied, "To those who have not yet attained it, one must simply remain silent. The Master said, "Setting aside that word of silence for a moment, how would you express the word of total blankness?
Zhaozhou stepped forward three paces. The Master then gave a shout. Zhaozhou made a gesture of shrinking his body.
The Master said, "How very fine, so silent! Thereupon, Xuangzhou went out.
On another occasion, when the Master had finished preaching the Dharma and the assembly was descending from the hall, he called them. The assembly turned their heads; the Master said, "What is this?"
Ascending the hall, he said: "The numinous light shines alone, utterly transcending the sense organs and their objects. Its essence reveals true permanence, unbound by words and letters.
The nature of mind is unstained, fundamentally perfect and complete from the beginning. Simply by detaching from delusive conditions, one is the Buddha of Suchness."
Chan Master Nanquan Puyuan.
There was a hut-dweller on the slopes of Nanquan Mountain. Someone said to him, "Lately, the Venerable Nanquan has appeared in the world;
why do you not go to pay him a visit? The dweller replied, "It is not merely that Nanquan has appeared in the world; even if a thousand Buddhas were to arise, I would still—"
He did not go. When the Master heard of this, he ordered Zhaozhou to go and investigate him. Zhaozhou went there and immediately prostrated himself. The host paid him no heed.

Zhaozhou walked from east to west, and again from west to east; the host still paid him no heed. Zhaozhou said, "The grass-robbers have been utterly defeated," whereupon he pulled down the curtain and returned.
He reported this to the Master, who said, "I have always suspected this fellow. On the following day, the Master...
Accompanied by a śrāmaṇera, he brought a bottle of tea and three cups to the hermitage. He threw them onto the ground and said, "Yesterday’s!
Yesterday’s! The master asked, "What is 'yesterday's'? The Master struck the śrāmaṇera once on his back and said, "You’ve had me fooled!
You’ve had me fooled! Then, shaking out his sleeves, he turned and departed.
Zhaozhou asked, "The Way is not outside of things; that which is outside of things is not the Way. What is the Way outside of things? The Master struck him.
Zhaozhou seized the staff and said, "In the future, do not strike people in error. The Master said, "Dragons and snakes are easy to distinguish; a patch-robed monk is difficult to deceive."
The Master went to attend upon Master Niepan of Baizhang. Baizhang asked, "Among all the sages of the past, was there any Dharma that they did not preach for others?
The Master said, "There was. Baizhang asked, "What is this Dharma that was not preached for others? The Master said:
"It is not mind, not Buddha, and not a thing. Baizhang said, "I have already spoken. The Master said, "I am simply like this; how about you, Reverend?
Baizhang said, "I am no great spiritual teacher (dàshànzhīshí). How could I know whether there is speaking or no speaking?
The Master said, "I do not understand. Baizhang said, "I have spoken for you quite enough!"
The Master was once with Luzu, Shanshan, and Guizong while they were drinking tea. Luzu lifted up his tea bowl and said, "This very thing existed even before the world was formed.
The Master said, "People today recognize only this thing; they do not yet recognize the world. Guizong said, "That is so.
The Master asked, "Does my elder brother not share this same view? Guizong, however, picked up his bowl and said, "Into the world!"
"Can you speak while [the path] is not yet formed? The Master made a gesture with his palm. Zong made a gesture with his face as if to receive the palm.
Magu, carrying his staff, arrived at Zhangjing; he circled the meditation seat three times, shook his staff once, and stood there upright.
Jing said, "It is so. It is so. Dagu went to the Master’s quarters again; he likewise circled the meditation seat three times, struck his staff once, and stood there upright.
The Master said, "It is not so. It is not so. Dagu said, "Zhangjing said it was so; why does the Master say it is not so?
The Master said, "Zhangjing is indeed right, but you are not. This is merely being turned by the force of the wind; in the end—"

The Abbot of Yanguan said to the assembly, "With space as the drum and Mount Sumeru as the mallet, what kind of person can strike it?
The assembly had no reply. A monk brought this up to the Master (Linji), who said, "Old Wang does not strike this broken drum."
The Master went together with Guizong and Magu to pay their respects to National Teacher Nanyang.

The Master said, "If that is so, then you will not go. Zong said, "What kind of mental activity is this? Thereupon, the Master called out to him, and he immediately turned back, no longer going to pay his respects to the National Teacher.
A head monk was taking his leave of the Master. The Master asked, "Where are you going? He replied, "Down to the mountains.

One day, the Master bolted the gate of the abbot’s quarters and surrounded the exterior with ashes, saying, "If anyone can speak a word that satisfies me, I shall open the gate.
Many came forward to respond, but most did not meet the Master's approval. Zhaozhou said, "Heaven! The Master then opened the gate.

The Master asked Shenshan, "Where have you come from? Shenshan said, "I have come from beating a sieve. The Master said, "Do you beat it with your hands or with your feet?
Shenshan was speechless. The Master said, "Ask me, and I will tell you. Shenshan asked as directed. The Master said, "Remember this clearly."

The Master asked a presiding lecturer (zhuangzhu), "What sutra are you lecturing on? The lecturer replied, "The *Maitreya’s Descent into the World Sutra* (*Mile xiasheng jing*).

The Master asked, "When will Maitreya descend into the world? The lecturer said, "He currently resides in the heavenly palace; he has not yet come. The Master said, "There is no Maitreya in heaven; [he is here on earth]."
There was no Maitreya below [the mountain].
While the Master was staying in his hermitage, a monk arrived. The Master said to him, "I am going up the mountain to work. Wait until mealtime;
prepare some rice, eat it yourself, and then send one portion up here. After a short while, that monk prepared the rice and ate it himself.
Having finished, he suddenly smashed up his household affairs and lay down upon his bed. The Master waited for him to leave before returning to his hut.
Seeing the monk lying there, the Master also lay down beside him. The monk then got up and departed.
After the Master had established his own residence, he said, "When I was staying in that former hut, there was a certain keen and intelligent practitioner whom I have not seen even until this day."
The Master encountered a dispute between the monks of the East and West Halls over a cat. He addressed the assembly, saying, "If you can speak the Way, I shall save the cat;

Zhaozhou took off his sandals, placed them on his head, and walked out. The Master said, "If you had been here..."

The Master said, "Neither as something precious nor as something cheap—how will you buy him? The monk was speechless.

The Master said, "Old man Wang lacks the power of cultivation; he has been spotted by ghosts and spirits. The attendant then asked:
"Since the Master is a good spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra), why was he seen by ghosts and spirits? The Master said, "Offer another portion of rice before the local deity."

The butcher set down his knife, joined his palms, and said, "Prefectural Administrator, which of these is not the finest? The Master [remained silent].
At this, there was an awakening.

"What? the Patriarch asked. "Look at the water," he said.
The Master, together with Nanquan and Guizong, went to visit Jingshan. On the road, they encountered an old woman and asked her, "Which way does the path to Jingshan go?
The woman replied, "Go straight ahead. The Master asked, "The water ahead is deep; can one cross it? The woman replied, "It will not get wet."
[The Master] asked again, "The rice on the upper bank is so excellent; why is the rice on the lower bank so poor?
The woman said, "It has all been eaten by the crabs. The Master said, "The grain is so fragrant! The woman said, "It has no scent at all. The Master asked again.
“Where does the old woman live? they asked. The old woman replied, “She is right here. When the three men arrived at the shop, the old woman brewed a pot of tea and took three cups with her.
She approached them and said, “Monks, those who possess supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*) may drink this tea.
While the three were looking at one another, the old woman said, “Watch as I, an old crone, display my own supernatural powers! Thereupon, she lifted a cup, poured out the tea, and walked away.

The Master said, "I have heard that Guangnan possesses the 'Taming-the-Seas Bright Pearl. Is this true? Yangshan said, "It is. The Master said, "What is this pearl like? Yangshan said, "Black."

The Master said, "Why do you not present it to this old monk? Yang placed his palms together, stepped forward, and said, "Yesterday I arrived at Mount Mui and was also asked for this pearl;
I was left with no words to respond and no reason to proffer. The Master said, "A true lion cub; excellent!"
Nanquan was able to roar. Having finished prostrating himself in worship, he withdrew to the guest seat, assumed his dignified demeanor, and went up again to pay his respects to the Master.
As soon as the Master saw him, he said, "We have already met. Nanquan said, "If we meet in this manner, would that not be improper?
The Master returned to his quarters and shut the door. Nanquan returned and related this to Guishan. Guishan said, "What kind of mental activity is this from Jizang?"
Yang said, "If it were not so, how could one recognize him?
When Minister of State Cui Gongqun was appointed as the Inspector of Hunan, he visited the Master and asked, "By what means did you attain realization?"

The Master said, "One attains it by seeing one's nature. At that time, the Master was suffering from an eye ailment, so the official ridiculed him, saying, "If you say one attains it by seeing one's nature, what can be done about the eyes?
The Master replied, "Seeing one's nature is not the eyes; how could an ailment of the eyes cause any harm? The official bowed his head in gratitude.
The Duke saw a bird dropping dung on the Buddha’s head and asked, "Does a bird have Buddha-nature or not?
The Master said, "It has. The Duke said, "Why does it drop dung on the Buddha’s head? The Master said, "Why does it not drop it on the hawk’s head instead?"
Chan Master Xitang Zhizang was a disciple who entered the hall of Dayi (Mazu) together with Baizhang and Nanquan. Once, Minister Li asked a monk, "What teachings did Master Mazu have?
The monk replied, "The Master sometimes said, 'This very mind is Buddha,' and sometimes he said, 'Neither mind nor Buddha.'"
"Not a Buddha. Li said, "Let us all go over to this side. Li then asked the Master, "What teachings did Master Mazu have?
The Master called out, "Li Ao! Li responded. The Master said, "The drums and horns are sounding."
A monk asked, "When there is a question and an answer, the roles of guest and host are clearly defined. But what is it like when there is neither question nor answer?
The Master said, "I am afraid you will rot away."
A layman asked, "Are there heavens and hells? The Master said, "There are. He asked, "Are there the Treasures of the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha? The Master said, "There are.
He asked further questions, and the Master answered them all by saying, "There are. The man said, "Does it not happen that you, Reverend, are speaking erroneously?
The Master said, "Have you ever met a venerable elder? He replied, "I have once attended upon the Abbot of Mount Jing."
The Master asked, "How would Jingshan answer you? He replied, "He says that everything is entirely non-existent.
The Master asked, "Do you have a wife? He replied, "I do. The Master asked, "Does the Monk Jingshan have a wife? He replied, "No.
The Master said, "In that case, it is appropriate for the Monk Jingshan to say 'no'. The layman bowed in thanks and departed.
The Dharma Master Daoguang asked Zen Master Dazhu Huihai, "What mind does the Zen Master employ to cultivate the Way? The Master replied, "This old monk has no mind to employ and no Way to cultivate.
Daoguang said, "If there is no mind to employ and no Way to cultivate, why do you gather [disciples] every day?"
[The monk] said, "I am encouraging people to study Chan and cultivate the Way. The Master said, "This old monk does not even have the space to plant a single awl;
where could I gather a crowd? This old monk does not even have a tongue; when have I ever encouraged anyone? [The monk] said, "Chan Master, you are lying right to my face!"
The Master said, "This old monk does not even have a tongue to exhort others; how could he understand false speech?
[The student] said, "I, however, do not understand the Chan Master’s discourse. The Master said, "I myself do not understand it either."
The Dharma Seat Master asked: "The Sūtra says that all the Bodhisattvas each entered the gate of non-duality, and Vimalakīrti remained silent.
Is this the ultimate? The Master said: "It is not yet the ultimate. If the Sage’s intention were exhausted there, what would he have further explained in the third fascicle?
After a long silence, the Dharma Seat Master said: "I request the Chan Master to explain the meaning of why it is not yet the ultimate. The Master said: "As the Sūtra states:"
Volume One. This section introduces the assembly’s censure of the ten great disciples for their attachment to mental abiding.
In the second part, the various bodhisattvas each speak on entering the Dharma-gate of non-duality, using words to manifest the wordless. Mañjuśrī then uses the wordless to manifest the wordless.
Vimalakīrti neither spoke nor remained silent; therefore, he was silent. This was because he had withdrawn his previous words.

From this silence, the third fascicle begins its discourse, further manifesting the function of his supernatural powers. "Do you understand, Preceptor? [The student] replied, "How extraordinary it is!"
The Master said, "It is not yet like this. [The student] asked, "For what reason is it not yet so? The Master said, "I have spoken thus merely to shatter people's attachments and deluded sentiments.
According to the true intent of the scriptures, they speak only of the emptiness and stillness of form and mind, in order to cause one to see one's original nature and to abandon false practices."
Enter into true practice. Do not seek the underlying meaning within words, paper, or ink; you will simply attain it by understanding the two characters "Pure Name" (Vimalakīrti).
"Pure" (*jing*) is the fundamental essence (*tǐ*); "Name" (*míng*) is the manifested trace and function (*yòng*). From the fundamental essence arises the manifested trace and function;

from the manifested trace and function one returns to the fundamental essence. Essence and function are non-dual; the fundamental and the manifested are not distinct. Therefore, the ancients said: "Though the fundamental and the manifested are distinct..."

The inconceivable is one; yet even this "one" is not one. If you understand that the two characters "Pure Name" (Vimalakīrti) are merely provisional designations, what more need be said of the ultimate and the non-ultimate?
It is without before or after, neither beginning nor end, neither pure nor named.
It simply reveals to sentient beings the inconceivable liberation of their own original nature. Those who do not see this nature will never see it throughout their entire lives.
Li Hua-yan, the Master of the Avatamsaka Sūtra, asked, "Chan Master, do you believe that insentient things are Buddhas? The Master replied, "I do not believe it.
If insentient things were Buddhas, then living people would be inferior to the dead; even dead donkeys and dead dogs would be superior to living people."
The Sūtra says: "The Buddha-body is the Dharma-body. It is born from precepts, concentration, and wisdom; it is born from the three clarities and the six supernormal powers;
it is born from all wholesome dharmas. [A monk] asked: "If you say that insentient things are the Buddha, then Venerable Sir, should you not become a Buddha now that you are about to die?
The Master said: "How can one become a Buddha? The Master replied: "This very mind is the Buddha; this very mind makes the Buddha. [The monk] asked: "The multitude..."
"When a person is born and enters hell, does their Buddha-nature enter as well? The Master said, "At this very moment when one is committing evil, is there still any goodness present?
He replied, "No. The Master said, "When sentient beings enter hell, it is the same for their Buddha-nature."
The Tripiṭaka Master asked, "Does True Suchness undergo change? The Master said, "It does undergo change. The Tripiṭaka Master said, "Zen Master, you are mistaken.
The Master then asked the Tripiṭaka Master, "Does True Suchness exist? He replied, "It exists. The Master said, "If it were not subject to change, it would certainly be an ordinary monk.
Have you not heard that a Good Friend (kalyāṇamitra) can transform the three poisons into the three collections of pure precepts?"
"Transforming the six consciousnesses into the six supernormal powers; transforming afflictions into bodhi;
transforming ignorance into great wisdom and suchness—if there were no such transformation, the Tripitaka would truly be the path of the natural heretics. Zang said, "If that is so,"
“True Suchness (tathatā) indeed undergoes transformation. The Master said, “If you cling to the notion that True Suchness undergoes transformation, you are likewise an outsider (tīrthika).
The monk asked, “Master, you just now said that True Suchness undergoes transformation, yet now you say it does not transform.
How can this be the definitive truth? The Master said, “If one clearly realizes the nature (prakṛti), it is like a mani jewel manifesting colors; I speak of transformation.”

"It can be said either way. It can be said that it does not change, and it can also be said that it changes. If a person who has not seen their nature hears it said that True Suchness changes, they will understand it as changing;
if they hear it said that it does not change, they will understand it as unchanging. Zang said, "I truly know that the Southern School is indeed unfathomable."

Question: Regarding the similarities and differences among the three teachings. The Master said: "For those of great capacity, they function as one; for those of limited faculties, they are grasped as different.
They all arise from the single nature, yet through the differentiation of faculties and views, they become three. Delusion and enlightenment depend on the person;
it does not lie in the similarities or differences of the teachings."
Master Yuan asked, "Does the Master still apply effort when practicing the Way? The Master said, "I do. He asked, "How do you apply effort?
The Master said, "When hungry, I eat; when tired, I sleep. He asked, "Everyone does this; is your application of effort the same as theirs, Master?
The Master said, "It is not the same. He asked, "Why is it not the same? The Master said, "When others eat, they are unwilling..."
When eating, they demand a hundred things; when sleeping, they refuse to sleep, devising a thousand schemes. This is why they are not the same as others.
Thus, the Vinaya Master kept his mouth shut.
When Zen Master Shishan Zhijian was first traveling as a mendicant with Guizong and Nanquan, they encountered a tiger on the road; each passed by the side of the tiger.
Jianquan asked Guizong, "What was that tiger you just saw like? Guizong said, "It was like a cat.
Guizong then asked the Master, who replied, "It was like a dog. He then asked Nanquan, who said, "I saw it as a great beast."
While the Master was eating his meal, Nanquan gathered up the raw rice. He said, "Is this raw? The Master said, "It is not raw.
Nanquan said, "Even 'not raw' is still secondary. After Nanquan had walked a few steps, the Master called out, "Elder! Nanquan turned his head and asked, "What is it?
The Master said, "Do not say that it is secondary."
While they were collectively gathering and selecting bracken, Nanquan picked up a single stalk and said, "This one is excellent for making an offering. The Master said, "It is not only this one;
he would pay no heed even to a hundred flavors of rare delicacies. Nanquan said, "Even so, each and every one must be tasted before it is acceptable."
Chan Master Shigong Huizang originally made his livelihood by hunting. He held monks in contempt. Once, while chasing a deer, he passed before Mazu’s hermitage.
Mazu went out to meet him, whereupon the Master asked, “Did you see the deer pass by? Mazu replied, “Who are you? The Master said, “A hunter.”
The Master said, "Do you understand archery? He replied, "I understand archery. The Master said, "With one arrow, how many can you shoot?
He replied, "With one arrow, I shoot one. The Master said, "Then you do not understand archery. He asked, "Does the Master understand archery? The Master said, "I understand archery."
[The Master] asked, "With one arrow, how many do you shoot? The Patriarch said, "With one arrow, I shoot a whole flock.
[The Master] said, "Since both parties possess life, why shoot a whole flock? The Patriarch said, "Since you know this to be so, why do you not shoot yourself?
[The Master] said, "If you were to have me shoot myself, there would truly be no place to apply my hand. The Patriarch said, "This fellow’s ignorance and afflictions from kalpas past—today..."
[The Master] suddenly stopped. The Teacher cast down his bow and threw himself at the Patriarch to leave the household life.
One day, while he was performing chores in the kitchen, the Patriarch asked, "What are you doing? He replied, "Tending the ox. The Patriarch asked, "How do you tend it?
He said, "Whenever it goes into the grass, I pull it back by the nose. The Patriarch said, "You truly tend the ox. The Teacher then—
"Stop! After the Master took up residence there, he constantly used the bow and arrow to test his students' mettle.
Zen Master Nanyuan Daoming went to visit Dongshan;
as soon as he stepped onto the Dharma Hall, the Master said, "We have already met. Dongshan then descended. The next day—
Qiaoshang asked, "Yesterday I already received the Master’s compassion; I do not know where it was that we met.
The Master said, "Mind after mind, without interruption, flows into the ocean of nature. Shan said, "How many times could I have let this pass?"
Master Hong'en of Zhongyi was asked by Yangshan, "How can one come to see the meaning of Buddha-nature? The Master said, "I will give you a parable.
Suppose there is a room with six windows, and inside there is a monkey. Outside, a monkey calls out from the east, 'O gibbon!'"

The orangutan immediately responded. Thus, when called from all six windows, it responded from each. Yangshan bowed in thanks and rose, saying, “I have now understood everything through the Master’s analogy.
However, there is one further matter: if the inner monkey has fallen asleep while the outer monkey wishes to meet with it, what then?
The Master descended from his rope-corded seat, took Yangshan by the hand, and danced with him.
He said: "The *xingxing* has met you. It is like a *jiaoming* insect building a nest upon the eyelashes of a mosquito, crying out at a crossroads:
'The land is vast and the people few; those who meet are scarce.'"
Chan Master Sanyue Zongyin addressed the assembly, saying:
"In preaching the Dharma, one must always accord with the time and the season. At that time, a monk asked:
"What is it like during the 'four yellows' and 'four reds'? The Master said: "Carried on the tip of the staff in the third month. The monk asked: "Why is it stored full within the belly?"
"Qi. The Master said, "What can you do about this single rope? [The monk] asked, "How can one get out of this qi? The Master said, "Wait until the skin is worn through."
A monk asked, "What are the Three Jewels? The Master said, "Rice, wheat, and beans. The monk said, "I do not understand, Teacher. The Master said, "The assembly joyfully accepts and upholds them."
Chan Master Wuye of Fenzhou went to visit Mazu.
Upon seeing that his appearance was extraordinary and grand, and his voice resonant like a bell, Mazu said, "How lofty and majestic!"
There was no Buddha within it. The Master prostrated, knelt, and asked: "I have roughly exhausted the essential meanings of the literature of the Three Vehicles.

I have often heard that in the Gate of Chan, 'the mind itself is the Buddha,' yet I truly have not yet understood this. The Patriarch said: "It is precisely this very mind that you have not yet understood;
there is nothing else besides it. The Master asked: "What is the seal of the mind that the Patriarch secretly transmitted when he came from the West? The Patriarch said: "Virtuous One..."
"Right in the midst of the clamor! Go now; come back at another time. As soon as the Master had stepped out, the Patriarch called out, "Virtuous One!

The Master turned his head. The Patriarch asked, "What is this? At that, the Master attained realization and prostrated himself. The Patriarch said, "You dull-witted fellow! Why do you prostrate yourself?"
After the Master had taken up residence, whenever students came to question him, he would mostly answer them by saying: "Do not engage in false conceptualization. The Master said:
"The Buddhas have never appeared in the world, nor have they bestowed a single dharma upon anyone. It is only according to the illness that the remedy is applied;
thus there are the twelve divisions of the teachings. This is like exchanging honeyed fruit for bitter gourds—it serves to wash away the karmic roots of you all."
Furthermore, it is said that after the ancients who were true men of the Way attained their realization, they dwelt in thatched huts or stone chambers, eating rice cooked in a broken-legged cauldron.
For twenty or thirty years, fame and profit did not enter their hearts, nor did wealth and treasure occupy their thoughts.

They utterly forgot the ways of the world and concealed their traces among the mountain crags. Though kings summoned them, they would not come; though feudal lords invited them, they would not attend. How could they be compared to—
"We are people who crave fame and love profit, submerged in the ways of the world like petty peddlers.
When Chan Master Taoyu was serving food and reached before Layman Pang, the Layman prepared to receive it, but the Master withdrew his hand and said, "To give rise to a mind [of grasping]..."
[The Master] received the offering. Pure Name (Vimalakīrti) had already rebuked him; setting aside that particular case, would you say the Layman [Wuzhuo] was still sweet?

The Layman said, "At that time, was Subhūti not a master of his craft? The Master said, "It has nothing to do with him. The Layman said, "When the food reached the edge of his mouth, it was snatched away by him.
The Master then set down the food. The Layman said, "Not even a single phrase will suffice."
The layman asked again, "Does Master Ma’s point of truly benefiting people still remain entrusted to you, Master?
The Master said, "I have not yet seen him; how could I know his point of being true? The layman said, "Even this very seeing and knowing has no place to be sought.
The Master said, "Layman, you must not speak with absolute finality. The layman said, "One..."
"If you speak in two directions," the Master said, "you lose your thesis again. If you speak in two or three directions, would you still be able to open your mouth?
The Master replied, "It is simply that one cannot open the mouth; this may be called reality. The layman clapped his hands and departed.
A monk asked Master Rishan, "When all forms return to emptiness, where does emptiness return? The Master said, "My tongue does not leave my mouth.
The monk asked, "Why does it not leave your mouth? The Master said, "Because inner and outer are one and the same."
Master Sōzan was drinking tea with Layman P’ang. The Layman held up his tea bag and said, “Everyone has a share;
why is it that no one can speak of it? The Master said, “Precisely because everyone has a share, they cannot speak of it. The Layman said, “Brother!”
"Why did you nevertheless speak? the Master said, "It was impossible not to say anything. The scholar said, "Truly so! Truly so! The Master then drank his tea.
The scholar said, "Brother, when you drink your tea, why do you not bow to your guest? The Master said, "Who? The scholar said, [pointing to himself].
Regarding Pang Gong: The Master said, "Why must you bow again? Later, when Danxia heard of this, he remarked, "Had it not been for Songshan, I might have been led astray by that old fellow.
When the scholar heard this, he sent someone to deliver a message to Danxia, saying, "Why do you not understand him before he even lifts his bag?"
Prime Minister Yu Di asked Chan Master Datong of Ziyu Mountain:
"What is it like when a black wind blows one's ship, causing it to drift and fall into the realm of rākṣasa demons?"
The Master said, "Yuti, you hired laborer! Why do you ask such a question? At this, Lord Yu turned pale with alarm.
The Master then pointed and said, "This very thing is what causes one to drift and fall into the land of the rākṣasa demons. The Lord asked again, "What is the Buddha?
The Master called out, "Lord! The Lord responded, "Yes? The Master said, "Seek nothing else. When Yaoshan heard of this, he remarked, "Alas! What a pity for the Yu family!"
Han was buried alive within Mount Ziyu. When the Duke heard of this, he went to visit Yaoshan.
Yaoshan asked, "I have heard that you, Excellency, are performing great Buddhist rites on Mount Ziyu; is this true? The Duke replied, "I dare not say so.

He continued, "I have heard that you possess words capable of saving others, and today I have come specifically for that reason. Yaoshan said, "If you have any doubts, ask away. The Duke asked, "What is the Buddha?"
Shanshan summoned Yu Di. The Master responded with an "Amen. Shanshan asked, "What is this? At these words, the Master attained realization.
Zen Master Yinfeng of Wutai Mountain asked Shitou, "How can one become in accord with the Way? Shitou said, "I, too, am not in accord with the Way. The Master said, "Finished."
"How was it in the end? Deshan said, "How long have you been obstructed by this?
While Deshan was weeding, the Master stood to his left with his hands folded. Deshan threw the weeding tool toward the Master and weeded a blade of grass before him.
The Master said, "The Master can weed only this; he cannot weed that. Deshan picked up [the tool].
The Master picked up a grass-cutter. He then made the gesture of cutting grass. The Head said, "You only know how to cut that;
you do not understand how to cut this. The Master was speechless.
As the Master was pushing his cart, Mazu sat on the road with his legs extended. The Master said, "I ask you, Master, to withdraw your feet.
Mazu replied, "Once extended, they do not shrink back. The Master said, "Once advanced, one does not retreat," and he pushed the cart over, crushing Mazu's feet.
Mazu went to the Dharma Hall, took up an axe, and said, "Come out, whoever it is that just now crushed my feet! The Master then came forth before Mazu.
The former master extended his neck forward; the Patriarch smiled and set down his axe.

Upon arriving at Nanquan, he encountered the assembly in the midst of formal inquiry. Nanquan pointed to a water pitcher and said, "The copper pitcher is an object; there is water within the pitcher."
"Do not touch the object; bring water for the old monk. The Master picked up the *karakā* (water pitcher) and poured it toward the front of Quan’s face;
Quan then desisted. Upon arriving at Mt.
Wei, he entered the hall and hung up his robes and bowl at the head of the upper platform. Hearing that his "uncle" had arrived, Wei [Shan] first...
Maintaining his dignified demeanor, he descended into the hall to look around. When the Master saw him coming, he assumed a reclining posture.

Baizhang then returned to the abbot’s quarters. Shortly thereafter, the Master departed. A short while later, Mount Yuanshan asked his attendant, "Is my uncle still here? The attendant replied, "He has already left. Yuanshan said:
"What words were there when you left? he asked. The Master said, "There were no words. Miaoyan said, "Do not say there were no words; the sound was like thunder.

When the Master was at Xiangzhou, he broke the formalities of the hall and wore only his undergarments. Standing by the mortars and pestles, he took up a mallet and said, "If you can speak, I shall not strike you.
At that time, the assembly remained silent. The Master then struck once.
One day, while Chan Master Tanzang of Xiyuan on Mount Nanyue was bathing by himself, a monk asked, "Why do you not have a novice attend to this? The Master clapped his hands three times.
In the eastern kitchen there was a great python several *zhang* long, with its mouth agape and fangs bared, emitting a blazing fire of venom.
An attendant requested that he avoid it, but the Master said, "Can death be escaped? It comes with poison; I receive it with compassion. Poison has no inherent nature."
"When stimulated, it becomes strong. If compassion lacks a causal condition, then enemies and kin are of one accord. Having finished speaking, the python lowered its head and walked away slowly;
suddenly, it was gone.
Chan Master Shenzang of Maitou Peak in Cizhou ascended the hall and said:
"To know while being without knowing—this is not a state of non-knowing that one speaks of as 'non-knowing. He then descended from his seat.
The monk Wujou was visited by the two senior monks Xuanshao and Shao. The Master asked, "From where have you two Zen travelers set out? Xuanshao said, "Jiangxi. The Master struck him.
Xuanshao said, "I have long known that the Master possesses such a vital pivot. The Master said, "Since you do not understand, [you are no more than a wooden man]."
The monk behind him merely looked on. Shao intended to step forward, whereupon the Master struck him and said, "I knew there would be no difference in the soil within the same pit. Go to the hall."
He asked a monk, "Where have you recently come from? The monk replied, "From Dingzhou. The Master said, "How is the Dharma-way in Dingzhou compared to here? The monk replied, [silently].
"Not different. The Master said, "If they are not different, go back there again! and he struck him. The monk said, "There is an eye at the head of the staff;
one must not strike people so recklessly. The Master said, "Today I have hit one," and he struck him three more times. The monk then went out.
The Master said, "It turns out there was someone to eat the brunt of this staff. The monk replied, "What can you do? The handle of the ladle is still in my hand."
[The Master] still held it in his hand. The Master said, "If you want it, I shall give it back to you when I return.
The monk stepped forward and snatched the staff, striking the Master three times. The Master said, "An unjust blow! An unjust blow! The monk said, "There is someone who has eaten [of its fruit].
The Master said, "In haste, I have struck a man. The monk bowed. The Master said, "And so he goes away. The monk laughed loudly and departed. The Master said, "He is worthy."
"It is so. It can be digested as such. An ancient temple master was visited by Danxia for an audience.
After staying overnight, when the morning congee was ready, the attendant served the Master only one bowlful and then served [himself] another.
He ate the bowl himself, paying no heed at all to Danxia. Danxia also served himself some porridge and ate it.
The attendant said, "Rising early at the fifth watch of the night, there are still travelers on the road. Danxia asked the Master, "Why do you not instruct this attendant? He has become so impolite.
The Master said, "One must not defile the pure ground with the sons and daughters of others. Danxia said, "..."
I almost asked that old fellow about his transgression.
When Master Shijiu first visited Mazu, Mazu asked, "Where have you come from? The Master replied, "From Wujiao. Mazu said, "Wujiao..."
"What have you been saying lately? the Patriarch asked. The Master said, "How many people are utterly bewildered by this? The Patriarch said, "Set aside the bewilderment for a moment;
as for that silent phrase—how about it? The Master then stepped forward three paces. The Patriarch said, "I have seven blows to deliver to Wujiu.
Are you willing to take them? The Master said, "The Master shall eat them first; I will be willing to take them afterward."
Master Benchxi was asked by Layman Pang: "When Danxia struck his attendant, what was his intention? The Master said, "An old fellow like you is still concerned with the long and the short.
The Layman said, "Because I am a fellow student of yours, I venture to ask this question. The Master said: [He remained silent.]
"If it is so, I shall bring it up from the beginning and deliberate with you. The layman said, "Great elder, you must not speak of people's faults with me.
The Master said, "I am mindful that you are advanced in years. The layman said, "My fault, my fault!"
When Master Shilin saw Layman Pang approaching, he held up his whisk and said, "This does not fall within the scope of Danxia’s device; try and say a single phrase.
The Layman snatched away the whisk and instead raised his own fist. The Master said, "That is precisely Danxia’s device."
The layman said, "Give me something that does not fall into the trap of conceptual viewing. The Master said, "Danxia suffers from muteness; Pang Gong suffers from deafness.
The layman said, "Exactly so. The Master was speechless. The layman said, "I told you it would be a mere coincidence.
On another day, the Master asked the layman, "I have a question to ask. Layman, do not be stingy with your words. The layman said, "Please go ahead and pose it. The Master said:
"Originally, I was sparing with my words. The Layman said, "This greeting of yours has unconsciously fallen into his trap.
The Master then covered his ears and said, "An adept! An adept!"

The Oxhead Monk of Zhenzhou used to prepare his own meals to provide for the assembly of monks. When it was time for the midday meal, he would carry the rice bucket to the front of the hall, perform a dance,
and laugh heartily, saying, "Sons of the Bodhisattvas, come and eat!"
One day, Master Baoling and Layman Pang encountered each other on the road. The Master asked, "Have you ever shared the phrase by which you attained realization at Mount Heng with anyone?
The Layman said, "I have. The Master asked, "To whom did you share it? The Layman pointed with his hand.
