Left Vice-Minister Fan Chong, the Layman Cizhu, while serving as Director of the Hanlin Academy and governing Yuzhang, visited Yuan Tong Temple to pay his respects to Chan Master Min. After the tea was finished, [Fan] said: "I am about to depart..."

"I am old now," he said. "Having fallen among those of the *jinzi* (purple-gold) rank, I have become somewhat distant from this matter. The Attendant (*tong*) called out, "Director of the Secretariat! The Master responded, "Yes? The Attendant said, "How could there be any distance?
The Master leaped up with joy and said, "I beg the Master to grant me further instruction. The Attendant said, "From here to Hongdu, it is four stages' journey.

The Master stood in thought for a moment. The Attendant said, "If you see it, you see it immediately; if you attempt to deliberate upon it, you are already mistaken. At these words, the Master was suddenly enlightened.
However, there was one who attained realization. While he and Yuantong were huddling by the brazier, the Master asked, "The karmic conditions of the various houses need not be brought forth;

I ask the Master for a direct, single phrase of instruction. Yuan Tong pointed with a stern voice and said, "Look at the fire! The Master quickly pulled back his robe and suddenly attained great enlightenment, whereupon he offered his thanks.
He said, "It is evident that the Buddha-dharma is not something vast. Tong shouted, "Put it down! The official responded with repeated assent.
The scholar then asked Yuantong, "This Dharma cannot be understood through thought or discrimination; how can one find a point of entry?"
Tong said, "The whole body enters the mass of fire. The official asked, "Ultimately, how does one understand this? Tong said, "Go straight ahead. The official hesitated.
Tong said, "Would you like some more tea? The official said, "There is no need. Tong said, "Why do you not understand it in this way?"
Master Gong said, "Originally, it is far too near. Tong said, "One hundred and eight thousand [miles].
Master Gong composed a verse of divination: "Inconceivable! This is a great mass of fire. To go thus, one does not leave this very place. Tong said, "Ei! There is still this thing remaining.
Master Gong said, "I beg the Master to grant me further instruction. Tong said, "To go thus, the cauldron is cast of iron."
The Duke bowed his head in thanks.
Chan Master Tudu Zhice of Mount Jingshan first visited Jishi Guang, where he attained a clear realization. He next visited Dayuan at Wanshou Temple, who asked him:
"Where have you come from? The Master said, "From Tiantai. [Daoyuan] asked, "Did you see the Great Master Zhizhe?
The Master said, "Even now, he is not lacking. [Daoyuan] asked, "Why is he under your very heels? The Master said, "You have missed him right before your face.
Daoyuan said, "The Master has flourished without weeding and stands straight without support. One day, the Master took his leave. Daoyuan saw him to the gate and patted him on the back, saying:
"The place where the treasure lies is near; this city is not real. The Master nodded in agreement. He then traveled to Yuzhang to visit Dian Niu.
On his way, he passed through Yunju, where wind and snow blocked the roads for forty-two days. At noon, the sound of a wooden board rang out sharply, and he attained a sudden, great enlightenment.
Upon arriving at the gate, Dian Niu pointed specifically at the Master and said, "Where have you come from seeing gods and ghosts? The Master replied, "Yun..."
While staying there, he heard the sound of a wooden board being struck. The Ox asked, "What is that? The Master said, "It breaks through empty space;
it has no handle or shaft at all. The Ox said, "The matter beyond this is not yet settled. The Master said, "The neighbor to the east sits in the dark; the neighbor to the west scolds one another.
The Ox said, "You have emerged far above Buddhas and patriarchs. When you establish yourself in the future, a single unicorn will suffice."
Chan Master Shao-long of Huqiu:

The Master first visited Chan Master Xin of Changlu and grasped its general outlines. When someone brought a transmission of Yuanwu’s words to him, the Master read them and sighed, saying, "It is like imagining the brine of fermented vinegar;
though it has not yet washed one's intestines or moistened one's stomach, it nonetheless brings a sense of exhilaration."
My only regret is that I have not yet had the opportunity to hear his voice. Consequently, he proceeded from Baofeng to Zhandang, stayed as a guest at Huanglong, and called upon Chan Master Sishin.
He next visited Yuanwu. One day, he entered the hall. Yuanwu asked, "When seeing the seer, the seeing is not the seeing;
even when seeing is separated from seeing, seeing cannot reach it. He raised his fist and said, "Do you see? The Master replied, "I see. Yuanwu said, "..."
"Placing a head upon a head. Upon hearing this, the Master attained a sudden realization. Wuzu shouted, "What have you seen?
The Master replied, "The dense bamboo does not hinder the flowing water from passing through. Wuzu approved of him. He was subsequently appointed to oversee the library.
Someone asked Wuzu, "Master Long is so gentle and easygoing; how can he accomplish anything? Wuzu said, "He is a sleeping tiger."
Chan Master Fozhi Duanyu of Yuyang Monastery ascended the hall and said:
"When walking, there is no trace of walking; when speaking, there is no mark of speaking. If walking and speaking reach their destination, one merely sets up a target to invite an arrow.
If walking and speaking are not yet clarified, the divine blade cuts through them all. Even if one’s speech is without leakage and one’s conduct is without delusion—"

For the time being, you remain stuck in the husks of outflows. If you were a great garuḍa, soaring with vigor for hundreds of thousands of yojanas, or a divine ten-shadows horse, galloping across the four quarters and the eight extremities, not pecking at food haphazardly nor burying its body wherever it lands—if you were such a being, would you still have any need to rely on anything at all?
Every land and every atom is the essential ford.
Chan Master Hugu Jingyuan ascended the hall and said:
"Before King Bhīṣmagarjitasvararāja, this lot of fellows were all wrong by seven or eight; after King Bhīṣmagarjitasvararāja, they were likewise."
This group of men fell two, three, four. Now this group of men sits and stands with solemn dignity.
Tell me, is this "mistaken seven, mistaken eight," or "falling two, falling three"? Can you yet discern the definitive truth? Raising his whisk, he said: "HŪṂ."
HŪṂ. The Master, because the monks were reciting the discourse from Dead Heart’s (Sixin) *Xiaocan*, said: "Since there is delusion, one must attain awakening.

Since there is awakening, one must recognize delusion within awakening and awakening within delusion. When both delusion and awakening are forgotten, one then establishes all things from the state where neither delusion nor awakening exists."
When Master Fa heard of this, he was filled with doubt. He immediately hurried to the Buddha Hall and pushed open the door panels with his hands;
suddenly, he attained great enlightenment. Subsequently, his administrative duties were performed with such spontaneous eloquence that Yuanwu dubbed him "The Headstrong Chan Attendant.
Yuanwu himself inscribed a portrait of him, saying: "Throughout my life, I have spoken only of headstrong Chan; when one encounters such a headstrong person, it is like hitting an iron wall."

The layman Zeng Kai, a former Secretariat Drafter, was a long-time student under various masters. In the *Xinwei* year of the Shaoxing era, he came to visit Master Huiyuan of Lingyin while the Master was presiding over Guangxiao Temple.
Kai asked, "What is a person of true realization? The Master replied, "The lanterns, the pillars, the cats, and the dogs."
Yangshan Kai said, "Why is it that praise brings joy while disparagement brings affliction? The Master said, "Attendant, have you ever seen a true teacher (a *kalyāṇamitra*)?
Kai said, "I have spent thirty years in inquiry and study; why do you say I have not seen one? The Master said, "See them in the midst of affliction; see them in the midst of joy.
As Kai hesitated, the Master let out a thunderous shout and struck him with his staff. As Kai was about to respond, the Master said: [The Master then departed.]
The one who opened his mouth was not Master Gong. He opened his mouth and was utterly bewildered. The Master called out, "Attendant Kai, where have you gone?
Kai suddenly attained realization and nodded his head, then spoke this verse: "Alas, the blind donkey! A calamity to the monastic community! With a single roar that shakes the earth—"
The celestial mechanism has been leaked. Someone asked further, "What is the meaning? The Master picked up his whisk and struck him across the mouth.
The Master said, "He too only attained a single peg."
Ge Zhan, the Prefectural Governor, aspired to the Chan school for a long time without attaining realization. One day, he was brought to a sudden awakening upon hearing the statement:
"It is not mind, it is not Buddha, it is not a thing. He spoke this verse: "Not mind, not Buddha, nor yet a thing;

Before the Five-Phoenix Pavilion, the mountain looms high. In the midst of the radiant sun, I turn my body upside down; The wild fox leaps into the golden-haired lion’s den. [He then went to pay his respects.]
The Master asked for verification. The Master said, "In your realization, Layman, you may have entered the realm of the Buddhas, but you have not yet entered the realm of the Māras.
Hege bowed. The Master said, "Why did you not say, 'The golden-haired lion leaps into the den of the wild fox'? Thereupon, Hege attained sudden enlightenment.
Master Huazang Anmin went to visit Master Fojian.
Fojian asked, "Foguo has a phrase that he never spoke of to others in a confused manner; has he ever spoken it to you?
The Master said, "Shut your dog’s mouth! Fojian raised his voice and said, "This is not the principle. The Master said, [silently].
"No one has stolen your bag of tea and salt. What is it called? Jian said, "If Foguo would not explain it for you, I shall explain it for you.
The Master said, "If you have doubts, O Monk, leave this monastery and go elsewhere to study. Jian laughed heartily.
Chan Master Xuansha Shengzao ascended the hall and said:
"In the heavens there is no Maitreya; beneath the earth there is no Maitreya. Tell me, where is Maitreya?"
After a long silence, he said: "When walking at night, do not tread upon the white; it will be either water or stone.
Chan Master Yunbian of Nanfeng went to visit Yuanwu.
Upon entering the inner chamber for instruction, as soon as he stepped through the door, Yuanwu said, "Look under your feet! Yunbian struck the pillar once.
Xuawu said, "Why do you not speak one word of actual substance? The Master said, "If the teacher shakes his head, the disciple wags his tail.
Xuawu said, "Try wagging your tail for me. The Master performed a somersault and left. Xuawu laughed heartily.

Ascending the hall, [the Master] said: "How pleasant it is that mid-spring is gradually warming! Yet how can one bear the Cold Food Festival and Qingming? Ten thousand layers of cloud-covered mountains tower with emerald green;
a single expanse of wind and moon is a fine neighbor. Everywhere, flowers are red and willows are green; the lake and sky are calm, with waves stilled and winds hushed.
The mountain birds on the branches chirp repeatedly—over and over again, in fragments and details, their instructions earnest and insistent. But tell me, what are they saying?"
"What is it that you are entrusting? [The Master] struck the meditation staff and said, "Remember this for next year’s day; it will still be Cold Food Festival and Qingming.
A monk asked, "Throughout the twelve periods of the day, how should a student apply their mind? The Master said, "Dipping into snow to eat a winter melon."
Question: "In the midst of the vast confusion of the mundane world, how does one discern the master? The Master said: "At the tip of the wooden ladle, the sickle cuts the vegetables.
[The questioner] asked: "Is this not precisely where you, the Master, act for the sake of others? The Master said: "The pestle stirs the steamed buns."
Chan Master Daomiao Fuxing Fatai ascended the hall and said:
"If you wish to know where the Buddha has gone, it is simply this sound of my voice. *Du!* (A shout) Fu Dashi did not recognize good from evil!"
Using his radiant and numinous presence, he corrupted the men and women of people’s households.
Master Zhigong gave him a shout, saying, “Great Being, do not speak such words; try saying something else. The Great Being spoke again: “Empty-handed, yet holding a hoe;
Walking, yet riding a water buffalo. A person passes over the bridge; The bridge flows, but the water does not flow. Master Zhigong laughed heartily.
It is said: "The beginning seems acceptable enough, but the end is even more distressing.
Zen Master Zhenshan of Gushan ascended the hall and said:
"To seek the ox, one must follow its tracks; in studying the Way, one prizes the absence of mind. When the tracks are there, the ox is also there; when there is no mind, the Way [is found]."
Easy to find. [Fashi] held up his whisk and said: "This is the track; where is the ox?
Even if you can see its horns with perfect clarity, its nostrils remain in the hands of Fashi.
When Shaojue Daozu was first with Yuanwu, he attained enlightenment upon hearing the words, "The very mind is Buddha. After some time, Yuanwu ordered him to share the seat [of the abbot].
One day, while leading the assembly into the room for instruction, Yuanwu suddenly asked, "When birth and death arrive, how can one evade them? The monk had no reply.
The Master threw down his whisk and passed away suddenly; the assembly all stared in astonishment. When Wuzhuo heard of it, he went to summon him, calling out, "Head Seat Zu!
The Master opened his eyes and looked at him. Wuzhuo said, "Rouse your spirit and pass through the barrier. The Master nodded his head and immediately entered nirvana.
Chan Master Huiri Mo’an Dao ascends the hall:
The gathering clouds are about to snow but have not yet snowed; the beloved sun seems radiant but does not truly shine. Cold sparrows chirp noisily among the fences;
the piercing northern wind dances through the curtains. If you wish to understand the intimate verse of Shaoyang, today I shall reveal it face-to-face for you.
"Awaken! He planted his staff upright and descended from the seat.
The State Councillor Xu Fu, the lay practitioner Shichuan, visited Yuanwu for a formal audience.
Yuanwu was delighted by his transcendent realization. One day, he went to the office of the Secretary and pointed to Yuanwu’s head.
Xiang said, "This old fellow’s heels have not yet even touched the ground. Wu turned his face away and said, "How could the turtle ever have escaped from the jar?
Gong said, "I am glad that this old fellow’s heels have finally touched the ground. Wu said, "Do not slander him; it would be better for you to stop.
Gong then withdrew.

When Zen Master Longya Zhicai first took up residence at Yue-lu, on the day he opened the hall for formal instruction, a monk asked: "De-shan’s staff and Lin-chi’s shout—today I ask the Master to pick them up and set them down.
The Master said: "Suru suru. The monk said: "Suru suru—does this still contain the meaning of the West?"
[The student] said, "No. The Master said, "Suru suru. From this, the monastic community called him Cai Suru.
Chan Master Shouchun Fodeng of Heshan went to visit Chan Master Foguan;
he joined the assembly to seek instruction, yet for a long time he made no progress. He then wrapped his bedding and said, "If in this life..."
He did not penetrate it and vowed never to leave his seat. Thereupon, he sat during the day and stood through the night, as if mourning for a deceased parent.

After more than seven weeks had passed, Master Fojian ascended the hall and said, "The myriad phenomena of the universe are all sealed by a single Dharma. Upon hearing this, the Master attained sudden enlightenment.
He went to see Guanjian. Guanjian said, "What a pity that this bright pearl has been picked up by this madman.
He then interrogated him, saying, "Lingyun said, 'Since the moment I first saw the peach blossoms, until now I have had no further doubts.
What is it about him that he has no doubts? The Master said, "Do not say that Lingyun had no doubts; even now, try to find a place where he doubted."
"It is utterly unattainable. Jian said, "Xuansha said, 'It is precise; it is most precise. I dare guarantee that you, elder brother, have not yet reached the ultimate.
Where, then, is the point where he has not yet reached the ultimate? The Master said, "I deeply understand that the Master’s compassionate heart is most earnest.

Jian agreed. As the Master rose from his prostrations, he presented a verse, saying: "Throughout the day I gaze at the sky without raising my head; Only when the peach blossoms are in full bloom do I lift it."
Mou said: "Even if you had a net that covers the heavens, once you have penetrated this secure barrier, you may simply rest. Jie instructed him to protect and uphold [the teaching].
That evening, he addressed the assembly with a stern voice, saying, "This time, Seat-Holder Xun shall sleep soundly. Yuanwu heard of this.
Doubting that this might not be the case, Wuzhuo said, "I must first put him to the test. He then had someone summon the Master. They went out for a walk in the mountains and happened upon a pond.
Wuzhuo pushed the Master into the water and immediately asked, "What was it like before Niu-tou saw the Fourth Patriarch?
The Master replied, "The pond is deep, and the fish gather there. Wuzhuo asked, "What was it like after he saw him? The Master replied, "The tree is tall, and it beckons [the birds]."
Feng asked, "What is it like when one has seen and when one has not yet seen? The Master said, "To stretch out one's legs is to be within the drawing back of them.
Wuzhuo greatly praised him.
The Attendant-in-Ordinary Pan Lianggui followed the Master for a long time without reaching a point of accord. He said to the Master, "I simply wish to die;
what should I do? The Master replied, "A fine outer wrapping! Keep it for future use. If you do not resolve this matter now, you should not depart.
Suddenly, if it is replaced by another wrapping, there will be no way to rectify it. The official then asked about the story of Nanquan killing the cat.
[The monk] said, "I have been looking at this for a very long time, yet I have never fully penetrated it. I hope the Master will show me compassion.

The Master said, "You are merely occupied with trying to understand the cat of another's house; you do not realize that you have lost your own dog. At these words, the monk was as if awakened from a drunken stupor.
The Master spoke again, saying, "This is no small matter. Once you have taken this step forward, you must further know that there is a matter 'above' this."
"It is so. Nowadays, when scholars and officials speak of Chan or the Way, they merely rely on intellectual principles and feel satisfied.
For the most part, it is like using money to buy oil-cakes; once eaten, one is no longer hungry. To say that anything else is deceiving them is also laughable.
The Master replied, "Yes, yes."
The Master once said to the assembly, "Brothers, if you have a moment of realization, regardless of the time or occasion, please come and reveal a sign of it.
One snowy night, a monk knocked on the door of the abbot’s quarters. The Master rose and held up a candle, then let out a thunderous shout:

"In the middle of the night under a heavy snow, you seek to resolve your doubts; why is it that your deportment is so lacking? The monk looked down at his robe and satchel, whereupon the Master drove him away.
He was discharged from the hospital.

Chan Master Shigui of Longxiang had devoted his heart to the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* for over five autumns. He then traveled south to visit various venerable elders; it was only upon first ascending Longmen that he...
On an ordinary day, he obtained an audience with Baizhang Huaihai. Baizhang said, "Your understanding of the mind is already ultimate;

you simply lack the exertion required to open your eyes. He was subsequently appointed to serve in the Hall Administration. One day, while standing in attendance, Baizhang asked, "What is it like when all dualistic dependencies are transcended? Baizhang replied:

"It was just like when you were striking the gavel in the Sangha hall. Master Wǎngcuò was at a loss for words. Later, Yǎn arrived at the Hall Office, and the Master recounted the previous conversation.
Yǎn said, "That was idle talk. At this, the Master attained great enlightenment.

Chan Master Huanglong Fazhong studied the teachings of the Tiantai school and attained realization of the principle of the three contemplations within one mind. Yet, unable to completely efface his traces, he traveled extensively to consult renowned masters.
Upon reaching Longmen, he observed a water mill turning and thereby clarified the essential point of the mind. He then composed a verse, which begins: "Turning the Great Dharma Wheel..."
The former [master] wrapped him up; he asked again, "How is it? [Fayan replied], "Water pushes stones along. He presented this to Foyan. Foyan asked, "What is the matter within it?
The Master said, "The water flows long beneath the ravine. Foyan said, "I have a final phrase; I shall entrust it to you. The Master covered his ears and departed.
Shortly thereafter, he took his leave, crossed the Nine Rivers, and ascended Mount Lu, where he slept in the open air and lodged among the grasses.

He wandered leisurely among the mountains and waters, dwelling wherever his mind found inspiration. Sometimes he would go several days without eating; sometimes he would not sleep for consecutive nights.
He did not cut his hair when it grew long, nor did he change his clothes when they became worn. Thus, those at the Chan assembly called him Zhongdao (the Loyal Wayfarer).
During the Xuanhua era, there was a great drought in Xiangtan. Although prayers were offered, no response was received. The Master leaped into the Dragon Abyss and cried out, "You wretched beast!
It shall rain one chi! Rain followed immediately. Residing at Mount Nanyue, he constantly rode a tiger when going out for excursions; both Confucians and Buddhists would bow upon seeing his dust.

The head seat master Shi Qi traveled extensively throughout various regions. In his later years, he arrived at Longmen. One day, while sitting in meditation, he dozed off; suddenly, a chorus of frogs began to croak.
Mistaking the sound for the clatter of a shaving board, he hurried toward it. Someone enlightened him, saying, "Those are the cries of frogs, not the sound of a board."
The Master was suddenly enlightened. He went to the abbot’s quarters to disclose his realization. Foyan said, "Have you not seen Rāhula?
The Master abruptly stopped him, saying, "Master, there is no need to cite that. I will go and see for myself. Not long after, he attained further insight and composed this verse:
"In a dream I heard the sound of the wooden board; Upon waking, a frog croaked. The frog and the sound of the board— All at once, they are equal to the mountains. From this point on...

He redoubled his efforts in investigation until he thoroughly penetrated the profound mysteries. Foyan ordered him to share the teaching seat, but the Master firmly declined, saying, "This is no small matter.
It is like piercing the eye with a golden needle; were there a discrepancy as slight as a hair's breadth, the eye would be destroyed.
I wish instead to remain at the stage of a student throughout my lives, refining myself by my own effort. Foyan then praised him with a verse.
As for Chan Master Husheng Juqing, at the age of fourteen he paid homage to Anhui of Baima as his teacher. Having heard of the renown of Nantang, he went there to rely upon him.

When Nantang raised the koan of Xiangyan regarding the dragon’s roar within the withered tree and engaged in a series of exchanges and interrogations, the Master attained great realization beneath these words.
Wu attained enlightenment. One day, Nantang asked him, "Do not guard the green grass on the cold crags; sitting amidst white clouds, the essence of the school is not subtle.
What do you say to this? The Master said, "One must directly brandish the sword. If one does not brandish the sword, the fisherman will nest in his dwelling.
Nantang looked startled and said, "This little fellow! The Master said, "Take care," and then departed.
Master Kaixian Zhi addressed the assembly, saying:

"The distinction between the school (Zong) and the teaching (Jiao) is a provisional path; the titles 'Buddha' and 'Patriarch' are but forced designations. Receiving the teachings and transmitting the mind are both equally empty and false.
To seek the true and pursue the real only leads to further divergence. If one takes one's own self and one's own mind as the ultimate, [one finds it]."
"There must necessarily be other things and other people acting as antidotes. At that time, a monk asked, "What is it then?
He replied, "If it were so, there would be 'is-not'. The monk asked, "How does one enter? He replied, "In what kalpa have you been outside? The monk asked, "What is the Buddha? He replied:
[The Master] said, "Which one do you call a sentient being? [The monk] said, "If that is so, then there are neither Buddhas nor sentient beings.

[The Master] said, "This very sentient being. [The monk] asked, "What is the ordinary mind? [The Master] said, "Bees, scorpions, wolves, and greed. [The monk] said, "If that is so, then it is entirely the mind of a sentient being.
[The Master] said, "Tell me, which one is the ordinary mind? [The monk] said, "I do not understand. [The Master] said, "You will understand it later."
[The Master] was present. A questioner asked, "By what cause do the four great elements possess form? He replied, "Tell me, by what cause does empty space lack any image?
The questioner said, "At this point, I do not understand. He said, "Neither do I understand. He added, "Tell me, you say you do not understand; I say I do not understand."
"Is this one? Is this two? [The Master] said, "I beg the Venerable One’s compassion. [The Master] said, "Have I ever reviled you, morning or evening? [The student] asked, "What is the Great Way?
[The Master] said, "I have no small paths. [The student] said, "What is a small path? [The Master] said, "I do not know there is such a thing as a Great Way.
[The student] asked, "How is it that you, Master, perceive things? [The Master] said, "It is not within your realm. [The student] said, "As for how I, the student, perceive things..."
"What? he asked. [The other] said, "How could I dare to dispute your instructions? He said, "I have not deceived you for countless eons."

The lay practitioner Wang Xiao, whose courtesy name was Guanfù, was a Dragon Diagram (Longtu) official. While staying at Zhaojue Temple, he had an awakening upon hearing the sound of the board signaling the end of meditation. He asked Nantang:
"I have a certain point of view," [the official] said. "Yet, as soon as I am questioned by someone, I find myself unable to speak.
I do not know where my fault lies. Nantang said, "The fault lies in having a certain point of view. Nantang then asked, "When did you arrive at your post?
The official replied, "On the fourth day of the eighth month last year. Nantang said, "How long has it been since you left the yamen as an Inspector-General? The official replied, "Last..."
On the twentieth day of the month, Nantang said, "Why is it said that one cannot open one's mouth? Thereupon, Gongsu attained awakening.

Later, when a monk asked Master An of Nantai, "What is it like when all is silent and there is nothing to rely upon? An replied, "As for that which is silent. He then composed a verse, which begins: "Nan..."

Sitting in meditation by a single burner of incense, I remain motionless all day long, forgetting all myriad concerns. This is not for the sake of stilling the mind or eliminating discursive thoughts;
it is simply because there is nothing whatsoever to be pondered.
Chan Master Tianfalu ascended the hall.
He let out a shout and said, "The lion roars. Again he let out a shout and said, "The elephant king snorts.
Again he let out a shout and said, "A mad dog chases after a clod of earth. Again he let out a shout and said, "A shrimp cannot leap out of its measuring bucket. Then he said:
Among these four shouts, there is one shout capable of serving as a teacher to the patriarchs and Buddhas. Let the clear-eyed monk try to discern it.
If he cannot discern it, he is very much like one who has lost his way in broad daylight.
Chan Master Guangxiao Shen ascended the hall.
"Vimalakīrti’s single silence and Samantabhadra’s extensive exposition—throughout the ages, the sages have alternately displayed their 'ugliness' and 'clumsiness.
Do you not see that when the flowers fall in the third month, the nightingale cries; every single cry is a drop of blood?"
Ascending the hall: The wind whistles; the leaves drift. Clouds in fragments; waters vast and boundless. Standing alone at the river’s edge, to whom can one speak?
Beyond the heavens, two or three rows of wild geese fly.

A monk asked Zen Master Chichan Xuamiao of Zhongzhu, “What is the phrase that cuts off all streams? The Master said, “Even Buddhas and Patriarchs have no opening for it. The monk asked, “What is the phrase that encompasses heaven and earth?
The Master said, “It pervades the earth and fills the heavens. The monk asked, “What is the phrase that follows the waves and drifts with the current? The Master said, [“... (text fragment)
A "Wandering Phrase. The Master said: "Sometimes one enters the wild grass; sometimes one ascends the solitary peak.
Imperial Preface:

Since last winter, I have been reading the texts of the Chan school. Consequently, while attending to the affairs of government, I encountered this compilation of the records of the ancient virtuous masters.
In my leisure time, I have occasionally spoken of this with the Wang Grand Ministers and others within the inner court.
From spring until summer, in less than half a year, eight among the Wang Grand Ministers have attained a thorough and penetrating understanding.

Indeed, throughout ancient and modern times, fellow practitioners of Chan have either secluded themselves in forest groves, dwelling among springs and rocks, or have traveled on pilgrimage to various quarters, visiting monasteries everywhere to seek instruction.

Those who discourse on emptiness and speak of the wondrous are as numerous as millet or hemp seeds; yet those who have attained realization of their own minds are as rare as phoenix feathers or qilin horns.
Now, within half a year, through my brief guidance, the King and his ministers have achieved such a moment of great penetration.
Is this not a magnificent event for the Dharma assembly? As the selection and carving of the recorded sayings (yulu) are now complete, I have therefore taken the King’s...

Among the works composed by my minister that I have previously presented for my perusal, I have selected those deemed appropriate and compiled them into a single collection, entitled *The Dharma Assembly of the Present Age*.
This is appended here for publication. I, the Emperor, reflect that the Tathāgata’s treasury of the true Dharma-eye and his wondrous mind of nirvāṇa—
It is like the bright sun in the sky; those with eyes behold it together. Those who are deluded remain deluded of their own accord, while those who have awakened have no words.
If one truly transcends and enters directly at this point, then to weave together the myriad existences is, in reality, to perform "non-action.

As for me, day and night I attend to ten thousand matters of urgency, and my ministers do not cease from their posts morning or evening; all of this is nothing other than the endeavor to bring peace and order to the world. And yet—
In this matter, one has deeply tasted the flavor of the profound, sudden, and perfect nectar.
It should be understood that this reality is the ground of ultimate truth (*bhūtakoṭi*), and it cannot be relied upon through reckless inquiry or the path of intellectual understanding.

As for me, residing in the position of a sovereign and performing the duties of a ruler, what connection have I to the hollow reputation of being well-versed in the *zong* (Dharmakāya) teachings? Furthermore, these several high ministers...
He is a gentleman of profound and vast learning, public-spirited, loyal, and upright. In word and deed, he has never been deceitful or false;
how could he ever resort to such means to curry favor or engage in the sycophantic acts of a petty man?

Nor would I ever secretly transmit oral instructions to serve as a pretext for defiling one’s spiritual life. It is because a person must, within the realm of their own mind and nature, directly penetrate the very root.
As for its source, its benefit to oneself and others is both supreme and universal. That I have been so earnestly devoted to this is certainly not without reason.

The words within these volumes—such as how the Lion [Śākyamuni] was able to let out a great roar at the age of three—can inspire profound faith in people and widely disseminate the lamp of the True Dharma;
such is the transmission of the selection, whether regarding the ancestral style of the school.

It is not without some small benefit. As for the śramaṇas and fangxiang (Daoist practitioners) who engage in ascetic cultivation within the monastery, there were also six individuals who simultaneously attained realization;
their compositions are likewise appended here for publication. This serves as the preface.
On the full moon day of the ninth month in the Gui-chou year, the eleventh year of the Yongzheng era,
selected by Imperial Decree for the present Dharma assembly:
His Royal Highness the Sixteenth Brother, Prince Zhuang, the Layman Ai-yue.

In prostrating to the Buddha throughout the entirety of heaven and earth, there is but one True Buddha. Whether they be hundreds of thousands of myriads of clay Buddhas or wooden Buddhas, they are all but this One Buddha.

If you seek by clinging to appearances, you will instead create obstructions. There is no need for deliberation or seeking through questioning; simply prepare yourself to realize it right where you stand.
Take this up. If you wish to recognize the true Buddha, there is nothing that is not it. How can you see him unless you have completely exhausted the ignorance of kalpas?
How can you exhaust it thoroughly? Simply remove the fetters. As for the word "fetter," the karmic consciousness of sentient beings has deep roots;
for thousands of births and myriad kalpas, they have been entangled by it without ceasing. Form can fetter seeing; sound can fetter hearing.
Contact conditions bondage; confronting objects leads to delusion. The more one seeks, the further one wanders; the more one searches, the deeper one sinks.

If one wishes to be liberated from these bonds, there is no other expedient means than to turn the light back for a single thought-moment, whereupon one beholds the Buddha’s countenance. It is neither mind nor Buddha; it is ten thousand miles of white clouds.
This mind is the Buddha. Amidst ten thousand miles of white clouds, the Buddha is precisely this seeing. This seeing is fundamentally free from causes;
it is like a blue lotus, unstained by a single speck of dust. One sees as if not seeing; one hears as if not hearing. Form does not obstruct seeing; sound does not obstruct hearing.
The faculties and their objects are empty and still; they are distinct and luminous. The moon is one in a thousand rivers; the moon is one, yet it is in a thousand rivers.

When the wind comes upon the water’s surface, clouds encircle the tiered ridges. Whether in the world of Ultimate Bliss or in the east or west—what barriers could there be? There is no need for further investigation.
The Buddha is precisely me; I am precisely the Buddha. The Buddha and sentient beings are non-dual and without distinction. Who is lacking? Who is in excess? Who is superior? Who is inferior?
To be deluded regarding this is to be an ordinary person; to awaken to it is to be a sage. When both the ordinary and the sage are utterly extinguished, the whole body is the great function.
If detachment from characteristics is false, then characteristics themselves are true; if characteristics themselves are false, then detachment from characteristics is true.

When both "is" and "is not" are forgotten, the True Buddha appears in the world. The Buddha’s birth is identical to the One: there is no emerging and no entering, this and that are not two, and there is neither coming nor going.
The Great Compassionate Father has established this compassionate vessel to rescue the deluded multitudes, unbinding their fetters and releasing them from their reins.

This kindness and virtue are difficult to discuss and impossible to measure. Having now tasted the unsurpassed *amṛta* of clarified butter, I pray that all sentient beings may together ascend to the site of enlightenment.
I bow my head in refuge; I prostrate before the Dharma King.

The Patriarchal intent was not transmitted by the Sixth Patriarch as a robe; Bodhidharma left behind but a single sandal. If one wishes to distinguish between difference and sameness, one must penetrate through to realize the profound principle.
If one were to reveal the message directly, what harm would there be in adding further annotations within the thousand rivers of a single month? Realize it beneath the heels of your feet.
Regarding one case of question and answer:
A monk asked Yunmen, "What is the phrase that penetrates the Dharma-body? Yunmen said, "The Northern Dipper."
"Concealing the body within. What is the meaning? King’s verse says: "Piercing through the Dharma-body, concealing the Big Dipper.
'Is' is 'is not'; 'is not' is 'is'. The mud-bull roars at the moon; Mulang drinks his fill of wine. Thus it is, thus it is. Do you know? Do you know?"

The Verse on the Six Faculties: The six faculties are originally gathered within a single thing; who would have known that the price of this one thing is difficult to repay? The locks and bolts are busily obstructing mice in vain;
the whip and stick laboriously strike the ox in error. Green waters and blue mountains are Avalokiteśvara; the clear breeze and bright moon are left to you as you please.
Leisurely and unhurried, uprooting oneself to respond to the assembly and take root in the ground. Listen as the cool cicada announces the early autumn.
The great earth is but a single hair-tip; originally, no soil is seen. Once you recognize what lies beneath your feet, let them swallow or spit out as they will.
A single scoop of water is the entirety of the vast ocean; yet the vast ocean contains not a drop of water. The ocean and the mulberry fields—the sea and the fields are just like this.
Fire.
Like sparks from flint and flashes of lightning, why need one distinguish between self and other? Once you recognize the cause of fire, you will know for yourself its fruit within the flames.
The wind pervades the entire realm yet is never hidden; it pervades the entire realm yet is never possessed. Simply observe movement and stillness, and sound—all are the lion’s roar.

The Way reaches the source of the Way; originally there is not a single word. What prevents one from chanting and reciting spontaneously? Whether in stillness or clamor, speech or silence, let all be in harmony.
There is nothing that can be affirmed, nor anything that can be denied. Where is the Land of Ultimate Bliss? Within form and emptiness lies the mystery. This is called the Demon.
It is said that the Buddha is not anything else at all; yet from the very beginning, there is no self.

On the first day of the month, when has it ever been obscured? Its radiance remains full throughout the three thousandfold world-system. Do not say that three or five [phases] constitute the perfect circle—the Great [Fullness] is already here.
The earth remains in darkness. Clarity negotiates within the dark; the dark revolves within clarity.
With clarity and darkness both free from partiality, this moon has only now appeared.
A single lamp can divide into a thousand lamps; one must know from where this single lamp comes. Even if it illuminates a nine-storied tower, how could this ever be an obstruction?
When applied, it is distinct yet without illumination; when its essence is realized, it is not separated from the dust of the world. The lotus flower...
In an instant, it blooms amidst the flames; only then can it be called "sovereign.
The mirror is just like the bright moon suspended on high; naturally, form and shadow are not concealed. Why need one scrape away impurities or polish its luster further? Only then...
The wondrous marks of suchness are manifest; even if covered by dust, how could they be obscured? Thus, there is no hindrance even when enclosed within a cage.
To distinguish between darkness and light is but a hair’s breadth; all fears and obstructions arise solely from the mind’s own barriers.

The nature of the mind-jewel and the nature of the water follow the same path; this realm and other lands are fundamentally no different. When the jewel shines brilliantly, it is contained within the deep, still water;

where the water is clear and pure, the round jewel is seen. When the light-wind and bright moon are present, the whole body appears; in the emerald pond and the cold, deep pool, it is but a single inch.
The shadow is non-existent. From antiquity to the present, there has never been a single thing. Why must one copy the gourd after the model?

These two recorded sayings show that all phenomena are as if present before one's eyes. Small yet without interior, vast yet without boundary—where could this universally pervasive single nature possibly come from?
Go! A green mountain beneath the water, a lotus within the fire.

Noble and precious, yet one has never known it oneself. Fortunately meeting this pressing inquiry, one may practice well. Who would have known that a single drop of Caoxi’s water was right here with me?
At the Imperial Taiye Pond.
Regarding the sequence of worshipping the Buddha at Bolin Temple, Shiming Ding said: "The Buddha left the home life for the sake of one great matter; how could it be merely for..."
Having personally realized the end of birth and death, one vows to rescue those sentient beings who are submerged and sinking; one vows to awaken those sentient beings who are deluded and mistaken;
one vows to liberate those sentient beings who are bound by fetters; and one vows to open the way for those sentient beings who are obscured by hindrances.
All holy ones and ordinary people alike can surely understand this principle. Yet, to rescue and pull out sentient beings is precisely to rescue and pull out oneself; to awaken sentient beings is...
"To bring beings to life" means to awaken oneself. "To liberate sentient beings" means to liberate oneself. "To enlighten sentient beings" means to enlighten oneself.
Thus, in this rescuing, awakening, liberating, and enlightening, there is truly no "I" that performs the rescue.

When I have attained awakening, attained liberation, and attained illumination, there is likewise no sentient being who has been rescued by me, awakened by me, liberated by me, or illuminated by me. This is what is called "delivering others."
This is what is called "self-deliverance. Therefore, since ancient times, those of great virtue who have already attained and realized [the truth] must be recommended by humans and devas as teachers.
Fundamentally motivated by compassion, they guide others according to their needs;

yet, while they themselves have not yet fully attained or realized [the goal], they remain diligent and urgent, neglecting both sleep and food, and exerting themselves without sparing even their own lives.

They sought with diligent effort, concealing their forms and extinguishing their voices; they closed their gates and sealed their lips, relying solely on their fundamental nature and refusing to concern themselves with others.
They went so far as to sit motionless upon empty crags or travel to distant lands; some severed their own arms while standing in the snow, as if their heads were ablaze.
Their bitter resolve and ascetic endurance were not measured by years; through relentless pressure and rigorous friction, they vowed to achieve thorough awakening. Once they had grasped it—
The nostrils—as if severed and then revived—thereupon accord with both phenomena and principle, free from obstruction.
Thus, even in the inclinations of humans and devas, from holding the whisk to opening the hall, the benefit of self and others is simultaneously perfected.

Indeed, throughout the ten directions and all eternity, it is impossible for one whose own matter is not yet clear to be able to guide others, nor for one who cannot guide others to have finally realized their own matter. This is certain.

There is certainly no such teaching; there is no such Dharma. Yet now you wear the saṃghāṭī robe and eat from the fragrant kitchen, serving as a disciple of the Buddha and known to others as a "good friend" (kalyāṇamitra).
You dwell in a renowned monastery, ascend the Dharma seat, and have been gathering both monastics and laypeople to preach the Dharma for many years.
The Emperor, in the dignity of a sovereign ruler, has realized the fruit of Tathāgata-hood. Wherever his sympathetic joy reaches, he constantly receives your instructions;
this is no different from the light of the sun and moon, which is ever-present. For all beings, such an opportunity is difficult to encounter throughout kalpas.
Yet, as I observe you, the bottom of your bucket has not been pulled out and you have not advanced even a step beyond the tip of the pole.

Although you pass your days through walking meditation, chanting, and recitation, never forgetting your two daily meals, you have truly failed to partake of even a single flavor of the realization of nature and the illumination of the mind. You cling to names and forms and are entangled in words and language;
your searching has been fruitless, and your "sipping" and "pecking" can offer no remedy. Is this not a failure to repay your superiors above?
O Holy One, you bear a heavy debt to yourself. To wish to become a human being while acting in such a manner is like leading the deaf with the deaf or transmitting blindness to the blind;

it deludes others from perfect enlightenment and severs their life-force of wisdom. It is like an iron serpent blocking the path—both self-deluded and deluding others, one falls into the cycle of saṃsāra.
Who will be able to endure the consequences for this? I feel deep shame and fear on your behalf. You must immediately seize this moment of fierce diligence.
Reflection: To penetrate the critical point and to deliver oneself and others is not two separate matters.

You should know that the Emperor’s grace is vast and difficult to repay, and you must acknowledge that my words are not false. The Buddhas of antiquity have already passed away, and those of future generations have not yet arrived.
If one does not seek deliverance in this present life, what can be done when it is too late for regret? Moreover, to err for oneself is a minor matter; to lead others astray is a grave sin.
Great! The tongue does not follow the mind; those with eyes need not ask the mouth. Exert yourselves in dedication; let there be no blemish upon the śramaṇas.
Cause the great assembly of three thousand to each give rise to faith, so that the essential doctrine may spread far and wide.

Do not merely say that the prediction was given at Vulture Peak, for one will surely obtain the blessings and retributions of humans and devas—is it so? Is it so? How is it? How is it? Do not say, "The Tathāgata..."
The teachings below are verbose and trivial; they bear a strong resemblance to the "Buddhism of old wives. Therefore, you must cherish this [instruction] and not neglect it.
This is the Epitaph for the Realization of the Layman Zide, Prince Guoqin, the Seventeenth Brother of the Emperor.
Sentient beings of the three realms, from time immemorial, have suddenly given rise to ignorance, thereby establishing the sense organs and their objects.

This very ignorance is identical to the Buddha’s perfect enlightenment; yet through deluded attachment, one undergoes the karmic consciousness of ascending and sinking. When awakened, there is neither folly nor wisdom; when realized, there is neither ordinary person nor sage.
It does not come from that, nor does it go from this; its prior and posterior limits are severed. It is neither identical with nor distinct from [phenomena];

it has no basis yet stands firm, and though it has support, nothing is established. It is level and uniform; truth and falsehood are non-dual. Both subject and object are transcended; it universally responds according to the various types [of beings].

To have a fixed method is to be obstructed; to cling to a place is to fall into error. To be deluded by stillness and empty darkness, or by the shadowy reflections of the six sense-objects, is to be stained while remaining unstained, and to mistake what is for what is not.
Every sound and every form is like flowers appearing when one presses on the eyes; that which is luminous and conscious is like the hair of a tortoise or the horns of a hare.

Both paths are extinguished; perfect realization is achieved in the snap of a finger. It is the realization of non-realization, the cultivation of non-cultivation. Gradually and successively, the habitual tendencies of past lives are eliminated.
The six classes of beings are equally saved; all sentient beings are of one suchness. Buddhas, demons, heterodoxies, and outsiders are all gathered within a single track.
Good and ugly are clearly distinguished; the precious mirror is free from defilement. It is eternally merged and eternally illuminating; eternally moving and eternally still.
There is neither "acceptable" nor "unacceptable"; it neither grasps nor rejects. Perfectly pervasive and vast, it is beyond thought and beyond deliberation.
Just as the Dharma of mind-transmission has been passed down from the Buddhas and Patriarchs above, it is without difference, without sameness, and without two tracks.

It is fundamentally not something that can be clarified by intellectual views, nor is it something that can be realized through the exertion of effort. The forms and appearances before one's eyes are all truly eternal; the sounds at one's ears' side are likewise [the same].

A wondrous teaching! Within this, even a hair’s breadth of deliberation falls into a thousand differences and ten thousand distinctions. Before any thought of conjecture arises, the host and guest are fully present;
there is no need to shift a single step to enter the Dharma hall. Perfectly complete and interpenetrating, it is free from purity and defilement;
rare, subtle, and profound, yet it is also ordinary. Unmoving and steadfast, it transcends kalpas of dust; silent and non-active, it raises the jeweled banner. In every land...
In every dust mote lies the true mark; what else remains to be taken up? It is not within nor without, neither Mount Sumeru nor a tiny speck of dust.
Ask again: it is like the bright moon reflected in a thousand rivers, and yet it is like a gale blowing through ten thousand pipes.
Squeezed, it does not coalesce; looked at, it has no form. Right before one’s eyes, it is present; sought, it is nowhere to be found.

If one can, for even a moment, turn the light back to illuminate within, without the slightest effort of a finger-snap, one shall achieve perfect realization. In the ultimate truth, there is neither saint nor non-saint; its wondrous meaning is neither arising nor non-arising.
When encountering the time of establishment, it accords with that establishment; when meeting the place of radiance, it merges with that radiance. Mountains, rivers, and the great earth—

The Tathāgatagarbha is the lamp of Buddhas and patriarchs for all moving and stationary sentient beings; what need is there to change the strings or alter the tuning? Let the moon remain white and the wind clear;
it is clear when settled and turbid when stirred, yet neither deluded nor awakened. This perfect fusion is itself the precious golden cord;
to indulge in its playfulness is instead to create a broken, frayed rope. Worldly toil and delusive thoughts are like the hair of a tortoise. *Bān*...
If nirvana were the same as a rabbit’s horns, then the Nāga would be eternally in samādhi amidst the bustle of activity;
traversing the entire realm without dwelling or attachment, he is the single vessel of compassion for the great trichiliocosm. Where could the incense pillar or the lantern hide?

If you seek the Patriarch’s intent on the tip of a blade of grass, it is just like searching for mandarin ducks upon a needle. The six sense faculties are themselves the seeds of Bodhi; ten thousand thoughts are none other than suchness.

The Banner of Mind resembles the cold plum blossoms after passing through the snow; though the flowers bloom, they do not bear last year’s fragrance. To hold fast at the single ford is not "entering";
to let loose a thousand streams is not "exiting. The state of mind is serene and profoundly clear; how could it require even a hair’s breadth of effort or power?
Without dwelling and without moving, one does not fall into emptiness; ever-luminous and ever-illuminating, it remains as dark as lacquer. The vast ocean...
Trickling streams enter the hundred rivers; filling the brooks and ravines, they form waves and surges. A single drop from Caoxi pervades the three thousand worlds;

why wait for the plucking of a flower before breaking into a smile? The moon shines upon the cold pond, and the waves reflect the moon; the moon and waves are vast and boundless, while the pond remains bright and pure.

Within this, essence and function are most clearly manifest; why must one insist on verbalizing them through conceptual analysis? Every single thing participates equally in the *nirmāṇakāya* and *saṃbhogakāya*;
even a single speck of dust is the Buddha of Pure Light. Where does the Buddha of Pure Light dwell? Seek him right within all the subtle atoms.
Whether drinking when thirsty or eating when hungry, from morning until nightfall, he is fundamentally no different from anyone else. As soon as one speaks of "liberation," [the duality vanishes].
This is precisely the pit and the moat. Why would the soles of one’s feet not be the Gate of Non-duality? To act and to condition is ultimately nothing but delusion;
to eliminate affliction and distress is likewise not the Truth. If you say that suchness constitutes two separate fragments, I ask you: have you heard this song or not?
To show those who are beginners:
the Dharma came from the West to point directly to the human mind, so that by seeing one's nature one becomes a Buddha, without relying on written words or language.

This was because sentient beings, due to the habitual defilements of their consciousness accumulated over immeasurable kalpas, have always sought outwardly and do not know how to return to the source. However...

To exhaustively pursue and follow after [objects], to cling to conditions and engage in discursive thought, only serves to increase one's learning and ultimately results in stagnation and obstruction.

Therefore, out of compassionate pity, the Patriarchs have bestowed teachings upon later students so that, within a single *kṣaṇa*, they may clarify the ground of the mind and directly reach the source.
Thus, every word is entirely the eternal and true; there is not a single phrase that does not point to the essence of purity, nor a single sound that does not expound the perfect [enlightenment].
"Exquisite Sound. The Sūtra says: "What was spoken by the Buddhas of the past, the Buddhas of the future follow accordingly.

The Tripiṭaka and the twelve divisions of the scriptures are language and letters, yet they are not language and letters. To understand this clearly from them, yet to have no one who understands, is what constitutes true speech and non-deceptive speech.
Failing to accord with this principle, but merely following the text to explain the meaning, one falls into the net of views. As it is said:
Like a solitary lamp beneath the sun, it loses its power to illuminate; one must urgently apply courageous and diligent effort to achieve immediate liberation.
Then, one will naturally attain clarity regarding the profound truths expounded within the boundless ocean of the teachings.

In these casual discourses on the ten [principles], it is said that existence arises from non-existence and non-existence arises from existence; existence and non-existence give rise to one another, all ultimately converging upon the Way, whether conditioned or unconditioned.
It transcends names and words. Is it the Way? Or is it not the Way?
The Way is not something towering, like the mountain that the benevolent delight in; the Way is not something vast and empty, like the water that the wise delight in.
Beyond mountains and water, where else would one seek the Way? If you cling to mountains and water as being the Way, it is like mistaking the eyes of a fish for a light.
A pearl. Now tell me, what is it ultimately like? Mountains are not mountains; water is indeed water.
Others speak of empty flowers; I discourse on the true mark (*dharmatā*). Others speak of mountains, rivers, and the great earth; I say they are dreams, illusions, bubbles, and shadows.

This is not intended to display one’s uniqueness to others; it is precisely to demonstrate the Great Sameness (Dàtóng). If one takes the different as the same and the same as different, they will be as far apart as a wind and a cow or a horse, failing to see for themselves.
Therefore, by seeing universally, one sees all; by not arising for oneself, one attains eternal life. Because there is no self-arising, the myriad things are of one great sameness.
Therefore, one regards unsurpassed bodhi as if it were a child’s play.

The Way is fundamentally without movement; thus it does not abide in movement. The Way is fundamentally without stillness; thus it does not abide in stillness. If the Way were in stillness, [it would be no different from ordinary stillness].

If you merely guard against the withered wood and cold ashes, you will immediately transcend the ocean of Dharma. If the Way were found in movement, you would merely be chasing after the dust of the wind or the wild horses of the desert;
thus, you would have no connection to True Suchness at all. Now, one who embodies the Way simply proceeds from profound stillness into the midst of turmoil.
The chaotic becomes the realm of profound stillness through realization;

a tree of a thousand fathoms is formed from inches, and a journey of ten thousand *li* begins with a single step. Thus, although the Way is lofty and subtle, it does not depart from the ordinary before one's eyes.
If one abandons what is near to seek what is distant, or loathes the mundane to admire the sage, this is to abandon [the Way].
To seek to reach the heavens with a sprouting tree, or to desire to travel far without stepping out of one’s courtyard—is this not called folly?
All things are spontaneous; to act with artificiality is to err. Because there is no artificiality, heaven and earth achieve their vastness, and the sun and moon [shine].
It manifests its radiance such that mountains, rivers, grasses, trees, birds, fish, and all moving and stationary life naturally merge into a single body; hence it is called the *Tathāgatagarbha*.

Just as a bright mirror reflects forms, whether they be short or tall, fat or thin, all appear exactly as they are. Yet if one were to remove the mirror and seek one's own reflection, it could not be found.
It is so. An empty valley responds to a sound; its magnitude, slowness, or rapidity is exactly like that of the original. Yet, if one goes to the valley to seek my voice, it cannot be found.
Therefore it is said: when it is in the mirror, it is simply the mirror; when it is in the valley, it is simply the valley.
The Great Way is rarefied and silent; it cannot be venerated, nor can it be prized. One should settle within it and follow it, harmonize with it and identify with it.
To have without possessing, to act without acting—this is called the Great Way.
Vast and empty is heaven; there is nothing it does not encompass. Profound and expansive is the sea; there is nothing it does not contain.
Therefore, those who model themselves after heaven share its greatness; those who take the sea as their law share its abyssal depth. As for the Way, it is inconceivable and beyond all measure.
Five Verses from the Random Notes:
The Buddhas and Patriarchs extend their great compassion to rescue all who are drowning. This is because sentient beings’ original reality is firmly obscured and buried by adventitious defilements;

as the waves of karma surge and boil, they cling to and reject with hatred and love, binding and fettering themselves. Thus they wander through the cycle of birth and death, finding it difficult to escape.

To loathe the ordinary and love the holy, to seek stillness and detest clamor—all these are attachments; they all belong to the realm of conditioned grasping. When one is among the holy, one is holy; when among the ordinary, one is ordinary.
When in stillness, one is still; when in clamor, one is clamorous. Fundamentally, there is no fixed location; it is like a pearl rolling upon a tray.

Acting according to one's natural station: the Way of the Buddha and the Way of Confucianism are one and the same. The laity abide in their homes; the monastics uphold the teachings. As a minister, one should be loyal; as a son, one should be filial.

To be able to fulfill these fundamental human relations is itself the profound mystery. To sever worldly ties and contravene natural sentiments, abandoning what is clear to seek some other illumination, is not the path.
Some, by following the teachings of Śākyamuni, abandon the fundamental social norms and compete with one another in mutual denigration, like the followers of Mozi or Yang Zhu.

Others, admiring heterodox practices, tear their clothes and ruin their garments, scar their faces and snap their fingers, recklessly inflicting injury upon themselves. Both groups slander the Buddha and deviate from the Way.
To pick up one thing and let go of another is not yet to reach a state of even repose. Water does not wash water; gold is not bartered for gold.

Outside the mind there are no objects; outside objects there is no mind. Objects are simply objects; the mind is simply the mind. Why do you remain so muddled, casting aside appearances to seek something else?
Contemplating the mountain, one sees its height; it is composed of many stones. Though the stones are many, the mountain is a single form.
A thousand-fathom mountain is but a single fist-sized stone; the stone is the mountain, yet the mountain is not the stone.

When looking at bubbles on the water, their forms differ while their substance is the same. When they coalesce, they become bubbles; when they disperse, they become water. The bubble is not the water, yet the water is the bubble.
It is better not to fixate one's gaze, but to let them flow as they will.
The Verse on the Fundamental Nature:

The Buddhas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, share this same single nature. This nature is neither cultivated nor realized; yet if one departs from cultivation and realization, one falls into madness.
It is neither movement nor non-movement, neither stillness nor non-stillness—this is the nature.
Everything that meets the eye becomes a perverted view; who can describe the mountains, rivers, and the great earth?
Since beholding the morning star, it has been clear that things and self are originally neither different nor the same. (Eye)
If one seeks the Buddha-dharma through sounds, it is like attempting to take flight by merely attaching wings. How does this compare to casting off all constraints and walking upon level ground?
In silent stillness and amidst clamorous speech, there is but one single destination.
It is said that when sandalwood is seen, it is fragrant piece by piece; within this, who could know its perfume if one did not smell it?
If you say that Buddha-nature is separate from the faculty of hearing, where could one seek the field of quiescent extinction? (Nose)
Do not say that the hundred flavors are but one flavor; it is clear that the river is fresh while the sea is salty.
You must discern each one through me, only then will you take dust and sand for rice and salt (the tongue).
The illusory, empty body is itself the Dharma-body; even if one recognizes it as such, it is not yet the truth.
Directly taking rubble to form my own body—who says that body and mind do not serve the dust of every world-system?
Movement and stillness, contraction and expansion, are of one essence; front and back, left and right, all accord with what is appropriate.
If one seeks another path outside of this, how is it different from discarding gold to value clay? (The meaning is as stated.)

In my recorded sayings, I do not speak of emptiness within emptiness, nor do I speak of existence within existence. If you ask what I have to say: it is a single roar of the lion, a single moon’s reflection upon ten thousand rivers.
The single moon conditions the myriad streams; rising and falling with the waves, they change year after year. Do not engage in frivolous discourse regarding identity or difference;
when the one moon is full, the ten thousand moons are full.

I have briefly described that Buddha-nature is not to be sought through form and appearance; if one departs from form and appearance, one only exhausts the mind in vain. The body of True Suchness is like the hair of a tortoise or the horns of a hare;
the cawing of magpies and the hooting of crows are the sound of Prajñā. It is not that my own body is the same as wood or stone; rather, wood and stone themselves must be [the Buddha-nature].
My own person: the perceptions of sages and ordinary beings arise from birth and extinction. The mountains are naturally high and the waters are naturally deep.
*Juehai lun* by the Fourth Imperial Prince, the Great Prince Bao, Layman Changchun.
To use the ocean as a metaphor for awakening is merely a forced analogy. The ocean is itself but one thing within awakening; awakening cannot be illustrated by means of the ocean.
Indeed, awakening is inherently beyond metaphor. Because the ocean is the most massive of things among heaven and earth, it is used as a metaphor only by way of necessity.
Now, Heaven first generates Water. Descending, it becomes dew; ascending, it becomes the moon; moving, it becomes waves; congealing, it becomes ice;
pooling, it becomes ponds and marshes; flowing, it becomes rivers and streams. With their thousands of branches and myriad tributaries, none fail to flow toward and honor the sea as their source.
The sea receives them without appearing to overflow; the sea releases them without appearing to be exhausted. The sea—
How immense it is! Nevertheless, the sea inherently possesses form. Because the form of the sea exists, the name "sea" persists.
Yet, when it comes to that which cannot be sought through form nor approximated by name—where there is nothing received, yet in truth there is nothing not received;
where there is nothing emitted, yet in truth there is nothing not emitted—one does not perceive receiving, nor does one perceive emitting.
It flows forth. It is profound and serene; it is vast and expansive. This ocean—could it not be the ocean of awakening of one’s own intrinsic nature?
It does not emerge from within, nor is it produced from without. It has no beginning in the past and no end in the future. Above, its summit cannot be seen; below, its bottom cannot be fathomed.
Throughout the worlds of the ten directions, none can measure its boundaries; among all sentient beings upon the great earth, there are none who do not [partake in it].
Fully complete. This ocean of awakening belongs to the Tathāgata; this ocean of awakening belongs to the Bodhisattva;

all noble ones and ordinary beings, down to the wriggling insects and sentient creatures, are none other than this ocean of awakening. Dwelling together within the three realms, the living and the Buddha are of one essence.

That within this single essence there are vast differences is the distinction between the living and the Buddha. Though these differences are as wide as heaven and earth, they all ultimately return to the ocean of awakening.
This is the primordial source from which Buddhas arise. To take the ocean of awakening as one’s essence, yet neither cling to that ocean of awakening nor abandon it—this is the Tathāgata.
To dwell within the ocean of awakening, yet either cling to its essence or abandon the ocean of awakening—these are sentient beings.

The separate transmission outside the teachings causes people to penetrate beyond the sense bases and their objects, and to utterly sever emotional views; both [approaches] relate to the ocean of awakening.

Names likewise do not exist. To cultivate is to have no cultivation; to realize is to have no realization. It is like the myriad rivers returning to the sea, yet the sea does not consciously recognize its own capacity to contain them.
Now, cultivating worldly dharmas reaches their ultimate limit in the state of a sage. However, if one clarifies the supramundane dharma, it is vast and empty, where there is no sage.
Where it is vast and empty and there is no sage, sages and ordinary beings are viewed as equal. This applies even to precepts, concentration, and wisdom.
It is awakening (*bodhi*). Greed, anger, and delusion are also awakening. The awakening of greed, anger, and delusion is not perfect awakening (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*).
The awakening of precepts, concentration, and wisdom is also not perfect awakening. One cannot find greed, anger, and delusion; one cannot find precepts, concentration, and wisdom.
Within that which is unobtainable, there is thus attainment. Within such attainment, there is nothing to be attained. Only after this does that awakening become perfect. Perfect.

Nor is it circular; yet awakening is the ocean of awakening. An ancient said: "The depletion of the wealth of Dharma and the destruction of merit—none arise except from this mind, intellect, and consciousness.
He further said: "The true nature of ignorance is itself Buddha-nature; the illusory, empty body is itself the Dharma-body.
The distinction between the Buddha’s birth and non-birth lies in the difference between awakening and non-awakening. Nevertheless, the awakened and the unawakened are the same.
Abiding within the ocean of awakening, if one takes awakening as awakening, this is the awakening of mind, intellect, and consciousness;

it is that which diminishes the wealth of the Dharma and extinguishes merit. Thus, not taking awakening as awakening, it remains the true nature of ignorance within the illusory and empty body—it is not true awakening.
One must realize that the true nature of ignorance is itself Buddha-nature; it is an illusion.
The transformed empty body is itself the Dharma-body. Along with this ignorance and Buddha-nature, even the name "illusory Dharma-body" cannot be found.
Only then does it enter a mote of dust without leaking and pervade the great trichiliocosm without overflowing. If one takes it from a jar, it fills the jar;
if one takes it from a pitcher, it fills the pitcher; if one takes it from a marsh, it fills the marsh; if one takes it from a lake, it fills the lake.
It is like a marsh: if one takes from it with a river, it fills the river; if one takes from it with a sea, it fills the sea;
if one takes from it with heaven and earth, it fills heaven and earth. It is limpid and profound, tranquil and alert; though aware, it is unaware.
To be unawakened yet ever-awakened—is this not what is meant by the ocean of awakening?
The moon in the water is said to be but one moon in the heavens; yet when it is reflected in the waters, it becomes ten thousand. One moon universally manifests in all waters. Its...
Fundamentally they are identical. All moon-reflections in water are subsumed within a single moon; their ultimate destination is non-duality.

Even if one understands that the true substance is one, yet fails to understand that the illusory substance is also one, then the ancient sages’ exquisite metaphor of the moon in the water remains unexamined.
It is like a boat drifting upon a stream: this is the moon in the stream. By way of the stream, it proceeds to the lake.

The moon in the lake is precisely this moon of the stream. From the lake, it extends to the Yangtze and Yellow Rivers; the moon within the Yangtze and Yellow Rivers is precisely this moon of the lake.
From the Yangtze and Yellow Rivers, it extends to the ocean; the moon within the ocean is precisely this moon of the Yangtze and Yellow Rivers.
From one small sea, it extends to the four great oceans; the moon of the four great oceans is precisely this [moon].
It is the moon over a small sea, yet it is also the very same moon setting sail upon this small stream. There is but one moon;
two moons cannot be found. Suddenly, in that interval, a dike separates them, becoming two streams of water within a single brook.
When divided into two streams, even a single month is split into two months. Proceeding from this principle, within the four seas:
the Yangtze has its *tuó*, the Yellow River has its *xíng*, the Rǔ River has its *fén*, and the Hàn River has its *qián*. The point where water and grass meet is called *méi*.
When water breaks through a marsh, it becomes a *qiān*; when it pours into a stream, it becomes a *xī*; when it pours into a *xī*, it becomes a *gǔ*; when it pours into a *gǔ*, it becomes a *gōu*;
when it pours into a *gōu*, it becomes a *huài*. Made even finer than this, it becomes surface runoff; made even finer than that, it becomes the puddle in a cow’s hoofprint.
Each obtains water, and each obtains the moon, yet the moon does not know how many tens of thousands or millions there are. Made even finer than that—
They become jars, basins, ladles, vases, cups, and goblets; each receives the water, and thus each also receives the moon.
Yet the moon does not know that it is reflected in as many vessels as there are grains of sand in the Ganges.

If one were to pour the water from a hundred small vessels into a single large vessel, the hundreds of moons within those hundred small vessels would all vanish, and they would merge into one great moon.

It is but the single moon within one vessel. If one were to pour the waters of hundreds of thousands of millions of vessels into a single stream, then the hundreds of thousands of millions of moons within those hundreds of thousands of millions of vessels would all vanish, becoming the single moon within that one stream.
From this, the moons in the streams, the brooks, the lakes, the rivers, and the seas—though as numerous as the sands of the Ganges—each become a single moon once more, just as at the beginning.
Truly, the moon within the water is fundamentally one; that it appears otherwise is due to obstructions causing such a state, not because it is inherently so.
Viewed from this perspective, it is clear that not only is the moon in the heavens universally one...
It is the same. The moon in the water is likewise universal. The moon in the heavens is *tathatā* (suchness); the moon in the water is illusory existence (*māyopama*).
Illusion issues forth from suchness; through illusion, the myriad things are formed. Yet in illusion there are no myriad things; the myriad things of illusion are also one.

Even that "one" does not stand as a fixed entity. It is for this reason that there are the myriad things. Thus, the moon of *tathatā* is already within the water; it is the moon of illusory existence.
The moon is also in the heavens. People still take pleasure in striking earthenware vessels until they break them, and digging through embankments to let the water flow;
might this not be their aspiration to sit in tranquil meditation within the Water-Moon Dharma-hall?

On the Discourse of Rebuking the Buddha and Scolding the Patriarchs. Someone asked: "In the Chan school, there are frequent expressions of rebuking the Buddha and scolding the patriarchs. Why is this? The Master said:
"The Buddha-body fills the Dharma-realm, appearing universally before all sentient beings. It responds to conditions and accords with stimuli without exception, yet it remains eternally..."
This Bodhimanda and the four-line verse from the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* truly constitute the essential purport of the patriarchs’ vital instructions.

Nevertheless, if a person generates conceptual understanding based on the words, they will become worlds apart [from the truth]. It is precisely this mind that generates conceptual understanding based on the words [that creates the separation].
This is precisely what is meant by "karmic consciousness drifting aimlessly, with no foundation to rely upon. If one has not yet attained such clarity here, how can the life-root be severed?

Even if the entirety of the mountains, rivers, and the great earth were transformed into teeth, lips, throats, and tongues, and each of those teeth, lips, throats, and tongues produced immeasurable sublime sounds to praise the Buddha simultaneously, it would still have no connection to the matter. As for the one who is able to offer such praise—
That which is praised is none other than the one who praises; that which is reviled is none other than the one who reviles.
If this is so, what praise could there be, and what revilement could there be? Moreover, since both subject and object are empty, where could praise or revilement possibly find a place to abide?
Sentient beings regard the Buddha as holy and those who are not Buddhas as ordinary; yet, regarding the ordinary and the holy—[they are likewise empty].

These two paths are the sickness of views held by sentient beings since beginningless time. Only when the sentiments of both the holy and the ordinary are exhausted can one forget both self and others.
Because the ancient masters possessed such a compassionate and urgent heart, they reviled the Buddhas and scolded the Patriarchs;
this was merely to eliminate the manifestations of these views. Someone might say: "If that is so, then..."
As for Your Majesty’s rebuking people and reviling the Buddhas and patriarchs, what is the meaning behind it? The King said:
"The ancient worthies did this merely to guide beginners; how could they have ever considered this the ultimate or final principle?
There are many skillful means (*upāya*) for guiding beginners, so why must it necessarily involve reviling the Buddhas and patriarchs?"
His Majesty’s Father manifests the body of the Tathāgata through the Buddhas of the present; his compassion is inexhaustible and his transformative guidance is boundless.
