The sun of wisdom shines everywhere, and the clouds of Dharma constantly bestow moisture. That which he perceives and realizes far surpasses that of all ancient worthies by ten thousand times;
how could it be fathomed by ordinary means? I, your humble servant, merely believe in, honor, and uphold [this teaching]; how could I possibly analyze or verify its meaning? Although...

Nevertheless, having respectfully received your instructions, I have been able to grasp your profound voice. Although I too am but a recipient of a mere fragment of understanding, I cannot bear not to reveal it to the world and future generations as a guide for those to come.
Therefore, I shall specifically elaborate upon this for you. Now, both empty space and the great earth are entirely illusory.
It is thus bound together. Yet this great earth and empty space are themselves the ground of ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi*). True reality is entirely illusion; all illusions are true.
Illusion is entirely true, and even that single truth is itself an illusion. Within this illusory reflection, at every step one does not depart from the ground of truth.
This nature of *tathatā* (suchness) passes through these illusory conditions in every moment: the pine tree was originally straight, the thorn bush was originally crooked, and the crow...
The crane is originally black; the crane is originally white. Pines are straight and thorns are curved; crows are black and cranes are white.
One cannot even alter these natural illusory forms, let alone the human being, who is the most spiritual among all things. Therefore, as a minister one should be loyal; as a son one should be filial;
as a citizen one should practice benevolence; and toward all things one should exercise compassion. When all virtues are fully realized, one can then perfect this illusion.
The shadow and the illusory shadow are true suchness; they are non-dual and without distinction. When the illusory shadow is perfected, it is itself true suchness.

To depart from this single word is to belong to the realm of demons and heterodoxies. Now, as for the Buddhas and Patriarchs: if discussed according to the supramundane dharma, they are that which arises from the body of non-arising.
If discussed according to the mundane dharma, they are the former sages and former teachers. Is it appropriate to utter disparaging words against them?
Is this not so? Only when both the sage and the ordinary person are extinguished can the boundaries of past and future be severed; this is certainly the case.

However, if one regards scolding and reviling as the extinction of both sage and ordinary person, then even this very view of the extinction of sage and ordinary person will leave no distinction from the views of the ordinary—how then could one avoid falling into the realm of animals?
Furthermore, the followers of our school cite that the ancient masters once said: "One must turn toward the heterodox classes..."
To walk the Middle Way, where the six realms of rebirth are all equally level—only then is one truly penetrating heaven and earth.

What cause and effect could there be to speak of? To fail to realize this is merely the deluded view of attachment; it only leads to the prospect of falling into the realm of animals. It lacks the capacity to penetrate heaven and earth as the ancient worthies did.
As for the mental conduct of those ancient worthies, one has not even dreamed of it in a lifetime as long as a donkey’s. If people truly step across the threshold...
Section: The Illusory and the Real are One and Identical. One must precisely fulfill the true fruit within the illusory. How could one possibly revile the Buddhas and scold the Patriarchs?

If you have not yet attained this, then how can the reviling of Buddhas and scolding of Patriarchs be tolerated? It is merely the talkative words of a tongueless person attempting to guide those at the beginning stage of practice.
"Does Your Majesty not see through this? Have you awakened? I and you shall believe, accept, and practice it together. Or have you not awakened?
The Imperial Decree cannot be disobeyed. The man responded with deference and withdrew.
After showing Chao Ding the joy of Chan, [the Master] said to Chao Ding: "The Buddha-dharma is the ladder and raft for transcending the world; worldly dharmas are the pivot for abiding in the world.
Their paths diverge and their directions differ—like a southward-bound carriage and a northward-bound track—and it is likely that everyone speaks thus. Nevertheless, were one to..."

If such a person is indeed able, within the Buddha-dharma, to realize their own mind and attain that which is non-attainment, they will manifest the marks of following conditions with an unstained mind.
Free from hatred and love, free from grasping and rejecting, they naturally do not pursue the flow of the waves nor abide in the shadow.
Thus, they attain the oneness of principle and phenomena, and the non-duality of emptiness and form; worldly dharmas are precisely the Buddha-dharma.
If the mind relies upon sense objects and lands, allowing entanglements to arise at will— amidst a chaotic jumble of grasping and rejecting, love and hate—

even to the point of rushing after fame and profit or hoping for favor and honor; if one’s conduct differs according to whether one is hidden or manifest, and one’s habits differ internally and externally— then,

even if one were to pour out the entirety of the Tripiṭaka and the twelve divisions of the canon, or the seventeen hundred public cases, as clearly as water poured from one vessel into another, such a person is not a Buddha.

As for those who possess knowledge and vision, they have already moved far beyond the spittle of foxes and the drool of wildcats; how much more so when they rely upon the subtle words of the ancient masters to create sharp tools for their times?
Yet, with these truths clear in their mouths while their minds remain busily distracted, how many will not end up defiling their own wisdom-life and staining the ancestral halls?
One should simply value the diligent practice of the Buddha’s teachings and faithfully uphold the vows of a śramaṇa in all worldly affairs.

If one does not give rise to a mind of joy within the Dharma, yet maintains the precepts against greed and anger, then even if an iron snake crosses one's path, one can ultimately regard it as a dead snake to be handled with ease.
It has never been the case that one who fails to practice discipline (*śīla*) and concentration (*samādhi*) can suddenly achieve full realization.
To borrow the Buddha-dharma to carry out worldly affairs, without falling into habitual defilement or increasing various delusions, so as not to obscure the Buddha-nature—this is the way.
Regarding those entangled in the worldly net:

our Imperial Father, taking the present Buddha as his guide, has awakened the *tathāgatagarbha*. In the leisure moments between his myriad state affairs, he occasionally expresses sympathetic joy (*anumodana*).

Whenever he reveals even a few words, they are like pouring clarified butter (*sarpirmaṇḍa*) upon one; thus, he upholds the Zen robes and rectifies the ancestral school with earnest and sincere devotion.
Directly citing [the scriptures] while employing indirect metaphors, the hope that each shall achieve their own fulfillment was originally the intent beyond the Tathāgata’s formal teachings.

Truly, it can universally benefit the ten directions and extensively save the myriad species. Those who meet with it realize it spontaneously; it is exactly as it is within one's own lot. It is right here and now, requiring no external seeking.

Yet, regarding the cultivation of oneself and the ordering of society, the governance of the state and the pacification of the world, military and agriculture, ritual and music, government, law, virtue, and instruction— [The text continues: ...and so forth. (Note: The provided source text appears to be a fragment of a classical Chinese Buddhist commentary, likely discussing the relationship between direct and indirect teachings (*kengyō* and *hikyō*) and the realization of the Way through one's own inherent nature.)
Whether in eating, drinking, sitting, or rising; whether in coming and going or resting and working—all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) are fundamentally free from obstruction.
Therefore, one desires to protect this single lamp so that it may never be extinguished.

His compassion is most earnest, and his illumination is impartial; thus, the distinction between self and others is entirely forgotten. This is surely something in which both the monastic and the lay can have common faith—is my word not so?
You have fortunately encountered this flourishing era and been graced with his instructions;
this must surely stem from past causes, allowing you to possess right view. It is precisely now that you ought to exert yourself; do not merely close your eyes and bury your head in neglect.

Enter the gate of shame and remorse; cultivate the practice of dedication; vow to reach the very bottom and fully comprehend this one matter, so as to look up and repay the profound and vast grace of the Sage, and successfully succeed to the Sun of the Buddha.
Thus, having recently listened to your speech and examined your conduct, it is like a bird about to soar—

Heaven! Though his feet have not yet touched the ground, and though he has momentarily severed the entanglements amidst the thorns and brambles, he still occasionally mistakes the reflection of flowers for the moon in the water.
To speak so garrulously before others is surely not the compassionate heart of one who guides;

to manifest his form everywhere is but the demonic artifice of one who seeks to curry favor. I ask you: in this field where Buddhas are selected, a single patch of pure earth—since it is neither... [the text ends].
One might be able to shave one's hair and wash one's marrow, yet as one turns away, the eyes grow dizzy and the ears ring;

regarding such trifling matters of profit and honor, one is still unable to penetrate them through investigation—how then can one hope to explore the fundamental and transcendent matters so as not to fall into decline?
Or rather, that one can deliver others—does this have its cause here, or does it have its fruit here? Let us not even speak of the absence of seeds; why is the sowing of them so imprecise?
A saying goes: "To see the Way is easy; to cultivate the Way is difficult. And again: "To know it is easy; to practice it is difficult.
When separated by a mere gauze curtain, one cannot distinguish objects; how much less so at Mount Jiuyi? Even within the space of a few inches, one cannot...

If you cannot reach home when you are already there, how much less so when you are ten thousand *li* away! You must wake up with urgent mindfulness at once and cut away [delusions] from within with great pain.
Do not harbor improper thoughts; simply practice the contemplation of suchness (*tathatā*). Before you have lost your way on the journey, press straight ahead.

In this way, perhaps this one matter may still allow you to return to your former self. Otherwise, as soon as Mañjuśrī gives rise to a thought, the Iron Ring Mountains follow it. To go lower and lower is hell.

What words can be used? The Buddha-dharma is fundamentally without abiding; those who cross over the drowning all do so by taking it up for themselves. Ultimately, it has nothing in common with worldly dharmas.
Exert yourselves! Exert yourselves!
Written by the Fifth Imperial Prince, the Duke of Huo, the Layman Rising Sun (Xuri).
Sixty Verses for Beginners in Poetry:
Self and others are originally not two; host and guest are naturally distinct. Before one, there is no shifting or exchange; the single moon is complete in ten thousand rivers.
Emptiness itself is fundamentally not empty; existence itself is fundamentally not existent. When both emptiness and existence are forgotten, the three times three are originally nine.
A reflection of fire cannot quench thirst; a painted cake cannot satisfy hunger. The ignorant often misrecognize this, while the realized understand its essential principle.
The moment one intends to depart from emptiness, one has already fallen into existence. Not knowing the interval between emptiness and existence, what thing is most enduring?
An ancient mirror buried in dust—how many people search for it with care? As the east wind brings the season of warmth, the sunlight outside the window is fresh.
The scenery of the Eastern Cloister is fine; a single oar on a light skiff. A thousand mountains sink in emerald shadows; as I travel by land, the boat does not move.
Having leaped out of the Diamond Circle and shattered the *liji* thorn-bush, if one asks what I have gained, I carry a shoulder-pole of spring breeze.
Once the fish and the rabbit are caught, there is no further need for them; why then must one guard the trap and the snare? Occasionally I read the Golden Sutra, merely to cover my eyelids.
Knowing only how to turn the palm leaves, I chant "Tāra" day after day. I do not listen to the birds in the forest, though they all sing the Mahā songs.
Taking sound as the direct pointing and seizing form as the single transmission—merely by means of this very sound and form, Avalokiteśvara contemplates in this way:

first he realizes the difference within the same, then he clarifies the sameness within the different. The three thousand realms are originally illusory; the four great elements are fundamentally not empty.

Closing one's eyes, one vainly seeks to see; contemplating the mind, one mistakenly looks for penetration. How pitiable are those who merely explain the teachings; they are just like bees bumping against a window.
Riding backward upon dragons and elephants, they rush about; in spring and summer, their hair hangs in disarray. When departing, there is no shadow at all; when arriving, no trace is seen.
The clouds of compassion spread thickly; the rain of Dharma falls in layers. Though he is but a fellow playing with mud balls, he is able to stand atop a steep peak.
To realize Buddhahood, one must eliminate the very concept of Buddha; to master Chan, do not become mired in Chan. If you seek it from a pillar, you will fall by the side of a water jar.

When the mind lingers on delusive objects, it is obstructed; when time is penetrated, the Buddha-nature is perfect. Vast and boundless as if wading through water, one should board the Dharma King’s boat.
The Buddha-land appears according to every direction; the Western Heaven lies right here in the East. Simply open the Pavilion of Maitreya, and ascend the Peak of Virtuous Clouds.
The bright moon lingers at the treetops; the fine breeze passes by the flowers. In these places of singular wonder, from antiquity to the present day, all remains the same.
Dwelling in this realm of non-action, what prevents one from being amidst the clamor of the marketplace? Returning, one sits within the embers; departing, one hides away in the snow.
The Great Way transcends subject and object; it is as immeasurable as empty space. When the World-Honored One presses down a single finger, the Ocean Seal reflects light everywhere.
Having smashed the black lacquer bucket, one walks within the realm of lapis lazuli. The ten directions are naturally pervasive; throughout the three periods of time, one acts with total freedom.
Where there is fire, it is as good as darkness; where there is no lamp, it is truly light. This body is equal to the sun and moon—why need one inquire about its birth year?
When meeting illness, one finds the excellent remedy: the land of longevity and ultimate bliss. Mountains and rivers become one’s vocation; rain and dew serve as the vessel for drink.
Subduing the tiger is but a waste of effort; taming the dragon is merely a display of wildness. You must know that both dragon and tiger are, in their very essence, the Mind-King.
Entering meditative absorption is originally no absorption; resting the mind is further mistaken as "rest. The flowers on the steps flourish together; the mountain stream flows along its course.
Who goes to seek the forest hermitage? What hinders one from holding the fishing hook? Year after year, on this very day, warmth and cold mark the seasons of spring and autumn.
How could illusion ever be illusory? One must behold the lotus within the fire. A single pond remains eternally serene; the eight waters are naturally profound.

Only when there is no Buddha does one speak of a Buddha; only when there is no immortal is one an immortal. To mistake the Buddha and the immortal by even a hair’s breadth is to remain utterly lost in two worlds as vast as heaven and earth.
A single thread connects heaven and earth—what person can perceive it? Unaware of the dream within a dream, they seek further confusion within their delusion.
The years and months pass like a swift wind; time flows like a rushing bolt of lightning. At this very moment, one must be alert and mindful; quickly seek the Dharma King as your teacher.

In the twelfth lunar month, one rides the cool breeze while loosening one's belt; during the three months of midsummer, one faces the fire while wearing a fur robe. The foolish deride this as perverse, but the wise smile in silence and nod their heads in agreement.
The Dharma-body of sixteen feet and three thousand worlds is but a tiny grain of dust; a mustard seed and Mount Sumeru are no different.
Mountains, rivers, grasses, and trees are his entire body:
one person eats constantly yet remains unsated, while another does not eat and yet suffers no hunger. Who has penetrated this meaning? Speak directly!
Not a single thread of attachment remains.
Black charcoal cannot match its blackness; white ice cannot compare to its whiteness. After all, when asked what it is, he replies:
"White charcoal, black ice."

If you wish to use stillness to stop movement, it is like trying to escape one's shadow while standing in the sun. If you wish to cultivate unsurpassed Bodhi, you must surely open your eyes and fall into a well.
The spring days bring a biting, piercing wind, while the three months of winter bring warm and mild air; this is not because spring and winter have been exchanged, but simply because—
Having once seen Amitābha, two selves appear before the mirror;
in the end, upon which of these do you fixate? At that very moment, both person and mirror are forgotten together, and "other-self" and "self-of-self" are clearly realized as one.

Yesterday, the garden flowers were in full bloom; several branches were white and several were red. Because I was so intent on gazing at their fragrant colors, I refused to step into the midst of the clusters.
In the four directions and ten quarters, there is only me; all that flies, hides, moves, or grows is Buddha. Buddha and I are originally not two; it is not otherwise.

Vague and indistinct—only when studying the Way do you not abandon yourself; only when seeing the Way do you truly become intimate with it. Let go of the six sense objects and the six sense faculties, and the entire great thousandfold world-system is but a single True Person.
Profoundly deep and purely clear is the primal qi; limpid and unmixed is the spirit. Having penetrated the three thousand worlds, one can command the twelve hours of the day.
A single pool of autumn water serves as the body; a hundred-foot pine by the mountain stream serves as the form. The golden light behind the crown of the head is an illusion;
the clouds rising from beneath the feet are not real.

If you intend to transcend and ascend to the Pure Land, yet remain without affinity for the Buddhas, then even a single grain of mustard seed remains unexhausted; how could the three thousand worlds be limited to just three thousand?
Once you recognize that [the mind] is torn asunder like a flower scattered in seven or eight pieces, what distinction can there be between the six desires and the four dhyānas?
To speak idly of the soaring hawk and the leaping fish is to be separated by a gulf as vast as heaven and earth at the slightest hair’s breadth.

At all times, I follow conditions for food and drink; when free from affairs, I sing aloud as my whim takes me. I have seen through the realization of *bodhi* as being illusory, and understood that Buddhas and patriarchs are all but demons.
Having recognized that the six sense-faculties are devoid of self, I let the five aggregates go their own way.
This is simply the exhaustion of principle and the end of nature—like a block of wood, like a vulgar commoner, ha ha!

Let there be no discussion of who observes or who listens; cease questioning whether there are words or no words. If you wish to realize the path of ultimate truth, you must know how to explore the root and seek the source.
If you wish to meet the ancient Buddhas face-to-face, you must tread them underfoot with your straw sandals.
Once you have mastered cleansing the defilements within your breast, who could possibly run about outside of all things?
The small gathers the fine hairs yet remains vast; the great pervades the universe yet is subtle. Without conscious recognition, there is Buddha-wisdom;

neither arising nor ceasing, it is the celestial mechanism. When winter days bring snow falling in heaps, and spring mornings see rain sprinkling in mist, let the snow and rain follow their seasonal course as they may;
I simply observe the times and put on my robes.

What fear is there when a fierce tiger stands in one's path? From the beginning, things and self have been fundamentally the same; in this sameness, there is originally no distinction between "self" and "other.

Only at different times do we distinguish male from female. To nurture the unadorned and preserve the true is not a strategic maneuver; to harbor the pure and embrace the simple is not a meritorious achievement.
If one were thus to take south as north, in the end, one would still not perceive east or west.
The forms of wind and clouds have no fixed nature; the dispositions of monkeys and horses are difficult to settle. Relying on stillness while remaining in motion, one acts out of delusion;
taking the conditioned to be the unconditioned, one deceives oneself. A floating bubble is not the surging waves; it is the ocean water itself that constitutes the billows.
Allow not even a hair’s breadth of obstruction; let a single precious jewel roll across the tray.
Within a single speck of dust, an entire Buddha-land resides. When one speaks of the Way, it seems dense and substantial;
when one speaks of emptiness, it is vast and entirely void. Whether near or far, there is no duality; east, west, south, and north are all the same.
Do not marvel at the brilliance of an ancient mirror; its roundness is nothing but common bronze.
In delusion, one possesses much knowledge and wide learning; yet upon awakening, one is like one who is drunk or insane. Only when there is no seeing does true seeing arise;
that which is conditioned is itself the unconditioned. The Great Way is neither difficult nor easy; what need is there for worldly anxiety or thought?
Why does a parrot have a tongue? Ultimately, why does a spider have no silk?
The appearance of form is fundamentally not form; how could emptiness be emptiness? Samādhi has always been entirely illusory; wherever the six sense organs abide, all are as such.
This very place is clearly where "I" am; where else in another realm would one seek me? The Western Heaven lies right beneath one's feet;
there is no need for the trouble of riding horses or driving carriages.
How can one investigate the matter within one's own person? Sitting upright on the grass mat, the mind finds no satisfaction;
in a single morning, past and future are suddenly severed—everywhere, in all directions, is Gautama.
Where is it right and where is it wrong? Laughing, he knocks over the wooden door-panel before the courtyard. Only this gate is non-dual;
fundamentally there is not even one—where else could one return?
Form, emptiness, clarity, and darkness comprise a thousandfold appearances; earth, water, fire, and wind constitute a single body. If you seek to abandon them, you increase delusion and error;
only when every particle of dust is mutually interfused is one truly real.
Only by realizing that which is like an illusion is it not an illusion; do not seek to eliminate the hundredfold manifestations of illusion.
If you wish to find that which is truly non-illusory, it is like trying to catch the wind within the wind.
The peach blossoms bloom year after year by the stream; only Lingyun saw them without doubt. I wish to ask Shaoshi about these flowers:
are they the marrow, or are they the skin?
In this very state, how could there be awakening or delusion? Without excess and without deficiency, all is perfectly equal.
If you say that awakening is only achieved today, how is this different from saying east while facing west?
Ultimately, there is no separate dharma prior to form; this is truly because beyond sound there is the direct transmission. What expedient means is there for riding upon sound and covering over form?
Let form and sound be as they are, according to their own nature.
No awl can be stuck into it, yet a body still remains; the other shore is still far away, and the sea of poison is deep.
Only when one has exhausted the body in poverty will a handful of earth suddenly become gold.
Clearly it was settled yesterday; what is settled today? A single phrase encompasses the gateways of ten thousand dharmas.
Yet, if you still seek them at the edge of sensory objects, you are merely thrusting your own head into a vat of glue.
The precious hall and the sixteen-foot golden body; for ten thousand years, the Dharma King’s wheel ever turns. How many people prostrate themselves upon the single mat?
Who can truly see it with open eyes?
In the midst of domestic affairs, all matters are as they should be; why need one hold up the staff to question Fuxi? Mountains, rivers, and the great earth are none other than oneself;
day and night revolving is not "it. A single moon shines afar across a thousand Buddha-lands; throughout the six periods, dreams manifest the four dignified postures.
Standing tall and solitary, there is truly nothing to do; through kalpas, it remains ever as this brief moment.
A single cry of a bird emerges from the treetops; it speaks as clearly as a pearl rolling across a jade platter. The five teachings are clearly and completely integrated;
the stages of the three vehicles are all perfectly encompassed. The great trichiliocosm is already entirely contained within; how could this tiny fragment ever deceive?
If you are still unable to cast off the lacquer bucket, what does the broad and long tongue have to do with it?

A stirring thought—how could it not be the root of birth and death? Failing to give rise to even a single thought, one again sinks into delusion. In the great ocean of perfect enlightenment, there is no gate or path;
the two Iron Ring Mountains stand tall against the vast heavens. When released, the snow lion melts into a mass of fire; when grasped, the flowing mercury enters the dust.
If the center and the periphery are not brought into equal balance and cast away, it will be difficult to form pure causes with the King of Emptiness.

All manner of wondrous marvels are cast aside; in the single flavor of *tathatā*, one goes wherever one will. Is this not penetrating both heaven and earth? Originally there is no self, nor is there "he.
The three bodies are entirely without distinction of long or short; how could there ever be compliance or opposition on this path?
It is laughable that Nanquan herds the water-buffalo; at every fork in the road, it branches off again.
Directly beneath, there has originally been not a single thing; do not seek peace of mind by starting from this "nothingness. Diligent cultivation is fundamentally a matter of ordinary daily life;

secret practice follows solely what one’s capacity allows. Within, there is no room for anything else but pure wisdom; without, there is nothing to inquire about regarding the past, future, or present.
Carrying firewood and drawing water within the state of suchness—this is precisely the ancient zither without strings.
All sentient beings are entirely of vajra-nature; the four marks fully manifest the light of prajñā. Sitting, one cuts off both bodhi and afflictions; treading, one overturns both hell and heaven.
Stepping out the door, a laugh fills the vast blue sky; leaning on a pillow at the third watch, the white moon is cool.
When the tree falls and the vines wither, what is this? It is clearly the precious seal emerging from the Wheel-Turning King.
Mixing water with mud, he comes forth in this manner; yet where could he ever be defiled by dust? Having untied the six knots, there remain no further knots;
having washed away the ordinary body and the saintly body alike. Casting off his hands at the precipice, he treads upon level ground;
opening his eyes in the well, he ascends the lotus pedestal. A man of spirit should take such steps: in a single thought-moment, a thousand years and ten billion eons pass.
Even a child of three feet tall shares in this; yet through a thousand lifetimes across kalpas, one has long forgotten it.
When the nostrils are pulled, the void roars; when the crown of the head is struck, the great earth knows. How could there ever have been even a fraction lacking?
Do not further deceive yourself before your own eyes. If you dally with this outside of it, a painted cake can never satisfy your hunger.
A thousand gates and ten thousand doors all point south; one need only pick up this and examine it closely. Do not say that within this there is still only "one";
know that even within a single phrase there is no "three. The mud ox enters the sea to seek news; the iron horse faces the wind to deliver a wondrous discourse.
This is the true seed of the Wondrously Awakened Empty King; atop a single hair-tip sits Gautama.

Layer upon layer of mountains, and layer upon layer of waters; the precious mirrors reflect one another, their light inexhaustible. When subject and object are suddenly dissolved, what rules or patterns remain?
Only when the distinctions between sage and ordinary are utterly cleansed does perfect fusion begin. The straw sandals turn upside down across the three thousand worlds;
the tattered robe stands high, encompassing the sixteen-foot void. Not even a single trace of contrivance is required—why seek a "host" any further?
Epitaph for the Layman Ru-xin, Prince Fupeng of Duolu Pingjun:

The ocean of the nature of True Suchness (tathatā) is the perfect penetration of the Dharma-realm; the paths of sages and ordinary beings are one and the same, and the way to Buddhahood is identical. It is only because of delusion regarding oneself [that this distinction arises].
Chasing after objects to the east and west, they turn their backs on existence from existence and on emptiness from emptiness. Their conscious minds are inverted; birth and death follow one another.
Hatred and love arise in succession, giving rise to good and evil karma. They transmigrate through the six realms, taking up and discarding bodies without ceasing. O Great Compassionate Father!

Out of compassion for the deluded masses, I have established this precious raft to rescue and deliver them from suffering. These sincere words and precious instructions—take refuge in them with all haste.
If you seek liberation, it is neither distant nor difficult; with a single resolve of faith, it lies right before you, requiring not even half a thought.
No single word is used. Crows cawing and magpies chirping, wooden chips and common bricks—all together perform the Mahāyāna, universally manifesting its adornment.

If you can realize this right now, who would distinguish between self and other? The three realms are mind-only; the myriad dharmas are but the one self. This is not a matter of intellectual understanding or conceptual realization.

Yet there is no connection [between them]. If one has not truly realized this, how can one speak of rest? To do so is to mislead oneself and others; it is the practice of demons and heterodox teachings.
That mind is the object, and that object is the Buddha—mind, Buddha, and object: what difference is there, and what sameness? There is neither one nor two.

The two and the one are perfectly interfused; form and emptiness, light and darkness, are harmoniously integrated wherever they appear. With no mind directed toward dharmas, there are no dharmas within the mind.
When both mind and dharmas are simultaneously extinguished, this is called "the Real. Yet even "the Real" is but a provisional designation. This is universally proclaimed for all time.

In the teaching of ultimate unity, speech and silence, movement and stillness, are not different; what distinction is there between darkness and light, or penetration and obstruction? To realize that this and that are non-dual, the great chiliocosm of sand-grain worlds is suchness itself.

In this painting of clouds and mountains, the green mountains are simply green mountains; the white clouds are simply white clouds. If you wish to understand the meaning of the clouds and mountains, observe them closely: are they divided or undivided?
This is the song of truth and delusion.
Arising from delusion and dispelling delusion both result in further delusion; employing the true to seek the true—where is the truth?
When the dualistic emotions of both the true and the deluded are exhausted, the cold ashes and withered wood suddenly burst into spring.
Delusion and awakening:
those who are deluded take emptiness for form; those who have awakened take form as emptiness. Delusion and awakening are like a dream;
form and emptiness are fundamentally the same.
A Song on the Essence of Mind:
In every land and at every dust mote, all is but the One Mind; Amidst the sands of worlds, the body alone is revealed. Who among men can recognize this wondrous essence?
Even if one were to recognize it, it would not be the true reality.
Not abiding in the east, one abides in the south; yet being in the south, one is actually in the north. All things abide in this manner. The mind that has no place of abiding is thus.
This is the discourse on self and others.
Humanity and phenomena are fundamentally non-dual; things and self are originally one and the same. Within this, delusions give rise to barriers, causing difficulties in penetrating all situations.
To transform these objects and attain liberation—
Transforming mountains and rivers so they return to oneself; transforming oneself so one becomes mountains and rivers. Two yellow orioles sing among the green willows;
a flight of white egrets alights upon the level slope.

In movement, seek stillness within stillness; in stillness, seek movement within movement. To resolve this crux of movement and stillness is called the functioning of True Suchness (*tathatā*). This is the subtle interplay of mind and object.

Many people say that external objects obstruct the mind; they do not realize it is the mind that obstructs objects. If one can eliminate this mind, the myriad objects will naturally accord with reality.
— *The Verses on the Three Times by Jñānaprabha*

When both object and mind exist, they together form a phantom. When mind exists but the object is empty, it is half-phantom and half-real. When both mind and object are empty, one transcends both reality and illusion.
This state of emptiness that is not empty is beyond compare.

To speak of True Suchness as existing is slander; to speak of it as non-existent is entirely deceptive. Setting aside both words of existence and non-existence, [I] sing of the living mercury beneath the earth and above the heavens.

I have a ball of mercury that scatters throughout the three thousandfold world-system; it expands and contracts, unites and separates according to conditions, flowing unhindered through the ten directions whether they be open or obstructed.
This is what I call "talking in a dream."
In peaceful sleep, dreams are illusory; upon awakening, one realizes the dream was not real. The deluded person is like a guest within a dream;
the awakened one is like a person who has woken from sleep.

Commentary on the "Nail in Empty Space": It is easy to drive a nail into empty space; it is difficult to drive empty space into a nail. If you can realize the meaning within this, the great trichiliocosm will be settled wherever you are.
*The Discourse on the Three Periods*.

The present is entirely devoid of present phenomena; how could there be a future time in the future? Being able to know that the three periods of time are fundamentally without boundaries, one may simply let things be, whether now or in antiquity.

Six Poems in the "Xijiangyue" Meter Although the characteristics of dharmas transcend the substance of form, the true mechanism does not reside in the contemplation of emptiness. When Vimalakīrti scattered flowers in mid-air, those who saw him were told they must leave behind the very act of seeing.
If one can harmonize with the six sense objects without being stained by them, what hindrance is there to the myriad phenomena appearing before one? Behold!
Cloud shadows rest upon the tranquil cold pool; when geese pass by, do they ever linger?
Suddenly one hears the crane’s cry in the sky, utterly forgetting the lowing of the ox beneath the bed. One cannot distinguish the melody of the flute from the sound of the bell;
ten thousand sounds naturally each find their stillness. People say the drum of poison should be avoided; I say the wheel of fire may be mounted. Follow conditions as they arise.
Immovable, quiescent, eternal, and luminous—this is the very nature of the Tathāgata.

Through the five teachings and three vehicles, there has been earnest exhortation; across fifty-eight thousand scrolls, there has been repeated instruction. Yet the separate transmission does not reside within the scriptural texts;

it is to be realized through silent resonance with one’s own mind, which is itself the seal. Simply by returning to this single wondrous truth, one immediately penetrates the Dharma-gate of non-duality. Thus it is attained.
Whatever comes to hand is the family treasure; yet one must guard against clinging and mistaken recognition.
The great earth is not the great earth; a single thread is simply a single thread. Within this, few people know the secret pivot.
It is neither right nor wrong, neither is nor not-is. If you ask how to practice, I tell you: do not rely on artificial cultivation. Do not say—
There is no activity and no conditioned action; yet one delights in performing Buddha-work within dreams.

To encompass the entirety of the worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges—where then would the True Sūtras of the Dharma-treasury come from? Was not Vimalakīrti’s single silence truly without sound?
Why engage in such lofty talk and expansive discourse? Try listening to the rhythm of the bamboo by the window; naturally, the wind arises upon the leaves. The wind arises.
The rustling of leaves is doubly causeless; at the ancient ferry, the boat lies across, unsettled.

If you ask about the root and the core of the mind, the spiritual sprout does not change with spring or autumn. Seeking the snake by parting the weeds requires exhaustive searching, as if looking for it before the frost or after the snow.
Subject and object are originally of one color; the solitary cloud wishes to depart but remains. The third watch.
The bright moon is directly over the pavilion; yet again, it is half-concealed and half-revealed.

These two verses count the black to seek the white, stirring up wind and waves of their own accord. Pointing east while drawing west, they mistakenly search for the ancient path—the mud ox at the bottom of the sea.
Dwelling securely, what more need one fear within the mountains of Shih-hu?

Without name or surname, unbound and unrestrained; like floating duckweeds upon the sea’s surface, a single mote of dust within the void. Do not marvel at the green mountains hidden by the morning mist;
look instead at the clear waters where fresh lotuses grow ever longer.
Four Gāthās: A single thought of purity is the Buddha; a single thought of affliction is a sentient being. Purity does not exist apart from affliction;
thus, Buddha and sentient beings share the same name.

Conditions arise from the confrontation with objects; where there is no confrontation, there is no cause. The single mind spontaneously gives rise to the myriad dharmas, yet the myriad dharmas fundamentally do not obstruct the mind.

From this, likes and dislikes arise; through likes and dislikes, one grasps and rejects, flowing in the cycle of rebirth. When one recognizes that high and low are equal, the three thousand [worlds]...
The world is a single body.
Sentient beings grasp at emptiness as form; those of the Two Vehicles grasp at form as emptiness. Grasping at emptiness and grasping at form are both erroneous.
One should know that it is both emptiness and form.
A Warning for Disciples:
Earth, water, fire, and wind circulate through the three realms; this illusory body is but a transformation of these four great elements.

Within them, the nature of ignorance and consciousness rushes about in confusion; one falsely clings to them as "self," with hatred and love attacking one another. Thus one is both greedy and angry, and both angry and deluded.

Delusion constitutes its essence, while greed and hatred function as its activities. Causes give rise to effects, and life after life, birth follows death; yet with every cessation, there is inevitably further rebirth.
Even for kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, one may feel sorrow and remorse, vowing to sever ignorance and seek to realize the Buddha-way in order to liberate all sentient beings.
It is like one running in the midday sun who wishes to be without a shadow; yet as the body moves, the shadow follows. To regard this shadow as an obstruction is to give rise to deluded views.
All things are empty: what Buddha is there, and what birth? Good and evil are blended as one. Holding to this single thought, the myriad existences are all erased.
What is this thought? It is the Great Iron Ring Mountains. Failing to realize the nature of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), one forcibly rejects the conditions of existence.

What basis is there for a solitary emptiness when the myriad phenomena manifest before us? Existence is itself emptiness; emptiness is not different from existence. To loathe existence and rejoice in emptiness is like fleeing in terror from one's own head.
The illusory body and the Dharma-body, consciousness-nature and Buddha-nature—all lack even a single inch of substance. It is but the one great perfect mirror;

it is solely because of delusion regarding its original truth throughout kalpas that one forcibly gives rise to discrimination, thereby creating the cause of illusion. Out of the compassion of the Buddhas and Patriarchs, they have bestowed various skillful means.
Regarding the matter within one's own person, one must simply recommend oneself.
Recorded by the Grand Secretary, the Layman Bo Er Tai, "Tantan."

For ten years I have clung to objects of perception, traversing the four heavens before a hundred billion Mount Sumerus and Iron Ring Mountains. Through this, I realized that the tongue exists only to perpetuate karma;
even if one uses no needles [to prick oneself], it is still not Chan. Entering the gate of shame and remorse, I seek further progress. — Gratitude.
The power of compassion is heavy and overturning; how can one tread to the bottom of the three barriers? The wind at the treetops, the moon over the river—these are the Zen verses.

Having finished speaking of the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, there is again the *Laṅkāvatāra*. The Dharma words never deviate by a single character. After all, when has there ever been a single word left behind?
A mere word; according to conditions, simply drink Zhaozhou’s tea.
Yunmen and Linji each stir up confusion; their blows and shouts are groundless, yet they further raise their fists. Cut through these entanglements and the Buddha-dharma appears:
the autumn wind in the eighth month is a fine, cool day.
The willow-raft coming from the West—does it have intent or not? The flax-seed and cypress-cone are far too blurred. Last night I caught a glimpse of the moon at the edge of the sky;
it was just like the pearl beneath the throat of a black dragon.
The incense burner stands firm upon the ground, passing through many years; yet even when the needle-point reaches its limit, it is not yet exhausted. When the rice is ripe, is it sifted or not?
How often has the innate nature of the barbarian been fully realized?
Who can take up the practice of rolling the ball? Having attained one, it is already not enough—how could there be three?
Recognize the pivotal mechanism within this: when hungry, eat; when weary, sleep.
Wind and banner interact, each realizing its own truth; why trouble yourself with further words to explain the mind? Ultimately, there is no place to be found herein;
the ancient master’s secret essence cannot be sought through inquiry.
The causes and conditions of the three periods of time pass in the blink of an eye; how often have they ceased their coming and going? Sometimes look at the tree before the steps:
the autumn dew is like pearls, each leaf perfectly round.
Stepping out the gate, one brushes away the sleeves, only to encounter the dust. Letting go—how could this not be entering the Truth? The entire courtyard’s wutong trees have shed their leaves;
along the steps, the autumn weeds grow once more in spring.

In vain do we speak of the Lesser Vehicle and the Greater; severing and permanence, arising and ceasing, are fundamentally without sentience. Once the Pratyekabuddha has attained fruition and the dust and smoke are purified, he continues as before to walk within the sands of the Ganges.
The merit of Nirvana is utterly without cause; in the transformation of the Dharma, how could there ever have been two bodies? The golden light pervading all realms sinks into the midst of darkness;
beneath the palm of the Tūla-cotton hand, those who are truly deluded are brought to clarity.
Is this delusion? Is this awakening? This is Mañjuśrī. At the gate, one must call out once or twice. Once you have entered the gate, the gate is outside;
does the fragrant rain through the single curtain not fall upon the flowers?
The wind and moon of Xitang are entirely without merit; one tries to seize them as they come from the West, yet they drift toward the East.
Though the nose-string has been pulled taut, liberation is not yet attained; where in the void can one grasp the void?

The mountain springs return to their source, and the jade is without flaw. If one can act at such a time, one shall leave the household life. Having left the household, the household remains as it was;
within the Jeta Grove, one beholds the *tiantianhua* (dharma-flower).
Sitting alone before the crags, the lunar disk is full. Facing the moon, you need only view it as the moon. To point at the moon is the mind;
the mind is the moon. Hanshan’s words require deep investigation.

Picking tea leaves at the foot of the tree, one seeks out form and sound; having sought them, form and sound reveal an ancient path stretching wide. Crimson leaves and green mountains—the autumn is at its finest.
Nirvāṇa and Prajñā are fundamentally names for the same reality.
Difficult and difficult, easy and easy—how many different kinds! Within, rely on him to apply his hand. Having worn through iron shoes, one sits securely;
the wind and moon of the Snowy Mountains are cold as ever, past and present.

These twenty-one verses concern delusion and non-delusion, awakening and non-awakening. When you recognize delusion, it seems as though you have shed your entanglements; yet when you fixate on the state of awakening, it immediately becomes a bond.
Awakening and delusion, delusion and awakening—neither has anything to do with the other. A single orb of autumn moon shines upon the eastern pavilion.
Yesterday the paulownia flowers bloomed; this morning the paulownia leaves have fallen. What is the cause of the blossoming? What is the fruit of the falling leaves?
At dawn, cold dew drenches my autumn robes. Year after year, flowers and leaves bloom and fall of their own accord.
Bodhi is fundamentally without cause; planting a cause brings forth its fruit. With a fruit, one further plants a cause; thus, in inverted confusion, one finds no place of rest.
What words did the World-Honored One have? Holding up a flower and smiling—nothing can be said.
The sunlight is faint beneath the water; the yin-qi manifests within the fire. Yin and yang are not two separate things; how could water and fire be opposites?
Abiding in the taking of water and fire, there is no inhaling or exhaling. Within the fire of the golden lotus, nectar is sprinkled; the nectar forms a pearl and the fire ignites itself.
In the end, this is precisely the path of turning back.
Turning back, what house is this? Within the eyes, the three realms are complete. Though the physical form is fundamentally empty, one must still maintain the pure precepts.
Master Lu possesses great faculties; for now, he eats the vegetables at the edge of the meat.
Traveling east, west, south, and north, it is only this path beneath the mountain. Smash the black lacquer bucket, and suddenly the crystalline light is revealed.
Where it is revealed, it turns back to black; when you come, you must go straight ahead.
Old Zhaozhou’s withered Chan: a seven-pound hempen robe. Crossing bridges, treading over horses and donkeys—it has vanished until not a single fragment remains.
Even though there is not a single fragment, this half still meets you. To preserve this half for the sake of meeting is merely to be a fellow who plays with lumps of mud.
A mustard seed contains Mount Sumeru; this is an ancient sage’s idle tale. Mount Sumeru has not diminished, nor has the mustard seed been made larger by anyone.
Last night I walked along the stream; the azure sky was like a painted picture.

Of the myriad dharmas, there is not a single dharma; even the absence of dharmas is not a non-dharma. When non-dharmas abide in the station of dharmas, where else could one distinguish between the real and the false?
Yunmen’s iron staff is as swift as thunder; it shatters empty space, yet you must strike yourself.
The great earth is but a single eye. When asked, the mouth speaks three leaps. Even if one were to ask further of the ears and nose, when would these leaps ever end?
North and south are the long rivers; east and west are the official roads. Oxen and sheep only cherish the mountains; they do not cherish the grass within the mountains.

In the morning I gaze upon the clouds atop the mountain peaks; at evening I face the moon by the riverside. The clouds and the moon are fundamentally without intention; the streams and mountains each have their own distinctions.
If the streams and mountains were not distinct, there would be idle clouds across a thousand ridges and moons in a thousand pools.
A single string of mani-jewels, each linked one to the next; who would know that within this continuous threading, at every point there is a severance?
Whether it be continuity or severance, severance or continuity, the precious light of each gem rotates like a flash of lightning.
Huangbo comes bearing his mattock; being buried alive is swifter than fire. With cremation there is deliberation; with burial alive there is no room for evasion.
Even were one to possess an indestructible diamond body, it would be buried away just like everyone else in ordinary practice.
Having formed a society at Dongping, they recommended the mirror of Guishan. What was the cause of this coincidence? Both sides shall become the subject of a public dispute.
This old monk adjudicates lawsuits like Shang Yang; in an instant, they are struck down, leaving no evidence. No evidence? Yet there is still evidence.
In the empty forest, the moon leaves behind its lingering clear shadows;
rising at dawn, I walk along the steps. As I tread before the steps, dust rises; this rising dust has no root. I wish to sweep it away, yet though I sweep, it does not cease.
Put down the broom and wander forth; the Tathāgata has spent his life amidst the dust.
People of the east and west each ask about the fruit of Buddhahood: what is this fruit of Buddhahood like? East and west, each remains attached to their own views.
In a casual moment, he topples the green lion throne; Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra are neither him nor me.
The Boatman, with a single stumble, takes up his oar and strikes out recklessly. Whether he hits the mark or misses it, it all results in a screen behind the wall.
The oar is broken and the boat overturned; the shimmering green waves overflow for three thousand fathoms.
As for the bell beneath the lion’s neck—by whom was it originally tied? To untie it, one must find the person who tied the bell; once untied, where would that person go?
The one who tied the bell knows how to untie it; the clay ox enters the sea, leaving no trace.
The moon rises from the west; the sun sets toward the west. Rising and falling are fundamentally like a ring—where can one find a hook or a lock?
Everyone claps their hands and laughs heartily. The permanent abode, the permanent abode—sitting together in a circle.

Because of bondage there is liberation; because of attachment there is detachment. Originally there is neither bondage nor attachment; why then seek liberation? Because of seeking liberation, one is bound once more.
Because of liberation, there is again attachment. If it were not liberation, from where would bondage and attachment arise? Feathers fly of their own accord; scales leap of their own accord.
Without knowing or perceiving, there is neither illness nor medicine.
Confucius, the Sage of Qun, left us his ultimate instruction: "To conquer oneself and restore the rites. He taught that one should first undergo hardship and only then attain the goal.

Who is it that exerts themselves in this practice? Now, the Way is like a great highway; whether far or near, all follow the same standard. Yet, with a single step taken upon it, why is it that some do not know how to return home?

This mind gives rise to subtle obstructions; with every step, it follows many divergent paths. If one claims that one’s strength is not yet sufficient, one must carefully avoid treading on dangerous ground by marking out the boundaries.

It is deeply fortunate that there is such earnest exhortation; this serves as a great aid for the worthy and the sages. When sincerity and clarity are non-dual with all things, whether sitting or standing, one is always upon the broad thoroughfare.

Great kindness is truly difficult to repay; what I have been moved by is none other than compassion. To accord with the wondrous principle of suchness, the consciousness-only (vijñaptimātra) is my true teacher.
There is no entry that does not lead to self-attainment; thus I have persevered until this very moment.
A Record of Questions and Answers:
Someone asked the Layman Tanyan, "The World-Honored One’s myriad words and ten thousand phrases were intended solely for people to see their nature.
Yet, as for this very word 'nature,' does it apply to Buddhas and sentient beings, to all things animate and inanimate, and even to asuras and non-humans?"

For all people alike, this is universally and equally possessed. Whether you ascend to heaven or descend to earth, from the rising of the sun to the setting of the moon, through light and darkness, the center and the periphery, from the past limit to future kalpas—at what place can it be escaped? At what moment can it be adhered to?
For all sentient beings, whatever is heard by the ear, seen by the eye, touched by the mind, or manifested through perception—all these various causes and conditions of empty form.
One is invisible; one is visible. Now tell me, what is this character "nature" (*xing*)? And how is it when seen? To adhere to it is to be bound;
to cast it off is to have nowhere to rest. Neither adhering nor casting off—whether it be adherence or casting off—it already becomes a mere conventional cliché.
You must point directly to its true falling place, so that the student may find their footing.
Proceed with firm resolve; go straight ahead. He replied: "This very nature is originally possessed by all people and is not lacking in any thing.

It is only because sentient beings have fallen into delusion that they obstruct their original state. Following conditions, they become inverted, recognizing forms and giving rise to arising and ceasing."
It is like a lost traveler who has forgotten his hometown and fallen into a pit of thorns; he cannot go forward, nor can he turn back.
Terrified and bewildered, he falls down only to stand up again, with no way out at all. As the Sutra says, "Like an infant who has lost its mother"—these words are most poignant.
The World-Honored One, giving rise to great compassion, points directly to the source of the mind, enabling people to...
Step by step one pursues [the Way], returning to the source and reverting to the root. Once awakened, it is just like recognizing the path and returning home, or as an infant seeing its mother;
the sorrowful longing and joyous celebration are beyond analogy, beyond description, beyond conception, and beyond comparison.
Wondrously luminous and perfectly enlightened, it is neither born nor extinguished, yet is not without birth and extinction. Because there is no birth, one realizes it.
Grasp non-arising. There is neither cause nor effect, yet it is not that there is no cause or effect. Because there is no fruit, one realizes and grasps the absence of fruit.
The student need only arouse great courage and march straight ahead. At times one is lucid; at times one is deafened; at times one is turbulent; at times one is tranquil.
Let arising and ceasing, and the cessation of arising, proceed as they will—arising after arising, ceasing after ceasing. Whether deluded or awakened, remain awakened.

Delusion. Delusion and delusion, awakening and awakening—there is no need at all for doubt or deliberation, nor for intellectual realization. When your practice reaches completion, it is like the ripening of a melon:
the stem falls away of its own accord. At that time, the original nature manifests spontaneously; fundamentally, it has always been just this way. The eye was originally the eye.
The ear is originally the ear; people are originally people; things are originally things; sentient beings are originally sentient beings; Buddhas are originally Buddhas.
All that is animate and inanimate, with form and without form, each returns to its original nature, together entering Prajñā-nirvāṇa, and collectively realizing Perfect Enlightenment.
Each recognizes Perfect Enlightenment; each possesses wondrous clarity; all possess wondrous clarity. This is regardless of—
The four characters "original face" (*benlai mianmu*) are like mere conceptual proliferation; even the three characters "what is it? (*jihe shi*) are superfluous words.

This is the foremost ultimate truth of the Tathāgata’s teaching, which is not something realized through the individual attainments of *pratyekabuddhas* or *śrāvakas*, nor can it be identified as the "plucking of the flower and the smile," regarded as a separate transmission outside the scriptures. Students should simply direct themselves toward this point.
Investigate thoroughly until you naturally receive a message; yet this is not a matter of seeking a message from within here.
He asked again: "The World-Honored One’s direct pointing to the source of the mind is indeed the primary ultimate truth. However, as for this word 'mind'—"
Yet it cannot be grasped, nor can it be pushed away; it does not stick, nor does it fall off.
It is originally vivid and distinct, yet it remains vast and boundless. Is it that the mind perceives because of objects? Or is it that objects are seen because of the mind?
If you say it is the mind perceiving because of objects, then when no object is present, this very state is naturally alert and awake—of which one cannot speak.
There is no mind. If you say that objects are seen by means of the mind, then at the moment when not a single thought has arisen, the myriad phenomena are already vividly arrayed;
one cannot say there is no object. Now, when you speak of "clarifying the mind," are you using the mind to clarify the mind? Or are you using objects to clarify the mind?
If you say you are using the mind to clarify the mind, then where is this "unclarified" state that you intend to take along with it? Take it!
Where is that which clarifies the other? If you say that one takes an object to clarify the mind, does this object enter from the outside or emerge from within?
Furthermore, as for this word "mind," it has nothing to cling to in either light or darkness;
how can one speak of it being already clarified or not yet clarified? As for this word "object," it cannot be applied to either the internal or the external; how can one recognize it?
From both within and without, the student vowed to clarify the mind. "But with what exactly does one clarify the mind? Please point this out for me once more. He replied:
"The character *xing* (nature) is that to which all things return; yet this character *xin* (mind) is possessed individually by every sentient being.
It is simply because ordinary people mistakenly take cognition and awareness to be the mind that they become bound by such cognition and awareness. Because of these bonds..."
These [notions] coalesce and thus become attachment; because of attachment, they become discrimination; because of discrimination, they become perversion.

The numinous faculty remains in a state of singular sameness, while sensory objects arise in chaotic profusion. Due to past karma and present conditions, one loses sight of the fundamental essence and fails to recognize this very mind.
Yet it is fundamentally empty, luminous, perfect, and wondrous. Even if the ten sages appear in the world, not a single atom of spiritual radiance is added;
even if the six realms manifest before one, not a single atom of the wondrous essence is diminished. It is profound and still, whether walking or standing.
In its state of profundity, it is like the sun and moon shining everywhere; in its state of stillness, it is like the silent operation of yin and yang. In its state of movement, it is like...
The wind turns and the clouds flow; the place of abiding is like water when ripples have settled.

Students should, for now, exert all their strength to investigate at the moment before a single thought has arisen and before a single object has been encountered. Let them investigate as they may, yet it does not emerge; ultimately, they must investigate with singular resolve.
When myriad thoughts arise in confusion and myriad phenomena are arrayed before you, exert all your strength to experience them. Even if he allows you to experience them, nothing will emerge;
simply experience with single-minded intensity. After a long, long time, there will suddenly come a moment of breakthrough, just like a single wheel of a precious mirror.
Possessing perfect radiance, it illuminates the mountains of karma and the oceans of desire all at once, leaving no trace of obstruction or defilement.
It penetrates the Brahma heavens and the pure lands with equal clarity, allowing not the slightest attachment to remain. This radiance does not arise from within.
Nor does it come from without. Whether it be the celestial Māra or a non-Buddhist (tīrthika), none can escape it. Whether it be a Bodhisattva of the Mahāyāna, they likewise cannot force their way in.
It is eternally quiescent and eternally luminous; eternally manifest and eternally hidden. This matter must be thoroughly investigated and realized, yet there is no need to investigate or realize it.
It must be diligently cultivated, yet one should not rely on fixed cultivation. As the Sūtra says: "When deluded, the teacher..."
To cross over: when awakening occurs, one crosses over oneself; the Buddha crosses over sentient beings, and sentient beings cross over the Buddha.
If a student can grasp this immediately upon hearing it, there will be no hindrance to becoming a Buddha on the spot, and they shall even become the teacher of all Buddhas.

If, however, you are unwilling to investigate and realize this, there is likewise no hindrance to sitting within the "black lacquer bucket" for a hundred or a thousand kalpas. It is only a pity that you pass it by right before your face, to no avail.
"I have indeed been wasting my time. I am truly one of those whom the World-Honored One described as pitiable. Either he rose up in trepidation and approached from another direction, saying:
"I have heard the general outline of the pointing-out instruction regarding the nature of mind; how could I dare not exert myself? Yet, there is still a small point that I do not understand."
This immediately results in obstruction. Even if one possesses some degree of understanding, there is no means by which to firmly establish faith and arouse courageous effort.

I venture to conclude my report on this. I dare ask: the words of Confucianism concern entering the world, while the words of Buddhism concern transcending the world. Confucianism brings the entire world, the state, and the family back to the body and mind;
Buddhism further subsumes the eyes, ears, nose, and tongue, gathering them all back into the nature and substance of the mind. Although both are without [attachment] to the world...
[The Master] said, "It is just that they all enter step by step in the same way. How, then, can it be called 'transcending the world'?
For example, at this very moment where you are sitting or standing, does your body enter space, or does your body exit space?
If you say the body enters space, we do not see any point of constriction at present; how then can you perceive an 'entering'? If you say the body exits..."
"In space, we currently do not perceive any boundaries. How, then, can one perceive 'coming out' and 'entering'?
Where, ultimately, do these two terms—'out' and 'in'—land? He replied: "It is simply because people fixate on one side that they are obstructed by both 'out' and 'in.
However, if one truly understands coming out and entering, then even that fixation on one side is itself precisely non-existent."
Regarding "entering and exiting": suppose a student intends to go out; this is because they are currently inside the house. Only when they say, "I am going out," does it become so.
If they had never entered the house at all, from where could there even be talk of going out? This point is extremely easy to see, yet how one speaks of "entering" is difficult to understand.
It is just like the myriad dharmas and myriad conditions in the world, each of which is presently manifest.
Worldly people have never yet emerged from that one thing. Since they have not yet emerged, how can it be said that they enter into that one thing?

Zen teachers and lecturers speak of entering and emerging from meditative concentration (*samādhi*), yet they do not say what concentration itself is; please tell me, what is this entering and emerging?

If a Confucian can explain these two words, "entering" and "emerging," he will be able to participate in the transformative power of the cosmos. If a Zen practitioner can explain these two words, "entering" and "emerging," [he likewise achieves mastery].
"Zi. One may then sit and realize Nirvana. Students should first investigate this point of entry. Close your eyes and bury your head; do not allow discursive thoughts to interfere.
Once you have understood the point of entry, the point of departure will naturally require no further explanation.
To speak of it again would be like riding a cow while searching for the cow—the foremost fool in the world. Nevertheless, there is no harm in speaking of it again. When speaking of it again:

This is merely seeing the moon and taking it for the moon; yet, right before one’s eyes is the Tathāgata in suchness (*tathatā*). Alternatively, he may remain silent, neither affirming nor denying, and ask again:

"In Confucian conduct, distinctions between the near and the distant, the close and the remote, are clear for every matter. In the Buddha-dharma, through skillful means and compassion, all things are equal.

If you say there is no need for such differentiation, then look at the world between heaven and earth: are the noble and the humble, the high and the low, the moving and the stationary, and the flying and the crawling not distinct?"
In the hidden depths [of reality], wisdom and folly, good and evil, right and wrong, hardness and softness—none of these are the same.
If there were such uniform equality, then one would have no need to implement rites, music, punishments, or governance; nor would it be necessary to plan out city walls, moats, or the grid of roads.

How could such a thing ever be put into practice? Even within the Buddha-dharma itself, there are the three miserable realms and the six paths of rebirth, as well as the five precepts and the four... [omitted].
Fruit. There are various kinds of conceptual distinctions; how can one speak of attaining equality?
If you say that Daoism and Confucianism are worldly dharmas while what the Buddha teaches is the supramundane dharma, then worldly dharmas necessarily cannot be equal.

If the Buddha-dharma can fundamentally be equal, then the Buddha is a Great Sage who is fully endowed with all dharmas, possessing wondrous clarity and perfect enlightenment, universally delivering all quarters. If one reaches this state...
If there were even a single place where one could not proceed, it would be a "lesser path" that may be admired for its appearance, yet would lead to stagnation when seeking to travel far.

How, then, could such a thing be called the World-Honored One? How could it be the Sage of ten thousand kalpas, to whom all universally turn in refuge? Now, we speak only of this Dharma-gate of equality.

"This practice leads to going; this practice does not lead to going. Furthermore, there must be a destination where this practice leads to going, as well as a destination where it does not lead to going.
This too must be analyzed and demonstrated so that students may find a point of entry. He replied:
"This principle is right before one's eyes, yet students have never realized it, and thus they produce all these idle words. Right now..."

There is no need to cite distant precedents; simply observe today. This day’s shadow of frost descends from the void, touching the grass and striking the trees, settling upon the water and floating over the mountains.
When this frost falls, it is uniformly impartial; one cannot say there is any further distinction.
Yet the pines and cypresses add luster, while the *piao* and *ai* grasses wither of their own accord; the old trunks remain upright, while the supple branches each turn withered.
The chrysanthemums are covered by it and vie for their splendor; the orchids are touched by it and contend to wither. The waves encounter it and become even clearer;
the peaks receive it and become even more precipitous. This is simply because this frost descends with uniform impartiality.
Therefore, it can respond to things as they come, so that all things each attain their natural state and each returns to its original source. If, however, when this frost descends...

One makes distinctions, treating each single object as a separate frostflake; this is indeed the great power of the Creator, who dispatches his minions to manage and transform things, yet it is still merely reaching one place while leaving another deficient.
Whether the deficient place is not [the truth], even that which reaches [the other] is not [the truth].
Extending this to the light of a mirror and the ripples on water, or the sun’s rays and the turning of the wind—all are like this. You must know this.
The two characters for "equality" apply thus to the Way of Heaven; they apply thus to royal governance; they apply thus to the Buddha-dharma; and they apply thus to the achievement of sagehood.

If a student can recognize this, it will not hinder their direct pointing to the wondrously luminous and perfectly enlightened state, nor will it hinder their straightforward acknowledgment of participating in the transformation and nurturing of all beings.
Pointed out at every turn, manifesting in every place, the *I Ching* says: "The sage has no mind."
And thus it is brought to completion. The Sūtra says: "All sages and worthies are distinguished by means of the unconditioned dharma (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*).
This is precisely the gloss for equality. Students must recognize this for themselves.

If one cannot comprehend this, the scholar merely clings to the two characters "sincerity" and "reverence," while the monk merely clings to the two characters "precepts" and "conduct. He then seeks out a patch of thatch to cover his head and dwells therein.

If you practice and investigate with diligence, you will surely attain a point of realization. Once you have attained such a point of realization, you will finally understand the efficacy of sincerity, reverence, and the observance of precepts.
Confucius’s *Analects* and Śākyamuni’s discourses on the sūtras both abide in this very place: truly abiding nowhere.
It is a single thread, non-dual, and fundamentally a great unity. Where there may appear to be slight differences, it is because of Confucius’s—
To speak of "nature" (xing), it ceases at the state of no sound and no smell; the Seal of the Tathāgata’s mind reaches the ultimate of no-nature and no-birth.
Within one circle and outside one circle—this is precisely where the names of the mundane and the supramundane originate.

If one does not pursue this to its ultimate conclusion but merely proceeds by treading on solid ground, and as soon as one has attained a mere fragmentary understanding, one speaks with false and狂妄 (mad) words, claiming that the rare and marvelous World-Honored One could not possibly be otherwise than this. Such a person disregards the fundamental tenets of the Buddha’s teaching;
it is like a fool speaking in a dream. Even regarding the Noble Path, how could there ever be a day of true realization? Shame, shame! Strive diligently!
Exert yourself!
This is "A Verse on the Buddha-Dharma by the Dharma-Teacher and Layman Chenghuai, Grand Secretary Zhang Tingyu," together with its preface.

I have heard that the Dharma-cloud provides universal shade, its numinous manifestations pervading the ten directions; the light of wisdom rises radiantly, its gracious brilliance shining across the eight extremities.

Grasping the precious mirror of the Benevolent King, the sun and moon shine with renewed splendor; turning the golden wheel of the Brahma-Emperor, thunder and lightning strike with simultaneous sharpness.
Only in this profound stillness does he abide eternally; the Great Hero encompasses the source of chaos, and in his silent non-arising, he is Perfect Enlightenment.
Transcending the realm of the ethereal mist, he is thus able to cause the ninety-six paths to be recorded within the single gate of Bodhi;
the thirty-three heavens are threaded through the four peaks of Mount Sumeru. Throughout all that is above and below heaven, the essence of universal illumination is ever-perfect;
throughout the trichiliocosm, the unconditioned compassion is widely extended. Truly, it is believed that the waters of the ocean may be measured, but empty space cannot be measured. Empty...
The void can be measured. But the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s maturation of sentient beings and their transformations according to conditions cannot be measured.

The stages and positions of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s cultivation have divisions that can be measured. Yet the true suchness (*tathatā*) of all Buddhas, the ocean of nature, is boundless and centerless;
it has no interior and no exterior—it cannot be measured. How sublime! How great! Even the mouth of Zou Yan could not [exhaust its description].
Tán Chānghài’s skills could not calculate its measure; the music of the Celestial Court could not reproduce its sound; even Yíyá’s palate could not discern its flavor.

Thus, though one might wish to praise it, by what means could one do so? Examining the ancient past, the meaning of the Tripiṭaka had not yet been revealed, and the workings of the Two Vehicles remained beyond our gaze.
Dull-witted sentient beings merely lived on, eating and breathing together with the rest of the world.

They rush about, receiving karma according to conditions; humans and devas follow divergent paths, while birth and death swirl in chaotic motion. Rising and falling, sinking and floating, they manifest in a thousand forms and ten thousand states.
The Tathāgata, riding upon his original vow to deliver beings, manifests the power of compassion to respond through transformation.

He restrains the six masters and rectifies the four inversions; he dispels the eight heterodoxies and returns all to the single flavor. He breaks the horns of worldly wisdom and silences the mouths of those with divergent views, guiding [all beings].

With the deluded mind seeking the jewel, he clears the cataracts obscuring the vision of the Great Image; holding the precious torch, he illuminates the path of awakening, and launching the Dharma-ship, he ferries those lost at the ford.
Administering medicine according to the ailment, he acts as the unsurpassed King of Physicians; blending milk with butter, he serves as the compassionate mother of all living beings.
Such is the supreme benevolence of this Dharma King. Through the patience of phenomena and the patience of wisdom, he leads others through what is difficult to endure.
All are empty. Where there is no mind, that is the mind itself. It universally encompasses all minds: the coral of the oceans and rivers stirs up waves with a single snap of the fingers;
the lapis lazuli of the sun and moon binds day and night with two hanging hands. A hundred thousand wondrous verses arise from between the wings of birds;
the twelve musical tones emerge from beyond the surface of ivory. When expounding Nirvana, wisdom transcends [all bounds].
In the three realms, when Prajñā was preached, the heavens rained down the four flowers; with a single roar of the lion, the heretics were shattered;

and with the brief sounding of the Dharma drum, the celestial Māras bowed their heads. This is the divine power of the Dharma King. Like a high ladder ascending straight up, he encompasses the great void;
like drawing a needle and casting it aside, he distinguishes the minute particulars. The verses that string the flowers possess a radiance like that upon the water.
The sound of the verses spoken by the Auspicious Lotus is as clear as the bright moon among the stars; it is neither with form nor without form.
Neither ordinary beings nor sages can fathom its subtle mysteries. Emptiness is form, and form is emptiness; few, whether wise or foolish, penetrate its essential subtlety.

It encompasses the vast and far-reaching, its profound principles extending to the distant depths. Within the eighty-four thousand treasuries [of the Dharma], it contains the two truths and the ten stages.
