The discourses on the Jeta Grove and the Deer Park, the teachings from the Dragon Palace in the ocean depths, the characters inscribed upon jade tablets and golden scrolls, and the words spoken during the seven locations and nine assemblies—
all these were nothing other than the manifestation of the wondrous Way throughout the heavens and the human realm, fanning the primordial wind across past and present, ancient and modern.
They open up the causes and effects spanning a thousand and ten hundred kalpas, and reveal the Dharma-nature of every phenomenon within the minds of billions.
Truly, he is the field of merit for the world; he is the ultimate refuge for all living beings. Those who hear him find the nectar of immortality entering their crowns;

those who awaken find the water of wisdom drenching their hearts. Among all classes of sentient beings who possess breath, and the multitudes of crawling and flying creatures, there are none who do not join their palms within their chests, longing to hear the sound of the Ten Virtues.
Even from within their shells, they raise their voices, nodding from afar at the teachings of the Four Heavenly Kings. Golden...
The wondrous meaning of his speech eclipses the two luminaries as it hangs long in the sky; the subtle words of his jade-axled scrolls penetrate the Three Powers without interruption.

This is the edification of the Dharma King. He takes the sublime Dharma as the carriage, meditative concentration as the axle-tree, patience as the hub, the observance of precepts as the linchpin, courageous diligence as the spokes, and the Diamond Prajñāpāramitā as the wheels.
It begins with carrying oneself and culminates in carrying others, so that those who seek the Way may recognize the path and those lost in their dwellings may know their home.
The wisdom-gem and the Dharma-mirror can be held by every person; the four patiences and five sciences hold hope for every household.
How could the merit of this be measured by the waters of the ocean or the sands of the Ganges? As for the morning bells and evening drums, they call back those in the dream-like realm—

O you who are stubborn and ignorant! The bright moon over the clear pool washes away the accumulated dust from the dusty breast. At the six periods of the day, one should offer prayers with the constant thought that the king’s land and waters are one's own.
In the diligent cultivation of the three karmas, one must always keep in mind the profound kindness of the sovereign and father.

This, then, is the cooling balm for the fever of passion; it is the resonant bell of loyalty and filial piety. Indeed, the moon has no intention to reject the water, yet the water possesses [the capacity to reflect]— [Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the available portion.]
The nature of the moon is like water that has lost its inherent clarity; if the water lacks this quality, the moon has no way to manifest itself.

One must necessarily attain *dhyāna* early on and long rely upon the waters of meditative concentration (*samādhi*). When the flowers of the mind are unstained, one expands the compassionate heart of supreme goodness, and the excellent fruits are vied for and grasped.
By examining the Middle Vehicle with the eye of wisdom, all accumulated stagnations will be swept away, like autumn winds falling leaves, and the profusion of doubts will vanish.
All [doubts] are now resolved, like spring sun melting the ice. This rough account of the supreme cause connects us to this initial stage (*ādikṣema*).
As for what lies beyond, it cannot be expressed through words. The verse says:
Lush and dense are the clouds of compassion, covering the ten directions; profound is the flavor of sweet nectar, spreading the light of lapis lazuli.

The lamp of wisdom shines eternally, and the sun of knowledge ever presides. This sun and this lamp are the heart of ten thousand ages; yet this mind is no-mind, and even these names are but provisional designations.
Manifesting the markless mark, extensively bringing forth the birthless birth; across the ten stages and nine heavens, he shatters the obscurity and illuminates the darkness.

With the light of moon after moon and the shores of sea after sea, he gallops eastward like an elephant or horse; his golden body, sixteen feet tall, supports the earth and upholds the heavens. He is the vessel for the sutras and the hub of the Dharma.
The transmission of the robe was but a single flower; the preaching of the Dharma was without words. It resounded with thunderous clarity, restoring hearing to the deaf and sight to the blind.

As for the succession of the patriarchs and the lineage of the school—whether it be skin, marrow, flesh, or bone—what truly exists therein? Even the Buddha is no Buddha. When the morning star leaked its light, the original mind was directly revealed.
Such is the natural law. Regarding the Great Intent of the West:
it is truly said that Dharma came from the Western Heaven to China solely to secretly transmit the Mind-Seal (cittamudrā) to seal one’s own original mind.
The Dharma-Seal Method: One seals the mind with the Dharma. Since the mind is thus, the Dharma is likewise thus. Therefore, it is said that not a single dharma can be apprehended;
this is merely to instruct one in realizing and grasping the original mind. At the moment of realization, there is no mark of realization and no mind that realizes.
When the mind and realization are fused as two, this is what is called True Suchness (Tathatā). Now, as for True Suchness, it is quiescent yet not non-existent.
Moving yet not existent; acting yet not shifting; abiding yet not stationary. Myriad forms manifest together, yet they cannot be colored by blue, yellow, black, or white.

A multitude of sounds resonate in concert, yet they cannot be characterized as clear, turbid, short, or long. Its function pervades the *sāhasra-lokadhātu* without leaving even a trace of subtle shadow;
its essence encompasses the great trichiliocosm without being attached to a single thread. From antiquity to the present, eighty thousand...
Throughout kalpas, one should never depart from mindfulness. Others see them as "others," and I see them as "I. The Buddhas of the three thousandfold world-system are all present before me.

The eight-sided transformation city is nothing other than the pure Dharmakāya; the thousand-layered lotus throne is entirely the majestic and wondrous marks. The four modes of birth and the six realms of existence—
Together we traverse the precious raft upon the waters of wisdom; from the Ten Stages to the Five Heavens, all become walls and ceilings of crystal.

There is not a single dharma that is inherently existent, nor a single dharma that is inherently non-existent. There is not a single dharma lacking, nor a single dharma left over. Center and periphery are obliterated;

before and after are severed; the false and the true are cut off; defilement and purity are made one. Subject and object are forgotten; form and emptiness are equalized. Identity and difference are sealed; sages and ordinary beings are made equal.
The taste of a single drop of water is no different from that of the eight great oceans; the substance of a single hair’s breadth of gold is no distinct from the entire ore.
A single pore can contain the vast void; a single tip of a hair can cover the great earth. Thus, essence is form, and form is essence;
principle is phenomena, and phenomena are principle; emptiness is existence, and existence is emptiness. This is the Dharma.

These are dust motes; indeed, these dust motes are the Dharma. Presently, heaven covers above and earth bears below; the sun rises in the east and the moon sets in the west; day is bright and night is dark; mountains stand firm and rivers flow.
There is not a single thread or a single hair that does not share in this hiddenness and manifestation.

Throughout the eighty thousand kalpas of the past and the eighty thousand kalpas of the future, there is not a single mote of dust or a single kṣetra that does not arise and perish together with it. When a person truly reaches this state, it is True Suchness (Tathatā).
The realm is like a mirror reflecting a mirror, like space merging with space, like water poured into water, like the moon encompassing the moon.
Like a mani jewel containing all colors within it, or a pure lapis lazuli vase where light and object are both forgotten: when withdrawn, they are withdrawn together;
when manifested, they are manifested together. There is no room for contrivance, nor need for arrangement; naturally there is neither action nor cessation, neither following nor extinction.

Furthermore, there is no acting in acting, no ceasing in ceasing, no relying in relying, and no extinction in extinction. Whether rolling up or unfolding, taking or giving, one distinguishes according to one's will;
regarding birth and death, coming and going, one possesses mastery over all phenomena. Thus, even the two characters "True Suchness" (Tathatā) are ultimately unobtainable.
How sublime is this principle! It is difficult to encounter and rarely heard; it is known only through realization, not through mere intellectual awakening.
To attempt to fathom it is to have already traveled a long distance before the words are even spoken; to intend to seek it with focused effort is as futile as marking the boat to find a lost sword.
In the past, at night on Mount Snow, [Śākyamuni] beheld the morning star—he beheld this. Kāśyapa broke into a smile—he smiled at this. At Shaoshi, he sat facing a wall for nine years—he faced this.
At midnight, the Sixth Patriarch transmitted the robe—he transmitted this. And so it was with all the great masters of antiquity.
Whenever there is a single accord or a single realization, a single blow or a single shout, it is none other than acceding to this, realizing this, striking this, or shouting this.

To seek elsewhere is to shift one's steps and change one's form; yet it is not said that [the truth] is not right here. Set aside a thousand heads and ten thousand threads, and you will know that, in the end, there is nothing much to it.
Blow the unperforated flute and listen to the Dharma drum in the sky—even until you behold...
There is nothing seen; there is nothing to laugh at, yet one laughs. There is no face, yet there is a face. There is nothing transmitted, yet it is transmitted.

Furthermore, there is nothing realized through accord, yet there is realization. There is nothing struck with the staff, yet the staff is wielded. There is nothing shouted with the roar, yet the roar is uttered.

Raising the fist and brandishing the whisk is merely a puppet appearing on stage. To "tip two and toss three" is to speak of another's wealth and treasures. How profound! As the World-Honored One said: "It is like..."
A person in a dream: while dreaming, it is not non-existent; yet upon waking, nothing at all can be found.
Thus, if there is still even a single thread of impurity remaining, one is still within the dream. Only when one reaches the state where nothing at all can be found is this called "great awakening.
Now, how could this state of finding nothing at all be reached through speech, thought, or deliberation? Please express this in verse: I have one...
The Perfect Buddha fills all of space. Though one wishes to speak of his original formlessness, he has no shape; though one wishes to paint him, he has no color from the start.

When he comes, there is the tide of faith; when he abides, there is the moon without trace. His wondrous flavor is difficult to express in words; if you wish to ask about it, you must ask with your tongue. Furthermore, a verse says:
The Tathāgata returns to suchness; coming and returning are suchness itself. This is called True Suchness (Tathatā). What is the nature of this settled True Suchness?

Singing the song of awakening, one thoroughly sweeps away the illusory and deluded body of the sensory faculties. First, one must recognize the original mind; the adornment of precious marks is all but form.
Phenomena. To see the beginning of reality without signs or mind, one holds the mind to observe the mind, yet this creates a confusion of subject and object.

"The very mind is Buddha" merely adds a name; "neither mind nor Buddha"—how could it be otherwise? Within this, the wondrous meaning is difficult to express in words. The vast, numinous hall is but a square inch;
it is profoundly still, neither having existence nor non-existence. Still, it does not stagnate; moving, it does not overflow. Transformation is not change.
Ah! Stillness is not barren. Who planted the tree of the mind to blossom with flowers of emptiness? Who released the fragrance of the heart to emit the scent of dust?
Who bestowed the eight waters to moisten the parched sprouts? Who grasped the two orbs to open the eyes of the ordinary?

A single point of numinous light is without obstruction; within it, the ten directions are universally contained. Within each and every realm, radiance is emitted; one Buddha and a thousand Buddhas are all present now.
Within the great void, the fragrance of the Dharma-rain falls; how many have tasted even a single drop of the finest cream?

Having tasted it, one finds that the flavor of the cream is flavorless—drinking water in summer and drinking broth in winter. In the Hall of Wondrous Victory, the Palace of the Muni, how many have ever beheld the face of the Tathāgata?
With the incense of precepts as a hand-held taper, I pay homage at Mount Ling; yet the mountain gates have long been closed, their two leaves shut fast.

"Mí, mí, mí—lost in delusion, one does not awaken. With a single roar, the lion thunders through the void; the sun shines upon Tongguan, opening it on all four sides. Why need one ask the way to the great road of Chang'an?
"Gòu, gòu, gòu—defiled and impure, though one were to draw from the Western River to wash them, they could never be cleansed. Lofty, it rises above the water.
The wondrous lotus flower, born from the mire, is by nature unstained. Mad, mad, mad—madness that knows no bounds. A fierce wind blows through, yet it is drenched in cold ice.
The moon enters the six windows; a fragment of cloud floats idly. Why need the monkey and the horse be restrained by ropes? Devious, devious, devious—deviousness that is not upright.
Chasing away the petty demons, one fears the sword may be blunt. The hundred-fold tempering of the diamond makes even a finger-bend soft. Hundred... [fold]... [temperings].
The myriad demonic armies all beg for their lives; the deluded awaken, the defiled are purified, the frantic find composure, and the heterodox become upright.
In an instant they are ordinary beings, in an instant they are sages. Are the sage and the ordinary two different persons? A single bright pearl is the seal upon the heart.

In the three months of spring, the phenomena of nature are richly flourishing; ten thousand trees of peach blossoms, ten thousand trees of flowers. How is it that they fill everywhere without deficiency?
Please investigate the root and sprout from within this very place. When the sun has risen three poles high, the myriad phenomena stand in dense array;
throughout the great trichiliocosm, there is universal radiance. Why is it that in a single opening, all becomes white? It pierces the darkness, penetrates the obscure, and is fundamentally pure.

The waters of the blue river flow vast and boundless; as level as a palm, they are without peaks or ridges. How can one completely obliterate all traces of high and low? Cast wide your gaze and let it be.
The contemplation of equality: In the dream of a brahmin, many are brahmins; in a single kṣaṇa, a dream contains the events of a thousand years. How can a thousand kalpas be but a single kṣaṇa?

One must understand the meaning of this sublime truth’s harmonious integration. With a clear, cool smile, the heavens and earth are empty. Hearing the sound, devas and nāgas praise and circumambulate.
Who is it that lets out a long啸 (shào) echoing through the mountain valleys? It is just like a cold insect chirping within a wall. Vast!
Ling raises his hand to cleave Mount Hua; how trivial—truly the strength of one who binds a chicken! I have heard that the Buddha’s power is vast and boundless;

with a single finger, he can rescue sentient beings drowning in the depths. A boat is not needed to cross; a staff is not needed to stand firm. The sea has no shore, yet he treads upon it with a single sandal.
All is dark and vast, yet all is bright and clear. Two and five are originally ten. Smash the beads of the abacus, and every bead returns to its source.
One by one. Why need one don the robe at midnight? Why wait nine years before facing the wall? Taking refuge, taking refuge again, I prostrate before the Buddha present before me.
Auspicious winds and sweet dew pervade the ten directions; may the blessings of this single-minded merit bring eternal peace to billions of beings.

Spontaneous Verses, Twenty Poems A single orb of perfect light is fundamentally empty space; The myriad phenomena of the universe meet one another face-to-face. The moon’s reflection seals the pool, and the pool seals the moon;
If you wish to distinguish guest from host, where can you turn?
The twin orbs revolve before one’s eyes; as summer passes and winter comes, which shall be first or last?
Having realized the principle of neither arising nor ceasing, the great cypress and the morning hibiscus are exactly equal in their years.

The hawks fly and the fish leap, each rising and sinking; the mountains are naturally verdant and the waters naturally deep. If you wish to recognize the meaning of the lofty mountains and flowing water, look at the bright moon that has come down to imprint its reflection upon the heart of heaven.
Seeking the true transmission along the path of conceptual thought is to wander in vain for thousands of miles in straw sandals.
To recognize that the ordinary mind is the Way is simply to eat when hungry and sleep when tired.
Originally there is neither form nor name; as soon as one engages in conceptualization, obscurations arise. Dust covers the mirror’s light and clouds veil the moon;
yet that which is most indistinct is the very essence of clarity.
Neither empty nor form, neither light nor darkness; Without self, without person, without past or present. One can only sigh that the people of this world mostly do not understand;
A single finger in the palm is the true connoisseur.
Seeking the Buddha, there is originally no place to find him; transmitting the mind, where else could it possibly reside?
It is better to forget both the real and the false, and laugh as one watches busy people hurrying in their dreams.

The Buddha originally has no mind; he only possesses the intent. What is this intent that came from the West? Do not say that people here find it difficult to understand; even the pillar does not know it.
To grasp at it remains untrue; do not weary your spirit in vain over words and phrases.
Alas, that single tree of cypress before the courtyard has deceived so many people throughout all time.
The seven characters of Yongjia point the way for those lost in delusion. When both mind and dharmas are forgotten, the nature is itself the truth.
Only then does one believe that the Tathāgata’s Great Perfect Enlightenment is still but an ordinary person within the universe.
Neither sitting upon a meditation cushion nor facing a wall; hearing sounds and seeing forms are all ordinary.
Since I have realized the flavor of the *amṛta*, the scorching winds of the sixth month have cooled my very bones.
A single lamp brightens a dark valley for many years; both light and darkness are produced from the realm of vision. How does this compare to after a practitioner has drunk their fill and slept:
a single red sun rising in the third watch?

The earth is vast and the sky is open; the square inch of the heart is wide. I laugh at those who grind like ants or fish with a rod. With a single staff, I have happened to ascend the peak of Mount Penglai;
millions of mountain ranges are seen beneath my feet.
Fearing clamor and seeking stillness—both are but entanglements. Whether it be Zang or Gu, they have both lost their sheep.
When not a single thing dwells within the mind, lotus flowers burst forth with rain, filling the pond with fragrance.
Who at the gate stops the traveler’s carriage? It is simply that the host wishes to save on household expenses. Let the spring breeze and butterflies revel as they please;
can they truly fly upon the snow-covered plum blossoms?
Performing ascetic practices morning and evening beside the lotus pedestal, you vainly conjecture with your holy vision and ordinary mind. The great earth, mountains, and rivers are all Buddha;
do not bother to move the pure water jar over here.
The pearl radiance of Hepu reflects the full moon; travelers on the shore mistakenly linger there.
Upon returning, recognize the treasure within your own clothes—what need is there to seek out the boat that sailed downstream?
Do not seek the profound meaning beyond words; do not seek the true exposition within phrases. Cast aside texts and discard intellectual knowledge;
blow the unperforated flute upon the autumn river.
When the mind is pure, one constantly perceives wondrous fragrances; what need is there for the laborious contemplation of the nose? All manner of dharmic characteristics return to non-existence;
let heavenly flowers freely form the site of the Way.
When inspiration strikes after reciting the Lotus Sutra, I lean against the railing and chant aloud the poems of ancient worthies: The moonlight falls into my breast from the wutong trees;
The breeze comes upon my face from the willows.
Twelve *Xiāngjiāngyuè* Verses:
Just as one perceives the biting cold of winter winds, one immediately beholds the fragrance and splendor of spring colors. Within this, is the message "yes" or "no"?
This principle is not difficult to comprehend. It is all said that the hawk soars and the fish leap; what prevents the hawk from leaping and the fish from soaring? Whether high or low...
Looking up and looking down, one aligns with the celestial mechanism; this is precisely what is meant by being "vibrant and lively.

Yet, without having removed the soiled garments from one's body, one is too lazy to polish the dusty mirror held in one’s breast. Unaware that one’s own obstructions are manifold, one instead claims the Buddha-dharma to be too lofty and grand.
To awaken is as easy as picking up mustard seeds; to remain deluded is as difficult as trying to fill a river. Suddenly—
Upon waking from the dream, I sing aloud: the mind and the Buddha are originally not two;
succession is fundamentally without birth or extinction. How could there be a beginning or an end in this cycle? Behold spring, summer, autumn, and winter;
their coming and going are like one footstep following another. Others see them as empty or as form, but I say they are neither different nor the same—this is the natural state.
Emptiness and form dwell within it; let the wind and banner move as they will.
Sailing upon the sea, riding the wind and breaking through the waves, one gazes into the vast expanse where neither shore nor limit is seen.

Suddenly encountering the precious raft that crosses the ford of delusion, there is no need to ask again about the other shore. Originally, there is neither true nor illusory; cease speaking of "neither illusory nor true. All phenomena...
Once [the mind] has ceased, what cause remains? A single point of numinous light is without inherent nature.

The Buddha’s intent is neither hidden nor revealed; the Buddha’s words are neither shallow nor deep. If one seeks the true mind through words and phrases, it is like a painted cake used to satisfy hunger.
Once the fish and the rabbit are caught, the trap and the snare are of no further use—why seek them again? Practice self-investigation.
Self-awakened and self-illuminated, I briefly take the scriptural texts as my seal of verification.

Who says the mind is subtle and elusive? At every moment it pervades heaven and earth. When the single moon reflects in ten thousand streams, one finally recognizes that the myriad differences share a single root.
In awakening to the Way, who distinguishes between sudden and gradual? In achieving success, does it depend on mere preservation of the mind? Heaven is long...

Since the beginningless kalpas, a single segment of the mind’s radiance has been obstructed by the habitual tendencies of delusion, such that one is not self-aware.

This is not limited to the four elements and six sense organs alone. Even when reading books, there is the obstruction of the book; when investigating principles, there is the obstruction of principle; and when practicing..."

Virtue is an obstacle; practicing virtue is an obstacle. Observing precepts and cultivating meditative concentration are obstacles to precepts and concentration. Studying Chan and learning the Buddha-way are obstacles to Chan and the Buddha-way.
Whatever one does is merely an affair of the mind’s shadows. If one does not reach the state of pure nakedness, the life-root will ultimately never be severed.
Thus, the state of pure nakedness is the shore. All various skillful means are intended to enable one to reach it.

This pure, bare ground is entirely a raft. Nevertheless, once delusion and ignorance are suddenly extinguished and the mind is opened and revealed, there is no obstruction regarding books when reading;
no obstruction regarding principle when investigating it; no obstruction regarding goodness when practicing it;
no obstruction regarding the observance of precepts or the cultivation of concentration; and no obstruction regarding the practice of Chan or the study of the Buddha.

There is no obstruction. Even regarding the six sense organs, the six sense objects, and the six consciousnesses, there is likewise no obstruction of the six sense organs, the six sense objects, or the six consciousnesses.
Every single thing is the Way; each and every one is fully manifest. All is Bodhi; all becomes nectar. Vertically, it exhausts the three periods of time;
horizontally, it spans the ten directions. There is not a single kṣaṇa that is not the Buddha-sun; there is not a single hair’s breadth that is not the Dharma-body. At the heels...
To point to the ground is for the shore to be right here. That which was previously called "pure naked ground"—is that not also a raft?

Nevertheless, to read books, exhaustively investigate principles, practice goodness, maintain the precepts, cultivate meditative concentration, engage in Chan, and study the Buddha—all of these are but flowers in the sky.

This is precisely like a dream or an illusion; it is utterly unattainable. Within this state of utter unattainability, thus and so, without interval or interruption, in pure, true suchness, one finally finds rest in the place where there is no resting.

Thus, as for "planting one's heels firmly on the ground," one must indeed never, at any moment, depart from the raft. The great ocean is originally the shore; furthermore, there is no [shore apart from it].

The terms "this shore" and "the other shore" may be spoken of; yet the shore is the pure *dharmakāya*, the raft is the hundreds of thousands of millions of *nirmāṇakāyas*, and boarding the raft to reach the shore is the perfect *saṃbhogakāya*. These three are one, and even as one they do not stand.
How then can one speak of three? Now, as I and you face each other in this room—am I the shore, or the raft? Are you the traveler, or am I? It is simply a guest.
They looked at one another and laughed, and thus recorded these words as a memorial.

When someone asked about "existence" during a tea discussion, he said, "Emptiness. When asked about "emptiness," he said, "Existence. As some still did not understand, he spoke this verse: Emptiness leans upon existence.
It is established by relying on emptiness to give it a name. All phenomena are entirely empty; even empty space is truly a form of existence.
The emptiness within a single pore dwells amidst all that exists. All such things that appear to be real possess the nature of emptiness within themselves.

Since "existence" cannot be apprehended, "emptiness" is likewise but a provisional designation. If one dwells upon the characteristics of emptiness and existence, how can one speak of *nirvāṇa*? This is what you have now asked.
Regarding "I" and "you," what names can there be for them? To call them "empty" is already untenable; to call them "existent" is surely not so either.

If there were no such things as "you" and "I," where could questions and answers be established? Within this absence of both, whether it be emptiness or existence—if emptiness and existence are as one, we forcibly name this "non-duality."
Zen Master Wenjue Xuehong of Juesheng Temple ascended the hall and said:
"Regarding the two words 'Buddha-dharma,' it is not that only the Buddha possesses this dharma, nor is it that sentient beings lack this dharma."

This is called the Buddha-dharma. "Buddha" has the meaning of awakening; awakening is itself the Dharma. Awakening is established in contrast to delusion; if there were no delusion, what would there be to awaken? What constitutes delusion?
It is to perceive mountains, rivers, and the great earth, and to identify them as being mountains, rivers, and the great earth, within the very acts of seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing.
To immediately establish seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing is itself delusion. What is awakening?

To see the mountains, rivers, and the great earth, and to call them "mountains, rivers, and the great earth," while within seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing, causing that seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing to function—this is awakening.

Since both are equally seeing the mountains, rivers, and the great earth, and both are equally seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing, why is there delusion and why is there awakening? *Psh!* Mountains, rivers, and the great earth!
Regarding seeing, hearing, perceiving, and knowing—when have I ever told you that there is delusion or awakening?
In short, whether speaking of awakening or delusion, or of the real or the false, all are merely provisional names used to guide sentient beings.

The nature inherently possessed by us is primordially perfected, primordially complete, and primordially free from arising and ceasing. It is neither empty nor existent; it is neither real nor false. It is not...
Delusion is not awakening; it is simply that sentient beings take what is without grasping to be grasping, and where there is no obstruction, they create obstructions.

They falsely perceive emptiness as having existence and existence as having existence; they perceive the real as the delusory, and delusion as awakening. If one can, in a single thought-moment, turn the light back upon itself, then all phenomena will naturally be fully understood.
Do you wish to know the principle of this understanding? Before the donkey’s business is finished, the horse’s business has already arrived.
Ascending the hall, [the Master] said: "One person has eyes but cannot see; has ears but cannot hear; has a tongue but cannot speak;
has a mind but cannot discern. Another person has no eyes yet can see; has no ears yet can hear; has no tongue yet can speak; has no mind yet can discern.
When these two people meet, which one is in front and which one is behind? He then added: "Now tell me, as for these two people—"
"Why is it that you have attained such a state?

[The Master] ascended the hall and said: "As for all verbal expressions, they are entirely devoid of real meaning. I, this mountain monk, dare to say that whatever is expressed in words is none other than real meaning.
Do you all recognize this principle? If you do recognize it, then even the dust motes speak and the world-systems speak, burning with brilliance."
However, it is said that while there is no interruption, there is only verbal expression and no non-real meaning.

If consciousness does not apprehend, then neither objects nor lands are spoken of; there is no burning discourse and no interruption, yet there is only verbal expression, entirely devoid of real meaning.
Ascending the hall, [the Master] said: "I have traveled all over the South on my pilgrimage, yet with the tip of my staff, I have never once struck anyone who understands the Buddha-dharma.
This talk of mine is very much like being unaware that the tip of one's own staff is too short. I, too, have come from the South;
I dare not so much as move the tip of my staff against a single person. Why? Because where there is no wound, do not inflict injury."
Thus it was. For an entire summer, he remained here, spending his days with everyone else carrying stones and hauling earth, tearing down the east to repair the west.
He insisted that the mountain gate must face south; he decreed that the pillar must touch the ground.

Whether the cauldrons were large or small, whether the handles of the ladles were short or long, where there were no rules he established them, and where there was no distinction between inner and outer, he demarcated the interior and exterior. The Hall...
Those within must know what is outside the hall, yet they must not leave the hall;
those outside must know what is within the hall, yet they must not leave their place outside. Tell me, among you, is this movement or is it stillness?
Leaning on his staff, he said: "For now, let us rejoice in peace."
Addressing the assembly: The people of Pūrvavideha in the east eat their meals; the people of Aparagoyānī in the west suffer from abdominal distension;

the people of Jambudvīpa in the south travel on foot; the people of Uttarakuru in the north have aching feet. These are the constant affairs that naturally belong to them. Why is it that the eye can see objects?
There are things that can be seen and things that cannot be seen. The ear can hear sounds; there are things that can be heard and things that cannot be reached by hearing.
The bottom. There is a bottom that hearing cannot reach. Is it because the nature of seeing and hearing is not all-pervasive? Or is it because the objects of seeing and hearing are obstructed?
It is entirely due to being deluded regarding what is before one's eyes, and consequently losing sight of what lies behind.

In principle, there is nothing that is not harmoniously integrated; yet in practice, one cannot avoid becoming stuck. Though one may claim that principle and phenomena are one and the same, in the end, phenomena and principle remain two separate pieces.
Śākyamuni himself was unable to manage it; he could only say: "The Dharma abides in its place; the characteristics of the world are eternally present.
One must know that this "place" (dharmatā) is where delusion resides and where awakening resides. It is from this that ignorance and affliction arise;
it is from this that false thoughts and attachments arise. One's entire being is within this very place; yet one seeks further outward. Entirely...
The body originally does not reside within its own position, yet one seeks it inwardly. From the left it is obstructed by it; from the right it is obstructed by it.
The mouth can eat food, and the hands can grasp and hold, yet they cannot function interchangeably: fire cannot be used as water, nor water as fire, for such borrowing is impossible.
Therefore, those who study the Way value knowing that there is a path for emergence everywhere. This is the nature of things.

Within all phenomena lies the pivot for turning the body. If one can turn and attain the body within the station of a single dharma, one will then be able to emerge from the body within the stations of all dharmas.
Spontaneously, the east will not obstruct the west, and the south will not obstruct the north. One may shift that to become this, or shift this to become that.

Only then will one enter the state of a Buddha without obstruction, enter the state of a Mara without obstruction, enter the state of an ordinary person without obstruction, and enter the state of a sage without obstruction.
Obstruction. Entering emptiness is unobstructed; entering existence is unobstructed; entering birth is unobstructed; entering cessation is unobstructed.

If one considers that fundamentally there are no Buddhas, demons, ordinary beings, or sages, and fundamentally there is no emptiness, birth, or cessation, and takes this to be "unobstructed," I dare say they have understood that all dharmas abide in their own positions;
yet they have not yet realized that the characteristics of the world are eternally abiding.
Addressing the assembly: It cannot be known by wisdom, yet it can be known by wisdom; it cannot be cognized by consciousness, yet it can be cognized by consciousness.

Fundamentally, there are no names or marks, yet there are names and marks; fundamentally, there is no speech, yet there is speech; fundamentally, there is no differentiation, yet there is differentiation;
fundamentally, there is no transition or change, yet there is transition and change. Because there is transition and change, one knows that which is without [transition and change].
Because of transformation and change, one knows there is no differentiation; because of the existence of speech, one knows there is no speech;

because of the existence of names and signs, one knows there are no names and signs; because of the existence of that which can be cognized by cognition, one knows there is no cognition that can cognize it;

because of the existence of that which can be known by wisdom, one knows there is no wisdom that can know it. Therefore, if even a single dharma were added, it would not be this very dharma; if even a single dharma were lacking, it would not be [this very dharma].
This very Dharma is like the saying: "Under heaven, there are no lands that are not the King’s;
along the shores of all the earth, there are no subjects who are not the King’s. Whether fertile or barren, it is all soil; whether great or small, they are all subjects.
Even so, does the King possess any active agency? Have you not heard it said: "It is manifest without appearing; it transforms without moving"?
"Accomplished without action—this must surely be the Way of the Sage! Suppose it were said that this mountain monk does not understand direct pointing and merely recites chapters and verses;
even so, I would consider myself fortunate."
Addressing the assembly: Bodhidharma came from the West to point directly to the human mind, so that one might see one's nature and become a Buddha.
You must know that there is no other method of pointing; it simply requires forgetting emotions and extinguishing views. Then, naturally, you will see your nature and clarify your mind.

If you do not clarify the mind, you will not know that the mind is fundamentally empty. If you do not see your nature, you will not recognize that nature is fundamentally all-pervasive. Because it is fundamentally empty, attachment is completely eliminated.
Because it is fundamentally thus, there is perfect interfusion and non-obstruction. Why? Because all attachment has been completely eliminated.
Form is not form; sound is not sound. Why is there perfect interfusion and non-obstruction? Because form is directly form; sound is directly sound.
Nevertheless, what is it like in the place where sound and form do not reach? Do not cling to emptiness.

Addressing the assembly: People only know that when the sentiments of ordinary and sage are exhausted, the true and eternal essence is revealed; they do not know that when the sentiments of ordinary and sage arise, the true and eternal essence is likewise revealed.

What is called "ordinary"? It is the Buddhas. What is called "sage"? It is sentient beings. What is called "true"? It is illusion and transformation. What is called "eternal"? It is arising and ceasing.
Nevertheless, you must open the eye that penetrates the barrier before you can attain it. If you have the eye that penetrates the barrier...
Unopened. The ancients said: "Mountains, rivers, and the great earth—these fully reveal the body of the Dharma King. Is this one? Or is it two?
A hair’s breadth of difference, and heaven and earth are separated; no hair’s breadth of difference, and heaven and earth are separated. *Can*.
Small Sermon. All dharmas possess counterparts; such are the dharmas of sentient beings and Buddhas, sages and ordinary people, sudden and gradual, partial and perfect, and so forth.

Only this dharma is without counterpart and without dependence; it cannot be encompassed by sentient beings and Buddhas, sages and ordinary people, sudden and gradual, partial and perfect, yet it can encompass sentient beings and Buddhas, sages and ordinary people, sudden and gradual, partial and perfect.
Therefore, do not attempt to seek this within the realm of dharmas that possess counterparts.
The Dharma cannot be apprehended. If one does not seek this Dharma within the realm of dualistic opposition, that Dharma likewise cannot be apprehended.
In these two instances where nothing can be apprehended, there is no teaching to be gathered; how could this not be "beyond the teachings"?
Since it is entirely unobtainable, how can it be transmitted? [He snaps his fingers once and says: "Do not indulge in deluded thoughts."
Small Assembly Sermon. The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: "Mind, Buddha, and sentient beings—these three are without distinction. I, this mountain monk, say they are distinct:
the mind is not the Buddha; the Buddha is not a sentient being; and a sentient being is not the Buddha. Why? Because when one is a Buddha, one certainly does not see the existence of sentient beings.

At the time of arising, one certainly does not see a Buddha; at the time of the mind, one certainly does not see the arising of a Buddha; at the time of the arising of a Buddha, one certainly does not see a mind.
Try to experience this for yourself.
Small Sermon: The sages of the Three Teachings all value "speaking of the Middle," whether they speak of "the moment of time," "maintaining the Middle," or "the Middle Way.
Yet, these are of no use within the Gate of the Patriarchs. If there were a Middle, then there would be partiality; with the Middle and partiality established as opposites, duality arises.
The emotions of grasping and rejecting arise; yet this Dharma is not a dharma of grasping or rejecting. Therefore, from of old, it has been said that this very "O" is it.
In reality, even this "O" is not established. Thus, square is as such, round is as such; high is as such, low is as such. One is as such, many are as such;
horizontal is as such, vertical is as such. Every atom is as such, every world-system is as such. This is called the Dharma-gate of Suchness (Tathatā).
Mind-Buddha is mind, which is Buddha; it is neither mind nor Buddha. Mind and Buddha are fundamentally empty; since they are not even "not," what could there be?
Being able to not abide in emptiness, the true source naturally flows through. Buddhas and patriarchs have established their school upon this.
The Verse on True Nature:
It is like a wealthy elder who bestows material gifts throughout the land, causing each person to be adorned and accomplishing all manner of tasks;
yet this wealthy elder dwells in his own enjoyment, entirely unaware that such things exist. Thus is the true nature, upon which all phenomena depend.
It is likewise so. Whether it be the Buddha or sentient beings, the body and mind, as well as the world, and even all immeasurable phenomena, all arise from the illusory nature.
The true nature is eternally pure, just like the ocean in this world that manifests mirages and illusory markets.
The appearance of the ocean returns to its original state. Therefore, those who practice and study should not be obstructed by any phenomena (*dharma*). All phenomena lack substantial reality;
they are seen only through the vision of non-seeing. By seeing this nature of no-nature, all become Buddhas who are no-Buddhas, constantly delivering beings who are unborn births.
A Verse on Dwelling in the Mountains:

Seven peaks rise and eight valleys sink along the mountain path below. Who comes to knock upon the white clouds of my door? I tear through the mists and constantly chant to the moon over a thousand peaks;
I leave the world’s distinctions of right and wrong in idle repose.
Abiding upon the green mountains, they grow deeper and deeper; tall pines and long bamboos fill the secluded groves. A single ray of divine light emerges from the unobscured void;
it is neither past, future, nor present, but penetrates all time.
The withered withers of its own accord, and the flourishing flourishes; spring comes, autumn passes, and winter follows again.
If you wish to know the mountain-dweller who resides upon the mountain, it is simply the old man dwelling within the mountains.
Prince Bǎoqīnyún bestowed a walking staff upon Chan Master Wùxiū of Shèngyīn Temple.
The Master received the staff, held it up, and said, "This staff is also seventy years old; it is of the same age as this mountain monk.
The Prince said, "Even one hundred and four would not be considered excessive. The Master laughed and said, "It is shared by all."
A Small Sermon for the Assembly.
The Buddha is the mind. The Dharma is the mind. The Sangha is the mind. Form and emptiness are the mind. Light and darkness are the mind.
Right and wrong are the mind. Good and evil are the mind. All such things as these belong to the mind.
Illusory and false, like flowers in the sky or the moon in water, they are utterly unattainable;
such are the phenomena of arising and ceasing. Now tell me, what is the true mind? The mind is the Buddha. The mind is the Dharma. The mind is the Sangha. The mind is form and emptiness.
The mind is light and darkness. The mind is right and wrong. The mind is good and evil. After a long silence, he said:
"Is this not the very mind itself? [The Master] strikes the desk twice with his whisk and says: "Do not deceive others! Small Assembly Sermon: "Thirty thousand acres of Lake Tai;
five *yojanas* of the Onion Range (*Gongling*). For every mote of dust and every leaf, it is easy to emerge above the heavens;
for every leaf and every mote of dust, it is difficult to let them drop from the void. Those who possess the eye atop their heads number ten thousand, all as pitch-black as lacquer."
With heels planted firmly on the ground, it stands revealed in its full majesty. If you seek it through form or sound, how is this different from drilling ice to find fire?
If you attempt to understand it through conceptualization or intellectual speculation, it is much like walking toward the west when you intend to go east.

This matter is not right if even one dharma is lacking; it is not right if even one dharma is in excess; it is not right if one dharma is grasped; it is not right if one dharma is abandoned. It is simply one dharma.
It is not so. It is not apart from a single dharma. Even if someone were to ask, "How does one attain this 'going'? simply speak to them in a low voice:
"The old monk, however, remains right within the realm of right and wrong."
A Small Sermon. Everyone, look! The entire monastic community, this mountain monk, and the great assembly; the halls and pavilions, the firewood, water, rice, and salt;
the chairs, desks, beds, and frames—all have been threaded together by a single cord, strung upon a single line.
Do you all see this cord? After a long silence, he said: "What is it? It is the severing of the binding rope."
Small Assembly Sermon. No words, no speech. No words, no speech. There is nothing at all; there is nothing at all. The Great Way is right before one’s eyes.
It is simply this emptiness and form before one’s eyes: form is itself emptiness, and emptiness is itself form. He is I, and I am he.

If your eyes flicker or move, you will instead find yourself ten thousand miles away amidst white clouds. (Holding up the whisk) Do not take it— (Note: The text ends abruptly with "Do not take it," implying the master would have continued by striking or making a gesture to demonstrate the point.)
A casual study of liberation; hoping to emulate the mind of the Patriarchs.

Small-scale discourse. Holding up a whisk, he said: "Mountains, rivers, and people; above, below, and in the four directions; the five metals and eight minerals; bricks, tiles, and rubble; zithers, lutes, bells, and drums;
wind, clouds, moon, and dew; cold, heat, warmth, and coolness; fragrance, stench, and filth; fine silk and cotton."
"Brocade. Rice, flour, sauce, and vinegar. Hermitages, pavilions, monasteries. Courtyards, halls, and palace steps—what are they?
He threw down his whisk and laughed loudly, saying, "How could one ever say it all?"
Small Assembly Sermon. It is the sixth month before our eyes; what a fine season! Where it is hot, it is cold; where it is cold, it is hot.
Amidst fire and water, the lotus is red and the lotus-root is white. Within the gate of the Buddha-dharma, there is the provisional and the real.
From the standpoint of a patch-robed monk, what is gained and what is lost? Silver bowls bring forth the snows of Mount Emei, just to relieve the heat and thirst of you all. Yunmen’s fan—*clap*.
The wind was piercingly cold; fanning the air, it made the hair on one's skin stand on end. Raising the fan, he said:

"Wait until the eyebrows of Cuiyan have fallen off, and then I shall explain this in detail to you all. He asked, "Tell me, what will he explain? Shaking the fan, he said: "A single piece of flesh for a tongue;
two rows of bones for teeth. Then, speaking to his attendant monk, he said: "By no means must this be recorded."
Ascending the hall, the Master said:
"Previously, I received the Imperial Grace of a full meal; it may truly be called a banquet from the celestial kitchen, complete with a hundred flavors.
Assembly, tell me: what kind of delicacy was it? The assembly replied, "We beg the Master to inform us. The Master said, "I shall speak to you all with utmost sincerity."
"It is nothing more than a piece of earth. [The Master] descends from his seat.
Having finished the questions and answers of the formal assembly, he raises his whisk high and says:
"This mountain monk is the whisk; the whisk is this mountain monk. Tell me, is the great assembly the whisk, or is the whisk the great assembly? [He holds up the whisk.]
He makes a single sweep toward the empty space, strikes the desk three times, and descends from his seat.
Entering the hall, he says: "The two classes of *kalyāṇamitras* and one old monk form a perfect analogy; this mountain monk is the fragrant bait."
The great assembly is each like one who, greedy for another’s fragrant bait, has climbed onto another’s hook.
Nevertheless, if there were among you a heroic spirit soaring through the heavens, it would be easy for him to swallow this mountain monk; it would be difficult for this mountain monk to swallow him.
How do you understand this, worthy ones? If you do not understand, listen as this mountain monk provides a further commentary. (He lets out a shout.)
He said, "I am going to make my living within the great elephant tusk at Jiazhou.
Entering the hall, he called to the assembly, saying, "Look, look! This handful of water in the old monk’s hand—from where did it come?"
The assembly remained silent, and he descended from his seat.
He ascended the hall, took up his staff, and said: "This wooden elder sometimes burns incense amidst surging waves;
sometimes he draws water within a fierce conflagration. You worthy ones, do not say that these are merely Buddhist rites performed in a dream; they are, indeed, manifest reality."
Regarding the merits of his physical marks, there was only one thing that was not clever; it happened to be the same as my own. What was it?

He did not know how to recite sutras or call upon the Buddha's name. A monk came forward and said, "If that is so, why does the Master repeatedly instruct people to practice *nianfo* (Buddha-recitation)?
The Master said, "Meng Babang has gone off in that way again."
Ascending the hall, a monk stepped forward from the assembly and prostrated. The Master shouted, "How can you, Venerable, receive the prostrations of this old monk?
The monk was at a loss. The Master smiled and said, "If you want it well, let the great conform to the small."
Ascending the hall, the Master said: "The old monk happened to have a dream. In the dream, I ascended the seat with the great assembly to preach the Dharma.
Everyone, try to interpret this omen for me. The assembly remained silent. The Master said, "It troubles me, it troubles me," and then descended from the seat.
Ascending the hall, the Master said: "Oṃ āḥ hūṃ. Adding the character *ān* beside the character for "mouth" (口), it is called *oṃ*.
With the character for "mouth" on the left and the character for "subtle" (亞) on the right, it is called *āḥ*. When the "mouth" and the "ox" (牛) are placed side by side, it is called *hūṃ*.
These are the Sanskrit words *oṃ āḥ hūṃ*; here they are translated as "A-ye A-ye, the tongue is stuck. No commentary can follow; shame, shame! He then descended from his seat.
Ascending the hall, the Master took his seat. After a long silence, the assembly requested him to preach the Dharma.
The Master drew a copy of the Heart Sūtra from his sleeve and recited it aloud once. He then descended from his seat.
Ascending the hall, he held up a portion of incense and said: "I offer this single grain of the Golden Elixir to the assembly.
It may only be spat out; it must not be swallowed. Is there anyone here among you who can receive it?
If you are unwilling to receive it, I have no choice but to take it back into the Treasure Storehouse of the Thirty-three Heavens. He then burned it in the incense burner.

Chan Master Tianning came to visit. As the Master went out to meet him at the gate, he saw him and pointed to the mountain in front of them, saying, "Lately, this old monk has been hanging high atop a solitary peak;
how will you save me? Tianning turned toward the ground and performed a dance in the manner of wielding a mattock.
The Master said, "The stake is released; the stake is buried. Tianning said, "A hundred-digesting pill—let it chew as it pleases. The Master laughed heartily.
Hand in hand, we return to the master’s chamber.
Ten stanzas of "West River Moon" are worthy of laughter;
for many years they have been neglected. One takes a brick and polishes it as if it were a mirror; hundreds of thousands of pivotal points have been passed over with a finger-snap from the sleeve.
The universe is contained within a grain of millet; let loose, it becomes the mountains, rivers, and the great earth; gathered together, the great earth and its mountains become one.
Now, as I please, I sing my song aloud: with a single stroke, I split the whole into two.
Before and after the vast chaos of primordial antiquity; from the beginning of Vipaśyin to the end of Maitreya—who can discuss the nine summers and three winters?

Let autumn and spring follow one another as they will. Form is emptiness, emptiness is form; within the same there is difference, within difference there is sameness. Form, emptiness, sameness, and difference unfold freely and spontaneously;
wondrous function accords with circumstances, whether still or moving.

How could the original source ever admit of fabrication? How could the field of the mind have any boundaries? Completely forgetting both the other shore and the lost ferry, one need not ask further once the path is trodden.
The Buddha said: "Depart from names and depart from forms. The Dharma says: "Neither false nor true. The myriad phenomena of the forest reveal the whole body;
in every single thing, the wondrous nature is manifest.
Opening the locks and bolts that bind the mundane and the sagely, in an instant one penetrates the profound mysteries. Without a mind, what is right and what is wrong?
It depends on the person themselves to realize it. The horned tiger lies peacefully; the featherless iron hawk soars aloft.
A single speck of dust is split asunder to reveal the true mechanism, swallowing and spitting out the stages of the Three Worthies and Ten Grounds.
Mount Sumeru, though eight thousand fathoms high, is not broad; the Fragrant Waters, though ten thousand feet deep, are not profound.

To seek the mind and find it not is itself the settling of the mind; one may take two balls of dough and make them into cakes. To seek the Buddha is not to be found in sounds or forms; what need is there to search for the Dharma?
From the beginning, it has never been obscured—this single, empty, and numinous clarity. To delight in it, one must verify it for oneself.
In the ninth month of autumn, the yellow chrysanthemums sway gently; in the three months of spring, the fragrant grasses flourish vibrantly.
Is this the ancestral meaning that comes from the West, or is it not? This matter must be urgently realized. With two hands clapping, a single sound is made; two solitary wild geese fly together.
Opening up the provisional and the real, one knows for oneself where one returns. With steady feet planted firmly upon the ground.
The ancient mirror originally possesses the capacity to reflect; yet it must rely upon polishing and scrubbing. Why have the years and months been spent in vain?
I am ashamed of this drifting life grown old. If one can realize that not even a single speck of dust is established, then the great earth, mountains, and rivers naturally manifest.
Walking empty-handed while performing a fist-dance in the Sahā world—what harm is there in taking what is mistaken and making it right?

Delusion is the very root of suffering; when awakened, sweetness permeates both the periphery and the center. To analyze it point by point is but a labor in vain—cease sowing the seeds of entanglement.
Hearing and seeing are neither sound nor form; mind and Buddha are neither different nor the same. When the myriad phenomena do not cling, they are simply emptiness;
like the bright moon in a clear pool, there is no movement.
Where there is mindfulness, mountain peaks stir up waves; where there is no-mind, the ocean floor raises dust. Awakening and delusion, delusion and awakening—none are true.
What can be cultivated or realized regarding birth and Buddhahood? The great void is purely clear and free from a single speck; it is like a bright moon on a cold pond.
Unstained by the midst of a hundred flowers, I grant you the realization of the mind and the seeing of nature.
Thoroughly penetrating form, fragrance, taste, and touch, one realizes there is no knowing, seeing, perceiving, or hearing. In the state of empty emptiness, every form reveals the true source.

Only when the "thunderous shout" [of realization] resounds across the earth can one truly act thus. Clearly, amidst the myriad grasses, the precious treasure of one’s own house is universally manifest.
Only by opening the eye at the crown of the head can one gaze upon the truth. This eye is the shared heritage of every person.
Four Verses on the Ground-Nature of the Three Ministers—Miaozheng, Zhenren, and Loujin—by Yuan San.
Brilliantly shines the great round mirror; both things and self are fully illuminated within it. Maitreya and Weiyin are but one body, bearing two names.

The mind is originally without anything to be enlightened; it is through enlightenment that its profundity is revealed. Nature is originally without anything to be seen; it is through seeing that its subtlety is manifested.
Within this very nature of mind, the true and eternal Way is equally contained. Its wondrous substance is perpetually serene, its radiant brilliance shining through the six gates.

Amidst the turmoil, the source is fundamentally still; within the vast expanse, there is constant bustle. When the contrivance of the mind is forgotten, grasping and rejecting vanish; returning to the root, there is neither old nor young.
If you wish to know the principle of the Buddhas and immortals, it lies solely within this mysterious pivot.
The world-system of three thousandfold worlds is but this square-inch vessel; at the tip of a hair, true nature is revealed, while upon the great earth, the illusory body is verified.
The mind exists not because of objects, yet objects appear because the mind is absent. If the mind does not pursue external things, where else could one seek "Me"?

The separation between the immortal and the mundane occurs in an instant; the distinction between the inner and outer reveals the refined and the coarse. Though the myriad phenomena are allowed to proliferate in confusion, the true mind remains loftily solitary.
Herein one accords with the wondrous principle: a single drop is hidden within the rivers and lakes.
The single orb of the moon in the heart of Heaven stamps my mind with purity. My mind and the bright moon stamp each other, their radiance deepening.

Where there is light, there are forms; how can one avoid the encroachment of external things? How much better it would be to extinguish that light, so that the myriad realms may drift and sink as they will.
This is what is called ultimate clarity. Transcending the five aggregates with ease—what a secret instruction on the Golden Elixir!
How many have sought it in error! From heaven, nothing has ever descended; from earth, nothing has ever emerged. Within this, there is this one matter: spontaneous and self-sufficient.
Like a jewel in the void, its radiance does not stain the color; like a drop of dew upon a lotus leaf, it rolls away without leaving a trace.

It manifests throughout the atoms of all lands, sporting through the realms of seers and Buddhas. Though these illusory transformations take diverse forms, they are like a thousand lamps in a single room.
In wisdom, there is fundamentally no wisdom; to speak of "attainment" is itself non-attainment. The sages of old had no teaching; later students have merely transmitted it by force of habit.
Buddhas and sentient beings share the same essence, yet their virtues differ. If one forms discriminatory thoughts, one will remain deluded by false attachments through kalpas.
Like the moon reflected in a thousand ponds, it contains the myriad within the one. Whether spoken of to the wise or the foolish, together they realize the *pāramitā*.
The mind-Buddha and the song of mind and Buddha are equal to empty space; the things within emptiness are wondrous beyond fathoming. The light of the azure sea contains a myriad forms of radiance.
The colors of the green mountains clear and bright, thousands of peaks loom high. Cease your groping; do not exert effort. Formless and imageless, it is utterly beyond trace.
The wondrous marks of True Suchness (Tathatā) are originally no marks; the six supernormal powers and liberating wisdom are likewise no powers.

Wherever the dust of phenomena arises, Buddha after Buddha appears; when every land is hidden, mind after mind is empty. To fully realize that the True Buddha dwells in the non-mind is to finally awaken that this non-mind is [itself the Buddha].
The true Buddha is such a mind; such a mind is such a Buddha. To speak of "mind" and "Buddha" is entirely false.

Once you recognize that single *maṇi* jewel, the light of the *Gaṅgā-sāgara* worlds will forever penetrate through. Whether cold or heat, they cannot invade it. Stripped bare, there is neither extinction nor non-extinction.
A Song of Joy: Joyful, joyful, truly joyful! All entanglements have been cast off. Now there is no need to seek the ultimate truth;
let me come and go with lively ease. People of this age do not understand the true meaning; they merely wait for conditions to arise before they practice.
The Living Buddha—yet who would have known that before the Living Buddha’s very eyes, ordinary people remain ignorant and deluded? How is this mind any different from a stubborn stone?
How is this body any more than the wood of the *chū* and *lì* trees?
By the Sage’s grace, a single finger shatters the skull; it is just like a blind man seeing the sun and moon.
Within this seeing, seeing and hearing are utterly severed—only then can it be called the Great Rest. With eyes that hear and ears that see, all is as usual;
without moving, one traverses eighty quadrillion worlds. The old nest and the habitual life—all have now been cast off. “I am not I.”
They do not know it; they are not that, yet I recognize it. The great earth is originally truly I; that all else is not I is the true teaching.
One does not know the past or the present; who speaks of longevity or of nirvana?
Relying on spring, summer, autumn, and winter, let the scorching heat and bone-chilling cold take their course. East, west, south, and north—I am too weary to even mention their names. I am dazed.
Faintly ignorant, forgetting discrimination; sovereign and unhindered, with no fixed essence. This is the celestial immortal and the Buddhas of the three periods of time:
at times they ride a clay ox across the ocean floor, or mount a wooden phoenix to traverse the clouds. Upon the peaks of a thousand mountains they act in wild abandon;
in the midst of the crossroads they create a commotion. In eating and dressing they are merely ordinary; mingling with the vulgar and sharing their dust, they respond to the world.
In these times, there is one cup of wine followed by another, and one verse of song followed by another.
The foolish laugh at me, saying my words are deceptive; who understands that my speech is truly sincere? Let them laugh at me or not laugh at me—it matters not;
for now, I shall simply enjoy myself.

The Chapter on Elucidating the Truth: Originally, the Dao has no name; it is because of names that names are established. Originally, the Dao has no form; it is because of forms that forms are manifested.
Name is the function of the Dao; form is the substance of the Dao. The substance of the Ultimate Dao originally has no fixed location; it is profound and vast.
Yet it abides in non-abiding. It is neither empty nor existent; neither coming nor going; neither beginning nor end;
neither facing nor turning away. It is luminously clear yet does not illuminate; it is distinct and vivid yet knows nothing. It merges emptiness and existence; it unites the true and the delusive.
Though the myriad phenomena are in chaotic profusion, they do not disturb its stillness—this is because I am the Dharma that turns. Like a single mirror, perfectly bright and lucid, when objects...
There is no form that can escape [the Dharma], for the Dharma is what I employ. Truth and falsehood depend upon one another; delusion and awakening are mutually caused.
To dissolve falsehood into truth is like ice becoming water; to turn from delusion toward awakening is like a shadow following a form. Such is the power of mirror-like awareness.

That one does not yet reach perfection is because the mind still possesses illumination. To dissolve this illumination and achieve perfect awakening, one must respond to circumstances with a mindless state.
Therefore it is said: "Heaven and earth share the same root; things and self are of one suchness. Its clarity rivals that of the sun and moon, universally bestowing its radiance;
its merit exceeds that of the two polarities, equally receiving its transformative molding. Were it not for the mindlessness of the Supreme Person, who could achieve this?

How could it have reached such a state? Therefore, the World-Honored One attained enlightenment upon beholding the morning star; the Most High rode a green ox to observe the transformations of the world;
and the Supreme Sage delighted in the waters of the Yi River to wander at ease—all because they clearly realized that the myriad things are complete within themselves.
Yet they have never harbored a mind toward the myriad things. Because they have no mind toward things, every moment of mind is the Buddha-mind.

Because they have no mind toward the Way, every place is the substance of the Way. Water is moist while fire is dry; Yang is still while Yin rises. One comes and one goes, mutually entering and exiting.
The Mother of Transformation conceives its numinous embryo, and the True Lord presides over its firm bones. Thus, the cinnabar—
Mercury is formed therein; the Valley Spirit nourishes therein. Within and without are clear and penetrating; exterior and interior are thoroughly understood.

By internalizing the spirit, the spirit becomes firm; by externalizing the body, the body is preserved. Only then can one transform that illusory form and perfect this true essence. Emerging from this true essence, one turns that illusory form.
Thus one knows that the great earth, mountains, and rivers are none other than my own body; insects, fish, phoenixes, and cranes are all [my body].

Having perfected my body, I may soar through the six realms and roam at ease across the eight directions. With a serene and limpid air, I shall ride upon the wind of brilliance and mount the auspicious clouds, wandering freely in the age of the Sage.
Thus beholding the sun of Shun and the sky of Yao, what further need is there to seek out Mount Penglai, the Garden of Langyuan, or to inquire after the Immortal’s Vase?

Is this the center of heaven and earth? Nevertheless, without the Three [Mysteries], there is no awakening; without awakening, there is no cultivation; and without cultivation, there is no realization.

One contains the myriad dharmas within a single emptiness, and one embraces that single emptiness within the myriad dharmas. Non-emptiness is itself emptiness; emptiness is itself non-emptiness. This is called wondrous existence and true emptiness.
True emptiness and wondrous existence—by means of true emptiness, one manifests wondrous existence; by means of wondrous existence, one [manifests]...
Realizing true emptiness: in practice there is truly nothing to practice; in awakening there is truly nothing to awaken to;
in cultivation there is truly nothing to cultivate; in realization there is truly nothing to realize. This is called true practice and true awakening, true cultivation and true realization.
It is this state of being profoundly serene and vast, abiding in non-abiding.

Twelve "Xijiang Yue" Verses: Behold the sun and moon within the alchemical vessel; upon the tip of a single hair, there are three thousand worlds. From the beginning, it is neither Buddha nor immortal;
who dwells in the jade halls and crystal palaces? This realm and other directions are not separated; the perfect luminosity of the one nature is bright and round. True roundness...
The luminous sphere illuminates the boundless; it is said that the profound night-treasury appears by day.
It brings forth the six kinds of divine functions and shatters light, darkness, form, and emptiness. This non-empty state of emptiness is true emptiness; let the wind and banner move as they will.
Arising and ceasing do not depart from the present moment; every head and every thing is perfectly interfused. Recognize this!
Ten thousand greens and a thousand reds; in a mere snap of the fingers, one reaches the immortal grotto of Peach Blossom Spring.

The water naturally does not retain the shadows of clouds; the moon is not eternally fixed in the heart of heaven. Deep and profound, it flows through the past, present, and future; light and dark both manifest and both conceal.
If you wish to find the reality within the vast void, you must seek it by tracing it back through the great earth. Water and clouds...
The celestial moon is already manifest; the soaring hawk and leaping fish all hear it.
Space and form have been one essence from the beginning—among them, who can forcibly establish names?

You, he, that, and I—we call upon one another, yet in the ultimate sense, when has anything ever been fixed as "this"? If you attempt to extinguish the flowers in the sky, ignorance will arise within your own eyes. You cannot.
Reality and illusion are both equally level—much like grinding a tile to make a mirror.

When one’s nature is awakened, every thing is the Way; when the mind is empty, every place is Bodhi. If a person can comprehend this profound mystery, it is the secret meaning of the Buddhas and Immortals.
Who would pay homage to Laozi at the Pass of the Box? Who would not study Śākyamuni of the Western Regions? Rootless.
Beneath the tree is the old hut; seeking what true teaching or wondrous truth?
All conditioned realms are adorned with hundreds of thousands of signlessnesses. These causes are pulled by those conditions;
both arise from emptiness, yet linger in attachment. The lion roars amidst the clouds; the azure dragon coils within the cave for a moment.
A single thread pervades the three thousand worlds; it unfurls as ten thousand strands of white silk.
Do not say that the Great Void has no substance; do not say that the Great Way has form. Whether with or without form, whether rising or sinking, it is all the perfectly luminous self-nature.
It is just like the moon reflected in a deep pool, yet like an echo transmitted through a hollow valley—manifestly clear.
Everywhere, the true nature is revealed. A single stream of wondrous scenes in the cold sky:
white waves blown by the wind as whales leap; green forests where the moon passes and sparrows startle. Laughing, one observes the causes within this up-and-down movement.
Who here can fathom this realm? The moon reflects in the cold pond, leaving a trace; dewdrops roll off lotus leaves, leaving no mark. Coming and going...
Every movement and stillness is perfectly distinct. One need only chant the *yueling* (regulations for the occasion) in accordance with the time.

Facing an object, when has there ever been an "object"? Sending forth the mind, where is there anything that is not "mind"? Fools falsely cling to the union of object and mind, thereby causing it to race about restlessly and without stability.
The green bamboos and yellow flowers reveal the truth; the crows’ cawing and magpies’ chirping proclaim it clearly. In a hundred ways...
This form and sound are illusory transformations; the true nature of all phenomena is suchness. Within form, there is no form;
apart from emptiness, there is no emptiness outside it. It is like the bright moon at the edge of the sky and the wind by the water—its lively mechanism is ever-shifting.
When yin reaches its peak, winter comes with piercing cold; when yang arises, spring arrives with warm harmony. Such is True Suchness.
Its wondrous application is difficult to fathom. Do not, by any means, attempt to deliberate upon or manipulate it.

This illusory body and that illusory body exchange places; the illusory form and the true essence travel the same path. Within this, the flavor resides—taste it within the ice-clear vessel, swallowing and spitting it out as you please.
Simply remain without a mind toward external things; what harm is there in the total merging of self and object? A single thread.
Supported by a staff, ten thousand people assist him; he traverses the ends of the earth, every step taken.

Whether large or small, high or low, he kicks and treads upon them all. Roaming through the ten directions and the six realms, wherever he encounters the source, every object and every phenomenon is his.
He realizes for himself that there is neither before nor after; in every touch, light, wind, clear sky, and moon.
The Sage’s grace is vast and boundless, difficult to repay. May you live ten thousand years and a thousand autumns. One phrase: "Heaven endures, earth lasts forever.
When encountering circumstances, the mind meets its own nature; four verses follow:
The spring flows to the bright moon, the moon flows to the spring. Above is the clear stream, below is the sky. Who within can recognize this profound mystery?
Attained! It should simply be entrusted to the fishing boat.

Whatever meets the eye is nothing other than the Great Dharma Assembly; it is luminously manifest throughout the entire world, never hidden. When the golden wind stirs once, the whole body is revealed;
the rock-orchid transmits its fragrance through the eighth month.
A single pond of autumn water takes the moon as its heart; the myriad phenomena of the universe reflect their shadows therein. The Northern Dipper conceals its body while the Southern Dipper remains;
a silent melody harmonizes with the stringless lute.

When illusion is extinguished, awakening is perfect; that perfection is itself illusion. What further difference is there between sentient beings and Buddhas? When the deluded mind is exhausted, the true mind is realized;
even to speak of "True Suchness" is already inadequate.
The late scholar Ziyang Zhang, the Patriarchal Master, said: "When you perceive an object, you perceive the mind; without an object, the mind does not manifest. He also said:
"To behold an environment and yet remain without a [discursive] mind—this is the very face of Bodhi. These two phrases alone fully encompass the essential purport of the entire *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*.
The wondrous Dharma taught by the World-Honored One over forty-nine years does not, in its entirety, transcend these four phrases.

The unified principle of the Buddha-Sage is entirely to guide future students by means of seeing one's nature and clarifying the mind. All the various phenomena of the world arise from one’s own mind;
therefore it is said: "When the mind arises, all phenomena arise; when the mind ceases, all phenomena cease. It is like a single fruit...
When the mind does not arise and the myriad dharmas are without fault, one is naturally able to transform all things without being transformed by them.
Ultimately, the self is everything; in the final analysis, everything is not the self. Whether transforming or not transforming is much like blowing upon light or cutting through water;
in the state of ultimate reality, what transformation or non-transformation could there be? This applies to all sentient and insentient beings alike.
This is like bubbles on the great ocean of the Tathāgata’s Perfect Enlightenment; all are formed from the seawater.
Yet, apart from the ocean there are no bubbles, and apart from the bubbles there is no separate seawater. Sentient beings, immortals, and Buddhas share the same Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom;

it merely manifests as a sage when encountering a sage, and manifests as an ordinary person when encountering an ordinary person. Because of these distinctions between the holy and the ordinary, one forcibly establishes [these categories] within the mirror.

Regarding this awakening-illumination: if the sage and the ordinary person share the same substance and the mirror of the mind is as one, then where could the function of awakening-illumination be established?
As it is said: "The myriad worlds of the great chiliocosm are but bubbles in the sea; all sages and worthies are like a flash of lightning.

Upon reaching this point, one finally knows that fundamentally there are no sages and no ordinary people, fundamentally no birth or extinction, fundamentally no coming or going, fundamentally no before or after, and fundamentally no...

Past and present are fundamentally without superior or inferior; they are fundamentally without defilement or purity; they are fundamentally without surface or interior. One cannot add even a single speck, nor can one subtract even a single speck;
one cannot discard even a single speck, nor can one grasp even a single speck. In this single state of equanimity, all things vanish of themselves.
